Process traceability is therefore recommended to ensure the continuous monitoring of the production process, modifying potential threats at source to avoid the wasted production and distribution of compromised products.

Thirdly, this study explored the benefits of traceability that enhanced the attainment of SCRes. Building on the detailed benefits specified in Table 7, it is concluded that the following have a relationship with SCRes: improved risk awareness and pro-activeness; improved consumer trust and confidence; improved monitoring of events and risk identification; real-time tracking and exchange of information; improved reliability and security; and, improved trust and confidence among SC actors. These benefits either directly enable the development of SCRes or have an indirect impact through other known enablers of SCRes – flexibility, velocity, visibility and collaboration. As summarized in Table 8 and Figure 3, these results advance understanding of the traceability-SCRes relationship and set the tone for further empirical research that seeks to validate this relationship. Previous studies have focussed on identifying strategies that enable SCRes, whilst this study has added emphasis on how to implement these strategies to successfully overcome the associated barriers.

6.2. Managerial implications

From a managerial perspective, this study increases practitioner awareness of the challenges and potential benefits associated with traceability systems, which are essential considerations in making strategic decisions. It addresses the opportunities inherent in various technologies to aid an objective cost-benefit analysis in selecting technologies thus guiding traceability-related SC initiatives. This study also offers valuable insights for both practitioners on the importance of building trust and confidence in SC relationships to maintain shared values among all SC actors.

Moreover, the study provides a justification for investment in digitalization in response to the increased susceptibility of SCs to disruptions by outlining the various benefits of traceability that help improve both the proactive capacity to prevent a disruption and the reactive capacity to respond appropriately after experiencing a disruption. Specifically, traceability increases a firm’s ability to monitor real-time events and obtain, update and transfer information quickly among SC partners to ensure a responsible partner takes the required action.

6.3. Research gaps and future research recommendations

The study identified the following broad gaps in the literature to steer future research.

The literature differed on the most important driver of traceability because of the varying complexity of the SCs studied and, to some extent, the theoretical lens adopted. To objectively determine the significance of the drivers and gain a better understanding of them, it is proposed that future studies consider the complexity of the SCs by focussing on cases from similar industries to gain literal replication, and/or contrasting industries to gain theoretical replication.

Unlike mandatory traceability, voluntary standards are likely to result in a restructuring of existing relationships because of the amount of information that must be shared among SC partners. Future research should explore the level of information firms are willing to share with partners and the potential benefits of stipulating boundaries on the demands for information that partners should realistically request from others.

Further research is needed to compare the effectiveness of alternative technologies, given that to date the comparisons in the literature have considered technologies that were at different stages of implementation, with some still being tested in specific industries. Surveys to compare the effectiveness of technologies at similar operational levels (such as according to years of adoption) are therefore recommended to better assess their potential for SC traceability. Case study research is also needed to analyse receptiveness towards advanced traceability and hence find effective implementation strategies for emerging technologies.

In contrast to traceability as an enabler of inter-firm trust and confidence, from a TCE perspective, Stranieri, Orsi, and Banterle (
Citation
2017) concluded that firms are more likely to implement traceability systems to mitigate their internal risks than to mitigate external risks in the SC. Further research is needed to explore strategies that jointly address these objectives and mitigate opportunistic behaviours in the SC.

Notwithstanding the capacity of traceability systems to improve risk awareness by identifying risk sources along the SC, a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between traceability and SCRes is missing from the literature. Although it is explicitly mentioned in a few studies on food SCs, traceability has either been ignored or merged with other enablers in studies of other industries. As highlighted in Section 5 above, traceability plays a significant role as an enabler of SCRes both directly and indirectly. Future empirical research is needed to verify these insights, thereby extending understanding beyond the purpose of traceability for monitoring and identifying risks to also consider its impact on developing vulnerability mitigation strategies.

The lack of a unified traceability standard obstructs the effectiveness of traceability since the various systems have different data manipulation attributes, creating compatibility problems. Survey research is recommended to understand the effects of this lack of standardisation on SC relationships and whether or not this blocks the entry of new potential partners.

Attaran (
Citation
2007) asserted that restricting traceability systems to regulatory requirements (compliance) because of the cost of technology may hinder the returns on investment (ROI) expected, suggesting a linkage between financial constraints and the level of traceability adopted. Further empirical investigation is needed to assess this assertion along with the severity of the other challenges identified in the literature. For example, case study research is recommended to investigate how an awareness of the challenges expected in the deployment of traceability systems can facilitate strategic decisions and subsequently determine the level of traceability to adopt.

6.4. Limitations

Despite rigorous efforts to ensure the validity of our findings, the study has some limitations. Firstly, there is potential for bias and subjectivity, as commonly attributed to literature reviews (Durach, Kembro, and Wieland 
Citation
2017). This study relied on papers published in ABS recognized journals compiled from the OneSearch Library and Scopus with a predefined search string. Hence, there is a possibility that some relevant articles were omitted because of the specified scope of the search strategy. However, the authors attempted to neutralize this limitation by adopting a comprehensive, transparent and systematic process, as described in Section 2, where the bounds placed on the sources of literature was justified as being necessary to ensure that only high quality articles were screened for inclusion. Secondly, this study was based on the viewpoints of other researchers, and hence the conclusions are limited to the scope of knowledge presented in the literature. This hindered the exploration of SC traceability as an enabler of SCRes because empirical investigation was beyond the scope of this study. However, the framework and conclusions lay the conceptual foundations for future empirical studies that develop this promising line of enquiry further.

column1: Digital Technologies for Food Loss and Waste Prevention and Reduction in Agri-Food Supply Chains: A Systematic Literature Review and Research Agenda
column2: Despite the benefits resulting from the use of Industry 4.0 technologies in the agri-food sector, the adoption of digital technologies for preventing and/or reducing food loss and waste (FLW) across the agri-food supply chain is still under investigation. In fact, enhancing and optimizing agri-food supply chain operations through digital technologies would just represent a partial effort if FLW prevention and reduction are not effectively addressed. Although companies are starting to adopt digital technologies for eliminating FLW from their operations, the implementation process and the achieved results are generally presented at a superficial level and practical guidance is still missing. This systematic literature review contributes to theory by developing a framework analyzing the state-of-the-art of adoption of each Industry 4.0 technology across the agri-food supply chain, and providing a research agenda structured around the main themes of research design, digital technologies, contextual differences, governance, and sustainability. Eventually, the study also informs managers in the agri-food industry about the potential implementation of digital technologies for preventing and reducing FLW in across the agri-food supply chain.
column3: The present study is an SLR to critically analyze cutting edge research focusing on the adoption of digital technologies for FLW reduction and/or prevention across the entire AFSC. Digital technologies find several applications in each stage of the AFSC, such as by collecting and monitoring agricultural activities through IoT and by analyzing large dataset through AI and machine learning; or supporting managers in decision making with data collected throughout the supply chain, fostering better demand–production coordination decisions [106]. However, only a limited number of publications analyze in depth how each digital technology contribute to the prevention and/or reduction of FLW across the AFSC, despite the recognized impact that wasting food has at a social, economic, and environmental level [27], [52], [135], [127]. Although in recent years we observed a significantly growing attention towards the topic among academics, as well as the increased interest among practitioners in the agri-food system, it emerges that the analyzed body of literature is still at an exploratory level, providing fragmented insights on specific implementation cases and often failing to provide practical guidance to practitioners in implementing digital technologies for FLW prevention and/or reduction. Summarizing the main results, digital technologies are more frequently adopted in the earlier stages of the supply chain and IoT and digital platforms are the most frequently cited technologies. IoT is diffused throughout the entire supply chain in order to measure and disseminate information, facilitate control, planning, and optimization, as well as promoting forecast accuracy of quantities to be planted by farmers, improving the use of natural resources and reducing waste. When combined with image processing, BDA, and machine learning, loT provides the data for enabling AI-based dynamic pricing by collecting data about the deterioration stage of fruit and vegetables with positive consequences for food waste reduction. Digital platforms are diffused instead in the downstream supply chain for avoiding food waste through food surplus redistribution. Moreover, none of the papers collected consider as unit of analysis the entire supply chain, thus resulting in only limited considerations about the changes in governance mechanisms occurring after the introduction of digital technologies targeting FLW reduction. Surprisingly, the real impact of FLW prevention and reduction through digital technologies on the aforementioned sustainability dimensions and indicators is rarely measured in a quantitative way. The external context does not play a central role in any of the analyzed papers, apart from Kör et al. [86], which provide an overview on the role of context and culture on FLW generation and management, by exploring the differences between developing and developed countries; thus, it is an important factor to consider in future analysis discussing about the adoption of digital technologies for FLW prevention and/or reduction. Finally, a research agenda is provided to identify future research opportunities and gaps and to provide guidance on the subject area that require further research, as the limited understanding of the evolution of the governance mechanisms occurring across the supply chain after the introduction of digital technologies for preventing and/or reducing FLW, the contextual information, the data management, and the opportunity to create a positive impact on sustainability from a triple bottom line perspective. This study presents some limitations. In particular, limitations are related to the generalizability of the findings, given that adopting digital technologies exclusively for reducing and/or preventing FLW is a niche topic.

column1: The Design of Hierarchical Consensus Mechanism Based on Service-Zone Sharding
column2: The byzantine agreement protocol has a disadvantage that there are many limitations on node scalability, because the performance degradation may occur due to a large amount of traffic. Hence, this classical byzantine agreement algorithm seems to be infeasible to achieve scale-out performance with the same level of security as a Bitcoin. In order to improve the performance degradation due to a large amount of traffic, we propose the hierarchical consensus mechanism based on service-zone sharding rather than how all nodes participate in the consensus process. In the proposed consensus mechanism (SZHBFT), a disjoint set of transactions is locally processed by a secure consensus subgroup or globally processed between consensus subgroups. Thus, the transactions that occur related to multiple Service-Zone Consensus Groups are updated and maintained in the Inter-Service Zone Public Ledger, whereas service transactions occurring locally are processed in parallel by each Service-Zone Consensus Group and then distributed into a local Service-Zone Private Ledger. The scheme of the proposed SZHBFT mechanism provides the hierarchical agreement solution along with distributed multiledger structure for the scalable byzantine resilient agreement by forming secure consensus subgroups in order to minimize the overhead of overall communication messages.
column3: Blockchain ecosystem can enhance significant economical and operational value to many services in different industrial domains. The value can be improved in terms of autonomous operational procedures, such as reduction of operations and administration costs, reduction of operations time delays, and reduction of human errors. In addition, the blockchain feature, such as digital identity for humans, organizations, and properties, can enable many new service models via the support for the agreement and security in the form of a distributed method without the need for an authoritative body. Leveraging both the added value and the capability of establishing new business service models will lead to enhancing the competitive capabilities and flexibility of many industries [25]. Thus, the blockchain ecosystem has the ability to revolutionize the paradigm of IoT services with a trusted and auditable open-sharing platform, where any exchanged information is reliable and traceable. The convergence of blockchain and IoT brings a number of benefits, such as [26], [27] decentralization and scalability; digital identity; autonomous operation; security and reliability; secure code deployment. Currently, although the development of blockchain has made great progress, the application of blockchain into IoT ecosystem is far from the ideal scale, in spite of IoT and blockchain convergence benefits. There are still many research issues that have to be addressed in order to seamlessly use these two technologies together by considering the benefits of IoT and blockchain convergence. Although the blockchain ecosystem converged with IoT brings many opportunities in upgrading the industrial automation, it can face a lot of challenges mainly in five aspects as follows: scalability; security; anonymity and data privacy; resource utilization; smart contract [5]. The scalability of blockchains limits the wide usage of blockchains in the large-scale IoT domain. Many blockchain systems are suffering from poor transactions throughput. Thus, most of the blockchain systems may not be suitable for the IoT services with a large volume of transactions. The transaction throughput is affected by the relevant factors with transaction propagation communication, consensus mechanism, and transaction verification. In the process of transaction verification and consensus, it is necessary to consume a lot of time and power, so the speed of transaction processing is limited. In order to address this issue of blockchain scalability, the proposed consensus mechanism has been designed according to the research direction which processes service transactions based on the sharding approach along with distributed multiledgers structure. The scheme of the proposed SZHBFT mechanism provides the hierarchical agreement solution along with distributed multiledger structure for scalable byzantine resilient agreement by forming secure consensus subgroups in order to minimize the overhead of overall communication messages. The key idea is to automatically parallelize the available processing power by securely organizing multiple consensus subgroups that process a disjoint set of transactions, record agreed transactions, keep track of their validity, and manage the state of objects. The proposed SZHBFT protocol can improve the performance for processing service transactions by the hierarchical agreement scheme that is performed in parallel in the form of distributed multiblockchains along with the Local SZone Private Ledgers managed on the unit of a service-zone consensus group. In addition, it supports the structure of efficient distributed service blockchain that can track the subsets of ledgers related to the corresponding service, so that the service function can be easily verified. The proposed SZHBFT mechanism requires the minimum number of rounds for messages exchange while tolerating the maximum number of allowable faulty nodes in order to reach a common agreement within the related multiple consensus subgroups. And, in the presented SZHBFT, the method of reconfiguration agreement integrated with the consensus for processing transactions does not increase the overhead of protocol messages and is also capable of the faster detection and removal of faulty validators.

column1: The impact of labor flexibility on operational efficiency in industry 5.0: a systematic literature review
column2: This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) on labor flexibility (LF) strategies and their integration into workload control (WLC) within the framework of Industry 5.0 (I5.0). As industries transition toward more sustainable, human-centric, and collaborative operational models, LF serves as a catalyst for enhanced adaptability, resource optimisation, and worker-driven innovation. Through synthesising LF strategies across diverse industrial sectors, this review underscores their contributions to productivity enhancement, cost reduction, and lead time improvement, all crucial pillars of I5.0’s resilience, sustainability, and human-centric ethos. Despite these advancements, significant research gaps remain regarding real-world validation, the integration of advanced and decentralised digital technologies (e.g. AI, IoT, digital twins, and blockchain), and the development of scalable, standardised frameworks for cross-sectoral application. Consequently, the authors promote for data-driven and collaborative approaches that leverage real-time analytics, predictive modelling, and human--machine synergy to enhance workforce adaptability and operational efficiency. The insights from this study lay the groundwork for future research and practical deployment, illuminating how LF can accelerate the transformation of modern industries in alignment with I5.0’s core objectives of resilience, sustainability, and human-centrism.KEYWORDS: Workload controllabor flexibilityoperational efficiencyindustry 5.0systematic literature review
column3: This study employed Snyder and Kitchenham’s SLR methodology (Kitchenham Citation2004; Snyder Citation2019) to analyze 48 articles, providing detailed insights into LF strategies across industries. The findings highlight key opportunities, research gaps, and future directions, aligning with I5.0 principles of resilience, sustainability, human-centricity, and adaptability. While LF research is heavily concentrated in manufacturing, with 28 studies focusing on workforce adaptability and operational efficiency, other sectors such as construction, hospitality, healthcare, education, and finance remain underexplored. These industries are often fragmented and seasonal, requiring tailored LF frameworks. Collaborative research between academia and industry can help adapt LF strategies to these contexts, while funding and policy support could encourage research in underrepresented sectors. The use of AI and IoT to optimise workforce management is well-established in manufacturing, yet their application in non-manufacturing sectors is minimal. Industry-focused journals, research consortia, and specialised conferences could boost academic interest in expanding LF applications across industries.Another major research gap is the lack of real-world validation and overreliance on theoretical models and simulations. Many studies fail to consider unexpected disruptions, long-term workforce fatigue, and dynamic environmental changes. Flexible job-shop scheduling models have been extensively explored, but empirical validation and real-world implementation remain limited. Without real-time data integration, adaptive LF frameworks cannot effectively respond to workforce and market demands. Future research should focus on scalable, robust, and context-aware workforce strategies that bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical implementation. There is also an underutilisation of emerging technologies such as AI, IoT, robotics, and blockchain. While AR, VR, and DTs have shown potential for improving adaptability, operational efficiency, and resilience, their integration into LF strategies remains limited. Future studies should explore predictive, real-time labor management systems, ensuring I5.0-aligned workforce adaptability.A key limitation in existing research is the lack of longitudinal studies. Most literature focuses on short-term outcomes such as cost reduction and productivity gains, neglecting organisational resilience, workforce retention, and long-term economic sustainability. Future research should analyze the long-term impact of LF strategies on employee well-being, cultural shifts, and financial viability to develop sustainable workforce policies. Human-centric aspects, such as LF strategies’ psychological effects and technological displacement, require further investigation. Understanding how advanced LF practices impact worker satisfaction, stress, and well-being is crucial for designing inclusive, worker-friendly policies. Cultural and geographical factors also influence LF adoption and effectiveness, yet comparative studies across regions and industries are scarce. These areas of inquiry align with broader I5.0 discourse, which emphasises proactive skill development and care for worker well-being to ensure both operational continuity and social sustainability. Future research should also examine how collaborative intelligence, where humans and machines adapt in tandem, can foster inclusive, innovative workplace cultures.Policy and regulatory considerations are another critical area requiring further exploration. Aligning LF strategies with data security laws, labor rights, and GDPR compliance is essential for ensuring transparency and stakeholder trust. Future studies should examine regulatory innovations that encourage LF adoption while protecting workers’ rights and organisational interests. There is also a need to analyze the legal implications of workforce flexibility, particularly regarding contractual agreements, employment protection, and ethical concerns. Integrated information systems that leverage real-time analytics and predictive modelling are also key to dynamic labor optimisation. The development of standardised LF metrics and methodologies is necessary to ensure consistency across organisations and sectors. Studies further show that regulatory adaptation is essential for decentralised and blockchain-based workforce management systems, especially for SMEs. Linking such systems with advanced compliance tracking can support ethical labor practices and bridge the gap between digital disruption and human-centered policy.SMEs struggle with LF implementation due to resource constraints, making scalability a pressing concern. Future research should focus on cost-effective solutions that align with SMEs’ operational and financial realities. Additionally, LF strategies’ impact on innovation and global competitiveness remains an underexplored area. Investigating how LF contributes to technological advancement and economic growth could provide valuable insights for strategic labor policies in dynamic markets. Addressing the outlined gaps can lead to robust, inclusive, and sustainable LF strategies that boost workforce adaptability, operational efficiency, and resilience. This study highlights the alignment between LF and I5.0 principles, offering a roadmap for future research and practical implementation. The findings are relevant for researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders aiming to cultivate a more human-centric, adaptive, and innovative workforce. Moving forward, integrating decentralised intelligence, machine – human collaboration, and advanced simulation environments can expand LF beyond cost-saving mechanisms. Embedding skill-based planning, real-time reconfiguration, and DT frameworks will help organisations align short-term efficiency goals with long-term workforce empowerment. In doing so, they can shape truly transformative labor policies, laying the groundwork for a resilient and inclusive I5.0 ecosystem.

column1: A fuzzy optimization-oriented decision support model to examine key industry 4.0 strategies for building resilience against disruptions in a healthcare supply chain
column2: Ensuring resilience in healthcare supply chains (HSCs) is crucial for maintaining the timely, accurate, and reliable delivery of common goods in health, especially in the face of disruptions such as pandemics or natural disasters. This study investigates the role of Industry 4.0 strategies in enhancing HSC resilience through a two-stage optimization-oriented methodology integrating Fermatean fuzzy numbers (FFNs), the Best Worst Method (BWM), and goal programming (GP). In the first stage, FF-BWM is used to determine the weights of HSC resilience factors derived from the SCOR model, based on expert evaluations. In the second stage, Industry 4.0 strategies are evaluated under these criteria, and the optimal strategy is identified using GP. The results reveal that among the evaluated strategies, the Internet of Things (IoT) is the most effective in enhancing overall HSC resilience. Blockchain and Digital Twin also demonstrate significant potential in this regard. Furthermore, the analysis highlights that Digital Twin excels in the Plan and Transform processes, Blockchain is most effective in the Order and Return processes, Machine Learning performs best in the Source process, and IoT leads in the Fulfill process. These findings provide actionable insights for decision-makers to prioritize digital investments and strengthen HSCs against potential disruptions. This study underscores the transformative role of digitalization in optimizing HSC operations and fortifying their resilience.
column3:
This study proposes a two-stage optimization-oriented methodology to provide a comprehensive understanding of Industry 4.0 strategies that enhance the resilience of the HSC by consulting with an expert team. To this end, after the key SCOR-based HSC resilience factors are determined, the weights of the factors are calculated by employing FF-BWM. Later, GP is utilized to obtain the ranking of the selected Industry 4.0 strategies ensuring the resilience of HSC.

Based on the results, the criteria considered concerning SCOR processes, namely accuracy and completeness, effective emergency planning, strategic capacity management, and cold chain management for temperature-sensitive healthcare products, are determined as the pivotal factors playing the most crucial roles in ensuring the resilience of HSC. The outcomes reveal that in the context of Order and Return processes, Blockchain (A1) has secured the topmost position. In the Plan and Transform processes, Digital Twin (A4) has emerged as the frontrunner. The leading position in the Source process has been claimed by Machine Learning (A5), while Internet of Things (A2) has taken the lead in the Fulfill process. In this manner, it is possible to assert that HSC managers have the opportunity to enhance and advance their SCs’ resilience against potential disruptions by harnessing the capabilities offered by these Industry 4.0 technological solutions.

This study’s findings highlight the critical role of Industry 4.0 technologies in strengthening HSC resilience across SCOR processes. These include accuracy and completeness, effective contingency planning, strategic capacity management, and cold chain management for temperature-sensitive healthcare products. The implementation of specific technologies uniquely benefits each SCOR process. Blockchain technology emerged as the top choice for improving transparency and traceability within the order and returns process. In the Plan and Transform processes, Digital Twin technology was the top choice. It provides real-time visualization and scenario analysis to support better decision making. In the Source process, Machine Learning was the dominant technology, primarily due to its predictive capabilities, which help manage supplies and resources efficiently. Finally, the Internet of Things (IoT) proved instrumental in the Fulfill process by enabling end-to-end visibility and improved control of healthcare assets. These results highlight the potential for HSC managers to make strategic use of these technologies to improve resiliency, operational efficiency, and responsiveness to healthcare interruptions.

This paper ensures the following central contributions from two main perspectives:

(i)

In teoretical terms, the study introduces an effective two-stage optimization-orientied evaluation methodology that integrates expert insights. This approach investigates Industry 4.0 strategies to bolster the resilience of HCSs. A noteworthy innovation is the adaptation of FFNs to BWM, enabling precise weighting of SCOR-based HSC resilience factors. Additionally, a GP approach is employed for a comprehensive strategy analysis.

(ii)

In practical terms, this innovative evaluation methodology is executed by a team of proficient experts, yielding valuable managerial insights. Both academics and practitioners focusing on Industry 4.0 and HCS resilience benefit from these findings. It’s important to highlight that this method not only contributes effectively to existing literature but also offers a straightforward application for any systems.

The study has certain limitations that must be acknowledged, despite its promising findings. Focusing on SCOR processes, while comprehensive in its approach, may limit the applicability of the findings to broader healthcare supply chain contexts that do not precisely align with these processes. In addition, the study is limited to evaluating Industry 4.0 technologies that are currently prominent. This may overlook emerging or future technologies that could further enhance HSC resilience. There are also challenges to implementing these technologies. These include significant upfront costs, the need for specialized technical expertise, and potential integration issues with existing healthcare systems. Furthermore, varying levels of technological adoption and infrastructure across healthcare facilities may affect the generalizability of the findings, especially in settings with limited resources.

This study provides several recommendations for future research and practice based on the findings and limitations. First, future research could extend this analysis by investigating the scalability of Industry 4.0 technologies in healthcare facilities of different sizes and types, especially in settings where resources are constrained. Furthermore, exploring how these technologies interoperate with existing systems would provide further insight into overcoming integration challenges. Practical recommendations for HSC practitioners include prioritising the adoption of technologies that align with specific resilience goals, while planning for long-term sustainability and flexibility. Building on the insights and methodologies provided, several promising avenues for future research and practical application in enhancing HSC resilience through Industry 4.0 strategies emerge. Future endeavors could explore the long-term resilience of HSCs, consider dynamic interactions between evolving Industry 4.0 technologies, develop real-time decision support systems, expand resilience assessment dimensions, conduct case-based analyses, investigate adoption challenges, emphasize human-centric strategies, establish quantitative resilience metrics, and assess the scalability and generalizability of findings across industries. By examining these aspects, researchers and practitioners can advance the understanding and implementation of Industry 4.0 strategies, contributing to the creation of more adaptable and robust HSCs that can effectively withstand disruption and uncertainty.

column1: Industrial Dataspace for smart manufacturing: connotation, key technologies, and framework
column2: Smart manufacturing is a popular concept for smarter decision-making and more efficient production. Although distributed methods for data management and processing in smart manufacturing have many advantages such as low cost of adaptation and convenience for local database, some methods are hard to manage variable data sources and discover proper range of data for smart decision-making. Therefore, Dataspace is considered in this article to be a feasible and effective method. From the relation-defined perspective of utilisation of industrial Big Data, the contribution is a novel industrial Dataspace design with static structure and working flow paths for smart manufacturing. In design, the industrial Dataspace platform has been proposed to accommodate smart manufacturing characteristics with the intelligence of pay-as-you-go, like harnessing distributed heterogenous data from industrial enterprises, understanding industrial data by ontology or knowledge, corelating the data with smart applications, and enabling related decisions. A further analytical case in Surface Mounting Technology manufacturing of welding procedure is provided to illustrate the execution of customisation, focused and related decision support, and system evolution within industrial Dataspace.
column3: Dataspace, a concept raised before Big Data, has its advantage in the distributed data source, comprehensive analysis, pay-as-you-go, and smart service support, making it a proper system in smart manufacturing and realisable utilisation of industrial Big Data. After reviewing the concept and existing technologies of Dataspace, an original industrial Dataspace structure is proposed in this article to accommodate industrial enterprise and data scenarios. On the achievement of most Dataspace features, industrial Dataspace focus on the constructing of relations and supporting related periphery decisions. By explaining the static structure and flow paths in industrial Dataspace, the basic design and how it fits with industrial needs is descripted. With an SMT manufacturing case, the detail of industrial Dataspace working procedures, information transformation, and presentation of focused and related decisions are illustrated. Future work could focus on solving technological difficulties in the current design, including a streaming method for large data and system capacity, new data sources analysis and update process, data security design, potential conflicts in system evolution and feedback. Also, techniques for smart manufacturing could be combined with industrial Dataspace, such as digital twins or blockchain, for flexible decision model, safer data transmission, and decentralisation design.

column1: Smart city for sustainable urban freight logistics
column2: ABSTRACT Sustainability has become an important objective of city logistics management. Smart city, being a technology and data driven paradigm for a city’s sustainable development, has entailed new research opportunities from different perspectives. It is foreseeable that smart city will keep evolving in the domain of city logistics, which plays a key role in this game changing evolution. Recent research in this field is characterised by interdisciplinary approaches and disruptive innovations. We review the state-of-the-art of this general area and conduct a bibliometric analysis. We conclude with a new conceptual framework of smart city for sustainable urban freight logistics and the relevant key perspectives.
column3: One of the main objectives of smart city logistics management presented in this paper is that of sustainable development by reducing the consumption of natural resources and improving the quality of service provision to the city citizens. Smart city, being a technology and data driven paradigm for a city s sustainable development, has entailed new research opportunities from different perspectives. It is foreseeable that smart city will keep evolving in the domain of city logistics, which plays a key role in this game changing evolution. Recent research in this field is characterized by interdisciplinary approaches and disruptive innovations. This paper conducts a bibliometric review and provides a conceptual framework of smart city for sustainable urban freight logistics. The paper and the Special Issue encourage further research on the problem, and here we point out some of the important research avenues towards sustainable smart city logistics: Stress on interdisciplinary research: operations, information systems, computer and data science, and industry specific fields (civil engineering, food and agriculture, transportation engineering, energy, etc.); New methodological contributions: novel analytical models, empirical evidences, qualitative research, design approaches; Use both holistic and reductionist approaches: top-down problems like multi-echelon network design, door-to-door integrated logistics services, reverse supply chain, land use, freight transportation and mobility combability, etc.; bottom-up solutions such as warehousing, micro-hubs, facility location, real-time vehicle routing problems, etc. Smart and autonomous systems development: vehicle-to-infrastructure or vehicle-to- vehicle communication, delivery droid, autonomous underground systems, self- organizing last-mile delivery (van Duin et al., 2020), blockchain and smart contract- enabled autonomous process management, etc. Digital sustainability (Osburg and Lohrmann, 2017) related to smart technologies and devices: energy consumption, life-cycle assessment, social-technology, impact on human behavior.

column1: Prediction of aircraft trajectory and the associated fuel consumption using covariance bidirectional extreme learning machines
column2: Abstract Accurate prediction of the aircraft trajectory and associated fuel consumption has become an important research topic owing to the increasing importance of air traffic management. Currently, trajectory prediction and fuel estimation are usually accomplished via complex mathematical energy-balance methods. In these methods, the prediction error could get increased due to the possible usage of global values and outdated database, resulting from that most of the information regarding aircraft operations is unavailable. In this paper, we propose a covariance bidirectional extreme learning machine (CovB-ELM) for predicting aircraft trajectories and estimating fuel consumption. The selection of randomly generated parameters for the hidden unit, such as the input weight and bias, to improve the accuracy and numerical stability of the extreme learning machine (ELM), is an open problem. The fundamental idea behind the proposed method is to maximise the covariance between the hidden unit and network errors through partially updating the hidden-unit parameters randomly generated in bidirectional ELM so that the output weight norm value is minimised and the convergence gets improved. The merits of the proposed CovB-ELM are demonstrated by the experiments involving regression problems and international airline historically flight data, which suggests that the CovB-ELM outperforms, in terms of generalisation performance, several existing methods, e.g., airline mathematical approach, backpropagation neural network, and constructive ELM methods.
column3: 5 Conclusion and future work To cope with the possible errors in predicting aircraft trajectories and estimating fuel consumption resulting from unavailable information, we proposed a covariance bidirectional extreme learning machine, referred to CovB-ELM for short, that was capable of achieving a more accurate and robust performance than existing methods. This was accomplished by iteratively updating some of the hidden-unit parameters randomly generated in bidirectional ELM (B-ELM) so that the covariance between the hidden unit and the network error was maximised. Such a strategy successfully made our method perform more accurate prediction and estimation as well as produced the smallest output norm values in comparison with many other constructive ELM methods. To further examine the model’s performance in the context of real-world applications, we obtained historical high-dimensional data for real operated flights from an international airline operating in Hong Kong, which was then used to predict the aircraft trajectory and estimate the associated fuel consumption. The effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method were demonstrated by the comparative study with an existing airline approach (AMA), a BPNN, and constructive ELM methods. Regarding trajectory prediction, the CovB-ELM exhibited minimum and maximum accuracy improvements of 18.90% and 898.88%, respectively, compared with the AMA; 8.68% and 83.53%, respectively, compared with the BPNN; 6.09% and 92.45%, respectively, compared with the EI-ELM; 3.54% and 77.66%, respectively, compared with the B-ELM; and 4.33% and 73.68%, respectively, compared with the CB-ELM. As for fuel estimation, our method achieved improvements in the performance of 34.24%, 119.25%, 103.65%, 85.37%, and 79.01% compared with AMA, BPNN, EI-ELM, B-ELM, and CB-ELM, respectively. The better performance of the CovB-ELM made it a promising and suitable method to accurately predict trajectories and estimate fuel consumption for airlines so as to ensure a higher level of safety and profitability. The limitations and future work of study can be concisely summarized as follow: 1) Facilitate in managing problems related to transportation management and electricity market participant The better prediction results in predicting aircraft trajectory and associated fuel consumption give insight that the proposed method may facilitate in managing several challenging problems of transportation management such as improving transportation mobility by solving traffic congestion problems, enhancing traffic efficiency by meeting travel demands, recommending routes to automotive, such as taxi, for finding passengers, forecasting transportation of goods, road accidents, and container volume, optimizing sediment transport, and many others. Besides, the current work can be extended in the future to contribute to the electricity market. In the modern era, sector such as automotive is passing through rapid changes from fuel operated engines to rechargeable batteries to reduce overall exhaust emissions. The present work considers the fuel category and how the proposed method can contribute to the electricity market participant needs future investigation. 2) Update training datasets periodically especially under the Covid-19 pandemic. We recommend modellers to take the timeliness of data used in training sets into a special account. Air traffic flows have obvious seasonal features; the passenger volume is prone to vary significantly with respect to holidays and different seasons. Therefore, the training set must be updated periodically so that the newly-obtained data and the historical data in the same period as that of the application scenario are involved. Additionally, when the operations objectives and/or the operations environments change dramatically, the training set should be modified accordingly and timely. For example, under the worldwide pandemic of Covid-19, the aircraft sectors in many countries have witnessed a deep recession. In this case, apart from reducing operations costs, airlines may also concern about hygiene levels in aircraft, which could call for prediction regarding related aircraft specifications. However, the related training data could be very scarce since the global has not encountered a similar pandemic over the past decade. Thus, airlines are encouraged to share the latest data under the condition of data security being ensured and without conflicts of commercial interests. 3) Comparison with other machine learning methods and activation functions The research is focused on improving the generalisation performance by improving the convergence, reducing the testing RMSE, and minimising the output weight norm. According to the generalisation performance theory of the FNN, obtaining connection weights with the smallest norm values is more important than the network size for enhancing the generalisation performance. However, in future work, we plan to make the network structure more compact without losing generalisation performance. The limitation of the present study is that the regression problem and the sigmoid activation function were considered. In the future, we recommend studying classification problems and the use of other differentiable and non-differentiable activation functions. How the results of trajectory and fuel consumption prediction can be made better and more accurate using other activation functions need considerable attention. Current work is limited in scope by making a comparison of proposed CovB-ELM with AMA, BPNN, and constructive ELMs. Attributed to good generalisation, one of the challenging but promising future work is to conduct the comparison of CovB-ELM with other popular machine learning methods to demonstrate effectiveness.

column1: Competency or investment? The impact of NFT design features on product performance
column2: This study investigates how NFT design features affect project performance. From the consumption perspective, NFT design features are divided into competency-related (image complexity, consistency) and investment-related (initial price, royalty). Using transaction data of 3297 NFT projects, we find that image complexity has an inverted U-shaped effect on long-term performance, while consistency boosts both short-term and long-term performance by formulating brand symbolism. Royalty as investment cost negatively affects short-term performance, while royalty and initial price exhibit inverted U-shaped impacts on long-term performance due to their mixed roles of costs and quality signals. Market uncertainty amplifies the impacts of complexity and royalties while diminishing the initial price impact in the long term. Findings support NFT project design, enhancing Web3 consumer behavior understandings.
column3: 6 Discussion and conclusion NFT technology has revolutionized the creative industry. To provide decision support for creators in designing NFT projects, this study investigates how the general features of NFT collections influence project performance, and their heterogeneity in terms of market uncertainty. Based on the dual nature of NFTs as information goods and tokens, it is argued that NFT general design features can be categorized into competency-related (i.e., image complexity, consistency) and investment-related (i.e., initial price, royalty) features from the perspective of consumption. Additionally, the performance of NFT projects can be assessed based on the primary and secondary markets. Theoretical implications. First, in response to the call for research on NFT project design, performance measurement, and consumer behavior, this study is among the earliest empirical research on the NFT market. Prior literature has mostly focused on the investment aspects of NFTs (e.g., NFT pricing [ 10 ]). This study contributes to the existing literature by exploring the impact of general NFT design features on project performance, thereby expanding the understanding of blockchain technology applications in innovative industries. Acknowledging that creative work is inherently subjective, this exploration of image complexity and consistency is not intended to dictate how artistic styles or specific content should be designed. Instead, it aims to provide basic design considerations that meet public preferences. Second, this study focuses on the impact of theoretically driven interpretable NFT design features on project performance. On the one hand, we extend traditional consumption theory into the web3 context and classify the general NFT design features accordingly. This classification provides a new analytical perspective for future product design in the NFT market and information goods market. On the other hand, contrary to prior literature which analyzed the uninterpretable image features using deep learning algorithms to predict NFT price [ 12 ], this study focuses on interpretable and managerially significant image features (such as image complexity and consistency), providing a new perspective for NFT image analysis. Third, this study proposes a systematic NFT performance measurement, considering both the primary and secondary markets from short-term and long-term perspectives. This provides specific evaluation metrics and a systematic assessment framework for evaluating the performance of the NFT project. The empirical results reveal that competency-related and investment-related design features have different impacts on NFTs' short-term and long-term performance. This highlights the importance of analyzing the primary and secondary NFT markets separately in future work. Managerial implications. By comprehensively understanding the impact of different design features on NFT performance, our findings offer decision support for the design of blockchain-based digital assets in the emerging content creation market. Additionally, the moderating results of market uncertainty also provide an important reference for creators' decision-making in a dynamic market environment. Specifically, image complexity and consistency are important for the performance of NFT projects, and creators can use moderately complex color combinations and consistent visual features when designing and creating NFT projects. Moreover, creators can use our results to design appropriate initial prices and royalties to achieve their expected financial goals. Limitations and future research . First, the NFT projects examined in this study are limited to those with a fixed circulation, and the primary market performance is evaluated based on the supply. Future research could explore NFT projects without a predetermined circulation at launch (such as CryptoKitties) and investigate the factors that impact their performance. Second, royalty serves as an incentive mechanism for content creators, yet this mechanism is still in the exploration phase. To the best of our knowledge, many NFT platforms are beginning to embrace a flexible royalty policy. It means that royalty is no longer static nor solely determined by creators. The dynamic nature of royalty presents new challenges and opportunities for NFT market analysis. Finally, with the introduction of NFT profile authentication on Twitter and the combination of Web2 and Web3, the social aspect of NFT consumption will be strengthened. The proposed conceptual framework may require additional expansion from the perspective of social influence.

column1: Equilibrium analysis of bitcoin block withholding attack: A generalized model
column2: Abstract Block withholding attack is an action where a miner who has found a legal block chooses not to submit it but rather directly abandons it. This attack makes the mining pool lose all bitcoin rewards contained within the block. In this paper, we construct a generalized model where two participants can choose to either cooperate with each other or employ a block withholding attack in the mining pool. To make the model more realistic, we consider both the cost of partial proof of work and the cost of cooperation. We also calculate the reward-per-time instead of profit-per-time to better measure the payoffs of each party. Further, we discuss the case where the payoff function and cost function are directly related to the computational power. The pure strategy and mixed strategy are analyzed respectively and the segmentations of the equilibrium are shown. We demonstrate that increasing the information asymmetry by utilizing information conceal mechanisms could lower the occurrence of the BWH attack.
column3: 5 Conclusions and future research In this paper, we proposed a generalized model in the blockchain mining pool game. There has been a lot of previous research in this field, but such research ignored several key factors that could influence the profit and the corresponding equilibrium solution. Some works compared the profits in a different time period, which lead to misleading conclusions. Others analyzed the BWH attack game by calculating the profit per time but made a mistake in the model foundation: they assumed that cooperation can enlarge the payoff and cost at the same time, which obviously contradicts the reality. Moreover, they did not consider the cost participants spend under cooperation or that partial of proof work might also consume some resources, such as CPU or electronic power. We corrected all these mistakes and found a generalized model that better captures all features of the BWH attack game in blockchain. By conducting the equilibrium analysis and calculating the payoff per time, we found that the equilibrium can be divergent under different cases. We performed the optimal choices in different segmentations, as shown in the Figures. We analyzed the cases where both participants can allocate part of their resources on BWH attack, and we obtained the corresponding solution under different parameter alterations. By introducing two major effects in this game – competition effect and signal effect – we explained why these phenomena occur under diverse cases. In the extensions, we extended our model to the case where payoff per time, cost of cooperation and cost of partial proof of work are directly related to the computational power, and we obtained a more universal conclusion. Throughout the deductions, we proved that the best way to avoid the BWH attack in a Bitcoin system is by increasing the information asymmetry between parties, which is counterintuitive. This is because, when the participant does not know what resource its opponent has allocated to BWH attack, it will not judge whether it is in a dominating status; thus, it might be more likely to take the strategy of cooperation. Moreover, our results show that setting a proper limitation for the cost of partial proof of work, or designing a rational relationship between function of cost of cooperation and function payoff per time, can be useful in eliminating the BWH behavior in a Bitcoin system. Regarding managerial insights, our paper is the first to propose a more generalized model in BWH attack, which features the reality more completely and veritably. Researchers can employ our model to find out more interesting conclusions by using game theory in Bitcoin. Managers can calculate the payoff per time to help them make more reliable and convincing decisions. Moreover, as we found that some information conceal mechanisms can help to decrease BWH attack, the platform or other Bitcoin firms can try to design such mechanisms to better solve the issue of BWH (and similar) attacks. Also, we put forward a limitation of cost of partial proof of work and a cost-payoff relationship, which can both be employed as the guarantee for the cooperation behavior of participants or miners in a mining pool. Managers can raise the cost of partial proof of work to a certain threshold to remove the incentive for participants to involve themselves in BWH attack. Similarly, a well-designed cost of cooperation-payoff per time relationship can limit the profit under BWH attack and encourage the participants to cooperate. There are still some limitations of our paper. First, we only consider the case where two participants can employ the BWH attack in one mining pool. In reality, participants might own computational power in different mining pools, which makes the strategy of employing BWH attack in one pool to save computational power so that it can then be transferred to another mining pool to cooperate in digging blocks an optional choice. Moreover, multiple participants and the corresponding optimal strategy combinations are worth discussing. In the Appendix, we only conduct a brief study; this could be extended to include a more complicated model. The cases where there is more than one mining pool or more than two participants could also be researched. For the case where there are two mining pools, both pools can try to attack the other pool by employing BWH attack. Moreover, there should be some cases that BWH attack can be employed by the mining pool instead of the miners. Also, there are many other types of attack, such as the fork after withholding attack, and our work could be extended to find out whether our conclusions would change when other types of attack are employed. Our paper shows that information asymmetry can ease the occurrence of BWH attack, but it does not show what level of asymmetry is required to decrease the probability of BWH attack to its lowest, and it does not measure the effect of information conceal mechanisms. Future works could concentrate on the BWH attacks and other moral hazard issues and the corresponding solving mechanisms in the Bitcoin system. Our model could also be extended to a dynamic occasion where long-term profit is analyzed.

column1: Establishing buyer-supplier self-organization through LSP brokered learning and information technologies: The effects on relational performance in logistic service triads
column2: Logistics service providers (LSPs) can have a profound impact on other companies operating in supply chains. To investigate the role of LSP, we propose and develop the concept of brokered LSP learning (i.e., supply chain learning run by the LSP) as exploitation and exploration practices imposed by the single actor to run organizational learning among supply chain actors. The research examines how supply chain learning run by the LSP affects self-organization of the buyer-supplier dyad and triadic relational performance. Our results provide insight into whether LSP-brokered learning alone is sufficient to improve triadic relational performance. The study shows that LSP-brokered learning, supported by decentralized technologies, has a positive effect on buyer-supplier self-organization. As a resulting effect, the study also operationalizes triadic relational performance composed of the joint impact of relational performances produced by three dyads in the logistics service triads, which can be improved by buyer-supplier self-organization. • LSP-brokered learning, supported by decentralized technologies, has a positive effect on buyer-supplier self-organization. • The direct effect of brokered learning run by the LSP on the triadic relational performance is significant and negative. • Buyer-supplier self-organization partially mediates the relationship between LSP learning and triadic relational performance. • There is a positive link between buyer-supplier self-organization and triadic relational performance.
column3:
5. Discussion
5.1. Theoretical contribution
This study advances the SCM literature by conceptualizing and empirically investigating how LSP learning affects self-organization of the buyer-supplier dyad and triadic relational performance. The theoretical contribution provided by our research is threefold.
First, we develop and test the concept of LSP learning, that is, supply chain learning run by the logistics service provider. In light of the obtained results, brokered LSP learning has two basic dimensions. The first dimension refers to performing exploitation and exploration practices to cultivate and disseminate knowledge in addressing organizational problems among multiple supply chain actors (Ojha et al., 2018; Silvestre et al., 2020). Exploitation practices are associated with rigid control, tight discipline, systematic reasoning, scrutinizing, and upfront planning, based on experience. Exploration practices, on the other hand, are linked to complex search, relaxed control, loose discipline, and flexibility, in the hope of finding new alternatives (Pereira et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2023).
The other dimension pertains to lead-organization learning, in which exploitation and exploration practices are imposed by a single actor. Although in brokered LSP learning all actors share a common interest, major organizational learning decisions and activities are coordinated by the lead organization. This is parallel to the mechanism of brokered governance, where a lead organization orchestrates the network and/or facilitates the activities of member organizations in their efforts to achieve network goals (Provan and Kenis, 2008). Building upon the study of Spekman et al. (2002), we argue that while the supply chain structure is a ‘vehicle’ for the multiple supply chain involved in knowledge gathering and learning, the LSP can be perceived as an engine of this vehicle, which triggers the supply chain learning process. The results obtained thus corroborate the prior studies, which highlighted the role of a lead company at the start-up stage of the supply chain learning process. Such a leading position can be held either by a core company or a third party which promotes a learning environment either under crisis or finding new opportunities (Bessant et al., 2003). In our study, the logistics service provider is the lead company that strives to develop and share knowledge to solve problems between multiple supply chain actors.
In general, our survey-based research provides quantitative evidence that the LSP is frequently able to act as the intermediary between suppliers and buyers. Likewise, by running the mechanism of broker learning, the LSP, to some extent, is able to orchestrate the operations performed in supply chains. In this sense, the obtained results complement previous studies (Liu and Lai, 2016; Wang et al., 2020) by providing evidence for an increasing role of LSP in the way the supply chain operates. However, our study extends the prior research by demonstrating that the effect of LSP depends on the increasing number, complexity, and greater customization of service offerings from the second-party logistics (2 PL) through the third-party logistics (3 PL) to the fifth-party logistics (5 PL). This result indicates that the better position of LSP in a triad guides the higher role of LSP-brokered learning and its stronger contribution to triadic relational performance.
Another contribution refers to the way our study perceives a triad. Prior research (Swierczek, 2023a, 2023b) admittedly investigated the determinants of self-organization in triadic supply chains (including decentralized information technologies and information governance), nonetheless, a triad in this research is still treated as a simple collection of dyads. Our study goes one step further and attempts to grasp how a certain actor and its relationships affect the other two actors and their relationships. In this vein, our study shows that a triad should not be reduced into a conglomerate of relations, quite the contrary, it corroborates that in business reality, each of the collective actors makes up more than the sum of its relations (Swierczek and Szozda, 2024). To operationalize that, the research explores the learning mechanism run by the LSP to underscore the role of a single company in imposing learning rules and practices on self-organization of two other supply chain actors (buyer and supplier).
More specifically, the study shows that brokered learning run by the LSP has a strong positive impact on buyer-supplier self-organization. Therefore, we argue that self-organization may require organizational learning composed of both exploration and exploitation practices. As exploration practices are more focused on revealing future chances and searching for useful new adaptations, exploitation practices are concentrated on using existing and known adaptations. In other words, exploitation is more related to control, while exploration is more related to chaos and uncertainty. The impact of LSP brokered learning thus ensures a balance between chaos and stability, required when performing buyer-supplier self-organization. This restrains the triad from falling into chaos or total inertia.
More importantly, buyer-supplier self-organization partially mediates the relationship between LSP learning and triadic relational performance. The results obtained might, at least partially, reconcile the dilemma concerning the real influence of supply chain learning on organizational performance. Specifically, some of prior studies found a positive impact of supply chain learning on performance (Flint et al., 2008; Jean et al., 2016), while the other portion of the research did not indicate such an impact (Nguyen and Harrison, 2019; Suh et al., 2019).
Our results show that the direct effect of brokered LSP learning on triadic relational performance is significant but negative. However, when a specific mediator is included, learning can yield certain benefits. In light of our study, when organizational actions are included and, for instance, take the form of self-organization, then the indirect effect of brokered learning, through buyer-supplier self-organization, on supply chain performance is significant and positive. Consequently, the results obtained complement the prior studies by providing evidence for an increasing role of LSP in relational performance (Forslund, 2012; Sodhi and Tang, 2021).
The results obtained from this study can, to some extent, solve the dilemma of the relationship between supply chain learning and performance. However, one should also consider the fact that while brokered learning is mostly run by individual companies, they can act solely in their own interest. This may explain the negative impact of LSP learning on relational performance, which highlights the role of joint effects and reciprocal influence between the triadic parties.
Third, by testing the effect of buyer-supplier self-organization on triadic relational performance, we advance and empirically operationalize the joint effect and reciprocal influence of relational performances yielded by the three dyads. The results obtained establish a positive link between the self-organization of the buyer-supplier self-organization and triadic relational performance. Consequently, the empirical results suggest that self-organization contributes to the relational effects produced by the three dyads. Similarly, our findings extend previous studies (Carter et al., 2017; Swierczek, 2022), by operationalizing and examining the construct of triadic relational performance, which attempts to grasp differences in relational performances produced by supply chain dyads. In doing so, our study further advances the research methodology presented in the study of Swierczek (2022) by applying a more robust assessment of the relational performances of three dyads in triads. In the current work, the identification of certain relational performances was validated by the use of CFA, complemented by HRA. Furthermore, our study extends the work of Swierczek (2022) by adding a triadic relational performance as a component in a regression analysis demonstrating the interaction among the dyads and contributing to the supply chain performance. However, contrary to the study of Swierczek (2022), this research shows a more dynamic picture of the contribution of relational performance produced by a certain dyad to the operation performance of the supply chain operational performance. Specifically, our results show that the relational performance produced by certain dyads within triads does not contribute equally to the operational performance of the supply chain operational performance. Unlike previous conceptualizations (Lavie, 2006; Carter et al., 2017), this study demonstrates that not all three relational performances of dyads contribute to the overall supply chain performance. Specifically, two dyads, located close to the market and ultimate customers combined with triadic relational performance, positively contribute to the overall supply chain performance, though to a different extent. Interestingly, dyads constituted by actors located more upstream in a supply chain, without direct contact with the market, have a negative impact on supply chain operational performance. These results appear to be consistent with the study by Swierczek (2022), which showed that two dyads formed with an actor having direct relationships with the market and ultimate customers contribute to supply chain performance.
5.2. Managerial implications
When practitioners are considered, the findings may be of interest to both the managers of companies providing logistics services and to the managers of companies that use these services. Importantly, for LSPs, decentralized information technologies, such as blockchain, Internet of Things, Big Data, and cloud technology, might have a positive, though rather weak, effect on LSP learning. Among those technologies, blockchain is traditionally perceived as a cutting-edge solution that can transform and remodel the relationships between all members of the supply chain. For instance, the study by Lacity and van Hoek (2021) showed the case of Walmart Canada and its LSPs, which used Blockchain to innovate the freight invoice process. In this vein, our results corroborate that decentralized technologies can support exploration by creating innovative opportunities. However, our findings seem to contradict that decentralized technologies are primarily instrumental when performing exploration practices (Hald and Kinra, 2019; Koryak et al., 2018). For instance, Lacity and van Hoek (2021) demonstrated that Blockchain can be instrumental in exploitation practices leading to a gradual improvement of contemporary processes. Similarly, in a broader sense, our study shows that technologies such as Blockchain, digital platforms, cloud systems, or IoT can be used to enhance exploitation practices. This provides evidence that decentralized technologies support both exploitation and exploration, which constitute organizational learning. Put in a more specific way, these technologies can be instrumental when organizational learning is run by logistics service providers within triads. This may also suggest a growing role of LSPs in establishing buyer-supplier relationships. Importantly, as suggested by our results, the LSP that uses brokered organizational learning is capable of adjusting exploitation and exploration practices to facilitate buyer-supplier self-organization. This gives third parties a powerful role in creating a favorable environment of self-organization for the buyer and supplier. In such a setting, they are able to take up bottom-up initiatives and make volitional, autonomous decisions. They contribute to devising creative ideas and innovative managerial methods that provide higher triadic relational performance.
The study shows how the relational performances produced by dyads affect each other to generate triadic relational performance. However, important for managers, the contribution of the relational performances of dyads to the overall performance of the supply chain can be unequal and also inexistent. Specifically, when considered individually, supplier-LSP performance turns out to have a positive effect on supply chain performance, but when combined with the relational performances of two other dyads (buyer-supplier and LSP-buyer), its impact is negative. Interestingly, however, supplier-LSP dyadic performance has an important role to play in the ability of supply chains to obtain triadic relational performance. Excluding the supplier-LSP performance from the model, and applying only the relational performances of two remaining dyads (buyer-supplier and LSP-buyer) make triadic relational performance negative and insignificant for the supply chain operational performance. This may corroborate the role of the relationships between the supplier and the LSP in the operational performance of the supply chains.
Likewise, in line with our results, while buyer-supplier self-organization partially mediates the relationship between LSP-brokered learning and triadic relational performance, the direct relationship between these variables remains negative. From a managerial perspective, this is probably due to the fact that the LSP learning activity is not enough to generate relational performance, and the engagement of two other supply chain actors is required to finally produce the joint effects at the triadic level.

column1: Implementation of digital twins in the food supply chain: a review and conceptual framework
column2: Digital Twins (DTs) hold significant promise in addressing the challenges faced by food supply chains (FSCs). This paper aims to provide critical insights into the potential for Digital Twins to meet the key challenges of the FSC and establish a comprehensive conceptual framework for their implementation. Following a systematic literature review (SLR), the study identified 81 peer-reviewed, high-quality papers published over the last decade (2012–2023). The typology-driven thematic analysis emphasises the emergent nature of DTs within FSCs, highlighting their key characteristics including monitoring, real-time simulation, and scenario analysis. The identified characteristics, applications, implementation drivers and barriers of Digital Twin form the basis for a novel conceptual framework for implementing DTs in FSCs. Leveraging insights from Innovation Adoption Theory and the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, the study outlines a structured five step implementation process divided into three stages. Notably, technology assessment and performance evaluation emerge as two innovative steps necessary for the successful implementation of DTs specifically, not previously considered by the theory. The study identifies promising avenues for future research. These findings provide invaluable guidance to researchers and practitioners seeking to embrace the potential of Digital Twin within the food industry.
column3: 7.1. Conclusion This study aimed to answer two research questions following a systematic literature review. To address RQ1: How can adopting Digital Twins address food supply chain challenges? Five themes were identified from the selected literature and assessed using thematic analysis. FSC challenges, characteristics of DTs, applications, implementation drivers and barriers were used to derive comprehensive insights. The challenges of the FSC were established: complexity and uncertainty, food safety, food waste, information asymmetry, and traceability. The characteristics of Digital Twins, including monitoring, real-time simulation, scenario analysis, data and technology integration, and visibility, were identified. The combination of complementary characteristics of DTs was identified as a key enabler for addressing FSC challenges. Furthermore, the study identified a number of current applications of Digital Twins in the food industry. These real-world examples help validate the need and opportunity for adopting Digital Twins in the FSC. A comprehensive understanding of the relationship between FSC challenges and the characteristics of DTs, along with applications of DTs, answers RQ1. To answer RQ2: What is the process for implementing Digital Twins in FSCs? The study explored the drivers, barriers, and examples of successful adoption of DTs in the FSC. Specifically, internal drivers such as improving operational efficiency and enhancing visibility and transparency and external drivers including wider technology support and competitive pressures (cost, production, and quality) are expected to drive organisations towards implementing Digital Twins. Similarly, barriers were identified which hinder the implementation of Digital Twins, including data security and storage, data processing, lack of collaboration, synchronisation and system integration, and high implementation costs. These insights are brought together to develop a theory-driven conceptual framework for implementing Digital Twins in FSCs. This framework proposed three main implementation stages: pre-adoption, adoption, and post-adoption. The TOE framework provides technological, organisational, and environmental characteristics critical for the pre-adoption stage. Technology assessment and performance evaluation were established as two innovative steps to implementing DTs successfully. The presentation of this conceptual framework for implementing DTs in FSCs (Figure 9) provides the answer to RQ2. Finally, detailed synthesis of the findings of the thematic analysis has allowed us to propose five avenues for future research. 7.2. Contribution to theory The study makes the following contributions to theory. This review enriches existing knowledge at the interface between Digital Twins and FSCs. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first systematic literature review study to explore the potential of Digital Twins in the food supply chain context. Our SLR provides researchers with insights into the attributes, characteristics and applications of DTs at different stages of the supply chain, complementing the research conducted by Ivanov ( Citation 2023), which conceptualised a Digital Twin framework for supply chain and operations management. We have employed Innovation Adoption Theory and the TOE framework to develop a novel conceptual framework for implementing Digital Twins in the FSC. This novel conceptual framework divides the implementation process into three main stages: pre-adoption, adoption, and post-adoption.
