In the pre-adoption stage, the TOE framework provides three dimensions for analysing the potential factors of pre-adoption. Building on Innovation Adoption Theory our framework extends the original three-step IT adoption process into five steps, with technology assessment added to the adoption process and performance evaluation metrics added to the post-adoption stage. Our proposed conceptual framework for the implementation of Digital Twins within the FSC should be tested and validated by researchers in the future. More importantly, our five proposed research directions offer a sound foundation for researchers to explore further development and evaluation of Digital Twins in the supply chain. 7.3. Contribution to practice This systematic literature review offers insights which enable food industry managers and practitioners to understand the characteristics and applications of DTs in the FSC context. The insights generated by this review can assist managers in assessing the current status of technology adoption in their organisations and determine if there is a requirement to implement Digital Twins in their operations. It is unlikely that Digital Twins will be able to alleviate all the challenges of the FSC and companies are likely to have already invested in other IT systems (such as EDI, ERP, Blockchain or IoT). Considering the inherent complexity and uncertainty of the food industry, managers need to think about their existing information technology and consider how Digital Twin-based solutions can be integrated with these existing technologies. Our novel conceptual framework provides detailed guidelines for implementing Digital Twins in the food industry. The framework is divided into three main stages, in the pre-adoption stage the framework enables practitioners to assess the key factors from technological, organisational, and environmental viewpoints. In the post-adoption stage the performance evaluation metrics will assist practitioners in determining if the implementation of DTs will benefit their businesses. Following full validation, this framework will provide an invaluable guide for policymakers and governments to better understand the benefits of Digital Twins in the food industry and help formulate future policies and regulations for encouraging wider adoption of this disruptive technology in other supply chains. Overall, this review has highlighted the importance of establishing a standard roadmap for adopting DTs in supply chains. 7.4. Limitations of the study This study has the following limitations. First, the study is based on 81 papers from a range of research areas. The inclusion of papers was limited to literature discussing Digital Twins within the FSC context. Only papers discussing DTs and FSCs published between 2012-2023 were selected. Thus, valuable literature on FSCs published earlier or later may have been neglected. Furthermore, this study only selected peer-reviewed journal papers and excluded other ‘grey literature’, thus potentially missing useful insights. Secondly, although an SLR provides a rigorous process, the mechanical method of extracting relevant data may have limited the findings. The selection of keywords and the screening process can be subjective and biased as it depends on the interpretation of the research team. Meanwhile, the potential for human error is unavoidable during the search, screening, and data extraction process, which may lead to erroneous review results. The use of text mining/data mining tools would have helped with establishing themes and validating other findings. Finally, as the application of Digital Twins in the FSC is a relatively new field of research, and there is limited empirical evidence to support their effectiveness in a real-world setting. This makes it difficult to draw generic conclusions from the available literature.

column1: Solving the Capacitated Dispersion Problem with variable neighborhood search From basic to skewed VNS
column2: The topic of this paper is the Capacitated Dispersion Problem (CDP). To solve the problem, variable neighborhood search (VNS) based heuristics are proposed. The proposed heuristics are Basic VNS, General VNS and General Skewed VNS. Their performances are assessed on the benchmark instances from the literature and compared against the state-of-the-art ones. Comparing to the state-of-the-art results, it turns out that Basic VNS is able to provide competitive results, while General VNS and General Skewed VNS advance the state-of-the-art results by establishing 57 new best-known solutions on the data set of 100 instances. Twenty nine new best-known solutions are solely due to the proposed General Skewed VNS.
column3: 4 Conclusions In this paper, the capacitated dispersion problem (CDP), an extension of the max–min diversity problem is studied. Unlike to the max–min diversity problem, the CDP imposes the minimum capacity requirements on the selected subset of elements. To efficiently solve the problem three heuristics based on Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) methodology are proposed. The proposed heuristics range from very simple Basic VNS, via General VNS (GVNS), up to the very sophisticated General Skewed VNS (GSVNS). The Basic VNS heuristic includes examination of only Swap Neighborhood, while GVNS examines two neighborhood structures (Swap and 2-out-1-in). On the other hand, GSVNS has the same ingredients as GVNS but uses more sophisticated rule for accepting new incumbent solution. This rule allows acceptance of even non-improving solutions and efficiently resolve the premature convergence issue detected in GVNS. The computational results reveal that BVNS is able to produce competitive solution values, while GVNS and GSVNS significantly advance the state-of-the-art results. Moreover, GSVNS is only heuristic able to reach all best-known solutions established in the literature and in this paper. In addition, the paper provides an empirical study on different improvement procedures varying from simple local search routines up to more advanced variable neighborhood descents that use two and three neighborhoods. The empirical study reveals the local search within swap neighborhood as the best local search routine, while as the best VND procedures are identified V N D 1 which explores Swap and 2-out-1-in neighborhoods, and V N D 3 which explores Swap, 2-out-1-in, and 1-out-2-in neighborhoods. However, further analysis disclosed that 1-out-2-in neighborhood becomes redundant if Swap and 2-out-1-in neighborhoods are already explored. The future work may include studying new capacitated dispersion problems as well as the development of GSVNS heuristics for other problems of max–min type.

column1: Through the looking glass: Unveiling geopolitical risks and sovereign bond spillovers in the eurozone
column2: This study introduces a novel time-varying parameter vector autoregressive (TVP-VAR) frequency connectedness approach for measuring the frequency transmission mechanism and dynamic spillovers among the sovereign bond markets of 13 Eurozone countries. Furthermore, the impact of global geopolitical risk (GPR) on the spillovers is examined through a time-varying Granger causality test. The results reveal strong spillovers in the Eurozone over time, especially since the spillover is predominantly driven by the short-term frequency domain. Besides, an asymmetry exists in the spillover effects between positive and negative returns, with spillovers being more pronounced for positive ones. The predictivity of geopolitical threats (GPRT) and geopolitical acts (GPRA) show significant time heterogeneity, particularly in response to specific extreme geopolitical risk events. Additionally, GPR, GPRT, and GPRA can significantly predict the spillovers for aggregate market return, specifically for positive ones, but it does not hold for negative returns (except for a temporary predictive capacity during COVID-19 of 2020). Finally, the Russia-Ukraine conflict predominantly influences sovereign bond market return spillovers through GPRT.
column3: 5 Conclusion In response to the economic disturbances caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the energy crisis ensuing from the Russo-Ukrainian conflict, Eurozone nations have implemented expansionary fiscal measures. These measures have led to a considerable escalation in sovereign debt levels, culminating in a historical peak in 2023. This development has sparked concerns about the potential resurgence of the Eurozone debt crisis, which could precipitate an extensive economic downturn across the region. To avert the transformation of sovereign risk spread into a systemic crisis within the Eurozone, it is imperative to delineate the paths of contagion and the fundamental drivers behind them. To this end, we utilize the SovCISS to gauge the risks in the Eurozone sovereign bond markets. Our research focused on the transnational spillover effects associated with both the escalation and de-escalation of sovereign debt risks across various frequency domains. Additionally, we explore the mechanisms driving sovereign risk spillovers, particularly from the perspective of geopolitical risk shocks. The key findings of our study are summarized as follows: Firstly, there exist strong spillovers among European SovCISS over time, especially since the spillover is predominantly driven by the short-term frequency domain since the spillover in the medium-term and long-term frequency domains is relatively smaller. In addition, an asymmetry exists in the spillover effects between rising and falling SovCISS, with spillovers being more pronounced during increasing SovCISS. This discovery still holds even in different frequency domains. Secondly, there exists significant Granger causality from GPR to the aggregate return TCI and the positive return TCI, but it does not hold for negative return TCI (except for a temporary predictive capacity during COVID-19 of 2020). The predictive abilities of geopolitical threats and geopolitical acts show significant time-varying differences, particularly in response to specific extreme geopolitical risk events. Additionally, this study demonstrates that the Russia-Ukraine conflict predominantly influences SovCISS spillovers through geopolitical threats. This study underscores critical policy applications. Firstly, the Eurozone to enhance its surveillance and early warning mechanisms concerning sovereign debt risks, particularly during periods of escalating risks within member states. The implementation of a regional risk assessment framework is recommended to facilitate the prompt identification and assessment of how geopolitical events might affect the debt markets of member countries. It is vital to foster enhanced fiscal coordination and cooperation among the member states to alleviate the negative repercussions of geopolitical risks and to avert market turmoil triggered by unilateral measures. Secondly, the establishment of a mechanism to buffer against geopolitical risks is proposed. The Eurozone might consider creating a specialized fund or insurance scheme designed to cushion economic and financial volatilities stemming from geopolitical conflicts. This mechanism would offer short-term fiscal support to member states, aiding in the stabilization of their debt markets and economies during geopolitical disturbances. Enhancing partnerships with international bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is crucial for ensuring swift access to additional financial and technical assistance during crises.

column1: A modified memetic algorithm with multi-operation precise joint movement neighbourhood structure for the assembly job shop scheduling problem
column2: This paper presents an adaptive memetic algorithm based on a new neighbourhood structure (AMA) for solving the assembly job shop scheduling problem, with the aim of minimising the maximum completion time (makespan). To utilise the knowledge of problem, a theoretical analysis is conducted to explore the criteria for feasible and effective movement of operations under assembly constraints, and a multi-operation precise joint movement neighbourhood structure is proposed accordingly. In the AMA, to ensure the feasibility of solutions during the evolution process, a feasible encoding mechanism based on the constraint degree of operations is designed, a greedy active decoding method as well as feasible crossover operation based on independent operation chains are designed specifically for this encoding method. To avoid premature convergence of the population, a population update operator with diversity adaptive control is proposed. Finally, by comparing the results with five state-of-the-art algorithms, the superiority of AMA in terms of solution quality and stability is verified, particularly with the update of known optimal solutions for 11 instances.

column1: Shareholding strategies for selling green products on online platforms in a two-echelon supply chain
column2: Abstract Observing the practical vertical shareholding phenomena in platform retailing, this paper considers two shareholding rates (forward and backward) and proposes three shareholding strategies (forward, backward and cross-shareholding) in a supplier-lead green supply chain to investigate the operation mechanism behind it. Shareholding’s impacts on green investment, prices and profits are provided and the players’ strategy preferences are discussed. We interestingly find that cross-shareholding can be joint optimal when the two shareholding rates are both sufficiently low and thereby Pareto region goes with it. Meanwhile, both the players’ performances can be further improved through certain coordinated ways.
column3: 8 Conclusions and implications 8.1 Conclusions In a platform supply chain that faces with green sensitive consumers, the upstream supplier will invest in the greenness of the products to improve the sales volume and through which increase its profit. However, the downstream platform retailer can gain more profit costless when the green level increases and can be regarded as a free-riding, which will conversely lead to the under-investment problem of the upstream. To address this issue, a novel coordination scheme—shareholding is proposed in this work. Forward and backward shareholding rates as well as three shareholding strategies including forward, backward and cross-shareholding strategy have been exploited. Under this approach, the supplier and the platform retailer can redistribute the wholesale and retailing stages’ profits depending on the shares held by them. In the further investigation of the shareholding, holding share effect and incentive effect are derived in the shareholdings. Particularly, in forward shareholding strategy, through holding partial shares of the platform retailer, the supplier can access the market more directly and acquire the retailing profit to some extend in the form of holding share effect. Meanwhile, the retailer may also benefit from the progress through incentive effect while the supplier has the incentives to increase the profit in retailing. Similarly, in backward shareholding strategy, partial shares of the supplier is allocated to the retailer. The supplier incurs a loss in its shareholding but may benefit from the retailer’s operation decisions. Specifically, the platform retailer will consider the profits in wholesale progress while making decisions and thereby the incentive effect arises. At last, in cross-shareholding strategy, the characters of both single-way shareholdings exist. Shareholding rates’ interaction also appears under this shareholding strategy. Using the classic reselling scheme as the background, this work has examined the optimal green level, wholesale price, retail price and profits of the players while using different shareholding strategies. The contributions of this study are threefold: Firstly, we analyze the impacts of shareholding rates on the optimal green level and wholesale price of the supplier, and the optimal retail price of the retailer. For the optimal green level, it shows that the optimal green level increases in response to either of the (forward or backward) shareholding rate under all shareholding strategies. Revealing the positive effect of shareholding on the coordination of the green level. Moreover, when adopting this method, promoting the retailer to hold the supplier’s shares will be more capable than promoting the supplier’s holding shares. Meanwhile, in observing the optimal wholesale price and retail price, we note that both the prices are increases in the backward shareholding rate and decreases in the forward one in most occasions. However, these two prices may change in opposite directions when the forward shareholding exceeds a certain threshold in using the cross-shareholding strategy. That is, when the supplier holds a sufficiently high partial of the retailer’s shares, and meanwhile it’s partial shares are held by the retailer, the holding share effect becomes less attractive and the supplier inclines to raise its profit in the wholesale progress. However, to stabilize the demand, the retailer can’t adjust the retail price in the same way. It also indicates the pricing decision of supplier is more flexible than the retailer and the supplier’s further extraction of the platform retailer’s margin. Secondly, the shareholding strategy preferences of the supplier and the platform retailer have been investigated. On the view of the supplier, the holding share effect can exert strictly positive effects on the supplier’s performance for a positive forward shareholding rate, which can cover the negative impacts from less favorable operations of the retailer. For a higher backward shareholding rate, although loss part of its own profit, the retailer’s more favorable operations as incentive effect can bring benefits to the supplier. Meanwhile, as the leader of the chain, the supplier can increase its wholesale price to possess a higher marginal and maintain the profit gains from the remaining shares. Consequently, the supplier’s profit is always increasing in both the forward and backward shareholding rates, leading cross-shareholding strategy to be its optimal shareholding strategy under any circumstance. On the view of the platform retailer, although it may suffer from a loss of shares in using the forward shareholding strategy, the incentive effect of a lower wholesale price and higher green level allows it to gain more profits overall, leading the platform retailer’s optimal strategy to be the forward shareholding in most cases. However, when the forward shareholding rate continues to grow, the wholesale price becomes unfavorable and the marginal of the retailer is shrinked, resulting the retailer’s optimal shareholding strategy converts to backward shareholding if the backward shareholding rate is low. In this situation, the holding share effect dominates the negative incentive effect, leading to an improvement of the retailer’s profit. Moreover, when both shareholding rates are high, the retailer will not accept any shareholding strategy and choose to be totally independent. Interestingly, the retailer’s optimal shareholding strategy changes to cross-shareholding when both the shareholding rates are sufficiently low. Under this occasion, both players of the chain will optimally choose the same strategy and thereby Pareto region goes with it. This conclusion helps explain the phenomena that many firms enjoy a low-level of the cross-shareholding in the real financial market like the Japanese one. Furthermore, under the alternative scheme of agency selling, cross-shareholding strategy remains their mutual optimal strategy if the agency sharing ratio is sufficiently high. Therefore, when the agency selling is not available in the practice, the related companies can consider to adopt the cross-shareholding to their performances. Thirdly, from the perspective of the entire supply chain, whilst the increase in the forward shareholding rate always raises the aggregate profits, a higher backward shareholding rate may cause damages when it exceeds a certain level. Thus, if the upstream shareholding rate is high and downstream rate is medium, cross-shareholding strategy achieves and the aggregate profits of both parties reach its highest level. Comparing the chain’s preference with both players', it shows the chain’s highest favorable shareholding rates are larger than the retailer’s. Consequently, if the supplier can compensate the retailer’s holding share or being held in specific range of the shareholding rates, Pareto improvement can be achieved. This conclusion echoes some shareholding subsidy policies or stock options for the retailers provided by the suppliers (e.g., Haier and Luzhou Laojiao platform retailers) in the practice. Comparing with the agency selling scheme, the whole supply chain will acquire more profit under cross-shareholdng strategy when the agency sharing ratio is sufficiently high. We also check the robustness of our insights through introducing a specific form of endogenous share price and extending the green investment cost function to a more complicated one.

column1: Exploring the impact of climate change on traditional and energy cryptocurrencies: A cross-sectional approach
column2: Cryptocurrencies have experienced a dramatic rise in popularity, evolving into major financial instruments. However, this surge has intensified concerns regarding environmental impact, particularly their energy consumption and carbon emissions. Understanding the relationship between environmental factors and cryptocurrency markets has thus become increasingly crucial. This paper investigates how regional and global CO₂ emissions influence the valuation of traditional and environmentally oriented cryptocurrencies. Using cross-sectional OLS regression models, we find that CO₂ emissions and inter-cryptocurrency dynamics significantly affect digital asset prices. Traditional cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum tend to rise with regional emissions but decline with global emissions, suggesting growing environmental concerns. In contrast, energy-focused cryptocurrencies such as Power Ledger and WePower exhibit the opposite pattern. They are negatively affected by regional emissions but positively associated with global emissions. This indicates growing investor interest in sustainable assets as climate awareness increases. These findings highlight the importance of investor sentiment, environmental expectations, and regulatory factors in shaping cryptocurrency markets.
column3: 5 Conclusion This paper offers new insights into the relationship between environmental factors and the valuation of both traditional and energy-focused crypto assets. In particular, our findings from cross-sectional OLS models show the significant influence of both CO₂ emissions and inter-cryptocurrency dynamics on digital asset valuations. Our results rely on the existing literature and extend it in several ways. In line with Papp et al. (2023) and Bilirer and Zeren (2024) , we find that environmental factors, such as carbon emissions play a significant role in shaping the value of traditional cryptocurrencies. However, while prior studies have focused on one region using time-series models and Granger causality ( Krause & Tolaymat, 2018 ; Stoll et al., 2019 ), our study uses a cross-sectional approach that allows for variations in carbon emissions across different locations including China, India, the US, the EU27 & UK, and the world. Our findings display significant disparities between regional and global contexts. In particular, traditional cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum are generally positively impacted by regional CO₂ emissions, reflecting increased mining and trading activity that leads to a rise in price. Conversely, their prices are negatively affected by global CO₂ emissions, suggesting a growing public awareness of environmental effects and, consequently, reduced demand for these assets. Moreover, our study contributes to the existing literature by incorporating green energy tokens, which have received little attention to date ( Manahov & Li, 2025 ; Ul Haq et al., 2023 ; Yousaf et al., 2023 ). While previous studies have mainly focused on the connectedness between energy-focused cryptocurrencies and traditional financial markets, our study is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to investigate the impact of CO₂ emissions on these cryptocurrencies. Our results reveal a clear divergence in how environmental factors impact energy-oriented digital assets, compared to traditional cryptocurrencies. Specifically, their values are negatively impacted by regional emissions, indicating that local environmental degradation is associated with intensified fossil fuel dependence and a less favorable context for green investments. In contrast, these environmentally oriented cryptocurrencies are positively associated with global emissions, suggesting that rising environmental concerns may enhance the transition to clean technologies and promote the adoption of sustainable digital assets. This study emphasizes that investor sentiment, environmental expectations, and regulatory policies play a crucial role in shaping the dynamics of cryptocurrency markets. As environmental awareness and regulatory pressure increase, understanding how climate-related variables interact with digital asset valuations becomes essential for investors, policymakers, and financial analysts when making investment decisions and shaping legislation. This highlights the need for more nuanced modeling approaches that incorporate investor sentiment, renewable energy trends, and regulatory risk. Overall, this paper contributes to the emerging field linking digital finance with environmental sustainability. It offers new insights into how climate change impacts the valuation of various cryptocurrencies, including green tokens. The results are relevant to investors, policymakers, and financial institutions seeking to reconcile digital innovation with sustainability goals.

column1: FinTech Finance and External Audit
column2: Synopsis The research problem This study investigated how national financial technology (FinTech) finance influences the external audit decisions of private, nonfinancial firms in developing economies. While FinTech is transforming financial systems and audit practices globally, its impact on audit demand in low- and middle-income countries remains underexplored. The test hypotheses The study tested two main hypotheses: first, that higher levels of FinTech finance are associated with increased firm-level demand for external audits; and second, that this relationship is mediated by institutional audit conditions and firm characteristics such as size, industry, and international orientation. Target population The analysis focused on private audited and unaudited firms operating across a range of low- and middle-income countries worldwide, drawing data from 2013 to 2020. Adopted methodology The study employed cross-country panel data econometric techniques, using probit models with country and year fixed effects. To strengthen causal inferences, the analysis incorporated instrumental variable regressions, Oster’s coefficient stability tests, and dominance analysis. Analysis The binary outcome variable, whether a firm’s accounts are externally audited, was regressed on national FinTech finance expenditure and a wide set of firm- and country-level controls. Robustness checks included sensitivity tests for sample restrictions, nonlinearities, and lag effects. Mediation was assessed via interaction terms with auditing standards, registration status, and employee training. Findings Results revealed that FinTech finance significantly increases the likelihood of firms undertaking external audits, especially in countries with strong regulatory environments. The effect is stronger for larger, digitally engaged, and export-oriented firms. Mediating factors, such as audit regulations, formalization, and workforce training, amplify this relationship. These findings underscore the growing role of FinTech in shaping audit behavior and highlight the importance of institutional support to maximize its transparency-enhancing effects.
column3: This cross-country study identified a strong and statistically significant positive association between FinTech finance expenditure and firms’ demand for external audit services. The relationship proved robust across a range of sensitivity tests and endogeneity checks, reinforcing its empirical credibility. By analyzing data from diverse national contexts, our study advances understanding of how FinTech investment shapes audit practices, regulatory adaptation, and technological integration within the auditing profession. Our findings show that increased FinTech finance not only raises audit demand but also prompts strategic responses from audit firms — such as adopting technology-driven audit tools and refining service differentiation. Mediating factors like regulatory strength, formal registration, and worker training further amplify this effect, confirming the importance of institutional context in leveraging FinTech’s transparency-enhancing potential. Importantly, this study contributes to the literature on the intersection of FinTech and audit practices. It highlights how FinTech-driven digitalization influences firms’ perception of external audit necessity, drives demand for specialized audit services (e.g., audits of digital assets or automated processes), and accelerates the adoption of data analytics in audit methodologies. These shifts underscore the continued relevance of external audits even in tech-intensive environments and reveal emerging technology-specific audit needs. Policy implications include updating audit standards to reflect the risks and complexities of FinTech, promoting digital skills among auditors, strengthening FinTech-related financial transparency requirements, and fostering collaboration between FinTech firms and auditors. Enhanced data protection regulations and ongoing research will be vital to ensure adaptive, secure, and effective audit practices. While the study offers broad cross-national insights, it was constrained by the limited temporal scope (2013–2020) and by the use of a binary outcome variable that may understate the nuances of firms’ audit behaviors. Future research should examine industry-specific patterns, firm-size heterogeneity, and country-level regulatory differences in greater depth to refine understanding of how FinTech finance influences audit demand. In sum, our findings provide a timely and evidence-based contribution to both academic and policy discussions on how FinTech reshapes audit engagement. They underscore the need for coordinated regulatory, institutional, and professional responses to ensure the integrity and effectiveness of audits in an evolving digital financial ecosystem.

column1: Digital inventory audits: an alternative approach to physical observation in audit evidence gathering
column2: PurposeThis study examines whether digital streaming and observation technologies can serve as an alternative approach for collecting inventory audit evidence, the challenges faced in their adoption and the factors contributing to their non-adoption.Design/methodology/approachThis study adopts a two-stage, mixed-method approach, beginning with pilot study interviews that informed the comprehensive survey with qualitative and quantitative data. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, t-tests and Pearson’s correlation coefficient, while qualitative data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.FindingsOur findings revealed a positive perspective concerning the effectiveness and reliability of these technologies for inventory audits and the efficiency of internal controls within them, despite challenges such as obtaining a holistic view of the warehouse, observing obsolescence, ensuring inventory completeness and general reliability concerns. Additionally, preferences for physical inventory audits and skepticism about these technologies’ potential to enhance audit quality were identified as factors contributing to their non-adoption.Research limitations/implicationsThese findings have important implications for cost-conscious firms because they reveal that carefully adopting intermediate technologies can enhance the audit process. Our findings are relevant to audit regulators and firms interested in determining whether such technologies enhance audit efficiency and quality. This study highlights the need for updated auditing standards and directives and technologies that meet auditing requirements.Originality/valueThis study contributes to the literature by uncovering whether less advanced technologies can be used as an alternative approach to collect audit evidence. Consequently, the finding adds to the growing body of literature underscoring the potential of technologies, even less sophisticated ones, to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of audits, despite their challenges. Additionally, it underscores the need for clear regulatory standards, suggests that auditors embrace emerging technologies and acquire relevant skills and offers insights for technology developers on audit firms’ concerns regarding digital technologies.
column3: This exploratory study examines whether digital streaming and observation technologies can serve as alternative tools for collecting inventory audit evidence, the challenges in their adoption, and the factors contributing to their non-adoption. Therefore, the study explores the staying power of these technologies. The findings suggest that less advanced technologies can be somewhat effective and reliable for collecting audit evidence, but they are not without significant challenges. Audit representatives generally found these technologies adequate but preferred physical over digital inventory audits and expressed skepticism about whether they improved audit quality. Although the internal control mechanisms within these technologies were seen as effective and secure, there was uncertainty about the thoroughness of their scrutiny and attention to security challenges. Despite their potential, these technologies face significant challenges, such as difficulties in gaining a comprehensive view of warehouses, observing obsolescence, ensuring inventory completeness, and addressing reliability and technical issues, as well as dealing with uncooperative personnel and the lack of proactive auditing standards. Moreover, the inability to engage in sufficient social interaction, a crucial source of audit evidence, is a significant limitation. These challenges raise doubts about the staying power of these technologies. The primary reason for the non-adoption of these technologies appears to be the perceived superiority of physical inventory audits over digital audits, primarily due to the less advanced nature of these technologies. Non-adoption was not due to a lack of competence or availability, although representatives expressed uncertainty about their functionality and whether the absence of regulatory standards hindered their adoption—a recurring theme in the study. We contend that adopting more advanced technologies can address the current limitations and enhance the audit process. In summary, integrating TAM and DOI provides a robust and holistic approach to analyzing our findings regarding the acceptance and adoption of digital technologies for inventory audits. This approach underscores the importance of perceived usefulness, ease of use, and innovation attributes (relative importance, compatibility, complexity, observability, and trialability) in shaping audit firms’ perceptions and attitudes toward technology. This study contributes to auditing literature and practice in numerous ways. Scant empirical evidence exists (e.g. Christ et al., 2021; Appelbaum and Nehmer, 2017) addressing the use of digital technologies for inventory audits because of the novelty of these technologies and the difficulties in accessing them (Austin et al., 2021). This study focuses on the recent phenomenon accelerated by the pandemic, which provided a natural experimental setting (e.g. Altiero et al., 2024; Barr-Pulliam and Carlson, 2024) to examine whether less advanced technologies can serve as an alternative approach to collecting audit evidence. It contributes empirical evidence concerning the effectiveness, reliability, and challenges associated with less advanced technologies, as well as factors affecting their non-adoption, filling a gap in research that has predominantly focused on advanced technologies. These findings are especially relevant for cost-conscious audit firms—particularly smaller firms impeded by the cost of adopting advanced technologies—who may be interested in using less advanced technologies in the audit process. However, to benefit effectively from these technologies, audit firms must thoroughly address their limitations or use them in combination with other audit evidence-gathering procedures. The study also provides empirical insights into how audit procedures were adapted in response to restrictions imposed by the pandemic, illustrating how technology was leveraged to establish a virtual audit room that accelerated audit evidence collection and client communication. It highlights ad hoc improvisations made in using technology as an alternative approach for performing specific audit procedures, such as inventory audits, and identifies the challenges, factors contributing to their nonuse, their potential staying power, and the need for explicit regulatory guidance and standards. The empirical evidence presented in this study has the potential to inform and shape the adoption of less advanced technologies in performing audit processes. Furthermore, the findings add to the growing body of literature underscoring the potential of technologies, even less sophisticated ones, to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of audits. Our findings have several practical implications for auditors. First, the findings suggest that audit firms should adopt emerging technologies that could potentially enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of inventory audits and audit quality (Christ et al., 2021; Appelbaum and Nehmer, 2017). Second, this study joins prior research in underscoring that auditors should obtain the relevant skills to use these technologies. Finally, the study may also benefit technology developers by highlighting specific concerns, including reliability and internal control issues, and emphasizing that generic technologies may not meet audit firms’ unique needs. Addressing these concerns is crucial for developing audit-specific technologies that can enhance audit efficiency and effectiveness. Collectively, these changes align with the crucial socio-technical expectations of the digital economy, incorporating technology, actors (audit firms, audit regulators, and auditors), and audit tasks/structures (e.g. Reid and Castka, 2023). Our findings have significant regulatory implications and are relevant to audit standards setters and regulators. The study underscores the need for clear standards and guidelines on using technologies to perform audits. Consistent with prior findings, auditors are hesitant to adopt these technologies due to uncertain regulatory responses and concerns about being first movers (e.g. Austin et al., 2021; Christ et al., 2021). Our findings suggest that audit regulators should expedite the process of crafting standards for collecting audit evidence using digital technology. Audit standard setters and regulators should develop standards or, at a minimum, provide explicit guidance on using these technologies in auditing. For instance, regulators might guide auditors on the extent to which these technologies can be used to conduct audits. Such regulatory guidance could mitigate the slow adoption of technologies in audits. The findings of this study provide numerous avenues for future research. Future studies could explore how adopting less advanced technologies affects the nature, timing, and extent of inventory audit procedures, as well as how auditors’ potential biases influence technology adoption. From an institutional perspective, it would be valuable to investigate whether the use of these technologies in audits are symbolic or ceremonial (e.g. checking boxes) or whether they are rigorously and effectively implemented. Additionally, comparative analyses could evaluate the efficacy and efficiency of traditional physical inventory audits versus digital inventory audits. Long-term impact assessments could examine the effects of audit digitization on audit quality, efficiency, and cost implications over time. Further research could also explore ethical concerns, particularly related to data privacy and security, and investigate cross-cultural differences in the use of digital technologies across diverse regulatory frameworks and cultural contexts. I thank the editor and reviewer(s) for their time and insightful feedback. I am deeply grateful for the invaluable assistance and suggestions provided by Johan Lorentzon throughout the data collection and analysis phases. I also appreciate helpful insights from Bertrand Malsch, Tatenda Mugwira, Aasmund Eilifsen, and the three reviewers of the Hawaii Accounting Research Conference (HARC) in 2023 and 2024.

column1: Disclosing transparency: A review of B2B marketing and supply chain research
column2: This study investigates the relationships within information transparency in business-to-business (B2B) marketing and supply chain management, focusing on the interplay between transparency, trust, and credibility among supply chain (SC) actors and customers. Drawing from a cross-industry literature review, it synthesizes previous studies and utilizes contingency coefficients to explore the connections among various transparency constructs and their associated elements. Derived normative indications for innovation and regulation are informed by empirical findings. While emphasizing B2B marketing and SC literature, study emphasizes the significance of downstream transparency for customers and direct vertical transparency distribution in trust-building efforts. Notably, clear and accessible information regarding product, price, cost, and process is found to enhance transparency, subsequently influencing perceptions and attitudes. However, these transparency components alone are insufficient to address customer trust, innovation, and regulatory oversight. A key contribution lies in comprehensive analysis of transparency, encompassing all elements from established conceptual frameworks, and identifying associations across them. The application of empirical ethics to derive normative indications adds a novel dimension to the research. The findings explicate how information access impacts trust, innovation, and regulatory processes. Additionally, this research provides valuable guidance for policymakers and interest groups in evaluating transparency legislation holistically and within specific contexts. • Comprehensive review of transparency in recent B2B and supply chain literature. • Comparison of the conceptual transparency frameworks of Granados et al. (2010) with Hultman & Axelsson (2007) . • Contingency analysis of transparency components and directions in scholarly research. • Transparency components framed in empirically informed ethics.
column3: 6 Conclusion, limitations, and further research The research aims of this study address two primary inquiries: the interactions of information transparency elements in B2B marketing and supply-chain relations' intricate dynamics, and how empirical research can aid in forming an ethics of transparency. The study offers insights on the present transparency levels in B2B interactions and suggest ways to improve transparency in the future using ethical and empirical frameworks. The research substantially contributes by clarifying the intricate connections of information transparency elements in B2B marketing and supply-chain relationships and promoting ethical transparency through practical research. Results provide a detailed understanding of how transparency operates in different business environments by examining important structural components like competencies, normative frameworks, and context and showing how they impact transparency dynamics. Moreover, it links the idea of transparency to the ethical structure of moral responsibility, indicating that being transparent necessitates a base of moral values, abilities, and situational understanding. Results also indicate practical suggestions for future studies, stressing the need for real-life data to improve ethical frameworks and create transparency plans that can be implemented. By adopting a thorough strategy, the research not only advances the academic discussion on transparency but also provides useful recommendations for companies looking to incorporate moral transparent measures in B2B transactions. This study shows the complexity of the web of information transparency in marketing and supply-chain management. Just as empirically informed ethics seeks to determine what moral agency is and how it works, our research shows the importance of transparency in building trust and trustworthiness, enriching the discourse beyond the contemporary, technology-driven discussion in B2B marketing (e.g., Falkenreck & Wagner, 2017 , Falkenreck and Wagner, 2022 ; Lacka et al., 2020 ; Paparoidamis et al., 2019 ). Transparency cultivates a culture of openness and responsibility, aligning with the idea that moral actions depend on their context. Just as moral agency appears on different spatial and temporal scales, our study shows that transparency is multifaceted and has diverse effects on different business contexts. As moral agents, both B2B vendors and buyers can improve their supply-chain performance by enhancing transparency's degree (increasing) and direction (unidirectional) and making its actions (disclose) and elements (process) more open. As moral agents need skills, clear processes are needed for openness on both sides (buyer and seller). In moral agency, the idea of an ethical reference frame resembles the importance of clear process information. The fact that both moral agency and transparency are affected by context shows the importance of finding a balance between practical efficiency, legal compliance, and mutual well-being. Because moral agency differs with respect to its facets, our work pushes transparency into many diverse domains covered by Granados et al.'s (2010) and Hultman and Axelsson's (2007) frameworks. It has different effects on immediate actions, deliberations, organizational growth, and even social change, just as moral events can be grouped by space and time. Our results are important for a wide range of stakeholders or actors in various roles in B2B marketing and supply chains, just as moral freedom and transparency are important for a broad range of people. In the ever-changing world of modern business, just as moral agency involves groups of people working together, transparency is pushed by interest groups that support it. So, just as moral agency comes from many fields, so does our study, bringing together scholars, practitioners, politicians, and pressure groups. To exploit the potential of transparency, businesses involved in the effort must work together to improve strategies, because moral agency requires skills. Just as moral beings need a normative frame, companies need data tools to understand how customers act. Because the parts of moral agency are all connected, it is important to consider transparency policies as a whole contributing to openness. In the evolving history of business ethics, moral agency is based on interactions and circumstances, and transparency grows when people work together. Just as moral theory, psychology, and character are all connected, so are marketing, supply-chain management, and ethical concerns. Both logical perspectives agree that we need to look at the effects of openness in both space and time. We believe our results, by shedding light on the relevance of transparency, add novel elements for developing empirically informed B2B marketing ethics. Just as moral agency calls for the study of competencies, normative frames, and context, transparency calls for strategic application, legislation that takes context into account, and joint efforts. By aligning with the above, our study indicates how to get to a place where transparency is valued, where stakeholders' voices are heard, and where trust is built. In conclusion, this study's proposed conceptual framework illuminates the intricate dynamics of transparency in B2B marketing and supply chains, drawing parallels with the structural components of moral agency. The interplay of key elements, including supplier , vertical , complementary strategies , disclose , systems and mechanism design , process , and increasing , forms a complex landscape that demands a comprehensive understanding from a moral and ethical philosophical stance. Examining the structural components of moral agency — ‘competencies’, ‘normative frame’, and ‘context’—provides valuable insights into their nuanced interactions and significance. The concept of competencies highlights the diverse skills needed for success in B2B marketing and supply chains and the need for multiple abilities to navigate this intricate landscape successfully. While process does involve adherence to ethical principles (normative frame) and is influenced by the broader context of interactions and external factors (context), it primarily belongs within the competencies component due to the multifaceted practical skills required to effectively handle and manage organizational processes. The normative frame, aligned with ethical principles, becomes evident in practices such as disclose , emphasizing honesty and openness, and systems and mechanism design , focusing on ethical infrastructures for transparency and accountability. The directional factor in increasing emphasizes a commitment to ethical behavior, illustrating its integral role in the normative frame of moral agency. The resonances between the items in B2B marketing and supply chains and the normative frame underscore the role of standards and goals in guiding decision-making. Much as with moral agents, decisions within these domains are shaped by desired outcomes and benchmarks, emphasizing the importance of establishing clear reference points and objectives. The concept of context holds profound implications in both moral agency and B2B dynamics. Just as moral agency's behavior is linked with its context, the relationships among items such as supplier and vertical are influenced by external factors and interactions. Recognizing the significance of context within B2B dynamics reflects the understanding that behavior is intertwined with external conditions and stakeholder interactions. In spirit, this study not only unveils the complex dynamics of transparency in B2B marketing and supply chains but also establishes a connection to the foundational principles of moral agency. It emphasizes the importance of competencies, ethical principles, and contextual considerations in navigating this intricate landscape, offering valuable insights for practitioners and scholars alike. 6.1 Limitations This research has several limitations. First, it focuses on a specific set of structural components (competencies, normative frames, and context) within B2B marketing and supply chains. Future research could expand on this work by incorporating real-life data to further improve ethical frameworks and create transparency plans that can be implemented. Additionally, while the study has aimed at establishing a connection between transparency and moral agency, more empirical research is needed to test these conceptual linkages across different B2B settings.

column1: The Value of Being Greener: Untangling the Relationship between Environmental Investment and Firms' Access to Trade Credit
column2: This study investigates the relationship between corporate environmental performance, as captured by environmental investment, and firms’ access to trade credit. Using data from Chinese listed firms in heavy pollution industries, we find that corporate environmental performance significantly increases firms’ access to trade credit. The positive effect of environmental investment appears more pronounced for firms with stronger internal incentives to conduct eco‐friendly practices, lower external regulatory pressure and located in regions with higher economic growth rates. Two factors – namely, increased information transparency and reduced exposure to environmental risk – are found to be channels through which environmental investment affects trade credit. This paper provides a nuanced understanding of how a supplier as a stakeholder plays a significant role in financing environmental sustainability. The results are robust to alternative proxies, model specifications, sample compositions and endogeneity concerns.
column3:
This paper investigates the relationship between corporate environmental performance and firms’ access to trade credit and the channels through which environmental investment influences firms’ access to trade credit in China. Whilst environmental investment and how to finance it has provoked an extensive public debate, little systematic research has been carried out on whether and how environmental investment influences access to trade credit. This paper therefore contributes to the environmental sustainability literature by showing how a firm's environmental performance influences its access to trade credit, suggesting that the customer–supplier relationship provides an important means for financing a firm's environmental investment.

The results of this study have significant implications for firm managers, regulators and policymakers. First, the positive relationship between environmental investment and trade credit calls into question the notion that trade credit only serves as short-term finance to meet working capital needs. Our results demonstrate to managers that trade credit can also be used to meet the grand challenges associated with financing environmental sustainability. Consequently, firms should endeavour to engage suppliers and use trade credits provided by suppliers in their sustainability practices. Second, the results show that increased information transparency and reduced firms’ exposure to environmental litigation risk are important channels through which investment performance affects trade credit, implying that managers should pay attention to these factors in their quest to finance environmental sustainability.

Given that a firm's performance depends crucially on its relationship with stakeholders (Freeman, 1984), the study provides insights for firm managers to improve their supplier–customer relationships. Thus, our results imply that information transparency and stakeholder engagement matter for a firm's access to trade credit as informal finance for environmental investment. The result that corporate gender diversity positively moderates the relationship between environmental investment and access to trade credit calls for greater gender diversity in business; firms should be encouraged to recruit more female leaders. Finally, the study provides additional insights for regulators and policymakers about the costs of tighter environmental regulation.

Despite the interesting and significant findings of this study, it is important to point out that the study focuses only on a single country's data, that is, China, limiting its generalizability to countries that have different institutional environments and legal enforcement mechanisms. We suggest that future research could explore the relationship between environmental investment and informal sources of finance using cross-country data.
