In this study, we build an analytical framework to find the optimal strategies for the token‐based and non‐token‐based blockchain (as a special application scenario) platforms and derive the essential model properties and characteristics. We analytically show how the optimal mining bonus depends on the fraction of reserved tokens sold to customers and on the price‐to‐sales ratio. Furthermore, we obtain several actionable findings for choosing suitable platform types under different scenarios. The shift from the non‐token‐based platform to the token‐based platform may yield greater social welfare unless the non‐token‐based system operates with a much larger ride price, which we show to be unrealistic for the considered Beijing case through numerical studies. Moreover, we find that the matching probability for the token‐based platform is predominantly higher than that for the non‐token‐based one. Besides, government interventions may encourage a path toward a fair consensus mechanism or a high decentralization level in order to enhance social welfare. One unanticipated finding is that a higher decentralization level may lead to a lower mining capacity shortage and so to a more efficient system, indicating that the combination of blockchain and the sharing economy has much potential.
column3: Motivated by the increasing popularity of blockchain platforms, we study both the token-based and nontoken-based versions, where the former becoming more mainstream in recent years and the latter offers an alternative solution, especially in countries with cryptocurrency bans. Specifically, we explore the way to set optimal mining bonuses to ensure user involvement and contribution to the community, considering the effects of mining on the platform's profit. Our framework incorporates users’ usage level heterogeneity in the ride-hailing market and captures the changing market conditions and business characteristics. We also analyze the effects of platform decisions on users’ asset purchase and sharing decisions in the peer-to-peer market and the associated social welfare of both types of blockchain platforms. For the more popular adoption of the token-based platform, we specify the industry and blockchain technology features that are more profitable for its development. Our findings help practitioners in terms of optimally setting the mining bonus, consensus mechanism design, and choosing the industry to work in for blockchain platforms.To answer the question of whether the token-based or nontoken-based platform (traditional platforms adopt blockchain technology without changing their earnings model) should be developed, which is one of the main concerns of both platforms and governments regarding blockchain adoption, we compare the outcomes in terms of platform profit, social welfare, matching efficiency, and decentralization level to capture the effects of tokenization. After analytically characterizing the conditions under which the token-based/nontoken-based platform generates higher social welfare, we further conduct extensive numerical studies based on the Beijing market to test the analytical framework. The results suggest that the token-based platform is more profitable for that market.Somewhat unexpectedly, our numerical results suggest that applying blockchain in a peer-to-peer market is a possible solution for the current dilemma of efficiency versus fairness. We observe that as the minimum required mining time per transaction increases, implying an increase in the decentralization level and thereby the fairness of the blockchain, the mining capacity shortage of both systems is mitigated, that is, the efficiency of the blockchain operation increases. This indicates that the combination of blockchain and the sharing economy has much potential. Moreover, we provide practical and actional guidelines accordingly to improve the social benefit of the system by influencing the blockchain's decentralization level, ride price, and mining system design.We next discuss further limitations of our research that provide interesting avenues for future research. First, our modeling framework is static and we consider the operator's equilibrium optimization. One future research direction is to explore dynamic decisions considering short-term supply and demand fluctuations affected by, for example, real-time traffic conditions, locations, time of a day, etc. Second, one could consider user behavior in more detail, for example, cancellation behavior related to the availability of alternatives such as underground transport, buses, bicycles, etc. Third, our analysis is deterministic, for example, we consider an expected mining time, but in real life the mining time is random, which may depend on the processing speed, memory scalability, information processing costs, data pool liquidity, and privacy level. One could consider a random mining process by optimizing the block size, privacy setting, etc. Besides, we ignore the risk of contingencies on the blockchain, for example, community members may vote for changes on the platform. One could explore the related coordination cost and its impacts on the protocol or smart contract, and so on the platform's profit. Fourth, we consider an expected mining bonus for all the miners; however, in real life, there are other incentive mechanisms to encourage users’ mining behavior. For instance, the sequence/speed of mining may affect the miner's bonus. Some platforms only offer a bonus to the first miner that finishes the calculation. Fifth, we consider that the nontoken-based platform charges the driver a fixed proportion of the ride price as commission. One could develop new business models for blockchain-based platforms, for example, charging the customer (as well). It is certainly worth comparing and contrasting different incentive mechanisms.

column1: Mainstreaming Versus Fairwashing in Fair Trade Operations
column2: This study explores the effects of competition on fair trade operations. Specifically, as a benchmark, we first consider a model with a single fair trade organization (FTO), that is, a monopoly FTO. We then extend the analysis to a setting with two competing FTOs, that is, duopoly FTOs. Although both FTOs share the common goal of alleviating farmers’ poverty, they adopt contrasting strategies: One FTO seeks to lower the barriers to fair trade, aiming to mainstream it, while the other maintains stricter standards to prevent fairwashing (or greenwashing). Following industry practices, we implement two modes of competition and compare them with the monopoly benchmark. We find that, while competition between FTOs increases the aggregate demand for fair trade certified products (mainstreaming), it results in less aggregate premium (fairwashing). Furthermore, we consider the potential application of blockchain technology in fair trade operations and demonstrate that it offers a promising solution to mitigate the fairwashing effects from competition between FTOs.
column3:
8. Discussion
This study examines the effects of competition between FTOs. The key implications of our findings are summarized as follows. First, Proposition 4 illustrates whether competition yields greater aggregate demand or greater aggregate premium; that is, whether it leads to mainstreaming or fairwashing. Particularly, in the multi-ingredient market, competition leads to mainstreaming but also causes fairwashing. In other words, the split between the two FTOs led to higher aggregate demand but lower aggregate premiums.
Our theoretical findings are consistent with real-world observations. Following the separation of Fairtrade America and Fair Trade USA, fair trade product sales surged, indicating mainstreaming. For instance, Fairtrade International recorded approximately one billion EUR in estimated sales of fair trade products in the U.S. market just before the 2011 split (FTI, 2013). By 2016, the estimated sales of products labeled by Fair Trade USA and Fairtrade America had grown to approximately six billion USD and one billion USD, respectively (Cooper, 2017).
At the same time, evidence suggests that competition also led to fairwashing, particularly in the multi-ingredient market. Under Fairtrade International, a multi-ingredient product previously had to contain not only 20% fair trade certified ingredients by weight but also use fair trade certified ingredients as much as possible (“All That Can Be”). However, beginning around 2013, Fair Trade USA allowed products with just over 20% fair trade certified content to carry the fair trade label, without requiring the “All That Can Be” standard (Lindgren, 2013) to be met. In 2018, Fairtrade International similarly relaxed its standards, launching the “Fairtrade Sourced Ingredient Mark (FSI)” (FTI, 2025b). Thus, both organizations lowered fair trade standards in terms of the minimum fraction over time.
More recently, the trend appears to be shifting. In March 2023, Fairtrade International announced an increase in the minimum price for coffee beans to better protect farmers from climate change and global economic volatility (FTI, 2023). In contrast, Fair Trade USA declined to adopt this change, citing concerns about a potential reduction in demand (FTUSA, 2023). Motivated by this divergence, we analyzed a new competition model where FTOs set different unit premiums. Similar to the minimum fraction competition model, the unit premium competition model results in mainstreaming accompanied by fairwashing, especially in the multi-ingredient market.
We attempt to mitigate the fairwashing resulting from competition by introducing blockchain technology as a novel solution. Proposition 5 shows that blockchain is especially effective under competition, as greater demand consistently accompany greater donations. Furthermore, Proposition 6 characterizes the conditions under which the aggregate benefit, which combines aggregate premium and donation (
), is greater. We find that maximizing farmer welfare under competition between FTOs requires not only a higher average consumer donation rate (
) but also lower thresholds 
, which decrease as the relative fair trade value (
) increases.
Finally, we acknowledge several limitations of this study and propose directions for future research. Our model relies on the disparity in fair trade information between consumers and firms, where consumers do not differentiate between the two labels or assess the premium amount in fair trade products. While our model reflects real-world consumer behavior, exploring a vertical differentiation model based on perfect information could offer valuable avenues for future research. Another promising direction would be to allow FTOs to make their decisions simultaneously, instead of sequentially as currently assumed. In addition, following Lim et al. (2019), our model does not endogenize decisions on regular products. Instead, we focus on fair trade operations and the competition between FTOs by simplifying the firm’s decision on regular (or noncertified) products using the term 
. However, endogenizing both decisions on regular products and fair trade products would be highly effective in completing the fair trade model. Furthermore, the objective function of FTOs in our model implies the interest of a focal FTO only. Since an FTO is also an NPO, it could be driven by not only its own interest but also those of others or competitors. Since both FTOs embody their philosophies into their premiums and have contrasting philosophies (e.g., “Smallholders vs. Large Plantations”), we assume that both FTOs are trying to maximize their total premiums. However, future models could incorporate the weighted average type of the objective function, such as the weighted sums of the total premium, total demand, or unit premium.
We also highlight the potential application of blockchain in the fair trade movement, where consumers donate to farmers through the blockchain. In this regard, it would be useful for future research to explore how to increase the amount of donations, such as utilizing the nudge. Additionally, while not addressed in this paper, there is a debate about fairwashing in volume. For example, when a firm sells only a small portion of fair trade certified products, consumers may have the impression that most of the firm’s products are fair trade certified (Jaffee, 2014: p. 200). We did not address this issue because both Fair Trade USA and Fairtrade America do not require a minimum volume commitment (Jaffee and Howard, 2016). Notwithstanding, it would be a fruitful direction for future research to incorporate these standards in the model. In addition, future research could endogenize the firm’s degree of perceived value of the fair trade label(
) in the model. Lastly, we explore fair trade operations using a stylized model. While we provide a number of implications regarding the competition between FTOs and fair trade operations, exploring this issue using an empirical model would also be meaningful for future research.

column1: Exact Nash-like solutions of blockchain gap games
column2: This note challenges the belief that mining processes are too complex for traditional game-theoretic analysis. We provide Nash-like equilibrium solutions for two-player gap games, focusing on the strategic delay of mining rig activation in Bitcoin’s Proof-of-Work (PoW) system. By delaying activation, miners can optimize profits, particularly as transaction fees become a more significant portion of their revenues (Carlsten et al., 2016). Building on the game-theoretic model of Tsabary and Eyal (2018), we offer a rigorous, proof-based analysis of this behavior, highlighting the importance of verifying simulation results through precise mathematical methods. The primary technical contribution of this note is a novel method for deriving closed-form equilibrium solutions for potentially non-differentiable ex-ante expected payoff functions Ui , defined as integrals in which the integrands—representing profit at time t —depend discontinuously on miners’ rig start times s .
column3: 4 Conclusion Although Tsabary and Eyal (2018) provided a complete symbolic description of gap games, their equilibrium analysis primarily relied on numerical and simulation methods due to the complexity of expected payoff functions. We simplified this by assuming each miner controls a single mining rig with equal computational power, differing from their assumption of multiple identical rigs. This assumption facilitated the calculation of the probability distribution function p B ( s, μ, t ) for the global block-finding time B in Section 2 , under the typical assumption that miners mine blocks as Bernoulli trials and that the time required for a successful result by each miner is a mutually independent random variable. We consider a gap game as a family of games parameterized by the rate μ , applying Nash equilibrium concepts to each game within this family. We identified a suitable notion of equilibrium as a Nash equilibrium denoted s ( μ ), subject to the condition BTI = E [ μ , s ( μ ) ; B ] . By defining a mapping Φ( μ, s ) and the Nash equilibrium mapping Nash ( μ ) = ( μ , s ( μ ) ) , we characterized the equilibrium of a gap game in Section 3 as a fixed point μ * = Φ ∘ Nash ( μ * ) , given that it is well-defined. In practical cases, Φ ∘ Nash behaves well within a suitably chosen domain Δ ⊂ (0, ∞). Focusing on two-miner gap games with transaction fees, we derived conditions for non-symmetric gap equilibria, presenting two examples satisfying s 1 * > s 2 * . Remark 3 indicates that our proof-based analysis for heterogeneous miners demonstrates that known simulation results obtained for homogeneous miners may not apply, suggesting that high subsidies do not necessarily reduce mining gaps among heterogeneous miners. In Section 3.2, we examined gap games with homogeneous miners, proving that if s * is a symmetric Nash equilibrium for either U i + or U i − , it is also a symmetric Nash equilibrium for the original game with U i , providing a novel method to derive the Nash equilibrium s * for possibly non-differentiable U i . Our results align generally with Tsabary and Eyal’s observations, except in low operational cost scenarios. We proved that gaps can exist at equilibrium even with c o p = 0 , counter to simulation results, and established a condition for a no-gap equilibrium when the total mining cost is small or the subsidy is sufficiently high. Remark 7 discusses measuring the degradation of the system’s total mining power due to gap formation. While numerical methods currently dominate the literature, our proof-based game-theoretic analysis establishes equilibrium conditions across different reward and cost structures, with plans to extend this to more players in future research.

column1: Regulation, Corruption, and Decentralized Autonomous Organizations: Insights from Bitcoin Trading and Platform Founding Between 2011 and 2023
column2: Decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) represent a novel organizational form enabling self-governed coordination based on blockchain technology. This study examines the prototypical Bitcoin DAO from an institutional perspective, focusing on how its core features—decentralization and autonomy—interact with the broader institutional framework in which it operates. Specifically, we study how regulative institutional environments (i.e., (il)legalization) shape the growth and development of DAOs while theorizing about the role of both petty and grand corruption (i.e., by higher-level officials) in influencing the effectiveness of these regulative institutions. Our empirical analysis focuses on the global rise of Bitcoin trading and platform establishment across 49 national contexts from 2011 to 2023. Utilizing a unique data set, we find that, although the number of Bitcoin exchange platforms in a country is positively associated with Bitcoin legalization, Bitcoin trading volume is positively associated with Bitcoin illegalization. In countries with higher levels of grand corruption, Bitcoin illegalization becomes even more strongly associated with trading. In contrast, grand corruption dampens the positive association between legalization and the number of Bitcoin exchange platforms. Further, the presence of petty corruption reduces the impact of grand corruption. Our study reveals that it is critical to distinguish between petty and grand corruption as an important factor that influences the interplay between the regulative environment and growth and development of the Bitcoin DAO and the related ecosystem of Bitcoin trading and platform founding.
column3: In conclusion, this study underscores the intricate relationship between the institutional environment and the development of DAOs, exemplified by Bitcoin. Our findings suggest that regulatory activities, such as legalization or illegalization, significantly influence Bitcoin’s expansion—through trading volume and the number of exchange platforms—depending on national contexts. Importantly, we demonstrate that both grand and petty corruption play a moderating role, amplifying or dampening the effects of these regulatory environments. Together, these insights highlight how the nuanced interplay of regulative frameworks and corruption shapes the trajectory of DAOs, offering essential considerations for policymakers, particularly as blockchain-based organizations continue to develop within diverse and dynamic institutional landscapes.

column1: Truth, trust, and trade-offs: When blockchain in supply chains backfires
column2: • Analyzing a newsvendor supply chain under a setting of information asymmetry • Comparing two options for information sharing: blockchain vs. commitment contract • Demonstrating that blockchain eliminates information risk • Commitment contracts can eliminate information risk and reduce demand risk • Characterizing when the supply chain may be better off without blockchain We study the role of blockchain in achieving information transparency and generating trust in a dyadic supply chain with one retailer sourcing from a single supplier. The retailer has superior information regarding the demand distribution, whereas the supplier sets the capacity in preparation for the selling season. Two sources of risk are identified: information risk, which captures the incentives of the retailer to portray a favorable market condition to the supplier to encourage the supplier to secure an ample capacity, and demand risk, which captures the potential for lost sales or excess capacity investment, even when knowing the correct demand distribution. We demonstrate how blockchain eliminates information risk for the supplier. As an alternative to blockchain, we analyze a commitment contract where the retailer can order in advance a certain number of units; this commitment can serve as a signaling tool to convey market information to the supplier. We argue that the commitment contract can eliminate the information risk for the supplier (as can blockchain), but it can also reduce the supplier’s demand risk. We conclude that in many instances, the supplier and the supply chain can become worse off when blockchain is used, while the retailer favors this technology.
column3: 7 Concluding remarks Blockchain is a decentralized, secure digital ledger that allows for transparent and immutable record-keeping of transactions. Blockchain technology can be found in applications in the fields of financial services, supply-chain management, healthcare, voting systems, and more. Its decentralized nature and cryptographic security make it a valuable tool for promoting transparency and trust in various transactions, leading to increased accountability. In this work, we focus on understanding the value of implementing blockchain in a newsvendor supply chain, where the retailer has superior forecasting capabilities and the supplier secures capacity prior to the selling season. In this setting, the challenge is centered around the question of how to share forecast information in a credible manner. Two main mechanisms are analyzed. In the first, blockchain is used and the supplier understands that the information provided is trustworthy; thus, blockchain eliminates the information risk for the supplier, namely, the risk of building capacity that is not in accordance with the realized demand distribution. In the second option, no blockchain is used and two possible solutions emerge: in the first (the separating equilibrium), the retailer uses the mechanism of commitment in order to signal the market state, whereas in the alternative option (the pooling equilibrium), no information is revealed to the supplier, who acts according to his prior knowledge. We demonstrate that when the alternative would be that the separating equilibrium is played, the supplier prefers this option over the use of blockchain technology. This is because the supplier correctly infers the realized demand distribution irrespective of whether blockchain is used, but when the separating equilibrium is played, the committed order also reduces the demand risk for the supplier. Furthermore, in some cases, the signaling cost for the retailer is so high that she chooses to order more than the minimum required separating quantity, effectively financing the entire capacity built by the supplier. In this case, it is not only the supplier that prefers the separating equilibrium, but the performance of the channel improves as well. In contrast with the supplier, the retailer (weakly) prefers to adopt blockchain technology in the case where, absent blockchain, a separating equilibrium would be played. This is because blockchain technology reduces the retailer’s signaling costs. Interestingly, we show that there are cases in which the supplier would even prefer to pay the retailer not to install blockchain technology. When the alternative to implementing blockchain is a pooling equilibrium, the choice of the supply-chain parties regarding whether to adopt this technology hinges on additional factors, including the prior belief that market demand is high and whether the demand distribution exhibits an IFR (or DFR) property. If the demand distribution is IFR, both parties favor blockchain implementation. However, when the demand distribution is DFR, the supplier prefers blockchain implementation, while the retailer benefits more from foregoing this technology. Our work offers significant managerial insights by providing guidance to supply-chain parties on whether to invest in blockchain implementation by identifying which party stands to benefit from it. Additionally, our findings shed light on concerns recently raised by industry leaders and scholars about the slower-than-expected adoption of blockchain technology. Specifically, we demonstrate that in many cases, one party in the supply chain may choose not to adopt blockchain, as it derives greater benefit from the alternative of a commitment contract. Moreover, we show that, in certain scenarios, the overall performance of the supply chain can be improved when blockchain technology is not implemented.

column1: The economics of resale royalties: Evidence from non-fungible tokens
column2: By constructing a comprehensive dataset of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) transactions, we investigate the impacts of resale royalties on the trading characteristics of market participants in the NFT platform. Our results show that one standard deviation increase in the royalty rate significantly correlates with a 7.04% decrease in market prices and a 4.8% decrease in the resale probability of NFTs. We also find that royalties have a greater impact on tokens with higher rarity during the NFT market boom. We deepen our analysis by incorporating several channels of the NFT royalty effects. Our analysis reveals that NFTs-enforced royalties have worse investment performance compared to royalty-free tokens. NFT investors attach less price premium to NFTs with royalties, since the information for the market value of NFTs is more symmetric when incurring royalty payments. Additionally, royalty tokens are less likely to be traded by speculative investors on the NFT platform. Our findings are robust across different estimation methods and transaction samples.
column3: 7 Conclusion In this paper, we investigate the relationship between resale royalties and trading patterns of investors in the non-fungible tokens platform. After constructing a comprehensive NFT sale transaction dataset, we adopt a two-stage least-squares regression to derive more exogenously-given proxies of NFT royalties. In the first stage, We utilize the implementation of lazying minting in OpenSea marketplace as the instrument variable to capture the variations of royalties driven by the upfront minting costs. By controlling a wide range of inherent attributes of individual tokens, we employ the hedonic regression model in the second stage regression to examine the impacts of the instrumented royalties on the trading patterns of NFT investors in the marketplace. Our results show that one standard deviation increase in the NFT royalty rate can significantly be translated into average 7.04% and 4.8% decreases in the secondary sale price and resale probabilities of NFTs respectively. We then explore the variations of the royalty effects across individual tokens. We find that high-value tokens command are more likely to be sold in comparison to the low-value ones when enforced royalty payment. Resale royalty may prevent the adverse selection of low-value tokens and boost the secondary transactions of high-value products. We further find that the effects of NFT royalties exert larger economic magnitudes during the boom period of NFT secondary market, i.e., NFT royalties can push back both volumes and prices to fundamentals during the time period of disproportional surge in NFT trading volume. To deepen our investigation of NFT royalty effects, we incorporate three channels through which resale royalties could affect the trading behaviors of NFT investors. First, we calculate the realized return of each NFT sale pair and find that investment in royalty-free NFTs is more profitable than tokens embedded royalty payment in the secondary marketplace. Second, we calculate the price-to-value ratio by scaling the NFT market sale price by its rarity proxies as the dependent variable. We find that market participants attach less price premium relative to the rarity value for NFTs embedded royalties, given that the information for the market value of NFTs is more symmetric to investors incurring royalty payments. Finally, we show that one standard deviation increase in the royalty rate significantly predicts 3.1% decrease in the probabilities of individual tokens being traded by speculative investors in the marketplace. The trading patterns of NFT speculators may serve as an explanation for the NFT royalty effects we identified in the baseline regressions. The results of this study are best explained through transaction cost theory ( Ghoshal & Moran, 1996 ) and information asymmetry theory ( Akerlof, 1978; Back, 1993; Kim, 1985 ). From the transaction cost perspective, resale royalties add an additional cost, which reduces the attractiveness of NFTs to buyers and decreases both prices and resale probabilities. At the same time, information asymmetry theory suggests that royalties act as a signaling mechanism, reducing price distortions in high-value tokens. However, they also create more symmetric information, making speculative trading less profitable and thereby reducing market activity. These findings emphasize the trade-off between incentivizing creators and the negative impact of royalties on market dynamics. This paper adds knowledge to the price formation process of non-fungible tokens and trading patterns of NFT investors by revealing the role of resale royalties in the NFT marketplace. Our findings show that the sale prices and market liquidities of NFTs are both adversely affected by the implementation of resale royalties. The utilities of NFT market participants investing in NFTs configured royalties decrease both pecuniarily and non-pecuniarily, drawn from the observations that royaltied NFTs generate worse investment performances and undifferentiated emotional dividends in comparison to royalty-free tokens. However, the negative impacts of NFT royalties are also driven by the symmetric information of NFT inherent value and lower volume of washing tradings in the secondary exchanges. Our results provide practical implications for NFT collections and marketplaces in optimizing their royalty decision to accommodate the diverse demands and trading patterns of NFT market participants, also, for NFT investors to fully utilize NFT royalties when assessing the market value of NFTs. This study has important theoretical, practical, and policy implications. Theoretically, it extends our understanding of how transaction costs, like resale royalties, influence market behavior and efficiency, especially in the context of informational asymmetries and speculative behavior. Practically, NFT creators should carefully balance royalty rates to avoid negative impacts on market liquidity and resale prices, while investors should factor in higher transaction costs when making investment decisions. From a policy perspective, clearer regulations on resale royalties are needed to prevent them from hindering market liquidity or creating barriers for investors. Policymakers should promote transparency and consider mechanisms to prevent excessive royalty rates that could undermine market efficiency.

column1: No trade under verifiable information
column2: No trade theorems examine conditions under which agents cannot agree to disagree on the value of a security which pays according to some state of nature, thus preventing any mutual agreement to trade. A large literature has examined conditions which imply no trade, such as relaxing the common prior and common knowledge assumptions, as well as allowing for agents who are boundedly rational or ambiguity averse. We contribute to this literature by examining conditions on the private information of agents that reveals, or verifies, the true value of the security. We argue that these conditions can offer insights in three different settings: insider trading, the connection of low liquidity in markets with no trade, and trading using public blockchains and oracles.
column3: 3.4 Multiple securities In the current model, only one security, X , is traded. In this section, we discuss how trading can be generalised to multiple securities, { X i } i ∈ I , one for each agent, so that ∑ i ∈ I X i = 0 . First, we fix the set of priors and show that common knowledge trade with X implies common knowledge trade with { X i } i ∈ I . Suppose, without loss of generality, that the only common knowledge event is the whole state space Ω. Then, our definition of common knowledge trade with X is that each agent i 's expected value given each of his partition cells is e i , yet e i ≠ e j for at least two agents. If e i > e j , then Agent i is willing to buy the security from Agent j at some intermediate price e i > p > e j . We can model this trade by having two new securities, X i = X − p and X j = − X + p , where p is the security that pays p at all states, so we have X i + X j = 0 . Both agents have strictly positive expected value from their respective securities, and this trade is feasible because the two securities add up to 0 at all states. The two approaches are complementary. We can view X as the ‘fundamental’ asset which pays according to the state (e.g. the value of the oil well), whereas securities X i , X j denote the actual trade that has been agreed. With n agents, where n is even, we can order e 1 > e 2 > … > e n > 0 . By setting p such that e n / 2 > p > e n / 2 + 1 , we can define X i = X − p for i ≤ n / 2 and X i = − X + p otherwise. We then have common knowledge trade with multiple securities. The converse is not necessarily true. To see this, suppose that { X i } i ∈ I satisfy common knowledge trade with multiple securities. We can define X = ∑ j ∈ I λ j X i , so we need to find λ = { λ 1 , … , λ n } such that ∑ j ∈ I λ j E p i [ X j | Π i ( ω ) ] = e i , for all ω ∈ Ω and i , j ∈ I . As there are many more equations than unknowns, the system may not have a solution. We now allow for all possible priors and extend our analysis to multiple securities. We say that a collection { X i } i ∈ I of securities is tradable if they add up to zero at all states, ∑ i ∈ I X i = 0 , so that the trade is feasible, and every Agent i 's maximum value of X i given each of his partition cells is strictly positive. If the last condition was not satisfied for some partition cell, then the expectation of X i would be negative for all priors, hence Agent i would not agree to participate in the trade. Definition 8 Securities { X i } i ∈ I are tradable if ∑ i ∈ I X i = 0 and max ω 0 ∈ Π i ( ω ) X ( ω 0 ) > 0 , for all i ∈ I and ω ∈ Ω . We say that there is common knowledge trade given a collection of tradable securities if it is common knowledge that each Agent i 's expected value of X i is e i > 0 . Definition 9 There is common knowledge trade at ω (with tradable securities { X i } i ∈ I ) if the event “agent i 's expectation of X i is e i > 0 , for all i ∈ I ” is common knowledge at ω . Note that e i in this definition denotes the expected profits of Agent i , whereas e i in the original definition denotes i 's expected value of X . Samet (1998) uses a weaker definition, which only requires that the expectations are strictly positive. He shows that there is a common prior that generates a given collection of posterior beliefs, one for each agent and his partition cells, if and only if there is no common knowledge trade with multiple securities. We extend threshold verifiability in a similar way. Definition 10 Tradable securities { X i } i ∈ I are threshold verifiable at ω if, whenever X i ( C ( ω ) ) is not constant for some i ∈ I , there exist i ∈ I and ω ′ , ω ″ ∈ C ( ω ) such that max ω 0 ∈ Π i ( ω ′ ) X i ( ω 0 ) < x < min ω 0 ∈ Π i ( ω ″ ) X i ( ω 0 ) , for some x ∈ R . We finally have the following Proposition, which is an extension of Theorem 1 . The proof is almost identical so it is omitted. 9 9 Note that we do not require that each X i pays differently across states, as in the proof of Theorem 1 . The reason is that e i = e j is allowed here, as they are the expected profits, not the agents' expected value of X . Proposition 1 Tradable securities { X i } i ∈ I are threshold verifiable at ω if and only if there is no common knowledge trade at ω, for any set of priors.

column1: Decoding blockchain data for research in marketing: New insights through an analysis of share of wallet
column2: Blockchains are often associated with anonymity and illicit activities. However, public blockchains offer an unparalleled level of transparency because they record all transactions openly. This transparency allows firms to observe in real-time and at a low cost the transactions of both their customers and competitors. This article outlines how to use the transparency of blockchain data to gain valuable insights into real-world behaviors, such as customers’ share of wallet. The empirical study uses blockchain data from the entire NFT trading market, which covers 22.7 million sales transactions from 1.3 million customers across eight competing firms, and totals to over US$500 million in fees. The study reveals that a customer’s current spending (size of wallet) is not a valid indicator of future growth potential because it has little correlation with the share of wallet or potential wallet size.
column3: 8 Summary and conclusions While blockchains have long been perceived as decentralized databases for anonymous (illicit) activities, we suggested that this perception is incorrect. We outlined how public blockchain data can be made transparent and how to use it to examine marketing phenomena such as share of wallet. In so doing, we made several contributions. We provided a comprehensive knowledge base for decoding and analyzing blockchain data. Our detailed exposition of blockchain infrastructure, transaction recording, and data decoding processes will enable researchers to access and utilize blockchain data as a rich source for empirical investigations. We examined the relationships between the four customer metrics—namely wallet size, total wallet, potential wallet, and share of wallet—across all eight firms of an entire market by using data from the Ethereum blockchain. We analyzed Non-Fungible Tokens (NFT) sales involving over 1.3 million customers and 22.7 million transactions, which generated over US$500 million in fees. This extensive data source allowed us to explore three research questions (RQs). In addressing RQ1, we found that theoretically, there are three possible combinations of correlation between size of wallet and total wallet and between size of wallet and potential wallet. Regarding RQ2, we found that a customer’s size of wallet is not a valid indicator of a customer’s growth potential in the NFT market because it fails to be a valid indicator of potential wallet (RQ2a). Similarly, size of wallet is not a valid indicator of a customer’s share of wallet (RQ2b). However, size of wallet is a valid indicator of a customer’s total wallet because estimation results indicated that an increase of US$1 in size of wallet also increases total wallet by about the same amount. This result is not too surprising as almost 60 % of customers only trade at one firm. Regarding RQ3, our analysis suggests that firms’ market positions moderate the strength of size of wallet as an indicator for the other metrics. However, the effects remain marginal. To summarize, our empirical investigation reveals that traditional assumptions about customer metrics require reconsideration in the NFT market. Specifically, we found that a customer's size of wallet is not a valid indicator of growth potential and that the firm’s market position only mildly moderates the relationships among our four customer metrics. As conclusion, our study pointed out the challenges and opportunities of utilizing blockchain data in marketing practice and research, with particular attention to how blockchain data provides the opportunity to observe and measure, individually and together, marketing success and marketing actions. Thus, while the empirical part of this study focused on a firm’s success via customers’ size of wallets, blockchain data provides further opportunities for marketing researchers.

column1: On the role of provenance in NFT trades
column2: This study explores the role of provenance in bidding behavior in a blockchain marketplace for NFTs. We analyze how the information inferred from the ownership chain of NFTs affects valuation. The products we study are a hybrid of consumption goods and collectibles, and so provenance is expected to manifest in both use value (how the item is used) and collectible value (how the item can resell) inferred from the ownership chain. We conduct our empirical analysis using a trading dataset of an online card game on OpenSea, a blockchain marketplace for NFTs. We find that provenance of NFTs passes through past owners, dating back to the first owner, largely as collectible value in our context.
column3: 6 Conclusion This work explored how provenance information about the ownership chain influences the bids for blockchain assets whose value derives from a combination of collectible and use value. We gather data on digital game cards designed as NFTs and are bought for both collecting and playing purposes. Our findings indicate that provenance information influences the perceived value of an NFT item, with previous owner characteristics shaping how bidders evaluate the current worth of an NFT. This study is the first work to demonstrate that provenance information is influential for items with use value, such as the card games examined in this study. Managerially, we posed two questions at the start of this work; namely, can platforms leverage accessible provenance information to impact trading dynamics, and can traders enhance their premiums by attaching trader identity from outside of the trading platform (such as their celebrity gamer status in our case) to their trading identity. Regarding the first managerial question, it appears that provenance information is valuable to traders and, because game cards are more likely to pass through experienced traders, the commission-driven platform is better off with accessible provenance information. Regarding the second question, we find that the trader identity outside the trading platform impacts their items’ valuations. Specifically, if traders are prominent in the game itself, they enjoy a premium on their items’ valuations. The importance of collectible value embedded in provenance increases as items increase in rarity. We find that liquidity value—indicating ease of resale--is critical and that it passes through subsequent traders all to the way from the initial owner. Thus, in designing markets with use value, it is advisable to attract and promote both traders with established trade reputations as well as gamers with established gaming reputations. The future of NFTs outside of collectibles is still uncertain. While three out of four NFT buyers indicate use value as a primary reason for buying an NFT, there have been no large-scale use value applications outside of gaming and profile pictures ( Qian, 2024 ). Experimentation into use value NFTs includes fan tokens (both fungible and non-fungible), which give sports fans access to events and perks 5 5 How Blockchain is Transforming Fan Loyalty in Sports; retrieved from https://www.protokol.com/insights/how-blockchain-is-transforming-fan-loyalty-in-sports/ . and there are other NFT products in development that promise to offer perks and rewards. 6 6 The Future of NFTs − What’s Next?; retrieved from https://www.protokol.com/insights/the-future-of-nfts-whats-next . Our research indicates that the success of such products in NFT format will largely hinge on the ability of such products to harness provenance. Looking ahead, the impact of blockchain technology in online marketplaces could generalize well beyond NFTs. There are calls and plans for Blockchain-based peer-to-peer marketplaces that would eliminate or reduce the role of traditional online intermediaries by recording transactions directly on the blockchain ( Ranganthan et al., 2018 ; Fonseca Cacho et al., 2021 ; Koscina et al., 2021; Cao, 2022 ). In parallel, blockchain technology is increasingly being used for traditional physical goods to track supply chains and ownership chains. Our provenance findings likewise extend beyond NFT markets. By showing provenance in these markets, and indicating how to identify and harness provenance, we have opened the door to employing that information in these new markets. In the traditional realm of physical goods markets, a seller's reputation has always played a pivotal role. For instance, Cabral and Hortacsu's (2010) study on reputation and feedback in online marketplaces highlights how a positive transaction history can positively influence buyers' perceptions, potentially affecting their bidding behavior. Our study adds to this body of literature by providing empirical evidence of the effects of provenance captured by seller and initial owner reputation in a novel setting characterized by significant changes in both moderating factors. Specifically, our research explores a market structure that relies on a distinct trust mechanism compared to traditional markets and it involves a new type of product where all items are digital and in the form of NFTs. Our results show evidence of the importance of provenance and the existence of reputation effects in bidding behavior. The evidence provided in this study lays a groundwork to investigate whether such transformative shifts made by blockchain technology will change our understanding of seller-bidder dynamics in peer-to-peer markets. As discussed in the front end, the main insight is that in blockchain markets there is a transference between previous owner attributes to product value. In this work, we limited our attention to reputation effects tying into value dimensions. However, attribute transfers need not be limited to reputation dimensions. Blockchain markets can be used to segment markets, target promotions, and price differentiation by attributes of past owners, as art markets already do. The transformative impact of blockchain-based marketplaces lies in their ability to facilitate direct user-to-user value exchanges through protocols that ensure consensus without requiring trusted middlemen ( Cao, 2022 ). This opens intriguing research possibilities; for example, examining how the absence of these intermediaries, akin to sellers on platforms like eBay ( Resnick et al., 2006 ), alters dynamics such as the influence of seller reputation and reputation system designs. Moreover, we have yet to explore the specific mechanisms driving these effects. Investigating whether transactions in these marketplaces adhere to traditional norms or if users are indifferent to the underlying technology would greatly enhance our understanding. In our analysis, our findings stem from a scenario where the NFTs serve a functional purpose in gameplay. Presently, most NFTs are usually non-functional, such as artwork. This situation closely mirrors the use of digital items beyond the blockchain sphere. Given this context, it would be valuable to investigate if the impacts of reputation vary depending on the specific nature of NFT products and to understand the mechanisms driving these effects. To map the mechanisms behind these effects, future research could investigate the potential spillover effects of celebrity value on the future market value of other tokens within the same card type, as these tokens share the same card name and visual rarity. This can be framed as an indirect celebrity value and can be operationalized by seeing whether any other token of the same card type has previously been purchased by a celebrity. If a spillover effect can be established, the follow up would be to study the time interval between the current bid and the celebrity's prior bid moderates this effect. Additionally, the analysis could be expanded to explore differences at the card name level. Such research would contribute valuable theoretical insights into the broader influence of celebrity value.

column1: It is a matter of trust: Literature reviews and analyses of human trust in information technology
column2: Trust is one of the most important constructs for understanding the adoption of information technologies (IT). In this paper, we review and analyze two literatures on the construct of human trust in IT artifacts and in the entities that source, operate, and govern IT. The first literature review focuses on defining of the construct of trust across a range of disciplines. Our analysis of this literature identified 13 assumptions about the nature of trust. The assumptions illustrate the complexities of human trust. The second literature review focused on 214 empirical studies of the construct of trust published in the AIS Senior Scholars’ Basket of Eight journals. We analyze this literature to identify IS scholar’s most common assessments of trust from qualitative studies and most common measures of trust from quantitative studies. As a cumulative body of knowledge, IS scholars have deeply examined the multidimensional aspect of trust by examining different types of trust, including affective trust, cognitive trust, institutional trust, instrumental trust, intrinsic trust, knowledge-based trust, relational trust, swift trust, disposition to trust, trusting beliefs, and more. IS scholars have also extensively examined the assumption that trust is dynamic, as evidenced by the many qualitative papers that examined trust as a process. Our review also finds that IS scholars have conducted extensive research examining trust in Web2 technologies, which are characterized by centralized applications and centralized governance. While the IS scholarly community has established a substantial tradition around the construct of trust, there is still interesting work to be done. With recent releases of open generative AI and with the rise of Web3 technologies like blockchains that purport to be “trustless,” the construct of trust in IT needs to be re-examined in these emerging contexts. We also encourage more research on trust in bi-directional relationships, on the limits of transitive trust, and on the construct of distrust.
column3:
Despite all the work IS scholars have done on the construct of trust, we believe there is more to investigate. From our review of the assumptions of trust from across disciplines and of the empirical IS research in the AIS Senior Scholars’ Basket of Eight journals, we encourage IS scholars to continue researching trust in emerging IT artifacts like blockchains, generative AI, and metaverse. So far in the cumulative IS research record, there seems to be a “pro-trust bias,” meaning that trust in technology is seen as a positive influence on adoption and success. In these newer contexts, perhaps there are downsides of trusting emerging technologies too soon or too much. In addition to calling for more research on emerging technologies, we identified gaps in our understanding of trust in bi-directional relationships, on the limits of transitive trust, and on the construct of distrust.
We encourage IS scholars to investigate trust in the context of Web3 technologies like blockchain (Assumption #3)
Trust in IT needs to be re-examined in the context of Web3 technologies, characterized by decentralized infrastructures, a.k.a. blockchains (Raddatz et al. 2021; Shao et al. 2022). Blockchains purport to ensure “trust by design” through the implementation of provable security and transparency within their transactions due to mathematics and cryptography (Anderson et al. 2023). Some authors argue that blockchains shift the perspective from trusting people to trusting math and algorithms (De Filippi et al. 2020; Lacity 2022; Lumineau et al. 2020; Utz et al. 2023; Völter et al. 2023). However, blindly relying upon the trust in the algorithm itself, and ignoring the other significant actors within the development, management, maintenance, and use of the system can lead to significant issues (Lumineau et al. 2023). While we have seen significant successes in blockchain platforms such as Bitcoin and Ethereum which have stood the test of time over a decade with continued adoption and development, we have also seen a flood of failed projects, fraudulent projects, and network manipulation by human actors hiding behind the limited understanding of the general public utilizing these networks who were told to simply trust the algorithm. Understanding the role and object of trust in evaluating emergent systems is crucial. Users and organizations need clear expectations of the potential risks involved with adopting and participating in networks generally outside of their direct control, especially as they enter the 4th industrial revolution. This era is characterized by increased interconnectivity and reliance between systems and humans (Lumineau et al. 2023).
So, what IS research has been done on human trust in blockchains? In reviewing articles published in the AIS Senior Scholars’ Basket of Eight journals up to July 2023, there are several recent articles on blockchain that tangentially relate to trust. For example, Du et al. (2019) studied a FinTech blockchain solution to identify blockchain affordances. One affordance, called “subsidiaries and suppliers can settle payment directly,” identifies that blockchains build trust based on a crowd rather than on a specific institution. The other recent articles on blockchains have not examined trust directly but did investigate other important aspects of this emerging technology, such as setting a research agenda (Beck et al. 2018; Rossi et al. 2019) examining stakeholder attitudes on privacy (Renwick et al. 2021), legal issues surrounding smart contracts (Drummer and Neumann 2020), blockchain use case for voting (Helm 2021), the stability of Bitcoin’s transaction fees (Ilk et al. 2021), and blockchain community discourse on Twitter (Miranda et al. 2022).
Despite some initial examinations within the AIS Senior Scholar’s Basket of Eight journals discussing the potential research avenues for blockchain, we believe there are ample areas of opportunity to explore further the relationship of trust in blockchain technologies across multiple layers (individuals, organizations, and collectives) and targets of trust (e.g., algorithm, developers, infrastructure miners, and users).
For individuals, users place their trust in public blockchains such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other cryptocurrencies which lack an underlying organization driving most of development and instead rely on a decentralized and potentially anonymous collective of developers and users. We have seen significant success and adoption with this open-source approach in platforms such as Bitcoin and Ethereum which are largely driven by an open collective but managed by a central group of core developers and influencers. For these open-source projects, there typically lacks a focal entity driving the majority of the design and development decisions, therefore balancing designs and reducing the potential for manipulation and abuse of the code being introduced within the projects. However, in many of the subsequent projects built upon or forked from Bitcoin and Ethereum, the development of specialized projects (e.g., exchanges, DeFI, wallet providers, and applications) are driven by focal actors (developers and organizations) who have their own incentives to design, implement, and control the participation and rules of the project in their favor while hiding behind the guise of the often misunderstood “trustless” nature of blockchain projects. For example, while stable coins are touted as alternatives to decentralized cryptocurrencies and a hedge in the trading market, these specific systems are designed with account blacklists, global exchange rules, and final authority given to a central organization which can lock or eliminate a user’s funds instantly without recourse.
Further, with public blockchains allowing participation in the network by anyone, and in many cases anonymously, users must rely on the trust in the technology even more so due to the lack of ability to verify the reputation, behavior, and intentions of others in the network. While this permissionless nature allows participants to reduce bias and increase inclusion within specific networks, it also allows the introduction of knowledgeable and malicious actors to infiltrate and manipulate the network as well. Blockchains are touted as being open and “trust-less” for users, which provides a large honeypot for malicious actors attempting to exploit the system and the unexperienced users within it by exploiting their trust in the technology (ur Rehman et al. 2019). While the public networks are open to participation by anyone, many users still rely upon centralized exchanges and providers to conduct their transactions, placing trust within a centralized organization and secondary platform, which we have seen have their own failures and manipulations of the market (e.g., FTX, QuadrigaCX, and Mt. Gox).
For organizations, blockchains have been developed and marketed as specifically helping to develop trust within interorganizational relationships by increasing shared data, agreeing upon shared transactional rules, and ensuring verifiability of transactional events (Batwa and Norrman 2021). However, many of these private and permissioned blockchain projects were proposed, developed, and maintained by centralized organizations that lead the decision making and on-going development of the projects which bring forth a new requirement of trust in the developing organization’s ability and benevolence. With the closing of several prominent enterprise blockchain solutions in 2022, including Tradelens, Everledger, Australian Securities Exchange, and we.trade, there needs to be post-mortem studies on the causes of failure—was it a lack of trust, and if so in which object of trust (e.g., system, developers, and organization), or something else?
We encourage IS scholars to investigate trust in the context of generative AI (Assumption #3)
The recent exponential growth of generative AI technology adoption has led to similar concerns regarding trust in the technology. While organizations have used AI tools like Robotic Process Automation (RPA) and AI-powered text generators for over a decade (Lacity and Willcocks 2016), generative AI tools are now open to the public. The veracity of Generative AI’s outputs relies heavily on the quality and validity of the data inputs. AI technologies rarely if ever showcase the actual data that was used to develop insights and recommendations (Willcocks 2023), leaving users to trust in the developers, platform, and the data integrated into these technologies without the transparency to verify their validity.
Additionally, most generative AI implementations are developed by a single organization. The exploitation of data by large AI organizations has led to significant pushback in the market and a lack of trust in these organizations to provide ethical usage of their training data (Zuboff 2019). Therefore, in the case of trust in generative AI, there might be a significant focus on trust in the developing organization who have made the decisions for the model and data utilized.
Recent articles published in the AIS Senior Scholars’ Basket of Eight journals have investigated AI in terms of algorithmic biases (Nishant et al. 2023), algorithm aversion (Turel and Kalhan 2023), explaining decisions made by AI systems (Fernández-Loría et al. 2022), but so far, none have examined specifically user trust in generative AI.
We encourage IS scholars to investigate trust in the context of metaverse (Assumption #3)
Davis et al. (2009) was the first paper in AIS Senior Scholars’ Basket of Eight journals that addressed the topic of metaverse, which the authors defined as “immersive three-dimensional virtual worlds (VWs) in which people interact as avatars with each other and with software agents, using the metaphor of the real world but without its physical limitations” (p. 91). Aiming to set an agenda for metaverse research, the authors called out trust as a particularly important construct to examine. Since then, JAIS had a special issue on virtual worlds in 2012, and one paper found that trust significantly affected workplace collaboration (Chandra et al. 2012), which was included in our coding.
More recently, metaverse received significant attention in 2021 when Facebook’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that Facebook was changing its name to Meta. While the intense interest in metaverse has since pivoted to generative AI, Herman Narula, author of Virtual Society: The Metaverse and the New Frontiers of Human Experience, argues that metaverse is inevitable because it’s part of human history to create mythical worlds that become socially constructed realities, like longstanding notions of “heaven” and “hell.”
Given metaverse’s immaturity, IS research has focused on defining metaverse (Dolata and Schwabe 2023), identifying its unique affordances (Dincelli and Yayla 2022), potential promises and perils (Dincelli and Yayla, 2022; Lacity et al., 2023; Nirmalee et al., 2023), and encouraging the inclusion of DEI considerations in metaverse strategies (Marabelli and Newell 2023; Mirbabaie et al. 2022). One recent paper by Seymour et al. (2021) examined the trustworthiness of avatars and found that subjects trust human realistic avatars more than non-human realistic avatars—the images in the paper are fascinating!
We encourage IS scholars to examine trust in the context of combinatorial innovations (Assumption #3)
IS scholarship has focused on trust in specific technologies, but trust in IT artifacts may be different for technologies that are used in combination. For example, some experts have argued that combining blockchains and AI may lead to even more trustworthy AI systems by ensuring the underlying data, algorithms, and privacy are protected and verifiable within AI implementations (Salah et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2019). As another example, combining metaverse and blockchains creates decentralized virtual worlds, like Decentraland and Spatial (Lacity et al. 2023). Will decentralized metaverses engender more trust than relying on a single company to operate a metaverse, like Meta or Roblox? As these combined systems of relatively emergent technologies continue to advance, understanding which components of the system and which external actors must be trusted and to what level are critical in helping understand and recommending adoption.
We encourage IS scholars to study bi-directional relationships between subjects and objects of trust (Assumption #11)
Studies we reviewed regularly considered a subject’s trust in a trustee, but not the trustee’s trust in the subject. From Assumption #11, we know that the relationship between a trustor and a trustee is an open question in the management discipline. Researchers are not quite sure under which conditions relationships are reciprocal, mutual, or asymmetrical (Korsgaard et al. 2014). In the field of IS, there has been some work on mutual dependency, mutual understanding, and one-way trust in the context of outsourcing, mostly from the perspective of the client trusting the IT provider (Lacity et al. 2011). We found only a few papers that considered bi-directional trust. Bapna et al. (2017) examined trust, reciprocity, and forgiveness in social ties using a field experiment on Facebook. Guo et al. (2021) looked at how a sourcing platform (an example of an IT artifact) mediated trust between the client and sourcing provider. The authors found that governance of the platform was important for building mutual trust.
We encourage scholars to research the limits of transitive trust (Assumption #12)
From assumption #12, we assume that trust is transitive to a degree, but we do not know where the boundaries may lie and under what conditions. Scholars have studied “one hop” transitive trust, such as a subject’s trust of a recommender or reviewer of a product, service, or vendor on an IT platform, but we did not find any research on longer transitive distances. On Facebook, for example, to what extent does a subject trust the friend of a friend of a friend of a friend…? On Linkedin, to what extent does a subject trust a colleague of a colleague of a colleague…? The limits of transitive trust is an important empirical question because hackers are known to exploit transitive trust (Webb 2008) and because some newer applications, like the Ripple and Stellar blockchain networks, find paths of transitive trust to process transactions that are more than a single hop (Lacity and Lupien 2022).
We encourage IS scholars to research distrust more (Assumption #13)
From assumption #13, it follows that trust is a different construct than distrust. Here we find a large gap in IS empirical work. In the AIS Senior Scholars’ Basket of Eight journals, we found only eight papers that considered distrust (Charki and Josserand 2008; Dimoka 2010; Heiskanen et al. 2008; Lim et al. 2012; McKnight et al. 2017; Moody et al. 2017b; Wright and Marett 2010). McKnight et al. (2017), for example, studied both trusting beliefs and distrusting beliefs, and hypothesized different antecedents to each. However, the results showed high correlations; information quality and system quality were both negatively related to distrusting beliefs and positively related to trusting believes. One construct, service quality outcomes, was negatively related to distrusting believes, but had no significant effect on trusting beliefs.
Using an experiment with 632 students and a Delphi method to study susceptibility to phishing, Moody et al. (2017a) measured disposition to trust using the sub-constructs benevolence, competence and integrity and the disposition to distrust using the sub-constructs malevolence, incompetence, and deceit. The authors found that the constructs of trust and distrust did not significantly affect susceptibility to phishing. However, they found differences at the sub-construct levels that were interesting. Both malevolence and benevolence were negatively associated with susceptibility to clicking on a phishing text link from known sources. The authors concluded, “This is likely due to the mixed signals inherent within this situation. The source is known, and thus more likely to be trusted, yet the link is entirely unknown. Building on the work of Moody et al. (2017a), we propose that the mixed signals cause the individual to engage in deeper processing, as both trusting and distrusting signals are present within the situation” (p. 574).
Beyond the IS discipline, management scholars have also called for more research on the construct of distrust. Six and Latusek (2023) write, “compared to trust, there is much less research on distrust” (p. 1). These authors claim that there is still confusion and lack of consensus as to the relationship between trust and distrust, calling for more investigation.
In conclusion, trust remains an important and relevant construct to understanding the adoption and use of IT artifacts and in the humans and entities that source, support, and govern IT. As our friends from the Trust over IP Foundation posit, “Technology can only help humans build trust if humans trust the technology” (ToIP 2021b. p. 51).

column1: Resale Royalty in Non-Fungible Token Marketplaces: Blessing or Burden for Creators and Platforms?
column2: Resale royalties, first introduced in the 1920s to support artists through a share of future resales, have now adopted by nonfungible token (NFT) marketplaces for digital art trading. Although these royalties are often viewed as beneficial for creators, our research reveals unexpected consequences. Using data from a major NFT marketplace, we find that NFTs with higher royalty rates sell for significantly lower prices and take longer to sell. Surprisingly, creators do not recoup these initial losses through royalty payments within four years. We discover that higher up-front minting costs lead creators to set higher royalty rates. We reveal a delayed gratification effect where creators with higher royalties accept lower up-front prices in hopes of future royalty income. We also find an overconfidence effect where confident creators, measured by their past sales and follower count, are more likely to lower initial prices. Our research contributes to the ongoing debate about royalty enforcement in NFT marketplaces and offers empirical evidence to inform platforms and creators. Platform managers should carefully consider both reducing up-front minting costs and implementing royalty rate limits to improve market liquidity. Creators should be cautious about setting high royalty rates as they may not provide the expected financial benefits.
column3:
This study investigates both the antecedents of royalty-setting behavior and the consequences of royalty rates in NFT marketplaces. We find that a higher minting cost for the
focal NFT as well as higher (sunk) minting costs for other NFTs lead creators to set higher
royalty rates for the focal NFT. Our analysis also reveals that NFTs with higher royalty
rates are traded at significantly lower prices on the primary market than their counterparts with lower royalty rates. Although resale royalties are intended to financially support
NFT creators in the long run, our findings indicate that they do not consistently benefit
NFT creators. Specifically, our estimates show that NFT creators do not accrue financial
benefits from resale royalty within the four years following the initial sale of their NFTs.
Additionally, we provide evidence that NFTs with higher royalty rates are less likely to
be sold and take longer to sell than NFTs with lower royalty rates. Conventional wisdom
suggests that resale royalties benefit NFT creators and, in turn, increase platform revenue.
However, our findings suggest that the opposite may be true for NFTs with higher royalty
rates, as the market becomes less liquid and the average commission decreases due to significantly lower primary sales prices. These findings indicate that resale royalties may lead
to unintended consequences for both NFT creators and platforms.
8.1.

Theoretical Contributions

To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first empirical investigation into
the long-debated question of the impact of resale royalties on NFT marketplaces. While
prior literature has investigated royalty rates in other physical artworks, no study has
empirically studied royalty rates in the NFT context, likely because NFTs are a relatively
new phenomenon in the realm of digital artworks. Moreover, the underlying blockchain
technology and the traceability of secondary sales offer a novel setting for exploring royalty
rates. Our findings contribute to existing theories in IS and other related disciplines in
several ways.
First, we provide empirical evidence and enrich relevant theories in IS. NFT marketplaces
are considered as novel digital goods markets, though they bear similarities to markets
for physical goods. For instance, the costs associated with content creation in NFT marketplaces resemble those in other markets where the production is costly. However, it is
unclear whether theories associated with costs, such as the sunk-cost fallacy, apply to the
novel context of NFT marketplaces. We found evidence that NFT minting fees can indeed

37

trigger a sunk-cost fallacy, albeit a short-lived one. NFTs minted within a 3-day window
influence the royalty-setting behaviors for the focal NFT, even though the minting costs
for the other NFTs are sunk. This suggests that the sunk-cost fallacy plays a role even in
digital goods markets, specifically in NFT marketplaces.
Second, we contribute to settling the long-standing debate about resale royalties, a topic
of interest among academics and policymakers since the 1920s. Our findings suggest that
resale royalties can lead to a delayed gratification effect. In other words, NFT creators
forego immediate rewards in the primary market in the hope of greater future monetary
benefits.
Lastly, we find evidence for a partial ownership effect for NFT buyers due to resale royalties. We observed that the partial ownership effect influences buyer behaviors, resulting
in fewer sales or prolonged time to sale for NFTs with higher royalty rates. These findings
not only provide empirical support for existing theories but also pave the way for future
research to expand these theories in the context of NFT marketplaces, which differ fundamentally from the market for physical goods. We believe our study offers an empirically
grounded contribution to the understanding of NFT marketplaces, providing a solid foundation for future scholarly work in this rapidly evolving field. We anticipate more studies
on NFT marketplaces, and our study pioneers this research direction, calling for further
evidence to support or refine existing theories as well as development of new ones in the
context of NFT marketplaces.
8.2.

Managerial Implications

Our findings have significant implications for NFT marketplace managers and creators.
Contrary to the widespread belief that economic incentives through resale royalties benefit
NFT creators, our research suggests that creators may be financially harmed by minting
NFTs with high royalty rates. Although creators have received substantial royalty payments—over $1.8 billion worth of royalties were paid out to creators of Ethereum-based
NFT collections as of October 2022 (Qadir and Parker 2022)—our findings indicate that
these royalty payments do not compensate for the reduced prices in the primary market
for at least four years.
Moreover, our research suggests that platform managers may not always profit from
implementing resale royalties. The average sales price in the primary market decreases
significantly, and commission revenue from sales becomes less frequent for NFTs with

38

higher royalty rates. These findings may shed light on recent developments in the NFT
ecosystem regarding royalty enforcement. In August 2023, OpenSea, the leading NFT
marketplace, announced that it would no longer enforce royalty fees for buyers of new
NFTs, and for existing NFTs, royalty enforcement would cease after February 202429 . This
decision shocked many NFT creators who had come to rely on royalties for their economic
well-being. In response, other NFT marketplaces took opposing stances. For instance,
Rarible announced they would continue to enforce royalties permanently30 . Our findings
contribute to this ongoing debate about whether marketplaces should enforce royalties,
offering empirical evidence to better inform platform managers and policymakers.
Platform managers must carefully craft their information policies and design incentive
mechanisms to survive and thrive in the long run. Maintaining a balance between the number of NFT creators and resellers in NFT marketplaces is vital for the economic viability
of such two-sided markets. NFT platforms compete to attract creators, as their primary
source of income is commission revenue from NFT sales. On the other hand, NFT creators
financially rely on buyers that ultimately become re-sellers in the secondary market. One
could not survive without the other. Hence, platform managers must ensure the economic
sustainability of both NFT creators and resellers. Many NFT platforms adopted the resale
royalties as a potential solution to offset the high minting costs, which undermine the
financial stability of creators, and stifles the emergence of new NFTs. The adoption of
resale royalties, however, might have unintended consequences for primary sales prices and
market liquidity, beyond the probable benefits for NFT production. Our findings call for a
more comprehensive assessment of the value of resale royalties, considering their effects on
market dynamics beyond simply stimulating the NFT production. Sustaining the long-term
economic viability of NFT marketplaces requires other important factors such as engaging
and rewarding active users, attracting new creators and buyers, and generating loyalty
mechanisms to encourage buyer retention. Moreover, platform managers should strive to
balance strategies between amateur and professional creators with respect to royalty rate
setting.
