column1: Optimal product line design strategy for green and non-green products with blockchain technology
column2: In practice, manufacturers have three typical product line design strategies to produce green products, i.e., only producing green products ( $$OG$$ OG strategy), producing both green and non-green products ( $$GN$$ GN strategy) and only producing non-green products ( $$ON$$ ON strategy). Moreover, the implementation of blockchain technology is beneficial for consumers to verify the authenticity of product information, then increasing the possibility of consumers making informed purchasing decisions. In view of these backgrounds, an interesting question arises regarding the impact of blockchain technology adoption on the manufacturer’s strategy for product line design. To investigate this issue, we consider a manufacturer facing three product line design strategies under traditional information disclosure and blockchain-driven information disclosure scenarios. By comparing the manufacturer’s optimal decisions in two different scenarios, we find that (i) regardless of the implementation of blockchain technology, as the production cost difference between green and non-green products increases, the manufacturer’s optimal product line decision is from $$OG$$ OG strategy to $$GN$$ GN strategy and then to $$ON$$ ON strategy; (ii) after adopting blockchain technology, it will be more profitable for the manufacturer to choose $$OG$$ OG strategy and less profitable to choose $$ON$$ ON strategy; and for $$GN$$ GN strategy, the profitability depends on the quality difference and the operation cost of blockchain technology; and (iii) a high cost of operating blockchain leads to a reduction in total market demand, which in turn mitigates the negative environmental impact.
column3: In practice, manufacturers have three typical product line design strategies for the production of green products, i.e., only producing green products, not producing green products, and producing both green and non-green products at the same time. The product information disclosure seriously affects consumers’ ability to effectively distinguish green products from non-green products, and thus may harm the sales of green products. The implementation of blockchain technology is beneficial to consumers because it allows them to verify the real information of products, increasing the possibility of consumers buying. Motivated by the important application of blockchain technology in green and sustainable supply chains, we develop analytical models to explore the effect of blockchain technology on a manufacturer’s product line design strategy. We also numerically analyze the impact of blockchain on the environment. We have extended the model to inspect its robustness and demonstrated that the main findings remain unchanged. Our conclusions can provide practical guidance for a manufacturer’s product line design and information disclosure decisions. Our main conclusions and managerial insights are summarized as follows. First, our analytical results revealed that as the production cost difference between green and non-green products increases, the manufacturer’s optimal product line decision moves from 𝑂 𝐺 strategy to 𝐺 𝑁 strategy and then to 𝑂 𝑁 strategy. Second, after adopting blockchain technology, it will be more profitable for the manufacturer to offer green products, while it will be less profitable to offer non-green products. Moreover, when the manufacturer produces both green and non-green products, whether the adoption of blockchain technology makes the manufacturer more likely to benefit depends on multiple factors, namely, the quality difference and the operation cost of blockchain technology. Specifically, when the quality difference is sufficiently large, the manufacturer’s profitability is more likely to be improved when incurring a low blockchain operating cost; otherwise, the optimal decision of simultaneously producing two products may undermine the manufacturer’s profitability. Third, we present numerical examples to observe the influence of the adoption of blockchain technology on the environment. We find that a slight cost of operating blockchain will stimulate an increase in market demand that exacerbates overall negative environmental impacts. A limitation of this study is that we only consider the manufacturer disclosing information directly to consumers and postpone another third-party platform or retailer sharing information to future research. We also consider a green supply chain, which consists of a manufacturer and consumers. In future studies, competitive parties can be brought in to investigate product line design in the blockchain era. In addition, it is valuable to extend the model with government policies, such as government subsidies and penalties, to explore the optimal decisions for product line design and information disclosure.

column1: Blockchain-based traceability system adoption decision in the dual-channel perishable goods market under different pricing policies
column2: The blockchain-based traceability system (BTS) can reduce product losses in the perishable goods market, which yields a loss-reduction effect, and offer authentic information, which triggers a premium effect. In a dual-channel perishable goods supply chain (DPGSC), including one supplier and retailer each, the supplier can operate the price of the direct channel, different or non-different from that of the traditional channel. To study the adoption of BTS in the supplier-led DPGSC, we employed a game-theoretical model to capture BTS adoption strategy under the differential and non-differential pricing policies and proposed an improved cost-sharing contract to boost the DPGSC performance. The results indicated that both the supplier and the retailer are willing to improve product quality, broaden the saleable region, and lower the production cost. The adoption of BTS mainly depends on the losses-reduction effect, premium effect, production cost, and tag cost, which is affected more by the premium effect than by the loss-reduction effect. Furthermore, their adoption is not always easier when the production cost is higher. Except for symmetric base demands, they benefit asynchronously from BTS. Synchronised adoptions can be realised only when the improved cost-sharing contract generates more profits and introduces excess momentum. Highlights Blockchain-based traceability system handles product losses and forged information Adoption decision-making processes under two different pricing policies are studied In the adoption process, the premium effect outweighs the loss-reduction effect Contract may introduce insufficient momentum, excess momentum, or new inefficiency Once excess momentum is formed, supply chain members' adoptions become synchronised
column3: We investigate the application of the BTS and propose an effective contract to improve the DPGSC's performance. First, we explore the applicability of the BTS in the DPGSC under differential pricing. Second, to expand the applicability of the BTS, pricing strategies under non-differential pricing are discussed. Finally, three extended cases are addressed to confirm the validity of our results. The key findings are summarised as follows. First, without the adoption of BTS, the supplier has an incentive to improve product quality while lowering the production cost, which is encouraged by the retailer. Second, differential pricing always benefits the supplier but may hurt the retailer, specifically in the case of symmetric base demands, determined by the traditional market's potential market size, cross-price sensitivity, production cost, and tag cost. Furthermore, retaining the existing pricing policy is the optimal strategy in the adoption process. Third, adopting the BTS or traditional traceability technologies is not always more profitable, and the BTS is more easily accepted than traditional traceability technologies and has the potential to broaden the saleable regions of perishable goods. Furthermore, the supplier bears a stronger positive impact of the premium effect than the retailer, which surpasses the loss-reduction effect. Fourth, the effect of the production cost in the adoption process for the coordinated supply chain is complicated than that for the uncoordinated supply chain. Specifically, for the uncoordinated supply chain, it is always the case that the higher the production cost, the easier it is always for the BTS to be accepted. However, for the coordinated supply chain, it is not always the case. Fifth, the supplier and retailer do not always synchronously benefit from the BTS adoption, except for symmetric base demands and the IC that provides excess momentum. Finally, the IC is proposed to generate more profits and plays various roles in this adoption. Specifically, the IC introduces insufficient momentum, but does not work well for adoption. Alternatively, it introduces excess momentum and works well. An equilibrium cost-sharing proportion exists under non-differential pricing, making it easiest to benefit from this adoption. Conversely, it introduces new inefficiency, and the cost-sharing proportion is closely related to the retailer's bargaining power. The key managerial implications are as follows. First, both players are committed to taking corresponding measures, such as adopting the BTS, to shorten circulation time and improve product quality. Second, to obtain the supplier's willingness toward stable cooperation, the retailer should strengthen the traditional channel's advantages. Once the BTS is implemented, the supplier retains the original pricing policy and sells perishable goods to regions where they previously could not be supplied owing to long-distance transportation. Third, compared with traditional traceability technologies, both players favour the BTS. The DPGSC, such as Sunkist Growers Inc and its retailer, should update their existing traditional traceability technologies to BTS, which is incorporated into their production, logistics, and retailing processes. Moreover, the supplier, like Yunnan Chu's Agriculture Corporation, enhances the premium effect by offering authentic information links on its website and showing real-time illustrations, and participating in social interactions during the live-stream time (Pan, Feng, and Zhao Citation 2022). Simultaneously, the retailer formulates certain countermeasures to provide convenience for consumers to access authentic information. Fourth, the role of the production cost in the adoption process differs for uncoordinated and coordinated supply chains. Specifically, given the tag cost, the uncoordinated DPGSC is always more likely to adopt BTS for perishable goods with a higher production cost, however, the coordinated DPGSC is not always. Fifth, the supplier and retailer do not always benefit synchronously from the BTS, and the IC introducing excess momentum can be implemented to make them accept the BTS synchronously. Finally, they adjust the cost-sharing proportion to ensure the effective execution of the IC. Specifically, they may obtain insufficient momentum and reject the adoption. Alternatively, they acquire excess momentum, determine the equilibrium cost-sharing proportion, and adopt the BTS, which is more easily accomplished under non-differential pricing. Conversely, they bear new inefficiency and are devoted to improving their respective bargaining power. Some potential directions would enrich our findings. First, we excluded some retailers, such as Walmart and FreshHema, who have developed their direct channels. Thus, future research should focus on mixed channels, which include the supplier's direct channel and the retailer's traditional and online channels. Second, we ignored the clear relationship between the premium effect and tag cost. More detailed and authentic information implies a higher cost (Wu, Fan, and Cao Citation 2021). Thus, further research should investigate the relationship between the premium effect and tag cost. column1: imseStudio: blockchain-enabled secure digital twin platform for service manufacturing
column2: The manufacturing industry is experiencing a service-oriented transformation in the digitalisation era. However, many small and middle enterprises (SMEs) still rely on traditional manufacturing patterns in which they can hardly servitise manufacturing resources due to the limited budget and poor digitalisation capability. To servitise manufacturing resources, this paper proposes unified five-layer blockchain-enabled secure digital twin platform architecture, followed by its core enabling components and technologies. Firstly, a service-oriented digital twinning model is developed to transform physical resources into digital services. Secondly, a rule-based off-chain matching mechanism is designed to bridge customers’ orders with manufacturing services. Thirdly, service-oriented architecture (SOA) is adopted as the major methodology to design and develop the whole blockchain platform. Four blockchain frontend services are developed using React.js, whilst the blockchain backend is developed using private Ethereum blockchain and InterPlanetary File System (IPFS). Finally, an experimental case is conducted based on the 3D printing scenario to verify the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed platform, named imseStudio. The results show that it not only provides an effective solution to digitalise manufacturing resources but also promotes the transformation towards service manufacturing. Highlights Blockchain-enabled secure digital twin platform is developed to servitise manufacturing resources Service-oriented digital twinning model is developed to transform physical resources into digital services Rule-based off-chain matching mechanism is built to bridge customers’ orders with 3D printer Four blockchain explorers are developed to facilitate 3D printing services
column3: To facilitate the service-oriented transformation in SMEs, this paper introduces a blockchain-enabled secure digital twin platform. Firstly, the architecture of blockchain-enabled digital twin platform for service manufacturing is proposed and developed, named imseStudio. It provides a secure and trustable environment for digital twins through the blockchain s immutability and reliability. Secondly, service-oriented digital twinning model is built to transform diverse manufacturing resources into digital twins, which are securely stored in the blockchain ledger. Finally, an experimental case of 3D printing service is given to verify the feasibility of the imseStudio. This paper's main contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) This paper builds a blockchain-enabled secure digital twin platform. Not only does it servitize manufacturing resources into digital twins, but also provides an effective solution to promote the transformation towards service manufacturing. (2) The rule-based off-chain matching mechanism is developed to achieve the flexible and trackable matching service between customer orders and 3D printers. Moreover, basic matching rules (e.g., size, material, accuracy) and advanced scheduling rules are considered to develop the flexible matching solutions, such as order priority, customer importance, etc. (3) Blockchain-based services, including order placement service, asset digitalization service, matching & scheduling service, and execution & monitoring service, are enabled by four blockchain explorers. Through the experimental case study, customer explorer provides a straightforward approach to place orders and track the printing statuses. Printer explorer facilitates the printing servicers to servitize their manufacturing resources. Matcher explorer plays a role as a matchmaker to schedule customer orders to suitable printers. Executer explorer provides a solution for the front-end operator to streamline the printing operations and helps the managers supervise the real-time printing activities and make production decisions flexibly. Further research could be conducted as following aspects. Firstly, collaborative service manufacturing could be considered using the developed imseStudio platform. For example, imseStudio could servitize multiple service manufacturing resources, such as grinding, laser-engraving, CNC, etc. It is worthwhile to explore the blockchain-enabled collaborative mechanism among different manufacturers to fulfill customer demands. Secondly, the implementation of a smart contract-enabled matching mechanism needs to be explored, such as development, deployment and versioning mechanism, etc. It could facilitate a practical and flexible matching solution for manufacturing industry. Thirdly, the current platform is only implemented and verified in the 3D printing service scenario. It could be extended in other service manufacturing scenarios, such as mold manufacturing, assembling, etc.

column1: Multi-period price competition of blockchain-technology-supported and traditional platforms under network effect
column2: ABSTRACT We build a multi-period pricing model between a blockchain-technology-supported platform and a traditional platform, where the blockchain-technology-supported platform provides a higher value for customers. Customers are influenced by network effect, that is, they value a platform more if the platform has more users. As either platform can adopt static pricing or dynamic pricing, four scenarios may occur. By deriving the equilibrium of each scenario, we reveal the 'Matthew effect' caused by network effect, that platform advantage (from adopting blockchain technology) or disadvantage (from not adopting blockchain technology) accumulates as time goes by. Thus, platforms are advised to adopt the blockchain technology antecedent to the competitors. Network effect, which amplifies the benefit of initial users, may intensify price competition and harm both platforms. By comparing the four scenarios, we derive the equilibrium pricing strategies: when network effect is weak, one platform adopts static pricing and the other adopts dynamic pricing; when network effect is medium, the blockchain-technology-supported platform adopts static pricing and the traditional platform adopts dynamic pricing; and when network effect is strong, both platforms adopt dynamic pricing. Dynamic pricing is more desirable for the traditional platform relative to the blockchain-technology-supported platform.
column3: To examine the impacts of network effect, we study a two-period price competition between a blockchain-technology-supported platform and a traditional platform which provide differentiated products or service. The adoption of blockchain technology can increase the utility of using the platform. The customers are influenced by network effect, that is, they value a platform more if the platform has more users. The platforms can adopt static pricing (i.e. charging the same price for the two periods) or dynamic pricing (where the platforms can responsively adjust the second-period price and set different prices for the two periods). We derive the analytical results of the optimal decisions under the four possible pricing scenarios: (S, S), where both platforms adopt static pricing; (S, D), where the blockchain-technology-supported platform adopts static pricing and the traditional platform adopts dynamic pricing; (D, S), where the blockchain-technology-supported platform adopts dynamic pricing and the traditional platform adopts static pricing; and (D, D), where both platforms adopt dynamic pricing. By letting each platform choose between static pricing or dynamic pricing, we find the equilibrium pricing strategies. We obtain some interesting results on user behaviour, pricing strategy and platform profitability, and provide important managerial insights, which are summarised in Table 9. Table 9. Summary of results and managerial insights. Download CSVDisplay Table A number of issues remain unaddressed in this paper, and will be worth future investigation. First, we build parsimonious models to obtain tractable results. Our results may be subject to the model assumptions and should be interpreted with care. For example, we use the linear Hotelling model to depict the price competition. In line with some marketing and operations management literature, our demand function is deterministic and does not incorporate a random part. Moreover, we consider that the product value and differentiation degree are exogenous. Future studies can examine the effects of network effect on product design. Second, with the support of blockchain technology, more pricing strategies are feasible, such as customised pricing (Choi, Guo, et al. Citation 2020). Future studies can examine such innovative pricing strategies. Third, to focus on the impact network effects on platform competition, this paper only accommodates two competitive platforms. More sophisticated supply chain interactions can be considered in the future, such as operations of upstream suppliers (e.g. Cai, Choi, and Zhang Citation 2020) and bilateral platforms (e.g. Liu, Pan, and Zheng Citation 2020).
