column1: The effect of blockchain implementation on supply chain disputes
column2: Although the significance of blockchain implementation has been broadly recognized, it is uncertain how a firm's blockchain implementation may further influence its supply chain relationships. This study fills the gap by exploring the relationship between blockchain implementation and supply chain disputes. Specifically, this study proposes that buyers with blockchain implementation are more likely to foment disputes with their suppliers, based on a substitution interaction between governance mechanisms. It also investigates how this impact may be moderated by corporate ethics and resource availability factors. A unique panel dataset of listed Chinese firms from multiple resources is created to test the hypotheses. The results suggest that a buyer's blockchain implementation is positively associated with supply chain disputes. Moreover, this positive relationship is weaker when buyers exhibit a higher level of technology for social good (TSG) orientation and engage in fewer financial misconducts. Conversely, the positive relationship is stronger when buyers operate in environments with higher supplier concentration and receive lower analyst recommendations. Our study makes both methodological and theoretical contributions. Specifically, we employ GPT-4 to help identify supply chain disputes with the buyer's violation. We also use a machine learning approach through combining the “continuous bag of words” (CBOW) method with the BERT NLP model to extract TSG orientation from unstructured annual reports, enabling both efficient and comprehensive understanding of semantic information. Our findings provide valuable insights for buyers, suppliers and policy makers in developing strategies to mitigate the adverse effect of blockchain implementation on supply chain relationships.
column3:
5. Discussion and implications
5.1. Methodological contribution
Our research significantly enriches research methods of the operations management (OM) field by employing machine learning language models to analyze massive unstructured textual data. In terms of measuring supply chain dispute, previous research primarily relied on surveys (Bai et al., 2016), analytical modeling (Chen et al., 2016), or case studies (Tuladhar et al., 2024). Our study advances these methodologies by utilizing a large corpus of unstructured court verdict reports to measure supply chain disputes. Specifically, we demonstrate the feasibility of employing the GPT-4 large model for processing extensive unstructured textual data. In addition to qualitative data analysis software such as MAXQDA and NVivo, GPT offers an alternative time- and labor-saving method. Regarding firm strategic orientation, previous studies typically investigated it using surveys (Jiang et al., 2023, Jiang et al., 2023, Jiang et al., 2023), manual scoring (Gatignon and Bode, 2023), or case studies (Danese et al., 2021). While some advanced research has incorporated machine learning techniques, such as the “bag of words” (BOW) method for word frequency analysis (Niu et al., 2024), these approaches may overlook the deeper semantic structures within the text. Our study innovatively combines the CBOW model with the BERT model, leveraging the strengths of both approaches to enhance text analysis and achieve a more nuanced understanding of complex semantic information in corporate strategic orientation.
5.2. Theoretical contributions
First, our study advances the understanding of blockchain implementation by extending its impact from the firm level to the supply chain context. Existing studies have primarily examined blockchain implementation from the perspectives of an individual firm or the supply chain as a singular entity (Chod et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Unlike other digital technologies, blockchain technology plays a role that is closely integrated within the supply chain context. Consequently, blockchain implementation initiated by a focal firm inevitably transforms the way of operation of the entire supply chain. Our study extends the understanding of blockchain implementation by focusing on the buyer's behavior and its impact on supply chain relational outcomes. The finding provides empirical evidence that the buyer's blockchain implementation could trigger supply chain disputes. Moreover, it also highlights the necessity for buyers to recognize the importance of coordinated actions with supply chain partners to avoid potential inter-firm issues (Gligor et al., 2021).
Second, our study enriches the literature of blockchain in the OM field by uncovering the mechanism underlying the dark side of blockchain implementation. Existing research predominantly highlights the positive effects of blockchain implementation, such as positive stock returns (Zhang et al., 2024) and increased supply chain efficiency (Hastig and Sodhi, 2020). While there is also a recognition of its potential drawbacks (Cui et al., 2024), the underlying mechanism has been unclear. Our study employs RDT to uncover how blockchain implementation may serve as a tool for reshaping inter-firm dependence structures. We show that buyers facing higher supplier concentration—indicative of resource dependence—are more likely to leverage blockchain to reduce reliance on powerful suppliers, thus heightening the risk of dispute. This extends the use of RDT by illustrating how firms not only respond to dependence, but also actively reshape it through technology.
Third, we build on TCE by illuminating the contingencies under which blockchain complements or substitutes for relational governance (Lumineau et al., 2020). Rather than assuming governance modes are static or mutually exclusive, we show how buyer behavior varies depending on organizational orientation and resource environment. Buyers with a strong TSG orientation are more likely to coordinate with partners and maintain trust, reducing the risk of conflict. In contrast, buyers with a history of financial misconduct may exploit blockchain opportunistically, undermining cooperation. Moreover, firms with stronger external reputations are more likely to pursue collaborative and trust-preserving blockchain strategies.
5.3. Managerial implications
First, buyers should acknowledge the potential dark side of private blockchain implementation in supply chain management. While private blockchains provide greater control and governance capabilities, they may also introduce trust-related challenges. When implementing a private blockchain, buyers can strengthen their data governance framework by establishing clear rules for data access to mitigate potential supplier opportunism. However, the governance role of blockchain may lead buyers to undervalue inter-organizational relationships and underestimate the importance of inter-firm trust, potentially harming supplier relationships. As a result, buyers may face an increased likelihood of legal disputes. To avoid unnecessary legal conflicts, firms should adopt a principle of sharing the benefits of blockchain implementation with all supply chain members. During the blockchain implementation period, buyers should prioritize both data governance and trust maintenance as essential components of their supply chain strategy. Additionally, to address supplier dissatisfaction, resistance, or misunderstandings—such as those arising from perceived data monopolies—firms should engage in frequent communication and dialogue with suppliers to foster collaboration throughout the implementation process.
Second, suppliers should be aware of the potential risks associated with buyers' implementation of private blockchains. Our research highlights that buyers might exploit blockchain adoption as a means to engage in speculative profit-making behavior. In response, suppliers should proactively engage in discussions to establish a consensus on data governance principles when a buyer implements a private blockchain. Forming alliances with other suppliers to collectively negotiate with the buyer can strengthen their bargaining position. This scenario also provides an opportunity for suppliers to establish fairer relationships and negotiate more favorable terms, using the buyer's blockchain implementation as leverage to create a more balanced and mutually beneficial dynamic. When contracting with buyers that have implemented blockchain, suppliers should prioritize partnerships with firms that exhibit strong corporate ethics and maintain a good reputation, thereby reducing the likelihood of buyer exploitation. To further safeguard their interests, suppliers should conduct thorough due diligence and implement protective measures to mitigate the risk of exploitation, especially in cases where there is evidence of financial misconduct by the buyer. Additionally, our findings suggest that higher supplier concentration increases the likelihood of supply chain disputes, as buyers may be motivated to reduce their dependence on key suppliers. To mitigate this risk, suppliers should diversify their customer base, reducing reliance on a single dominant buyer who has implemented a private blockchain. By diversifying their client portfolio, suppliers can decrease potential supply chain risks and enhance their resilience against opportunistic behavior.
Third, governments and industry associations should proactively promote the reliable application of blockchain technology. On one hand, governments should develop regulatory standards that ensure the compliant use of private blockchains. Our findings suggest that buyers may exploit technological asymmetry in blockchain implementation for opportunistic gains, potentially increasing supply chain disputes. Strict regulations can deter such violations and ensure fair practices. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of TSG orientation and good reputation in mitigating disputes. Governments can encourage blockchain adoption by providing subsidies and tax incentives to firms with demonstrated TSG goals and strong reputations. Governments can also support small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) by offering training programs on blockchain technology, enabling these firms to overcome technical barriers and participate in blockchain-enabled supply chains. Special funding incentives could further promote the development and application of blockchain technology, fostering innovation and ensuring its equitable and effective use across industries. On the other hand, industry associations can collaborate with governments to establish pilot programs in key projects, such as food traceability blockchain initiatives, which can provide valuable compliance guidelines and practical insights. Additionally, industry associations can create industry-wide platforms to offer technical services for data governance and develop effective dispute resolution mechanisms. They can also play a critical role in bridging digital gaps among supply chain partners, facilitating smoother blockchain implementation.
5.4. Limitations and future research
This research has certain limitations that future studies might further explore. First, given that our research context is confined to China, the specific economic and cultural environment may limit the generalizability of our results. Therefore, future research could extend these findings to both emerging and advanced economies to enhance their applicability. Second, our study is limited to the implementation of private blockchains in supply chain management due to data constraints. Future research could explore a comparative analysis of the effects of private and public blockchain implementations on supply chain-level outcomes. Third, our study is limited to supply chain disputes that may require court judgement for resolution. Future studies could explore the impact of blockchain implementation on various types of disputes between supply chain partners, classifying these disputes by severity (e.g., dispute, litigation) and type (e.g., collaboration breakdowns, informational fraud, cultural shock). Due to data limitations, further research needs to be conducted by using questionnaires or interviews to gather more comprehensive conclusions. Fourth, our research only considers the moderating roles of corporate ethics and resource availability. Further research could explore legal liability as a moderator to understand how this ex-ante trust factor influences the supply chain relationship impacted by blockchain implementation. In addition, future research could examine the antecedents of supply chain disputes, such as the characteristics of supply chain managers. Fifth, while the use of the GPT-4 model demonstrates the potential of advanced large language models (LLMs) in textual data analysis, its high computational costs present a limitation. Future research may explore alternative models, such as DeepSeek, Claude and Gemini, which can offer complementary advantages in resource efficiency.

column1: Decoding the premium: The effect of name fluency on NFT artwork valuation
column2: This paper examines how the fluency of an NFT's title affects its market valuation. Leveraging sales data from Damien Hirst's renowned NFT collection, The Currency, we find a positive association between name fluency and NFT price. Tokens with higher name fluency, measured by shorter titles and simpler syntax, achieve significantly higher prices. These findings extend heuristic-based theories in finance and economics by demonstrating that fluent cues influence investors’ valuations in the emerging blockchain-empowered NFT markets.
column3: 4 Conclusion Building on the literature on heuristic decision-making, we show that NFTs with more fluent names achieve higher valuations. Both shorter title length and simpler syntax are positively associated with sale prices, underscoring the influence of name fluency on investors’ heuristic-based choices in the NFT market. These findings extend prior research on NFT pricing and offer practical guidance for platforms seeking to optimize information presentation. More broadly, our study contributes to behavioral economics by demonstrating that an artwork’s title acts as a critical reference point shaping investor judgment under uncertainty.

column1: Digital Technology Adoption: Go Together With Supply Chain Partners
column2: With the rapid development of digital technology, such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, and big data, digital technology adoption has become a strategic choice for firms to maintain competitiveness in a dynamic market. As an important technology investment input, firms should have a holistic consideration of their level of digital technology adoption, focusing on the entire supply chain. Using empirical evidence from the data of listed companies in China from 2007 to 2022, we find that a higher discrepancy in the level of digital technology adoption between the focal firm and its suppliers and customers negatively affects the focal firm's financial performance. Additionally, the focal firm's own capabilities, including bargaining and innovation capabilities, play a negative moderating role in the impact of digital technology adoption discrepancy, which can mitigate the negative impact of the gap in digital technology adoption between itself and its suppliers and customers on the firm's financial performance. Our findings thus provide implications for firms to implement a “go‐together” approach to match their digital technology adoption level with their partners' to synchronize the adoption level of digital technology along the entire supply chain and enhance their negotiation and innovation capabilities to improve their resilience and sustainable development.
column3: The business environment is rapidly changing due to the increased rate of new digital technologies as well as higher consumer expectations. This forces firms to be proactive in their digital transformation. Our study shows that the financial outcomes of digital technology adoption depend not only on the decisions made by the individual firm, but also on their supply chain partners' conformity. A higher discrepancy in the level of digital technology adoption between the focal firm and its suppliers and customers negatively affects the firm's financial performance. In addition, the firm's internal capabilities, including its bargaining and innovation capabilities, can mitigate the negative effect caused by any digital technology adoption discrepancy. Our results provide important guidance for firms in their digital technology adoption. Specifically, firms should implement a “go-together” approach to match their digital technology adoption level with their supply chain partners. In this way, digital technology adoption can achieve its optimal financial effect by synchronizing adoption across the supply chain.There are several fruitful directions for future research. First, our study focuses on digital technology, but further research is needed to explore other technologies, such as green technologies. These future studies can investigate the impact across supply chains. In addition, the effect of digital technology adoption studied in our paper is concentrated on financial performance, namely, ROA. Although ROA is a common measure for firms' financial performance, digital technology adoption may also influence firms' risk control or organizational performance, which can be further explored. Finally, future studies can explore other firm characteristics, such as firm culture, that may moderate the impact of digital technology adoption discrepancy across the supply chain.

column1: The International Supply of Reserve Currency
column2: This paper provides insights into the historical inefficiencies and instabilities of the international monetary system, spanning from the gold standard to modern "paper" currency systems. It analyzes the historical limited supply of safe assets within the reserve currency, as indicated by positive liquidity premia, both from government and private issuance. Additionally, it explores the macroeconomic and financial instabilities of shortages in the supply of safe assets with respect to the challenges of stabilizing inflation and economic activity. Innovations stemming from the competition of cryptocurrencies and the associated blockchain technology hold the potential for improving these outcomes.
column3:
The challenge of establishing a stable and efficient international monetary system appears to have no clear solution. Looking at the provision of liquidity, this study has argued that it cannot be left to the will of a monopolist, that even were benevolent has no incentive in providing the efficient supply. The reason is the improvement in the country’s current account.Footnote 21 The system becomes prone to instabilities due to shifts in the external demand of liquidity. These vulnerabilities can be quite evident under certain monetary regime, like it was the gold standard. The innovation of a monetary policy framework in which policy is conducted setting the interest rate on reserves, which determine also the interest rate on liquidity, can help to insulate the issuer country from external demand shocks, unless the zero lower bound is reached.The residual rents remaining in the market due to a government monopolistic supplier can be eliminated by the competition among private intermediaries seeking to benefit from lower borrowing costs in the liquidity market. Ideally, when these intermediaries adequately back the supply of safe liquidity, competition enables the efficient provision of liquidity. This backing can even be achieved through risky securities by allowing equity to absorb potential losses. An efficient private supply of liquidity does not pose a challenge to monetary policy’s control of inflation and money markets.However, deviations from this ideal framework reveal sources of inefficiency and instability, necessitating government and central bank intervention. This discussion highlights a multi-task role for the central bank, encompassing liquidity provision, macroeconomic stability, and acting as a lender of last resort for intermediaries and often, the treasury. These interconnections create environments characterized by nuanced financial and fiscal dominance.Footnote 22In this somewhat gloomy scenario, there is a glimmer of hope stemming from recent developments in the currency market, thanks to the emergence of cryptocurrencies and their accompanying blockchain technology. These innovations introduce three significant changes that could potentially transform the international monetary system.Firstly, we now have currencies that can transcend national boundaries, effectively disconnecting the traditional link between a nation, its government, and its currency. This cross-border adaptability is a notable departure from the past.The second innovation lies in the potential advantages that come with the competition in supplying these currencies, something governments typically lack an incentive to pursue, as they typically enforce their own national currency. In an ideal world, we might foresee a future where individuals can choose their monetary system, deciding which units they wish to transact with, settle contracts, or handle debit and credit operations. As envisioned by Hayek in 1976, there is no reason to doubt that this could lead to an enhancement in currency quality, driven by users seeking the best currency in terms of its macroeconomic stability.The third novelty is the blockchain technology, which introduces a means of certifying and verifying information through cryptographic guarantees–a highly objective approach compared to the traditional paper-based, subjective guarantees, see Chainlink (2022). This technology has the potential to evolve to enable cryptographic-guaranteed assessments of securities, offering users trustworthy information about the quality of financial securities, that is more accurate, accessible, and auditable than current alternatives. This would replace, for example, the reliance on subjective evaluations from rating agencies, potentially reducing the sources of instability outlined in this work. In the context of the model discussed in this work, this innovation has the potential to substantially reduce the barriers that hinder the smooth interaction between the supply and demand for private safe securities. Using the notation of the model, as the parameter \(\phi _{t}\) approaches 1 and \(\delta\) approaches 0 due to this innovation, the efficient supply of liquidity could be reached.
With these three innovations in mind, it is conceivable that in the near future, competition for superior currencies could lead to the emergence of automated monetary policies solely focused on maintaining currency value stability, without the interferences arising from fiscal and financial dominance. Simultaneously, cryptographic truth could accurately price the risk associated with securities denominated in the currency’s units, allowing private entities to compete in efficiently providing liquidity with a trustworthy backing.

column1: Incentives in decentralised autonomous organisations
column2: This study examines the impact of competitive incentives on member effort and organisational success, providing insights for practitioners aiming to optimise the performance of DAOs (Decentralised Autonomous Organisations). By leveraging the power of economic incentives through token rewards, DAOs, a novel form of member-owned organisational structure built on blockchain technology, are able to foster engagement and contributions from their members. Since tokens represent a DAO’s value, in contrast to equity investors, token financing motivates members to apply effort, enabling a DAO to incentivise higher efforts than other member-owned organisations such as cooperatives. This study aims to investigate whether the association between efforts and tokens can effectively motivate members to generate value for DAOs. Our findings seek to assist practitioners in decision-making when selecting the optimal organisational structure based on the number of members and the share of tokens allocated to community rewards.
column3: 6 Conclusion In this section, we provide a summary of our findings and managerial implications and outline avenues for future research. 6.1 Theoretical implications Our game-theoretic model explores incentives within cooperatives and DAOs, revealing both similarities and significant differences between these organisational structures. Traditional cooperatives face challenges with free-rider behaviour, where unlinked rewards to individual efforts lead to suboptimal member contributions ( Ben-Ner and Ellman, 2013; Van Dijk et al., 2019 ). Holmstrom’s (1982) team production model notes that cooperatives often fail to align individual rewards with individual contributions, leading to reduced effort levels. By contrast, DAOs have a mechanism that directly addresses this issue by tying rewards to observable individual efforts. Our findings show that DAOs achieve higher levels of member effort and engagement through an effort-based reward system, effectively mitigating free-rider problems and increasing member satisfaction. Our analysis demonstrates that DAOs can reach first-best effort levels when token allocations reflect each member’s marginal contributions to the organisation’s value. In situations where all tokens are distributed solely as rewards, members of a DAO are incentivised to exert maximum effort, achieving optimal outcomes. This approach starkly contrasts with cooperative models, where effort levels generally fall below the optimum due to collective distribution structures. When cooperative and DAO models are compared, DAOs exhibit the potential to drive member contributions significantly higher, especially when tokens are allocated based on individual efforts, directly linking personal effort to personal reward. Furthermore, our study highlights how DAOs might maintain equivalent or even superior effort levels compared to cooperatives under specific conditions. For instance, in scenarios with additive effort functions or where a limited token supply is allocated to community rewards, DAOs can maintain comparable efforts. However, as membership increases, cooperatives experience a decline in equilibrium efforts, while larger DAOs continue to incentivise higher member engagement even with a modest community reward allocation. These theoretical insights offer a foundation for understanding how DAOs leverage token-based incentives to sustain higher member efforts, especially in larger organisations.

column1: Foundations of Decentralized Metaverse Economies: Converging Physical and Virtual Realities
column2: ABSTRACT Decentralized metaverse economies leverage blockchain cryptocurrency and asset tokens to enhance the concepts of digital ownership and scarcity, uniquely combining aspects of real, virtual, and blockchain economies. This study applies and extends token adoption and valuation theory to conceptualize and empirically analyze the dynamics in decentralized metaverse economies. We analyze over 4.5 million blockchain transactions from two blockchains across two years in the “The Sandbox” metaverse using vector autoregressive models. Our findings reveal complex dynamics among exchange rates, economic actors, and their activity, highlighting the exchange rate’s central role in fostering growth, particularly regarding creating scarce digital assets. The results provide insights for designing and regulating decentralized metaverse economies and offer a novel conceptual framework for understanding these emerging information systems. Our research contributes to the literature by bridging economic theories with the technological realities of blockchain-based metaverses, providing a foundation for future studies on the convergence of real and virtual economies in the metaverse.
column3: Blockchain-based metaverses leverage blockchain cryptocurrency and asset tokens to enhance the concepts of decentralized digital ownership and scarcity in virtual environments. Their decentralized metaverse economies uniquely combine aspects of real, virtual, and blockchain economies, contributing to merging physical and virtual realities [ Citation 94]. Understanding their economic foundations is essential for creating, operating, and regulating these emerging systems. This study provides new insights into the nature of decentralized metaverse economies, which exhibit characteristics of real, virtual, and blockchain economies, creating a unique hybrid that requires new conceptual frameworks to understand fully [ Citation 37]. This study set out to explore the economic foundations of decentralized metaverse economies. Our analysis of over 4.5 million blockchain transactions in The Sandbox metaverse reveals complex interactions that support and challenge existing theoretical frameworks. We draw on token adoption and valuation theory and extend it by accounting for digital assets and metaverse government actions. Our empirical results reveal the central role of exchange rates in stimulating economic activity and attracting economic actors while also highlighting the potential for speculative behavior that may not translate into sustained economic engagement. We demonstrate that in decentralized metaverse economies, the relationship between the adoption by economic actors and the exchange rate is more nuanced than previously thought. While new economic actors positively influence the exchange rate, the total number of economic actors does not have the same effect, suggesting a more complex adoption dynamic. Second, our findings highlight the crucial role of digital assets in these economies, a factor not fully accounted for in existing theories of blockchain-based platforms. This extends our understanding of how value is created and exchanged in these novel information systems. For metaverse operators and developers, our findings underscore the importance of carefully designing market mechanisms for future blockchain-based metaverses. The ability to trade digital assets in multiple cryptocurrencies on various marketplaces while providing flexibility may reduce demand for the native cryptocurrency. Operators must balance this trade-off to maintain a healthy economy. Additionally, our results suggest that the strategic creation of digital assets by the metaverse government can stimulate economic activity and attract new economic actors, confirming theories from real economies [ Citation 34], traditional digital platforms [ Citation 41], and virtual environments [ Citation 54]. For policymakers and regulators, this study highlights the need for nuanced approaches to governing these new economies. Decentralized metaverse economies, combining virtual and real economies, present unique challenges. Regulators must consider how to protect consumers while fostering innovation. However, coordinating regulating efforts on a global scale remains challenging and potentially hinders the widespread adoption of blockchain-based metaverse and their economies. This study opens several avenues for future research. Longitudinal studies across multiple metaverse economies could provide insights into how these systems evolve and how economic dynamics change as they mature. An investigation into the quality of digital asset creation, not just quantity, could yield valuable insights into value creation in these economies. Moreover, research into user motivations and behaviors in decentralized metaverse economies could help bridge the gap between economic theories and actual user engagement. This work contributes to research and practice by providing a novel framework for understanding the economic foundations of decentralized metaverse economies. As the metaverse emerges and decentralized metaverse economies evolve, this research provides insights for designers, operators, , regulators, and researchers. By bridging economic theory with the technological realities of blockchain-based virtual environments, we lay the groundwork for future studies on the convergence of real and virtual economies for the metaverse. column1: Can Fintech Development Contribute to Mitigating the Greenhouse Effect? A Global Perspective
column2: Fintech leverages blockchain and smart contracts for decentralized economic coordination. Its emerging applications in green finance and supply chain transparency hold promise for mitigating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This article evaluates the global impact of Fintech development on GHG emissions (GHGE). Based on cross-sectional regressions using data from 124 countries (2014–2018), the article finds that Fintech development significantly reduces GHGEs—with each 1% increase in the Fintech development level, GHGEs are reduced by 0.546%. This reduction is significant in low-, lower-middle-, and high-income countries, but not in upper-middle-income countries. Furthermore, the article finds that three components of Fintech activity—equity investments in Fintech companies, usage of Fintech credit, and digital payments—significantly reduce GHGEs, with digital payments proving the most effective. This article broadens our understanding of Fintech's role in achieving global climate goals, demonstrating its substantial potential for sustainable development. Subgroup analyses further validate Fintech's key function within the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) framework, highlighting how EKC moderates Fintech's emission reduction effects. Overall, these findings provide valuable insights for policymakers, financial institutions, and technology entrepreneurs aiming to mitigate the greenhouse effect through enhanced Fintech development.
column3: A. Contribution In this article, we examine Fintech development excluding cryptocurrencies. This is important because a lot of public attention and research has been focused on the energy expenditure of cryptocurrencies. This article examines the aspects of Fintech that are more widely used and established, such as electronic payments and green financing. Our findings are important for policy-makers, managers in financial institutions, technology entrepreneurs, and firms in general that are concerned about sustainability. The contribution of this article is two-fold: first, we have established that Fintech (excluding cryptocurrencies) on average reduces GHGEs globally. The results show that an increase in the Fintech development level by 1% leads to a 0.546% reduction in GHGEs. Meanwhile, analyses based on the subindices of Fintech activity demonstrate that improvements in three subindices can also significantly contribute to reducing GHGEs. Before this article, some evidence of Fintech's impact on GHGEs had been observed in China [69], though we were unable to find studies testing this globally. Our findings support and extend prior article that investigated the links between Fintech and green finance and found that Fintech enabled green initiatives [4], [14], [15]. At the same time, the findings further align with conclusions about the role of financial innovation and sustainable technologies in achieving environmental objectives. As research has found, Fintech promotes the use of funds for energy and environmental projects, as well as the construction of renewable energy and environmental infrastructure through innovative financial instruments, supporting sustainable climate and social goals [10], [11], [16]. Green innovation and positive shifts in environmental-related technologies drive positive environmental benefits [70], [71]. Additionally, the result that digital payment usage is the primary Fintech driver of GHG reduction supports existing research highlighting the positive environmental impacts of digital technologies [28], [72], [73], offering new evidence for the role of digital technologies in reducing GHGEs. GHGEs represent one of the most pressing challenges of our time, with direct implications for global warming, climate change, and the future of our planet. The findings underscore the transformative potential of Fintech in reshaping financial systems to align with global climate goals and offer robust empirical evidence for the critical role of financial and technological innovations in promoting environmental sustainability, particularly in reducing GHGEs. Second, the article finds that the GHGE reduction effect of Fintech development varies across country groups. The reduction effect is insignificant in an upper-middle-income country group compared to other groups, lending support to Hypothesis 2 about the EKC moderating the effect of Fintech. The EKC framework posits that environmental quality improves after reaching a certain income level. Our findings further illustrate how Fintech interacts with this dynamic. Specifically, Fintech has a greater GHGE reduction effect in low- and lower-middle-income countries and high-income countries but shows limited impact in upper-middle-income countries, where industrial activities and energy use often outweigh the benefits of Fintech adoption. This nuanced relationship enriches the broader discussion on the key role of Fintech in the operation mechanism of the EKC hypothesis and highlights the need for tailored Fintech policies in transitional economies [74]. These findings align with existing research. For example, Kashif et al. [39] found that Fintech positively contributes to ecological sustainability by reducing EFs in advanced countries; Butu et al. [75] noted that Fintech improves small-scale renewable energy financing in sub-Saharan Africa; and Croutzet and Dabbous [14] discovered that Fintech development promotes renewable energy use in OECD countries. B. Policy Implications This article provides the following implications. First, policy-makers should take a leading role in integrating Fintech into national sustainable development strategies, promoting the coordinated development of various dimensions of Fintech, and formulating country-specific strategies. For example, national funding programs targeting Fintech startups, green credit, and digital payment technologies can be established, supported by tax incentives and preferential policies. Additionally, a transparent and efficient regulatory framework for Fintech lending platforms should be established to encourage the development of green credit products targeting SMEs and low-income groups, enhancing financial inclusion and resource utilization efficiency. Regarding differentiated national strategies, for high-income countries, the focus should be on leveraging technological and financial advantages to foster green finance innovation in high-tech fields, particularly blockchain- and AI-based solutions, to strengthen Fintech's leadership role in international green finance. For upper-middle-income countries, policy efforts should emphasize supporting the adoption of Fintech solutions in high-emission industries and incentivizing the modernization of energy technologies. Additionally, the further development and application of digital payment systems should be encouraged. For low- and lower-middle-income countries, policies should prioritize digital infrastructure construction to expand Fintech service coverage, enhance the digitalization of financial services, and accelerate financial inclusion and energy-saving practices. Second, financial institutions should fully understand Fintech's role in green development, optimize organizational structures, and innovate financial products based on practical needs. Collaborations with tech companies could foster public–private partnerships to develop integrated platforms. These platforms could combine the convenience of digital payments, the financing capabilities of equity investment, and the flexibility of credit, offering one-stop green financial solutions. Moreover, financial institutions should tailor products to meet local community needs, such as microloans for renewable energy adoption and affordable green housing solutions for low-income populations, ensuring that green principles are incorporated into efforts to enhance financial inclusion. Third, technology entrepreneurs and firms concerned about sustainability should keenly observe the expanding demand for low-carbon transitions worldwide and invest resources in developing cutting-edge technologies to address critical low-carbon development challenges. For instance, in fields such as blockchain, AI, and Big Data analytics, entrepreneurs and firms could develop technological solutions for carbon footprint tracking, energy management, and green financing. This would not only enhance the market competitiveness of their enterprises but also contribute to achieving global sustainability goals. They can also design affordable, user-friendly products for low- and lower-middle-income countries, such as mobile financial tools tailored to small farmers or SMEs, facilitating their integration into sustainable development practices. C. Limitations In addition, this article has some limitations. First, the study was unable to obtain a panel dataset that has variation over time in Fintech development. Thus, a within-country effect, that controls for all time-invariant country-level confounders, could not be estimated. Second, while this article uses IVs to address endogeneity, unobserved confounders may still influence Fintech development and GHGEs. Factors such as environmental regulations, regional economic policies, or technological readiness might indirectly affect the observed relationships, introducing endogeneity bias. Last, this article provides initial macrolevel evidence showing that Fintech does reduce GHGEs, and several pathways of how that happens are suggested in the theoretical development section. However, the importance and relative significance of these pathways require further elucidation and testing to clearly establish the causal mechanisms by which Fintech reduces GHGEs. Based on the above limitations, future article could enhance and extend this article in three ways. First, panel data should be used to validate the findings. Panel data would help control for time-invariant country characteristics and provide stronger evidence of causality. As the topic of Fintech generates interest and curiosity, we expect better data to be available on the topic. Second, where data availability permits, additional variables related to economic policies, technological innovation, and environmental regulation should be incorporated to reduce potential omitted variable bias. Third, future article should explore the intrinsic mechanisms driving Fintech's GHG reduction effects, offering more actionable insights for policymakers. For example, the capability of Fintech to lower transaction costs and increase financial accessibility supports the expansion of green finance. This phenomenon is evident through innovative financing models such as green bonds and impact investments, which increasingly attract both individual and institutional investors. Green bonds specifically fund projects that have positive environmental and climate benefits, and their growth has been bolstered by Fintech platforms that enhance the transparency and efficiency of such transactions.

column1: Unveiling barriers to the integration of blockchain-based circular economy and Industry 5.0 in manufacturing industries: A strategic prioritization approach
column2: Although Industry 4.0 plays the role of a catalyst in the transition from a linear economy to a circular economy (CE), some sustainability goals are neglected by prioritizing machines over humans. Industry 5.0 insists on combining technology with human values to achieve sustainable development goals. Therefore, the integration of CE and Industry 5.0 leads to sustainable synergy in various industries, especially in manufacturing industries. However, their integration is always associated with challenges and barriers. This study identifies a set of these barriers in the electric vehicle battery production industry from the financial, technical, supply chain, cultural, and regulatory and processes perspectives through a deep literature review. The fuzzy weighted influence non‐linear gauge system method is used to analyze the relationship between identified barriers and their prioritization. Finally, we leverage the knowledge of four experts from an electric vehicle battery manufacturing company in Southeast Asia to validate the proposed approach and to rank the barriers. The results demonstrate that immature technology providers are the biggest obstacle in the integration of blockchain‐based CE and Industry 5.0 in the electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry.
column3: Applying CE principles in SCs leads to increasing their sustainability; it enables the reuse of waste, reduces energy consumption, and makes the use of virgin resources more efficient. On the one hand, the technologies based on Industry 4.0 have a considerable effect in pushing SCs towards circularity and sustainability; on the other hand, Industry 4.0 is in contradiction with some sustainability goals since it focuses on machines instead of human values. Industry 5.0 solves this problem and helps SCs to achieve sustainable development goals by linking human values and technology. Therefore, the integration of CE, Industry 4.0, and Industry 5.0 concepts is a powerful tool to increase the sustainability of SCs. But integrating these concepts and implementing them in SCs are challenging. Identifying and prioritizing the challenges and barriers of integrating these concepts are very important. Hence, in this study, we comprehensively reviewed the literature and identified the effective barriers to integration of blockchain-based CE and Industry 5.0. Then, by applying a method based on structural models called fuzzy WINGS, we ranked the barriers to the integration of blockchain-based CE and Industry 5.0 in the electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry. The results showed that financial and technical barriers are the most important engagement barriers for the integration of blockchain-based CE and Industry 5.0 in the electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry. However, an important difference between them is demonstrated. The technical barriers have cause properties, while financial barriers have attribute effects. It means that although both are highly connected to the other barriers, the technical barriers influence the others, while financial barriers are influenced. It can be inferred that to defeat the financial barriers, the initial focus should be on the technical barriers and maturing the technology. Likewise, intensity of immature technology providers possesses the cause attribute, as evidenced by the positive values of the role. However, high capital expenditure for upgrading the system works as an effect property which means that it is more influenced instead of influencing. This means that the less experience and maturity in developing and maintaining the technological systems is the main reason contributing to high financial costs. Other interesting point is that it seems that the decision-makers may not have so much concern about collecting the waste for recycling. Such results may be related to the type of industry. The battery industry's wastage is not remarkable; it does not have impurities and is not generated daily. Due to these facts, they likely do not have concerns about customer resistance against contributing to wastage collecting. At the same time, they do not have a focus on human concerns.This research identifies and ranks the integration barriers of Industry 5.0 and blockchain-based CE and does not provide strategies to deal with them. It is suggested that in future research, strategies to deal with these barriers will be introduced and those that have the greatest impact on overcoming these barriers will be identified through organizational theories (Govindan, Demartini, et al., 2024). Although the fuzzy WINGS method considers both the weight and influence intensity of barriers, it does not use a systematic method for weighting barriers. Therefore, we suggest that in future studies, by integrating effective weighting methods such as fuzzy best-worst method with fuzzy WINGS, an approach to ranking barriers is developed and its results are compared with the results of this paper.

column1: Reward-Based Crowdfunding Versus Initial Coin Offerings
column2: Inspired by emerging financing techniques that offer additional financing options for entrepreneurs, we establish a stylized model to compare two prevalent crowdfunding strategies: Reward-based crowdfunding and Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs). First, we highlight that the fundamental difference between reward-based crowdfunding and ICO lies in the distinct types of price distortion, resulting in different agency costs. Specifically, compared to the first-best benchmark, reward-based crowdfunding sets a lower funding price to attract more consumers to pre-order, while ICO sets a higher market price due to speculators’ revenue-sharing in the market stage. Second, we show that the financing limit (i.e., the maximum funds raised) of reward-based crowdfunding is driven by the platform traffic, whereas that of ICO is driven by the marginal production cost. Therefore, even with numerous speculators, ICO may result in a lower financing limit than reward-based crowdfunding when the platform traffic or the marginal production cost is high. Third, we explore how products’ cost structures shape entrepreneurs’ financing preferences. ICO suits intangible products with high fixed cost and low marginal production cost, while reward-based crowdfunding aligns better with products exhibiting the opposite cost structure. Finally, we extend our model to show the robustness of our findings and offer some additional insights. For example, ICO may amplify the risk of market uncertainty compared to reward-based crowdfunding; Security Token Offerings (STO) benefits from the absence of agency costs between the entrepreneur and speculators compared to ICO while it may suffer from equity loss, particularly in risky and regulated markets, etc.
column3: Inspired by emerging financing techniques, we construct a stylized model to compare the efficacy of two prevalent crowdfunding strategies: Reward-based crowdfunding and ICO. Our analysis reveals that the suitability of each approach largely depends on the product’s cost structure. Specifically, ICO is more suited for intangible products with high fixed costs and low production costs, while reward-based crowdfunding suits tangible products with the opposite cost structure. This result arises from their divergent fundraising mechanisms. In reward-based crowdfunding, the entrepreneur accumulates funds through revenue during the funding stage, bearing all production costs. In contrast, ICO raises funds by transferring revenue (affected by the marginal production cost) over two stages, spreading the production costs to speculators. Interestingly, speculators can act as a double-edged sword in ICO. They can increase the success of fundraising, but the revenue sharing between them and the entrepreneur in the market stage can undercut the entrepreneur’s pricing power and overall profitability. We further explore several extensions to substantiate our primary findings and derive novel insights. With market uncertainty considered, ICO is more likely to dominate reward-based crowdfunding with relatively low market uncertainty. When incorporating production costs in the financial constraint, reward-based crowdfunding gets worse than ICO when factoring in the first-period production costs. In contrast, ICO experiences more negative impacts when all production costs are considered. Also, with high marginal production costs, cash diversion behavior can expand the dominance of ICO. As for STO, compared to ICO, the advantage stems from the absence of agency costs between the entrepreneur and speculators. More tokens can be sold to increase the success rate, which is crucial for high-cost projects. However, it may result in higher financing costs due to equity losses in a risky and regulated market.To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to theoretically compare reward-based crowdfunding and ICO from an analytical perspective. This research can be extended in several promising ways. First, we employ a simplified two-phase game to address this problem. However, in reality, ICOs often involve additional phases. For example, many ICO projects include a pre-ICO stage, during which the startup sells tokens to early investors or allocates tokens to key employees. Moreover, startups commonly adjust their token supply based on market demand to ensure price stability. Considering a multi-period game that incorporates the strategic behavior of firms as token suppliers may reveal intriguing dynamics. Second, our model assumes that all information is common knowledge for all participants. However, given that both reward-based crowdfunding and ICOs gather funds from backers before product market entry, this could engender information asymmetry. Entrepreneurs may signal critical product information by showcasing a functioning prototype during the campaign. Thus, exploring the entrepreneurs’ strategies to signal such information via campaign design presents a compelling research direction. Third, we consider the total consumer base as an exogenous factor in our model. Yet, in practice, entrepreneurs can manipulate consumer visits to crowdfunding platforms via various marketing strategies, including social media promotions. Considering the consumer base during the funding stage as a variable could provide further valuable insights. Last, our model focuses on a single entrepreneur’s fundraising effort, but in reality, numerous entrepreneurs vie for funding on the same crowdfunding platforms. Future studies could explore how entrepreneurs design the optimal campaign in a competitive environment.

column1: Trusting the trust machine: How does blockchain-enabled governance configuration enhance financing credibility?
column2: This study highlights the role of blockchain technology in addressing the trust crisis in supply chain operations and financial activities. While previous research has acknowledged blockchain as a response to trust issues, limited studies have explored its specific contributions and its impact on accelerating cash flow in supply chains. Drawing on governance theory, this study investigates the relationship between blockchain technology and supply chain finance (SCF) through multiple case studies. The central argument is that blockchain technology alone does not automatically generate trust. Instead, trust is established through the configuration of various governance mechanisms. We propose that trust in blockchain applications is derived from two main factors: the requirement of codifiability and verifiability. Through a cross-case analysis, we found that in situations where both the requirement of codifiability and verifiability are high, blockchain governance tends to dominate. When only one factor is high, a configuration of blockchain governance and relational governance emerges. When both factors are low, contractual governance proves to be efficient. This study underscores the need for a nuanced understanding of trust dynamics in blockchain applications and highlights the importance of considering contextual factors in trust research related to blockchain technology.
column3: 7 Conclusion This study examined the adoption and usage of blockchain technology in SCF by three companies. It outlined the stages involved in building trust and compared how blockchain technology functions within different governance structures. The study also explored how companies with limited information on SMEs can establish trust and make financial decisions based on the capabilities of blockchain service providers and changes to their own governance practices. 7.1 Theoretical implication This study challenges the traditional view of blockchain as merely a trust machine or algorithm trust to make financial decisions. Blockchain technology enhances financial institutions’ confidence on SMEs and their operations ( Dubey et al. 2019 , 2020 ). However, the fundamental characteristics of the blockchain are just the starting point of establishing trust or the initial stage of trust. Although technical confidence is the source of trust, trust cannot be generated solely based on technological features. An effective approach to building trust among participants, who are along the pipeline to guarantee authenticity of operation and avoid falsification, lies in combining blockchain with SCF scenarios while promoting business efficiency and effectiveness. Therefore, blockchain as a trusted machine needs to earn its own credibility through specific promotion strategies rather than relying solely on its technological features. This study suggests that while blockchain-based capabilities can be an internal motivator for trust, external factors such as governance reconfiguration are the driving force behind generating trust. Trust is based on a party's perception of their counterpart's reliability and predictability. Therefore, it is not only important for counterparts to have blockchain-enabled capabilities but also for users to accept and trust the operational process utilizing blockchain. This finding aligns with previous research in e-commerce which found correlations between trust, perceived risk, and perceived usefulness ( Goundar et al., 2021 ). In the SCF context, financing risks mainly stem from SMEs' financial information opaqueness, operational information, and behavior information (e.g., innovation or negative events) ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhao and Li 2022 ). If transaction processes and asset/behavioral data are deemed to be credible and have high-quality through the use of blockchain technology, its value can be realized. Therefore, this research enriches our understanding of how blockchain generates trust. The trust generated by blockchain originates from the interaction process between service providers and customers. It requires joint action from both internal and external aspects to establish credibility in the transaction process. Our research also explored how blockchain technology fit with specific SCF scenarios. Blockchain is an important pivotal element for generating trust, but its role needs to be combined with other technical means according to the specific SCF scenario. As the cases show, different SCF businesses (e.g., order financing, inventory financing, asset-backed securitization) often have distinctive applied scenarios and encounter different challenges ( Bal et al., 2018 ). Therefore, the generation of technical confidence and the contribution of blockchain to trust building depend on how the blockchain adopters (or blockchain service provider) structure resources according to business scenarios and establish a systematic governance mechanism. Through the two-dimensional matrix of verifiablilty and codifiability, we distinguish the three SCF scenarios. We found that, in situations where both verifiability and codifiability are high, blockchain governance dominates; when only one side is high, there exists a configuration between blockchain governance and relational governance; finally when both sides are low, contractual governance would be efficient. Thus, we emphasize the importance of contextualizing research on trust in relation to blockchain technology within specific business contexts.

column1: How can blockchain-based lending platforms support microcredit activities in developing countries? An empirical validation of its opportunities and challenges
column2: The aim of this paper is to explore the opportunities and challenges of using blockchain technology to support microcredit activities of microfinance institutions operating in developing countries. Microfinance is widely regarded as a tool for poverty alleviation and a means of integrating the unbanked population into the financial system. Using expert interviews from several industries including microfinance and blockchain, we explore the potential and challenges of blockchain-based platforms in microcredit settings. The findings suggest that blockchains could create credible financial profiles for lenders, automate contracting through smart contracts and attract funds at lower costs. However, coordination complexities, strategic issues, and privacy concerns are key challenges to blockchain implementation. The study advances the understanding of blockchain applicability in the microcredit space and carries practical significance for microfinance institutions as to how blockchain can — in combination with mobile money — improve operational efficiency and strengthen governance on microcredit activities.
column3: 6 Conclusion MFIs are critical organisations but face many operational challenges that impact their ability to provide microcredits to the poor at affordable interest rates. Although there is considerable research on microfinance and the conceptual possibilities of blockchain technology, no empirical study has investigated blockchain's operational challenges in this context. This study provides novel insights into how blockchain could facilitate microcredit as well as the associated issues that impede its diffusion in developing countries. A blockchain-based decentralised ledger could be used to create unique borrower profiles that can be used for verification and assessment purposes. It can minimise opportunistic behaviours, reduce microcredit service costs, and improve loan governance. In addition, smart contracts can be used to customise loan products and to align the interests of borrowers and lenders. However, blockchain technology also causes a set of concerns that impede its implementation. This includes coordination complexities, strategic considerations and privacy issues. Relevant stakeholders should try to overcome these problems proactively with suitable polices and industry-led research collaborations. Our results may facilitate such initiatives to enable social change.

column1: Is decentralization sustainable in the bitcoin system?
column2: The Bitcoin system is a decentralized monetary system in that any participant can potentially verify and record transactions onto a public ledger. Using a simple model, we show that the number of miners could be negatively (positively) related to the expected rewards if miners with low-operating costs also have less (more) severe financing constraints. We characterize the possibility of miners with low-operating (high-operating) costs facing less (more) severe financing constraints as large-size (small-size) miners. The empirical evidence supports the model's large- and small-size miner characterization prediction. The negative association between the number of miners and expected rewards is attributable to Bitcoin's exchange rate. Collectively, our evidence suggests that even though the Bitcoin system is designed as an egalitarian system, it is likely to evolve into a near-centralized system because of economic forces.
column3: 5 Concluding remarks Decentralization is a crucial feature required to sustain the verification and the recording of transactions in the Bitcoin system. The “hype” among the exuberant tech community is that blockchain-based decentralized digital currencies such as the Bitcoin system would disrupt traditional financial transaction systems. We show that this exuberance may be premature. In this concluding section, we summarize our analyses and findings, highlight some managerial implications, and emphasize some limitations that can lead to pathways for future research. 5.1 Summary of analyses and findings We examine a game-theoretic model where miners choose their level of computing resource that, in turn, determines the miner's probability of being the first to solve the crypto-puzzle and obtain the mining reward. The miners incur operating costs and a fixed cost for acquiring a minimum level of the computing resource that depends on the level of difficulty of the crypto-puzzle, i.e., blockdifficulty. The miner's competitive advantage stems from the differential operating costs and the capital available to finance the computing resource, operating costs, and fixed costs. We derive insights from the model by considering two cases: one, where the two sources of competitive advantage are complements, i.e., miners with low (high) operating costs also have more (less) capital; and two, where the two sources are substitutes, i.e., miners with low (high) operating costs have less (more) capital. We show that if the two sources of miners' competitive advantage complement (substitute) each other, the number of miners is negatively (positively) related to expected rewards. These insights provide empirical tension, where the relationship between the number of miners and fees will provide insights into the nature of miner's competitive advantage. We empirically examine the predictions by obtaining data between February 2012 to October 2017 from blockchain.info (BI). To compute the number of active miners that compete to solve the crypto-puzzle in a calendar week, we use the identity of miners that successfully solve the crypto-puzzle in the nine-week window surrounding the treatment week. The reward is the total of a fixed component and a variable discretionary component that the buyers/sellers of the transaction offer the miner. The Bitcoin reward is converted to US dollars at the exchange rate obtained from Yahoo Finance. We partition the sample into two periods: we classify the period after November 2014 as the High BlockDifficulty period, i.e., the period when the severity of the financing constraint is high. We find that the number of miners is negatively associated with the reward, and this relationship is attributable to the High BlockDifficulty period. These results are consistent with the two sources of competitive advantage being complements – large-size miners have lower operating costs and more capital than small-size miners. We then perform a battery of robustness and additional tests to support this inference. Collectively, this evidence suggests that few miners capture the mining market, and as such, the Bitcoin system is ultimately likely to be non-egalitarian.

column1: The nexus between ReFi, carbon, fossil energy, and clean energy assets: Quantile timeâ€“frequency connectedness and portfolio implications
column2: Leveraging blockchain and Web3 technologies, Regenerative Finance (ReFi) is dedicated to advancing the financing of climate initiatives. A key innovation within ReFi is the tokenization of carbon credits. Consequently, this study explores the return connectedness among ReFi, carbon, fossil energy, and clean energy markets, employing a quantile time–frequency connectedness framework. Our findings indicate a relatively weak and time-varying trend in return connectedness. Notably, the pairwise connectedness within the ReFi-carbon-energy system becomes more pronounced during extreme market conditions compared to normal conditions. Moreover, clean energy markets of all sub-sectors serve as net spillover transmitters across different quantiles and time–frequency domains. In contrast, ReFi markets act as net receivers in the short term but evolve into net transmitters in the medium term, especially under extreme market conditions. Next, we examine the impacts of determinants on total connectedness, which demonstrate heterogeneity across different time horizons and market conditions. Finally, we confirm the usefulness of ReFi assets as effective diversification and hedging tools for carbon-energy portfolios. Our findings not only provide guidance for ReFi investors in constructing more cost-effective investment strategies, but also assist ReFi policymakers in cultivating a broader and trustworthier application of ReFi.
column3: 6 Conclusion This study explores the return connectedness between four ReFi tokens (BCT-Toucan Protocol, Klima-KlimaDAO, M CO 2 -Moss Earth, and Regen-Regen Network Tokens), carbon assets (CCM and VCM), fossil energy assets, and sub-sector clean energy assets based on a quantile time–frequency connectedness framework. Next, this study examines the determinants of total connectedness across different quantiles and time-frequencies, from a large number of candidates including economic and financial factors, cryptocurrency behavior, COVID-19 sentiment, and uncertainty indicators. Moreover, this study calculates the static and dynamic optimal portfolio weights, hedging ratios, and hedging effectiveness for portfolio allocations between ReFi and carbon-energy assets. The study unfolds several key findings. First, the return connectedness among ReFi, carbon, fossil energy, and clean energy markets tend to be relatively weak, with time-varying dynamics influenced by major events and policy reforms. Notably, the pairwise linkages within the ReFi-carbon-energy system become more pronounced under extreme market conditions compared to normal conditions. Second, clean energy markets play a pivotal role as the primary net spillover transmitters across all quantiles and time–frequency domains. Conversely, the spillover patterns within ReFi markets exhibit diversity: Toucan and Klima assets emerge as net transmitters in the time domain and short term under normal market conditions, while Moss and Regen assets serve as net receivers. However, during periods of extreme market shocks, nearly all ReFi assets act as net receivers in the short term, transforming into net transmitters in the medium term. Thirdly, the influence of determinants on total connectedness demonstrates heterogeneity across different time horizons and market conditions, with a more significant impact during economic upturns than downturns. Finally, ReFi assets prove valuable in achieving diversification profits and reducing downside risks within a carbon-energy portfolio, particularly when accounting for tail risks. They also demonstrate effectiveness as hedging tools for carbon-energy assets. Our findings offer policy implications for sustainable investors and policymakers. From the perspective of sustainable investors, our findings highlight the diversification and hedging potential of ReFi tokens in carbon-energy assets. We suggest that investors leverage our quantile time–frequency connectedness results to enhance their diversification or hedging strategies, customized according to their time preferences and the current market conditions. Simultaneously, the distinctions among various attributes of ReFi projects and clean energy sub-sectors should also be thoroughly considered for a targeted investment. We also recommend investors avoid static buy-and-hold strategies and instead dynamically adjust ReFi’s diversification and hedging shares in the presence of changing market conditions, aiming to ensure stable adjusted returns, even under extreme market shocks. Additionally, investors should monitor the changes in key spillover determinants based on different market conditions and time horizons. For instance, during an economic downturn, attention should be directed towards short-term changes in cryptocurrency market sentiment that may impact spillovers and, consequently, the appeal of ReFi assets in a portfolio. From a policymaker’s perspective, our findings indicate relatively decoupled relationships among the ReFi-carbon-energy system, implying that the on-chain carbon credits currently face challenges in competing within the global carbon market, primarily due to a lack of trust in on-chain data. Hence, we recommend that policymakers implement more robust regulatory measures in the ReFi sector to accurately identify low-quality carbon credit projects and address other forms of misconduct. These actions are essential to mitigate the proliferation of false climate solutions and speculative activities in ReFi trading. Moreover, policymakers should consider the heterogeneity of spillover determinants across different time horizons and market conditions, so as to mitigate the cross-market contagion during the crypto bubble period. For instance, during economic upswings, short-term policies need to address geopolitical risks, while medium-term measures should focus on controlling term spreads and guiding COVID-19 sentiment. Some limitations can be addressed in future studies. First, due to the data limitation of the ReFi asset, this study involved a small sample period with a beginning date of November 2021. As more ReFi data (or more mature ReFi practices) become available, new insights might be gained regarding the comovement between ReFi, carbon, and energy markets. Second, the four representative ReFi projects selected in this study are primarily related to carbon markets or incentives for renewable practices. Future research could explore additional types of ReFi projects, such as those aimed at protecting and restoring ecological capital (Kolektivo, Astral Protocol, Curve Labs, dClimate), and those aimed at restoring social justice (Impact Market). Additionally, exploring the interaction between ReFi and ESG investments is intriguing, as it helps unveil their potential synergies, which may foster a transformative shift towards a renewable and sustainable economy.

column1: Probably something: a multi-layer taxonomy of non-fungible tokens
column2: Purpose This paper aims to establish a fundamental and comprehensive understanding of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) by identifying and structuring common characteristics within a taxonomy. NFTs are hyped and increasingly marketed as essential building blocks of the Metaverse. However, the dynamic evolution of the NFT space has posed challenges for those seeking to develop a deep and comprehensive understanding of NFTs, their features and their capabilities. Design/methodology/approach Utilizing common guidelines for the creation of taxonomies, the authors developed (over 3 iterations), a multi-layer taxonomy based on workshops and interviews with 11 academic and 15 industry experts. Through an evaluation of 25 NFTs, the authors demonstrate the usefulness of the taxonomy. Findings The taxonomy has 4 layers, 14 dimensions and 42 characteristics, which describe NFTs in terms of reference object, token properties, token distribution and realizable value. Originality/value The authors' framework is the first to systematically cover the emerging NFT phenomenon. This framework is concise yet extendible and presents many avenues for future research in a plethora of disciplines. The characteristics identified in the authors' taxonomy are useful for NFT- and Metaverse-related research in finance, marketing, law and information systems. Additionally, the taxonomy can serve as an information source for policymakers as they consider NFT regulation.
