Appendix B. Matching Patent Filings to Data on Public and Private Firms
We attempt to gather data on key characteristics of the public and private firms that filed patent applications in Categories 1 through 8 (finance-related innovations). Starting with all of the assignees’ names reported in BDSS, we conduct a name match against CRSP/Compustat, D&B Hoover’s, Standard & Poor’s NetAdvantage, LexisNexis, Bloomberg, company websites, Google, and other publicly available websites.

The name matching process for public and private firms often involves some ambiguity. In some cases, an assignee firm appears in the USPTO database with multiple names. In other cases, different assignee firms may have similar names. To ensure that name matches are valid, we extract from USPTO filings the city and state of each assignee firm and look for an exact name-city-state match. If either the assignee’s name or address does not match, we use additional information from online Google searches, Bloomberg company profiles, or company websites to determine whether the match is valid.34 Another source of ambiguity arises from the fact that assignee firms are occasionally acquired by other firms during the sample period, and both acquirers and targets appear in the databases we use. Given the large number of private assignee firms, tracking the merger and acquisition histories for all firms is difficult. Therefore, we screen for cases in which the assignee’s name contains keywords in its current parent company’s name, and in such cases we use the parent’s information for matching.35 Also, we note that some filers are coded in BDSS as being U.S. firms, but they are in fact universities, foreign companies, or subsidiaries of foreign companies.36 We remove from the sample a small number of filings that correspond to such cases.

For each public and private firm in the name-matched sample, we gather available data on financials, stock prices, SIC and NAICS industry codes, and the firm’s year of founding. The data on stock prices and financials are from CRSP and Compustat. Data on industry codes and founding year are drawn from D&B Hoover’s, Standard and Poor’s NetAdvantage, LexisNexis, Bloomberg company profiles, Google, Bizapedia, and other web-based sources.

Finally, we observe that, due to IPOs and exchange listings, a small number of filers are publicly traded at the disclosure of an application but were privately held when the application was originally filed. Thus, for each patent filing by a public firm, we compare the filing date to the time window of the firm’s available stock prices in CRSP/Compustat. If the filing date does not locate in the time window, we treat the filer as a private firm in the Poisson regression analysis of Table 6.

Appendix C. Using Two-Stage Bootstrapping to Calculate 
-Values (Tables 7 and 9)
As described in Footnote 24, standard tests for significance of means and medians are not appropriate in the context of Table 7 due to measurement error, heteroskedasticity, and nonnormality. Therefore, we develop a two-stage bootstrapping approach for testing whether the means and medians reported in Table 7 are significantly different from zero (see, e.g., Efron (1979), Efron and Tibshirani (1986), and Mooney and Duval (1993) for general treatments of bootstrapping methods).

In the first stage of our procedure, we bootstrap each of the 24 Poisson regressions in Table 6 to obtain distributions of the estimated innovation intensities. Specifically, we resample each regression sample 200 times with replacement to obtain bootstrapped samples, each of which has the same number of (filer-year) observations as the original regression sample. We then conduct the Poisson regressions on each bootstrapped sample and obtain predicted innovation intensities for each filer-year observation. Pooling the results together, we obtain a distribution of 200 fitted innovation intensities (lambdas) for each filer-year observation in each regression.

The second stage involves building upon the fitted lambdas from the first stage to bootstrap innovation values at the filing level. Specifically, within each innovation category in Table 7, we resample the set of patent filings 1,000 times with replacement to create bootstrapped samples. Each bootstrapped sample of filings is then merged with the appropriate set of 200 possible fitted innovation intensities from the first stage. Simulated private values are calculated like in Equation (9) from a filing’s CAR and from each of the 200 fitted lambdas. Note that each of the 1,000 two-stage bootstrapped samples of values consists of 
 observations, where 
 is the number of actual filings in the innovation category. We then calculate the mean and median values from each two-stage bootstrapped sample to obtain distributions of the two statistics. Without assuming normality of the distributions, we can use the nonparametric percentile method (see, e.g., Mooney and Duval 1993), which entails sorting each statistic and using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the lower and upper bounds of the 95% confidence interval. Similarly, we can obtain specific 
-values of the statistics by comparing the bootstrapped distributions of the statistics against zero.

For Table 9, we can also apply two-stage bootstrapping to compute 
-values for tests of whether median industry-level values differ from zero. The bootstrapping procedure used here resembles the one used for Table 7 but differs in two respects: (1) the filing-level bootstrap resampling is conducted within each technology type-industry pair; and (2) the bootstrapped industry-level value impacts are computed using Equation (12) rather than Equation (9).

Appendix D. Permutation Tests (Table 10)
Estimation error from the Poisson regressions in Table 6 could systematically affect the calculation of industry-level values. Therefore, for Table 10 we rely on nonparametric permutation tests (see, e.g., Good 1994) to assess whether the median value impact of disruptive technologies on an industry is significantly more negative than that of nondisruptive technologies. The permutation test for a given industry is implemented as follows. First, we first divide the original sample of all patent filings by individual inventors into those that are disruptive and those that are nondisruptive and then calculate the median values for each group. The difference between the two (i.e., disruptive median minus nondisruptive median) is taken to be the original statistic.

We then compute, for each filing in the original sample, all of the 200 possible industry values using the fitted innovation intensities from the first stage of our two-stage bootstrapping procedure (see Appendix C). We then resample this bootstrapped sample without replacement, randomly assigning 
 observations to an artificial disruptive group and the rest to an artificial nondisruptive group, where 
 is the number of disruptive filings in the original sample. For a given resampling iteration, we calculate the difference in median values of the two artificial groups (i.e., disruptive median minus nondisruptive median). The resampling is repeated 1,000 times to obtain 1,000 permutation statistics. Finally, we locate the original statistic on the permutation distribution. The 
-value for the permutation test is the fraction of the 1,000 permutation statistics that are no larger than the original statistic.

column1: Affordances, experimentation and actualization of FinTech: A blockchain implementation study
column2: Abstract Blockchain, the technology underlying bitcoin, is an emerging financial technology (FinTech) that is poised to have strategic impacts on organizations. Because it is a new phenomenon, there are few studies on blockchain, and those studies have focused mainly on the technology’s potential impacts, whereas how to effectively implement it in an organization remains unknown. Our study intends to fill that gap. Using affordance-actualization (A-A) theory as the theoretical lens, we conducted a case study of blockchain implementation in an organization that has effectively implemented it. We identify three affordances of blockchain in the organization and a process model whereby these affordances are actualized. The process model extends A-A theory by adding an experimentation phase where blockchain’s use cases within the organization are identified, developed and tested through conceptual adaptation and constraint mitigation. Our study makes important theoretical contributions to the literature on A-A theory, blockchain, information technology (IT) implementation, and strategic information systems (SIS). Our study can also help IT practitioners to implement blockchain effectively and extract value from their investment.
column3: Concluding remarks Although the theoretical and practical contributions are rich, they must be considered in light of the limitations. First, a common criticism of single-case studies is the issue of generalizability ( Walsham, 2006 ). Although our findings are generalizable at the analytical level because they are supported by the literature, generalization in a statistical sense is impossible with our research design ( Lee and Baskerville, 2003 ). Future research could achieve statistical generalization by collecting data from multiple cases of blockchain implementation and statistically validating our findings. Second, our study is based on a large organization and thus the findings may not be readily applicable to startups. Startups have fewer formal routines and face less resistance to the adoption of new digital technologies than their larger counterparts ( Chen et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017 ). Future research can investigate how startups effectively implement blockchain and compare the results with our findings. Third, our findings are derived from a case in an emerging economy where the financial infrastructure is underdeveloped. For example, the difficulty faced by SMEs in securing loans from financial institutions may not be as salient in a developed economy. Although our case selection makes the theoretical phenomenon more salient ( Eisenhardt, 1989 ) – FinTech such as blockchain is likely to play a more significant role in regions where the financial infrastructure is immature ( Gupta and Knight, 2017; Morrison, 2016 ) – it would be fruitful to conduct a similar study in a developed economy and compare the results with our findings. The added experimentation phase is a key contribution of this study and more research can be done to further unpack this phase. First, future studies can systematically examine blockchain’s constraints in an organization and investigate how to mitigate them. For example, the distributed database’s inability to process large amount of data constrains efficient processing of transactions. This represents a critical constraint that needs to be mitigated when applying blockchain to streamline transactions. Second, although the extended A-A theory has the potential to be generalized to other emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and virtual reality, these contexts may have their own specific experimentation activities. Further research could apply the extended model to these contexts and compare the results with our findings. Finally, in addition to the designated experimentation phase, our study also observed another type of experimentation whereby advanced affordances were recognized as the basic affordances were actualized. This type of experimentation is a continuous process rather than a designated step. Future research might further examine this experimentation, exploring how it best improves learning and subsequent implementation outcomes.

column1: Initial coin offerings (ICOs) to finance new ventures
column2: In an initial coin offering (ICO), new ventures raise capital by selling tokens to a crowd of investors. Often, this token is a cryptocurrency, a digital medium of value exchange based on the distributed ledger technology. Both the number of ICOs and the amount of capital raised have exploded since 2017. Despite attracting significant attention from ventures, investors, and policy makers, little is known about the dynamics of ICOs. This initial study therefore assesses the determinants of the amount raised in 423 ICOs. Drawing on signaling theory, the study explores the role of signaling ventures' technological capabilities in ICOs. The results show that technical white papers and high-quality source codes increase the amount raised, while patents are not associated with increased amounts of funding. Exploring further determinants of the amount raised, the results indicate that some of the underlying mechanisms in ICOs resemble those found in prior research into entrepreneurial finance, while others are unique to the ICO context. The study's implications are multifold and discussed in detail. Importantly, the results enable investors to more accurately understand crucial determinants of the amount raised (e.g., technical white papers, source code quality, token supply, Ethereum-standard). This reduces the considerable uncertainty that investors face when investing in ICOs and enables more informed decision-making.
column3: 8 Discussion and conclusion 8.1 Discussion of the main results Patents do not seem to constitute an effective signal in the ICO context. This finding is surprising and in contrast to prior research in entrepreneurial finance (e.g., Baum and Silverman, 2004 ; Hsu and Ziedonis, 2013 ). An explanation might be that patents are of limited usability for DLT and blockchain ventures because code (and software) is not generally patentable in various jurisdictions ( EPO, 2018 ). In these jurisdictions, only supporting technologies or very specialized elements of code would be patentable. Closely connected, most blockchain ventures reveal their code freely on GitHub. Because patents require a technological invention that is previously undisclosed, they cannot be obtained if the code is already revealed. Another explanation might be that most ventures are in such early stages that they may not yet have a technology advanced enough to be patented ( Kaal and Dell'Erba, 2018 ; Russo and Kharif, 2017 ). Also, the results indicate that ICO ventures may not consider patents to be an important part of their strategy when raising funds because patents are used so rarely by these ventures. Recent evidence suggests that blockchain patents are often filed by large, established companies, such as Bank of America or IBM ( O'Neal, 2018 ). A final explanation refers to the receiver's ability to interpret and then act upon the signal ( Connelly et al., 2011 ). Because patents may not be as suitable in the ICO context, investors may not be overly familiar with the concept of patents. In contrast, venture capitalists and business angels pay a lot of attention to patents and are familiar with them ( Block et al., 2014 ). A technical white paper may be an effective signal in ICOs in contrast to patents. Interestingly, both patents and technical white papers constitute a detailed description of a venture's technological efforts. However, while they are similar in terms of general content, a technical white paper is less restrictive with respect to legal necessities (e.g., paying fees, involving a patent lawyer, referencing prior knowledge). Most importantly, however, patents require that an invention is previously undisclosed, while a venture can publish a technical white paper to demonstrate its technological capabilities even if it has already revealed its code. To some extent, technical white papers may constitute a substitute for patents in the specific context of ICOs. However, the link between a technical white paper and higher technological capabilities is not completely straightforward. Research in crowdfunding finds that ventures that are able to communicate as precisely as possible raise more funding (e.g., Davis et al., 2017 ; Kim et al., 2016 ; Parhankangas and Renko, 2017 ). This may be reflected in technical language, but it may also lie in being able to describe a highly technical problem in a very nontechnical and understandable way, so that those who have particularly high technological capabilities are actually able to communicate in a nontechnical way. Also, it may be that ventures with low technological capabilities try to hide behind technical language ( Jafery, 2018 ). However, the results do indicate that investors seem to be persuaded by a more technical appearance of a white paper. Finally, a high-quality code is associated with an increased amount of funding. The source code is a relatively objective characteristic that most investor's guides suggest investors assess when making an informed decision about investing in ICOs (e.g., Bhowmik, 2017 ; ICOcrowd, 2018 ; Mulders, 2018 ). While most investors may not understand the detailed technicalities of source code, GitHub presents multiple aggregate metrics that seem to help investors make reference to the venture's underlying technological capabilities.

column1: Enterprise architecture as a responsible data driven urban digitization framework: enabling circular cities in India
column2: Major global urbanization has burdened cities, necessitating circular use of scarce resources, demanding superior service delivery for citizens while expecting increased operational efficiency in governance. Responsible use of smart systems like AI, cloud etc. can address contemporary socio-economic-governance problems. Digital technology can integrate various urban functions into a common service delivery platform. Platform-based public services enable resource sharing and circular economy, building smart communities that treat nations as digital enterprises and their citizens as customers while achieving operational efficiency in governance. Integration of several urban functions into a single platform facilitates ubiquitous urban public service delivery and efficient government operations. Digital platforms can be built by horizontal integration of several technologies like analytics, cloud, IOT, blockchain etc. by breaking silos. Multi-functional urban digitization is complex, especially for a diverse country like India; this also requires responsible use of technologies like AI, cloud etc. which use public data. This necessitates a robust and secure transformation architectural framework. Academia, industry, and policy-makers are currently evaluating an Indian city specific adaptation of Enterprise Architecture as a potential urban digital transformation framework. This study produces a design artifact that defines elements of enterprise architecture adaptation for Indian cities. The study recommends cross industry horizontal integration in business architecture by converging urban functions such as mobility, safety, communities etc. The study also suggests horizontally integrated and responsible use of analytics, IOT and cloud in technology architecture to build a uniform urban public service delivery platform. This research uses design science research methodology, which is popular in practice due to its problem-solving approach and emergence in contemporary IS research.
column3: Major urbanization globally demands a sustainable circular economy towards scarce resource sharing, superior urban public service delivery and operational efficiency in governance. All three requirements need integration of various urban functions. This can be achieved by an integrated digital public service delivery platform that binds various urban functions together, leveraging emerging technologies. Platform-centric governance facilitates better public services, brings operational efficiency in government, and enables cross functional resource sharing. However, the question remains if such a design framework exists that can implement unified urban service delivery platform by responsibly using technologies on public data. A robust urban digital transformation framework and architectural design is needed to ensure strategic and socially responsible use of technologies like cloud, IoT and analytics. The framework needs to be aligned with “whole of government” vision, rather than an isolated and siloed approach in technology implementation, integration, and management. This paper evaluates the fitment of “Enterprise Architecture”, widely used in industry, as a potential digital transformation framework for smart cities of India. This research highlights integration of cross functional urban use-case with several digital technologies in building a unified technology architecture. The proposed city Enterprise Architecture also ensures socially responsible use of technology, such as AI, on public information. This paper finds that cross-industry and cross-functional integration into a single business architecture, integrated horizontally, together with scale and complexity, differentiates a city Enterprise Architecture from traditional Enterprise Architecture within an organization. Business architecture integrated horizontally brings together multiple civic and public services delivered by multiple agencies; this is the most important element of City Enterprise Architecture. This is followed by technical architecture that defines the use of emerging technologies in a uniform service delivery platform to deliver many services to one customer. The need of service integration of various departments, private and public players together, to improve operational efficiency in government is a driver behind city Enterprise Architecture. However, in India, challenges lie in the complexity of the geo-policy variation of requirements and the stakeholder ecosystem of federated governance structure. Active private participation along with government policy and regulatory support can help address these challenges. The study concludes that connected cities should have various functions or enterprise use cases connected to each other. City is an ecosystem of various enterprise use cases. It finds mobility, safety and communities as prime interdependent functions that need digitization on a single technology platform to bring in a sense of connectedness. As a result, these enterprise functions should be digitized with priority in an integrated way to generate connected city benefits. The study also finds connected devices in the form of IOT as fundamental to a connected city. Socially responsible use of analytics in conjunction with IoT to process sensor generated data helps in meaningful data driven governance decisions. Cloud is seen as the default enabling technology which provides elastic computing and data storage capabilities to combined IoT and analytics use cases. A cloud first approach is relevant in a city due to its scale, complexity, shared and collaborative computing capabilities needed for inclusive public service delivery to every citizen. The study also suggests IT architecture to evaluate fitment of horizontal versus vertical approach, to ensure maximum sharing of technology and data across different industry use cases. It also suggests that technology selection should depend on ease of implementation, total cost of ownership, localization capabilities, along with data privacy and responsible use of AI on public data.

column1: Circular Economy and Digital Technology-Enabled Innovation: Advances, Applications and Prospects
column2: There is a major promise in the fusion of the circular economy (CE) principles with digital technologies—such as internet‐of‐things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and blockchain—in transforming innovation, sustainability, and industrial practices. This editorial article discusses this intersection and introduces a special issue dedicated to exploring how digital technologies enable the business transition towards the CE in a variety of ways. We initially provide an overview of the context, scope, and perspectives of this special issue. The discussions in the papers illustrate a breadth of theoretical perspectives and practical approaches considered by the academic community in addressing real‐world phenomena related to CE and digital technology‐enabled innovation. Furthermore, we propose a single integrative conceptual framework of the CE and digital technologies, encompassing both the multi‐level insights from the special issue and future research opportunities. This unified framework is structured along macro (ecosystem/supply chain), meso (organisational), and micro (individual/product) levels, highlighting key findings as well as open research avenues.
column3:
This special issue covers recent theoretical and practical knowledge that provides valuable insights for academics and practitioners concerned with a better understanding of the role of digital technologies in enabling organisational and industrial transitions to the CE. The manuscripts in the special issue collectively emphasise the transformative role of digital technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, AI, and blockchain in advancing CE practices. Based on existing literature and the special issue contributions, we proposed an integrative framework of CE and digital technologies, highlighting different levels of analysis. Building on the framework, we extended a call for further research on micro, meso, and macro levels, as well as across the levels. Given the rapid rate of digital technological advancement, as well as the changing landscape of the CE, our special issue is, of course, a cross-section of knowledge at a single point of time. Nonetheless, the papers in this special issue make valuable contributions to advancing knowledge in the field, and we expect that this focused issue will stimulate continued interest in the area, as well as further research concerning CE and digital technology-enabled innovation.

column1: Artificial intelligence and circular supply chains: framework for applications and deployment from the triple bottom line model perspective
column2: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to automate processes in the manufacturing and supply chain domains, thereby assisting in the attainment of the three pillars of circular economy, namely, recycle, reuse , and reduce . Furthermore, implementing transparent and responsible AI is foundational to achieving sustainable and ethical Circular Supply Chains (CSC). This research explores how AI transparency and responsibility mechanisms are critical enablers for aligning technological advancement with sustainable practices in CSC operations. Furthermore, technologies such as Digital Twins, Industrial Internet of Things, and Blockchain provide frameworks for cyber-physical systems that create smart or intelligent factories and contribute to CSC. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, it became crucial for businesses to begin focusing on Society 5.0, which resulted in the development and deployment of strategies based on the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework, wherein profit is achieved by keeping people and the environment in mind. Through the lens of the TBL framework, this study compiles and organizes AI in CSC research by identifying the enablers of AI as predictive maintenance, real-time monitoring, society 5.0, sustainable development, and cyber-physical systems and barriers like privacy, transparency, etc. We believe that the benefits of AI technology will outweigh its initial costs. Implications for the future and enablers and barriers under the themes of AI in CSC are also discussed.
column3: This study addresses the gap in the literature where AI and CSC were not explored in detail in alignment with the I5.0, society 5.0 for which the TBL model framework is suggested. This framework emphasizes AI to be transparent and responsible by listing multiple challenges of current CS. This study also highlights how this framework will achieve the SDG goals through the three components of TBL model (People, Profit, Planet) which are in alignment with the CE. By making current AI systems more agile, resilient, and sustainable industry can solve the problem of “Black Box” and make it transparent and responsible. I4.0 technologies are embedded in each stage of the SC, generating a mountain of data. This has led to the need for the workforce to get upskilled in digital technologies for efficient working (Agrawal et al., 2022). AI is helping the manufacturing industry prevent downtime, improve production with a digital twin, generate product design, optimize the production process, manage inventory, and enhance safety at the workplace. The merging of cyber and physical space has encouraged researchers to study various dimensions of people, profit, and the planet. AI has helped organizations reduce costs and increase workforce productivity (Benzidia et al., 2021). Sustainable development integrates all three dimensions with concepts like augmented reality-based maintenance applications. SSCM incorporates technologies like smart contracts, blockchain technology, and big data to develop the industrial Internet of Things, providing multiple benefits related to the CE and the 3Ps of the TBL framework. To overcome multiple challenges posed by the current AI in CSC, this study highlights the effectiveness of the TBL framework which will make AI transparent and responsible. 8.1 Theoretical implications This paper has several theoretical implications. Firstly, this study makes a significant theoretical contribution by developing an integrated framework that combines the domains of transparent and responsible AI with the TBL framework in the context of CSC. The framework advances the theoretical understanding of how responsible AI practices serve as fundamental mechanisms for aligning technology with sustainable operations in CSC. By demonstrating how AI transparency enables trust and accountability in supply chain operations, this research expands the theoretical foundation for responsible technology implementation in sustainable business practices. The framework synthesizes concepts from multiple disciplines, including AI ethics, cyber-physical systems, sustainability, and SC management, providing a comprehensive understanding of how transparent and responsible AI can be effectively utilized to optimize CSC operations while maintaining ethical standards. By integrating these diverse perspectives, this study advances theoretical knowledge by offering a holistic framework that captures the complex interactions between responsible technology implementation, sustainable processes, and ethical considerations in the context of CSC. The framework contributes to the theoretical understanding of AI and CPS and provides a foundation for future research on the interplay between these domains and their implications for responsible CSC management. Secondly, this research contributes to the theoretical understanding of trust and transparency in adopting and implementing AI in CSC. It explores the challenges and barriers associated with AI adoption, such as data quality, privacy, and algorithmic accountability. It proposes theoretical models and frameworks that emphasize the importance of trust and transparency. The study highlights the need for XAI and accountable decision-making processes to foster trust among stakeholders in CSC. This research provides a foundation for developing ethical guidelines and best practices for AI-enabled CSC by deepening the theoretical understanding of trust and transparency. The theoretical insights from this study contribute to the growing body of literature on AI ethics and governance, particularly in the context of CSC, and offer a basis for future research on the ethical implications of AI adoption in SC management. Thirdly, this study advances theoretical knowledge by examining the dynamics of human-AI collaboration and decision-making in CSC. It explores the role of AI in enhancing human performance, decision support, and automation while considering the psychological and organizational challenges associated with AI adoption. The research provides theoretical insights into the paradoxes of automation, the need for human intervention, and the concept of XAI to facilitate effective collaboration between humans and AI in CSC. By delving into the complexities of human-AI interaction, this study contributes to the theoretical understanding of how organizations can leverage AI technologies while preserving human judgment and expertise in CSC. The insights gained from this research provide a foundation for developing frameworks and guidelines for optimizing human-AI collaboration in CSC, thereby advancing the theoretical discourse on the integration of AI and human decision-making. Fourthly, this research contributes to the theoretical understanding of sustainable development and CE principles in AI-enabled CSC. It examines how AI can promote resource efficiency, waste reduction, and environmental sustainability in CSC operations. The study highlights the potential of AI in optimizing inventory management, demand forecasting, and SC logistics to minimize waste and maximize resource utilization. By exploring the intersection of AI, sustainability, and CE concepts, this research provides theoretical insights into the transformative potential of AI in promoting a more sustainable and environmentally conscious CSC. The theoretical contributions made by this study pave the way for further research on integrating AI and sustainable practices in CSC, enabling organizations to adopt more responsible and environmentally friendly approaches to SC management. Finally, his study contributes to the theoretical understanding of barriers and challenges associated with adopting and implementing AI in CSC. It identifies critical barriers such as the competency of humans, data quality, understanding of AI benefits, security and privacy concerns, and integration complexity. The research explores these barriers in-depth, shedding light on their theoretical underpinnings and implications for AI adoption in CSC. By offering a comprehensive analysis of the challenges, this study contributes to the theoretical discourse on AI adoption in CSC. It provides a foundation for future research on strategies and interventions to overcome these barriers. The theoretical insights gained from this research contribute to the broader field of AI adoption and implementation, particularly in SC management, and provide valuable guidance for organizations seeking to leverage AI technologies in CSC. This research significantly contributes to understanding how transparent and responsible AI serves as a foundational element in achieving sustainable and ethical CSC operations. By emphasizing the importance of AI transparency and responsibility throughout the supply chain, this study demonstrates how organizations can align technological advancement with sustainable practices while maintaining ethical standards. The findings suggest that implementing transparent and responsible AI is not merely a technical consideration but a fundamental requirement for building trust, ensuring accountability, and achieving long-term sustainability in CSC operations. 8.2 Practical implications From the results of this research, several practical implications are suggested. First, this research offers practical guidelines and recommendations for organizations adopting and implementing transparent and responsible AI in CSC. Based on the synthesized findings, a set of actionable steps and best practices are provided to assist organizations in effectively integrating AI technologies, optimizing processes, and promoting sustainability in CSC. The practical guidelines address challenges related to technology integration, data quality, privacy, and algorithmic accountability, enabling managers and decision-makers to navigate the complexities of AI adoption in CSC and maximize its benefits. Second, this study provides practical contributions by highlighting the importance of ethical, transparent, and responsible AI practices in CSC. Practical strategies and approaches are proposed to address ethical challenges such as privacy violations, discrimination, and biased decision-making. Guidelines for establishing governance mechanisms, promoting transparency, and ensuring accountability are offered, assisting organizations in aligning AI adoption with ethical principles and societal values. The practical insights this research provides enable organizations to mitigate risks, build trust, and ensure responsible AI practices in the context of CSC. Finally, this research offers practical insights and recommendations for leveraging AI to enhance efficiency and sustainability in CSC. Practical strategies are suggested for optimizing processes, reducing waste, and maximizing resource utilization through AI-enabled technologies. The study emphasizes the potential of AI in areas such as predictive maintenance, real-time monitoring, and demand forecasting, providing practical guidance for organizations to improve operational performance, reduce costs, and minimize environmental impact in CSC. By offering actionable recommendations, this research enables organizations to harness the transformative power of AI for sustainable and efficient CSC operations. The practical contributions of this study highlight the critical role of transparent and responsible AI in CSC (CSCs). Shifting from I4.0 to I5.0 requires overcoming barriers related to trust in AI. This study provides insights into transparent and responsible AI by pinpointing key enablers such as sustainable development practices, cyber-physical systems, predictive maintenance, and real-time monitoring. This will help in achieving society 5.0 goals through SDG mapping and addressing the social component of TBL model. This research provides a thorough framework for leveraging AI to boost sustainability and operational efficiency through the merger of cyber and physical space which will help in carbon neutrality, waste management, green material usage (Benzidia et al., 2021), and smart CSC. Practitioners can utilize these insights to ensure that AI systems remain transparent and accountable throughout their application. The business side of this industry will benefit through understanding the importance of making AI transparent to increase the efficiency of processes. Transparent AI can help in overcoming the Black box problem of current AI. Implementation of responsible AI helps in predictive maintenance which provides targeted actions towards business and environment components of TBL model and CE. Moreover, this study emphasizes the importance of addressing challenges related to AI transparency and ethical considerations. The guidance provided is essential for developing AI systems that can be trusted and relied upon for responsible decision-making. Policymakers can draw from these findings to establish regulations and standards that foster ethical AI practices while encouraging innovation in CSCs. This research provides several concrete recommendations for managers implementing AI in CSC operations. First, managers should establish clear governance frameworks for AI transparency, including regular audits of AI decision-making processes and documented explanation mechanisms for stakeholders. We recommend creating dedicated transparency teams responsible for monitoring and explaining AI decisions to various stakeholders, from suppliers to end customers. Second, organizations should implement a phased approach to responsible AI adoption. Managers should begin with smaller, well-defined projects where AI decisions can be easily monitored and explained, gradually expanding to more complex applications as transparency mechanisms prove effective. This includes establishing clear metrics for measuring AI transparency and responsibility, such as decision explanation rates and stakeholder satisfaction scores. Third, managers must invest in developing comprehensive training programs for employees at all levels. These programs should focus not only on the technical aspects of AI systems but also on understanding transparency mechanisms and ethical implications. We recommend quarterly training sessions that combine technical knowledge with practical exercises in explaining AI decisions to various stakeholders. Fourth, organizations should establish formal feedback mechanisms across the supply chain. This includes regular stakeholder surveys, dedicated communication channels for AI-related concerns, and structured processes for incorporating stakeholder feedback into AI system improvements. We recommend monthly stakeholder reviews to assess transparency effectiveness and identify areas for improvement. Fifth, managers should develop specific KPIs for measuring AI transparency and responsibility. These might include metrics such as time taken to provide explanations for AI decisions, stakeholder satisfaction with AI transparency, number of successfully resolved AI-related queries, and rate of stakeholder adoption of AI-driven recommendations Finally, organizations should create cross-functional teams responsible for maintaining AI transparency across the supply chain. These teams should include representatives from operations, IT, sustainability, and stakeholder relations, ensuring a balanced approach to transparent and responsible AI implementation. Regular monthly meetings should be held to review transparency metrics and address emerging challenges.

column1: And No One Gets the Short End of the Stick: A BlockchainBased Approach to Solving the Two-Sided Opportunism Problem in Interorganizational Information Sharing
column2: In interorganizational information sharing, opportunism has two sides: information poaching by the information recipient and information manipulation by the information provider. The threat of such opportunism can entirely preclude business relationships. Prior countermeasures either failed to reliably prevent opportunistic behavior or addressed only one of the two sides. To overcome these shortcomings, we develop three design principles of an information system that facilitates reliable interorganizational information sharing without revealing the underlying data. We instantiate the design in a blockchain system for wear-based leasing contracts for machine tools. We demonstrate and evaluate the efficacy and utility of our design through in-depth interviews with business and technology experts and a survey of 85 machine tool users and 77 lessors in the manufacturing industry. Our study conceptualizes information poaching and information manipulation as two sides of the same problem and shows empirically that opportunities for beneficial business relationships arise when both are addressed together. Our design principles provide a blueprint for a shared information system that prevents both information poaching and information manipulation, thereby enabling new interorganizational information sharing relationships based on data that would otherwise be considered too sensitive to share or too untrustworthy to rely on.
column3:
In this study, we designed, instantiated, demonstrated,
and evaluated an IS that prevents both information
poaching and information manipulation in interorganiza­
tional information sharing. The results have implications
for the research on interorganizational information shar­
ing, opportunism, and blockchain systems. In the follow­
ing, we elaborate on the key contributions of this study as
well as its limitations.
7.1. Contribution
The study provides three key contributions. First, at a
conceptual level, we contribute to the literature on inter­
organizational information sharing by identifying infor­
mation poaching and information manipulation as two
sides of the same problem and showing empirically that
opportunities for beneficial business arise if both forms
of opportunism are addressed simultaneously. In doing
so, we broaden the discourse on opportunism in interor­
ganizational information sharing, which has long
emphasized the importance of each side of opportunism
in isolation (Williamson 1985, Clemons and Hitt 2004,
Lumineau and Quélin 2012, Skowronski and Benton
2018) but has not considered them interdependently.
Our study provided empirical evidence that interorga­
nizational information sharing relationships can be sub­
ject to two-sided opportunism concerns. We showed
that information providers are willing to provide more
sensitive data if their information poaching concerns
are addressed, whereas information recipients are
more willing to rely on provided information if their
information manipulation concerns are addressed.

Thus, countermeasures that prevent both forms of
opportunism simultaneously enable new interorganiza­
tional information sharing relationships based on data
that would otherwise be considered too sensitive to
share or too untrustworthy to rely on. If only one side of
the two-sided opportunism problem is addressed, one
party must always take precautions against the poten­
tial opportunism of the other, such as not sharing sensi­
tive data or not relying on received information. As a
result, business opportunities may remain unexploited.
As Williamson (1993, p. 97) observes: “Huge numbers
of interesting problems of economic organization are
missed or misconstrued if opportunism is ignored or
suppressed.”
By uncovering the two-sided nature of opportunism
in information sharing, we add to prior research aimed
at understanding the triggers for and safeguards against
information poaching (Skowronski and Benton 2018,
Skowronski et al. 2020) and information manipulation
(Lumineau and Quélin 2012). We emphasize the duality
of these threats and the need to consider them simulta­
neously, challenging the prevailing approach of investi­
gating opportunism in interorganizational information
sharing solely as either information poaching or infor­
mation manipulation. Shifting from a one-sided to a
two-sided view, it becomes easier to understand why
some interorganizational information sharing relation­
ships are difficult to establish or fail. According to trans­
action cost economics, business relationships become
increasingly risky and costly as the threat of opportun­
ism grows. Because of the duality of information poach­
ing and manipulation, the risks encountered by both
parties may influence and even exacerbate one another.
Therefore, a two-sided view calls for new theoretical fra­
meworks and empirical investigations to better under­
stand this interdependence of information poaching
and manipulation as well as its consequences.
A second conceptual contribution to the literature on
interorganizational information sharing is our set of

design principles for a shared IS that enables reliable
(i.e., verifiably truthful) information sharing between
business partners without revealing the data underlying
the shared information. The design principles constitute
a generic approach to solving the two-sided opportun­
ism problem in interorganizational information sharing.
Although we have designed a blockchain-based system
to implement the design principles in a technical solu­
tion, there may also be other ways to implement the
design principles based on different underlying technol­
ogies. In fact, blockchain technology has several proper­
ties that are often considered challenging (Beck et al.
2018, Siegfried et al. 2020, Beverungen et al. 2021), and
implementations of our design principles based on
other technologies could potentially have technological
advantages. Nonetheless, our solution goes beyond
existing organizational measures, such as contractual
governance (Dyer 1997, Clarkson et al. 2007), relational
governance (Mayer et al. 1995), and third-party involve­
ment (Lumineau and Quélin 2012, Du and Mao 2018).
Specifically, our solution prevents opportunistic actions
ex ante, whereas existing organizational measures disin­
centivize and discourage such actions or sanction them
ex post. Our work also goes beyond existing technical
solutions proposed for interorganizational information
sharing by simultaneously addressing both information
poaching and information manipulation. Although var­
ious technical approaches have been proposed to
address either side (e.g., Kumar and van Dissel 1996,
Grover et al. 2002, Heller et al. 2004, Hyvärinen et al.
2017), virtually all existing technical approaches that
prevent information poaching are incompatible with
those that prevent information manipulation. Our solu­
tion also complements the idea of multiparty computa­
tion, which avoids this incompatibility. Whereas some
conceptual papers (e.g., Zyskind et al. 2015, Ackerman
et al. 2016) suggest that multiparty computation could
prevent both information poaching and information
manipulation in sufficiently large networks, our solu­
tion is applicable even in networks as small as two orga­
nizations sharing information. The implementation of
IS based on our design principles can therefore impact
interorganizational relationships involving few or
many parties. Given that opportunistic actions such as
information manipulation and poaching are closely tied
to the power distribution in interorganizational relation­
ships (Frazier et al. 2009, Cho et al. 2017), the introduc­
tion of a new IS implementing our design principles
may lead to significant shifts in power dynamics and
potentially trigger evasive maneuvers—an area that
requires thorough investigation in future research.
Third, at a technological level, we contribute to the lit­
erature on blockchain systems by recombining specific
blockchain technology components—private data col­
lections, smart contracts, and joint governance—in
a new way to achieve novel results. Prior work in

industry and academia has used private data collections
to share data among some actors in a larger network,
effectively hiding data from illegitimate access by third
parties but sharing it with legitimate parties (e.g., Gug­
genberger et al. 2020, Amend et al. 2021). In contrast, we
utilize private data collections as a truly private data
store that keeps sensitive data completely confidential
to the information provider while performing prespeci­
fied computations on the data through smart contracts.
The latter have been used to automate conditional trans­
actions based on publicly available data on a blockchain
(Beck et al. 2018, Lumineau et al. 2021). In contrast, we
combine a specific type of smart contract (i.e., smart con­
tracts with nonreversible functions) with private data
collections to compute and share reliably truthful infor­
mation derived from undisclosed, confidential data.
Furthermore, we combine private data collections and
smart contracts with joint governance mechanisms of
blockchain systems to prevent information providers
and information recipients from unilaterally changing
the computation logic or access rights to information.
Thus, we recombine existing technologies in an uncon­
ventional way and show that there is value in doing so.
Our demonstration with professional blockchain and
business experts attests to the efficacy and novelty of
this solution. The specific recombination of existing
blockchain technology components guarantees the
confidentiality of sensitive data for the information pro­
vider and verifiably correct information for the informa­
tion recipient. By offering this recombination, our
study bridges two distinct strands of research on block­
chain systems: managerial blockchain literature, which
explores the effects of blockchain’s transparency and
manipulation resistance on transaction costs and poten­
tial opportunism (e.g., Lumineau et al. 2021), and techni­
cal blockchain literature, which examines the feasibility
of data confidentiality in blockchain networks (e.g.,
Chanson et al. 2019, Ma et al. 2019). Our study draws
attention to the issue of information poaching, which has
largely been overlooked in the managerial blockchain lit­
erature, and emphasizes the need to address information
poaching and manipulation together—an aspect not yet
considered in the technical blockchain literature. In doing
so, our study may foster cross-fertilization between these
strands of research and stimulate the development of
alternative technical solutions and new managerial appli­
cations. Our specific recombination of blockchain tech­
nology components may also be able to solve related
problems where blockchain technology was previously
considered inadequate. For example, although block­
chain technology has been proposed to combat tax fraud
in prior work, its inherent transparency was considered
an “unacceptable property” (Hyvärinen et al. 2017,
p. 445). In this case, our recombination of private data col­
lections, smart contracts, and joint governance could
potentially be used to make a verifiably correct claim

about tax payments without sharing unwanted details
about the taxpayer.
Relatedly, from a practical perspective, we envision
the transfer of our conceptual and technological solu­
tions to areas beyond the bilateral information exchange
in machine tool leasing. For example, another applica­
tion case can be found in supply chain management,
which is an active area of research on opportunism
(Lumineau and Oliveira 2020, Skowronski et al. 2020).
With growing pressure to ensure and certify compliance
with human rights regulations throughout the entire
supply chain (Hofmann et al. 2018), downstream ven­
dors are demanding increasingly detailed information
from suppliers several levels upstream. However, sup­
pliers may be reluctant to provide detailed information
about their own supply chain because of concerns over
the downstream vendors’ potential for backward inte­
gration and encroachment into their business operations
(Lin et al. 2014). Our design principles offer a blueprint
for developing a shared IS that enables suppliers to pro­
vide reliable attestations regarding specific process and
delivery characteristics to downstream vendors without
revealing more information than necessary. Similarly,
other domains of interorganizational relationships, such
as IT outsourcing (Huber et al. 2013, Mathew and Chen
2013), coopetition (Wiener and Saunders 2014), and stra­
tegic alliances (Das and Rahman 2010), could benefit
from our two-sided view of opportunism and the solu­
tions we propose. In IT outsourcing relationships, clients
may manipulate information by setting unrealistic tar­
gets for vendors, whereas vendors may engage in infor­
mation poaching by using confidential client data for
their own purposes (Mathew and Chen 2013). In coope­
tition settings, competing service providers who are
required to cooperate may fear for their own informa­
tion while simultaneously seeking to exploit the infor­
mation shared by their peers (Wiener and Saunders 2014).
In strategic alliances where independent organizations
collaborate in one business area while competing in
others, information exchange and data confidentiality
are particularly challenging issues (Das and Rahman
2010). Our two-sided view of opportunism, along with
our conceptual solutions, may support the development
of multifaceted governance frameworks and informa­
tion systems that address opportunism from both sides.
7.2. Limitations
Our study has several limitations and boundary condi­
tions. First, our solution is most effective when both the
information provider and the information recipient fear
opportunism at the same time. If only one party fears
opportunistic behavior, then simpler technical solutions
than ours may be sufficient to address the one-sided
threat. In addition, our solution requires that both the
information provider and the information recipient
have the necessary technical expertise to effectively

1583

perform their roles in defining appropriate nonreversi­
ble functions (DP2) and in governing and operating the
system (DP3).
Second, jointly defining and approving appropriate
nonreversible functions can be time-consuming and
costly. Therefore, our solution can be expected to per­
form better under relatively stable conditions with infre­
quent changes to the nonreversible functions and the
logic of the smart contract. Appropriate nonreversible
functions must be found for each application context.
We invite researchers to work on such context-specific
metrics that derive meaningful and instrumental infor­
mation from the underlying data without revealing it.
Third, our solution relies on the integrity of the under­
lying blockchain network. Previous research has shown
that the integrity of blockchain networks can be com­
promised by various attacks (Mueller-Bloch et al. 2022).
Our solution for interorganizational information shar­
ing is designed for relatively closed networks of rela­
tively well-known participants who wish to share
information based on sensitive data for business trans­
actions, and it is built on a permissioned blockchain.
Although these characteristics should make our solu­
tion less susceptible to many of the threats prevalent in
open, permissionless blockchain networks (Bakos et al.
2021), the integrity of the blockchain network must be
monitored and enforced.
Fourth, our solution depends on the provision of cor­
rect and unaltered data to the shared IS. Technologi­
cally, our solution is subject to the “first mile problem”
of blockchain systems (Reyna et al. 2018, Lumineau et al.
2021), as preceding systems and their components
(e.g., at the hardware level) could be targeted for
manipulation before the data enter the shared IS. Put
differently, our solution can only prevent both forms of
opportunism—information poaching and information
manipulation—once the data have entered the IS.
Blockchain-enabled hardware that combines sensing
and transaction management could help overcome this
limitation, but it is still under development (Chanson
et al. 2019).
Finally, we evaluated the utility of our solution using
an artificial, rather than a naturalistic, evaluation strategy.
A vignette-based survey with business experts allowed
us to examine the solution’s utility in the diverse contexts
of many organizations. Although DSRM evaluation
guidelines recommend such artificial evaluation strate­
gies for systems with the technical characteristics of our
solution and similarly long and complex implementation
cycles in practice (Venable et al. 2016), artificial evaluation
strategies have limitations. For example, the business
experts in our survey may not have been intimately
familiar with the inner workings of our solution, which
could have biased their utility assessments. Similarly, the
selection process focused on business experts whose pro­
files could be found online. Business experts without

1584

online profiles may evaluate the utility of our solution dif­
ferently. Thus, future work should include additional nat­
uralistic utility evaluations.

8. Conclusion
The threat of opportunistic behavior in the form of infor­
mation poaching and information manipulation is a
persistent problem for interorganizational information
sharing. We conducted a design science study to
address the two-sided problem of opportunism. We
derived three design principles for IS that compute
shared information from sensitive data in a confidential
and manipulation-resistant manner, enabling the reli­
able use of sensitive data for information sharing with­
out revealing the data. We instantiated, demonstrated,
and evaluated our design principles using blockchain
technology in the domain of wear-based leasing con­
tracts for machine tools, leveraging access to a multifirm
research consortium. Our study is one of the first to
address the need for technical countermeasures against
the potential opportunism of both information provi­
ders and information recipients in interorganizational
information sharing based on sensitive data, thereby
providing a springboard for future research in the
domains of interorganizational information sharing,
opportunism, and blockchain systems.
Endnotes
1

We use the terms data and information following Floridi (2005). We
use data for any digital record and information for meaningful, wellformed, and contingently truthful data that convey a certain mean­
ing in a specific context (Floridi 2005). In principle, both data and
information can be shared. Sensitive data are data from which infor­
mation can be derived in certain contexts whose availability to
others runs counter to the data owner’s business interests.
2

We use the term recombination following the work of Yoo et al.
(2010), Henfridsson et al. (2018), and Hund et al. (2021), where it
refers to the creation of valuable novel artifacts through the combi­
nation of existing ones in new ways.
3

In contrast to other forms of opportunism in interorganizational
relationships, such as shirking (Skowronski et al. 2020) and forced
renegotiation of contracts (Wathne and Heide 2000), information
poaching and information manipulation strictly relate to the infor­
mation level in an interorganizational relationship.
4

We initially proposed four design principles. We appreciate the
input of the anonymous reviewers and associate editor, which
emphasized that one of our initial design principles, source-to-sink
protection, was presented in prior research (e.g., Chanson et al.
2019) and constitutes a key boundary condition of our system rather
than a design principle (see Section 7).
5

column1: The Blockchain Newsvendor: Value of Freshness Transparency and Smart Contracts
column2: Motivated by blockchain applications in the fresh produce industry, we consider a newsvendor problem in which a retailer faces stochastic and freshness-dependent consumer demand. The retailer can adopt blockchain technology to have more transparent information on the freshness of supply. We quantify the value of blockchain-enabled freshness transparency by deriving closed-form expressions for the retailer’s expected profit growth and food waste reduction brought by blockchain adoption. Using publicly available data, we provide a numerical example illustrating that for Walmart’s strawberry business in the United States (which is about only 4% of Walmart’s fresh produce sales), blockchain can increase annual profit by [Formula: see text] million while eliminating 23 million pounds of food waste annually through operational improvements. Despite this substantial value for the retailer, blockchain adoption can decrease the expected profit of the retailer’s supplier. We design a family of threshold-type smart contracts contingent on a blockchain-based freshness consensus and examine when such contracts offer a win-win proposition to the retailer and the supplier. Moreover, when the retailer offers freshness-based price discounts, we find that less fresh supply leads to less food waste. In contrast, when the supplier adjusts the wholesale price based on freshness, less fresh supply causes more food waste. We also generalize our findings to the cases of (i) dual sourcing, (ii) noisy measurements in the Internet of Things sensors feeding data into blockchain, and (iii) the retailer’s culling processes. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.02949 .
column3:
Our paper presents a framework for analyzing the benefits of blockchain-enabled transparency in fresh produce supply chains. Our analysis reveals a number of managerial implications for grocery retailers seeking
to adopt blockchain technology. First, we show that by adopting blockchain, grocery retailers can better
match supply with demand so as to increase profits and reduce food waste. In particular, we show that the
value of freshness transparency is the highest for fresh produce that generates stable consumer demand
but is perishable and vulnerable to storage conditions (e.g., temperature). Some of the products for which
blockchain can provide substantial value are berries, avocados, lettuce, kale, and protein such as beef and
fish. Second, our results indicate that adopting blockchain could decrease the profit of a retailer’s supplier,
even when the supply chain is better off. In such a case, the retailer can design a smart contract to compensate the supplier. By doing so, the retailer can filter out unsatisfied products and maintain profitability.
Meanwhile, the supplier can also gain from blockchain adoption. Third, we find that when the retailer who
adopts blockchain jointly optimizes the retail price and order quantity based on freshness information, the
retailer generates more food waste when supplied products are fresher. To mitigate the adverse effect on
food waste, the retailer can set an upper limit on the retail price to avoid surge pricing. In addition, we analyze the case of a supplier with the market power to set the wholesale price, in which food waste increases
with less fresh supply.
As a first study on the impact of blockchain-enabled freshness transparency and smart contracts, our
framework can be further generalized in future research. For example, one direction is to study the supplier
incentives to adopt blockchain in dual sourcing. Another direction is to investigate how smart contracts
can be designed to automate freshness-based wholesale pricing decisions in addition to ordering decisions.
Other future directions include studying the simultaneous pricing decisions of the retailer and supplier
based on freshness transparency. We show that the freshness-based pricing decisions of the retailer and

26

the supplier have opposite effects on food waste, and it would be interesting to explore the joint impact of
freshness-based retail and wholesale prices.

column1: Supporting Intellectual Property Protection: Blockchain Technology as a Catalyst for Open Innovation
column2: As the access, sharing, and transfer of intellectual property (IP) are central to open innovation (OI) projects, preventing the leakage of IP is critical. The emergence of blockchain has prompted organizations to seek support from this technology to protect IP. However, the potential applications, challenges, and benefits for OI projects at the technology/legal interface are not well understood. This article shows that while blockchain technology is not the solution to all IP protection problems, it has the potential to significantly improve the status quo by creating an immutable record of the existence, integrity, and ownership of files at specific points in time. It also offers guidance to practitioners on how to extend and complement their existing IP protection, ultimately enhancing their negotiating leverage and collaboration with OI partners.
column3: This study explores novel tools to support IP protection by combining encrypted storage with a public blockchain. We map the workflow of these tools, clarify their scope, and explore the potential impact on innovators’ IP strategy and OI practices. While use cases are still rare and difficult to access, we collect empirical data from providers and users to understand the scope and limitations of these tools. Our results show that relying on blockchain technology is not a panacea for ending all IP protection problems but holds the potential to significantly improve the status quo by creating an immutable record of files’ existence, integrity, and possession.Managerial Implications: How to Get Started?Blockchain technology offers innovative firms opportunities to extend and complement their existing IP protection, ultimately leveraging their negotiating leverage and OI projects. Blockchain-based records can reduce appropriation concerns and impact innovators’ IP strategies by streamlining the filing of registrable IP rights and supporting the enforcement of non-registrable IP rights. In addition, it can facilitate the establishment of OI projects and help surmount well-known obstacles in the course of OI projects, such as the distribution of jointly created IP and the reluctance to share IP.Using blockchain technology is not always useful or easy. Therefore, managers should carefully evaluate the trade-offs and determine whether and how to implement blockchain technology. The following five key steps provide guidance for the evaluation and implementation:•Evaluation of IP Strategy and Capabilities—IP rights can create and sustain a competitive advantage if strategically managed. Both formal (e.g., patenting) and informal (e.g., technological lead-time advantage, signaling seriousness about IP through blockchain documentation) mechanisms are relevant for IP protection strategy. Furthermore, an overarching IP strategy does not solely include measures to protect, but also to commercialize IP. Blockchain should not be used in isolation, but as a component of the overarching IP strategy. Thus, innovators should evaluate how blockchain technology might leverage the potential of IP protection to extend and contribute to their IP strategy. Since blockchain-based IP protection provides the most direct benefits for non-registrable rights, managers will need to discuss the current and future role of non-registrable rights in their IP strategy. When non-registrable rights play a negligible role, managers should refrain from investing in them. Furthermore, we advise innovators, particularly in smaller firms, to carefully evaluate their firm-specific IP contingencies and capabilities. For instance, the users in our sample differ considerably in size and experiences with IP protection. Hence, their resources dedicated to IP protection, the maturity of their IP strategy, and the tools operationalizing their IP strategy differ accordingly. Blockchain-based IP protection can have a more fundamental meaning for individual entrepreneurs and startups since it acts as an initial protective layer—from “having nothing” to “having something.”•Evaluation of OI Projects—Managers should closely analyze their existing and upcoming OI projects. Depending on the project type and related partnership, the involvement of IP and its protection will differ. Managers will need to ask: What type of OI projects and partnerships do we have? What type of IP is involved in these projects? How can this IP benefit from blockchain-based protection? Moreover, managers should carefully align their OI projects with their IP strategy to reap the benefits of blockchain-based IP protection. While the answer to the question of whether to use blockchain technology contains a large gray area, the simple evaluation matrix shown in Figure 2 is a starting point for companies to discuss the trade-offs and applicability of blockchain-based IP protection for their IP strategy and OI projects. The matrix represents a propensity rather than a clear binary decision tree. Once the firm decides to consider blockchain to support IP protection, steps 3 through 5 follow.•Scouting and Selecting a Blockchain-Based IP Protection Tool That Is Fit for the Purpose—There are many companies and platforms on the market that offer mature solutions for blockchain-based IP protection, such as Bernstein.io (founded in 2016) or IPwe (founded in 2018). Although the tools offer the services described in the findings section, the exact scope of the products offered often differs due to unique selling points and specific features. For example, IPwe offers additional features such as estimates of the financial valuation of the IP portfolio. Therefore, we recommend selecting a blockchain-based IP protection tool that meets the needs of the focal firm’s IP strategy and OI projects.•Gradual Implementation of Blockchain-Based IP Protection Tools—Since users and providers are obliged to wait for upcoming court decisions and legislation, they can primarily overcome obstacles that do not pertain to the remaining legal uncertainty. Innovators and innovating firms should start using the tool internally, relying on trial versions to determine whether it fits their firm-specific needs before expanding it to external stakeholders.•Development of Communication Guidelines—According to our informants, convincing other OI partners to use a relatively new technology might be an uphill battle. While financial reasons are a minor consideration, they encounter much skepticism about blockchain technology and the accompanying legal uncertainties. Thus, we strongly recommend developing a concise communication guideline when using the tool. This includes communicating the use, required changes, and potential consequences to internal stakeholders, such as an IP department in larger firms or co-founders in startups, and external stakeholders, particularly partners in OI projects. Fostering communication and exchange with associated departments and partners is necessary to align stakeholder interests. While our study was conducted in Europe, where IP enforcement is strong, these managerial recommendations are not only valid, but even more suggested when doing business in countries with weak IP protection, such as China, India, and Russia. Some of the claimed benefits of blockchain for non-registrable rights (in countries with strong IP enforcement) can also be reaped when IP enforcement is weak, thereby improving de facto IP protection. For example, an IP infringement recorded on blockchain may be easier to detect. While the breach may have occurred and damage may have been done, companies can take immediate action and refrain from doing business with the offending party in the future. Also, in countries with weak IP enforcement, plaintiffs’ attorneys require strong evidence of IP infringement and damages,45 which blockchain-based documentation can provide.Open in ViewerFigure 2. Evaluation matrix for trade-offs, applicability, and benefits of blockchain-based IP protection.Some Considerations for the Legal and IP SystemsThe assessment of the current IP system is puzzling. On the one hand, it is under pressure. The patent system, for example, dates back to the fifteenth century and largely follows the same principles, while being confronted with twenty-first-century technologies that allow data to be shared with extreme ease. As a result, many critics have predicted the end of the existing system, arguing that it is outdated46 or even rejecting its basic principles.47 On the other hand, especially in Europe, patents enjoy an excellent reputation; their signaling and marketing effects go beyond their protective purpose.48 Patents are therefore very popular.There is still legal uncertainty in Europe about whether courts will recognize blockchain evidence. While there are several laws and court decisions recognizing blockchain evidence in the United States and China,49 the situation in Europe is more fragmented. However, at least three indicators point in the direction of the recognition of blockchain evidence in European courts: the blockchain-related initiatives and conferences by IP institutions such as the European Patent Office; the case-by-case acceptance in France and Italy; and the related existing recognition of digital signatures in the EU.50 Despite these indicators, some managers are still reluctant to implement the tool before a final court decision or legislation is in place.We argue that new technologies put pressure on the IP system and at the same time offer new ways to support it. In particular, blockchain technology affects the IP system at the institutional and user levels. With respect to the former, de Rassenfosse and Higham51 propose that distributed ledger technologies can support the work of patent offices and fundamentally change the patent system by decentralizing it. This decentralization could rectify several well-documented shortcomings, such as inefficiencies in the patent examination process.52

column1: Less trust, more truth: Implications and design choices for business models and platform ecosystems in the age of Web3
column2: Business model literature, while insightful, primarily focuses on the Internet and Web 2.0 contexts. The emergence of pioneering digital technologies, especially the Web3 anchored by blockchain, necessitates reevaluating business model paradigms, particularly those of platform business models within related ecosystems. This study delves into blockchain's unique affordances, investigating how they mold novel Web3 business model patterns and integrate into specific platform ecosystems. We scrutinize the characteristics, trajectories, and synergies of value creation and capture. Using a mixed-methods approach involving 171 interviews and a subsequent sample of 126 Web3 ventures, we delineate a taxonomy of Web3 business model dimensions, clustering emergent decentralized platform ecosystems into pertinent archetypes. Our theoretical model delineates how blockchain affordances influence these configurations, emphasizing the dynamic between a platform's nucleus and its fringes. We highlight Web3 platform design choices leaning towards data sovereignty, emphasizing how the degree of blockchain integration within platform governance—leading to information symmetry and platform disintermediation—transitions digital trust to what we term as digital truth . • Blockchain-based platforms enable new decentralized governance structures in platform ecosystems. • Two distinct Decentralized platform archetypes are identified: Federated and Web3 platform ecosystems. • Platform-inherent token is crucial for incentivization and coordination schemes in fully decentralized platform ecosystems. • Blockchain affordances offer innovative pathways for overcoming B2B platform challenges. • Our study provides managerial insights for designing blockchain-based platform strategies.
