column1: A critical insight into the intersection of sustainability and technology
column2:
Purpose
This paper aims to explore the role of blockchain (BCT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in enhancing and incentivizing environmentally responsible, socially inclusive and economically viable tourism practices within the hospitality and tourism (H&T) industry.

Design/methodology/approach
This study is based on a critical reflection research approach that enables a synthesis of information derived from existing literature's insights and the authors' experiences and observations. By examining frameworks and theories in the literature, critical reflection also helps develop a more comprehensive understanding of the topic.

Findings
This study portrays how BCT could be used to track the sustainability credentials of tourism providers and how AI can optimize energy usage in hotels. This study depicts how adopting technology-driven sustainable practices in the H&T industry can increase profitability, improve reputation, compliance with regulations, efficiency and a better guest experience.

Practical implications
The study suggests targeted actions and policy frameworks that can be tailored to different stakeholder groups (hospitality businesses, policymakers and tourists) to overcome barriers and maximize the positive societal and environmental impacts of adopting BCT and AI for sustainable tourism.

Originality/value
The originality of this study lies in its ability to offer new perspectives and novel recommendations on the diverse uses of AI and BCT in the context of sustainable tourism. Furthermore, the study provides strategic and policy elements (Targeted actions and policy frameworks) for stakeholders to integrate sustainable tourism practices using BCT and AI successfully. This study differs from earlier review studies that primarily focused on adopting emerging technologies and ignoring the sustainability angle in the use of technology.
column3:
This critical reﬂection study revolves around the growing importance of technologies like
BCT and AI in fostering sustainability in H&T businesses. The study illustrates how
including targeted programs and frameworks for different stakeholder groups can help
promote sustainable tourism using AI and BCT. Furthermore, our study is also aligned with
some suggestions by Liu and Dong (2021) in the context of BCT in promoting sustainability.
They explored the potential applications of BCT in sustainability marketing, knowledge
management, and service improvement for tourism and hospitality ﬁrms. The current study
covers the different strategic and policy elements that can assist the stakeholders in fostering
sustainable tourism practices. The ﬁndings of this study are also in line with the studies of
Kashem et al. (2023), which state that BCT can tackle the challenges of managing waste in
the H&T business and monitor excessive energy usage in the industry. Another study by
Joshi et al. (2023) presents a viewpoint similar to ours that states the effectiveness of BCT
for effective supply chain management. Other common elements in previous studies are
using BCT to promote local economy and culture (Erol et al., 2022). A study by

Dadkhah et al. (2022) used the Delphi study approach. It stated that BCT can be an effective
medium to address challenges like fraud and ineffective processes in the tourism industry. It
also highlighted that effective BCT implementation can achieve security and transparency in
the tourism industry. Furthermore, a study by Kashem et al. (2023) conducted a systematic
literature review on the role of BCT in tourism businesses. It illustrated beneﬁts like trust,
effective supply chain management and transparency using BCT.
Previous studies mainly focus on human behavior and social phenomena in adopting
blockchain technology (BCT) for sustainability in tourism. Some research uses theories like
technology diffusion and decision-making to highlight BCT and AI's growing relevance in
hospitality. The necessity of technology for sustainable solutions is becoming more popular
among researchers. However, fewer studies apply theories to BCT adoption for
sustainability, with only 26% being theoretically based (Joshi et al., 2023). This indicates
BCT for sustainability is still developing. Future research can integrate theories from various
ﬁelds, such as software engineering for system development (Afaq et al., 2023) and social
sciences for understanding user perceptions. This paper advises the H&T sector on using
technology to enhance sustainability, improve operations and enrich guest experiences.

7. Implications
7.1 Theoretical implications
The current research ﬁndings respond to multiple calls from the literature on sustainability
and technology integration in the H&T industry. The ﬁrst is a research call from Treiblmaier
(2021) to explore further how emerging technologies can promote sustainability. In response,
our results show that BCT and AI enhance sustainable practices by improving transparency,
optimizing resource use, and facilitating customer engagement. Additionally, the research
addresses gaps identiﬁed by Erol et al. (2022) and Sharma et al. (2021) regarding the
applications of digital technologies in achieving sustainability goals. Speciﬁcally, our
ﬁndings illustrate successful examples demonstrating how these technologies can lead to
measurable improvements in sustainability outcomes. Furthermore, we highlight the
importance of stakeholder acceptance in adopting these technologies by utilizing established
frameworks such as the TPO framework and the Diffusion of Innovation Theory. Overall,
the research responds to these calls and contributes to the theoretical understanding of
integrating sustainability and technology in the H&T sector.
7.2 Practical implications
The current study's ﬁndings respond to several calls from the literature on integrating the
latest technologies like BCT and AI in the H&T industry. One such call is the necessity to
provide technological solutions for managing environmental issues and promoting
sustainability practices in the H&T industry. This study addresses Rashideh (2020) concern
regarding why H&T companies should use BCT. The study also tries to answer the question
by Acikgoz et al. (2024) about what barriers different stakeholder groups can face in
accepting BCT and AI in the H&T industry and what potential capabilities of these
technologies can be used to promote sustainability. This study illustrates how different
stakeholders - hotel businesses, policymakers, and tourists can incorporate BCT and AI to
promote environmentally responsible, economically practical, and socially embracive
tourism options. BCT, for example, can be used by the hospitality industry to track the
provenance of sustainable products, guaranteeing environmentally favorable methods.
Policymakers can foster the use of BCT-based certiﬁcation systems for upright tourism
operators, promoting ethical behavior.

7.3 Limitations and suggestions for future research
This study poses limitations in terms of its generalizability to other industries. Moreover, the
emphasis on BCT and AI leaves behind the role of different technologies like IoT and

using particular keywords to address the research questions is another limitation. Given the
speciﬁc keywords the authors employed in their research, there's a chance that some items
might have been overlooked in the screening process. The limited availability of literature on
the relationship between technology and sustainability in the H&T industry highlights the
necessity for more extensive investigations. Therefore, future studies could address
signiﬁcant research questions, such as the following:
RQ3. How can integrating technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT),
Blockchain, and Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) enhance operational efﬁciency and
guest experiences in sustainable tourism practices?
RQ4. What role does community-based tourism play in achieving sustainable
development goals (SDGs), and how can local communities effectively leverage

column1: Blockchain technology for building buyer-supplier trust and transparency in supply chains: An experimental study on P2P online marketplace vendors
column2: This study aims to examine blockchain technology's impact on transparency and trust within the context of the buyer-supplier relationship of vendors and P2P (peer-to-peer) platforms. This research employs a scenario-based experimental design and an online dataset comprised of 243 vendors on an online P2P platform to empirically test the effect of blockchain features. The findings indicate that the relationship between blockchain features and the vendors' willingness to continue selling is fully mediated by the vendors' perceptions of transparency of the P2P platform and their trust in it. Moreover, switching costs moderate the relationship between trust and willingness to continue selling on the P2P platform, but not the one between transparency and willingness. Unlike the previous research, this study examines the relationship with online platforms from the perspective of vendors (B2B), rather than end customers (B2C). This research contributes to social exchange theory and resource dependence theory, as well as to the emerging research at the intersection of business relationships in P2P online platforms, microenterprises, and emergent technologies. Further, we augment supply chain literature on buyer-supplier trust by offering insights into the impact of blockchain.
column3:
7. Limitations and future research
The results of this study should be interpreted by considering the
following limitations. First, having an experience of damaged/lost cargo
claim and selling internationally were the inclusion criteria for this
study. On the one hand this provided a rich context testing the relationship between the vendors and the P2P platform, but on the other
hand it might limit the generalizability of the results. Future research
could examine vendors’ perceptions of trust and transparency by
considering both domestic and international vendors with and without
damaged/lost cargo claim experience and compare the results. Second,
this research focuses only on a single P2P selling platform and vendor
perspective. Additional studies and further investigation are required to
draw consensus about the results across various platforms and explore
the impact of blockchain adoption on both vendor and buyer experiences. Third, we used a post-test only control group between-subjects
design, which does not include measuring pre-existing perceptions of
the participants. Although the randomization in our design helps mitigate the impact of any pre-existing perception by ensuring that such
biases are equally distributed across both groups, experimental designs
controlling for preexisting perceptions might yield better results. For
this purpose, future studies could use the pretest-posttest control group
design and measure the preexisting perceptions of the participants.
Fifth, our scenario does not allow us to establish which blockchain
features are more important, which can be tested in future studies and
might provide valuable insights for managers. Sixth, our study is limited
in empirically testing why blockchain features may not lead to higher
perceptions of trust and transparency. Moreover, future studies can
improve our switching cost items to better align with micro-enterprises.
Future studies could explore alternative dependent variables beyond
willingness to continue selling, taking into account network effects and
the high switching costs associated with platform-based businesses.
Additionally, while this study contributes to understanding the role
of trust and transparency in P2P platforms, future research can further
deepen this understanding by integrating other variables of social exchange theory into our proposed model. Specifically, future research can
employ reciprocity, support, commitment, fairness, justice (Cropanzano
& Mitchell, 2005), satisfaction, cooperation (Lambe et al., 2001),
collaboration (Davis-Sramek et al., 2022), attractiveness, and power
balance (Tanskanen, 2015).
Finally, future research may apply transaction cost theory to further
explain the role of trust and transparency in P2P platforms. By
enhancing transparency, limiting opportunistic behavior and ensuring
compliance with standards through smart contracts, blockchain technology can potentially reduce transaction costs (Schmidt & Wagner,
2019). Given the call for research on applying transaction cost theory to
e-commerce platforms (Cuypers et al., 2021), future research can
explore the impact of blockchain within this context.

column1: Green cryptocurrency and business strategies: Framework and insights from a stewardship literature review
column2: This study critically evaluates the extant research on green cryptocurrency (GC). It incorporates the systematic literature review (SLR) approach of research executed through the analysis and compilation of 54 relevant studies. The focus is on identifying and interpreting the thematic foci and existing gaps about GC to inform potential areas of future research. The SLR findings aggregated the research around key themes: interconnectedness, portfolio diversification, environmental impact, green blockchain, behavioral impact, and regulatory policy. Additionally, the study develops the research profile of the selected studies in terms of data analysis methodology, research findings, variables investigated, and critical knowledge gaps in the literature corpus. The study proffers an integrated framework and actionable inferences for supporting the merits of novel research and regulatory project applications in GC. It is crucial for understanding and advancing research in the GC domain, which currently has scant academic literature and efforts toward sustainable investment.
column3: Cryptocurrencies are popular investment tools today, but their environmental impact has become a key concern given the vast energy consumption and environmental risks. The emergence of GCs has implied the potential for clean energy and carbon footprint reduction, as clean cryptos have a more vital linkage with the green economy and other green assets (Ren & Lucey, 2022a; Sharif et al., 2023) and cryptocurrency algorithms are now more environmentally-friendly and low-carbon (Shao et al., 2023). The emergence of new types of cryptocurrencies, such as green and Islamic cryptocurrencies, can contribute to the ongoing evolution of the cryptocurrency market and influence the development of new technologies and applications. (Mnif & Jarboui, 2021). To the best of the authors' knowledge, no current SLRs have talked about GC in the digital currency domain. The current study addresses that gap by providing insights into the contribution of various researchers in this domain and theme-based critical gaps in the literature. We selected a specific type of cryptocurrency as there is a dire need to reduce the carbon footprint and achieve carbon net zero. By contrast, research has focused chiefly on cryptocurrency as a primary study area, with less attention accorded to GC. This is indicative of a requirement to stimulate research in the field. The study meticulously adheres to the SLR approach to discover, combine, and assess the 54 papers on the subject to uncover their research attributes and thematic foci. The six themes found through content analysis are diversification, interconnectedness, green blockchain, behavioral impact, environmental and social impact, and regulatory policy.Furthermore, we have created a framework using the stakeholder's theory approach to illustrate the intricacies of the topic and the various aspects that reduce the carbon footprint. The study also highlights that engaging in collaboration with stakeholders can create more efficient and enduring solutions for businesses. The study not only presents the current status of research in the field but also identifies gaps in existing studies and posits tangible suggestions in the form of theme-based potential research questions, paving the way for future empirical investigations. This study contributes to a panoptic understanding of GC research findings and identifies gaps and areas that warrant more attention. It can guide future research and inform stakeholders and policymakers on potential strategies for sustainability promotion in the GC ecosystem.

column1: Generative Blockchain: Transforming Blockchain from Transaction Recording to Transaction Generation through Proof-of-Merit
column2: ABSTRACT This paper proposes a new type of blockchain, generative blockchain, that aims to transform the conventional blockchain from the focus of transaction-recording to transaction generation. The key to our design of generative blockchain lies in a novel consensus mechanism, proof-of-merit (PoM), that is uniquely designed for environments where businesses must solve complex problems before transactions find their place on the blockchain. PoM integrates the generation and recording of transactions within a unified blockchain system, differing fundamentally from prevailing consensus mechanisms whose primary objective is to record existing transactions. Specifically, PoM delegates the task of solving complex transaction-generating problems to a pool of independent problem solvers, whose solutions govern the generation of transactions, and selects the winning solutions based on merit. The winning solvers register these transactions onto the blockchain and are rewarded accordingly. We introduce a decentralized control parameter (DCP) to balance two key performance metrics of a generative blockchain: efficiency and equity. The applicability of our designed generative blockchain is illustrated through a ridesharing context, where a group of matchers (solvers) take on the task of matching riders with drivers. We demonstrate PoM’s performance and nuanced properties using agent-based simulation and explore how to find the proper value of DCP toward achieving a desirable balance of efficiency and equity in a generative blockchain. We also implement a prototype blockchain using PoM mechanism to validate its feasibility and evaluate its performance.
column3:
This paper introduces a novel generative blockchain framework, seeking to integrate the transaction generation process into the conventional transaction recording process facilitated by extant blockchain systems. Towards this end, we propose a general-purpose blockchain consensus mechanism, PoM. PoM solicits solvers to solve users’ complex problems that determines transaction generation and selects a winning solution based on merit of the solutions. The selected solution governs generating and recording of these transactions onto the blockchain. In contrast, existing consensus mechanisms, such as PoW, PoS, and PoUW, are used to record existing transactions but not generate new transactions. Even when the computing power is being used for solving a problem, as in the case of PoUW, the problem is being solved for an external party rather than the problem at hand.

Furthermore, PoM effectively balances efficiency and equity. It factors in the historical quality of each solver’s contributions when choosing the winner, thus entailing a merit-based system; it assures equity by leveraging DCP to reduce the likelihood for dominant solvers to monopolize the wins, preserving the decentralization principle of Blockchain. The implications of varying DCP on PoM’s performance were explored through ABS, demonstrating the inevitable trade-off between efficiency and equity. Our simulation also established the appropriate DCP level from a system designer’s perspective, revealing that the desired balance between equity and efficiency can be contingent on various circumstances.

Our study contributes to blockchain literature. First, our proposed framework of generative blockchain has the potential to transform the blockchain industry, by switching the focus from transaction recording to transaction generation in complex environments. Second, we devise a new consensus mechanism to decentralize the task of transaction generation. In so doing, we allow solvers to solve a meaningful social-benefiting (business) problem as opposed to miners who only solve an energy-wasting puzzle in PoW. PoM goes beyond the extant consensus mechanism from record-keeping of the existing transactions to providing a solution that allows for new transactions to be created. This represents a significant leap in the design of consensus mechanisms. Third, our PoM mechanism, as a merit-based system, determines the winner based on the quality of the solution a solver provides. As such, it diverts the precious computing resources towards providing high-quality solutions, thus improving sustainability of blockchain. Fourth, our use of ABS offers several new insights on the performance and properties of PoM. For example, it answers “what-if” questions, such as what proper levels of DCP one should choose to best balance efficiency with equity under a specific business environment.

column1: Blockchain innovations for addressing pharmaceutical counterfeit in the global supply chain: a PLSâ€“ANN approach
column2: There are obvious benefits of the adoption of blockchain innovation within the supply chain of pharmaceutical businesses, but there are significant obstacles hindering widespread adoption. This research aims to explore the relationships between transparency and three variables: reliability, responsiveness, and agility of the pharmaceutical supply chain. Besides, we examined the impacts of these three factors on the perceived value of blockchain. The influence of the perceived value on the blockchain adoption intention was also examined. Furthermore, this research examines the relationship between the intention to adopt blockchain technology and the perceived medicine safety. A new model of adoption is developed based on the Resource-Based View (RBV) and evaluated from the perspectives of stakeholders in Malaysian pharmaceutical and healthcare companies. The model is analyzed using two sequential approaches of Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). The findings revealed that supply chain transparency positively influences perceived reliability, responsiveness, and agility. These factors positively influence perceived value, which influences the adoption intention. Moreover, the results demonstrated that the adoption of blockchain can lead to safer medicines throughout the supply chain.
column3: In this research, we explored the influence of the transparency of blockchain in the pharma SC on several factors, including agility, responsiveness, and reliability. We also checked the impacts of these constructs on the perceptions of the stakeholders of the added value of blockchain. The impacts of perceived value on the intention to adopt and the following impact of the intention to adopt on the perception of medicine safety were also inspected. To assess the proposed hypotheses, we used PLS-SEM. On one side, the PLS-SEM results highlighted the significance of all hypothesised relationships, among which the link between SCT and AGI is the most significant. We also employed an ANN to rank the significance of the impacts of all factors on medical safety. As the ANN’s results revealed, the perception of medicine safety is triggered mainly by RES, REL, and AGI. 8.1. Theoretical contribution This study attempts to address the research questions that explore the complex relationship between SC transparency, SC reliability, SC responsiveness, and SC agility of blockchain, while also explaining the impact of these factors on the perceived value, adoption intention, and perceived medical safety. The study aims to fill the gap in the literature through the theoretical and empirical support for the suggested hypotheses. By integrating these factors into a theoretically-based model and examining them empirically, the significance of these factors can be deemed acceptable, and research implications can be drawn. Although researchers have shown increasing attention to the adoption of blockchain on both the individual and organisational levels, research approaches and findings are scarce. First, the majority of research papers have focused on presenting frameworks, while less research has assessed the adoption of blockchain from different perspectives. Such examples of these studies in the context of the pharma industry are (Abdallah and Nizamuddin Citation 2023; Akram et al. Citation 2024). Another route is the review of the literature and the proposition of the research agenda (Kumar Singh et al. Citation 2023). However, in the specific context of exploring the drivers of blockchain adoption in the pharma industry, there is less focus on research. The study explored the participants’ perceptions of the value presented by the blockchain to the pharma industry. While the exploration of attitudes toward technology has dominated the adoption of technology studies, we integrated the perceived value in our research model (Ko, Kim, and Lee Citation 2009). The integration of the perceived value enables us to examine the trade-off among time, effort, and cost within the specific context of the study (Kleijnen, De Ruyter, and Wetzels Citation 2007). Particularly, we aimed to explore the factors as drivers of the adoption, while emphasising the perceived value of blockchain in pharma SC. For researchers, the study provides insights into exploring complex paths among constructs. Both methodologies (PLS-SEM and ANN) enable robust analysis and offer valuable interpretation of results. SEM might be seen as a simplification of complicated paths through linearity assumptions (Xu, Gao, and Jia Citation 2023). Particularly, we argue that in research topics that integrate the perceptions of stakeholders from different sectors, a more in-depth exploration is preferred. ANN overcomes the shortcomings of SEM, with its higher prediction capabilities (Liébana-Cabanillas, Marinković, and Kalinić Citation 2017), which is efficient in exploring complex non-compensatory and nonlinear relationships (Chong Citation 2013). By supporting the research hypotheses, the study builds on the literature that adopted the RBV as a theoretical model to explore technology adoption as an important resource for organisations (Ahn, Kim, and Lee Citation 2022; Chen, Meng, and Li Citation 2018). Particularly, the integration of blockchain technology in the SC can leverage synergistic advantages, thus leading to the creation of SC capabilities. These capabilities, which are difficult to replicate, characterise the organisation and help in positioning it within the competitive market (Wu et al. Citation 2006). 8.2. Practical contribution The study offers several outcomes that can be utilised by policymakers in the pharma industry. For instance, policymakers who hold different managerial roles in the industry can encourage the use of blockchain within different production stages. To facilitate this behaviour, the awareness of the advantages of utilising blockchain should be improved among them, thus raising the investment in blockchain. This can be facilitated by sharing stories of success (Iranmanesh et al. Citation 2023), promoting the advantages of blockchain adoption, and sharing the risks of counterfeit drugs. The study emphasised the important role of SC transparency, enabled by blockchain adoption, on the agility, responsiveness, and reliability of SC, which accordingly improves the perceived value. Several practical and industry-specific examples demonstrate the real-world application of blockchain technology in pharma SC. For example, LeewayHertz Technologies has created a blockchain-based system called TraceRx that aims to revolutionise the SC of the pharmaceutical business (Akram et al. Citation 2024). This creative technology aims to enhance medicine shipment tracking, handle several threats, including recalls and theft, and guarantee transparency in the provision of medicines. Another example is Merck’s SAP Pharma Blockchain POC application, which has greatly enhanced traceability and security throughout the pharmaceutical SC (ManufacturingChemist Citation 2019). Barcodes can help in mitigating the threats of fake medications, enhancing transparency, authenticity, and data integrity. Real-time accessibility of critical data can also increase transparency, authenticity, and data integrity. However, blockchains should be integrated among many SC nodes, presenting a critical challenge. One of the promising initiatives is Novartis, in which blockchain was integrated with IoT, with successful tracking of temperature changes and identification of fake drugs (Akram et al. Citation 2024). Essentially, the project brings a partnership between pharma business, patient representatives, SME blockchain, clinical labs, and hospitals, by incorporating clinical trials, patient data, supply chain, and counterfeit drug detection (Morris Citation 2018). The study also proved the importance of several factors within the adoption process. Responsiveness, reliability, and agility are the most significant factors in the adoption process, based on the results of the ANN. Hence, more focus can be allocated to the improvement of these factors by the developers of the technology. To infer practical solutions for designers and developers of blockchain technology, it is important to investigate the details of each factor. Reliability, for example, focuses on the performance of the functions as expected, which in the context of blockchain refers to providing secure and efficient data sharing of pharma products. On the other hand, responsiveness is reflected by the swift response to the requirements of the customers in relation to the services and products (Lima-Junior and Carpinetti Citation 2019). Agility is reflected by the adaptability to market demands and emerging conditions, which in the realm of blockchain can be addressed by efficient recovery of errors, easy integration of new functionalities in the system, and adaptation in the context of unexpected events. For instance, in pandemics, adopting the blockchain will lead to enhanced management of the inventory, distribution, and delivery of medicines. This will help in addressing the unpredictable changes in the market during such a crisis. All these aspects should be carefully considered in the design of blockchain. On the other side, among the explored hypotheses in the PLS-SEM stage, the impact of the intention to adopt the blockchain on medicine safety is the most significant. Hence, according to this, stakeholders perceive that the adoption of the blockchain can enhance the safety of medicines and healthcare products. Particularly, this hypothesis is linked to the important issue that raised the need for innovative solutions such as blockchain, which is counterfeit drugs. While the majority of the studies in this context have proposed solutions in terms of designs and frameworks for blockchains in the pharma industry; with the integration of innovations such as IoT in the work by (Turki et al. Citation 2023) or the integration with smart contracts (Abdallah and Nizamuddin Citation 2023); there is a lack of research that explores how stakeholders perceive the blockchain as a potential solution for counterfeit drugs. The research brings the attention of researchers to the importance of delving more into the user-centric evaluation of such emerging technologies while exploring the enablers of adoption and the relationship among them. 9. Limitation and future work The findings of this study can be utilised as a ground for future research in blockchain adoption within the pharma SC. Still, there are some limitations and future routes that should be reported. The data collection process was carried out in Malaysia, which might restrict the generalizability of the findings. The level of significance of the factors might differ in other nations. Second, the study has targeted stakeholders in the pharma industry, in which these stakeholders hold different positions and might have different perceptions. As can be seen in the demographic data, participants come from different sectors including manufacturing, marketing, sales, supplying, and management. Hence, a future study that compares the perceptions of stakeholders among different sectors can provide more detailed results. The study examined the perceptions of stakeholders who hold positions in pharma SC, while the perceptions of end customers, particularly patients and doctors, were not explored. The lack of sufficient awareness about the blockchain is the main reason for this choice. However, a future study could explore the perceptions of end customers, who also have sufficient knowledge of the technology. Additionally, the study explored only three main factors that impact the perceived value of blockchain technology (reliability, responsiveness, and agility). However, there are several factors that can be explored in relation to the perceived value in future studies such as the factors derived from the conventional acceptance models including perceived ease of use (Davis Citation 1989) and perceived behavioral control (Ajzen Citation 1991). Other factors could be also explored as moderators such as demographic data, level of experience of participants, and firm size. Particularly, there are several obstacles encountered by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the adoption of the blockchain, in terms of cost and the need for experts to facilitate the adoption process. As our research focuses on the drivers of the adoption of the blockchain on the organisational level, other factors could be explored in this context, such as top management support, competitive pressure, human factors, regulations, and so on. Future studies could emphasise the long-term impact of adopting the blockchain on the pharmaceutical SC, and how it influences other metrics rather than medication safety, including sustainability and cost reduction. While the blockchain is offering opportunities to enhance the performance of pharmaceutical SC, the integration of the blockchain with other emerging technologies could lead to enhanced performance in data collection, analysis, and decision-making. This could be achieved with the integration of AI innovations, IoT, and RFID.

column1: Discovering technological opportunities of cutting-edge technologies: A methodology based on literature analysis and artificial neural network
column2: This paper presents a methodology for discovering technological opportunities of cutting-edge technologies by capturing information from literature. Technological opportunities are expressed in the form of business applications of technologies in untested contexts, i.e. unexplored industries and business processes. The paper underscores the advantages of discovering opportunities starting from existing emerging practices presented in scientific papers, in contrast with the current state of the art that prefers other datasets. The business cases presented in journals are converted into the triad technology-industry-process and the impact on the business performance is reported. From the analysis of 33,285 papers, 14,739 existing triads have been captured. An artificial neural network has been trained using this dataset, enabling accurate forecasting of the potential impact of vacant combinations technology-industry-process. The methodology has been tested on 11 cutting-edge technologies: 3D printing, artificial intelligence, blockchain, computing, digital applications, geo-spatial technologies, immersive environments, internet of things, open & crowd-based platforms, proximity technologies, robotics. For each technology, a technological opportunity map is provided to show the best vacant areas for future implementation. The methodology distinguishes between combinations with uncertain and confident expected impact, so that companies can focus on the most promising areas. Implications for both practice and academia are discussed. • A methodology using academic papers to discover technological opportunities. • Business cases mapped in technology-industry-process combos with business impact. • An artificial neural network forecasts the business impact for vacant combos. • Technological opportunity maps are presented for 11 cutting-edge technologies. • Companies can leverage methodology to target confident and promising areas.
column3: 5 Conclusions This research suggests a methodology for discovering technological opportunities of cutting-edge technologies by capturing information from literature and exploiting the power of artificial neural networks. Results demonstrate the predictive power of the methodology, tested on 11 cutting-edge technologies. However, it is necessary to underscore some limitations of this research, which are linked to the type of dataset used for the analysis. In order to achieve the expected results, to date it is necessary a time-consuming manual content analysis, as already discussed. In addition, time plays a crucial role due to the vast number of scientific papers published annually in the realm of implementing cutting-edge technologies in business settings. However, it is possible that numerous applications utilizing cutting-edge technologies may not lead to scientific publications. As a result, the database of current emerging practices might be missing certain combinations, potentially leading to an overestimation of the number of available combinations through this methodology. Moreover, if a new technology emerges, it is necessary to assess the positioning of this new technology within the current classification of technologies. Additionally, it will be necessary to retrain the model from scratch to incorporate the effects of the new variable. This paper demonstrates that scientific literature can be used as a source of emerging practices to build a tool for discovering technological opportunities. To establish a more precise impact of every cutting-edge technology category, it is imperative to concentrate on each particular technology described in Table A.1 for future research. Moreover, a continuous monitoring of scientific literature is necessary to find new emerging technologies to add to the methodology. Enabling a thorough examination of the proliferation of each technology can provide insight into whether there is substantial progress for commercial endeavors or if the technology is still in its early stages. Further efforts will be dedicated to reducing the work performed by experts for the manual content analysis. A tool for natural language processing will be developed to analyze and filter abstracts of scientific papers, allowing experts to prioritize their analysis of the most promising works. This will accelerate the time required for the analysis. Moreover, with the diffusion of artificial intelligence tools that can be integrated with external software, it will be possible to pass a paper to an application in order to find the emerging practice within the corpus of the scientific paper.

column1: A novel hybrid decision-making framework for measuring Industry 4.0-driven circular economy performance for textile industry
column2: The sustainability strategy focuses on conscious production and consumption, with the circular economy (CE) as an innovative approach to maximize resource value and minimize waste. Industry 4.0 technologies like AI, robotics, and blockchain play a significant role in enhancing the competitiveness of businesses pursuing the CE. These advanced technologies help organizations achieve their sustainability goals, particularly within the CE framework. The study analyses how Industry 4.0‐driven CE practices impact sustainable business performance, using the Indian textile industry as a case study. The researchers developed a three‐stage hybrid decision‐making framework, integrating various methods to assess sustainable performance. A novel three‐stage hybrid decision‐making framework was developed by integrating Kendall's agreement test (Kendall's W), fuzzy Delphi, best–worst method (BWM), full consistency method (FUCOM), and combined compromise solution (CoCoSo) methods. The findings highlight positive outcomes such as enhanced incentives, government support, greener logistics, and improved monitoring of emissions, waste, and pollution. However, there is room for further improvements to address market demand and increase the profitability of green products.

column1: Resolving the information reliability issue in live streaming through blockchain adoption
column2: With live streaming becoming an integral part of a seller's business strategy, a retailer can choose an influencer from a multi-channel network (MCN) to attract consumers. However, since the MCN may benefit from exaggerating the influencer's historical live sales data, information asymmetry between the retailer and the MCN exists. This may lead the retailer to misestimate the influencer's demand-enhancing capability (DEC), and then suffer loss. As the usage of blockchain in providing trust becomes more common, an MCN can apply blockchain technology to signal its data reliably to a retailer. However, conditions for MCN to adopt blockchain and its impact on retailer's influencers choice has not been investigated so far. To fill this gap, we built a signaling model in which an MCN knows the actual information reliability whereas the retailer does not. We find that the retailer opens a live-streaming channel only if the operating cost is low but the retailer will use its own staff in the live streaming rather than an influencer from MCN if the commission is high. This makes the MCN to refrain from adopting blockchain technology. Meanwhile, the blockchain adoption decisions of the MCN and its impact on the retailer's influencers choice not only depend on the adoption cost but also the commission. Specifically, when the adoption cost is low, a high-reliability MCN benefits more from adopting blockchain technology, which incentivizes the retailer to choose a high-DEC influencer; as the adoption cost increases, retailers become unable to judge the MCN's information reliability, especially when the commission level is too low or too high; when the adoption cost increases to a moderate range, multiple equilibria co-exist, indicating that an MCN's willingness to adopt blockchain technology depends on the retailer's belief. We find that all equilibria survive the intuitive criterion, but, from both types of MCN's perspectives, the equilibrium without blockchain adoption is always Pareto-dominant. When the adoption cost is high, an MCN has no incentive to adopt blockchain technology.
column3: 6 Conclusion and discussion 6.1 Concluding remarks and answers to research questions A retailer can choose an influencer from Multi-Channel Network (MCN) to attract consumers in live streaming to pursues profit. However, since the MCN may benefit from exaggerating the influencers’ historical live sales data, the knowledge on influencers’ ability to increase demand is asymmetric between the retailer and MCN. This study addresses the issue by considering that the MCN can apply blockchain technology to generate reliable data and signal its true type to the retailer. Hence, we focus on the conditions for MCN to adopt blockchain and its impact on retailer’s influencers selection. As a concluding remark, we highlight the answers we have derived with respect to the research questions: • (1) The retailer’s willingness to open a live-streaming channel by selecting an appropriate influencer depends on its operating cost and commission level. The retailer opens a live-streaming channel only if the operating cost is low, but prefers to choose a staff without DEC over an influencer when the commission level is high. • (2) MCN’s willingness of adopting blockchain technology depends not only on the adoption cost but also on the commission level. Interestingly, when the adoption cost is non-negligible, the high reliability MCN is willing to adopt blockchain technology only when the adoption cost is low and the commission level is moderate, which results a separating equilibrium. This means that the MCN cannot benefit more from adopting blockchain technology when the commission level is too low or high. • (3) Impact of MCN’s adoption on the retailer’s influencers choice mainly depend on the MCN’s reliability. High-reliability MCN adopts blockchain technology will promote the retailer choose a high-DEC influencer, while low-reliability MCN adopts blockchain technology reduces the retailer’s willingness to choose a high-DEC influencer. Meanwhile, we find that an increase in the probability of the retailer perceiving the MCN as low reliability reduces the retailer’s incentive to choose a high-DEC influencer.

column1: Great partners: how deep learning and blockchain help improve business operations together
column2: Business operations have entered the digital era in which artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and blockchain (BKC) have emerged as major disruptive forces. In AI and ML, deep learning is a critical area. In this paper, we aim to investigate how deep learning and BKC together can help improve business operations. We first examine the operations research (OR) literature related to the applications of deep learning for business operations. Then, we discuss the prior studies on using BKC for operations. After that, we explore deep learning’s applications for BKC, BKC’s applications for deep learning as well as how deep learning and BKC have been used together for business operations. Then, we construct a research framework and propose future research directions.
column3: 6.1 Concluding remarks Business operations have entered the digital era in which deep learning (DL) and blockchain (BKC) have emerged as major disruptive forces. Motivated by the importance of DL and BKC in real world applications, in this paper, we have explored how DL and BKC together can help improve business operations. We have first reviewed the OR literature related to the applications of DL for business operations. Then, we have discussed some prior studies on using BKC for practical operations. After that, we have explored applications of DL for BKC, applications of BKC for DL as well as how DL and BKC have been used together for business operations. Then, we have constructed a research framework. Finally, we conclude this paper by showing a future research agenda in the following sub-section. 6.2 Future research agenda 6.2.1 Using DL-BKC systems in business operations First of all, real case studies should be conducted to show real world applications of DL-BKC systems for practical business operations (especially for some timely topics such as ethical operations and sustainability (Li, Li, et al., 2020). Second, it is important to identify the critical success factors behind the implementation of DL-BKC systems. Empirical studies should be conducted to generate more insights. Third, new computational DL algorithms and BKC consensus schemes can be developed to further enhance the applicability and performance of DL-BKC systems. Finally, it is important to quantify the values that DL can be brought to BKC and vice versa. 6.2.2 How to share DL-BKC systems costs in supply chains Implementing DL-BKC systems to enhance supply chain operations is potentially effective. However, the involved investment and operations costs are non-trivial. In the context of a multi-echelon supply chain system, there are many agents. Then, how to share the incurred investment and operations expenses is a very practical problem but still under-explored. Future studies should be devoted to it. 6.2.3 Cryptocurrencies BKC has its root in bitcoins. Many interesting features of cryptocurrencies and their applications for business operations deserve deep explorations. Among others, initial coin offering (ICO) schemes are very timely and important (Choi and Ou, 2021). It is not only a way to get funding similar to crowdfunding, but it also makes use of BKC based platforms to provide additional functions and applications (e.g., for startups). Further studies can be conducted on cryptocurrencies and the associated applications and functions for business operations. 6.2.4 Decentralized and distributed systems A fundamental difference between BKC based systems and many traditional information systems (such as ERP systems) is their decentralized and distributed nature. This is very innovative for operations and may change many industrial practices. Future studies should focus more on this aspect and see how DL-BKC systems perform with respect to their decentralized and distributed nature. 6.2.5 Multi-tier high-tech supply chains In supply chain operations, some supply chains exhibit the multi-tier structure (Villena & Gioia, 2018). For example, for the high-tech industry (such as the “semi-conductor and consumer electronics” industry), multi-tier supply chain operations are very common (Villena, 2019). However, sourcing, auditing and quality control problems are very challenging which require the use of advanced technologies to enhance product provenance information. The use of DL-BKC systems is hence a good choice, which deserves further investigations.

column1: Blockchain-based connectivity within digital platforms and ecosystems in international business
column2: Digital globalization enabled by disruptive technologies has opened a myriad of ways to create value, warranting a cross-disciplinary research agenda on digital connectivity in international business (IB). Given the scarcity of understanding about the role of specific technologies enabling value creation through digital connectivity, we investigate how blockchain-based digital connectivity shapes value creation in international digital platforms and ecosystems (DPEs). Building on a comparative empirical analysis of international DPEs enabled by different types of blockchain technology, we develop a typology of blockchain-based connectivity in IB. The typology demonstrates how different blockchain technology types enable different kinds of connectivity, resulting in diverse approaches to value creation within newly emerging forms of DPEs. These findings contextualize the concept of digital connectivity, enabling more precise explanations of blockchain's adoption in DPEs, and expand the conceptualization of DPEs, with three new types emerging from the utilization of blockchain-based connectivity. Moreover, this interdisciplinary explanation reveals why certain features theoretically attributed to blockchain (e.g., decentralization, trust) do not always realize or support value creation in practice in IB based on the DPE business model.
column3:
5. Discussion: creating value with blockchain-based connectivity in international DPEs
Digital connectivity (Luo, 2022), enabled by connectivity technologies (Ahi et al., 2022; Luo, 2022; Xu et al., 2018), opens many new avenues for creating value in DPEs that are partly integrated into MNEs' business models or become the main business model for the MNE, creating value across broders (Banalieva and Dhanaraj, 2019; Nambisan et al., 2019). This is because digital connectivity allows firms to benefit from network effects in addition to traditionally available resources (Banalieva and Dhanaraj, 2019; Li et al., 2019; Nambisan et al., 2019; Stallkamp and Schotter, 2021). Our study further contributes to this debate by exploring how digital connectivity, enabled by a specific blockchain technology type, affects interconnectedness and how this interconnectedness further shapes value creation in DPEs.
Based on our empirical findings, we suggest that, to understand value creation in DPEs that utilize blockchain for value creation, we need to explore three blockchain-based connectivity types: (1) semi-centralized and distributed connectivity without crypto-economics, (2) combined, and (3) decentralized with crypto-economic connectivity. These blockchain-based connectivity types are created through the use of specific types of blockchain. Some types of blockchain technology lead to similar blockchain-based connectivity types, but different approaches to creating value in the DPE. We elaborate on each blockchain connectivity type, explaining how it is utilized in emerging forms of DPEs.
5.1. Semi-centralized and distributed blockchain-based connectivity without crypto-economics, and platforms as venues for co-opetition
As illustrated by the cases of IBM Food Trust and Alastria, the connectivity that permissioned blockchains provide is conditional. The creators of the DPE clearly define who will access and record information in the blockchain-enabled network, and how, who will host and validate the nodes storing the information in the distributed network, and who is allowed to further co-create or enhance the technological infrastructure. Thus, the connectivity such blockchains provide is semi-centralized, yet (partly) distributed (Zheng et al., 2017).
Even if the transactions among the stakeholders are encoded and executed by programmed commands, they are initially defined by contractual agreements among the participating firms, or by an established management system within the firm. These social agreements, and not the motivators embedded in crypto-economics, are the foundations of control used to monitor the behavior of the permissioned blockchain-enabled network. As a result, trust among the DPE participants is not automatically given (it needs to be negotiated), even if the technology itself allows information to be secured and supports trustworthy transactions. The lack of trust upon entering the conditioned network is due to the possibility that permissioned blockchain can be tampered (Zheng et al., 2017), existing social mistrust, and other social barriers present among the consortium members, especially when they are competing or semi-competing firms within the value or supply chain (see Jovanovic et al., 2022).
The creators of such DPEs, just like in the currently conceptualized DPEs (Nambisan et al., 2019), have power over other stakeholders and can decide who enters the network, since the technology supports conditional access. If access to the network is granted, the stakeholders also have a copy of the stored network data (part or all of it, depending on the conditions regarding who can become a node for which information) (Zheng et al., 2017). Moreover, unlike in the currently conceptualized DPEs (Nambisan et al., 2019), the permissioned blockchain-enabled network is typically created to address a shared issue across the stakeholders, such as reducing unnecessary or untrustworthy intermediaries, ensuring the quality of product certification, reducing mistakes in multilayered transactions, or speeding up payments, among others. For example, in the studied cases, the issues concerned enhancing transparency in the food supply chain (IBM Food Trust) and the need for an infrastructure for creating solutions that would benefit multiple stakeholders in multiple industries (Alastria). Due to the shared nature of the issue to be solved via permissioned blockchain-based connectivity in such DPEs, the DPE leadership may be transferred to a third party representing consortium members, e.g., to an established association (see details in Jovanovic et al. (2022) or Alastria).
Given all the above, we conceptualize the DPEs that use semi-centralized and distributed blockchain-based connectivity without crypto-economics (such as IBM Food Trust or Alastria) as platforms as venues for co-opetition.
5.2. Combined blockchain-based connectivity, and platforms as venues for boundary-spanning
Public permissionless blockchain is based on the decentralized governance mode and provides connectivity for anyone anywhere on the open network (Sunyaev et al., 2021). To make such interconnectedness function, it employs crypto-economics embedded into the programmable code of the blockchain to motivate stakeholders to transact and trust the network (Davidson et al., 2018; Freni et al., 2022; Voshmgir and Zargham, 2020). The adoption of crypto-economics and tokens of different kinds to enable public, peer-to-peer connectivity, which happens beyond the control of the third party, has prompted a significant number of regulatory questions (Yano et al., 2020), since its principles fall beyond the currently used policy framework (Šilenskytė et al., 2022). Most importantly, decentralized blockchain-based connectivity with crypto-economics also introduces an entirely new mindset for defining and exchanging value through digital connectivity (Davidson et al., 2018), thereby resulting in many successful and not-so-successful applications in DPEs, as well as good and bad practices in the industry (Šilenskytė et al., 2022).
Under such conditions, many firms, such as Animoca Brands that we analyzed, try to combine the old way of defining and exchanging value in the networks (captured in capitalist principles), and the new way (captured in crypto-economics). As a result, a number of firms combine semi-centralized connectivity in DPEs with the new, decentralized, peer-to-peer connectivity incentivized by the use of diverse tokens. When MNEs create value in DPEs by utilizing various constellations of two-sided (semi-centralized) and peer-to-peer (decentralized) connectivity, we call them platforms as venues for boundary-spanning.
Combining the two economic logics, platforms used as venues for boundary-spanning (e.g., Animoca Brands, OpenSea, Binance, CoinBase, HyFi) enable inexperienced users to become familiar with decentralized connectivity. For example, in addition to the offerings of Animoca Brands discussed above, OpenSea allows the purchasing of NFTs, i.e., unique digital assets, in the platform, which acts as a multisided marketplace (Nambisan et al., 2019). CoinBase and Binance, as intermediaries, allow the exchange of fiat and cryptocurrencies in the semi-centralized DPE without direct participation in DeFi platforms, enabling boundary-spanning for users unfamiliar with peer-to-peer currency exchanges.
Thus, platforms as venues for boundary-spanning simultaneously have both (a) the legal entity that is meant to enable known DPE forms (Nambisan et al., 2019) and manage core and peripheral technologies (Banalieva and Dhanaraj, 2019) and (b) the decentralized DPEs for fund-raising and/or consumer engagement (e.g., through the issuing of their own tokens), or decentralized interaction elements based on crypto-economics embedded in their offerings for customers (e.g., the possibility to trade assets in the game, peer-to-peer, using tokens). By operating traditional DPEs (Nambisan et al., 2019) governed as limited companies, MNEs can hire and manage employees, create, purchase, and manage tangible and intangible assets, thus stabilizing DPE operations under turbulent crypto-market conditions, and manage and record fiat transactions, complying with existing institutional expectations for the business (Šilenskytė et al., forthcoming 2024). Simultaneously, by having decentralized governance enabled by public permissionless blockchain (i.e., decentralized authority organizations (DAO)) and a token of some kind, DPEs expand their offerings, funding sources, and customer pool globally.
The combined blockchain-based connectivity allows DPEs to combine physical and digital assets, too, like in some traditional DPEs (Rong et al., 2022; Stallkamp and Schotter, 2021). For example, HyFi – a publicly traded fintech company – utilizes peer-to-peer public permissionless blockchain-enabled connectivity to provide a funding platform for green initiatives. This means that sustainability-driven projects (e.g., solar power plants, wind farms, green hydrogen plants) developed by individuals or firms can be financed through the CeDeFi – centralized, decentralized financing mechanism – thereby merging classical regulated financing with the decentralized crypto-economy.
5.3. Decentralized blockchain-based connectivity with crypto-economics, and platforms as venues for virtual co-creation
The public permissionless blockchain enables the decentralized connectivity described above and therefore the creation of DPEs in which none of the intermediaries or leaders, including the MNE itself, is needed to produce value in economic activities, because technology and crypto-economics solve the issues of distrust and market inefficiencies (Freni et al., 2022; Zutshi et al., 2021). For example, Ethereum is global by nature DPE, which is shared among its co-creators and participants (Tönnissen et al., 2020). Empirical equivalents of such DPEs are, e.g., Solana, Cardano, NEAR. The socio-technical economic interactions on the public permissionless blockchain network allow the creation of DPEs that are entirely decentralized but have a trusted value creation and exchange mechanism (a native token or programmable money, e.g., Ether). In addition, these DPEs have a socio-technological infrastructure in which any other individual or firm in the world can innovate by building dApps (Ethereum, 2022; Tikhomirov, 2018). These DPEs promote related and unrelated virtual business and product development, create virtual monetary and other value for DPE co-creators and stakeholders (e.g., suppliers and customers), foster virtual relationships (e.g., market exchanges), and contain virtual assets and identities. This is why we call them platforms as venues for virtual co-creation.
These DPEs adhere to the changing global market needs, in which consumption is also exclusively virtual – the newly emerging consumer highly values digital rather than physical assets and products (Baranowski and Pandari, 2021) and the possibility to secure their personal data when consuming digitally (Banotra et al., 2021). Different tokens incentivize participation in the interactions within the DPE (Freni et al., 2022; Tönnissen et al., 2020), some of which serve as digital currency: “digital assets designed to work as a medium of exchange using cryptography to secure the transactions and to control the creation of additional units of the currency” (Osterrieder et al., 2017, p. 58). For example, the users of Ethereum's DPE are charged “gas” fees that make transactions in the network economically feasible (Tikhomirov, 2018). Since these DPEs have a unit of value for exchanges among the DPE participants, they do not need to be related to any fiat currencies existing in the current markets. Participation in the DPE exchanges happens exclusively virtually.
The co-creation is central to the success of this type of DPE, because these DPEs create value only when widely used and adopted (Voshmgir and Zargham, 2020). Those like Ethereum can be used in multiple ways, as they do not define or limit how they can be used. Thus, on top of the infrastructure providing DPEs like Ethereum, second-layer protocol solutions (Web3Foundation, n.d.), such as SushiSwap, or empirical equivalents such as Balancer, Uniswap, or AAVE, are developed. Co-creation between the first and second-layer protocol solutions is symbiotic, i.e., they enhance the value and usability of the DPE when co-existing. They do not create value in exactly the same way, but can still be meaningfully grouped under DPEs that aim for virtual co-creation enabled through decentralized blockchain-based connectivity with crypto-economics. This is because, crypto-economics is adopted together with the technology, and features in programmable assets, trust, ownership, money, identity, and contracts (Pouwelse et al., 2017; Weber and Staples, 2022), along with socio-economic incentive mechanisms that oppose market internalization ideas (Davidson et al., 2018). In other words, when public permissionless blockchain is adopted in DPEs as a venue for virtual co-creation, this technology becomes an institution (Davidson et al., 2018), eliminating institutions that regulate the market in a capitalist economy. The trust that no misbehavior, misjudgment, operational error, or uncertainty will happen in the DPE is further reassured through smart contracts (Bashir, 2018). All these technological mechanisms become feasible because the DPE is open to anyone on equal, pre-programmed terms, without any conditions.
This means that decentralized connectivity enabled by public permissionless blockchains with crypto-economics shifts away from the idea of value creation through resource orchestration led by the DPE's leader (Banalieva and Dhanaraj, 2019; Nambisan et al., 2019), and instead advocates economic entities that are capable of co-creating value for the entire network. This co-creation is enabled through tokens of a specific kind that may allow network participants to simultaneously be a ‘shareholder,’ ‘rightsholder,’ stakeholder, customer, and co-creator of the ecosystem if they wish. Consequently, if a DPE-based MNE were to entirely embrace such connectivity, it would cease to exist in the form we theorize in the extant IB literature. Instead, a new techno-socio-economic entity would emerge, which could be referred to as a digital community enterprise – a virtual, decentralized MNE co-creating and co-sharing value with all DPE users and participants through the trusted technological institution.
5.4. Typology of blockchain-based connectivity
The theoretical implications above are summarized in Fig. 2, representing a typology of blockchain-based connectivity that can be utilized for value creation in newly emerging forms of DPEs.

These new types of connectivity and DPEs have remained undiscovered before now because blockchain technology has usually been discussed without any exploration of its technological particularities (e.g., Lumineau et al., 2021; Morkunas et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2021; Torres de Oliveira et al., 2020). We demonstrate that exploring each connectivity technology on a separate basis can produce significant improvements in our understanding of digital connectivity, leading to a more precise theorization on how it is used to create value in DPEs. For example, our findings explain why emerging empirical evidence (e.g., Du et al., 2023; Jovanovic et al., 2022; Šilenskytė et al., 2022) sometimes counters the theoretical blockchain promise of decentralized, code-based interconnectedness in which trust is automatically given (Lumineau et al., 2021; Morkunas et al., 2019; Torres de Oliveira et al., 2020). These findings further reinforce the calls to explore implications of particular technologies on value creation in IB (Ahi et al., 2022; Strange and Zucchella, 2017).
Our findings and interdisciplinary typology synthesize and enrich the literature on connectivity (Berman et al., 2020; Castellani et al., 2022; Lorenzen et al., 2020; Luo, 2022), blockchain (Davidson et al., 2018; Filippi and Hassan, 2016; Lumineau et al., 2021; Morkunas et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2021; Torres de Oliveira et al., 2020), and DPEs (Nambisan et al., 2019; Stallkamp and Schotter, 2021), inviting scholars to further explore and test the relationships we have identified when studying blockchain technology's particularities.
5.5. Limitations and suggestions for future research
While making considerable contributions, this paper is not without limitations that highlight further research directions. First, we analyze a limited number of cases in an industry developing at the speed of light. It is very likely that, while we selected representative cases of each blockchain type and its connectivity, more constellations have emerged. Moreover, we do not broadly explore the diversity within token economics (Freni et al., 2022; Sunyaev et al., 2021) and various consensus mechanisms (Zheng et al., 2017) to completely shed light on peer-to-peer connectivity implications in DPEs. Thus, the typology we provide should be tested and further refined by expanding the case analysis and considering other potential types of connectivity and the DPEs in which they are applied.
Second, we do not elaborate on smart contracts (De Filippi et al., 2021; Herian, 2021), their standards and mechanisms, or their influence on blockchain-enabled peer-to-peer connectivity. Researchers should further explore whether the bundling of blockchain technology groups we provide is sufficient, or if it is necessary to delve deeper into technical aspects of protocol-level solutions to give an accurate representation of the connectivity that specific types of technology, such as blockchain, create. This would likely deepen the insights on various governance models and their applications. Overall, peer-to-peer connectivity enabled by public permissionless blockchain and crypto-economics is an exciting and novel direction for IB scholars to explore.
