column1: Beyond the Block: A Novel Blockchain-Based Technical Model for Long-Term Care Insurance
column2: ABSTRACT The insurance business is characterized by complicated transactional interrelationships among various stakeholders involved in insurance-related activities. Given this unique nature, the century-old challenge in the insurance industry is to effectively reduce transaction costs among the stakeholders while maintaining business privacy and trust. Although blockchain is a promising technology to mitigate this challenge, two technical issues, namely (1) inefficiency in data auditing and (2) difficulty in verifying encrypted data, are of strategic importance when applying blockchain to the insurance industry. To address these technical challenges, we propose an innovative blockchain-based technical model, InsurModel, in the context of newly initiated long-term care insurance in China. Specifically, we utilize cryptographical methods including “zero-knowledge-proof” to 1) represent business interdependence and 2) verify confidential business information without disclosure of specifics. We demonstrate the scalability and applicability of InsurModel and explore its strategic implications in constraining adverse behaviors of the stakeholders.
column3: In this study, we designed, developed, and evaluated a blockchain-based technical model, InsurModel, for a new LTCI initiative in China. Our study affords three primary contributions. First, following the design science paradigm by Gregor and Hevner [ Citation 20], we deploy transaction cost economics (TCE) as a kernel theory to inform IT artifact construction and its strategic implications. Despite its prevalence in the IS literature, TCE has been rarely applied in design science research. Previous literature has argued the pivotal role of blockchain in mitigating transaction costs [ Citation 1, Citation 40], but there has been scant research that demonstrated this effect in a specific business setting. Thus, we attempt to fill this research gap by utilizing TCE in innovative blockchain design and application in the insurance industry. More specifically, blockchain, as a decentralized and immutable database, enables efficient and transparent transactions, which constitute a transactional environment with enhanced institutional trust [ Citation 39]. The TCE literature shows that the establishment of trust among contracting parties constrains the respective opportunism, thereby reducing transaction costs and increasing economic efficiency. Therefore, the extant literature has theorized that blockchain technology is an effective governance proposition to complement TCE [ Citation 39, Citation 40]. However, although it is clear that blockchain contributes to constraining opportunism and reducing the overall transaction costs, how to reduce the ex-post transaction cost further has not been clearly demonstrated in the literature. In response, InsurModel is designed with two primary features, that is, representation of business interdependence in blockchain and utilization of the ZKP protocol to reduce the ex-post transaction cost for the LTCI initiative. Our computational experiments reveal that the representation of business interdependence can significantly strengthen traceability, thereby reducing the cost of auditing. In theory, the proposed design can significantly reduce the cost of auditing by saving considerable human resources and increasing the auditing accuracy. As stated by the data security manager (DSM), “We have to allocate a lot of human resources in auditing for anti-fraud procedures (at present) … If the blockchain (with your design) can extend to all of our (insurance) business (in Tai-Chi Group), the current large team can be downsized to a much smaller one (in terms of headcounts).” In addition, the deployment of ZKP into blockchain contributes to reducing the ex-post transaction cost by mitigating the dilemma of business privacy and authentication integrity. Such a cryptographic method can help verify and authenticate the encrypted data without disclosing the real value. In the LTCI context, the leading insurance company can apply the ZKP protocol to attain a specific business goal, such as the proof of price range without disclosing the real selling prices of distributing insurance companies. Meanwhile, the business privacy (e.g., the real selling prices) of the distributing insurance companies is also protected to avoid opportunistic use by the leading insurance company. As indicated by the IT manager (ITM) at Tai-Chi Insurance, “We (Tai-Chi and other insurance companies) are competitors. The mutual trust is not very high among us. But we still need to cooperate to comply with the regulations from China Insurance Regulatory Commission … The ZKP for validating the price range in LTCI is a good start … ” Collectively, our research findings expand the literature that blockchain technology accounts for the reduction in transaction costs because this technology establishes a trusted transaction environment. Moreover, we apply TCE as a kernel theory in design science research. Our proposed InsurModel can further reduce the ex-post transaction cost by facilitating traceability and authenticating the required information without disclosure. Second, the proposed InsurModel achieves necessary scalability in terms of scalable implementation and the number of connected business nodes. The scalable implementation can increase the accessibility of InsurModel to a large number of users without disrupting their routine operations. Users are reluctant to switch to a new technology or system if they perceive significant differences between the extant and the new one. Thus, InsurModel is packaged as an SDK that can be set up by the stakeholders in their back ends only, thus alleviating the individual reluctance to use the new information system or infrastructure. As stated by the ITM at Tai-Chi Insurance, “I used to be reluctant to implement a new system or application because of the uncertainty. You never know whether people are willing to use it or not. Therefore, we prefer to keep the front end (interface) but make radical change at the back end (infrastructure or design).” More importantly, our computational experiments suggest that the performance of InsurModel does not deteriorate rapidly with the increasing number of connected business nodes and workload, which is far better than the performance of the Traditional Database and Bitcoin-like Blockchain Models. In other words, the proposed design assures the efficiency of the authentication and verification despite the presence of additional connected devices or infrastructures. This finding provides an important strategic implication for organizations that plan to implement blockchain technology to a large landscape of the market, including Tai-Chi Insurance. For example, Tai-Chi Insurance is planning to implement InsurModel in a third-tier city with around 5,000 insured and many organizational stakeholders. Our experimental results on scalability suggest that InsurModel can also run efficiently in first-tier cities, such as Beijing or Shanghai. As commented by the VP, “ … The scalability (in blockchain application) is what we really want to examine, because other insurance products may involve more entities if we apply the blockchain to all other business in the future.” Overall, the proposed scalable design affords accessibility to a large number of concurrent users or business nodes but does not sacrifice the effectiveness of functionality, thereby establishing an exemplar model for the future design of blockchain applications. Third, our proposed InsurModel provides significant implications for organizations promoting a data-sharing strategy. Data are the new fuel in the digital economy. However, many companies keep their data as closed silos, which hinder the process of gleaning data and developing deep and actionable insights from the data. Therefore, recent literature has encouraged organizations to share data and facilitate cooperation [ Citation 26, Citation 33]. Although some organizations have attempted to enable the authenticated API requests for data sharing, such an API-based sharing mechanism has its drawbacks in data security because the unauthorized third party can intercept the data in transit [ Citation 42]. In addition, it is difficult to prevent the secondary usage of data retrieved from the API requests [ Citation 21]. Accordingly, many organizations are still reluctant to share their data with others in the present API-based sharing mechanism. The emergence of blockchain technology has shed light upon data sharing due to its transparent governance structure and advanced encryption. However, the encrypted data carry the challenge of utilizing the shared data. Therefore, it is necessary for organizations to master a new method to utilize the shared data in an encrypted format, thereby eliminating/mitigating the cost from data transactions. In our proposed InsurModel, the ZKP is integrated into the blockchain to prove the price range without disclosing the real selling prices of distributing instance companies. The implication can yet inspire future research from different disciplines despite the technical solution. For instance, future research can extend prior literature to explore the data-sharing strategy supported by blockchain-related technology [ Citation 18, Citation 52]. Moreover, future research can also integrate more advanced cryptographical technology, such as ZKP of membership, homomorphic encryption, and neural cryptography, with blockchain, thereby exploring additional means of data cooperation. As the VP stated in the interview, “We (Tai-Chi) want to become a leader (in insurance industry) to leverage the blockchain technology to facilitate more data exchange in the future.” Although InsurModel was designed for the LTCI context, its ideas (i.e., representation of business interdependence and ZKP) can be generalized to not only other insurance products but also other industrial sectors. Future studies are urged to explore additional application scenarios to expand the generalizability of our proposed design. For example, the logistics industry has a high demand for traceability, namely registering and identifying a goods from its origin (production site) to its final destination [ Citation 35]. Thus, our proposed design (i.e., representing business interdependence in blockchain) can be adopted and extended by the logistic industry to enhance traceability. In addition, blockchain technology can possibly transform health care operations. Our proposed design of the integration between blockchain and ZKP contributes to compromising the debate between privacy protection and data verification in health care. Take the example of a blockchain-based Covid-19 contract tracing app [ Citation 24], in which the ZKP can allow users to check whether they were in close contact with a confirmed patient without disclosing his/her identity. Last, but not least, evidence from the applicability check supports the pivotal role of blockchain and the proposed InsurModel in improving individual productivity and efficiency. We urge future studies to collect additional evidences and statistically validate the effectiveness of blockchain function in the organizational context. column1: Barriers to the adoption of blockchain technology in business supply chains: a total interpretive structural modelling (TISM) approach
column2: Blockchain is an emerging technology with a wide array of potential applications. This technology, which underpins cryptocurrency, provides an immutable, decentralised, and transparent distributed database of digital assets for use by firms in supply chains. However, not all firms are appropriately suited to adopt blockchain in the existing supply chain primarily due to their lack of knowledge on the benefits of this technology. Using Total Interpretive Structural Modelling (TISM) and Cross-Impact Matrix Multiplication Applied to Classification (MICMAC), this paper identifies the adoption barriers, examines the interrelationships between them to the adoption of blockchain technology, which has the potential to revolutionise supply chains. The TISM technique supports developing a contextual relationship-based structural model to identify the influential barriers. MICMAC classifies the barriers in blockchain adoption based on their strength and dependence. The results of this research indicate that the lack of business awareness and familiarity with blockchain technology on what it can deliver for future supply chains, are the most influential barriers that impede blockchain adoption. These barriers hinder and impact businesses decision to establish a blockchain-enabled supply chain and that other barriers act as secondary and linked variables in the adoption process.
column3:
This paper analyses the barriers to successful adoption of blockchain technology in supply chains. A contextual relationship between barriers that impact the offtake of blockchain technology has been developed. The TISM explores the dynamic interactions and transitive linkages between the barriers and provides a hierarchical model depicting appropriate behaviours of each barrier to blockchain adoption in the supply chain. Further, this paper identifies influential barriers that need to be addressed and eliminated for effective adoption of blockchain in supply chains. A structural model was developed using TISM, which revealed that the lack of familiarity with blockchain technology and a lack of critical awareness on what it can deliver for future supply chain are the most influential barriers. These barriers impact the decision to establish a blockchain enabled supply chain and other barriers act as linkage variable in the process, as confirmed by the MICMAC analysis.

By analysing the interactions within barriers using TISM and identifying the influential barriers using MICMAC analysis, this research minimises the lack of clarity around the adoption of blockchain. This paper has contributed to the supply chain literature addressing blockchain applications and innovations. It adds to the existing literature [see Kurpjuweit et al. (

This paper examines the capability of TISM to explore the reasons for transitive links, which enables a deeper understanding of the system and validates the developed TISM model for the nine barriers to implement blockchain in supply chains. This is a step forward in the applicability of TISM proposed by Sushil (

This study contributes to the current literature on blockchain technology in supply chain management. Though the various adoption and maturity models like TAM, DOI and TOE etc., provide insights on adoption behaviour and maturity levels of adoption, these do not address the barriers to implementation. The adoption of new technology by focusing on enablers of adoption is important and the adoption managers can tackle the task of eliminating the barriers for successful implementation of blockchains across the supply chain. Once the barriers are eliminated the success of the adoption process becomes inevitable. Also, the Pareto 80-20 principle suggests that 80% of the effects are due to 20% of the causes.

Thus, we argue that the novelty of the research lies in supporting managers in identifying top barriers that must be eliminated for blockchain adoption in supply chains. The TISM method coupled with MICMAC analysis provides the information on influential barriers with a higher driving force which must be eliminated first so that the other dependent barriers in the system can also be eliminated. In this regard, our results reveal that barriers, lack of technical knowledge about blockchains and the uncertainty around the benefits of this technology are the driving barriers, which trigger dependent barriers. Hence, the adoption managers should focus on knowledge development on blockchain functionalities with the employees and inform the top management about the benefits blockchain adoption could bring to the firm, will improve the adoption process.

This study suggests that, for successful adoption of blockchain, companies should begin by mapping the potential applicability of blockchain within their own business and invest in developing knowledge of the technology. With assistance of an expert, a team creating blockchain strategy and designing a demonstrable case on a smaller scale before wholesale adoption is recommended. Finally, through iterative process rapid progression on the prioritised cases, the industry can move towards creating a successful business case on a commercial scale. Though barriers exist to blockchain based transformation in the supply chain, these barriers are not insurmountable. Despite its relative infancy, this technology has attracted many business owners irrespective of industrial sector to which they belong. Talking about supply chains, blockchains offer a wide range of applications dealing with issues like transparency, traceability, anti-counterfeiting, provenance, shared resource management, contract management, demand/forecast management, and robust cyber security, etc. Blockchain adoption, however, demands more resources in terms of capital, time and processes to eliminate the barriers in the way of its adoption and to realise its full potential.

column1: Designing a blockchain enabled supply chain
column2: While blockchain technologies are gaining momentum within supply chains, academic understanding of concrete, real-life design and implementation is still lagging, hence offering very limited insights into the true implications of blockchain technology on supply chains. This paper reports a two-year design science research (DSR) study of a smart contract initiative piloted by a consortium in the UK’s construction sector. We seek answers to the research question, ‘How should a blockchain enabled supply chain be designed?’ Guided by the theory of business model, we explore how a group of supply chain actors collectively designs and pilots a blockchain solution that addresses the supply chain transparency and provenance problem. Our research is one of the very few longitudinal empirical studies to offer in-depth evidence about how blockchain is deployed in complex multi-tier supply chain networks. In compliance with DSR research paradigm, we make contributions at three levels: designing and instantiating the blockchain architect and proving its utility in addressing the target problem; developing a set of design principles as a mid-range theory that can be applied and tested in different blockchain supply chain contexts; and refining and extending the kernel theory of business value at supply chain network level.

column1: Characteristics of a Blockchain Ecosystem for Secure and Sharable Electronic Medical Records
column2: Blockchain technology is a secure and distributed information accounting, storage, and retrieval modality which has the ability to disrupt and revolutionize business practices. One such disruption resides in the capability of Blockchain to serve as a secure method for storing and sharing electronic medical records in new and innovative ways. Current medical record storage and transmission methods are proprietary and have interoperability and security problems. To that end, secure, effective, and interoperable electronic records options are highly prized. This article uses a grounded theory approach to qualitative analysis of electronic medical records users in the United States to develop a perspective from industry and scholarly practice on the suitability of Blockchain technologies for electronic medical records, security, and storage.
column3: Blockchain is a novel technology which, as its proponents assure, will be the solution for many existing problems in current healthcare information systems [3], [10], [12], [20], [23], [30]. Expected benefits of healthcare Blockchains include providing access to sensitive health-related information for specified user groups, while at the same time ensuring the confidentiality of the information by restricting current and future disclosure. In this article, we scrutinized the applicability of Blockchain for the storage of health information by contrasting different opinions from experts in that area. The results of the study indicated several key points for critical consideration. One was that the hype surrounding the technology was well ahead of the healthcare industry's understanding and appreciation for the Blockchain ecosystem's features. Among the healthcare provider market, Blockchain is still an untried and uncertain entity. Providers are largely either skeptical or unaware of Blockchain capabilities in regard to the ability to store, share, and secure electronic medical records. And, as noted, providers are not dissatisfied with the capabilities of the current HIE solutions. For these users, Blockchain may very much be the case of a solution in search of a problem, at the present moment. While there is a lot a Blockchain can do for healthcare providers in regard to managing and sharing the electronic records they use, the learning curve is steep and the will to introduce a new system in the face of a currently adequate solution from leading HIE providers is low. There is much yet to learn about the differential advantages Blockchain will bring, in order to overcome this nascent “perfect is the enemy of pretty good” mindset regarding current EMR solutions in place. Another point for consideration is that the leading HIE providers in the application developer market, who do appear to have a reasonable understanding of Blockchain technology, do not appear to consider it essential to the enhancement of the existing government-specified protocols already established for the sharing and security of electronic medical records among healthcare providers. HIE providers see the generic advantage of Blockchain, in other words, but do not see the necessity of implementing a Blockchain ecosystem as part of their present product offerings. A final point for emphasis is that it appears that an alternative route to widespread Blockchain-based EMR adoption is presently being exploited by entrepreneurial application developers and that the current trends toward involvement of patients in clinical trials and the desirability of big data analysis access to patent-generated health information from increasingly popular wearable devices augurs for increasing and wider adoption of Blockchain-based EMR apps by patients, individually. The degree to which healthcare providers are motivated to begin using Blockchain-based EMR applications, then, appears to depend in large part on the patterns of individual patient adoption and use. The subsequent motivations of the HIE industry to accommodate Blockchain enhancements of their offerings also depends upon this dynamic, if indirectly, as healthcare providers increasingly accede to the demand-pull pressure of patient adoption, and as the providers increasing inquire of their technology developers as to possible Blockchain enhancements for their own records systems. A. Provider and Developer Perspectives of Electronic Medical Records Sharing It must be emphasized that this article and the theoretical development arising from it are induced from interactions with the technology development industry for healthcare EMR solutions and from healthcare providers belonging to health services organizations who serve medical patients. In this perspective, the Blockchain adoption process we introspect upon is central to the service providers who operate and provide patient access to electronic medical records systems and/or the health information exchange systems that application developers provide the health services industry for electronic records management. Future research will expand this perspective to the patient side of the equation. 1) Patient-Centric Route for an Industry-Instantiated Innovation What we theoretically induce is a putative patient centric route to Blockchain adoption of EMR solutions, but this is based entirely on the perceptions of the companies that are developing such analysis of health and technology industry perceptions of the causes and effects of the influence attempts with which they are targeting patients as customers. The individual patient perspective of adoption—as an individual innovator for personal use—is not part of this analysis, at least not the early theoretical stages of our inquiry. Nor should it currently be, since the diffusion of innovation process we study here instantiates with technology development on the seller side and promulgates from the developers and services providers forward to the patient. The decision on the part of individual patient users in response to market campaigns from technology and services providers is an entirely different theoretical proposition, which is also quite deserving of study but which will be more probative once we completely understand the process by which the application developers will successfully bring the Blockchain technology to the market. From the perspective of diffusion of innovations, the innovation developer is the party tasked with inventing the Blockchain-specific applications and making the adoption target for the innovation aware of its existence, benefits, and uses. The initial target for such an innovation would be the healthcare provider market, those organizations which serve individual patients. We have seen in this article that the healthcare provider market is not at present prepared to adopt, being largely uninformed and doubtful of the benefits brought by the Blockchain ecosystem. This does not mean that Blockchain will not find its way into EMR solutions, but rather that the initial entry point is not likely to be on the side of the hospitals and clinics that create and store medical records. 2) Lack of Immediate HIE Incentivization The developers of currently used EMR systems, the companies that create Health Information Exchanges such as Cerner and Epic, likely do not see the immediate benefit of adopting Blockchain as an enhancement of their present implementations. That is because 1) their customers, the health services providers, are not clamoring for the solution and 2) they believe their current product offerings achieve the necessary ends adequately without Blockchain enhancement. There simply is no market-centric basis from which to derive a demand for adopting the innovation on the part of the HIE developers: continuecontinue I have a sense that industry is not really wild about this idea. Can you imagine having a consortium of healthcare providers coming together to exchange information that is directed by consumers. You have to ask what's in it for the provider, why would they do that? It's not going to benefit them monetarily (RS). B. Reasons Why Blockchain Might Not be an Immediate Healthcare Provider Innovation Left on their own, health providers would probably not adopt Blockchain for medical records use quickly. They are, as yet, largely uninformed, unconvinced, and unconcerned about the areas in which Blockchain can contribute value to the EMR situation. 1) Lack of Current Awareness in Healthcare Our clear sense from the data is that the Chief Information Officers of the Healthcare Organizations we interviewed did not know as much about Blockchain and the implications of Blockchain technology for the sharing of healthcare information in HIE-like networks as did we researchers. The implication to be found in this is that academics have the luxury of “armchair quarterbacking” in regard to speculating on the future of Health Information Exchanges and likely Blockchain applications for such HIE applications, while members of the practice are actually living it, day-to-day. The centrality of records-keeping and record security in the healthcare industry dictates a high degree of organizational overhead devoted to the collection, administration, and sharing of medical records information. Innovations that are not immediate, mission critical adoptions (such as the original Medicare mandate for keeping medical records electronically, for example) probably do not have immediate priority in the face of critical daily operations. This is an informed supposition, but it seems reasonable in the face of our analysis. For that reason, our sense from interacting with healthcare organization executives is that Blockchain might be something that the healthcare industry will not rush to adopt. To that end, a key recommendation for researchers is not to assume that the healthcare industry knows or cares as much about Blockchain technologies as the more informed researcher might. This is not to imply that Blockchain has no future in healthcare, nor that managers in healthcare are uninterested. Rather, researchers who seek to more fully understand the emerging role of Blockchain technologies in medical record keeping and sharing simply have to be patient with the realities of the present HIE situation. While it seems to us that Blockchain could do a better job in many ways, it is not universally acknowledged by our respondents that present HIE implementations, problematic though they might be in certain cases, are as yet unsatisfactory enough to merit immediate replacement. On one hand, we had a clear sense of awareness of the technology; on the other hand, we also had a similarly clear sense that medical professionals considered the Blockchain innovation to be still an unproven quantity, so to speak. Clearly, researchers will have to engage in the twin missions of education and understanding when they undertake Blockchain research on the potential applications in HIE and healthcare. 2) Knowing the Technological Limitations A second general recommendation about engaging in HIE research on Blockchain technology is also related to the unexpected finding that industry professionals simply are not as aware as academic researchers are of the several high-profile HIE/Blockchain proofs-of-concept from Azaria, Ekblaw, Halamka and colleagues seen in the current research literature [3], [12], [18]. To approach research with healthcare industry professionals expecting them to know about MedRec [3] and its various academic experimental implementations of Blockchain-based medical records systems is unrealistic; the information has not yet filtered out to industry. To that end, if we go to respondents with the presumption that they might be aware of several well-conducted and efficacious demonstrations of Blockchain HIE systems, we are likely to be disappointed and lose the advantage of learning what we can from the respondents as regard to the current state of knowledge and the likely path for future adoption and implementation for this important technology. Even then, there is a wide-scale perception of Blockchain technology among our respondents that potential healthcare applications are “faddish.” As can be easily seen in the Appendices where we display our coded statements of meaning, the terms “buzzword” and “early days” are frequently noted. Clearly, Blockchain is early on the diffusion curve of awareness in the healthcare industry, whereas academics are a step or two ahead. It is well to be mindful of this when undertaking Blockchain research in industry. 3) Knowing What Is Needed It bears consideration to ask what healthcare industry executives feel they need in records-sharing capabilities. Although our results, here, are not industry-wide, they do span Healthcare Organizations that embrace both Epic and Cerner HIE systems, as well as including key government and industry consultancies. This is a qualitative study, so we are careful not to claim any specific generality to what we say here, but the data do present a regular and consistent point in regard to the functional capabilities which managers are seeking for HIE-type implementations that might include Blockchain technology. First, record identification is front and center on the minds of these executives. Granted, Blockchain implementations are very good at preserving identifying information that is entered and in providing secure nonrepudiation capabilities for information that is entered, but the question of “who manages the data flows to the system” arises in our study. The notion of a centralized authority, or gatekeeper, in order to certify the front-end integrity of data is notable in the response of the executives we talked to. Clearly, there is the perception that Blockchain is a powerful security protocol but that the weak point of the security lies on the input side, where (as in all information systems) GIGO is a cardinal rule. Your records are only as good as the quality of the input, essentially, in the view of the respondents. This is an area of research that could well benefit from more introspection. The portability of patient data is a highly popular idea related to the potential of Blockchain in electronic medical records storage and transmission. This cannot be overstated; to the extent that many respondents felt Blockchain was a popular buzzword, a faddish concept, as many others understood and approved of the capabilities of the technology to make patient information securely portable. Benefits of such approaches include the capability to provide a trustworthy audit trail of patient visit histories, at the least, and to provide ready access on subsequent visits to new providers to the entirety of the patient health record, at most. Much is made by patient-facing applications developers about the attractive possibilities for patient-directed portability of their own medical records data as the move from provider to provider. This implies a fruitful venue for further research that draws in considerations of the patient in addition to the healthcare organizations, since portability would appear to hinge dually upon the capabilities and desires of the providers and their patients, alike. 4) Realities on the Ground As exciting as Blockchain is to us as researchers who are interested in healthcare organizational research, it is important to be mindful of the real state of industry as we consider how to investigate the potential for a future role for Blockchain technologies. The majority of respondents in this study were either Epic users or supporters of the Epic system. The Epic HIE system is broadly seen by our respondents as generally effective in its current state, and while there are most certainly shortcomings that a Blockchain implementation could overcome in present Epic HIE operations, there is not a strong sense of a rush to replace it. It is the system they know, and even with its limitations (largely related to interoperability with non-Epic systems) it is fondly regarded. Blockchain may be an excellent solution to certain storage and sharing problems, but until the system users recognize a problem large enough with regard to the operation of current HIE systems, Blockchain may well be a solution in search of a problem, particularly considering the unexpectedly low level of specific knowledge about its capabilities among the sample. Perhaps, to that end, a better research focus going forward might be understanding the limitations and user satisfaction issues with present HIE implementations as a precursor to examining the likelihood of their replacement with Blockchain implementations. C. Blockchain Healthcare Adoption Leveraging the Patient Access Route The fact that the HIE market does not see immediate incentives to develop Blockchain options does not mean that Blockchain does not have a place in healthcare; it only means that the likely adoption path for the technology will not be along the traditionally utilized path. Among entrepreneurial technology developers—those who look beyond the present received view and status quo of EMR/HIE solutions—there is the recognition that Blockchain can provide features and benefits that private users might find compelling, even if industry presently does not. It is at this point that the consideration of the individual patient enters theoretical consideration, but only from the perspective as a market prospect for the innovative technology developer who sees promise in the invention of Blockchain-specific medical records storage and sharing. The key use envisioned for private patient access and storage of persona electronic medical records via Blockchain technology at this moment is more related to their likely participation in clinical trials than their need to provide records access to their clinicians: continuecontinue We think it's going to be even more valuable for clinical trials, where data provenance and data integrity is so critical. We think the distributed public ledger is really key when you are designing clinical trials (RS). For that reason, our theoretical development is aimed at understanding the resistance to initial introduction of a new EMR innovation to the markets of healthcare providers. It is a theoretical specification of the causes, effects, and processes by which a new innovation in electronic medical records storage and sharing becomes visible to potential adopters, the first of whom are likely to be the individual patients that healthcare providers serve and the second of which, of necessity, are the providers who respond to patient demand for EMR interoperability with their subsequent demands upon the technology development sector for interoperable applications. It is a matter of entirely different theoretical speculation as to how the potential patient adopters will choose to use, share, and understand the innovation, itself, once it reaches the market and is made available to individual users [13]. This is beyond the immediate scope of this article, having been focused on the initial innovation and market introduction of Blockchain EMR solutions, but the theoretical perspectives induced here provide the ready abductive starting point for such an expansion of inquiry. It is certainly a potent point for future research consideration. D. Reasons Why Blockchain Might be a More Compelling Innovation for Patients Than Providers or Developers Drawn from our interview with Raj Sharma of Health Wizz, the patient-facing Blockchain EMR application, our realization is that there are far fewer compelling reasons for healthcare providers to change the system they presently use, as limiting as it may seem to Blockchain enthusiasts, whereas there are generous pragmatic and financial incentives for the individual patient to access, download, and preserve copies of their own health records with Blockchain applications. As Sharma of Health Wizz stridently notes, continuecontinue Depending on who you talk to [health record analytics] is a 68-70 billion dollar market (RS). The financial incentives are strong for analytics providers to have access to patient data, and each day brings new accounts in the IT and healthcare news about big data providers seeking to expand their purview into the arena of health information. Emblematic of this intention is the news recently of Apple and its forays into health information markets,4 which stimulated informed speculation among financial commentators about a potential takeover bid for Epic. Sharma makes a cogent point that only part of what a patient-facing EMR application would store would consist of accounts of medical treatment. A goodly portion of such personal health records could also be comprised of dedicated feeds from wearable fitness sensors designed to track and record user activity, vital signs and other health-related information, in addition to easily accessible consumer market genetic testing products that are currently on the market: continuecontinue All those things come together on your mobile application and then you control who you share that information with and how you monetize it (RS). In this perspective, the individual patient becomes a very valuable source of information and potent arbiter of its flow and disposition, regardless of whether big data brokers are seeking their information flows for analytics purposes, or health industry researchers are seeking personal health histories for clinical trials. Future research should look to this point. Either way, a Blockchain-based EMR application that can provide a nonrepudiable source of accurate, secure, and sharable patient information will be increasingly valuable at the individual patient level, when individuals are empowered to monetize their own data via such applications. Blockchain ecosystems for individual health records storage, management and sharing are the avenue to such empowerment. As individuals increasingly adopt and use such applications, and as they more frequently bring them to encounters with their healthcare professionals, health providers are highly likely to take notice and seek to find ways to integrate such individual applications into the flow of patient record keeping at the provider level.

column1: To What Extent Will Blockchain Drive the Machine Economy? Perspectives from a Prospective Study
column2: The advancements in the fields of IT and robotics are provoking the fourth industrial revolution and transforming our economy toward the machine economy. Billions of economically autonomous machines engaging in business relationships raise novel requirements regarding security, privacy, regulation, business models, trustful transaction processing, and interoperability. A technology that promises to provide solutions to these challenges is blockchain. Neither practice has spawned productive solutions nor has research been able to assess the phenomenon profoundly. First investigations focus on specific use cases, but existing work does not examine the overall impact and role of blockchain in the machine economy. However, this knowledge is of particular importance for various stakeholders. In this article, we address this research and knowledge gap by conducting a study with 50 blockchain and machine economy experts. We establish a sound research fundament by following a literature assessment, group discussion, interviews, and qualitative data analysis. As main research instrument, we chose a Delphi study, which has a long-proven record of application in prospective studies and has been applied to examine future premises, estimates, and challenges across nearly all disciplines. This allows us to derive six key findings leading to a transparent picture of blockchain's role in the machine economy.
column3: Fast emerging digital infrastructure technologies, the phenomenon of ubiquitous computing and their increasing combination with advancements in the field of robotics might ultimately lead to fourth industrial revolution—called machine economy—which was controversially discussed [1]. Since blockchain was assumed to be a vital building block in this development, we had investigated the future role of blockchain in the machine economy. In a prospective study, we engaged a panel of 50 blockchain and machine economy experts to assess and discuss 13 projections related to blockchain and the machine economy. Our article contributes to current body of knowledge in the fields of blockchain and machine economy in the following way. First, we were the first to scientifically investigate and evaluate how blockchain might be able to fulfill requirements of the machine economy. This allowed us to better understand in which particular aspects blockchain could play an important role in the machine economy. Further, it allowed identifying in which direction the technology needed to be further developed. Here our key findings one, two, and four in particular provided starting points regarding, scalability issues, standardization and compatibility, and establishing a secure infrastructure for the machine economy. Second, our study provided first insights on events that humanity expects and desires to (not) happen. Our key findings three and six represented valuable starting points for ethical and legal guidelines that could frame a research strategy for blockchain and machine economy as well as their governance mechanisms. Third, our projections and study results laid the foundation for further additional in-depth analyses. For instance, the fact that there might be more than one machine currency (key finding five) requires researcher to analyze and conceptualize how exchange platforms and currency valuation could work in the machine economy. Besides our theoretical contribution, we provided practitioners with valuable insights. First, our findings allowed decision-makers to better understand and estimate the expected occurrence of specific events related to the emerging machine economy. Second, we provided practitioners with a comprehensive perspective on which role blockchain technology might play in the machine economy. Thus, they were able to make technology and investment decisions more informed. Third, our results suggested that a mix of technologies was required to propel the machine economy and indicated that organizations should not focus on blockchain as infrastructural technology only. As any research project, this study had limitations that also represented starting points for future research. First, although we followed established practices to select our panelist, the results might be influenced by biases of the experts. It requires additional research to further evaluate and generalize our findings. Following a case study approach to analyze specific results (e.g., the fact that blockchain alone might not represent the foundation of the machine economy) seems a very valuable and promising endeavor. Second, we discussed a limited set of projections. Although we followed a rigorous and transparent process of projection development, alternative approaches could lead to differing projections. Thus, future research might cross-validate results by different perspectives. Third, our research had a very strong focus on technical aspects of the development of our economy and only moderately touched on aspects such as regulation. Thus, we were able to receive distinct answers and estimates about potential technical requirements and use cases. However, additional aspects such as regulation, ethical issues, and user acceptance also heavily influenced the development of our economy. Having understood the technical aspects, future research should widen the scope and also include the aforementioned perspectives to provide a more comprehensive picture of the potential breakthrough of the machine economy.

column1: Decision Support for Blockchain Platform Selection: Three Industry Case Studies
column2: Blockchain technology has received significant attention recently, as it offers a reliable decentralized infrastructure for all kinds of business transactions. Software-producing organizations are increasingly considering blockchain technology for inclusion into their software products. Selecting the best fitting blockchain platform requires the assessment of its functionality, adaptability, and compatibility to the existing software product. Novice software developers and architects are not experts in every domain, so they should either consult external experts or acquire knowledge themselves. The decision-making process gets more complicated as the number of decision-makers, alternatives, and criteria increases. Hence, a decision model is required to externalize and organize knowledge regarding the blockchain platform selection context. Recently, we designed a decision support system to use such decision models to support decision-makers with their technology selection problems in software production. In this article, we introduce a decision model for the blockchain platform selection problem. The decision model has been evaluated through three real-world case studies at three software-producing organizations. The case-study participants asserted that the approach provides significantly more insight into the blockchain platform selection process, provides a richer prioritized option list than if they had done their research independently, and reduces the time and cost of the decision-making process.
column3:
Blockchain technology is evolving rapidly, and the number of blockchain platforms in the market is growing rapidly. Furthermore, software-producing organizations are increasingly considering blockchain technology for inclusion in their products. Therefore, a decision model was required to externalize and organize knowledge regarding the current state of blockchain technology, besides, to assist decision-makers at software-producing organizations with selecting right blockchain platforms based on their preferences and requirements.

In this article, the blockchain platform selection process was modeled as a MCDM problem that deals with the evaluation of a set of alternatives, and taking into account a set of decision criteria [1]. Moreover, we introduced a decision model for the blockchain selection problem based on the technology selection framework [2]. We had designed and implemented a DSS for supporting decision-makers with their technology selection problems in software production. The DSS provided a modeling studio to build such decision models for technology selection problems. The decision models can be uploaded to the knowledge base of the DSS to facilitate the decision-making process for software-producing organizations. The proposed DSS addressed common knowledge management issues, including capturing, sharing, and maintaining knowledge.

The novelty of the approach was that it provided knowledge about blockchain platforms to support uninformed decision-makers while contributing a sound decision model to knowledgeable decision-makers. Furthermore, it incorporated deeply embedded requirements engineering concepts, such as the ISO software quality standards and the MoSCoW prioritization technique, besides knowledge engineering theories, to develop the DSS. We conducted three case studies to evaluate the usefulness and effectiveness of the DSS to address MCDM problems. Our website7 is up and running to keep the knowledge base of the DSS up-to-date and valid. We aim to create a community around the platform that will regularly update the curated knowledge base with new blockchain platform features.

Probing more in-depth, the decision model presented in this article also provides a foundation for future work in MCDM problems. We intend to build trustworthy decision models to address software architecture pattern and model-driven development platform selection problems as our (near) future work.

column1: Blockchain in global supply chains and cross border trade: a critical synthesis of the state-of-the-art, challenges and opportunities
column2: Blockchain possesses the potential of transforming global supply chain management. Gartner predicts that blockchain could be able to track $2 T of goods and services in their movement across the globe by 2023, and blockchain will be a more than $3 trillion business by 2030. Nowadays, a growing number of blockchain initiatives are disrupting traditional business models in each sector. In this paper, we provide a timely and holistic overview of the state-of-the-art, challenges, gaps and opportunities in global supply chain and trade operations for both the private sector and governmental agencies, by synthesising a wide range of resources from business leaders, global international organisations, leading supply chain consulting firms, research articles, trade magazines and conferences. We then identify collaborative schema and future research directions for industry, government, and academia to jointly work together in ensuring that the full potential of blockchain is unleashed amidst the socioeconomic, geopolitical and technological disruptions that global supply chains and trade are facing.
column3:
6. Existing gaps and future research
Global SCM requires harmonised solutions supported by both industry and government, presumably with the aid of academia, for realising the disruptive potential of blockchain. Support from governments can ensure that a blockchain-based SC ecosystem for data sharing and information exchange encompasses requirements from both governmental agencies and the private sector. Furthermore, it is in the interest of governmental agencies to promote the adoption and the development of open architecture and standards, something that may not be always aligned with the interests of technology providers.

Currently, private enterprises are leading the blockchain effort and governmental agencies are falling behind. There is a lack of understanding of how governmental agencies across the world should be involved and how to leverage the initiatives led by the private sector. Few efforts have focused on the integration of the needs and requirements of governmental agencies.

Thus, while developing new technologies and novel business models based on blockchain, academia and industry should work closely with governmental agencies for further facilitating global trade and ensuring compliance with trade law and regulations. This can be achieved by taking advantage of the unique characteristics of blockchain and smart contracts (e.g. consensus driven, data exchange in decentralised/distributed IT environment, immutability of history, strong protection of data integrity, cyber-attack resilience, auditability) in order to: (i) streamline and harmonise information and process flows across SC networks; (ii) improve data quality; (iii) support the timely analysis of SC risks; and (iv) develop efficient business processes between governments and global SC stakeholders.

We conclude the paper by pointing out meaningful collaborative schema and future research directions.

While several initiatives have been under development in industry for automating and securing the data and information exchange, the triple helix of academia, industry, and government should assess (from technology, business, policy, as well as operational aspects) how governmental agencies could leverage these existing efforts to manage the flow of information and documents in trade, and analyse the resulting implications to the private sector. Jointly identifying SC areas where blockchain can be integrated for automation, data harmonisation, and information exchange is a critical step for both government and industry to understand the business flow, benefits, and potential use cases of blockchain for securing and facilitating global SCs and trade.

The triple helix should further cooperatively develop artefacts and relevant knowledge in forms of architecture specification, analysis, and recommendations (specifically for governmental agencies as they are falling behind). Such artefacts can include open architecture designs as well as visual representation and specifications of business flows and blockchain architectures. The analysis and recommendations should provide guidance on how government and the private sector could be involved and interact with each other in the ecosystem. While neither party would be the owner of the blockchain infrastructure, this effort may help to integrate and coordinate the two critical participants in the SC network to facilitate trade and secure transactions. The value proposition for governmental agencies and the involved businesses regarding the use of blockchain in global trade should be clearly developed and articulated.

Technical and non-technical challenges regarding the feasibility and viability of integrating blockchain into global trade and SCM from both industry and governmental perspectives should be identified. Such issues may include confidentiality assurance, access control, interoperability, open architecture specification, and integration with standardisation.

Both government and industry should jointly identify the path forward and solutions where interoperability can be attained. Blockchains are verticalising as they are tailored to specific business needs. Identification of the path forward and recommendations on this front can enhance the integration of blockchain with existing business flows and the use of international standards (e.g. World Customs Organization, The World Wide Web Consortium).

column1: Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech: a systematic review and case studies in the supply chain
column2: Abstract This paper aims to bridge the knowledge gap in the existing literature on Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech. It begins by clarifying the definition of these concepts. Through a systematic review and case studies in the supply chain industry, this paper brings out the applications, the benefits/value, and the challenges/issues of Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech in several industries. It also presents the research methodologies/approaches used during such research. The classification framework developed and used to perform an analysis of 141 articles from five top academic databases serves as a baseline study. It offers the opportunity to evaluate the level of knowledge on Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech, and their evolution over time. The findings show that these technologies are evolving, and organizations are embracing them for competitive advantage. Thus, organizations need to leverage research on these technologies to better understand them, optimize their business strategies, and develop critical insights for decision-making.
column3: This paper presents a systematic review of the peer-reviewed academic literature published from 2007 to 2017, pertaining to Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech, based on their perceived application domains, potential benefits, challenges, and applicable industries. It represents a baseline study for the 2007–2017 period that reveals the actual evolution of Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech as indicated in peer-reviewed research. It also provides significant insights for academia to establish new research domains, and for practitioners to assess their needs and ability to adopt any of these technologies. The findings show that these technologies are evolving, and organizations are embracing them for competitive advantage. Thus, organizations need to leverage research on these technologies to better understand them, optimize their business strategies, and develop critical insights for decision-making. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is the first review combining Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech, and spanning the 2007–2017 timeframe. The review and classification proposed in this study offer useful insights into Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech research. They place all three concepts in one paper, making a comparative analysis easier for readers. In addition, the proposed definitions and findings can be used as a research agenda in Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech orientations and related discussions, amid the perception that further research in this area should be aligned to its rapid development. Building a strong business case for Bitcoin, Blockchain or Fintech will require expanding businesses from their current state to more sophisticated applications in the emerging market. Further research could focus on developing explanatory and predictive theories and models for better understanding of these technologies. Specifically, emphasis may be put on strategies and techniques of creating business value from the well-known benefits of the technologies, as well as on the ways and means of overcoming the explored challenges of Bitcoin, Blockchain and Fintech. Another angle of research may consist of investigating these technologies in other domains, such as the healthcare sector, where the research is very limited.

column1: TWO SIDES OF THE SAME COIN? DECENTRALIZED VERSUS PROPRIETARY BLOCKCHAINS AND THE PERFORMANCE OF DIGITAL CURRENCIES
column2: There is a shared view among practitioners that the blockchain is a revolutionary, decentralized technology that will have a larger impact than the Internet. Firms are increasingly using blockchains for various applications; the most prominent of which to date are digital currencies. In this article, we aim to increase our theoretical understanding of the driving forces behind the success and volatility of digital currencies. We use a detailed dataset of 345 digital currencies for our explorative analysis and identify some of the key factors that can explain their performance. We find that the success and volatility of digital currencies depend on their business type (i.e., whether they relate to a platform business or not) and on their technology type (i.e., whether they are based on their own specialized blockchain technology or on a third-party standardized platform blockchain). Our findings suggest that, paradoxically, to obtain the promised benefits of this decentralized technology, firms need to centralize part of it to retain control over critical strategic dimensions (data and rules for transaction). We discuss the implications of our discovery for other contexts undergoing digital transformation.
