5.1 Theoretical Implications
While it is well established that founders' power can play a key role in influencing business performance and shaping strategic decisions within organizations (Daily and Johnson 1997; Clegg et al. 2006), existing literature does not adequately explain whether some success or failure cases of technology startups can be directly attributed to the power of their founders, nor does it address why some management behaviors (caused by different sources of power) are particularly detrimental in technology adoption. Our study enriches founders' power and blockchain literature by revealing that founders' power can significantly influence management behaviors during the two critical phases of blockchain adoption (Finkelstein 1992; Nakauchi and Wiersema 2015; Hastig and Sodhi 2020; Lumineau et al. 2021). While these two phases contribute to the development of blockchain services, effective execution relies on the founders' power. In other words, while the two phases are essential, these efforts may not be sufficient without the robust support of founders' power to implement effective solutions. For example, in the case of Delta, the founder's focus on designing less innovative blockchain services (stemming from investor pressure) highlighted a lack of power derived from prestige and expertise, which impeded the adoption of more innovative service designs. Also, the founder of Epsilon was unable to leverage power sources and consequently depended heavily on the IT department to drive blockchain adoption.

The scarce empirical evidence on the successful adoption of emerging technologies often attributes success to founders' ability to envision and pursue unique technological innovations. For example, Maamoun (2021) illustrates how Tesla's success is largely due to Elon Musk's vision of combining electric vehicles, renewable energy, and advanced technology into a cohesive business model. Similarly, Davenport and Harris (2017) explain how Reed Hastings, the founder of Netflix, envisioned a business model based on digital platforms, moving away from physical rentals of DVDs and Blu-ray discs. In our cases, it is suggested that founders imagined several potential uses of blockchain in operations and supply chains, but how were these initial ideas successfully pursued and transformed into effective adoptions? While previous research assumes that visions in emerging technologies are constructed rather than discovered (Mesgari and Okoli 2019), our findings challenge this view. We demonstrate that firms, influenced by founders' power, engage in behaviors that uncover preexisting meanings in their environments during blockchain adoption.

Moreover, while existing blockchain literature focuses on identifying drivers and CSFs for successful adoption (Hastig and Sodhi 2020; Danese et al. 2021; Klöckner et al. 2023), it often overlooks the challenges that arise during the adoption phases and the internal dynamics that influence success. By integrating founders' power with blockchain adoption literature, we address this gap and demonstrate that founders' different power sources can shape management behaviors—such as beyond-blockchain exploration and centralized decision-making—that are essential for successful blockchain adoption across different phases. This highlights the crucial role of organizational and behavioral dynamics, particularly the influence of founders' power, in navigating the complexities of adopting disruptive technologies like blockchain.

Additionally, our research aligns with OM's focus on power dynamics and management behaviors, which are crucial in shaping business processes and outcomes (Lovell 1993; Bendoly et al. 2006; Crook and Combs 2007; Loch 2017; Bendoly and Oliva 2024). Particularly, OM literature has extensively explored how different sources of power can influence buyer–supplier relationships and impact inter-organizational performance (see e.g., Benton and Maloni 2005; Zhao et al. 2008; Handley and Benton Jr 2012; Skowronski et al. 2022). Other OM scholars also stress the importance of power in shaping operational outcomes. For example, Li et al. (2022) investigate how the power of chief risk officers (CROs) affects the effectiveness of CRO appointments, risk reduction, and operational efficiency. In addition, blockchain is essentially a modern operations and supply chain technology and its successful development as a business is a central concern of OM scholars (Babich and Hilary 2020; Pun et al. 2021; Wang and Xu 2023; Lumineau et al. 2023). Our study provides valuable perspectives on how founders' different sources of power and management behaviors drive the adoption and effectiveness of emerging supply chain technologies. This bridges theoretical contributions to practical applications within OM, highlighting the strategic importance of leadership roles in technological transitions.

5.2 Practical Implications
Many startups dive into blockchain projects without fully understanding how the technology can benefit their operations or solve specific problems, leading to a high failure rate as misapplications of the technology occur when simpler solutions could be more effective (Omale 2019). For example, Sirin Labs, founded in 2014, launched the Finney blockchain smartphone in July 2018 after raising $255 million. The phone featured an embedded cold storage wallet and a decentralized application center, aiming to bridge the gap between blockchain users and the mass market. However, sales were significantly lower than expected, leading to workforce reductions and a strategic shift toward software development. As Blockchain Land (2019) commented, “There is no point in offering a product that might provide an attractive value proposition in a utopian decentralized world; because that's not the world we live in.” Our findings suggest that Sirin Labs' failure can be attributed to its narrow focus on the technical aspects of its blockchain-enabled smartphone, exemplifying a within-blockchain exploration approach that struggled to scale and align with market needs. In contrast, beyond-blockchain exploration has proven effective. High-performing cases like Alpha, Beta and Gamma identified significant improvements over existing systems by promoting a comprehensive understanding across the business ecosystem. This approach prevents firms from adopting blockchain merely for innovation's sake—a common pitfall in the rapidly evolving landscape—and encourages a holistic view that avoids unnecessary competition and resource misallocation. Moreover, beyond-blockchain exploration addresses key challenges such as interoperability and the need for legitimacy, which are crucial for gaining stakeholder trust and market acceptance (Hastig et al. 2020; Ziolkowski et al. 2020). By aligning blockchain initiatives with established industry practices, firms can not only enhance the comprehensibility and appeal of technology but also ensure their initiatives are adaptable to market demands and regulatory changes, thereby facilitating wider adoption and success.

The study also suggests the practical benefits of centralized decision-making in blockchain adoption, emphasizing its role in providing a clear, unified strategic direction crucial in the fast-evolving blockchain industry. Our findings show that the centralized approach not only expedited the adoption process but also ensured that blockchain solutions were effectively integrated into their business models, demonstrating a strong alignment with strategic business objectives and market demands. By centralizing decision-making, founders can effectively communicate the strategic importance of blockchain, align resources, and address stakeholder concerns, thereby facilitating a smoother transition from legacy systems and reducing resistance to new technologies. However, while decentralized decision-making promotes inclusivity and collaboration, it presents significant drawbacks that can impede blockchain adoption. For example, we found that the cases employing this approach face complications and slowdowns in decision-making. This decentralized approach leads to delays in adopting new technologies and scaling operations effectively. While beneficial for generating diverse ideas and input, decentralized decision-making may contribute to a higher blockchain failure rate by hindering quick adaptation to market changes and scaling blockchain solutions, highlighting the pitfalls of lacking a unified strategic direction.

For practitioners implementing or contemplating blockchain technology, our research suggests that founders should consolidate their authority, seek inspiration beyond the traditional blockchain ecosystem, and make decisive, centralized decisions while encouraging their teams to embrace innovation and adaptability. Also, it is imperative for them to be aware of the beliefs that become institutionalized within their organizations to ensure these beliefs support adaptive and innovative behaviors. While our findings highlight a consistent pattern (where founder power → {beyond-blockchain exploration, centralized decision-making} → performance) contributes to successful blockchain adoption, failure does not necessarily stem from the absence of these factors alone. Instead, external and internal challenges can hinder adoption even when founders possess power. For instance, external market dynamics, such as shifts in customer demand, competition from non-blockchain firms, and evolving regulations, can limit commercialization opportunities. Regulatory challenges, including legal uncertainties and compliance barriers, may further constrain scalability, particularly in industries requiring strict data security and governance. Additionally, execution misalignment, such as poor resource allocation, technological integration issues, or stakeholder resistance, can undermine the benefits of beyond-blockchain exploration and centralized decision-making. These suggest that while founder power and strategic behaviors are critical, blockchain adoption success depends on a broader set of organizational and environmental factors. It highlights the multifaceted nature of failure beyond leadership dynamics in blockchain adoption.

5.3 Limitations and Suggestions for Future Research
Both the primary strength and weakness of this research lie in the selection of all sample firms, which are startups operating as blockchain technology providers within a limited number of industries in a single country, observed over approximately 5 years. While this facilitated the selection of cases to gain a comprehensive understanding of the successes and failures of technology providers in developing blockchain services for operations and supply chains, it also restricts the generalizability of the findings. This approach was pursued due to the lack of empirical evidence explaining the failures of blockchain startups in the existing literature, despite their significant implications for both practice and theory. Although concentrating on a single country could be considered a limitation, it also allows for a more detailed and profound comprehension of the elements of competitive heterogeneity while maintaining various contextual conditions relatively consistent, which would be difficult in a multi-country study.

Nonetheless, future studies should be conducted across diverse contexts to account for environmental differences in blockchain adoption. Also, future research can be conducted to empirically examine the interactions among the different power sources and their impact on blockchain startup performance, particularly how these impacts vary in different phases of the adoption process. Furthermore, there is an opportunity for researchers to investigate the connection between effective technology providers' blockchain development and their customers' willingness to adopt the technology for their operations and supply chain innovations. These directions represent a starting point for a broader exploration of blockchain technology's transformative effects, encouraging diverse theoretical perspectives and methodological approaches to capture the complexity of blockchain in operations and supply chain management. Drawing on the high failure rate of blockchain adoption and incorporating the perspective of founders' power, this study represents an initial step toward understanding how startups navigate these emerging domains either successfully or unsuccessfully. It is hoped that this study will offer a unique approach to consolidating the diverse research on blockchain adoption and inspire future efforts from others in this field.

column1: A Brave New World: The Impact of Technology on Innovation Management
column2: This special issue—focused on the transformative impact of emerging technologies (e.g., artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, service robots, blockchain) on innovation management—identifies the ways that firms are rethinking how they generate ideas, develop products, and engage with stakeholders across organizational and societal levels. The articles in this special issue span multiple domains, including ride‐sharing, smart homes, health care, and digital communication. In addition, they demonstrate how new methods are reshaping new product development (NPD) processes. These contributions highlight how emerging technologies enable novel ideation through tools like large language models and topic modeling, as well as how they support agile, data‐informed NPD and dynamic commercialization strategies. Leveraging these insights, this editorial proposes a conceptual framework that encompasses a simplified, three‐step NPD process (ideation, development, and commercialization), along with key drivers of innovation and their implications for individuals, firms, society, and academia.
column3:
3 Implications and Avenues for Future Research
The synthesis of the special issue articles suggests several directions for further research across the elements of our organizing framework.

For example, focusing on the NPD Process, AI-driven ideation arguably should support improved efficiency and a greater quantity of ideas (Pescher and Tellis 2025); yet it remains unclear how various ideas perform over time in terms of novelty, implementation, and market success. Longitudinal studies could shed light on whether AI-generated ideas allow for sustained competitive advantages or if they might threaten to lead to convergence and redundancy with non–AI-driven ideation. Scholars should explore how AI-driven ideation influences inclusion, cognitive diversity, and value co-creation, as well as how organizations can maintain sufficient ideation novelty over time.

As firms increasingly adopt hybrid or remote models, team members may encounter fewer opportunities for informal communication or spontaneous idea sharing during the innovation development. Research could identify what strategies leaders need to adopt to build and maintain a culture of experimentation and psychological safety when teams are geographically dispersed and rely on digital communication tools. Co-creation strategies enabled by technology represent another, related target for research. Firms increasingly invite users to participate in product development through digital platforms, and Lee et al. (2025) demonstrate how platform ecosystems shift innovation from firm-centric to co-produced in nature. Studies could examine how co-creation affects brand trust, loyalty, and innovation outcomes, especially if mediated by AI or other digital tools.

The Role of Emerging Technologies raises new challenges such as digital platforms struggling in their efforts to balance firm growth with ethical stakeholder outcomes. Scholars should define mechanisms that might enable platforms to scale up their operations while still ensuring the equitable treatment of key stakeholders, such as rideshare drivers, content creators, and consumers. As Lee et al. (2025) show, Uber's shift from a democratic pricing model to a profit-driven one created both value and conflict. Continued research should investigate governance mechanisms that can align private and public value in innovation ecosystems, as well as explore how ecosystems might be managed to avoid trade-offs between efficiency and societal outcomes.

The impact of ecosystem configurations on innovation diffusion is another promising avenue. Innovation does not occur in isolation but is contingent on the organizational Innovation Context spreading through networks of firms, suppliers, and partners. Mahr et al. (2025) emphasize that innovation ecosystems—particularly those involving service robots—require coordination and alignment across micro (user), meso (organizational), and macro (societal) levels. Further research could analyze how different ecosystem structures influence the speed and scope of innovation diffusion, particularly in critical industry settings like health care and education. Such efforts also need to account for how innovation ecosystems adapt over time to deliver public and market value to broad sets of stakeholders.

Considering how agile approaches are redefining organizational designs, continued research could analyze how firms restructure their hierarchies, teams, and communication flows to support agile NPD processes. Hui and Tucker (2025) note a shift from linear to iterative, feedback-driven development; O'Connor (2025) identifies five organizational models that vary in their ambidexterity approaches. Research should explore which organizational configurations are most effective in delivering innovation outcomes for individuals, firms, and society at large. Case studies of successful transformations and potential pitfalls could give managers guidelines for exploiting structural enablers of continuous innovation.

Geographic and cultural contexts in innovation adoption also remain underexplored, despite their crucial relevance to assessments of geopolitical development and competition. Some cultures are more receptive to change and uncertainty; others favor incremental improvements over radical shifts. Ludwig et al. (2025) suggest that communication design logics can be pivotal in shaping perceptions of innovations. Additional research might specify how various cultural settings determine optimal ways to harness user- or stakeholder-generated communication (e.g., reviews, social media) to refine ideation and implementation.

Moreover, advancement in Methodologies like new metrics are needed to evaluate the effectiveness of innovation management efforts in dynamic environments. Traditional performance indicators fail to capture real-time adaptability or stakeholder outcomes linked to modern innovation efforts. Topic modeling and other natural language processing techniques might offer a solution, as indicated by Wetzels et al. (2025). Continued research should explore if these methods can track the evolution and interplay of innovation outcomes, as well as identify their limitations for reflecting multistakeholder perspectives.

Finally, innovation initiatives increasingly aim to generate societal value, yet metrics for evaluating such Stakeholder Implications remain scarce. Firm-level outcomes have traditionally dominated such measures, but there is increasing recognition of the need to integrate individual, societal, and scientific goals (Wetzels et al. 2025). Research could work to develop balanced assessments of the individual, firm, societal, and scientific outcomes of emerging technology projects.

Trade-offs between automation efficiency and creative diversity also deserve further investigation. If organizations automate repetitive tasks, they risk marginalizing human creativity and reducing diversity of thought. Pescher and Tellis (2025) caution that overreliance on AI may lead to homogenized solutions. Further research could explore how firms might harness automation while still preserving avenues for breakthrough innovation and cognitive diversity.

In summary, the role of technology and innovation management is shifting rapidly due to digital transformations, shifting stakeholder expectations, and increased complexity. By integrating insights from recent scholarly work and applying the innovation management framework to the contributions in this special issue, we demonstrate how organizations can navigate these challenges. Effective innovation management requires not only the adoption of cutting-edge tools but also the cultivation of a culture, leadership, and strategy that align with long-term stakeholder outcomes. Finally, the proposed research directions offer a fertile grounding for attempts to advance both theory and practice in this vital domain.

column1: Eliminating information asymmetry in supply chains: Blockchain-driven or not
column2: Blockchain technology is widely adopted to tackle information asymmetry within supply chains. However, a comprehensive assessment of the value of blockchain remains incomplete, particularly in markets where customers’ perceptions of product quality exhibit substantial polarization. This paper models a supply chain comprising a manufacturer and a retailer to analyze the impact of blockchain on information symmetry elimination. We examine two dimensions of blockchain's role in mitigating information asymmetry within supply chains. We focus on (i) the disparity in quality information between the manufacturer and retailer, and (ii) the discrepancy in quality information between consumers and the product. We find that if both the manufacturer and the retailer raise prices simultaneously due to blockchain adoption, the manufacturer should avoid claiming that the product quality is very high or low. When consumer trust in product quality is moderate and the benefits of blockchain are moderate, the value of blockchain is realized more at the production stage. Conversely, when consumer trust is either very low or very high and the blockchain benefits are substantial, the value of blockchain shifts to the retail stage. These insights offer strategic guidance for retailers and manufacturers in leveraging blockchain for competitive advantage.
column3: 7 Conclusion 7.1 Concluding remarks Upon witnessing the practical application of blockchain in mitigating information asymmetry within supply chains, we are compelled to explore the potential value of this disruptive innovation. To address the issues, we model a supply chain consisting of a manufacturer and a retailer, which uses blockchain to address information asymmetry in two aspects, i.e., information asymmetry between the supply chain entities, and between consumers and the product. Specifically, we develop models with and without blockchain to perform the analysis. We come to the conclusion about the value of blockchain-driven information asymmetry elimination. To assess the robustness of our results, we extend the models to consider the competitive advantages of blockchain adoption in different market structures. In conclusion, our findings underscore the strategic importance of blockchain adoption and its impact on pricing strategies and information transparency for the supply chain. Understanding the alignment between product quality, consumer preferences, and blockchain is paramount to making informed decisions for successful blockchain adoption.

column1: Interplay between manufacturersâ€™ blockchain adoption strategy and retailersâ€™ online channel introduction strategy in the presence of counterfeits
column2: This study explores the interplay between the manufacturer’s blockchain adoption and the retailer’s online channel introduction strategy in the presence of counterfeits. Subsequently, the impact of blockchain adoption and channel selection decisions on consumer surplus is analyzed. We examine four distinct scenarios: with and without blockchain adoption, and in both single-channel and dual-channel settings. The results demonstrate that blockchain adoption significantly impacts the retailer’s channel distribution decisions. With blockchain, the retailer is always willing to add an online store. However, without blockchain, the retailer prefers to launch an online channel only when customer acceptance of the online store is high, or both customer acceptance of the online store and the number of purely online customers are low. Moreover, the retailer’s online channel introduction strategy can, in turn, affect the manufacturer’s blockchain adoption strategy. Specifically, the manufacturer will adopt blockchain only when consumers’ acceptance of the online channel is sufficiently high. Finally, utilizing blockchain can support strategies for expanding online sales channels. And retailers can leverage dual-channel models to enhance profitability and increase consumer surplus, while manufacturers can benefit from increased consumer confidence and expanded sales channels. Furthermore, governments should support blockchain adoption to foster these benefits. • Explore manufacturer blockchain and retailer channel strategy interplay amid counterfeits. • Confirm retailer’s benefit of channel expansion with manufactuer adopting blockchain. • Manufacturers of authentic products are not always motivated to implement blockchain. • Overall, implementing blockchain technology is beneficial to consumers.
column3: 6 Conclusions Blockchain has the potential to enhance supply chain transparency by disclosing quality-related information to consumers. Its immutability and traceability make blockchain a more effective and reliable anti-counterfeiting technology compared to alternatives such as RFID or QR codes. However, there is limited research exploring the interaction between manufacturers’ blockchain adoption and retailers’ channel choices from the retailer’s perspective. To fill this gap, our study investigates the interaction between manufacturers’ blockchain adoption strategies and retailers’ channel decisions in the context of deceptive counterfeiting, and how this interaction impacts consumers. Our findings reveal that, compared to a single-channel scenario, the dual-channel model enables retailers to capture higher profits. Additionally, blockchain can enhance consumer trust in product quality, making the online channel more appealing. Moreover, when consumer acceptance of the online channel is high (or moderate) and the proportion of purely online customers is low, manufacturers are more inclined to adopt blockchain, and retailers are more likely to favor the online channel. These results provide several key managerial insights. First, under certain conditions, manufacturers should invest in blockchain technology and collaborate with retailers to integrate online and offline channels. Second, with blockchain adoption, retailers should implement a dual-channel strategy (offline + online) to attract both traditional and online customers. In the absence of blockchain, retailers need to carefully assess the size of their purely online customer base and the level of consumer acceptance of online stores to determine whether to adopt an online channel strategy. Finally, both manufacturers and retailers should adjust their pricing structures, as blockchain can help reduce double marginalization by aligning their pricing strategies. This study has several limitations, each providing opportunities for future research. First, our study does not consider the impact of government actions on the decisions of upstream and downstream supply chain members. Governments worldwide are increasingly focusing on counterfeiting issues and implementing various enforcement actions to combat it ( Shen et al., 2022a; Pun et al., 2021 ). Additionally, there have been reports of government subsidies for companies adopting blockchain technology ( Pun et al., 2021 ). Therefore, it would be interesting for future research to analyze how government actions influence the primary outcomes. Additionally, our study only explores the impact of blockchain on supply chain members and consumers. Therefore, another potential avenue for future research is to investigate whether consumer purchasing behavior (e.g., return rates, repurchase intentions, or brand loyalty) interacts with blockchain applications across different retail channels. Blockchain adoption requires coordination between upstream and downstream supply chain members. Our study assumes that if the upstream manufacturer adopts blockchain, the downstream retailer will also adopt it. However, in reality, downstream participants have the discretion to adopt or reject blockchain technology ( Iyengar et al., 2024 ). Future research could relax this assumption and explore the key barriers, including cost and regulatory considerations, that supply chain members face in adopting blockchain.

column1: Can blockchain implementation combat food fraud: Considering consumersâ€™ delayed quality perceptions
column2: Food fraud is driven by unethical enterprises’ economic incentives and endures due to consumers’ delayed quality perceptions, while present solutions make it impossible for ethical firms to verify food quality in a timely and convincing manner. To that end, this paper focuses on a duopoly competition between an ethical firm (H) and an unethical firm (L) incorporating consumers’ delayed quality perceptions. Considering the industry credibility crisis that food fraud may trigger, we analytically explore the conditions and effects of firm H to combat food fraud with the aid of blockchain technology (BCT). Counterintuitively, this paper finds that quality improvements beyond industry standards are not always beneficial to firms. Indeed, firms H and L will adopt quality improvements only when marginal returns are higher or delayed perceived time of quality (DPTQ) is longer, respectively. When deciding whether to adopt BCT, H should consider not only the implementation cost and DPTQ, but also the non-monotonic impact of DPTQ on the cost threshold. In addition, it is found that the application of BCT will always motivate H to make quality improvements and further enhance the goodwill, demand, and profits, but that the effect of combating food fraud is stage-specific. Within DPTQ, BCT will only serve as a marketing tool to enhance the competitiveness of H. It is outside of DPTQ that BCT can be effective in combating food fraud, not only by accelerating L's exit from the market, but also by increasing H's market share at the same time.
column3: 8 Conclusions and management insights 8.1 Main conclusions Food fraud is repeated, not only jeopardizing people's health, but also generating an ICC in the industry, greatly restricting the healthy and sustainable development of the food industry. Food fraud is due to the economic motivation of enterprises to carry out adulteration, adulteration, and forgery. Food fraud persists because consumers have delayed perception, often after a series of activities such as purchase, consumption, and experience to correctly perceive the quality of food. In addition, ethical firms often face consumer distrust and unhealthy competition from unethical firms due to the lack of timely and credible means of quality disclosure. Existing studies have mostly examined the impact of food fraud and coping strategies from the perspective of economic incentives of firms on the supply side, but have rarely considered the impact of delayed perceptions on the consumer side. To this end, this paper addresses the duopoly competition consisting of an ethical firm H that makes authentic quality inputs and an unethical firm L that has fraudulent quality inputs, and considers both the supply-side economic incentives and the demand-side delayed perceptions of food fraud, and uses BCT as a technological approach for the truthful, trustworthy, and real-time disclosure of food quality by the firm H to cope with DPTQ, as well as the ICC fraudulent behaviors triggered by firm L. With the help of delayed differential game theory and Hamilton's maximum value principle, this paper constructs a delayed differential game model for two scenarios of enterprise H not implementing and implementing BCT and obtains the equilibrium results of the enterprise's optimal quality improvement input decision, enterprise's goodwill, and profit in the two scenarios. Through comparative and sensitivity analyses, the conditions under which enterprise H implements BCT and its effectiveness in combating enterprise L's food fraud are obtained. Research Findings: (1) Previous studies have also generally concluded that firms always tend to make quality improvements because it can enhance goodwill and boost demand, which in turn makes firms profitable, and that the extent of quality improvement is mainly limited by costs ( De Giovanni, 2011 ; Lu & Navas, 2021 ). However, our findings suggest that while food products that exceed industry standards attract more consumers, firms H and L do not always produce beyond industry quality standards due to consumers’ delayed perceptions of quality, and the conditions under which they invest in quality improvement differ between them. Firm H conditions quality improvement on sufficiently high marginal returns, a result that is intuitive. Firm L, on the other hand, makes fraudulent quality improvement inputs when consumers’ DPTQ is long enough, rather than being constrained solely by costs or marginal returns, as intuitively assumed. At the same time, the study shows that the two firms’ adjustments to their quality improvement input strategies are affected differently by environmental factors. When BCT is not implemented, for firm H, the growth of DPTQ, the increase in industry quality standards, and the increase in the intensity of competition in the market inhibit its quality improvement inputs. For firm L, an increase in DPTQ, a decrease in industry quality standards, and an increase in the intensity of competition in the market will intensify its spurious quality improvement investment to capture more unjustified profits. (2) Previous studies have generally concluded that BCT implementation is mainly limited by implementation costs ( Pun et al., 2021 ; Shen et al., 2022 ; Ma & Hu, 2022 ). Considering the presence of consumers’ delayed quality perception, our study shows that BCT implementation by Firm H is also affected by the DPTQ, and the cost threshold is related to the size of the DPTQ. BCT will only be adopted when the DPTQ is long and the price of blockchain implementation meets a certain threshold. The competitive advantage in the goodwill dimension of BCT will increase the DPTQ threshold. Further, it was found that the effect of DPTQ on the cost threshold is non-monotonic. This finding explains the intrinsic reason why in reality BCT in the food industry can experience adoption blockage, i.e., the implementation of BCT by firm H is monotonic in nature. Thus, only when the DPTQ is not so long, firm H is able to credibly demonstrate its quality inputs to consumers through BCT in a timely manner within the delay period (the unexposed enablement of firm L), enhancing goodwill and boosting demand. At the same time, in the case where firm L is exposed relatively soon, it allows the effect of the BCT against firm L to present itself early, and yet protects firm H from being exposed to the ICC. When the DPTQ is too long, the fraudulent behavior of firm L will become unscrupulous, and the effect of H investing in BCT to confirm its own food quality will have a saturation effect, which will neither inhibit the quality improvement investment of firm L at lower cost to deceive consumers, nor be able to face the high-intensity competition brought about by firm L in the fraudulent situation through further quality improvement under the cost constraints. (3) Previous studies on BCT to combat fraud have shown that implementers can prove the authenticity of their products with the help of BCT implementation to increase demand and profits, but potentially reduce the quality of their products ( Pun et al., 2021 ; Shen et al., 2022 ). First, consistent with previous studies, this paper affirms the long-term value of BCT implementation for the development of firm H. To the extent that BCT is feasible, Enterprise H's market demand and profits are enhanced. However, this result is obtained from an increase in the level of quality improvement in Firm H, which is counterintuitive to the finding of a decrease in the level of quality in previous studies. This counterintuitive result is mainly closely related to consumers’ perception of quality delays. Specifically, this paper finds that when Firm H adopts BCT, DPTQ will no longer affect its quality improvement input decision and the implementation of BCT can lower the threshold for firm H to make quality improvement inputs. At this time, Firm H will increase quality improvement in the trustful trading environment created by BCT. Through the increase in goodwill and the improvement in the observed quality of the food products due to the increase in the degree of quality improvement, the market demand and profit of Firm H will increase significantly. Furthermore, previous research in other industries has shown that BCT can achieve supply chain transparency with significant combat effectiveness by virtue of its technical properties such as the difficulty of tampering with real records ( Naoum-Sawaya et al., 2023 ; Fang et al., 2024 ). However, considering the delayed perception characteristic of fraud in the food industry, the results are stage-specific. The research in this paper shows that in the long run, the implementation of BCT does not always enable the unethical firm to exit the market earlier mainly in the form of demand. However, the profit of the unethical firm declines more rapidly after the delay period and to zero in a shorter period of time. More specifically, within DPTQ, if L chooses to make false quality improvement, the strong competitive advantage of goodwill brought by BCT will promote L to improve quality, which in turn will greatly increase demand and profits. In that case, BCT implementation often fails to combat fraud directly, and can only be used as a marketing tool for firm H to accelerate the rate of decay of firm L's goodwill by enhancing its competitiveness. We illustrate this thought-provoking conclusion by looking at three aspects of the impact of BCT implementation on firm L's fraud quality improvement investment, firm goodwill, and market demand. First, firm H enhances its competitiveness with BCT, and within DPTQ, improving the quality of food observations with the help of fraudulent quality improvement becomes firm L's only means of coping with the situation at a lower cost. Therefore, the implementation of BCT not only lowers the threshold at which firm L chooses quality improvement inputs, but also induces firm L to increase fraudulent quality improvement inputs. Second, if the competitiveness resulting from BCT implementation by firm H is too large or the DPTQ is too long, the goodwill of firm L under BCT implementation instead exceeds that of the BCT non-implementation scenario. This is also due to the unidirectional impact of BCT implementation. While consumption does not fully trust firm L's quality improvement inputs, it also delays the perception period and is unable to confirm its fraudulent behavior. Continuous fraudulent quality improvement will confuse uninformed consumers with higher observed quality.

column1: The interplay between blockchain and big data analytics for enhancing supply chain value creation in micro, small, and medium enterprises
column2: This study explores the interplay between blockchain-based smart contracts and big data analytics for the supply chain value creation of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). We implement our Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) procedure with the ganache blockchain, and addresses generated by the Metamask wallet. Each supply chain player in the blockchain is assigned a wallet address to observe the hashes created when data is added to the blockchain. Our findings unfold that supply chain value creation emphasises traceability, transparency, security, and profit maximisation interlocked with how effectively companies utilise big data collected through blockchain-based smart contracts. This subsequentially assists managers in using data types and a variety of analytics, spanning from descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive to cognitive analytics. This synergy between the blockchain and the types of analytics provides opportunities to identify new interactions and directions for future research.
column3: 6.1 Key findings and contributions In this paper, the authors aimed to look at the interplay between smart contracts and big data key analytics for MSMEs’ supply chain value creation. To achieve this, we have taken a layered approach that brings together smart contracts and data analytics (presented in Fig. 5) to create supply chain value. We argue that technological adoption by MSMEs is an investment that leads to higher levels of transparency, traceability, security, and profitability level. Fig. 5 The alternative text for this image may have been generated using AI. Full size image Interplay between big data analytics and smart contracts Figure 5 brings the key components together and highlights the interplay between smart contracts/blockchain (SC3), technical tools, big data analytics, and supply chain value creation (i.e., traceability, transparency, and security) among supply chain players (e.g., suppliers/producers/retailers). The x-axis and y-axis depict supply chain value creation by applying the intensity of analytics, technical software tools, and types of data. We add a shade of green showing each analytical component's value and intensity. Figure 5 is one of our key contributions, laying out the synergistic relationships between secured big data collection and smart contracts, as part of the blockchain, Utilising the dynamic technical capability/technical resource-based view (Akhtar et al., 2019), we investigate the interplay between dynamic capabilities, i.e., smart contracts/blockchain and big data analytics. We find that MSMEs are facing continuous uncertainty and constant change, and there is a need to generate and modify practices to foster resource reconfiguration and adapt change to achieve competitive advantage. Hence, in our study, we embed smart contracts interlinked with blockchains and big data analytics to reconfigure and adapt as dynamic internal resources, processes, and routines to align with the decisions made by the interplay. These dynamic capabilities and resources play an essential role in enhancing MSMEs’ operations in the context of technology implementations, contributing to creating business value for MSMEs. We make two unique contributions as part of this research; firstly, we identify the key role of data analytics in creating a benchmark for pre-agreed conditions. Secondly, we find a linear processing approach that links data analytics and smart contracts in a trusted decision-making ecosystem for supply chain value creation. We now revisit our research questions to provide context for our findings. RQ1: How does the integration of smart contracts and big data analytics enhance supply chain value by addressing key challenges of transparency, traceability, and security for MSMEs, which often face limited resources and higher vulnerability to operational inefficiencies and fraud? In meeting RQ1 the authors establish the significance of MSMEs, highlighting their challenges in adopting advanced technologies like blockchain and big data analytics in the introduction and the literature review. We move beyond technical explanations to demonstrate how smart contracts and big data analytics enhance transparency, traceability, and security in supply chains. The discussion of blockchain applications, such as food traceability and combating counterfeit goods, provide relevant examples of how these technologies create value. In our experiments we create an environment of security and transparency/visibility, as all stakeholders have access to the data in an MSME environment. RQ2: How can the integration of smart contracts and big data analytics be applied in MSMEs’ supply chain operations to demonstrate tangible improvements in transparency, traceability, and security, and what specific operational insights can be gained from this implementation? For RQ2 we provide a deeper understanding of how smart contracts and big data analytics interact within supply chains, offering real-world examples of their application. The critical analysis of blockchain use cases, such as food security, reverse logistics, and tracking emissions, showcases the potential for visualizing these interactions in supply chain operations. Furthermore, we created a blockchain to monitor how transactions are added and how conditions are met on the Ethereum blockchain. This sets the stage for a visual framework, illustrating how these technologies can be leveraged together to enhance transparency, efficiency, and decision-making, particularly in the context of MSMEs. We highlight that the more complex the data analysis (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive, cognitive), the higher the value for MSMEs and the more accurate and secure supply chain value creation. 6.2 Implications In the literature review, we have developed a comprehensive overview of the key research in MSMEs’ food traceability and transparency. In most cases, we identified that there was research on the blockchain (Iranmanesh et al., 2023; Yadav et al., 2023) and big data (Akhtar et al., 2019; Hopkins, 2021; Yadav et al., 2020), but very little investigated the interplay between data analytics and smart contracts. We also found that the work was often conceptual; for example, Farnoush et al. (2021) conducted a literature review on blockchain analytics focusing on intent to implement. Similarly, Kaur et al. (2019) explored the use of blockchain in the context of vehicular technology but conducted a system modelling approach. This research takes a novel approach and creates a strong contribution by investigating the interplay between data analytics and smart contracts on a fully functioning virtual blockchain. Thus, as the discussion around blockchain becomes more popular, future research will focus on real-world applications of the blockchain using virtual systems. In the MSMEs’ supply chains, this paper is one of the first efforts to use an applied approach to research development. Additionally, Khan et al. (2021) believe that adoption with senior management is still an issue, and many projects fail due to a lack of support. This can be an issue for MSMEs that often do not have the financial or skills-based capabilities to conduct large IT projects or implement advanced analytics. Thus, implementing smart contracts within MSMEs may still lead to some reluctance, primarily due to the need for pre-agreed conditions and access to data. The other challenge is the lack of training and skills in using technical tools to supplement big data usage. One of the key implications at this stage is managing the tension between skills and technology adoption, encouraging managers to build big-data saving teams for better value creation in MSMEs (Akhtar et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2019). While smart contracts and big data analytics are a huge step forward within the MSMEs’ industry, there is a huge skills shortage in several sectors (Clohessy & Acton, 2019). To help manage this tension, this study provides guidelines for managers and companies on how effectively they can embed big data collected through blockchain-based smart contracts and then utilizes a variety of analytics for their supply chain value creation. 6.3 Limitations and future research In developing this paper, we identify several limitations and future directions that can help shape this interdisciplinary field's future. The first limitation we identified was the need to apply this solution to more case studies. In this paper, we propose and test a virtual blockchain solution that can act as a testbed to investigate the interplay between smart contracts and big data analytics in an industrial setting. The second limitation we put forward is the smart contract dataset; future datasets might be more complex as advanced technology emerges. In looking forward, we argue that investigating the interplay between smart contracts and data analytics is an exciting area of future research. The opportunities to research with different types of data open distinct possibilities to work with industry 5.0 technologies. Extended datasets could open solutions for AI implementations and the extensive use of automation. Various combinations of technologies, analytics, and automation could open new avenues for cognitive analytics for data-driven performance.

column1: Green data analytics, blockchain technology for sustainable development, and sustainable supply chain practices: evidence from small and medium enterprises
column2: With attempts being made by both governments and organizations to reduce environmental hazards, blockchain technology is becoming a crucial tool for attaining supply chain sustainability in small and medium enterprises (SME). Recognizing this fact, this study investigates the effect of blockchain technology on sustainable supply chain practices to improve organizational performance. In this investigation, data was gathered from 364 respondents, including middle and upper-level managers from SME manufacturing companies in China and Pakistan. The relationships among the endogenous and exogenous variables were tested by employing partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The primary results suggest that blockchain technology and green information systems positively influence sustainable supply chain practices. Moreover, green information systems and sustainable supply chain practices possess a significant positive association. Sustainable supply chain practices have a positive and significant relationship with sustainability; i.e., operational, environmental, and economic performance. The findings also reveal that three dimensions of organizational sustainability—i.e., operational, environmental, and economic performance—have a significant effect on organizational performance. Additionally, the results of this study provide valuable insights into blockchain technology and offer policy implications for manufacturers and legislators regarding the implementation and promotion of green supply chain practices.
column3: This study has explained and endorsed the acceptance of BCT in supply chain networks. The execution of blockchain-based supply chain management (SCM) is becoming common across many countries, permitting collective, safe, and dispersed ledgers, independent numerical initiatives, and trustworthy networks. Additionally, it facilitates transactions amongst peers by minimizing the role of distributors/intermediaries in the system. This study has statistically examined the relationship between BCT and green supply chain practices to improve ORM. The model's main variables included BCT, green supply chain practices, green information systems, environmental, operational, and economic performance, while the dependent variable was ORM. Data were collected via a questionnaire survey with 364 middle-level and upper-level managers working in the manufacturing sector in Pakistan and China. After conducting the preliminary tests, PLS-SEM was employed to examine the statistical relationships among the variables. 16 hypotheses were tested, among which 15 were accepted; only green transportation and operational performance did not show a significant relationship. Overall, the model showed a significant relationship between BCT-GSCP and BCT-GIS. A positive and significant connection was also revealed between GIS-GSCP. It was also revealed that green supply chain practices positively affect environmental, operational, and economic performance, resulting in improved ORM. Finally, it was also discovered that improved organizational sustainability eventually results in the improvement of ORM. There is a need to further examine green supply chain practices that may benefit from blockchain-enabled solutions to examine the strength of these practices in the overall blockchain environment. For instance, procurement and in-house or outbound logistics may have a stronger role as compared to internal management culture and practices, provided there exists a need for blockchain adoption. Organizations envisioning the adoption of BCT are required to carefully examine their existing processes and practices to identify which operations can benefit most from the implementation of such technology. They should carry out a cost–benefit analysis to aid them in decision-making related to the adoption of BCT. Based on their available finances, companies can prioritize the processes that are to be updated and require immediate attention. If traditional digital processes can meet the organization's information management demand, it is not necessary to adopt BCT in all situations. Further, the proper management of information throughout the blockchain process may benefit policymakers in making strategic decisions related to product inventory management for specific industries; e.g., which natural resources to rely on, which to reduce and increase, which substitute products or raw materials to utilize in the long run to benefit the community and meet government requirements. There is a need to examine inter-organizational and inter-industry relationships concerning BCT in order to recognize how they can benefit from reducing costs and enhancing efficiencies to improve ORM and environmental sustainability. The role of BCT with respect to inter-regional capabilities and the barriers that hinder organizational efficiency across industries can also be explored. Future researchers should also examine individual behavioural barriers related to BCT and its impact on the overall process's success. There also exists a need to examine top management support to enhance green supply chain practices. In addition to an outline of BCT and its applicability in the supply chain, it is imperative to identify the bottlenecks in BCT adoption from the institutional and financial perspective of firms and governments.

column1: Blockchain Systems in Food Supply Chains: An Interpretation Through the Lens of Agency and Technologyâ€“Organizationâ€“Environment Theories
column2: Blockchain (BC) systems are increasingly used by consortia to monitor ex‐post opportunism in food supply chains. BC systems differ for BC technical characteristics, complementary technologies, and organizational tools. Yet, little is empirically known about the link between different BC system designs and the context where they are implemented and how contextual factors influence the adoption of each BC system. This study analyzed different BC systems in 11 principal–agent dyads within one food supply network. Each dyad is composed of a consortium of fruit producers and packers (the principal) and a supply network actor (the agent). Inspired by agency theory, this research associates BC system design choices with levels of system trust (trust in the technology) that are consistent with the risk level of ex‐post opportunism. Compared to previous studies, a new studying perspective regarding the concept of ‘BC trust’ arises. Starting from technology–organization–environment (TOE) theory, this paper also offers an interpretation of how TOE factors intervene in the adoption of different BC systems by agents. By distinguishing between different BC systems, it offers a diverse perspective in grounding TOE in BC research. Together with relevant future research directions, these findings provide adopters and policymakers with important practical insights.
column3: Grounded on AT and TOE theories and based on the analysis of eleven principal–agent dyads, where the principal is a food consortium and its agents are the companies in the different supply network tiers, this study proposes a theoretical model (Figure 4) to interpret: Which BC system design configurations are appropriate for addressing the different levels of ex-post opportunism of supply chain members? (RQ1), and what contextual factors influence the use of different BC systems by supply chain member agents? (RQ2).One important limitation of this study is that the model in Figure 4 does not consider the influence of some contextual variables mentioned in the literature on BC and TOE theory (Table 3). The agents selected in this study showed some common traits, which set precise boundaries for the present study (see Section 4.2.2). However, in general, contextual variables—such as organizational readiness, agents' perceptions of technology maturity, or compatibility with a company's existing technologies—can affect BC adoption and should be investigated in future studies. Another area for further research is to understand whether the focus on other sectors and countries might highlight different influencing variables (e.g., mimetic pressure or technological barriers as Internet connection).In addition, the BC systems investigated do not represent all the possible existing BC systems. Future research could extend the analysis on the level of system trust of BC systems by considering further differentiating features, such as the use of AI.A further limitation relates to the nature of the ex-post opportunism issue (Lumineau and Oliveira 2020). During the interview process, the president and vice president of the consortium discussed the likelihood that an opportunistic event would occur and its consequences and provided the researchers with past examples of agents' opportunistic behaviors. The discussion with all agents focused on understanding where some potential opportunistic behaviors could potentially occur in their activities and in the SC and the monitoring mechanisms that were already in place (e.g., certifications, audits by a surveillance body). However, agents obviously did not disclose any intention to game the system or that there was a conflict between their goals and those of the consortium regarding food safety and quality.Moreover, dyads and the BC project were observed until a certain point in time, and it would be interesting to explore how the BC use could evolve over time to reach the ideal BC system initially designed. In some dyads, this is challenging, as changes in the regulatory environment can take a long time. In other cases, such evolution could be observed in scenarios in which the principal incentivizes actors who are reluctant to use IoTs or smart contracts. Future longitudinal case studies are also required to understand the dynamics in BC system adoption evolution. On the one hand, the flexibility of adapting a BC system to agents' needs can facilitate its adoption, as the present research supports. Yet, on the other hand, it requires additional costs to the technology provider and the principal, which may explain why in other BC cases (Table 1), principals use one BC system across the supply network.Finally, the case study investigated did not involve small family-owned fruit stores or neighborhood markets in the downstream network, as it focuses on large-scale retail chains. Future research could investigate the use of BC in these other channels, including differences in terms of food quality and safety as well as ex-post opportunism.

column1: Leveraging blockchain to optimize online strategies for remanufactured products with cannibalization
column2: Remanufacturing faces significant challenges including negative consumer perception and the complex dynamics of cannibalization between new and remanufactured product sales. This paper explores the potential of blockchain technology to enhance consumer value perceptions of remanufactured products and presents a decision-making framework that examines both blockchain adoption strategies and online sales channel strategies. Through theoretical analysis using game theory models and numerical analysis of real-world data, the study analyzes the optimal channel strategies and blockchain implementation. The results indicate that a mixed strategy, where manufacturers and platforms collaborate, is highly helpful for promoting the remanufactured market and usually has greater profits. Additionally, an agency–agency strategy, where the manufacturer and platform both leverage blockchain, can help mitigate the cannibalization effects. However, we find that only when consumers’ initial environmental awareness reaches a certain threshold can blockchain effectively promote the remanufactured market. To demonstrate the practical implications, we apply the framework to the remanufactured products on the JD.com and Amazon platforms. The results show that by transitioning to a mixed strategy, the overall profits for the brands can increase. Furthermore, the application of blockchain strategy can lead to further increases in the sales volume of remanufactured products and overall profitability. The paper concludes with managerial insights for fostering sustainable remanufacturing operations through leveraging blockchain technology and optimizing online sales channel strategies.
column3: 7 Conclusion This study constructs four Stackelberg models under scenarios with and without blockchain adoption to assist manufacturers in determining the optimal channel strategy for two product categories. From a profit maximization perspective, the ( A R , A R ) strategy emerges as the optimal choice for both product types. Moreover, blockchain adoption can benefit manufacturers and boost the earnings of online platforms. In this strategy, allocating more remanufactured products to agency channels and new products to reseller channels prove advantageous in augmenting the manufacturer revenue. When considering cannibalization, adjusting the channel strategy significantly impacts the cannibalization and market development of both new and remanufactured products. The ( R , A ) strategy exhibits the most pronounced cannibalization. With blockchain adoption, the new product market faces not only the encroachment from the remanufacturing market, but also the adverse influence of the double marginalization effect in the reseller channels, making it the least favorable strategy for the new product market. In the ( A R , A R ) strategy, although blockchain adoption intensifies cannibalization, the overall performance of both products surpasses that of the other channel strategies. For ( R , R ) strategy, blockchain exacerbates the double marginalization effect for remanufactured products, rendering it the least favorable mode for these products. Blockchain adoption has minimal impact on the cannibalization of new products in ( A , A ) strategy, thus favoring the stable development of the new product market. Regarding the impact of blockchain adoption, the decision to utilize blockchain depends on the channel strategies and the level of consumers' information sensitivity. Implementing blockchain may not be ideal for remanufactured products with low consumer acceptance. In the ( A R , A R ) channel strategy, adopting blockchain can enhance profits even when consumer information sensitivity is low. However, if other channels are considered, it is preferable to first elevate consumers' initial value perception towards remanufactured products through advertising or similar means before adopting blockchain. Moreover, the higher the initial value perception of consumers towards remanufactured products, the more substantial the positive effect of blockchain adoption. Note that with the adoption of blockchain, the difference in the improvement of consumers’ value perception will result in different levels of benefit for manufacturers. When consumers’ value perception increases only slightly ( k < k 1 ), manufacturers may choose to abandon the remanufacturing business. When k increases by a moderate range ( k 1 < k < k 2 ), the remanufactured products are sold with a small profit but in a quick turnover mode. When k 2 < k < 1 / δ , manufacturers can sell more remanufactured products at higher prices. Therefore, it is crucial to stimulate the remanufactured product market and enhance consumers' understanding and confidence in blockchain integrated remanufactured products. By coordinating blockchain adoption and sales channel strategies, manufacturers and platforms can leverage the transparency features of blockchain. This includes providing clear and accessible information on how blockchain ensures product authenticity, traceability, and quality. In the initial stages, platforms and suppliers can partner with well-known brands to lend credibility to blockchain-integrated products. For long-term development, addressing issues such as information sharing and data privacy, and enabling consumers to interactively track a product's lifecycle on the blockchain, can further demonstrate the value of the remanufacturing process. This study examines the impact of blockchain adoption strategies on marketing channels. The cannibalization effect suggests that changes in channel strategies could shift the market share between new and remanufactured products, affecting manufacturers' long-term sustainability. Future research should explore the coordination of channel strategies, forward production processes, and backward recycling processes for competitive products, while considering the interplay of technologies like blockchain and the Internet of Things. Additionally, optimizing closed-loop supply chain operations is crucial. It’s important to evaluate the economic and environmental benefits of closed-loop supply chains and how companies can adapt to regulations such as carbon taxes, carbon trading, and the EU carbon border adjustment mechanism. column1: Managing digital transformation with blockchain: Distributed ledger innovation platforms
column2: Realizing its overarching potential in achieving digital transformation, leading organizations, such as Air New Zealand, have recently employed blockchain technology to manage 3D printing innovation. Despite the potential benefits, including the key role of blockchain as a supporting technology in Industry 5.0, these applications of blockchain technology in 3D printing are still at a nascent stage in practice and mostly limited to producer innovation. Additionally, 3D printing and blockchain technologies are often independently revolutionizing value capture and value creation, whereas the theoretical implications of their combined impacts on innovation management remain an underexplored domain. Limited digital transformation efforts have been made to employ blockchain technology to create a synergy between producer innovation and community innovation in relation to 3D printing innovation. To solve these issues, we introduce a novel concept, distributed ledger innovation platform (DLIP), which refers to a network of firms and individuals that create and capture value on a blockchain through digital transformation efforts. In this research, we draw upon transaction cost and social production theories to investigate the potential benefits of blockchain to solve the digital transformation challenges associated with 3D printing innovation. We utilize these perspectives to propose the concept of DLIP as a new governance structure for managing digital transformation activities with blockchain. Additionally, we examine illustrative digital transformation efforts via 3D printing innovation and applications of blockchain technology. Then, we present future research directions for innovation management scholars to investigate the benefits of DLIP in digital transformation efforts via 3D printing. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of DLIP to manage other enabling technologies of digital transformation, including big data, artificial intelligence, and the metaverse.
column3: This research investigates the theoretical and managerial implications of employing blockchain technology in managing digital transformation efforts and proposes DLIP as a solution to do so. The combination of institutional and general-purpose technologies could not only revolutionize both producer innovation and community innovation, respectively, but also streamline these two types of innovation. In particular, our proposed concept of DLIP offers a new way to create and capture value in relation to digital transformation efforts via 3D printing innovation. Companies have recently started to employ blockchain technology in managing innovation via 3D printing, and most of these early applications are limited to producer innovation. Consequently, community innovation tends to be overlooked in the applications of blockchain technology. In particular, through streamlining producer innovation and community innovation, our proposed DLIP offers a futuristic view in relation to the managerial and theoretical impacts of managing digital transformation efforts with blockchain.In this article, first, we discuss issues with 3D printing, the benefits of applying blockchain to solve these issues, and propose the concept of DLIP to manage these digital transformation challenges. Second, we introduce illustrative digital transformation cases of both producer innovation and community innovation in relation to 3D printing. Third, we identify four areas of future research directions for innovation management scholars in relation to the benefits of DLIP for digital transformation efforts. Finally, we discuss potential applications of DLIP to manage other enabling technologies of digital transformation, including big data, AI, and the metaverse. To leverage their innovation potential, these distributed technologies should be managed on a distributed platform (DLIP). Consequently, DLIP would enable both firms and community members to create value in a sustainable manner, fairly capture value, and create synergies between producer innovation and community innovation in a futuristic governance structure.

column1: Blockchain technology as a driver for sustainability? A consumer purchase intention perspective
column2: PurposeBlockchain-based traceability labels is increasingly adopted in supply chain, yet there is little empirical research to examine effectiveness from consumer perspective. Can blockchain technology motivate consumers to purchase sustainable products? Drawing on signaling theory, this paper answers this question by comparing the effect of blockchain-based traceability labels with certification-based labels on consumer purchase intention of sustainable products. We further investigate consumers’ perception of sustainability level as a mediating variable and social enterprise as a boundary condition.Design/methodology/approachThis study uses three online between-subject experiments with a total of 750 participants. The proposed hypotheses are tested using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) as well as mediation analysis based on PROCESS macro.FindingsThe results suggest that (1) blockchain-based traceability labels lead to greater consumer purchase intention of sustainable products than certification-based labels; (2) such a positive effect of blockchain-based traceability labels occurs as consumers perceive a higher sustainability level; (3) however, the effect is attenuated when the company is a social enterprise.Originality/valueThis study contributes to the operations and supply chain management (OSCM) literature by studying the effectiveness of blockchain-based traceability labels from the overlooked yet emerging perspective of consumers. We provide a theoretical explanation and empirical evidence of how blockchain-based traceability labels influence consumer purchase intention during sustainable consumption compared with certification-based labels. We thus additionally contribute to the extant research on the intersection of blockchain and sustainability. Moreover, the incorporation of social enterprise as a moderator enriches the application of signaling theory on the context of sustainability signaling.

column1: Achieving economic sustainability: operations research for risk analysis and optimization problems in the blockchain era
column2: In the digital era, achieving economic sustainability requires proper management of risk with deployment of technologies. In this paper, we discuss how the popular blockchain technology can be applied for risk analysis and optimization (RAO) in real-world oriented operations research (OR) problems. We first present the OR approach and examine the related literature for some critical topics and key research issues in RAO. Then, we present the features and functions of blockchain technology. After that, we propose how the blockchain technology can be applied to support different steps in the OR approach and enhance our investigation and real-world applications of RAO models. Finally, we discuss future research directions and establish a research framework.
column3: 5.1 Concluding remarks In OR, there are many recent developments including all kinds of theories in optimization (Li & Sun, 2006; Luo et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019) and the use of technologies. In particular, in a global market full of uncertainties, business enterprises need to face all kinds of risks. To achieve economic sustainability, proper risk management and deployment of technologies, such as blockchain, are crucial. In this paper, we have discussed the OR approach and reviewed some related literature for many important RAO problems. We have also examined some solution methods for RAO problems. After that, we have presented several functions of BcT which are evidenced to be very helpful to improve business operations. We have further proposed how BcT can be applied in the six-step OR approach as well as address the issues associated with the mentioned RAO problems. As a conclusion, we further establish a research framework for future research in the following. 5.2 Future research agenda and research framework 5.2.1 Theoretical research First, in terms of theoretical studies, many topics deserve further explorations. For instance, for supply chain coordination with risk sensitive agents (including risk prone, risk averse and risk neutral), how stochastic risk sensitivities affect the design and coordination mechanism of supply chain systems is an important topic. How BcT may play a role deserves further explorations. For Bayesian information updating, considering both supply side and demand side information updating will be interesting, and how to quantify the values of BcT in the respective business operations will be important. For the duality control theory, more studies on how it can be applied to operations management and OR problems should be conducted. How BcT can support them will also be a meaningful area to investigate. In terms of financial applications, ICOs are very important for technology related start-up projects but there are very limited studies in the operations literature (e.g., Chod et al., 2020; Choi, 2020b). If we conduct a google search, we will find lots of on-going ICO projects. Footnote 3 ICO is very timely and practical. As such, future studies should explore ICOs in more details. Finally, even though the SoS theory is well-established in systems engineering, it is not widely applied in business operations. More studies on the use of SoS theory should be conducted and the roles played by BcT should be deeply explored. 5.2.2 Applications and implementation BcT is still a relatively new technology for business operations. Enterprises such as Chow Tai Fook Jewelry, LVMH, and Maersk have implemented (or are implementing) it in their business operations. Undoubtedly, using BcT in the real world is very challenging and involves a non-trivial level of risk by itself. Thus, further research should be conducted to examine the technology implementation process and challenges associated with BcT in the six-step OR approach. More real-world industrial cases should be examined with the use of scientifically sound methods.
