column1: Socio-technical phenomena involving blockchain use: Literature review, conceptual framework, and research agenda
column2: This paper reviews the emerging literature on blockchain, structuring key insights in a conceptual framework and setting out a research agenda from a socio-technical and information systems (IS) perspective. The review covers 234 blockchain-focused papers across IS, management, computer science and related fields. It categorises blockchain use into three main types and reframes blockchain use within the socio-technical phenomena of which it is a part. This broader framework enables us to aggregate, integrate and synthesise knowledge about blockchain, its values, drivers and barriers, social and technical subsystem(s), as well as potential consequences, both intended and unintended. Using this framework as a basis for analysis, we identify gaps in the existing blockchain literature and outline a research agenda for advancing blockchain studies within the IS field.
column3: Conclusion Socio-technical phenomena involving blockchain use, which involves several different types of blockchain use, play an increasingly important role in both IS academia and practice. In this study, we have proposed a conceptual framework of socio-technical phenomena involving blockchain use based on a literature review of 234 blockchain papers across IS, management, computer science and related disciplines. The conceptual framework comprises five themes: values (inherent values and value judgements); drivers and barriers; social subsystem(s); technical subsystem(s); and consequences (intended or unintended). This has allowed us to capture the relevant, research-based knowledge about blockchain use available today. This framework advances scholarly understanding by consolidating fragmented insights across disciplines, providing a cohesive lens to analyse the socio-technical interplay inherent in blockchain applications. It serves as a foundational platform for future research, enabling scholars to efficiently map existing knowledge landscapes and identify critical gaps as mentioned in Section 5. For practitioners, the framework offers actionable guidance to navigate implementation challenges. For example, deploying blockchain-based smart contracts may require balancing technical innovation with compliance risks or addressing unintended consequences like environmental criticisms stemming from energy-intensive consensus mechanisms. By foregrounding these interdependencies, the framework empowers stakeholders to anticipate trade-offs. As emphasised throughout this study, blockchain technology and its uses evolve at an unprecedented pace, continuously giving rise to new socio-technical phenomena and providing research opportunities for future IS researchers. The future of blockchain research is not just about understanding technology—it is also about architecting the very fabric of our society.

column1: Data-driven digital transformation in operations and supply chain management
column2: Data-driven digital transformation is a dynamic capability that enables organisations to derive actionable insights and achieve a competitive edge. Data-driven technologies have played a pivotal role in evolving operations and supply chains, making them more responsive and efficient. Data-driven technologies now support advanced functions such as supply chain analytics, blockchain for security and transparency, and AI for innovation and efficiency. Research has long stressed the benefits of improved visibility and collaboration in the operations and supply chain management (O&SCM). Despite rigorous research, there remains a disconnect between theoretical frameworks and their real-world application. This gap suggests further research to better align academic insights with practical implementations in OSCM and a more comprehensive and integrated approach to understanding and applying data-driven digital transformation strategies in O&SCM. This special issue (SI) aims to deepen the theoretical understanding of data-driven digital transformation within O&SCM. We believe the 20 accepted papers out of 97 submissions contribute meaningful theoretical insights to O&SCM research and practice. These contributions not only enrich the theoretical discourse in data-driven digital transformation and O&SCM but also provide practical pathways for future research and application in diverse industry settings.
column3: 5 Conclusions The SI published twenty excellent manuscripts from scholars from diverse geographic locations, each contributing unique perspectives and valuable insights into the various data-driven digital transformation initiatives implemented by the private sector, public sector, and non-governmental organisations (NGOs). These initiatives are aimed at addressing pressing challenges such as the climate crisis, economic instability, and a range of social and humanitarian issues. The contributions shed light on effective strategies and outcomes, enrich the theoretical framework, and deepen our understanding of this emerging field within O&SCM. The success of this SI can be attributed to the relentless support of numerous subject matter experts who generously volunteered their time and expertise as reviewers. Their dedication, demonstrated through multiple rounds of detailed feedback, was crucial in meticulously refining each manuscript to enhance clarity and impact. Furthermore, we would like to express our heartfelt appreciation to Professor Stefan Minner, EIC of the IJPE, whose guidance and assistance were invaluable in navigating the various challenges we encountered throughout the editorial process, ensuring that each submission was addressed with utmost care and attention. We hope that this SI triggers readers to address some unresolved questions and help advance the O&SCM field to the next level.

column1: The interplay of blockchain and channel structure with consideration of cyber-security in a platform supply chain
column2: This paper investigates the application of blockchain technology and channel selection strategies, considering an e-commerce platform vulnerable to cyberattacks that can defend itself through either effort or blockchain technology, which enhances the efficiency of defensive effort and has a certain impact on consumers. Utilizing a Stackelberg game model, we analyze the situation where the manufacturer can not only wholesale products to the retailer selling on the platform, but may also choose to encroach by establishing a direct channel through the platform. Research finds that the manufacturer's encroachment can incentivize the platform to increase its defensive effort, thereby expanding market demand. Consequently, the manufacturer increases the wholesale price after encroaching into the market, which worsens the double marginalization. Additionally, although blockchain can reduce the efficiency of increasing defensive effort, we find that due to consumers’ negative attitude towards blockchain, the platform may actually reduce its defensive effort after adopting blockchain. Furthermore, we discover that the negative impact of blockchain can be mitigated by the manufacturer's encroachment. Finally, we find that within a certain range, the platform may use blockchain to promote manufacturer's encroachment, while simultaneously, it may also forgo the use of blockchain to prevent encroachment. This suggests that when faced with cyberattacks, managers of e-commerce platforms can strategically design channel structure and utilize blockchain to defend against cyberattacks and secure profits.
column3: 8 Conclusion With the progress of e-commerce technology, the online platform has emerged as the primary channel for consumers to purchase goods The manufacturer may also move directly onto the platform to compete with the retailer. However, the issue of cybersecurity is becoming increasingly significant and cannot be overlooked, with online platform exerting efforts to defend against cyber-attacks. In this paper, we develop a Stackelberg game model to study the defense of platform cyber-attacks as well as the construction of direct channels for the manufacturer. We consider that the platform can exert certain defensive effort against cyberattacks and can also enhance network security by adopting blockchain technology. Our findings indicate that when the encroachment cost is high, the manufacturer doesn’t opt to engage in encroachment. This observation elucidates why certain small manufacturers refrain from establishing the direct channel when encroachment cost is elevated, opting instead to sell products on the e-commerce platform through the third-party distributor. When the encroachment cost is low, the benefits accrue to the platform rather than the retailer. Manufacturer’s encroachment can encourage the platform to exert defensive effort. Subsequently, we extend our analysis to study when the platform will adopt blockchain technology and how blockchain will affect the manufacturer’s encroachment decision. We find that the platform will only adopt blockchain technology when the cost of blockchain is low, and the use of blockchain can alter the encroachment strategy. To further investigate, we also explore the interactive effects of encroachment and blockchain on defensive effort and the profits of various enterprises, and provide the equilibrium strategies for the manufacturer and the platform. Our research indicates that when consumers prefer blockchain, it can encourage the platform to increase its defensive effort, whereas if consumers have a strong negative attitude towards blockchain, it can suppress the platform’s defensive effort. The encroachment not only consistently motivates the platform to exert defensive effort but also expands the range of blockchain’s promotion of defensive effort. Finally, we find that blockchain can not only change the preferences of the retailer and the platform for encroachment strategy but also alter the impact of encroachment on consumer surplus and social welfare. 8.1 Managerial insights The research findings have practical managerial implications and can provide directional guidance on channel selection for the manufacturer, as well as for cybersecurity-related concerns. For the manufacturer who trades on an online platform with cyber risks, this study offers an insight into effective encroachment strategies. When confronted with an online platform that lacks blockchain protection, a manufacturer may opt to initiate an encroachment, particularly when the cost of such action is low; this can stimulate the platform into enhancing its defensive measures. Following a manufacturer’s encroachment, the online environment observes enhanced security. Moreover, when the encroachment cost lies within a defined range, such encroachment proves beneficial not only for the retailer but also for the platform. Blockchain, an emerging technology, plays a crucial role in upholding cybersecurity and can significantly shape the manufacturer’s encroachment strategy. This paper finds that if consumers are not strongly averse to blockchain, the platform’s adoption of blockchain technology can promote encroachment and even amplify the positive impact of encroachment on corporate profits, conversely it may inhibit the manufacturer’s encroachment. Therefore, the manufacturer should consider a range of factors, including blockchain, encroachment cost, the probability of being attacked, and consumer attitudes towards blockchain, and choose to encroach the market at the right time. Regarding the online platform, besides the inherent defensive measures, this study suggests that it could incorporate blockchain technology to augment cybersecurity and decrease the success rate of cyber-attacks. However, the platform must evaluate factors such as the implementation cost, the likelihood of being attacked, and the consumer preferences for blockchain before deciding on the adoption of blockchain technology. This research indicates that the platform is likely to adopt blockchain technology when the implementation cost is low, and refrain from implementing it when the possibility of an attack is either minimal or extensive. It is noteworthy that if consumers are not strongly averse to blockchain, adoption of blockchain can facilitate the manufacturer’s encroachment, and the interaction between the two can lead the platform to exert the highest level of defensive effort. In other words, in this scenario, the network risks are the lowest, and the network environment is the most secure. As cyber-attacks become more frequent and complex, many e-commerce platforms, such as PDD, face challenges in completely defending against cyberattacks despite employing traditional security technologies, furthermore, issues such as data leakage persist. We suggest that these platforms can judiciously utilize blockchain technology to enhance cybersecurity, provided the cost associated with blockchain implementation remain manageable. This approach will not only effectively safeguard consumer data but also significantly influence manufacturers’ encroachment strategies, benefiting the platform and other members of the supply chain. Ultimately, through numerical experiments, this paper finds that encroachment consistently increases consumer surplus and social welfare, while the impact of blockchain on both depends on consumer attitudes towards blockchain. If consumers are more concerned about the environmental and cost burdens brought by blockchain, then considering social welfare, the platform should not adopt blockchain technology. Therefore, on the one hand, there is still a need for blockchain technology to progress in order to improve consumer perceptions of blockchain. On the other hand, the manufacturer and the platform need to weigh various factors and adopt relevant strategies to enhance social welfare.

column1: How does blockchain application impact on supply chain alliance?
column2: Recent advancements in blockchain technologies have attracted significant global attention in supply chain management due to their potential to revolutionize this field. Our study examines the relationship between a firm's blockchain application and its alliances with supply chain partners at a dyadic level. Furthermore, the study sheds light on the influence of geographical and technological proximities as critical contextual factors in this dynamic. This study predicts that blockchain integration within a firm fosters the formation of supply chain alliance between firms, with the positive effect being amplified when firms are geographically and technologically closer. Such proposition is evidenced by analysis based on a comprehensive dataset compiled from public annual reports, details of supply chain partnerships, and patent records of 3281 Chinese listed firms over the period 2012–2020. This research offers novel insights into how emerging technologies foster trust-based collaboration within supply chains, and contributes not only to the expanding literature on blockchain applications in supply chain management, but also addresses the need for a deeper understanding of how specific contextual factors, such as geographic and technological proximity, shape the impact of blockchain integration.
column3: 7 Conclusion To summarize, this research highlights how blockchain technology affects the formation of supply chain alliances, particularly between individual firms. By adopting blockchain, companies can improve transparency, build trust, and enhance operational efficiency, which ultimately strengthens their partnerships. However, our findings reveal that the effectiveness of blockchain varies depending on the context, with geographical and technological proximity playing key roles in amplifying its impact on alliance formation. Nonetheless, the focus on Chinese firms and dyadic relationships suggests that future studies could benefit from examining other regions and levels of analysis, such as entire supply chains or individual actors. Additionally, further work is needed to explore how blockchain interacts with different contextual factors, especially in globalized and digital supply chains where physical proximity may be less relevant. In conclusion, this research enhances the understanding of blockchain applications in supply chains, and initiates discussions on theorizing contextuality in terms of differences in geography and knowledge stock, contributing to a more thorough management debate.

column1: Platform-leading blockchain adoption for traceability under upstream competition
column2: Customers are facing quality uncertainty when purchasing though ecommerce platforms, which may hinder their purchase intention. The platform can use the traceability of blockchain technology to alleviate consumers’ doubts. We construct a game theoretical model to investigate the issue of platform-leading blockchain adoption in a supply chain where heterogenous suppliers sell products through the platform. There are different selling modes depending on whether the platform cooperates with suppliers as a marketplace (agency contract) or a reseller (reselling contract) or both (hybrid contracts). We find that blockchain would be adopted to improve the efficiency of the supply chain when suppliers have enough capabilities to provide high-quality product regardless of selling modes. Furthermore, the platform’s leadership in adopting blockchain benefits the entire supply chain. It stimulates the platform to provide subsidies for the capable suppliers to solve the incentive mismatch between suppliers and himself. We also make the comparison of blockchain adoption in different selling modes. In particular, we find that the platform is most likely to adopt blockchain when the supplier with higher quality management capability uses the agency contract and another supplier uses the reselling contract. If the suppliers use the same contract, the supply chain usually accepts a higher cost under the pure agency contract, however, it may not be true when the commission rate is very low and the upstream competition is relatively fierce.
column3: Blockchain creates a reliable traceability system for supply chain to disclose its capability of quality management. This study is motivated by the industrial practice. IBM has reported that blockchain brought an explosion of transactions for earning trust from customers, Footnote 1 and nearly 40% blockchain projects had positive returns. Footnote 2 JD, the China e-commerce giant, develops its own blockchain project “ZhiZhenLian” and provides service for its suppliers. For example, JD cooperates the suppliers of holothurian to trace each stage of holothurian cultivation from breeding to processing based on the blockchain technology and IoT devices. Footnote 3 Consumers can learn about the growth information of every holothurian through a specific digital certificate. In this way, consumers have more trust in products and have greater user stickiness with the brands. Footnote 4 The findings in our study are consistent with the above real-world observations. Moreover, our study further considers the subsidy mechanism and different selling modes, which provides some managerial insights into the platform’s leading blockchain adoption. First, it is important for the platform to collaborate with a supplier who has great capability of quality management. Only when the supplier has enough capability to provide high-quality product, the supply chain members will decide to adopt blockchain according to the costs. Blockchain improves the efficiency of supply chain by mitigating consumers uncertainty of product quality. In this paper, we explore that blockchain disclosing the heterogeneity between suppliers reduces their competition pressure and further benefits the supply chain. This implies that members adopting blockchain should pay attention to the supply chain structure, consisting of upstream competition and suppliers’ heterogeneity. Second, the platform’s subsidy strategy could create more collaboration of blockchain adoption. As the leader of blockchain adoption, the platform is motivated to reduce the cost pressure on suppliers, which promotes the blockchain adoption consequently. In fact, the blockchain leader has greater benefits than participants in the early stage of blockchain4; thus, it is reasonable that the leader is willing to provide incentive to adopt blockchain. Blockchain’s role in alleviating competition creates “free-riding” opportunity for both suppliers. Therefore, the platform’s leadership in adopting blockchain not only benefits himself, but also improves the performance of the entire supply chain. Third, the platform is the most likely to adopt blockchain in AR mode. The advantage of agency contract and superior capability of Supplier A makes blockchain works the best in AR mode. In the pure selling modes, the platform may accept a higher blockchain cost in RR mode than AA mode when the commission rate is very low and the upstream competition is relatively fierce even though the performance of supply chain is proven to be better in AA mode. Regarding to the blockchain participant, the superior supplier has more willingness to join blockchain than the inferior supplier in the pure selling modes, but this situation may be inversed by the asymmetry of hybrid selling modes. To promote the blockchain adoption, the platform always prefers to subsidize the superior supplier in AA, RR and AR mode. However, the platform may prefer to subsidize the inferior supplier in RA mode when the difference between suppliers’ capability is relatively small. Our study examines platform-leading blockchain adoption issue and the value of blockchain traceability under upstream competition. There still are some limitations, which provides directions for future research. First, it would be interesting to study how the platform motivates suppliers to improve their capabilities of quality management through adopting blockchain. As a result, there will be more coordination issues among the supply chain members about costs and benefits associated with adopting blockchain. Second, blockchain can solve the issue of information asymmetry between the downstream and upstream members and creates transparency inside the supply chain. For example, the downstream members could learn about the upstream members’ practice through blockchain, such as the sourcing behavior (Cui et al., 2022a). Although this paper focuses on the blockchain’s role in sending trustworthy messages to consumers, we also study the issue of information asymmetry in Appendix C. We find that since the platform and suppliers could reach a consensus about the blockchain adoption when it is adopted to eliminate the consumers uncertainty, the information asymmetry doesn’t make a significant effect in this case. Third, blockchain adoption could be considered as a signal about product quality when consumers are strategic. The game among consumers, suppliers and the platform will lead to more discussion about adopting blockchain.

column1: From bytes to sustainability: Leveraging supply chain digitization for enhancing energy resilience
column2: The escalating global energy demand, coupled with the urgency of climate change, underscores the necessity for innovative approaches to achieve energy resilience and security. This study critically examines the interrelationship between global supply chain breadth, digital transformation, and energy resilience, addressing the key themes of this special issue across different aspects of energy security. This study used robust static panel data models for the assessment. Utilizing unbalanced data of 87 countries in 5 models and 95 countries in 6th model (2008–2022), the analysis results reveal a non-linear relationship between supply chain breadth and the five dimensions of energy security: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability, and developability while digitization had shown the moderating effect. The findings suggest that while the initial expansion of global supply chains may heighten vulnerabilities due to complexity and interdependence, long-term development fosters energy security through diversification and operational flexibility. Digital transformation is identified as a crucial moderator, stabilizing this dynamic by optimizing energy flow, reducing inefficiencies, and enabling an effective transition to renewable energy systems. Technologies such as blockchain and IoT enhance monitoring and management capabilities, mitigating disruptions and supporting sustainable energy governance. This study's findings provide actionable insights into how digitization strategies can be leveraged to align supply chain management with energy resilience objectives. By integrating supply chain theory with energy economics, this research offers a unique contribution to understanding the transformative potential of digital tools in mitigating energy risks while addressing broader sustainability goals. The policy implications emphasize the importance of digital infrastructure investment and cross-sector collaboration to design robust energy security strategies. This research study advances the discourse on supply chain digitization within the context of energy resilience, providing novel insights for policymakers, energy economists, and stakeholders aiming to navigate the challenges of a rapidly evolving energy landscape.
column3: 5 Conclusion and policy implications At the wake of global energy-led environmental issues, households, businesses and governments are looking for ways to secure energy sources. Globalization has also led businesses to integrate across regions and borders forming value chains in their distinct products to define the energy composition that is suited for their growth. Environmental theories would suggest the limiting of value chains' growth in order to secure posterity. The exploration of the interaction of value chain growth with energy is required to understand how decoupling can be initiated. This study explores how the development of supply chains are influencing the energy security. The indicator of energy security is developed from the indicators provided by ( Le and Nguyen, 2019 ) which are assessed against the changes in the supply chain depth proposed by World Economic Forum. The study has explored the data from OECD database for 87 countries between 2008 and 2022. Using the panel FGLS model the results showed the non-linear effect to supply chain showed to have a U-shaped effect on energy security overall while its effects are different for different sub-indicators of energy security. The U shape effect implies that economies need to integrate and develop supply chains to beyond certain thresholds so that it can help increase energy security at the national level. However developing supply chains in time taking and costly process, this study adds to a policy intervention of digitization which an expectation that it can help increase the ability of supply chains to induce energy security. The results of the moderation effect showed that digitization counteracts the effect of supply chain on energy security which leads to stabilization. This stabilization helps in two ways, firstly it would lead to an increase in the predictability of the effects of supply chain on energy security. Secondly, it would lead to an increase in energy security at low levels of supply chain depth. More details insights from the nonlinear moderation is shown using the visualization of the results in Figs. 8 to 13 . Policymakers should ensure the expansion of supply chain breadth in order to increase energy security at the macroeconomic level. Further in order to expedite the energy security transition, policymakers should also need to explore the sub-indices. The results of digitization have shown the ability of the country to gain higher energy security even at low levels of supply chain breadth. The government should develop value chain friendly / supportive energy laws so that their presence in the country is secured but their counter effect on energy must also be catered, like the increase in value chains in one place increases energy security, it also reduces the use of fossil energy, thus policy makers need to put plans in place to develop renewable energy infrastructure. The digitization policy must also include energy use transparency and clean energy transition targets in mind so that with digitization businesses reduce their reliance of fossil energy. Each country should set their priority areas where green innovation is required in order to align the value chain growth and sustainable energy together which can help decouple the economic growth and environmental quality. The results of the study are limited to the data provided by OECD library for the selected variables. Future studies can explore the effect of other forms of supply chain breadth with other indicators of energy security so that its in-depth effects can be explored. The results can further be explored by going deep into the type of digitization the country is adopting, it can be financial technology, or it can be artificial intelligence. Further new forms of energy are also explored in other studies, so the definition of energy security can be further extended.

column1: Blockchain technology adoption mechanism for semiconductor chip supply chains considering information disclosure under cost-sharing contract
column2: To combat substandard semiconductor chips and enhance market control, a blockchain technology adoption mechanism is crucial in managing semiconductor chip quality within supply chains. This paper establishes two-stage Stackelberg game models treating the usage level of blockchain technology as an endogenous variable for semiconductor chip supply chains consisting of a single manufacturer and a single retailer, considering consumer preferences, decision-makers’ risk attitudes, technological enhancement cost, and additional testing cost. This study expands the application of blockchain technology, game models that treat the usage level of blockchain technology as an exogenous variable, and those that only address the design of single-type cost-sharing contracts. This paper further explores the blockchain technology adoption mechanism from the aspects of the optimal usage level of blockchain technology or enhancement level of information disclosure, pricing strategy, and utility profit. The results indicate when the semiconductor chip manufacturer bears the technological enhancement cost alone, the adoption of blockchain technology improves the information disclosure level, increase the market demand, and reduce the downstream testing demand, enhancing overall profitability. The fixed-ratio cost-sharing contract for additional testing does not prove effective. However, when the semiconductor chip retailer falls below a certain threshold, the fixed-ratio cost-sharing contract for technological enhancement further enhances the usage level of blockchain technology and overall profitability, fostering a win-win scenario.
column3: 8 Conclusions This paper examines the impacts of various factors such as quality information disclosure, consumer utility, additional testing cost, and technological enhancement cost on the equilibrium decisions within semiconductor chip supply chains consisting of a single manufacturer and a single retailer. Two-stage Stackelberg game models are constructed to analyse decision-making before and after the adoption of blockchain technology. Then, to alleviate the cost pressure of the semiconductor chip manufacturer, another two-stage Stackelberg game models are established under fixed-ratio sharing modes for additional testing and technological enhancement costs. Subsequently, the influences of the cost coefficient, cost-sharing ratio, and risk aversion coefficient on the adoption of blockchain technology in semiconductor chip supply chains are explored. Finally, this paper studies how the information disclosure level, regarded as an exogenous variable, affects equilibrium decisions in supply chains. This study makes three significant contributions. Firstly, this paper establishes a theoretical framework linking blockchain technology with semiconductor chip quality management from a supply chain perspective. By considering factors such as the information disclosure level, the decision-makers’ risk attitude, uncertain demand, consumer utility, and multi-type costs, this paper delves into the complexity of this problem and proposes viable solutions. This study not only extends the application scenarios of blockchain technology but also provides new approaches for stakeholders to combat the entry of substandard semiconductor chips. Secondly, this study addresses the adoption of blockchain technology in semiconductor chip supply chains by regarding the usage level of this technology as an endogenous variable and formulating two-stage Stackelberg game models before and after adoption. It further develops two-stage Stackelberg game models under fixed-ratio sharing contracts for technological enhancement and additional testing costs. These models extend existing research that previously treated the usage level of blockchain technology as an exogenous variable and considered single-type cost-sharing contracts. Thirdly, the findings confirm that blockchain technology can indeed enhance the overall performance of semiconductor chip supply chains. It is therefore recommended that the manufacturer and the retailer use blockchain technology to improve the information disclosure level. Nevertheless, the fixed-ratio cost-sharing contract for additional testing does not show significant impacts on improving supply chain performance through blockchain technology. On the contrary, when the semiconductor chip retailer shares the cost with a smaller ratio, the fixed-ratio cost-sharing contract for technological enhancement proves more effective in promoting the wide use of blockchain, thereby further boosting the performance of semiconductor chip supply chains. In practice, decision entities must carefully balance various production costs and set the appropriate cost-sharing ratio. This not only alleviates the cost pressure on the manufacturer but also ensures that the cooperation within semiconductor chip supply chains remains intact, promoting overall coordination and optimization. Future research could extend this work in several directions. Firstly, this paper focuses merely on semiconductor chip supply chains with a single manufacturer and a single retailer, further study is needed into the design of blockchain technology adoption mechanism in competitive environments with multiple manufacturers or retailers. Secondly, this paper primarily focuses on semiconductor chip supply chains composed of the manufacturer and the retailer, but the regulations of the government as the key regulator should be examined for their impacts on semiconductor chip quality management decisions from a supply chain standpoint. Exploring the role of government regulations in the blockchain technology adoption mechanism in semiconductor chip supply chains is the following work. Thirdly, the semiconductor chip quality management problem under symmetric information is the focus of this paper, future work aims to investigate decision-making mechanisms of semiconductor chip supply chains enabled by blockchain technology under asymmetric information conditions.

column1: Blockchain enabled traceability â€” An analysis of pricing and traceability effort decisions in supply chains
column2: Despite numerous use cases, enterprise-wide implementations of blockchains have seen limited success. This raises the question of when do firms adopt blockchains and do blockchains benefit supply chains. To answer this, we examine a dyadic supply chain consisting of a buyer and a supplier and analyze their traceability effort and pricing decisions. Our results show that the demand-side, supply-side and reputational factors influencing blockchain adoption are primarily complementary and in the absence of one of them, firms can still adopt blockchain. Furthermore, even in the absence of individual benefits for a supply chain partner, there exist conditions under which blockchain adoption benefits the supply chain that can incentivize players to join blockchain. Overall, we contribute by offering a framework that supply chain players can use to assess the likelihood of blockchain implementation success or failure and address the challenges pertaining to incentives and cost imbalances in blockchain implementation.
column3: Summary of findings. A key insight from our analysis is that (i) demand-side (consumer sensitivity), supply-side (unit cost saving) and reputational factors are strategic complements that drive a firm’s blockchain adoption decision. (ii) When the downstream entity (the buyer) has a relatively greater impact on traceability, the supply chain incurs higher profits than a single firm. Furthermore, the consumer welfare is also higher in the supply chain. (iii) We find that blockchain adoption creates a surplus in a supply chain that can incentivize players to offset the higher costs of technology implementation. (iv) Additionally, traceability has implications for supply chain design. When product collection and reuse is at the buyer’s end, it yields greater supply chain profits when demand and supply-side factors are favorable. Otherwise, the supplier’s involvement in product collection and reuse leads to higher profits. While several studies have focused on the benefits of blockchain technology, few have examined lesser-known aspects of blockchain adoption such as supply and demand characteristics and reputational factors that affect supply chain coordination. Yet, these are critical as evident from Maersk’s and other blockchain failures. Our paper attempts to address this gap. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2 , we discuss the relevant background literature pertaining to our study. Section 3 presents the model and analysis for the single firm. Section 4 presents the supply chain model and comparative results. Section 5 extends our analysis while managerial insights and concluding remarks are discussed in Section 6 .

column1: Should live streaming be adopted for agricultural supply chain considering platform's quality improvement and blockchain support?
column2: Platforms empower farmers to address the quality and safety issues of agricultural products by offering blockchain technology and improving product quality. Recently, live streaming becomes a new sales channel to sell products, and plays a key role in enhancing the visibility of agricultural products and introducing detailed information of agricultural products in real time. This disrupted the long-term cooperative relationship between the platforms and farmers. Based on this, our paper explores that whether and how the agricultural supply chain members should adopt the live streaming channel. We build a game model that consists of a farmer, a platform, and an influencer, and investigate the live streaming introduction strategies in the agricultural supply chain in the context of the platform assisting the farmer (the improvement of quality level and adoption of blockchain). We capture two characteristics of the live streaming channel, i.e., the live streaming channel's impact on market size (live streaming value) and additional profit per unit product derived from the influencer's personal influence (influencer value). We interestingly find that when the live streaming value is low, introducing live streaming negatively impacts the farmer's profit at the low influencer value in the farmer's live streaming. When the live streaming value is low (high), introducing live streaming damages the platform's profit at the moderate (low) influencer value in the platform's live streaming. Therefore, adopting the live streaming channel is not necessarily profitable for agricultural supply chain members. We also extend our model to check the robustness of our findings. This study is the first to explore live streaming introduction strategies in the agricultural supply chain in the context of the platform assisting the farmer, and significantly contributes to the literature and provides valuable guidance for farmers and platforms on when to adopt the live streaming channel in the agricultural supply chain.
column3: 6 Conclusions 6.1 Summary Current scholars have mainly investigated the live streaming introduction strategies ( Cui et al., 2023; Du et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2022 ) and the adoption of different parties ( Huang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Different from the existing literature, this study examines the live streaming introduction strategies in the agricultural supply chain in the context of the platform assisting the farmer (the improvement of quality level and adoption of blockchain) by capturing two characteristics of the live streaming channel, i.e., live streaming value and influencer value. Since both the farmer and platform are likely to introduce the live streaming channel in practice, we establish three models: the benchmark model without live streaming, the model with the farmer’s live streaming, and the model with the platform’s live streaming. Moreover, we extend our study by considering enabled live streaming channel, different influencers and production cost, and illustrate our main findings through numerical studies. We derive managerial insights for the agricultural supply chain dynamics.

column1: The Quantum Leap Toward a Sustainable Future: Exploring the Nexus Between Blockchain, Circular Economy, and Managerial Perceptions
column2: The planetary ecosystem currently confronts a myriad of dire environmental predicaments, necessitating immediate and decisive action to forestall irreversible damage wrought by economic activities. Embracing the tenets of circular economy (CE) presents a compelling and exigent opportunity to attenuate wastage and engender resource recycling. In this milieu, blockchain technology (BCT) emerges as a pivotal instrumentality in imbricating CE principles into the tapestry of environmentally conscientious supply chain practices. However, the enigmatic nature of the factors that undergird the seamless integration of BCT into CE practices bespeaks a pressing need for further elucidation. This inquiry endeavors to scrutinize executives' perspectives regarding adopting BCT as a fulcrum for CE and its multifaceted impact on organizational performance. A research model predicated on the belief–action–outcome (BAO) framework was conceptualized and scrutinized utilizing partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) with data gleaned from 164 responses from Malaysian manufacturing firms. The findings evince that respondents' attitudes were significantly swayed by the organizational CE culture, their cognitive grasp of BCT principles, and their normative inclinations. Furthermore, the investigation unearthed that personal norms and attitudes wielded a palpable influence on the inclination to adopt BCT to catalyze CE, thereby exerting a substantive impact on the organization's economic and environmental performance. A roadmap delineating a trajectory to further facilitate BCT‐propelled CE is proffered.
column3: The current study presented a comprehensive investigation into the utilization of BCT to promote sustainable green SC practices, specifically within the CE, to enhance organizational performance. The study utilized the BAO framework to develop a research model that incorporated belief, action, and outcome factors. Data was collected from 164 participants through an online-based questionnaire, which was then analyzed using the PLS-SEM approach via SmartPLS software. The findings demonstrated that CEC, PKB, and PNR had a significant impact on respondents' ATT, while ATT and PNR were significant factors in shaping their INA. Additionally, INA was found to be a highly predictive factor in both ECP and ENP.The study, however, faces several limitations. Primarily, our research was confined to manufacturing firms in Malaysia, thus potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings to other settings due to unique contextual nuances. Secondly, the cross-sectional nature of the study raises concerns regarding endogeneity, as causal relationships cannot be definitively established. Future investigations could overcome these constraints by conducting longitudinal studies spanning diverse industries and geographies to corroborate our findings. Moreover, exploring the impact of additional contextual variables and employing alternative research methodologies, such as experimental or case study approaches, could offer deeper insights into the integration of BCT in CE practices. Subsequent research avenues could also delve into the integration of proenvironmental theories, like the theory of planned behavior, NAT, or the value–belief–norm theory, to better comprehend the drivers and intentions behind BCT adoption for promoting CE practices. These theoretical frameworks could serve as valuable tools for analyzing the decision-making processes involved in adopting sustainable practices and devising strategies to encourage more environmentally conscious behaviors within SCs.

column1: Non-fungible tokens in retailing: Sources of value and strategic implications
column2: From Balenciaga to Bored Apes, non-fungible tokens (NFTs) have captured popular, managerial, and scholarly attention. However, despite some prominent exceptions, the question of whether and how NFTs can represent a real source of value for retailers remains open. This paper provides a framework to consider ways in which NFTs can be a source of value in retailing. We identify three technical features of NFTs (decentralization, immutable encryption, automated execution), which in turn offer potential utility to retailers in the form of three value propositions (transcendence, dynamic contingencies, flexible identification), which a survey study suggests are valued by managers but not yet connected to NFTs. To help make this connection, we use illustrative examples to demonstrate the ways in which NFTs can deliver these three value propositions in a single marketing tool. Taken together, we hope this framework's proposed relationships will spark future work in this area, leading to the development—and evolution—of theories of NFTs and their use in retailing as this technology continues to progress.
column3: Conclusion: Implications of the framework for the future of retailing We have provided a framework that offers a snapshot of the potential future uses of NFTs. However, NFTs will almost certainly continue to evolve, as will retailers’ understanding of their tactical and strategic use. We also anticipate individual differences in predispositions toward exploring and exploiting the value propositions of NFTs. For example, in the survey data reported above, we identified significant negative correlations between participants’ evaluations of NFTs' potential value for their business and both their age ( r = -0.20, p < .05) as well as years of work experience ( r = -0.32, p < .001). These findings suggest that managers tend to view NFTs more skeptically the older they are and the more professional experience they have. Moreover, NFTs themselves accumulate value through different value propositions, as they can accumulate value over time (dynamic contingencies) and space (transcendence), which persists independently of the current owner and transfers to future owners (flexible identification). While other products can also offer each of these value dimensions separately to some extent, NFTs provide one uniting entity. Thus, our framework can also help us understand what may happen when the technical features of NFTs change, or if firms design NFTs that emphasize one feature over another. Specifically, some scholars suggest that centralization may be increasing in the NFT market with tight networks of NFT owners and traders ( Nadini et al., 2021 ). Moreover, changes in the underlying approval mechanism of a blockchain can potentially lead to more centralized structures ( Asif & Hassan, 2023 ). Our framework suggests that should more centralization occur in the NFT market, less interpersonal trust may be required or generated by related transactions. Rather, trust will be contingent on consumers’ perception of the centralized hub through which NFTs become organized. Centralization may also reduce the transcendent capabilities of NFTs, creating greater separation between online and offline experiences. For some retailers, this may be desirable, as they see their online and offline consumers as distinct segments. However, for other retailers, the loss of transcendence may create undesirable silos, both between consumers and between online and offline marketing efforts. We may also consider the potential effects of designing NFTs that lack automated execution. If automated execution becomes a less central feature of NFTs, they may become more like typical digital goods, in that they offer a static meaning and lower levels of psychological ownership ( Atasoy & Morewedge, 2018 ). For some retailers, this may be acceptable and even desirable, as they are able to better control the “life” of the NFT. Rather than investing in smart contracts, they may simply release subsequent waves of NFTs, each tailored to the firm's current offerings and consumer preferences. For other firms, though, NFTs designed without smart contracts may have a short lifespan: the risk of satiation with NFTs may increase, undermining their value as means of maintaining consumer satisfaction over time. Furthermore, the ability to adapt to consumer experiences through the NFT will be reduced. Thus, such firms may need to rely on other means to collect data about consumers’ actions, to provide goal progress signals, and to reward beneficial activities. Finally, we can consider the possibility that immutable encryption becomes a less reliable feature of NFTs. For example, “fake” NFTs may be minted. If this is the case, the power of NFTs to help authenticate and guard against counterfeiting will obviously be disrupted. However, any gains from that an NFT or product might have via an accumulated ownership provenance may also be threatened. If NFT technology or related communities develop in ways that discourage transparency, we may expect NFTs to become increasingly associated with ethically questionable practices such as money laundering and the exchange of illegal goods. Given our framework, we would argue that the decision of whether a firm should engage with NFTs need not be rooted in its motivation to be seen as trendy or cutting-edge. Rather, this decision can be driven by an assessment of the consumer benefits that NFTs offer, particularly when these benefits are challenging to provide within their industry. Furthermore, firms can use this framework to determine which technical features of NFTs should be most focal given their strategic needs. Our framework offers a starting point to both academics and practitioners to broaden perspectives on NFTs and can contribute as this technology continues to expand and evolve.

column1: Use of non-fungible tokens in operations and supply chain management
column2: Non-fungible tokens (NFT) are secured storage methods for unique and non-interchangeable data items. While NFTs are commonly associated with digital arts and the cryptocurrency market, the paper explores their potential in industrial applications, particularly within operations and supply chain management. The paper introduces the technology and key processes of NFTs, providing a foundation for understanding their application in operations and supply chains. The design science method is employed by conducting requirement collection with a small group of experts and based on this a set of potential applications for operations and supply chain management is outlined. Five use case applications are presented from the requirements management point of view. The artefact developed in the process is a sample implementation, demonstrating how NFTs can be practically employed to address specific operational requirements. The results indicate that physical components, digital assets, uniqueness of the entity, contracts, security, and multiple stakeholders collectively enable various use cases where NFTs can provide value.
column3: The paper has aimed to contribute by exploring the use cases of NFTs in the context of operations and supply chain management. The examples demonstrate that NFTs offer intriguing opportunities for industrial applications within these domains. With the increasing importance of digital components in product development, manufacturing, and supply chain-related systems, NFTs can play an important role in authenticating licenses for accessing unique operation features. The possible impact of non-fungible tokens on operational processes is comparable to blockchains. Security of intangible tokens can provide solutions where centralised solutions are not feasible due to the long life-cycle of the physical asset or changing stakeholders in the market. Non-fungible tokens can link to financial transactions, such as change of ownership, rights to manufacture, rights to use software or a service, or automated transactions or material release. Linking non-fungible identification with serial numbers of parts and products can provide long-term documentation for authenticity, origin and manufacturing details related to safety, security and sustainability. The results of this study can be compared to studies conducted in the field of blockchain applications in operations and supply chains. It can be expected that the barriers to implementation are similar in non-fungible tokens as technology has similar challenges in implementation and cost of processing (Mathivathanan et al. Citation 2021). This study has limitations. The implementation of proposed use cases has not been very thorough as the purpose has been to develop a proof-of-concept type of description to answer the research question. Most definitely, all possible application areas have not been identified in this paper. Also, in terms of implementation, one can say that most use cases described follow a similar pattern, generating a sequential number in response to a minting request. This approach is rather trivial and does not address specific challenges like validation of the minter-provided information, or detection of minting multiple NFTs based on the same data, which would be needed for actual wide-scale application implementation. Also, the functionality of the contracts is limited. The sample codes could generate hash values based on input instead of using sequential numbers and access control, permissions could have been enhanced. Further research is needed to study the propositions presented, but the possibilities of non-fungible tokens should be explored further in practical applications. It can be argued that non-fungible tokens are not needed for all applications. Blockchain itself can solve several related use cases. However, non-fungible tokens can improve traceability, visibility, safety and security when the need is uniquely representing the production and operations. This should be the case when ownership and life-cycle-related features are important for product instance-level tracking nd tracing. Non-fungible tokens can add value compared to plain blockchain implementation when the cases are related to high-level uniqueness, e.g. for authenticity, ownership transfer, intellectual property of licensing, product safety, or other special value tied to product service bundle. The safety of pharmaceuticals, luxury items, expensive wines, intellectual property of custom-made unique 3D prints and special software installed on an IoT device are examples of possible domains where a higher resolution solution could be highly appreciated. The case examples presented were developed based on expert panel proposals and it must be admitted that some of the cases could be implemented with planned blockchain implementation. The conceptual difference presented in the framework aims to help to evaluate when the use of non-fungible tokens should make sense and when the use of it would be an overkill. By identifying and exploring the potential use cases of NFTs in operations and supply chain management, this paper sets the stage for future research and development in this area. It highlights the need for practical implementation studies and the importance of understanding how NFTs can bring tangible benefits to various stakeholders within the operations and supply chain ecosystem. However, further research is necessary to develop and test these applications in real-world settings. Conducting proof-of-concept studies will provide valuable insights into the feasibility and practicality of implementing NFTs within operations and supply chains. Additionally, understanding the managerial implications of utilising NFTs can pave the way for their effective integration into existing systems.

column1: The use of blockchain in organisations for sustainable development: a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis
column2: Blockchain research has proliferated in recent years, attracting more attention from academics and practitioners. However, the current body of management literature is widely scattered and lacks a comprehensive view of how the use of blockchain in organisations impacts environmental and social sustainability. To bridge this gap, our review comprehensively examines 238 academic papers sourced from the Scopus database, synthesising previous research on the convergence of blockchain and sustainability. Employing a systematic approach and incorporating bibliometric analysis, our study provides an analysis of the current management research landscape concerning blockchain and sustainability. Our study yields a comprehensive model comprising the antecedents, blockchain mechanisms, and sustainability outcomes of the use of blockchain in organisations. Based on our literature review, we establish a future research agenda and provide practical implications.
column3:
Our research synthesises evidence on blockchain applications in management and related sectors, emphasising sustainability initiatives. Through an SLR, we discover that, blockchain technology driven by regulatory, societal, and organisational antecedents, positively impacts environmental and social sustainability in organisations through mechanisms of traceability, transparency, and immutability. Our proposed model illustrates the relationship between antecedents, mechanisms, and environmental and social sustainability outcomes, filling a gap in current research. Our study uniquely combines bibliometric and content analysis, diverging from previous literature reviews that have not comprehensively analysed blockchain and sustainability across industries beyond supply chains.

Our study provides a few contributions. First, our findings, derived from our uniquely combined bibliometric and content analyses, offer researchers insights into the existing boundaries and research scope within the field, highlighting underexplored and innovative topics for future research, facilitating a deeper integration of blockchain in management contexts. Second, our bibliometric analysis helps identify key figures, institutions, and influential articles, guiding potential collaborations and advancing research in the field. And third, our approach has organised extant literature into a comprehensive model that considering antecedents, mechanisms, and outcomes establishes a clearer link between blockchain applications and sustainability.

column1: Blockchain empowerment: enhancing consumer trust and outreach through supply chain transparency
column2: Despite the growing interest in blockchain for supply chain transparency, a gap remains in understanding consumer perceptions and attitudes toward blockchain-supported initiatives. This study examines how consumers perceive blockchain's role in enhancing supply chain transparency, the factors influencing consumer trust in blockchain-enabled transparency, and the implications for consumer engagement and behaviour within the supply chain network. Through a scenario-based experiment, we find that technology-supported transparency enhances consumer trust not only in the focal firm but also in various stakeholders involved. Specifically, consumers exhibit higher trust in retailers and other stakeholders when firms adopt decentralised transparency systems compared to centralised ones. Decentralised technology-supported transparency significantly influences consumers’ decisions to interact directly with stakeholders, shifting their preference toward responsible supply chain actors over focal firms. While multi-stakeholder transparency does not directly affect consumers’ purchase intentions, high trust in the technology positively influences their intention to purchase. Our study provides actionable managerial insights, guiding decision-makers in adopting decentralised transparency practices to strengthen stakeholder relationships and align with consumer expectations. By understanding the nuances of consumer trust in technology-supported transparency, firms can make more informed strategic decisions, ultimately enhancing the overall performance of their supply chains.
column3: This study addresses a significant gap in production research by examining consumer perceptions of blockchain-enabled transparency in supply chains. Our findings show that adopting decentralised transparency mechanisms enhances consumer trust across the supply chain but does not directly increase purchase intentions. This increased trust fosters greater consumer engagement and collaboration among supply chain partners, which is crucial for optimising production systems and logistics operations. For engineers and decision-makers, implementing blockchain technology offers practical benefits in enhancing transparency, traceability, and accountability within supply chains. Viewing these technological investments as long-term strategic initiatives can lead to improved supply chain performance and resilience. Future research could explore the application of blockchain technology in different industries and its impact on production metrics. Investigating the challenges of implementing decentralised transparency mechanisms will further contribute to the advancement of production systems and supply chain logistics.

column1: Blockchain adoption in a green supply chain: Considering information asymmetry of consumersâ€™ privacy concern
column2: In this study, we consider a green supply chain (GSC) with one manufacturer producing green products and one retailer implementing the sales effort, and assume that blockchain adoption increases market demand while causing the consumers' privacy concern (CPC) and that the retailer privately knows the CPC level information. Subsequently, we conduct games in three scenarios: (i) no blockchain adoption (N), (ii) blockchain adoption and information symmetry (BS), and (iii) blockchain adoption and information asymmetry (BA). Then, we obtain the manufacturer's optimal contract schemes and the retailer's optimal sales-effort levels in the three scenarios. Further, we analyze the optimal preferences of GSC members for these three scenarios. The results show that: (i) supply disruption occurs in Scenario BA if the probability of the high CPC level is too low, otherwise, the retailer prefers Scenario BA the most; (ii) the manufacturer's optimal ex-ante expected profit in Scenario BA is always lower than that in Scenario BS; (iii) the manufacturer prefers Scenario BS or Scenario BA over Scenario N under specific conditions; and (vi) blockchain adoption can achieve the Pareto improvement of the GSC under specific conditions.
column3: 6 Concluding remarks 6.1 Conclusion discussion We build a two-echelon GSC comprising one manufacturer and one retailer. We discuss both the positive and negative effects of blockchain adoption on the GSC. We focus on studying how blockchain adoption affects the GSC performance. Here, the positive impact refers to the situation in which blockchain adoption makes consumers fully trust the products' greenness level and the negative impact refers to the blockchain adoption cost and CPC. Moreover, the CPC level is treated as the retailer's private information, which makes it more difficult for the manufacturer to make decisions on blockchain adoption. Based on these assumptions, three scenarios are developed: Scenarios N, BS, and BA. By analyzing the manufacturer's optimal contracts and the retailer's optimal sales-effort level in the three scenarios, we deduce the GSC members' optimal (ex-ante expected) profit in each scenario. Moreover, GSC members' optimal preferences for the three scenarios are analyzed. The main findings of this study are as follows. From the perspective of the manufacturer's optimal contracts, the retailer's preservation profit affects only the manufacturer's wholesale price and does not affect the supply quantity decision. The sensitivity level of the wholesale price on the preservation profit is related to the type of contract. For the type- L contracts, the sensitivity levels of the wholesale price on the preservation profit in Scenarios BS and BA are the same, and this sensitivity level is lower (higher) than that in Scenario N if the greenness level is relatively high (low); for the type- H contracts, the sensitivity level of the wholesale price on the preservation profit in Scenario BA is always higher than that in Scenario BS, but both sensitivity levels in Scenario BS and Scenario BA can be lower than the sensitivity level of the wholesale price in Scenario N if the greenness level is high enough. The retailer's sales-effort level is directly affected by the manufacturer's supply quantity. If the manufacturer sets a higher (lower) supply quantity after blockchain adoption than before blockchain adoption, the retailer should accordingly increase (decrease) the sales-effort level. In other words, blockchain adoption induces the retailer to set a higher (lower) sales-effort level than that before blockchain adoption if the greenness level is relatively high (low). Furthermore, we discuss the optimal preferences of the GSC members for blockchain adoption and information sharing. An important conclusion is that the manufacturer has no willingness to cooperate with the retailer in Scenario BA if the probability of the high CPC level is low enough ( β < β 0 ), which causes supply disruption. At this point, both GSC members' ex-ante expected profits are equal to zero, and they prefer the other two scenarios. Thus, the manufacturer has no way to screen the retailer's private CPC level. The retailer must actively take measures to share the CPC level information with the manufacturer if blockchain is adopted under a low enough probability of the high CPC level. Under the conditions that the manufacturer is willing to cooperate with the retailer in Scenario BA ( β ≥ β 0 ): ( i ) The type- H retailer always obtains the preservation profit in the three scenarios while the type- L retailer's optimal preference is always Scenario BA because of the information rent. Moreover, the higher the greenness level, the higher the information rent. ( ii ) The manufacturer's optimal ex-ante expected profit in Scenario BA is always lower than that in Scenario BS. However, her optimal ex-ante expected profit in Scenario BS or BA can be higher than her optimal profit in Scenario N under specific conditions, that is, β < β 1 for Scenario BS and β 0 ≤ β < β 2 for Scenario BA. Under these conditions, the GSC achieves a Pareto improvement through blockchain adoption. Moreover, an extended model in which the greenness level is endogenous is developed, and the robustness of the main conclusions is verified. By analyzing this extended model, we find that the manufacturer's greenness level in the type- L contract is not affected by information asymmetry, while she chooses a more conservative greenness level under information asymmetry compared with that under information symmetry in the type- H contract. In addition, the greenness levels in Scenarios BS and BA are both higher than the greenness level in Scenario N if the unit blockchain adoption cost is low enough. From the perspective of profit, when the CPC level is symmetric, the manufacturer prefers blockchain adoption if the probability of the high CPC level is low enough, that is, β < β 1 E ; when the CPC level is asymmetric, the manufacturer prefers blockchain adoption if the probability of the high CPC level is in the middle, that is, β 0 E ≤ β < β 2 E . However, it should be noted that the conditions under which the manufacturer is willing to cooperate with the retailer in Scenario BA become stricter if the greenness level is endogenous, that is, β 0 E − β 0 > 0 .

column1: Trends in the dynamic evolution of blockchain and circular economy: A literature review and bibliometric analysis
column2: The intersection of blockchain technology and circular economy (CE) practices holds significant potential for enhancing sustainability, transparency, and efficiency. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis to explore the current research landscape in this domain. Key findings indicate a rapid growth in publications, highlighting a burgeoning interest in leveraging blockchain for CE initiatives. The analysis identifies critical approaches such as enhancing supply chain transparency, improving resource management, and facilitating product lifecycle tracking. However, the integration of blockchain into CE practices presents challenges, including technical complexities, scalability issues, and regulatory hurdles. Addressing these challenges requires interdisciplinary and cross‐sectoral collaboration, as well as continuous research and innovation. Future research should focus on the integration of emerging technologies with blockchain, longitudinal studies on long‐term impacts, socio‐economic implications, and the development of regulatory frameworks. This study contributes to the existing body of knowledge by providing unique insights and outlining potential research directions at the intersection of blockchain and CE.
column3: This study has demonstrated the significant potential of BT in advancing the core objectives of the CE, particularly in improving transparency, traceability, and resource efficiency within supply chains. The results indicate that blockchain enables better tracking of materials throughout their lifecycle, from production to disposal, which is essential for circular business models that aim to reduce waste and extend resource use.Key findings from the analysis show that blockchain's ability to create decentralized, immutable ledgers significantly enhances accountability and supply chain visibility, supporting more sustainable practices in industries with complex supply chains. This study identified that blockchain not only improves material traceability but also fosters trust among stakeholders, which is crucial for implementing CE principles such as reuse, recycling, and closed-loop systems.However, the study also highlights critical challenges that must be addressed for blockchain to be widely adopted in CE practices. The main barriers include scalability, interoperability, and the need for regulatory frameworks that facilitate blockchain integration across global supply chains. Addressing these obstacles through collaborative efforts between industries, governments, and academia will be key to unlocking blockchain's full potential in the CE.7.1 Study implicationsThe implications of this study are twofold—contributing to both the theoretical understanding of blockchain's role in the CE and offering practical insights for industry leaders and policymakers.From a theoretical standpoint, this research expands the literature on how blockchain can enhance SCM within the CE framework. It shows that blockchain's core features—transparency, traceability, and decentralization—are vital for achieving CE's objectives of minimizing waste and maximizing resource efficiency.In practical terms, the study provides actionable insights for industries seeking to implement blockchain-based circular practices. By improving supply chain governance, blockchain allows for the more effective tracking and management of materials, which is crucial for industries such as manufacturing, electronics, and automotive. Furthermore, this research underscores the importance of developing regulatory frameworks that support blockchain's scalability while ensuring data privacy and security.For policymakers, the study emphasizes the need to create an environment conducive to blockchain innovation. Policies must address the technical and governance challenges associated with decentralized systems, ensuring that blockchain is implemented in ways that align with both sustainability goals and regulatory requirements.7.2 LimitationsWhile this study provides valuable insights, several limitations must be acknowledged. The analysis was primarily based on data from selected academic databases, which may have excluded relevant literature. Additionally, the study's theoretical nature limits the evaluation of blockchain's real-world implementation in circular supply chains. Future research should incorporate empirical case studies to validate the findings and explore practical challenges. Finally, the analysis did not fully account for regional regulatory differences, which may impact blockchain adoption globally.In conclusion, BT offers substantial opportunities for enhancing the transparency, traceability, and sustainability of supply chains in the CE. However, realizing its full potential will require overcoming key challenges related to scalability, interoperability, and regulation. This study contributes to the expanding discourse on blockchain and CE by offering both theoretical insights and practical recommendations. By improving transparency and fostering collaboration across industries, blockchain has the potential to drive the transition toward a more sustainable and circular global economy.

column1: Value of blockchain for scope 3 carbon disclosure: The moderating role of data processing technologies
column2: Disclosing carbon emissions in Scope 3 is essential for mitigating pollution and the associated environmental damage, and blockchain can enhance the disclosure. However, the effect of blockchain on Scope 3 carbon disclosure remains unclear due to a lack of empirical evidence. This paper investigates the value of blockchain for Scope 3 carbon disclosure and examines whether this value can be strengthened by integrating data processing technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, and big data analytics (BDA). Drawing upon the coordination theory, we posit that blockchain as a recording and tracing technology can improve the coordination among supply chain members on collecting carbon emissions data, thereby facilitating firms' Scope 3 carbon disclosure. Furthermore, data processing technologies enable efficient utilization and management of the collected data, potentially coordinating with blockchain to enhance Scope 3 carbon disclosure. We test these relationships using regression analysis based on a sample of 422 observations for Chinese listed firms during 2021 and 2022. The results show that blockchain adoption is positively associated with a firm's Scope 3 carbon disclosure. In addition, adopting each of the three data processing technologies—AI, cloud computing, and BDA—further strengthens the positive relationship. This study contributes to academic knowledge and evidence on blockchain and sustainable supply chain management with practical suggestions for managing carbon emissions at the supply chain level through the combined adoption of blockchain and data processing technologies.
column3:
6. Discussion
6.1. Findings
This study explores the role of digital technology adoption on Scope 3 carbon disclosure. Analyzing a sample of 422 firm-year observations from China, we find a positive relationship between blockchain adoption and a firm's Scope 3 carbon disclosure. In addition, the positive relationship is more pronounced for firms adopting higher adoption levels of data processing technologies, including AI, cloud computing, and BDA. These findings imply that adopting blockchain can enhance Scope 3 carbon disclosure, and data processing technologies can interact and complement blockchain to achieve better Scope 3 carbon disclosure practice.
6.2. Theoretical implications
This study provides several implications for research. First, it adds to the existing literature that explores the effect of digital transformation on supply chain sustainability by focusing on Scope 3 carbon disclosure (Lai et al., 2023; Lerman et al., 2022; Schilling and Seuring, 2024). Previous studies on this topic investigated whether digital transformation contributes to general SSCM (Khan et al., 2022) and carbon-related outcomes such as carbon management (Sharma et al., 2022; Sheng et al., 2023) and carbon emissions reduction (Huang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a,b). Our study represents the first attempt to empirically examine the effect of digital technology adoption on a specific aspect of supply chain sustainability—Scope 3 carbon disclosure. Such an investigation is relevant since Scope 3 carbon disclosure is unprecedentedly important for climate change mitigation and supply chain decarbonization (Blanco, 2021; Hettler and Graf-Vlachy, 2024). Our findings reveal that blockchain can help firms disclose carbon emissions in Scope 3. Our study lays the groundwork and offers a conceptual framework for future research concerning the influence of digital transformation on carbon disclosure.
Second, previous research on the antecedents to corporate carbon disclosure largely concentrated on external pressures from stakeholders (Guenther et al., 2016; Jira and Toffel, 2013; Reid and Toffel, 2009) and internal firm characteristics such as industry, type of ownership, and carbon performance (Borghei, 2021; Cowan and Deegan, 2011; He et al., 2022; Kim and Lyon, 2011; Ott et al., 2017), while the role of digital transformation has been neglected. Focusing explicitly on Scope 3 carbon disclosure, our study addresses this research gap by empirically examining the relationship between digital technology adoption and carbon disclosure.
Third, this study also extends the literature about digital technologies and SSCM by examining the moderating effect of data processing technologies on blockchain and carbon disclosure links. Most existing studies on this link focused on the effect of a single technology (Khan et al., 2022; Long et al., 2022), while the interaction between digital technologies and sustainable practices remains underexplored. This study provides a deeper look at the synergistic effect of blockchain and data processing technologies on Scope 3 carbon disclosure. We suggest that firms not only enable the recording of carbon emissions data through blockchain but also complement it with data processing technologies to manage the collected data effectively.
