Overview of the research findings.
First, blockchain capability and big data analytics capability can positively affect supply chain integration. This result extends the findings of Jabbar et al. (2024), who highlighted the theoretical benefits of these technologies in the supply chain but did not provide empirical validation. The empirical results show that blockchain enhances information sharing and real-time tracking, improving data authenticity, security, trust, collaboration, and supply integration efficiency. Big data analytics provides business insights, aiding in demand forecasting, inventory optimization, logistics efficiency, and accurate decision-making, thus boosting supply chain coordination and integration. This study also found that when blockchain capability and analytics capability are aligned, supply chain integration increases linearly with the growth of both. When misaligned, integration initially decreases before increasing as both capabilities rise. This finding is novel compared with those of previous studies examining individual technologies because it explores their interactions. The empirical results demonstrate that an aligned blockchain and big data analytics complement one another, enhancing supply chain transparency, efficiency, and security. However, when they are misaligned, integration costs and technical challenges initially burden the system, potentially reducing efficiency. As technologies gradually coordinate and optimize, supply chain integration efficiency improves.

Second, supply chain integration partially mediates the relationship between big data analytics capability and sustainable product innovation and between blockchain capability and sustainable product innovation. This finding extends the research results of Junaid et al. (2022), who argued that supply chain integration is a key factor in improving green innovation but did not consider the technological drivers in the digital era. Our results demonstrate that digital capabilities can promote sustainable product innovation by strengthening supply chain integration. Specifically, big data analytics improves supply chain processes through accurate demand forecasting, real-time monitoring, and intelligent inventory management, enabling more agile and sustainability-oriented product development. Likewise, blockchain capability enhances trust, traceability, and information transparency across supply chain partners, thereby facilitating coordinated actions that support the creation of environmentally and socially responsible products. These findings underscore that the value of digital technologies in sustainable product innovation is, to a significant extent, realized through their role in enabling supply chain integration.

Third, CSR positively moderates the relationship between supply chain integration and sustainable product innovation. The findings extend the work of Kong et al. (2020) on how green supply chain integration drives green innovation through the knowledge creation process, as they did not incorporate CSR into their analytical framework. Our findings show that CSR encourages companies to focus on coordination and transparency in various aspects of the supply chain, enhance trust and cooperation with supply chain partners, and prioritize sustainable sourcing, eco-friendly operations, and lifecycle thinking in product development, improving sustainable product innovation. Additionally, CSR does not significantly moderate the relationship between big data analytics capability and blockchain capability on supply chain integration. A plausible explanation is that blockchain and big data analytics, as efficiency-oriented tools, are primarily focused on enhancing transparency and operational efficiency rather than directly embedding CSR goals such as carbon tracking (Dubey et al. 2016). During the technology-driven supply chain integration phase, companies often prioritize functional optimization and efficiency improvement, which may weaken the influence of CSR in the integration process (Klassen and Vereecke 2012).

Finally, Study 2 provided in-depth insights into the relationships between blockchain capabilities, big data analytics, supply chain integration, CSR, and sustainable product innovation. In addition to reinforcing the conclusions of Study 1, Study 2 identified cost and market positioning as critical boundary conditions for the adoption of digital technologies in agricultural enterprises. This suggests that cost and market positioning not only shape the extent to which companies adopt and implement digital technologies but also influence the effectiveness of these technologies in enhancing supply chain integration and sustainable product innovation. These findings extend Study 1, demonstrating that combining two distinct analytical approaches significantly enhances our understanding of the research model.

7.2 Theoretical Contributions
The theoretical contributions of this study can be summarized in four key points. First, prior studies on the drivers of sustainable product innovation have predominantly focused on well-established factors such as horizontal coopetition (Wu et al. 2025), customer and supplier involvement (Zhao et al. 2018), and top management commitment (Bhatia and Jakhar 2021), while the roles of digital technologies (i.e., blockchain and big data analytics) remain underexplored, particularly their potential interaction effects. To address this research gap, we developed a model based on the IT-driven organizational capability perspective and resource complementarity theory to explore the effects of blockchain capability, big data analytics capability, and their interactions with sustainable product innovation. Consequently, this study contributes to sustainable innovation research by offering a novel perspective on how firms can leverage blockchain and big data analytics to enhance sustainable product innovation, thereby enriching the understanding of blockchain and big data analytics' value in improving product outcomes.

Second, the specific mechanisms through which digital technologies promote sustainable product innovation remain unclear. Supply chain integration is considered a critical mediating mechanism linking digital technologies to sustainable product innovation (Kong et al. 2020; Lin and Fan 2024); however, this mediating role has not yet been empirically examined. This study identifies supply chain integration as a mediator through which blockchain capability and big data analytics capability drive sustainable product innovation. Blockchain capability and big data analytics capability, through improved transparency and real-time intelligent data processing, foster collaboration and trust among supply chain partners, thus enhancing supply chain integration. In turn, the integration of information, relationships, and processes among supply chain partners enhances visibility, trust, and operational coordination, which enables firms to jointly identify sustainability opportunities, reduce environmental impacts across the chain, and embed sustainability into product design and development, ultimately driving sustainable product innovation. By demonstrating this mechanism, our study clarifies how these digital capabilities contribute to sustainable product innovation through the mediating role of supply chain integration.

Third, previous studies on the boundary conditions for sustainable product innovation have primarily focused on environmental factors as moderating variables, such as environmental uncertainty (Zhao et al. 2018), cooperation and competition similarity (Wu et al. 2025), neglecting the moderating role of CSR, a key stakeholder-related variable. This study finds that CSR positively moderates the relationship between supply chain integration and sustainable product innovation. Enterprises with higher levels of CSR are more likely to actively integrate information, relationships, and operational processes across the supply chain, which in turn facilitates the development of environmentally and socially responsible products. By revealing the internal driving force, particularly how CSR positively moderates the impact of supply chain integration on sustainable product innovation, this study provides clear insights into the conditions in which supply chain integration affects sustainable product innovation.

Finally, existing research on sustainable product innovation has predominantly relied on single-method designs, such as systematic literature review (Khan et al. 2021) or structural equation modeling (Zhao et al. 2018; Xie et al. 2019; Wu et al. 2025), which constrain the depth and breadth of insights. This study adopts a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and qualitative analyses to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how blockchain capability and big data analytics capability affect sustainable product innovation. In the quantitative analysis, we develop and empirically test a research model, demonstrating that both capabilities positively influence sustainable product innovation via supply chain integration, and that their interaction strengthens integration when well aligned. CSR further moderates the relationship between supply chain integration and sustainable product innovation, although it does not significantly affect the link between digital capabilities and supply chain integration. In the qualitative analysis, the findings not only corroborate the quantitative results but also identify two potential boundary conditions—blockchain implementation costs and market positioning—thereby offering additional insights. Overall, by integrating quantitative and qualitative methods, this study enhances the robustness and generalizability of the findings, reveals previously unrecognized boundary conditions, and advances methodological innovation in research on digital technologies and sustainable product innovation.

7.3 Managerial Contributions
The following insights are relevant to managerial practices for enhancing sustainable product innovation. First, improvements in sustainable product innovation increasingly rely on emerging digital technologies, such as blockchain and big data analytics. Enterprises should accelerate the integration of these technologies, forming blockchain capability and analytics capability to leverage technological advantages. Specifically, they should select appropriate blockchain platforms to secure key data and establish unified data collection systems with advanced analysis tools to promote data sharing and optimization across the supply chain. Internally, companies should train employees in these technologies regularly to boost technical skills and innovation. Forming cross-departmental teams responsible for implementing and maintaining these technologies ensures effective collaboration and successful application. Enterprises should establish unified data standards and interfaces, allocate resources appropriately, and facilitate these technologies' integration, interoperability, and balanced development.

Second, CSR is an intrinsic motivation for enterprises to improve sustainable product innovation. Enterprises can make efforts in various aspects to enhance their CSR level. First, they can integrate CSR into their core strategies, thus clarifying their CSR goals and visions. Second, they can actively participate in and support local community development projects, invest in agricultural technology innovation, improve production efficiency, and reduce negative environmental impacts. Third, they can actively conduct consumer education using both online and offline promotion methods to raise awareness of sustainable agricultural practices and the value of sustainability-oriented products. Fourth, they should regularly publish CSR reports to increase enterprise transparency and consumers' trust.

Third, cost and market positioning are key factors influencing the adoption of blockchain technology and big data analytics in agricultural enterprises. Companies should tailor their implementation strategies to align with their specific market positioning and cost structures. For those targeting high-end markets or those with strong profitability, increased investment in these technologies can boost supply chain transparency and enhance sustainable product innovation. For cost-sensitive companies, a gradual rollout focused on maximizing return on investment can help minimize upfront costs. Similarly, enterprises facing significant cost pressures can adopt a phased approach, starting with small-scale applications that yield immediate benefits and expanding incrementally to reduce the risks of large initial investments. This step-by-step approach also allows businesses to adapt well to the operational changes these technologies bring.

Finally, beyond the firm level, broader implications can be drawn for policymakers and industry alliances. Government regulators can introduce incentive policies, such as subsidies or tax benefits, to encourage the adoption of blockchain and big data analytics for sustainable product innovation. They can also establish regulatory frameworks and technical standards to ensure data security, interoperability, and alignment with environmental goals. At the industry level, agricultural alliances and associations can promote collaborative innovation by developing shared platforms, setting unified data standards, and disseminating best practices. Such collective efforts can reduce the costs of technology adoption, enhance supply chain transparency, and create an enabling ecosystem for sustainable product innovation across the agricultural sector.

7.4 Research Limitations and Future Research
This study has several limitations. First, we collected data from Chinese agricultural firms, which allowed us to control for cross-industry confounding but may limit the generalizability of our findings. Future research could incorporate samples from a wider range of industries, such as financial firms and manufacturing firms, to enhance the universality of the research results. Second, this study utilizes cross-sectional data for two main reasons. On the one hand, this method is widely used in research on digital technology, making it a suitable approach for examining the relationship between organizational capabilities and innovation outcomes (El-Kassar and Singh 2019; Shamim et al. 2020). On the other hand, blockchain and big data analytics capabilities in Chinese agricultural enterprises are still in the early stages of development, which makes it difficult to obtain longitudinal data that could capture their long-term effects. Although the cross-sectional design limits causal inference, it nevertheless offers valuable insights into how digital technologies are beginning to shape sustainable product innovation. Future studies could build on this by employing longitudinal or panel data to further validate and extend our findings once such datasets become available. Third, this study's data are based on self-reports, which may have subjective limitations. Future research could address this issue by utilizing secondary data. Fourth, it investigates the mechanisms through which digital technologies improve sustainable product innovation in the context of China. Although this approach strengthens internal reliability and mitigates issues arising from cross-country heterogeneity and uneven economic development, it limits generalizability. Future research could extend these findings to other countries to enrich the scope of the study. Fifth, the impact of blockchain capability and big data analytics capability on sustainable product innovation is influenced not only by CSR but also by other contextual factors, such as environmental uncertainty and government support. Future research could further consider the moderating role of other environmental factors. Sixth, the study is based on a static model and cross-sectional data, but firms have a long-term goal of improving sustainable product innovation, so conducting a longitudinal empirical analysis in future research is necessary.

column1: Full transparency or restricted visibility? Mechanisms of blockchain enabled data sharing in supply chain
column2: This study examines values and adoption conditions of Blockchain Technology (BCT) in horizontal demand forecast sharing among retailer, focusing on the influence mechanism of transparency-restriction approaches and BCT's endogenous effects on firms' sharing incentives. We model a supply chain with one manufacturer and multiple retailers, comparing four BCT-enabled data-sharing regimes: open access (permissionless) versus no-open access (permissioned), with or without encryption. Results show that restricted transparency, combined with selective accessibility, aligns individual and collective incentives by curbing wholesale price inflation and improving forecast accuracy. Contrary to intuition, higher transparency does not universally benefit retailers; supplementary encryption can balance data utility and privacy, enabling Pareto-superior outcomes. We further demonstrate BCT can reduces moral hazards in horizontal sharing (e.g. sharing biased forecast), allowing retailers to leverage aggregated demand signals without inefficiently verification. However, excessive transparency in BCT can accelerates retailers' profit erosion, akin to perfect competition. These findings offer micro-foundations for adopting visibility-restriction technologies (e.g. Zero-Knowledge Proofs) and guide the design of context-specific BCT systems. By reconciling transparency-privacy tensions and demonstrating BCT's endogenous role in forecasting, this study advances strategies for enhancing supply chain resilience through BCT innovation.
column3: This paper develops a theoretical model comprising one manufacturer and multiple retailers to investigate the value proposition and adoption conditions of BCT, the influence mechanisms of transparency-restriction approaches, and the endogenous effects of BCT-enhanced transparency on related decision-making. Focusing on combinations of (non-)open-access and (with/without) encryption, we characterise four BCT-enabled data-sharing cases, analyse their equilibrium outcomes, and conduct a comprehensive comparison from both the retailer's and the manufacturer's perspectives. Our study makes three key contributions: (i) It reveals the value and adoption conditions of BCT in horizontal demand forecast sharing among retailers, thereby enriching the literature on horizontal sharing in traditional systems (Ha, Shang, and Wang Citation 2023; Sanders and Wan Citation 2018; Taylor and Xiao Citation 2010) and contributing to prior BCT-related research on one-to-one vertical sharing and pull supply chain setting (Cui, Gaur, and Liu Citation 2024; Cui, Hu, and Liu Citation 2023). (ii) It sheds light on the mechanisms through which two major transparency-restriction approaches (access control and encryption technology) affect supply chain operations, providing micro-level theoretical foundations to support relevant empirical studies (Cong et al. Citation 2023), and offering deeper insights into existing qualified discussions (Koh, Dolgui, and Sarkis Citation 2020). Relevant analyses can also advance the understanding of the integration of BCT with artificial intelligence techniques, including federated learning (Manimuthu et al. Citation 2022). (iii) It extends the BCT literature by treating the adoption of this technology as endogenous, rather than exogenous (Cho et al. Citation 2021; Chod et al. Citation 2020; Dong, Jiang, and Xu Citation 2023). Based on Bayesian inference, we illustrate the endogenous interrelationships among BCT-enhanced transparency, forecast accuracy, and retailers' incentives to share information. This also contributes to the modelling paradigms on BCT enabled forecast sharing by extending insights into push supply chains and one-to-multiple horizontal sharing scenarios (Wang et al. Citation 2021). Our findings can also provide actionable implications and insights for implementation of BCT from tow-folds: firms' incentives for sharing data on BCT, and mechanisms of BCT enabled data-sharing. Towards the former fold, we show that retailers' incentives for sharing data on BCT depend on two components: effects on wholesale price inference and effects on ordering quantity inference. We find that the manufacturer's wholesale price can increase with BCT-enhanced verifiability and a higher level of demand forecast accuracy. Therefore, retailers' horizontal data sharing can constitute a Pareto equilibrium under both open-access and no-open-access cases, provided that no encryption technology is used to restrict visibility for non-sharing retailers. However, although retailers may prefer sharing data on BCT when visibility to non-sharers is restricted, we identify thresholds for the effectiveness of BCT in enhancing verifiability, the extent of data sharing, and the coefficient of variation. These results may be of interest to practitioners in supply chain management and BCT platform operation, since they provide micro-level explanations from a supply chain perspective for extant studies on BCT applications (e.g. Babich and Hilary Citation 2020; Dutta et al. Citation 2020; Wang et al. Citation 2021), particularly those empirical observations (e.g. Cong et al. Citation 2023) on why and how firms participate in BCT-enabled data sharing when visibility restrictions (e.g. access control, ZKP, Layer-2 solutions) are in place. Moreover, these findings can offer critical managerial implications for how to unlock BCT's values in horizontal data sharing. For instance, if without visibility restrictions and with low verifiability (i.e. transparency), either no retailer or all retailers share data; However, if wholesale prices are high and verifiability is low, no-open-access with encryption better incentivises sharing. Towards the latter fold, our analyses reveal that the decision sequence between the manufacturer and retailers plays a pivotal role in BCT enabled data sharing. Specifically, when the manufacturer's wholesale price precedes retailers' ordering quantity and shared data contents are incorporated, we find that supplementary encryption can serve as a powerful coordination mechanism. Under this setting, the manufacturer can anticipate retailers' behaviour and set aggressive wholesale prices to achieve her expected profit at the level of full retailer participation in data sharing. This is because retailers, when shielded by encryption, only need to consider the effects of shared data on ordering quantity inference rather than wholesale price inference. Therefore, supplementary encryption technology can mitigate the risk of wholesale price exploitation while still enabling downstream horizontal data sharing. This finding can be importantly, since it challenges conventional views on BCT's role in supply chain transparency: While prior studies argue that BCT inherently promotes full transparency (e.g. Dong, Jiang, and Xu Citation 2023; Pun, Swaminathan, and Hou Citation 2021) or that its benefits are diminished when transparency is restricted (e.g. Cui, Gaur, and Liu Citation 2024; Liang et al. Citation 2021), we demonstrate that encryption can act as a strategic enabler rather than a barrier. Furthermore, our findings offer practical implications for the design of BCT ecosystems, particularly in leveraging transparency-restriction mechanisms to incentivise data sharing. For instance, the rational deployment of supplemental encryption technologies can create a win – win scenario: retailers benefit from enhanced demand visibility and reduced competitive pressure, while the manufacturer gains access to aggregated forecasts, enabling more effective production planning and pricing decisions. We acknowledge several limitations that provide opportunities for future research: (i) Our theoretical propositions – such as the impact of BCT's supplementary encryption technology on supply chain decisions (e.g. wholesale pricing, ordering quantities) – require empirical validation. Future research could conduct field experiments or case studies in industries where BCT-enabled data sharing has been implemented (e.g. online-retail, pharmaceuticals) to test the robustness of our findings. For instance, examining how encryption affects retailers' willingness to share data in real-world BCT platforms could provide valuable insights into the practical applicability of our models. (ii) Our current model focuses on data sharing and encryption but does not account for other BCT features, such as cost-saving and automation. Extending the model to include these features could reveal new dynamics, such as how cost-saving impacts firms' sharing incentives or how smart contracts automate enforcement mechanisms in data-sharing agreements. Future research can also explore the effects of cost-sharing on initial construction of BCT network among technology provider and supply chain firms. (iii) Our supply chain structure is limited to a single manufacturer and multiple retailers, neglecting the role of upstream firms (e.g. suppliers) in a deep-tier supply chain. Extending the model to include multi-tier interactions (e.g. multi-supplier/one-manufacturer/multi-retailer, or M/1/M) could provide comprehensive understandings of BCT's impact on end-to-end supply chain coordination. In sum, we hope our work inspires future research to build on these insights and advance the field of BCT-enabled supply chain management. column1: Reconfiguring resource orchestration via social capital: a processual view of blockchain in supply chains
column2:
This study examines how social capital's cognitive and relational dimensions enable effective resource orchestration for blockchain implementation in global supply chains. It reconceptualizes blockchain implementation as a dynamic, cyclical process shaped by evolving interorganizational trust and collaboration.
 
 
 
 Adopting an abductive, multi-case qualitative methodology, this study examines data collected from a UK-based food manufacturer and nine of its suppliers from developing economies. Primary data, along with secondary documents, is analyzed using social capital theory as the primary lens and resource orchestration theory as a secondary lens.
 
 
 
 Findings reveal that while structural capital is foundational, advanced cognitive and relational capital are vital for successful blockchain implementation. Features of blockchain, like immutability and automated verification, enable trust to shift from interpersonal to system-based. Challenging linear models, the study shows a recursive loop where blockchain reinforces social capital, enabling ongoing collaboration and capability building.
 
 
 
 Managers should approach blockchain not merely as a technological upgrade but as a relational transformation. Successful implementation requires phased trust-building, capability alignment and tailored orchestration strategies suited to the digital maturity of supply chain partners.
 
 
 
 This research contributes a novel integrative framework linking social capital and resource orchestration in a digitally mediated context, a perspective largely overlooked in the existing literature. It challenges deterministic blockchain implementation models by introducing a co-evolutionary perspective grounded in trust dynamics.
column3: This research develops a framework for blockchain implementation using an abductive approach, examining how different levels of social capital influence resource orchestration. The key contribution is the proposed framework (Figure 2), which reveals the interplay between social capital and resource orchestration in enabling effective blockchain implementation within supply chains. Unlike prior studies that mainly emphasize blockchain s operational and security aspects, our findings uncover a cyclical interaction between cognitive and relational social capital during implementation. We reconceptualize the buyer supplier relationship by showing how trust, shared norms, and collaboration act as critical enablers of blockchain success. While structural capital is foundational, advanced relational and cognitive capital are essential for sustained implementation. Our findings challenge the traditional linear view, showing instead a cyclical relationship: relational capital is vital in early stages, but its role reduces as automation, smart contracts, and system-based trust increase. In addition to theoretical insights, we offer practical implications. Blockchain implementation should be seen as both a technological and relational transformation. Managers should prioritize trust-building through joint training, knowledge sharing, and collaborative governance, enhancing readiness and alignment among stakeholders in global supply chains. 7.1 Limitations and future research This study integrates Social Capital Theory and Resource Orchestration Theory to explain blockchain implementation; it does not fully incorporate other relevant theoretical perspectives such as Dynamic Capabilities and Institutional Theory. These alternative lenses may offer complementary or even competing explanations, particularly in understanding how firms adapt to technological change over time or how institutional pressures shape inter-organizational collaboration. Future research could build on our framework by incorporating these perspectives to provide a more holistic and multi-level understanding of blockchain adoption processes in diverse supply chain contexts. Second, the empirical evidence is derived from a qualitative case study consisting of a single buyer and its network of suppliers. Although this approach enabled in-depth exploration of context-specific dynamics, the findings may be subject to limitations in generalizability. Further research could enhance external validity via methodological triangulation. Large-scale surveys, experimental designs, and/or archival data can provide robustness of the identified relationships, particularly the cyclic interplay between trust and resource orchestration. Third, this study focuses on the UK food sector, which is highly regulated, compliance-oriented, and has a concentrated supply chain. These characteristics may have amplified the importance of social capital in resource orchestration, particularly due to the sector s strong focus on traceability and collaboration. Therefore, applying these findings to other sectors or regions, especially those that are decentralized or less regulated, requires caution. Future research should test the framework across varied institutional, cultural, and structural settings to better understand its generalizability and limitations.

column1: Blockchain and pricing strategies in supply chains considering consumer traceability preference and power structure
column2: Information asymmetry, a common challenge in supply chains, undermines operational efficiency and hinders effective decision-making. Blockchain has emerged as a transformative solution to address this longstanding challenge. This paper explores blockchain investment within supply chain contexts, incorporating varying degrees of consumer preferences regarding traceability. By developing a game-theoretic model with diverse power structures, we investigate chain members’ pricing and blockchain investment strategies under conditions of information asymmetry regarding consumer traceability preferences. Our findings indicate that blockchain investment strategies are jointly determined by the proportion of high-type consumers and the associated usage cost. Both the retailer and the manufacturer will invest in blockchain technology only if the proportion of high-type consumers exceeds their respective investment thresholds. Investment propensity declines with higher blockchain implementation costs. If the incentive is insufficient to meet both parties’ thresholds, neither will invest. When the high-type consumer proportion lies between the two thresholds, low blockchain costs prompt manufacturer-led adoption, whereas high costs shift the investment initiative to the retailer. Additionally, blockchain can create win-win outcomes in supply chains under specific conditions. However, the extent of blockchain value realisation depends on the power structure. From a social welfare perspective, blockchain investments can enhance consumer surplus and social welfare.
column3: Blockchain technology offers a transformative approach to addressing pervasive information asymmetry in supply chains. Its core features of immutability and traceability significantly enhance transparency throughout a product’s entire lifecycle. This not only bolsters consumer trust in brands but also creates distinct value for traceability-conscious consumers. However, because various consumers exhibit differing traceability preferences, the value they derive from blockchain technology can vary. Balancing the cost of blockchain with the value derived from its information traceability is a crucial consideration. This paper develops retailer-dominated and manufacturer-dominated game models. It investigates supply chain members’ product pricing and blockchain investment strategies under information asymmetry regarding consumer traceability preferences. The specific conclusions are as follows: First, supply chain members’ investment strategies are influenced by the interaction between the proportion of high-type consumers and the cost of blockchain usage. Firms consider investing in blockchain only if the share of high-type consumers exceeds a specific threshold. Their willingness to invest diminishes as investment costs rise. Notably, both the retailer and manufacturer will invest in blockchain technology only when the proportion of high-type consumers exceeds their respective individual investment thresholds. When the proportion of high-type consumers falls between the manufacturer and retailer investment thresholds, the investment leader is determined by blockchain usage costs. The manufacturer invests in blockchain when usage costs are low, and the retailer becomes the primary investor when they are high. Second, blockchain investment facilitates a win-win collaboration between the manufacturer and retailer under a unified power structure. When blockchain adoption costs are low and the proportion of high-type consumers is moderate, the retailer-led model can achieve a win-win outcome. However, when both the cost and the proportion of high-type consumers increase simultaneously, the manufacturer-led model becomes more conducive to mutual benefits. Third, from a blockchain value perspective, when high-type consumers constitute is moderate, the manufacturer and retailer prefer that the opposing party dominate the supply chain. But each prefers to dominate when that proportion is high. Finally, blockchain investment improves consumer surplus and social welfare. Building on the key findings outlined above, we can distil practical and actionable recommendations for supply chain enterprises applying blockchain technology. First, enterprises should adopt a systematic approach. They should assess their own profitability while also carefully considering the competitive landscape of the market and potential responses from upstream and downstream partners. This will enable them to formulate differentiated blockchain application strategies. In industries like organic food and luxury goods, high consumer demand for traceability justifies greater investment in blockchain. In the bulk goods sector, however, where this demand is low, a more cautious approach is warranted. Second, market research should be conducted to analyse consumer structure and demand characteristics, especially the preference for product traceability. This analysis will help determine the optimal timing for adopting blockchain technology. Finally, supply chain members should embrace a collaborative development approach. Vertically, retailers and manufacturers can optimise blockchain investments by sharing information and integrating resources through strategic partnerships. Horizontally dimension, enterprises should shift from traditional price competition to collaboration in technological innovation and value creation. This approach fosters a healthy competitive ecosystem that delivers win-win outcomes for all parties. For instance, Fresh food e-commerce platforms can enhance product competitiveness by collaborating with suppliers to implement blockchain traceability. This paper has several limitations that warrant further investigation. First, while the study highlights the consumer benefits of blockchain technology, it does not sufficiently address potential risks related to information leakage or the associated costs that may arise from adopting it. Second, although we account for consumers traceability preferences in blockchain investment, we have yet to fully incorporate product characteristics, such as perishability and value density. Future research could further explore how product attributes and consumer demand jointly affect blockchain adoption decisions. Finally, future research could explore scenarios where supply chain members share investment and usage costs proportionally, aiming to derive more practically oriented conclusions. These limitations offer clear directions for future research and enhance the understanding of blockchain applications in supply chain management. column1: Blockchain Innovation for Sustainability: Unraveling Its Market Impact Through Public Attention and Financial Performance
column2: This study investigates the dynamic interplay between blockchain innovation, public attention, and financial performance, with a focus on sustainability applications. Using a state-space model and the Kalman filter, it analyzes data from blockchain-related patents and Google Trends to assess their influence on the excess returns of blockchain-focused exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The findings highlight that innovation activity significantly enhances financial performance, underscoring blockchain’s role as a general-purpose technology with transformative sustainability potential. Public attention, measured through search interest, independently drives investor sentiment and market outcomes, while the interaction between innovation and public attention does not exhibit significant synergistic effects, suggesting distinct channels of influence. This study contributes to the growing stream of literature in sustainable finance, innovation management, and behavioral finance by introducing a real-time measure of blockchain innovation for sustainability into an asset pricing model, by showing that patent activity and public attention operate as separate predictors of financial returns, and by advancing methodological practice through the use of a state-space approach to capture latent innovation dynamics. The findings suggest actionable strategies: investors can track patent-based innovation and search trends as early signals of thematic-ETF performance; industry leaders can align blockchain projects with sustainability goals to unlock valuation gains; and policymakers can foster environmental, social, and governance innovation ecosystems by encouraging transparent patent disclosure and public awareness.
column3: This study provides critical insights into the dynamic relationship among blockchain innovation, public attention, and financial performance within the context of sustainability-oriented blockchain technologies. By employing a state-space modeling approach, we empirically demonstrate how targeted blockchain innovations significantly impact market valuations, as evidenced through ETF returns, and how public sentiment independently shapes these financial outcomes. These findings address a crucial gap in the literature, integrating perspectives from innovation management, behavioral finance, and sustainability research. Despite these contributions, several limitations offer clear pathways for future research. Our analysis relies on blockchain-focused ETFs (BLOK and BLCN), which, while insightful, may not fully represent market dynamics across other relevant financial instruments such as individual stocks, cryptocurrencies, or private equity investments. Expanding analyses to include these additional financial vehicles could provide richer insights into market-specific sensitivities and broader investment behaviors related to blockchain technology. Moreover, our study utilizes patent filings and Google Trends as proxies for innovation and public attention. Though established in literature, these indicators may lack granularity regarding commercialization, regional sentiment variations, and the qualitative nature of public engagement. Integrating supplementary data sources—such as direct blockchain deployment metrics, detailed media sentiment analysis, or advanced social media analytics—could enhance the precision and practical applicability of future studies. Additionally, the influence of external market conditions—macroeconomic trends, geopolitical factors, and sector-specific dynamics—was beyond this study’s explicit scope. Including these elements in future modeling could better isolate the intrinsic effects of blockchain innovation and public attention from external market influences, enhancing the model’s robustness and practical value. An empirical finding from our study—the absence of significant interaction between blockchain innovation and public attention—presents further questions for investigation. Future research might explore conditions under which these variables interact synergistically, considering contextual moderators such as technology maturity, cultural contexts, and strategic communication framing. Methodologically, while our state-space model offers valuable insights into evolving market dynamics, alternative analytical approaches could further refine our understanding. Machine learning techniques and network analyses, capable of capturing complex, nonlinear relationships and interactions, represent promising avenues to explore the multidimensional nature of these phenomena. Importantly, our study’s practical contributions have direct managerial relevance. The state-space modeling approach and related empirical insights developed here can serve as foundations for an actionable strategic decision-making dashboard. Managers can leverage this framework to systematically track and respond to blockchain innovation trends and shifts in public attention, optimizing their strategic investments and communication efforts. Such a dashboard would facilitate real-time monitoring of market sentiment and innovation signals, providing managers with critical insights into when and how to best align their blockchain initiatives with sustainability goals. This practical tool directly supports managers in effectively embedding emerging technologies into their strategic planning processes, thus enabling organizations to move beyond individual examples and toward systematic, effective approaches for sustainable business innovation.

column1: Blockchain Adoption in Competing Retail Channels
column2: Blockchain technology has been increasingly adopted in supply chains, offering new avenues for enhancing information transparency. This article investigates the role of blockchain in reducing consumer uncertainty, as well as its impact on competition between online and offline retailers under different market structures, using a game-theoretical approach. It highlights how blockchain enhances transparency and consumer trust, thereby influencing market dynamics and pricing strategies. The model incorporates consumer heterogeneity in terms of blockchain awareness and perceived product value, examining how these factors affect blockchain adoption decisions. A key finding reveals that blockchain can provide competitive advantages to online retailers, especially when consumer acceptance of the online channel is relatively low. Interestingly, if the online retailer adopts blockchain, higher mismatch costs could unexpectedly hurt profits. Moreover, our analysis shows that blockchain adoption does not necessarily benefit all retailers. Its effectiveness depends on consumer trust levels, awareness, and the magnitude of mismatch risks. Overall, this article offers managerial insights for retailers to tailor blockchain strategies based on market conditions, emphasizing the importance of consumer uncertainty and aligning blockchain’s benefits with specific market roles.
column3: A. Concluding Remarks This article develops analytical models to investigate the impact of blockchain on the competition between online and offline retailers across various market structures and game models. Through the Duopoly game and the Stackelberg game, with either the online or offline retailer as the leader, the study examines how blockchain influences profits, competitive advantage, and consumer surplus for both types of retailers. The core of the research focuses on identifying the conditions under which blockchain supports each retail channel and analyzing the key factors that influence these effects, including consumer awareness, product mismatch cost, and satisfaction. B. Managerial Insights Based on the analytical results, we derive the following specific management implications. For online retailers: They can use blockchain to increase consumer trust and improve the online shopping experience. Online retailers can enhance their competitiveness through blockchain, particularly when consumers are highly accepting of online shopping. By providing transparent product information—such as details on origin, production processes, and quality certifications—retailers can reduce uncertainty and foster consumer trust. For instance, an organic food e-commerce platform could utilize blockchain to display the complete production and shipping process of each batch, instilling greater confidence in consumers. Moreover, blockchain helps mitigate issues with fake reviews and low-quality products by recording the authenticity of each transaction and ensuring data integrity. This approach not only boosts consumer trust but also enhances customer loyalty. The online retailers need to assess consumer mismatch risk and blockchain awareness before adoption, and to target high-risk, low-trust segments, such as luxury goods or cross-border e-commerce, with traceability-focused blockchain applications. We also suggest pairing blockchain implementation with consumer education initiatives to improve awareness and perceived value. For offline retailers: They can use blockchain to strengthen trust and enhance brand image. When offline retailers are market leaders, they can leverage blockchain to further strengthen their market position. For example, luxury retailers can utilize blockchain to verify the authenticity of their products, significantly reducing the risk of counterfeit items. Consumers purchasing luxury goods can scan a blockchain certification tag to verify the origin and authenticity of the item, enhancing the brand’s credibility and increasing consumer trust in offline shopping. In addition, home appliance retailers can use blockchain to provide transparent records of maintenance and warranty services, offering consumers peace of mind regarding after-sales support. This level of transparency gives offline retailers a unique competitive advantage and helps them maintain their lead in the market. In addition, while the offline retailer does not adopt blockchain in our setting, they must strategically respond to the competitive implications of blockchain adoption by online rivals. To counter this shift, offline retailers can emphasize their inherent advantages, such as physical inspection, in-store service, and immediate product availability, to retain consumers who remain skeptical of online shopping. Moreover, our findings suggest that in markets with high mismatch costs or low trust in online channels, offline retailers may still benefit competitively. Managers in offline settings should monitor competitors’ blockchain strategies and consider reinforcing service differentiation or leveraging trust-based branding to maintain market position. Tailor blockchain strategies based on market structure and role: Retailers should assess their role in the market structure and their channel advantages when selecting blockchain strategies. For established market leaders, blockchain can reinforce their dominant position; for instance, a major supermarket chain could leverage it to optimize supply chain management, enhance product traceability, and build strong consumer trust in food safety. Conversely, new online retailers can use blockchain as a tool to establish trust and attract customers. For example, a new online clothing platform might showcase transparency in its supply chain and sustainability practices, appealing to younger consumers who prioritize environmental and social responsibility. C. Limitations and Future Research This study has several limitations that point to future research directions. It relies on specific assumptions about consumer behavior, blockchain costs, and market dynamics, which may not generalize across industries or regions; relaxing these assumptions could help assess the model’s applicability in varied contexts. The analysis also focuses on consumer awareness and trust without considering how education and marketing might influence blockchain acceptance—future studies could explore the impact of targeted campaigns on consumer engagement. Finally, the use of a Stackelberg game framework limits the scope of competitive dynamics; examining alternative models such as Bertrand or Cournot could offer broader insights into blockchain’s effectiveness under different market structures.

column1: Blockchain success in the post-adoption phase: extending the information systems success model with supply chain complexity
column2: This study investigates blockchain’s effectiveness and the drivers of its success in supply chain management. Drawing upon the Information Systems Success post-adoption model and Contingency Theory, we propose a moderated mediation analysis to analyze the relationships among extended use, user satisfaction, individual benefits, supply chain complexity, and their impact on performance outcomes at both the supply chain and individual firm levels. The model was validated by using survey data from a cross-sectional sample of 370 supply chain professionals from the United States with blockchain experience. Our findings indicate that individual benefits mediate the impact of extended use and user satisfaction on supply chain and operational performance, while supply chain complexity positively moderates the indirect effect of extended use on supply chain performance through individual benefits. This suggests that blockchain adoption is more impactful in complex supply chain contexts with numerous processes, stakeholders, and data sources. These results highlight the importance of adequately considering the supply chain context to fully understand the effectiveness of blockchain technology. This study contributes to the nascent literature on the blockchain post-adoption phase and proposes a new extension to the Information Systems Success model by incorporating supply chain complexity as a contextual factor.
column3: Blockchain has been praised as a promising technology for SCM, yet few cases demonstrate its sustained use. Grounded in the ISS model and Contingency Theory, this study investigates the impact of user satisfaction, extended use, individual benefits, and SC complexity on performance outcomes at both the SC and firm levels. Our findings show that individual benefits mediate the impact of extended use and user satisfaction on supply chain and operational performance. Supply chain complexity moderates the relationship between extended use and individual benefits. This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, we restricted our sample to supply chain professionals from the United States with blockchain experience to ensure homogeneity. Different results might be obtained from studies in other regions of the world. Second, this study employs a cross-sectional research design, which limits the ability to infer causal relationships. Furthermore, the design may be susceptible to common method bias. Although we introduced control variables, we cannot eliminate the possibility of omitted variables. Future research using longitudinal designs could further strengthen the validity of the findings. Finally, while supply chain complexity is treated as a moderator in our model, future studies could explore other dimensions of complexity, such as geographical coverage of the supply chain, product risk, and product complexity. Academics can benefit from our findings on how blockchain technology generates value in the post-adoption phase. Specifically, it provides insights into how blockchain post-adoption behaviours, such as extended use, and attitudinal responses, such as user satisfaction, translate into individual benefits and organisational performance outcomes. Our study also highlights supply chain complexity as a significant contextual moderator, emphasising the importance of incorporating environmental contingencies into the IS success model and acknowledging their role in technology adoption. Future studies should investigate how the constructs in our model interact with blockchain-specific variables, such as decentralisation, smart contracts, and consensus mechanisms, as well as supply chain factors such as a firm's position and geographical scope within the supply chain. Additionally, exploring the model's applicability across different blockchain implementations, such as public versus private blockchains, will help assess its generalisability and identify potential limitations. Such investigations will contribute to further understanding of blockchain’s effectiveness in diverse organisational contexts.

column1: Counterfeiting From an Operations and Engineering Management Perspective
column2: Counterfeiting poses a significant and growing threat to the global economy and has been examined through marketing, legal, manufacturing, and behavioral lenses. This article introduces new directions for research from an operations and engineering management (O&EM) perspective—including operations management, engineering management, and industrial engineering—with the aim of encouraging broader engagement from these disciplines. While drawing from insights in adjacent fields, the focus remains on applying O&EM-based models and tools to confront the practical challenges posed by counterfeiting. We develop a structured framework to guide researchers in exploring technological and strategic innovations that can help reduce the prevalence and impact of counterfeit products. These include approaches rooted in product and process design, global sourcing strategies, blockchain-enabled traceability, and circular economy integration. As we will suggest, both analytical modelling and empirical research can be applied to assess these solutions and their implications for operational performance, economic resilience, and sustainability.
column3: Counterfeiting is a widespread and complex issue with far reaching consequences for economies, societies, the environ ment, and public health. Sectors such as fashion, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and automotive increasingly contend with the proliferation of fake goods, resulting in significant financial losses, safety risks, and diminished incentives for innovation. The underlying causes are diverse and interrelated, encompass ing demand-side factors (such as consumer price sensitivity and purchasing behavior), supply-side conditions (including globalization, offshoring, and brand erosion), and deficiencies in regulation and technology. Tackling these challenges calls for coordinated interventions that move beyond conventional legal or marketing measures. This paper examines the strategic and operational role of O&EM in reducing exposure to counterfeit activities. Drawing on methods from operations management, engineering man agement, and industrial engineering, it demonstrates how firms can reinforce SC robustness, refine product and process con figurations to limit imitation, and align more effectively with partners across the value chain. O&EM-based approaches of fer actionable pathways to manage counterfeit threats through sourcing decisions, production setups, distribution structures, data governance, and the design of reverse logistics systems. Several directions for future inquiry are outlined, combining empirical analysis and quantitative modelling. These include the development of multi-period frameworks to evaluate long term effects on brand equity, studying competitions among counterfeiters and substitute goods, and integrating behavioral elements such as status signaling. Researchers can also explore how firms adapt their business models via leasing schemes, deposit-return programs, or modular product designs to exert more control over product circulation and reduce the likelihood of imitation. Circular economy efforts, though promising, in troduce additional vulnerabilities that must be examined with care. Recasting counterfeiting as an operational and structural issue opens new avenues for research and practice. Greater clarity on how O&EM instruments can be applied across industries and geographies will support the protection of IP, enhance consumer trust, and contribute to more resilient and ethically sound SCs. To enhance clarity and facilitate future work, Table V consoli dates the proposed research agenda across Sections IV-A IV-D. It outlines representative research questions and suggests suit able methodological approaches for focus area. Finally, given the multifaceted nature of counterfeiting, insights from adjacent fields such as information systems (e.g., technology adoption), behavioral science (e.g., consumer decision-making under deception), and public policy (e.g., reg ulatory frameworks) can enrich O&EM perspectives. These in terdisciplinary linkages offer promising avenues for both model building and empirical research.

column1: Exploring supply chain capabilities as drivers for willingness to adopt blockchain technology using a technologyâ€“organizationâ€“environment (TOE) framework
column2: Abstract As blockchain technology reshapes operations and supply chain management (OSCM), understanding its capability-driven adoption pathways is crucial for enhancing supply chain efficiency, resilience, and decision-making. This study applies Fuzzy-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) within the Technology-Organisation-Environment (TOE) framework to analyse data from supply chain managers with blockchain implementation experience. Our findings reveal three adoption pathways: (1) Dynamic Collaborators, who integrate blockchain through external collaboration and agility; (2) Resilient Specialists, who prioritise internal resilience over partnerships; and (3) Proficient Collaborators, who emphasise information sharing and agility without deep IT integration. These results highlight the causal complexity of blockchain adoption, demonstrating that firms follow multiple strategic configurations based on their capability portfolios. By uncovering scalable, context-specific adoption pathways, this study provides actionable insights for managers and policymakers, advancing both blockchain integration strategies and the broader OSCM literature.
column3:
This study advances the understanding of blockchain adoption in SCs by revealing configurational pathways rather than single-factor influences. The fsQCA results demonstrate that blockchain adoption is not driven by a one-size-fits-all model but instead follows multiple strategic routes, depending on industry context, firm size, and capability configurations.

6.1. Theoretical contributions
First, we advance the literature on factors influencing blockchain adoption by shifting the focus from individual drivers to combinations of capabilities. Previous research has highlighted various determinants, such as infrastructural facilities, government policies, top management support, and organisational readiness (Clohessy and Acton Citation2019; Orji et al. Citation2020), as well as technological challenges, market structures, and inter-organisational trust (Ghode et al. Citation2020; Janssen et al. Citation2020; Sciarelli et al. Citation2022). While these studies treat drivers as isolated factors, our findings demonstrate that firms adopt blockchain through specific configurations of relational, dynamic, and information capabilities. By identifying three distinct pathways�Dynamic Collaborators, Resilient Specialists, and Proficient Collaborators�we reveal that blockchain adoption is not determined by the mere presence or absence of a single capability but by the interplay among capabilities.

Second, we contribute to the literature on the link between DCs and blockchain adoption. Past research has shown that blockchain adoption enhances SC agility and resilience (Chowdhury et al. Citation2022;; Iranmanesh et al. Citation2023). While these studies focus on what occurs after blockchain has been adopted, less is known about what types of relationships exist between these concepts before blockchain adoption. In this vein, our study takes a step further by uncovering the causal complexity of these relationships by exploring the impact of SC resilience and agility on firms� willingness to adopt blockchain. Our results show that firms with high SC resilience (Dynamic Collaborators, Resilient Specialists) and firms with low SC resilience (Proficient Collaborators) both exhibit a willingness to adopt blockchain. Similarly, SC agility can be either absent (Resilient Specialists) or present (Dynamic Collaborators, Proficient Collaborators). These insights challenge the assumption that specific capabilities uniformly drive adoption and instead highlight the importance of examining capability configurations and their interdependencies.

Third, we expand the understanding of relational and information capabilities in blockchain adoption. Previous studies have indicated that firms implement blockchain to improve capabilities such as information sharing, external collaboration, communication quality, and information integration (Ghode et al. Citation2020; Gligor, Pillai, and Golgeci Citation2021; Ullah et al. Citation2022). For instance, Ghode et al. (Citation2020) illustrate that key factors affecting blockchain adaptability include issues related to organisational trust, data transparency, and interoperability. Furthermore, other research suggests that blockchain adoption enhances transparency and accountability (Kshetri Citation2018), visibility and traceability (Wang et al. Citation2019), as well as collaboration and trust (Longo et al. Citation2020).

However, to the best of our knowledge, no other studies have explored capability configurations and their influence on blockchain adoption intent. By contrast to the existing literature, our findings reveal that adoption can occur under multiple pathways where some of these capabilities are absent. For example, Proficient Collaborators exhibit high levels of information sharing and external collaboration but lack SC resilience and communication quality. This demonstrates that blockchain adoption is not contingent on uniformly enhancing these capabilities but depends on the firm�s specific capability combinations and adoption context.

Fourth, we make a notable methodological contribution by applying fsQCA to blockchain adoption research (Russo et al. Citation2016; Woodside Citation2013). Unlike traditional regression-based or SEM approaches that assume linearity and symmetry in previous studies (Chittipaka et al. Citation2023; Dong et al. Citation2024; Iranmanesh et al. Citation2023; Li and Fang Citation2022), fsQCA allows us to uncover the causal complexity and asymmetry in adoption decisions. This method highlights the principle of equifinality, showing that firms can achieve similar outcomes (i.e. blockchain adoption) through multiple, equally valid pathways. fsQCA provides richer insights into the nonlinear and context-dependent nature of blockchain adoption by capturing the interplay of capabilities across different adoption scenarios.

Finally, we extend the Technology-Organisation-Environment (TOE) framework by integrating organisational capabilities as critical enablers of blockchain adoption (Ganguly Citation2024; Malik et al. Citation2021). While the traditional TOE framework emphasises technological infrastructure, organisational readiness, and environmental pressures, our findings demonstrate that blockchain adoption is shaped by distinct capability configurations rather than isolated factors. Specifically, Dynamic Collaborators leverage technological enablers (e.g. information integration) and environmental factors (e.g. external collaboration and agility), showcasing high adaptability to external demands and highlighting blockchain as a tool for SC connectivity and efficiency. Resilient Specialists prioritise the organisational aspect, relying primarily on SC resilience to manage disruptions and regulatory compliance while minimising technological and environmental dependencies. Lastly, Proficient Collaborators balance organisational enablers (e.g. information sharing and agility) with environmental readiness (e.g. external collaboration), indicating that blockchain adoption can be strategically achieved even in the absence of profound technological capabilities integration.

column1: Competitive dynamics in blockchain-based supply chains under cryptocurrency volatility: a game theory approach
column2: The increasing integration of blockchain technology in supply chains has brought about significant challenges due to the volatility of cryptocurrencies, as it has become an essential aspect of customers’ risk considerations. This study addresses the problem of managing supply chain operations amid such volatility, focusing specifically on pricing, advertising, manufacturer subsidy, and cybersecurity strategies within a manufacturer-retailer framework involving two cryptocurrency-based retailers that have higher market capitalisation compared to others: Ethereum and Bitcoin. The proposed solution employs game theory – a simultaneous game and two Stackelberg games with either retailer as the leader – to identify optimal strategies based on the corresponding parameter values. Accordingly, the study uniquely delivers blockchain-related risks by applying game theory to analyze the decision variables, providing insights into competitive pricing adjustments and leadership strategies for the cryptocurrency-based retailers under varying volatility levels. Results demonstrate that retailer pricing strategies must adapt to changes in wholesale prices and to the difference in cryptocurrency volatility. It also identifies crucial subsidy levels for manufacturers and optimal strategies for retailers under different volatility conditions to sustain profitability and demand.
column3: This study offers insights into the intricate dynamics of blockchain-based supply chains, with a particular focus on the profound impact of cryptocurrency volatility. It investigates the dynamics of pricing, return policies, advertising, and cybersecurity in a supply chain comprised of a manufacturer and two cryptocurrency-based retailers (Ethereum and Bitcoin). The study utilises game theory models to analyze decision-making strategies under different volatility scenarios. The game model structure, comprising three central models, namely Nash game, Bitcoin leader, and Ethereum leader Stackelberg games, provides a nuanced understanding of the dynamic interplay between an Ethereum-based retailer ( ER ), and a Bitcoin-based retailer ( BR ). The research’s findings and related insights, obtained through a rigorous solving approach grounded in game theory and a thorough analysis of decision variables, illuminate critical aspects of this dynamic ecosystem as follows: The analysis demonstrates the intricate relationship between changes in the wholesale price ( 𝑤 ) and retailer pricing strategies. The impact of 𝑤 increase varies based on the level of Ethereum's volatility ( 𝜖 ). When 𝜖 is low, an increase in the wholesale price leads to lower retail prices due to increased demand in ER . In contrast, when Ethereum's volatility is high, a wholesale price increase leads to higher retail prices as demand shifts towards BR . This finding highlights the importance of dynamic pricing strategies that factor in multiple variables, including cryptocurrency market dynamics and wholesale costs. Retailers should closely monitor these factors and be prepared to adjust pricing strategies accordingly. By doing so, they can optimise their competitiveness and profitability in a rapidly changing blockchain-based supply chain environment. Overstock.com, which became one of the first major retailers to accept Bitcoin as payment, is recognised as an empirical evidence. Initially, they experienced a significant increase in orders paid with Bitcoin, highlighting the potential benefits of adopting cryptocurrency payments. However, over time, the impact of Bitcoin’s volatility led to a decrease in transactions. This fluctuation demonstrates how cryptocurrency volatility can influence retailer pricing and sales strategies, emphasising the need for businesses to adapt their pricing approaches to maintain profitability and remain competitive in a dynamic market. The results indicate a key threshold for the subsidy level ( 𝜆 ) provided by the manufacturer. In circumstances with significant volatility, the manufacturer has to provide a subsidy level larger than 0.4 to retain a profit for the Ethereum-based retailer. Otherwise, it may lead a considerable reduction in ER ’s willingness to spend on advertisement, as a result of demand increment due to the drop in ER ’s profit level. This research underscores the manufacturer's involvement in minimising the unfavourable impacts of volatility on the Ethereum-based retailer's profitability. The findings identify specific thresholds for the optimal strategies of Ethereum Retailer within different volatility ranges, wherein at lower ranges, the Nash game emerges as the cost-balancing strategy. However, as volatility increases and falls within the mid-range, the Bitcoin Retailer leader strategy becomes the preferred choice. The analysis highlights that, in scenarios of higher volatility levels, the Ethereum retailer leader strategy becomes the most favourable choice, in which it brings flexibility in the face of increased volatility, offering the highest profitability and demand resilience. It underscores the importance of leadership roles in managing the challenges posed by cryptocurrency volatility and its impact on customer behaviours, refund policies, and cyberattacks. These thresholds provide clear guidance for blockchain-based retailers to adapt their strategies based on the prevailing volatility conditions. Future research in blockchain-based supply chains and cryptocurrency dynamics could consider multi-platform competition, dynamic volatility models, regulatory impacts, and customer behaviour. Moreover, also competition between private (e.g. Ethereum) and public (e.g. Bitcoin) cryptocurrencies is shaped by their volatilities. With higher volatility, private cryptocurrencies need aggressive strategies like extensive advertising and return policies to compete. Public cryptocurrencies, with lower volatility, provide a more stable environment for pricing and marketing. On the other hand, the design of public digital currencies (as digital central bank money) has been a challenging topic for monetary policy authorities for almost ten years (Bech and Garratt Citation 2017). For example, the ECB is developing a concept for the digital euro, which raises questions such as the allocation to the money supply, the transaction possibilities of private households and the possible usability of the currency in the event of a crisis. The volatility of an introduced digital public currency is expected to be systematically lower than that of commercial currencies due to the lower risk (central bank as lender of last resort). Most of the results of this paper then apply to the volatility difference between Ethereum (or any other private cryptocurrency) and public crypto currency. Accordingly, further research could also explore how private cryptocurrencies can manage volatility through financial tools and strategic partnerships to stay competitive. Furtheremore, it is essential to study the resilience of blockchain-based supply chains against cyberattacks and evaluate security measures. Keeping up with blockchain technology advancements and their impact on supply chain operations is crucial. Additionally, it is of great value if researchers assess the environmental sustainability of blockchain-based supply chains and conduct real-world case studies across various industries to gain practical insights. To sum up, the findings of this study provide a foundation for several promising research directions that may further enhance the practical and theoretical contributions of blockchain-based supply chain models: Dynamic Modelling: Extending the current game-theoretic framework into a dynamic or multi-period setting would allow for modelling the evolution of volatility, adaptive decision-making, and long-term strategic adjustments in decentralised environments. Multi-Tier Supply Chains: Incorporating additional layers such as wholesalers, logistics service providers, or third-party platforms would enrich the analysis of coordination and risk-sharing across the full supply network. Regulatory and Monetary Impacts: Examining how public digital currencies (e.g. CBDCs), transaction regulations, or tax policies influence operational decisions in blockchain-integrated systems would align this research with ongoing financial digitisation trends. Behavioural and Strategic Extensions: Introducing bounded rationality, risk aversion, or reputation-based dynamics into the decision-making process may capture more realistic responses to uncertainty and volatility. Empirical Validation and Case Applications: Applying the model to specific sectors (e.g. digital retail, high-tech manufacturing, or food logistics) using real data would allow testing of theoretical insights and increase the model’s managerial value. Sustainability and ESG Alignment: Investigating how cryptocurrency-enabled systems interact with environmental performance, carbon tracing, or circular economy practices can bridge digitalisation with sustainability goals in supply chain management. These perspectives offer a roadmap for further enriching both the academic exploration and the real-world applicability of decision models in blockchain-enabled production and logistics systems. These areas collectively enhance our understanding of this evolving field.

column1: Harmonizing Fintech and Supply Chain Resilience: Unveiling the Role of Blockchain Integration, Incentives, and Resilience
column2: Motivated by the increasing adoption of blockchain technology in supply chain management, in this article, we examine the impact of integrating blockchain technology on incentive structures (e.g., data sharing, compliance with standards, and collaborative efforts), as well as the resulting implications for supply chain resilience. Recognizing the rising interest in blockchain applications, we identify a critical gap in understanding how firms’ cooperative and competitive dynamics serve as boundary conditions in this area. Grounded in transaction cost economics and goal interdependence theory, we empirically tested our hypotheses using structural equation modeling with data from 285 Chinese firms. Our results demonstrate that blockchain integration significantly strengthens incentive structures by enhancing security, reducing costs, and improving transparency. Increased cooperation among firms amplifies the positive relationship between blockchain integration and incentive structures. In contrast, competitive dynamics complicate this relationship, as privacy concerns related to transparency can diminish the benefits of integration. These findings offer crucial insights for managers seeking to leverage blockchain for enhanced supply chain resilience, highlighting the importance of considering both cooperative and competitive dynamics in this integration process.
