column1: Foresight Scenarios: The Future Impact of Technology in Freight Forwarding, an International Delphi Study
column2: The freight forwarding (FF) industry plays a key role in running global supply chains, with a sales revenue of $180.66 billion in 2021. Digitization in supply chain management, a thriving topic in the past few years, has been accelerated by the challenges of COVID-19 and presents both challenges and opportunities for the FF industry which requires freight forwarders to adapt. Since technological foresight studies for the FF space are scarce, the specific expected impacts of digitization in FF remain unrevealed today. The aim of this study is to examine upcoming changes in the FF industry expected by FF professionals and academics over the next 30 years against the background of current technological developments and to identify related resilience measures for FF organizations. Overall, 84 international experts shared their estimates in a Delphi survey. The results are clustered into four clusters that provide an outlook for the future of FF. The results show that FF organizations should adapt to developing customer expectations, a change in the FF profile due to new requirements and a change of vision for the development of human resources. Still, experts see a high relevance for FF services in the future despite all technological developments.
column3: Ghadge et al. [135] saw increasing competition in business and supply chains, leveraged by technological enhancements and by that, changing customer requirements. The same is true for freight forwarding, where developing customer requirements, the development and adoption of technology, and digital transformation drive the complexity and dynamics in supply chains and so with their execution, which is done by freight forwarders [136]. For freight forwarding services, which serve as a vital element of SCM to this day, there is a limited vision of how technology will affect the freight forwarding industry internally as well as externally and how technology will impact the organizational structure of freight forwarders. This study used strategic forecasting to answer these questions by means of an investigation on the future of freight forwarding, considering the impact of technology in the industry internally as well toward customers. In a web-based, real-time Delphi study with the perspectives of both freight forwarding professionals and academics, we collected both quantitative as well as qualitative input through a dynamic expert assessment. We provided descriptive as well as qualitative statistics and FCM-clustering to gather insights into the survey results and identified the following four clusters. Microenvironment: Shift of the freight forwarder profile. Tech capital: Shift in tech use and market dynamics. Evolution: Threat of technology and macrodynamics. Long term: Freight forwarders in a relevant position to manage global trade. The resulting discussion offered provoking insights that help and enable freight forwarders to evaluate the future of the freight forwarding industry and to build a foundational understanding of expected trends and developments under the perspective of technology use and digitization and its imposing impact on the organization role of freight forwarders to derive resilient action plans and strategies. Regarding the following initial research question: RQ1. How will digitization influence the future development of freight forwarders? our results from Section IV demonstrated that digitization and the use of technology are largely expected to expand further in the freight forwarding space and that freight forwarders of all sizes need to invest in IT and data expertise on various levels, such as software and system as well as in human capital and customer interaction. Our results show that more than 50% of all freight forwarders (projection 1) will have expanded their business models from the pure transportation of goods to additional supply chain consultancy and optimization services and that by higher tech standards, cargo owners will consider the pure transactional model of freight forwarders as inappropriate in the coming years (projection 3). To remain resilient and competitive, freight forwarders are likely to expand their service scope, which will result in deeper requirements for services from cargo owners (projection 4). With regards to technology adoption, previous research confirms that the implementation of technology and the migration into existing IT landscapes can be a hurdle for small and medium enterprises [137]. It remains questionable whether small and medium freight forwarders can keep pace with this development in a fast-paced tech environment. Freight forwarders call today's interaction with customers “people's business” where relationships and human interaction is a key driver for long-lasting, profitable relationships. This point remains under pressure as our results show that technology is likely to shift the perception of freight forwarding services and how freight forwarders have to operate to remain profitable and competitive, i.e., automatizing operations with the use of robotic process automation (projections 2 and 8). With regards to the second research question as follows: RQ2: How will digitization influence the organization of freight forwarders and dynamics involved? the human factor plays a key role in today's logistics environment and related services [124]. We discovered that freight forwarding is likely to shift toward a more data- and IT-driven approach, which might reduce the focus on human interaction. This has also been affirmed by other researchers from other disciplines [138]. Thus, freight forwarders might consider shifting their recruiting procedures toward more data and IT experts (projection 9), away from traditional freight forwarding skills such as transportation management. It will require further research as to how freight forwarders manage this shift without losing competencies in traditional freight forwarding operations. Another HR-related task freight forwarders should consider is the expected job development in the industry. While some researchers state that technology will displace jobs with repetitive tasks in particular [96], [139], our experts state that there will most likely be a mix of shift in expected skills for employees and a reduction of jobs, particularly in operational departments where repetitive tasks dominate (projection 10). We expect this change to be more difficult than in theory since people will have to retrain themselves to adapt to new job profiles which remains a challenge for HR departments. With regards to market development, we discovered that experts see the rising consolidation of freight forwarders through mergers and acquisitions. To remain resilient through change, freight forwarders need to make sizeable investments while remaining under pressure in a low margin environment. With today's highly defragmented freight forwarding market (projection 6), small- and midsize freight forwarders in particular will struggle with IT investments and the transition into more digital operations. Even though global supply chains became more profitable for freight forwarders in the COVID-19 pandemic, it can be expected that gross profit margin levels will again slip back to previous levels that are somewhere between 4% and 10% in air and ocean freight shipping [140], which will, in turn, put pressure on freight forwarders who are reinventing their service capabilities under the framework of digitization. We also raised questions about three technological trends [12], [13] that are currently gaining momentum, diving deeper into the means of blockchain technology, AI, and Big Data analytics. While blockchain technology (projection 5) is not seen as a threat to the role of freight forwarders, AI seems to have a promising value outlook on decision making and operational efficiencies. With regards to Big Data analytics, experts state that technology will help freight forwarders to manage data in a more structured way and this will enhance trust in the processing of data automatically, reducing operational maintenance of data, and thus, manual involvement in freight forwarding operations. It remains apparent that particularly regarding the concept of blockchain technology, freight forwarders need to massively improve their limited understanding of technology in order to realistically evaluate opportunities and risks posed by technology to the industry which has likewise been confirmed by previous researchers [128], [129]. With regards to AI (projection 8), the question remains unanswered as to how freight forwarders can embed technology in their daily standards. While key global players in freight forwarding have started to adopt AI into their operational portfolio [141], [142], it will be crucial for small and midsize forwarders to keep up with the global players to ensure adequate operational quality and proper data-driven decision making. Thus, we call for further evaluation of the application on AI in freight forwarding and how freight forwarders can use the technology to drive their own operations and to keep pace with the big freight forwarding enterprises. Under all these changing circumstances for freight forwarders, the results show that freight forwarding operations will still be required and that the asset-light model of today's freight forwarders will remain relevant. From our view, this requires further investigation, especially under the circumstances that the first asset-heavy carriers such as Maersk or CMA CGM are starting to migrate freight forwarding agents [131], [143]. From our perspective, it is questionable as to whether the asset-light model of freight forwarders will also be competitive against hybrid models from carriers under future technological developments and more automatized processes. As in every academic research, we also see some weaknesses in our research. Phadnis et al. [28] concluded in their study on strategic foresight that scenario planning can gain efficiency when it is done continually. Our study was a one-off over a certain period which is not able to evolve within the dynamic spaces of technological and freight forwarding developments. Furthermore, we decided to incorporate a broader base into our research design, putting more general questions to our panelists. Every stated projection could potentially result in a deep-dive to generate strategic development and action plans for freight forwarders. Our panelists were mostly freight forwarders, which could affect bias toward the single projections we took. Future research could broaden the basis, inviting more cargo owners to the panel who might provide more insights into the perception of freight forwarding customers. Finally, our focus on three technologies does not cover all relevant areas of technological development in supply chains such as Internet of Things, supply chain governance and security, 5G Networks, and virtual- and augmented reality. These technological trends are worth a separate study for themselves. With regards to the methodology, the Delphi method also shows some weaknesses as does every other research design. First, it lacks agreed standards of consensus [144]. Furthermore, Fink-Hafner et al. [144] state that even though anonymity has been stated as a strength of Delphi surveys reducing bias of participants, still the anonymity may also result in a reduced ownership of the panelists when it comes to ideas and contribution to the study. Furthermore, it remains difficult to generalize the results to a wider range of professionals and academics due to the sample size [145], [146]. The results of our study show that practitioners do understand that digitization is a “train that will not stop” in the next few years, still they admit to struggling with taking ownership of technological developments and with embedding them into their organizations, mindset, customer service, and freight forwarding products. Several challenges such as data quality [147] or freight capacity and allocation management, freight planning, and production of services could be supported by the technologies considered in this article. Thus, we call for further research, helping the domain and freight forwarding managers to set the foundation for conceptual frameworks and as to how freight forwarders could embed technology into their production environment and service portfolio. To this day, freight forwarding literature is scarce. By performing this Delphi research in the space of freight forwarding and investigating the future impact of certain technologies, we have expanded the existing literature landscape and provided the first, to the best of our knowledge, Delphi research study in the environment of freight forwarding and technology. The study provides useful insights into the mindset of freight forwarding practitioners and delivers indicators for strategic planning in order to support decision makers. Overall, the use of technology in freight forwarding is growing significantly, which puts freight forwarders under pressure to adapt. We anticipate the continuation of this development, and our Delphi results confirm this expectation. The increasing need for supply chain visibility, and thus, data quality will create the need for more automation in freight forwarding operations. We highlighted the expected “lack of talent” when it comes to technology adoption and the rapid speed of technology development. As freight forwarding organizations depend heavily on the people who run them, future research should attempt to aim toward cultural change and a more technology driven mindset of employees, which is mainly a topic for freight forwarding products and HR departments. To expand their findings, it could be helpful to consider these perspectives on the HR strategy of freight forwarding companies, helping to determine the required changes freight forwarders must undertake under the impact of digitization.

column1: The role of blockchain-related technologies in transforming the tourism and hospitality industry: an overview and research guidelines
column2:
Purpose
This paper aims to examine the relationship between the implementation of blockchain in the tourism and hospitality industry (T&HI) and its state-of-the-art. The aim is also to identify emerging research topics and gaps in this area.

Design/methodology/approach
A bibliometric overview is presented to examine articles from Web of Science published between 2018 and January 2024. The analysis was performed by VOSviewer software using the co-occurrence technique.

Findings
The results reveal the growing interest in blockchain technologies (BCT) applications in the T&HI. To reveal the conceptual structure and emerging research hotspots in this area, seven clusters were identified along with their interrelationships. This paper discusses the features and attributes of BCT mechanisms, including cryptocurrencies, distributed ledgers, smart contracts and consensus algorithms. The analysis highlights the drivers for increasing adoption and acceptance to promote smart tourism, transparency, trustworthiness and disintermediation. This paper explores the use of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) in the metaverse to promote authenticity and enhance tourists’ experiences, with emphasis on achieving cost-effectiveness and sustainability in the T&HI. In addition, key challenges are identified, with a focus on security and privacy.

Practical implications
This study provides timely and valuable insights concerning the application of BCT in the T&HI. It elucidates the factors that contribute to the optimal implementation of BCT, such as the collaboration between stakeholders and the key role of regulatory frameworks. Furthermore, it considers the implications for the design of new services towards enhancing sustainability and customer experiences.

Originality/value
This paper presents the first bibliometric analysis of the use of BCT in the T&HI. It identifies research gaps and future research avenues, which can guide further investigation in this area. This study provides valuable information for organisations, managers and academics who are considering future applications, benefits and challenges in the field of sustainability issues and technology acceptance.
column3: The adoption of BCT has revolutionised the T&HI. BCT ensures transparency of products with better traceability throughout the supply chain (Filimonau and Naumova, 2020; Cheng et al., 2023). This technology permits payments to be made using cryptocurrencies, increasing trust between hotels and users (Rashideh, 2020; Cheng et al., 2023). Additionally, smart contracts allow for agreements that secure tourists bookings without intermediaries (Filimonau and Naumova, 2020). Based on the results obtained, the inter and intra cluster relationships provide valuable information about the current conceptual structure of this field. From a methodological approach, this paper enriches the understanding of the scientific literature related to the incorporation of BCT in the T&HI. This analysis fills this gap in the literature, as there is no previous bibliometric analysis about this novel topic. This bibliometric analysis provides a general idea of the influence of the BCT breakthrough in the T&HI. Between 2018 and 2024, there is a growing evolution in the research. Since the COVID-19 crisis, T&HI organisations put more effort and interest into the implementation of BCT such as distributed ledgers, cryptocurrencies, consensus algorithms or smart contracts. The hotspot topics (RQ1) are focused on the features and attributes as well as advantages and disadvantages presented in the current literature about the joint use of BCT and AI, IoT and Big Data (red cluster). Drivers to enhance forecasting demand, to obtain tourists’ feedback and secure information. The distributed ledger and cryptocurrencies in the promotion of smart tourism are presented (green cluster), focusing on technology acceptance and the main challenges, such as transparency and the resistance to change, respectively (Walsh et al., 2021). Another hotspot topic is how the use of Bitcoin and consensus algorithms achieve sustainability and cost-effectiveness in the industry (blue cluster) by eliminating intermediaries and simplifying transactions between stakeholders (Treiblmaier, 2021). The yellow cluster focuses on the main drivers and barriers in mobile payment by cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, highlighting how the customers’ and organisations’ intentions play a fundamental role (Albayati et al., 2020). The application of smart contracts for disintermediation (purple cluster) in the sector (Balasubramanian et al., 2022) was identified as another major topic. The cyan cluster focuses on how the use of NFT promotes metaverse experiences, in terms of authenticity and trust (Lin et al., 2023) as well as its limitations. Finally, the orange cluster explores how BCT affects the industry in the post-COVID-19 era, for instance, by fostering T&HI revenue. Referring to the research agenda suggested, the proposals are associated with how the joint use of BCT with other Industry 4.0 technologies enable tourist experiences, putting more emphasis on the relationship in achieving the SDGs thanks to BCT, the regulatory framework required, the necessity for education and training campaigns as well as rewards and loyalty programs for tourists facilitated by BCT (RQ2). 6.1 Theoretical implications As there is no previous conceptual/thematic analysis of this field, to the best of our knowledge, this study is the first bibliometric analysis that uses co-occurrence to examine the evolution of the field of BCT and the T&HI. As such, providing a thematic analysis of this field is the main novel aspect of this article. This article presents a picture of the state of the art in this domain to shed light on its conceptual structure, capturing the dynamics of BCT adoption in the T&HI. This review identifies research hotspots and emerging trends based on the clusterisation displayed by VOSviewer software, which detects inter- and intra-relationships between the trending topics. In addition, this paper explains the characteristics, benefits and drawbacks of BCT connected to the T&HI and how to address the main gaps and barriers obtained from the analysis with the proposals suggested in the research agenda, similar to the study conducted by Shin et al. (2023) that considered other research areas. Previous bibliometrics in the T&HI focused on new technologies or ICT from a holistic perspective (Shin et al., 2023; Molina-Collado et al., 2022a) or other Industry 4.0 technologies (AI, Sharma et al., 2022b) but with no particular emphasis on BCT. Puri et al. (2023) focused on smart tourism without considering hospitality. Therefore, this paper fills this gap in the literature. The attributes of BCT in each cluster (thematic analysis) and their relationships with the T&HI were examined, providing valuable insights to this scientific field. Based on the advantages and disadvantages analysed in the co-occurrence of each cluster, from a theoretical perspective, this study provides an understanding in the field of BCT that enriches the literature. With regard to BCT adoption in the industry, this study provides information on attitudes towards transparency and data security (Leal et al., 2020), based on the core of the literature in this field. In addition, this review provides features and characteristics, as well as challenges and barriers to the implementation of BCT in the T&HI. In terms of acceptability, the findings also shed light on perceptions and ease of use, highlighting the need for education and training, and how resistance to change could be one of the main barriers (Walsh et al., 2021). A controlled use of BCT, such as cryptocurrency, allows for influencing customers’ decisions and acceptability (linked to the green cluster). However, a regulatory framework is still a necessity to improve trustworthiness (Albayati et al., 2020). From a theoretical perspective, this study provides an understanding of the field of BCT that enriches the TPB, and the TAM applied to the T&HI. This could guide future researchers and managers in implementing blockchain successfully. According to the TPB, it is important to clarify that the attitude towards blockchain adoption could be positive or negative depending on the perception of the benefits of blockchain (purple cluster). Furthermore, the ease of use and the challenges could impact blockchain application, found in the green cluster (Kumari and Devi, 2023), and the opinion of stakeholders could influence its adoption, as seen in the red cluster (Cheng and Chong, 2022). Taking the TAM into account, the perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of blockchain’s benefits could improve blockchain adoption, shown in the red and green clusters. In this vein, more emphasis on transparency can also enhance tourists’ and visitors’ perceptions while improving the ease of use, for example, by using Bitcoin in accommodation establishments (blue cluster). This in turn will impact attitudes toward BCT. In this regard, the security and privacy implied in the transactions plays a key role in the perceived risk by customers (connected to the yellow cluster). Ultimately, familiarisation with these technologies through information and education campaigns as well as training for employees (Celik et al., 2024) will potentially improve the ease of use, perception, acceptance and attitude of tourists towards the implementation of BCT in this industry. Based on the articles analysed in this sample, there is still a lack of empirical studies, and study cases analysing blockchain adoption by consumers and companies in the T&HI literature. The research agenda developed makes way for future opportunities and inspires further studies for scholars in this field, according to the emerging topics identified in the clusterisation analysis and the gaps detected in the literature. This analysis highlighted the lack of attention given to social aspects such as SDGs and empirical evidence about BCT acceptance in the T&HI. Training required for T&HI employees and information campaigns for users in the field of BCT (Ratna et al., 2023) is another prominent topic which arose in this research. The need for a regulatory framework for all its mechanisms involved including cryptocurrency (Bitcoin and Ethereum), smart contracts, distributed ledgers and consensus algorithms (PoS and PoW) is also put forward as another avenue for further research. Hence, this study enriches the literature guiding future research and enables a broader understanding of the theme. 6.2 Practical implications The co-occurrence analysis results can be used as a guideline with valuable information for governments, academics, managers and tourists in terms of practical implications (Sedighi, 2015). The practical implications of this paper can be split into two concepts – the first being the factors contributing to the optimal implementation of BCT; and the second being the implications for the design of new products and services. Factors contributing to optimal implementation included creating a regulatory framework, establishing collaboration and information systems, and integrating different technological tools. These different factors show how BCTs (seen in the blue and cyan clusters) make “privacy”, “openness” and “trust” possible (Nam et al., 2021). The findings reveal to governments the need to create a regulatory framework (presented in the green, purple and orange clusters) for BCT in the T&HI to promote trust (Irannezhad and Mahadevan, 2021), ensure legal compliance (Nam et al., 2021), prevent fraud (Barkel et al., 2021), and promote standardisation (Irannezhad and Mahadevan, 2021). In terms of privacy and security (red and yellow clusters) for T&HI customers, a regulatory framework will positively affect trustworthiness. The use of BCT mechanisms can affect the privacy of travellers, for example, smart contracts are vulnerable to breaches, and therefore more protocols are needed. Furthermore, regarding identity verification, if these mechanisms fail and this data is stolen, it could potentially result in identity scams. Hence, this risk should be addressed for better implementation in the T&HI by means of regulatory procedures; more robust cybersecurity and standards (Zamani et al., 2018); enhanced transparency; and educational training. While BCT can improve knowledge and information sharing, it requires collaboration between governments, hotels, local tourism organisations and tourists. Public-private investment thanks to government collaborations with T&HI firms on disruptive technologies – BCT, IoT, Big Data and artificial intelligence (presented in the red cluster) – play a key role towards digitalisation in this sector. However, the impact of blockchain on relationships along the value system in the tourism industry must also consider that certain participants may disappear and must consider how this will change the relationships of the remaining members. In this respect, a few case studies have shed light on this issue (Thees et al., 2020). In terms of practical implications for the design of services or products offered by the business or destination, both aspects of improving the customer experience and the sustainability impact of the customer must be considered. Although customers value the status of smart destinations (Nam et al., 2021), as shown in the green cluster, there is a need to better understand the acceptance of these technologies being used in these destinations, while also considering the post-pandemic era influence and changes in customer patterns and attitudes. The “human touch” is being lost with technological advances implemented in the T&HI, and it is necessary to contemplate what tourists and guests expect. Similarly, service design needs to consider non-tech-savvy travellers (Muharam et al., 2023). With that in mind, it is important to consider and to improve user acceptance, thus training and education for T&HI customers is fundamental. There is a gap in encouragement and support from tourism managers in terms of BCT education and training, which has been flagged as a potential resistance to change shown in the red cluster. There is a need for support on sustainability aspects related to the blue cluster. However, the implementation of blockchain must overcome the one-dimensional view of sustainability that links it to the environmental aspect. From a social perspective, this technology facilitates access to certain basic resources; holds up the quality of experiences; and allows for stakeholders (such as residents of these tourist destinations) to participate. Due to this, recent research has studied the case of the role of blockchain in social entrepreneurship (Sansone et al., 2023) and local relations. It is therefore necessary to study the adaptation of these cases to the service sector in general and to the tourism sector in particular. This pathway to sustainability should be linked to the achievement of the SDGs, emphasising how BCT can align the T&HI in achieving the 2030 Agenda. 6.3 Limitations and future lines of research This bibliometric overview has some limitations. Firstly, the database used for this study was the Web of Science, which only considers English-language articles. Other databases such as Google Scholar could be considered for further analysis. It might be interesting to consider and include international conferences and book chapters in future studies. Secondly, reading the results displayed by VOSviewer software may be somewhat subjective. Other bibliometric tools such as SciMat, BibExcel or CiteSpace could be used to provide complementary information about this field. Thirdly, the analysis was carried out with a small number of published articles (n = 70). Therefore, to broaden and consolidate the obtained results in this paper, a future bibliometric study could be addressed to monitor the evolution of this field and tracking if attention to this technology continues to grow over the years in relation to this industry. Other bibliometric techniques such as co-citation analysis between articles and co-authorship of researchers can easily shed light on the intellectual composition of this field and the opportunities for authors to collaborate. In addition, further research using qualitative methods or case studies could enrich the conclusions drawn in this article. More empirical research is required to examine tourists’ opinions, reviews and acceptance (green and orange clusters) of BCT use linked to experiences in this sector (Nam et al., 2021). However, a differentiation between tech-savvy and non-tech-savvy tourists’ demands needs to be addressed in further research. BCT could transform the T&HI’s supply chains, increasing the data transparency (blue cluster); therefore, it is interesting to conduct further research on the main challenges and barriers towards its implementation. The question of how to lower infrastructure costs and how complex these technologies are to integrate are also key aspects that require further investigation. Additionally, a comparison between countries or between developing and developed countries to identify what is currently being done in the sector can be addressed. More research is needed to investigate the impact of COVID-19 on tourism patterns, including a comparison of pre- and post-pandemic periods (Kim et al., 2021). It could be interesting to develop future research on improving information in the implementation of BCT in smart tourism destinations (green cluster), considering COVID-19 as the break point (orange cluster) to analyse changes in tourists’ patterns of behaviour. The use of BCT towards sustainability (blue cluster) and for achieving the SDGs in the hospitality and tourism sector are pivotal future lines of research, aligned with areas of future research from previous work, such as sustainable consumption or rural tourism development (Molina-Collado et al., 2022b). Further in-depth research is required to fully understand the use of PoS and smart contracts, among other mechanisms, for sustainability standardisation in the T&HI. column1: Exploring blockchain technologies in sustainable supply chainsâ€“unveiling the latent research topics using an AI approach
column2: Blockchain technology is reshaping sustainable Supply Chain Management (SSCM) by enhancing transparency, efficiency, and security. This study introduces an unsupervised machine learning approach, leveraging Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to systematically analyse over 4,000 scholarly articles and uncover latent research topics in blockchain applications for SSCM. Our findings reveal 60 key topics, with high-impact areas including food safety, healthcare, smart contracts, agriculture, and blockchain adoption barriers. The study identifies the fastest-growing research domains – food safety and implementation challenges – while highlighting underexplored areas such as trust and privacy protection. Additionally, we provide a first-of-its-kind systematic mapping of blockchain research trends across geographical regions, showing Asia’s dominance, particularly in China and India. Our integration of advanced topic modelling with bibliometric analysis offers a deeper, data-driven understanding of blockchain’s role in SSCM, bridging qualitative insights with quantitative evidence. By identifying research gaps and emerging trends, this study serves as a roadmap for future blockchain innovations in supply chains, emphasising their role in addressing sustainability challenges and enhancing operational resilience, efficiency and transparency.
column3: This paper explore the role of BCT in SSCM using a novel AI-driven approach, LDA, to identify key research trends and latent topics. The findings underscore the growing importance of blockchain in enhancing transparency, traceability, and efficiency across supply chains, particularly in sectors such as the food industry, healthcare, and agriculture. Despite its potential, the adoption of blockchain faces significant barriers, including technical, regulatory, and organisational challenges. Key topics such as food safety, smart contracts, and blockchain barriers are rapidly gaining attention in the academic community. Additionally, the analysis revealed a regional concentration of research, with Asia, particularly China and India, leading in publications. Underexplored areas such as trust and privacy protection present opportunities for further research. This study has the potential to influence future research on SSCM and BCT. By introducing an AI-enhanced methodological framework that allows for the large-scale identification and classification of latent research topics, the study provides a foundation for a more structured and data-driven development of the SSCM research field. The comprehensive topic map and territorial classification (e.g. uncharted, discovering, expanding) help researchers identify underexplored areas and prioritise future investigations. Moreover, the integration of bibliometric indicators with topic modelling offers a replicable model for monitoring thematic evolution, research impact, and knowledge systematization within SSCM. This work thus contributes to advancing theory-building efforts and promotes a more coherent and cumulative research agenda in the field of blockchain-enabled SSCM. After using this tool/service, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.

column1: Decarbonisation in supply chain management with blockchain technology: using multi-criteria decision-making in industry 4.0
column2: This study explores the role of blockchain technology (BT) in enabling decarbonisation within healthcare supply chain management (SCM) in the context of Industry 4.0. A novel hybrid methodological framework combining the fuzzy spherical analytical hierarchy process (FS-AHP) and the Z-number logarithm methodology of additive weights (ZLMAW) is developed to address the complexities and uncertainties inherent in this domain. The research identifies critical factors influencing the adoption of BT in decarbonised SCM and ranks healthcare companies based on their suitability for implementation. The results highlight the lack of a robust scope framework as a priority concern and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model in advancing sustainable practices. This work contributes to theoretical advancements, by integrating multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) techniques with blockchain in SCM, and practical insights, by offering a scalable approach to supply chain decarbonisation. The findings bridge gaps in the literature by addressing the intersection of blockchain, Industry 4.0, and sustainability in healthcare, presenting actionable strategies for supply chain optimisation.
column3:
This study identifies the key factors influencing the successful implementation of blockchain technology (BT) in decarbonising supply chain management (SCM) within healthcare facilities, specifically within the Industry 4.0 framework. Decarbonisation SCM has emerged as a critical priority in today’s global effort to combat climate change, and BT offers unique capabilities to enhance transparency, traceability, and operational efficiency. However, the real-world implementation of BT in SCM poses significant challenges, including technical, organisational, and regulatory obstacles. These challenges necessitate a robust and systematic approach to prioritising and addressing critical success factors.

The study introduces a novel hybrid methodological framework that combines the fuzzy spherical analytical hierarchy process (FS-AHP) and Z-number logarithm methodology of additive weights (ZLMAW) to evaluate and rank healthcare companies’ readiness for BT adoption. The use of Z-numbers ensures that uncertainties in decision-making are effectively managed, while the hybrid approach provides decision-makers with reliable and actionable insights. This framework extends theoretical understanding by integrating blockchain technology with advanced multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) techniques, addressing a significant gap in the literature. Additionally, the study demonstrates the practical application of these methods in ranking companies and prioritising factors critical to decarbonisation SCM, offering a scalable solution for broader use.

The findings highlight a practical roadmap for decision-makers to overcome barriers in adopting blockchain and Industry 4.0 technologies for decarbonised healthcare SCM. Key strategies include initiating pilot programs to demonstrate tangible benefits, fostering cross-sectoral collaborations to standardise frameworks, and leveraging government incentives or policies to offset the initial costs of implementation. Such initiatives can accelerate the adoption of advanced digital tools, enabling organisations to achieve both sustainability and operational efficiency goals.

Beyond the integration of blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI), emerging Industry 4.0 technologies like digital twins and edge computing offer significant potential. Digital twins, for example, can simulate supply chain operations to predict outcomes under varying scenarios, providing actionable insights for emissions reduction. Similarly, edge computing can process supply chain data locally, reducing latency and enhancing decision-making efficiency in dynamic environments. These technologies represent the next frontier in sustainable healthcare SCM.

One of the study’s major contributions is its focus on decarbonisation SCM within healthcare—a sector that accounts for approximately 5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, with 71% originating from supply chain-related activities. By emphasising BT’s potential for real-time carbon footprint monitoring, improved traceability, and enhanced data transparency, this research highlights how Industry 4.0 technologies can support environmentally sustainable and efficient operations. The findings demonstrate that BT not only enables more accurate data sharing and trust-building among stakeholders but also aligns seamlessly with the intelligent systems and automation supported by Industry 4.0.

This research aimed to address three primary objectives and demonstrated the following outcomes: (1) Identifying Factors for Blockchain Adoption in Healthcare SCM: The study conducted an extensive review to identify critical factors, such as transparency, trust, and operational efficiency, that influence blockchain adoption in healthcare SCM. These were validated using expert input, highlighting unique challenges specific to the healthcare sector. (2) Evaluating and Ranking Companies for Blockchain-Enabled Decarbonisation: By integrating SF-AHP and ZLMAW, the study evaluated healthcare companies’ readiness for blockchain implementation. The findings provide a practical roadmap for prioritising investments in blockchain to achieve decarbonisation goals. (3) Proposing a Scalable Framework Combining Blockchain and MCDM: The research developed a novel hybrid framework, offering actionable insights into real-time carbon emission tracking and decision-making under uncertain conditions. This framework bridges gaps in the existing literature by addressing both operational and sustainability challenges in healthcare SCM. For example, the framework was applied to prioritise blockchain adoption strategies for hospitals and clinics, which are significant contributors to CO2 emissions through their supply chain activities. These contributions align with the objectives of the Paris Agreement and demonstrate the feasibility of integrating Industry 4.0 solutions into healthcare SCM.

Future adoption frameworks must account for the unique regulatory, operational, and environmental challenges inherent to the healthcare sector. For instance, decision-makers must address data privacy concerns in blockchain implementation while ensuring compliance with industry standards. This study lays a foundation for such sector-specific strategies, emphasising the need for adaptable frameworks that cater to diverse organisational contexts.

This study presents several limitations that also provide opportunities for future exploration. A significant limitation lies in the reliance on expert interviews, which introduces potential subjectivity and bias. To address this, future research could adopt a broader, more diverse panel of experts from multiple industries and geographies to enhance the generalisability of findings. Additionally, the use of group decision-making approaches, such as the Delphi method with iterative feedback cycles, can further mitigate individual biases and improve reliability.

The scope of this research is currently focused on healthcare SCM, which accounts for a substantial share of global greenhouse gas emissions. Future studies could expand this scope to examine blockchain adoption in other sectors, such as logistics, manufacturing, and energy, where decarbonisation challenges and operational dynamics differ. Such investigations would provide valuable insights into the scalability and adaptability of blockchain technology across industries.

To address uncertainties in supply chain disruptions and supplier reliability, future research could integrate advanced modelling techniques such as fuzzy logic and stochastic models with blockchain. These approaches would enable decision-makers to better navigate variability in demand, regulatory shifts, and operational risks, thereby enhancing decision-making under uncertainty. Moreover, conducting sensitivity or what-if analyses could assess the robustness of proposed frameworks in diverse scenarios, strengthening their practical applicability.

Lastly, exploring synergies between blockchain and emerging technologies like digital twins, the IoT, and AI could significantly advance the field. For instance, integrating IoT sensors for real-time carbon tracking or leveraging AI for predictive analytics in supply chains can complement blockchain’s transparency and traceability. These future research directions align with the broader objectives of achieving sustainable and efficient SCM within the Industry 4.0 paradigm.

column1: Achieving Competitive Advantage Through Blockchain and Enterprise Metaverse Integration: The Role of Innovation Capabilities and Technostress
column2: This study examines how technology-organization-environment (TOE) factors influence innovation capability, which drives blockchain and enterprise metaverse adoption, ultimately impacting competitive advantage. This study uses the data from 258 managers to understand blockchain integration and enterprise metaverse to achieve competitive advantage. The findings of this study reveal that blockchain traceability, blockchain transparency, technology readiness, the threat of data ownership, and competitive pressure are significantly associated with innovation capability. Moreover, the findings suggest that innovation capability is positively associated with blockchain integration and enterprise metaverse adoption. Furthermore, blockchain integration is positively associated with a competitive advantage. Finally, the findings of this study reveal that technostress moderates the relationship between innovation capability and enterprise metaverse adoption. This study enriches the existing literature pertaining to blockchain, enterprise metaverse, and technology adoption. The research also enriches the TOE and innovation capability theory. Furthermore, this study will also be helpful to organizations that intend to adopt blockchain and enterprise metaverse in the future.
column3:
Implications
A. Theoretical Implications
This article holds important theoretical implications for scholars in the field. Positioned as one of the pioneering studies in exploring the factors linked to blockchain adoption and enterprise metaverse adoption, this study makes a substantial theoretical contribution in the domain of technology adoption, TOE framework, and DCT. This article aims to contribute theoretically to the understanding of the synergistic relationship between blockchain technology and the adoption of the metaverse by enterprises, with a particular focus on its implications for gaining competitive advantage. As both blockchain and the metaverse gain prominence in the digital landscape, their convergence presents a novel avenue for organizations seeking to enhance their competitiveness in the evolving business environment. This study contributes to the technology adoption literature by examining the combined adoption of blockchain and the enterprise metaverse, a unique and nascent technological convergence. While the TOE framework has been a cornerstone for understanding technology adoption, this research extends its applicability to a highly novel context. The findings also refine our understanding of how specific TOE factors interact with innovation capability in the adoption process.

Furthermore, by synthesizing the theoretical foundations of blockchain technology and metaverse adoption by enterprises, this article contributes to the growing body of knowledge in the fields of digital innovation and business strategy. The insights provided serve as a guide for organizations seeking to navigate the dynamic landscape of the digital era, offering theoretical frameworks that illuminate the pathways to competitive advantage through the strategic integration of blockchain in metaverse initiatives. As the digital landscape evolves, the convergence of blockchain and the metaverse presents a novel avenue for organizational strategy. There is a need to explore the organization's response toward this innovative technology to achieve competitive advantages. However, scant efforts were made in the existing literature to examine the role of blockchain integration and metaverse adoption in achieving competitive advantages. This article contributes theoretically by exploring the transformative impact of this integration on competitive advantage. This article uniquely contributes to the existing literature by exploring the potential for interoperability across metaverse platforms facilitated by blockchain standards. It theorizes how enterprises can strategically collaborate, leading to innovation, expanded reach, and a sustained competitive advantage in the digital landscape.

This study uses TOE and dynamic capability theories to explore the phenomenon. Investigating the adoption patterns of innovative enterprise metaverse and blockchain technology extends the theoretical understanding of this area. The framework combines crucial constructs within the three dimensions of the TOE framework: technology, organization, and environment. By incorporating these constructs, this study comprehensively analyzes the factors impacting the intention to use blockchain technology and enterprise metaverse to achieve competitive advantages. The findings also refine our understanding of how specific TOE factors interact with innovation capability in the adoption process. By demonstrating that TOE factors significantly influence innovation capability, this study sheds light on how these attributes can shape an organization's receptiveness to adopting emerging technologies.

This study also contributes to the existing literature, emphasizing the enduring relevance of DCT in navigating the complexities of the digital age. This article contributes to the theoretical discourse by providing a comprehensive exploration of DCT in the digital age, shedding light on how organizations can harness these capabilities to adapt, innovate, and gain a competitive advantage. This combined theoretical lens offers a deeper understanding of the decision-making process behind adopting these novel technologies. The findings also enrich our knowledge of the link between technology adoption and competitive advantage.

B. Managerial Implications
The findings of this study reveal that blockchain traceability, blockchain transparency, technology readiness, the threat of data ownership, and competitive pressure are significantly associated with innovation capability. Organizations should organize workshops and training sessions focused on blockchain traceability and transparency to enhance blockchain traceability and transparency. Organizations should educate teams on leveraging these features to enhance data integrity and security. Also, managers should encourage brainstorming sessions to explore innovative blockchain applications within different departments. Furthermore, managers should comprehensively assess technology readiness within the organization to identify gaps and invest in skill development programs tailored to enhance technology readiness. Organizations should establish clear data ownership frameworks and policies to mitigate concerns related to data ownership by ensuring transparency and accountability in data management. Furthermore, top management should foster trust among employees by clarifying rights and responsibilities concerning data control and access. Organizations should also foster a culture that thrives on innovation and experimentation. Managers should encourage cross-functional collaboration and idea-sharing platforms to capitalize on competitive pressure.

Moreover, the findings suggest that innovation capability is positively associated with blockchain integration and enterprise metaverse adoption. Organizations should develop a strategic roadmap for blockchain integration and enterprise metaverse adoption aligned with organizational goals by outlining specific objectives, timelines, and key performance indicators to track the progress of the adoption process. Organizations should then ensure leadership buy-in and commitment to facilitate seamless integration. Furthermore, blockchain integration is positively associated with a competitive advantage. Organizations should invest in acquiring and nurturing blockchain expertise within the organization. Furthermore, they should recruit or train employees with specialized knowledge in blockchain technology to maximize its potential across departments. Finally, the findings of this study reveal that technostress moderates the relationship between innovation capability and enterprise metaverse adoption. Organizations should provide specialized training programs focused on mitigating technostress while promoting the benefits of enterprise metaverse adoption. Furthermore, top management should educate employees about the functionalities and advantages of the metaverse to alleviate uncertainties and anxieties associated with adopting new technologies.

C. Contributions to Engineering Management
The research empirically examines the influence of technology readiness, competitive pressure, and blockchain features on innovation capability in firms. By an empirically validated conceptual model, the research provides engineering managers with a structured pathway to technology adoption, thereby contributing to managerial decision-making. The findings allow organizations to develop structured roadmaps for metaverse and blockchain adoption by emphasizing blockchain transparency, traceability, and competitive pressure.

D. Limitations and Future Research
Similar to other research studies, our study also faces several limitations. Primarily constrained by resources, this article relies solely on cross-sectional data. Future researchers could broaden their scope by incorporating data across a longitudinal period to facilitate a more comprehensive analysis of adoption intention and competitive advantage. Furthermore, blockchain and enterprise metaverse represent a novel phenomenon with limited organizational adoption, resulting in relatively small sample sizes. Therefore, forthcoming research endeavors could expand their scope by including diverse populations with varying cultural backgrounds, thereby extending the implications of this study to encompass a broader range of industries.

column1: Digital transformation for safer circular lithium-ion battery supply chains: a blockchain ecosystem-data perspective
column2: Lithium-ion battery (LIB) circular supply chains (CSCs) present unique safety challenges among operation processes. Blockchain technology can be a promising solution for addressing these challenges, by enabling effective tracking and verification of safety-related information throughout the supply chain. However, how blockchain can mitigate safety issues from a supply chain perspective is poorly understood. This study proposes a theory-supported framework through intervention-based research (IBR) to provide guidance for LIB CSC safety management. The conceptual framework and theoretical propositions set the foundation for research on a comprehensive blockchain ecosystem specifically designed for CSC safety management. The framework includes the design of a blockchain architecture with capabilities tailored to address safety concerns, the involvement of multiple stakeholders, and the development of a safety measurement matrix. This study suggests research and practical directions which lay the groundwork for leveraging blockchain technology to improve safety management in LIB CSC. This research contributes to sustainable supply chains by proposing a conceptual framework for mitigating safety concerns in LIB CSC, paving the way for effective blockchain implementation. In addition, this study contributes to advancing the theoretical design understanding and application of blockchain technology in CSC safety management.
column3: CSCs of the LIB industry present unique challenges in terms of safety, transparency, and efficiency. Blockchain technology offers significant potential for enhancing safety management by enabling effective tracking and verification of battery movement throughout the supply chain. However, there is a noticeable research gap regarding the utilisation of blockchain to address safety issues within CSCs. Further investigation and exploration of blockchain technology are needed to improve safety management in LIB CSCs, guided by theoretical frameworks. To bridge this research gap, we propose a theory-supported application of blockchain in LIB CSCs aimed at mitigating safety concerns. Our study presents a comprehensive blockchain ecosystem that encompasses the design of an architecture with specific capabilities tailored to safety management. This framework also emphasises the involvement of multiple stakeholders and the development of a safety measurement matrix. Additionally, we have developed theoretical-based propositions to explore the interactions and relationships within the conceptual framework, providing valuable insights for future research endeavours and practical blockchain implementations. While this research provides a foundation for applying blockchain to CSCs safety management, it is important to acknowledge certain limitations. Due to space constraints, specific investigations, such as the development of blockchain implementation algorithms, were not conducted in this study. Furthermore, the blockchain architecture requires further examination to enhance its practical implementation. Additionally, this study could be enhanced by empirically testing and verifying the proposed framework. In summary, this research contributes by proposing the application of blockchain technology to the safety management of CSCs. The developed model combines practical implementation strategies with theoretical considerations, offering a roadmap for future blockchain applications not only in LIB safety management but also in other industries and domains. Future research and explanation of the proposed model, along with addressing the identified limitations, will contribute to the advancement of safety management participants and the realisation of safer and more sustainable CSCs.

column1: Blockchain adoption in supply chains: implications for sustainability
column2: Abstract This study aims to systematically review the current academic literature on blockchain and supply chain management (SCM) to explore the antecedents and sustainable outcomes of blockchain adoption and identify factors that influence blockchain adoption at different stages of implementation in supply chains (SC). This review follows the 6 steps and 14 decisions of conducting a systematic literature review (SLR) to comprehensively review 69 papers published in Academic Journal Guide (AJG) 3 and above journals between 2008 and 2023. Based on the content analysis of the selected papers, this study identifies antecedents and outcomes for blockchain adoption. This study further identifies influential factors in each blockchain implementation stage. A conceptual framework is developed to facilitate the conceptual development of blockchain adoption for sustainability in SCs. This study extends the prior studies of blockchain adoption in SCM with the consideration of how blockchain affects the SCM from the aspects of economic, social, and environmental. This review identifies four major themes in the topic of blockchain implementation and SCM, thus assisting researchers in avoiding focusing on the investigation of mature and saturated topics. The research gaps are identified, and future research directions are recommended for scholars, thereby enabling the comprehensive development of blockchain adoption in SCs.
column3: Blockchain technology application in SCs has been established as an important research area in SCM; however, it requires further exploration by both academics and practitioners. This review has explored the relationship between blockchain adoption and SSCM and conducted a content analysis of relevant literature published from January 2008 to June 2023. This review makes an important theoretical contribution to the blockchain and SSCM literature. First, to the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first systematic review of blockchain implementation for SSCM. Previous literature review tends to emphasize the economic outcomes of blockchain adoption and focuses on the identification of enablers and barriers of blockchain adoption in SCs, thus limiting the contribution to exploring the effect of blockchain on SSCM. This review develops a theoretical framework to comprehensively explain how blockchain affects the SCM from the aspects of economic, social, and environmental. Also, the framework helps to clarify what factors can influence blockchain implementation in different stages of initiation, pilot adoption and implementation. This review identifies four major themes (antecedents, implementation stages, influential factors, and benefits to SCM) in the topic of blockchain implementation and SCM. These themes can assist researchers in avoiding focusing on the investigation of mature and saturated themes. In addition, the research gaps are identified, and future research directions are recommended for scholars, thereby enabling the comprehensive development of blockchain adoption in SCs. In the theoretical framework, blockchain implantation stages and related influential factors are concluded from case study research. This endows this SLR with managerial theoretical as well as practical contributions. Companies can employ this framework as guidance for their blockchain project initiation and large-scale implementation in the SC. Moreover, the identified relationship between influential factors and blockchain implementation stages can assist companies in evaluating their readiness for the progression to the next stage of blockchain implementation. In addition, this review has proved that blockchain can comprehensively improve sustainable SCM outcomes, which can provide some insight to policymakers, who can enact preferential policies to encourage organizations to initiate blockchain projects, to leverage the strength of this emerging technology to further promote sustainable development. This paper is not free from limitations. First this review only includes papers published in AJG 3 and above journals, while the conference paper and research reports are excluded. However, blockchain adoption is an emerging topic in SCM research, and thus including these grey references might facilitate a better understanding of blockchain and its related functions in SCM. Second, in the second-round selection, papers employing modelling methodology are excluded. Including these papers may generate more conclusions of the blockchain’s implications on sustainable SCM.

column1: A framework for modeling and simulating blockchain-based supply chain traceability systems
column2: Traceability improves supply chain operations transparency, benefiting the overall performance and the end customer perception. Blockchain technology is a promising alternative to create robust traceability systems, as it promotes trust and supports information sharing based on data immutability. Despite the hype surrounding blockchain technology and the vast literature in the field, the effectiveness and efficiency of blockchain-based supply chain traceability systems remain uncertain across multiple industry sectors, due to the lack of empirical evidence. Considering its characteristics, simulation is a valuable tool to evaluate the performance of supply chain management processes and technology alternatives. However, a structured guide to support the building process of simulation models regarding blockchain in the supply chain is still missing, making it hard for modelers to create realistic simulation models. Thus, this work proposes a novel methodological framework with guidelines to develop HS models regarding supply chain traceability capable of integrating the main blockchain concepts for managerial purposes. Scenarios with different granularity levels may be designed through the combination of both discrete-event and agent-based simulation paradigms. The proposed approach integrates concepts and terminologies from foundational references, including the Supply Chain Operations Reference (SCOR) model and the Global Traceability Standard (GTS). In addition, it is anchored on the ADACOR holonic architecture for the agentification process. Following the Design Science Research methodology, a proof-of-concept application is presented, based on a real-scale industrial case of a lobster supply chain from Canada. Results obtained reflect the framework's versatility to assist the development of a hybrid simulation model, as traceability is explored through the perspectives of time to react, item separation, temporal screening, and blockchain participation rate.
column3: 6 Conclusions 6.1 Methodological and managerial contributions In this paper, we have introduced a novel methodological framework designed to guide the development of hybrid simulation models that integrate supply chain management, traceability mechanisms, and blockchain technology. The main contribution of this work lies in providing a step-by-step multidisciplinary method that combines and adapts frameworks widely accepted in the business and research communities. Our framework supports the modeling of traceability from multiple perspectives, including origin, process, movement, and post-delivery, thus offering a comprehensive approach to capturing the complexities of supply chain traceability from the source of raw materials to final consumption. The proposed framework is particularly valuable for supply chain strategists looking to evaluate the performance of blockchain-based traceability systems. By incorporating agent-based and discrete-event modeling paradigms, our approach allows for the consideration of various blockchain configurations, levels of granularity, traceability information types, and smart contract conditions. This flexibility ensures that the framework can be adapted to different organizational needs and supply chain scenarios, making it a robust tool for both practical application and academic research. Our application of the Design Science Research methodology has ensured that the proposed framework is not only theoretically sound but also practically relevant. The framework has been validated through a real-scale proof-of-concept application in a live lobster supply chain in Canada. This validation has demonstrated the framework's effectiveness in addressing real-world challenges, thus bridging the gap between theory and practice. By providing modelers with specific capabilities and reusable components, our framework simplifies the adoption and use of advanced traceability and blockchain technologies in supply chain management. This contribution is expected to enhance the ability of organizations to optimize their supply chains, improve responsiveness to disturbances, and meet increasing consumer demands for transparency and traceability.

column1: Analysis of Industry 4.0 technological enablers for sustainable supply chain transparency in a fuzzy environment
column2: This study aims to identify various Industry 4.0 technological enablers and analyze their relationships in achieving transparency in sustainable supply chains. Initially, 17 Industry 4.0 technological enablers were selected based on an extensive literature review of sustainable supply chains and evaluated through Systems and Information Processing theories. Using the fuzzy Delphi method, these enablers were then narrowed down to 14 relevant ones. The reliability of these enablers was assessed by measuring their internal consistency using Cronbach's alpha (α) and McDonald's omega (ω). The fuzzy Decision‐Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) method was then used to demonstrate that blockchain, cybersecurity, big data, and artificial intelligence (AI) are the most prominent and influential enablers for enhancing transparency in a sustainable supply chain. Additionally, the cause–effect relationship of other key enablers provides evidence for a feasibility study that links sustainability with transparency across the supply chain. These identified Industry 4.0 technological enablers can assist external stakeholders and policymakers in improving transparency and advancing sustainable supply chain practices.
column3: The main objective of this study is to prioritize and analyze the cause–effect relationship among thirteen identified Industry 4.0-based technological enablers. This study investigated the importance of enablers by employing the fuzzy Delphi method to address the ambiguity in selecting these enablers, using insights from an extensive literature review and expert opinions. Further, fuzzy DEMATEL is applied, which is a widely accepted methodology that provides human judgment clarity in a fuzzy environment. In this study, fuzzy DEMATEL bifurcates the enablers into effect and cause groups. It is applied to identify the prominent enablers of sustainable supply chain transparency. The cause group enablers are intended to provide a platform to industry experts and academicians to transform their traditional supply chain into a sustainable supply chain. In addition, the enablers in the effect group provided evidence for assessing the feasibility of integrating sustainability and transparency into the supply chain. This study also encourages policymakers to re-evaluate their processes, supplier selection, inventory management, and procurement, reducing environmental impacts and long-term risks while increasing production efficiency. It will also assist policymakers in better organizing their assets and execution endeavors for supply chain digitalization. Moreover, Industry 4.0 integrated supply chains provide a holistic view and allow for huge performance improvements by incorporating advanced analytical capabilities, thereby leading to net zero. This study provides a novel approach for integrating Industry 4.0 technological enablers to connect sustainability and transparency in the supply chain. Consequently, the proposed study will motivate academicians and industry practitioners to establish an Industry 4.0 facility to overcome the technical hurdles in the sustainable supply chain and develop new theories or find the root cause of the real case problems of the industries.

column1: Battery recycling and coordination in information leakage prevention under blockchain technology in a new energy vehicles supply chain
column2: Retired battery recycling and information leakage prevention under blockchain introduction intertwine in the new energy vehicle (NEVs) supply chain, but rare literature has jointly investigated them. Therefore, we characterize the vehicle goodwill under recycling and marketing efforts as well as the automobile demand function with and without blockchain introduction, identify the long-run discounted profits of the manufacturer and retailers in the supply chain, and investigate the Stackelberg differential game equilibrium under four scenarios: no blockchain introduction, manufacturer introduction, manufacturer-retailer cooperative introduction, and cooperative introduction plus wholesale price discounts for preventing information leakage. The results show that the manufacturer can introduce blockchain when costs are below a certain threshold, which increases the recycling rate of decommissioned batteries and improves goodwill, consumer demand, and marginal profits for the manufacturer and retailer; the retailer participation in the introduction of blockchain solves the free-rider problem and reduces the thresholds introduced, but does not affect battery recycling, goodwill, consumer demand, and wholesale and retail prices; wholesale price discounts effectively discourage the retailer from leaking information about the manufacturer and lead to improved profits for the retailer, but results in higher earnings for the manufacturer only when discounts are below a certain threshold.
column3: 8 Conclusions Promoting the development of the NEV industry and accelerating the recycling of decommissioned power batteries for NEVs is crucial. This paper considers the decision-making of introducing blockchain technology in the automotive supply chain to improve the consumer demand for new energy vehicles and power battery recycling. It has investigated four scenarios for introducing blockchain technology: no introduction, unilateral introduction by the manufacturer, introduction by the manufacturer in cooperation with the retailer, introduction by the manufacturer in cooperation with the retailer, and wholesale price discounts to prevent information leakage. Using the differential game method, we solve the Stackelberg game between the manufacturer and retailer under the above four scenarios and obtain the following main conclusions and managerial implications. 8.1 Main conclusions It obtains the following conclusions: (1) Introducing blockchain technology on both supply chain sides depends on comparing costs and benefits. A rational economic agent can unilaterally introduce blockchain if the introduction cost is satisfied below a certain threshold. However, a manufacturer seeking to make a fair profit requires the cost of introducing the blockchain to be lower. If a manufacturer and a retailer cooperate to introduce the blockchain, the cost of sharing it depends on their bargaining power. (2) Marketing efforts for NEVs and recycling efforts for decommissioned batteries in the supply chain are complementary, i.e., if one improves, so does the other. The introduction of blockchain improves both. (3) The introduction of blockchain has the potential to significantly increase the demand for new energy vehicles and the recycling rate of retired batteries. This increase in demand and recycling rates, driven by blockchain, can lead to a more sustainable and environmentally friendly supply chain. The introduction of blockchain also pushes up the wholesale and retail prices of new energy vehicles. The greater the consumer preference for blockchain and the lower the truthfulness of the battery recycling rate announced under the no-blockchain, the greater the effect of the roles of the blockchain above. (4) The introduction of blockchain cost-sharing collaborations could address retailers' free-riding and the “unfairness” of improved margins for manufacturers and retailers due to blockchain. However, such a partnership would have no impact on wholesale and retail prices, recycling and marketing efforts, market demand, or recycling rates. (5) Building on the cooperative introduction of blockchain, manufacturers and retailers can establish a wholesale price discount pact. This pact, facilitated by blockchain, effectively prevents information leakage, providing a sense of security in the supply chain. The pact not only leads to a further improvement in the retailer's profit but also has the potential to increase the manufacturer's profit if the discount rate falls below a certain threshold. Simultaneously, the pact leads to an increase in marketing efforts, product goodwill, wholesale and retail prices, and product demand.

column1: Emerging digital technologies potential in promoting equitable agricultural supply chain: A scoping review
column2: The agricultural sector plays a pivotal role in global economies, providing livelihoods and sustenance for billions. However, it faces numerous challenges, including low productivity, and inequitable supply chains that only benefit some of its stakeholders. The study investigates the potential of emerging digital technologies such as blockchain, the Internet of things, artificial intelligence, and machine learning, in promoting equity within agricultural supply chains. Using a scoping approach to Systematic Literature Review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews, the study examines the extent of emerging digital technology deployment in various aspects of the agricultural supply chain. Emerging technologies have been found to focus heavily on some parts of the supply chain (such as transportation), with limited application in others, particularly cash crop supply chains. The evidence gathered informs innovation policies and prioritizes opportunities for future research and practices. Despite the promise of emerging technologies, further evaluation, re-development, and deployment considering the local context and innovation dynamics are necessary. The paper contributes by providing insights into the mediating role of emerging digital technologies in addressing equity issues within the agricultural supply chain emphasizing the need for continued exploration and refinement of these technologies.
column3:
This paper has systematically explored the synergy of Emerging Digital Technologies (EDTs) and equity in the Agricultural Supply Chain (ASC). The review revealed that the emerging technologies that can potentially enhance equity aspects in ASC included BCT, AI, IoT, GIS, and BDA. Moreover, these EDTs can address the equity challenges in the ASC in several ways. Blockchain (BCT) has shown the potential to address most of these challenges, including the ASC's lack of security, trust, transparency, traceability, and sustainability. The varied features of Blockchain technology, like smart contracts, decentralisation, transparency, traceability, data immutability, and data privacy, along with a consensus mechanism, make it suitable to be utilised in today's complex and multi-echelon supply chains. These factors improve the production processes and make the existing supply chains agile, resilient, and responsive in the long term. Blockchain also adds an aspect of sustainability that correlates with the phenomenon of the circular economy in today's world. Nevertheless, the integration of multiple EDTs is pertinent. Furthermore, the study indicated a potential implication of EDTs and equity for ASC policy and practice.
EDTs offer various potentials for supporting equity in ASC. Moreover, each EDT has its strengths and weaknesses in assisting equitable ASC. In order to comprehensively ensure equity in the ASC, governments, researchers, and practitioners are recommended to use a combination of EDTs, including BCT, IoT, AI, and Big data analytics since these technologies complement each other. Some weaknesses of these digital technologies appear as strengths in others. For instance, IoT and BDA can benefit from blockchain by providing and enhancing data security, anonymity, trust, anddecentralisation. Since BCT exchanges information in a distributed network, researchers and developers should create innovative IoT applications for distributed environments.
On the other hand, the valuable data generated from the IoT could enrich transaction details that are registered on the BCT. In turn, the accurate data provided by BCT can be used as input for ASC-based AI applications and to record their outputs. Besides, AI can enhance the IoT by developing innovative ASC applications to analyze data captured by sensors in real-time using machine learning algorithms. Machine learning and other analytic methods can also improve Big data analytics' predictive and prescriptive capabilities (decision-making) in ASC. Thus, combining the different technologies will enhance the ASC and make it more innovative, informed, efficient, secure, sustainable, and resilient.
