In general, EDTs will lead the ASC to evolve into a data-driven, intelligent, agile, autonomous, connected system of systems.

column1: Digital capabilities to manage agri-food supply chain uncertainties and build supply chain resilience during compounding geopolitical disruptions
column2: PurposeThe agricultural supply chain is susceptible to disruptive geopolitical events. Therefore, agri-food firms must devise robust resilience strategies to hasten recovery and mitigate global food security effects. Hence, the central aim of this paper is to investigate how supply chains could leverage digital technologies to design resilience strategies to manage uncertainty stemming from the external environment disrupted by a geopolitical event. The context of the study is the African agri-food supply chain during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.Design/methodology/approachThe authors employ strategic contingency and dynamic capabilities theory arguments to explore the scenario and conditions under which African agri-food firms could leverage digital technologies to formulate contingency strategies and devise mitigation countermeasures. Then, the authors used a multi-case-study analysis of 14 African firms of different sizes and tiers within three main agri-food sectors (i.e. livestock farming, food-crop and fisheries-aquaculture) to explore, interpret and present data and their findings.FindingsDownstream firms (wholesalers and retailers) of the African agri-food supply chain are found to extensively use digital seizing and transforming capabilities to formulate worst-case assumptions amid geopolitical disruption, followed by proactive mitigation actions. These capabilities are mainly supported by advanced technologies such as blockchain and additive manufacturing. On the other hand, smaller upstream partners (SMEs, cooperatives and smallholders) are found to leverage less advanced technologies, such as mobile apps and cloud-based data analytics, to develop sensing capabilities necessary to formulate a “wait-and-see” strategy, allowing them to reduce perceptions of heightened supply chain uncertainty and take mainly reactive mitigation strategies. Finally, the authors integrate their findings into a conceptual framework that advances the research agenda on managing supply chain uncertainty in vulnerable areas.Originality/valueThis study is the first that sought to understand the contextual conditions (supply chain characteristics and firm characteristics) under which companies in the African agri-food supply chain could leverage digital technologies to manage uncertainty. The study advances contingency and dynamic capability theories by providing a new way of interacting in one specific context. In practice, this study assists managers in developing suitable strategies to manage uncertainty during geopolitical disruptions.
column3: The present study explored the role of digital dynamic capabilities in enhancing SCRes within the African AFSC, particularly in the context of geopolitical disruptions such as the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The research identified the concept of “contextual dynamic capabilities,” which allows firms to adapt their strategies based on their size and the geopolitical landscape. Furthermore, the study extended the strategic contingency theory by incorporating geopolitical factors as a critical variable, enriching the existing literature. Moreover, the findings suggest that a nuanced understanding of the geopolitical landscape can offer supply chain managers more robust resilience strategies. Finally, the study implies that larger firms should actively involve smaller upstream partners in their digital transformation initiatives to maximize SCRes. Theoretically, this research contributes to the extant literature by uniquely positioning the African AFSC within a broader geopolitical framework, offering novel theoretical insights into how external geopolitical factors can influence supply chain strategies. Further, the study's holistic approach to examining digital capabilities across multiple supply chain tiers adds complexity to the existing literature on dynamic capabilities and SCRes. Finally, through case studies, the research provides empirical evidence that enriches the current understanding of SCRes, particularly in the context of geopolitical disruptions. While our findings offer valuable insights into the African AFSC during geopolitical disruptions, their transferability to other contexts should be cautiously approached. The unique socioeconomic and geopolitical characteristics of the African context might limit the generalizability of our results to other regions or supply chain scenarios. Like any research, our study has limitations that need to be acknowledged. First, our study's primary limitation lies in the scope of our empirical data, which, while offering a broad view of the impact of digital capabilities on the African AFSC, may need to capture the full depth and specific complexities of each case. Future research could benefit from detailed case studies or longitudinal analysis, enriching our understanding of digital capabilities in supply chains during geopolitical disruptions and providing more nuanced operational and strategic insights. Second, it is a single-context and single-sector explorative study. We recommend that future studies extend the findings by exploring other critical supply chains, such as healthcare, relief, medicine, etc. In addition, future studies are encouraged to examine other contexts, investigating less developed countries in other global areas such as the Asian sub-continent and South America. Finally, the study was conducted during the highly damaging Russian invasion of Ukraine. We recommend expanding the research into a longitudinal study in post-conflict to focus on digital transformation capabilities to support recovery policies. The authors express their sincere gratitude to the dedicated editorial team, handling associate editor, and the diligent reviewers for their invaluable contributions throughout the entire process—from the initial submission to the acceptance of the paper. The constructive comments provided proved instrumental in refining the clarity and readability of our study, enhancing its overall quality. Additionally, the third author extends a special note of appreciation to the British Council for the prestigious recognition and support granted through the “Education Partnership for Promoting High Value Manufacturing Supply Chain Systems (EPPHVMSCS)” project. Since submission of this article, the following author(s) have updated their affiliation(s): Mani Venkatesh is at the Asper School of Business, University of Manitoba, Canada.

column1: Correction to: Platform pricing and blockchain adoption for capacity sharing with cross-network externality and supply risk (Annals of Operations Research, (2024), 10.1007/s10479-024-05850-8)
column2: Platform-based capacity sharing is a new business format of sharing economy to reallocate spare production resources via industrial internet, generating collaborative manufacturing related platform operations issues. This paper examines the impact of cross-network externality and supply risk of the two-sided market on the pricing and blockchain adopting decisions of capacity sharing platforms. The mean–variance model is employed to depict the impact of purchasers’ or suppliers’ risk-sensitive types on platform pricing, where purchasers’ or suppliers’ risk-sensitive types can be identified by blockchain technology and be intertwined by the cross-network externality. The obtained platform’s optimal pricing under two scenarios with risk-sensitive capacity purchasers (D) and risk-sensitive suppliers (S) shows that the platform charges risk-seeking, risk-neutral and risk-averse users in descending order for the platform side containing risk-sensitive users, regardless of the comparison of bilateral cross-network externalities. However, for risk-neutral side users, the price ranking under three risk-sensitive types depends on the relative size of bilateral cross-network externalities. In addition, blockchain technology always decreases the surplus of risk-sensitive side users, whereas it increases the surplus of risk-insensitive side users. Further, we find that platform prefers to introduce blockchain technology when the fixed cost of introducing it is less than the profit increment it brings. In addition, by comparing platform profits and blockchain value in the two scenarios, we argue that platforms need to comprehensively balance the comparison of fixed costs of introducing blockchain on both sides and the importance of risk-preferring and risk-averse users to improve their profitability. Introducing blockchain technology to the side where the cost of blockchain technology is higher may result in higher blockchain value for the platform. Finally, we examine the platform with two-sided risk-sensitive users and the results are robust. This study proposes theoretical explanation for platform pricing considering the cross-network externality and risk-sensitive users, as well as some management insights for the application of blockchain technology in platform operations.
column3:
Inspired by the reality fact that platform users’ risk tendency to capacity supply variation affects the efficiency of platform-based capacity sharing economy, this paper investigates how risk attitudes and cross-network externality impact capacity-sharing platform pricing, platform profit and surplus of two sides. Specifically, this paper discusses three scenarios: hybrid risk-sensitive purchasers (scenario D), hybrid risk-sensitive suppliers (scenario S), and hybrid risk-sensitive purchasers and suppliers (scenario B). The analysis of above three situations yields some managerial insights.

In scenario D, we first discuss the platform pricing when the purchasers show the same risk-sensitive types. The result shows that the price on the demand side, the platform profit, and the surplus of bilateral users are higher with risk-seeking purchasers. However, the impact of risk-sensitive types on supply-side pricing depends on the relative size of the bilateral cross-network externalities. The supply-side pricing is higher with risk-seeking purchasers when the cross-network externality of the supply side is greater than that of the demand side; otherwise, the supply-side pricing is higher with risk-averse purchasers. The result is different from Choi et al. (2020b), which only focuses on demand-side pricing. Secondly, we discuss two pricing mechanisms of the platform when purchasers show different risk attitudes: uniform pricing (without considering the risk-sensitive types of purchasers) and differentiated pricing (charging different usage fees in terms of purchasers’ risk-sensitive types based on blockchain technology). We find the blockchain improves the surplus of suppliers but it hurts purchasers’ surplus by comparing the above pricing schemes. The result is the opposite in scenario S. However, Choi et al. (2020b) show that whether blockchain technology is beneficial to consumers depends on the significance of risk-averse and risk-seeking consumers in the market. Song et al. (2022) conclude that blockchain technology always hurts consumer surplus with the high application cost of blockchain. Furthermore, we find that it is wise for the platform to introduce blockchain technology when the fixed cost of introducing blockchain technology is less than the profit added for the platform. While Wu and Wang (2023) reveal that whether the platform adopts blockchain technology is related to the sales mode of suppliers. By comparing Scenario D and Scenario S, the result demonstrates that the platform needs to comprehensively trade off the relative size of the blockchain fixed costs on the two sides and the significance of risk-seeking and risk-averse users on the platform to improve its profitability. Introducing the higher-cost side of blockchain technology on the platform may result in higher blockchain value. Finally, we extended our research to discuss platform pricing when both sides of the platform contain risk-sensitive users, and the results are still robust.

This paper novelly focuses on the platform pricing problem considering two-sided users’ risk attitudes and the effect of bilateral cross-network externalities, the research of which adds new theoretical knowledge and expands boundary of platform-based capacity sharing field. Furthermore, this paper uncovers the impact of blockchain technology on platform's profitability and bilateral users’ surplus under various scenarios, and depicts the decision-making process of adopting blockchain and conditions of improving revenue and blockchain value. The findings provide suggestions for platform’s blockchain technology adoption decision.

Future research can be conducted in aspects as follows. Capacity supply reliability can be regarded as engogenous decision variable rather the exogenous in this paper. Further, complementary to our focus of the cross-network externality, the impact of same-network externality on users’ utilities can also be considered in the future, so is the fairness concern of users under differentiated pricing scheme. Finally, discussing how blockchain technology influences product delivery time under capacity-sharing platform will be another research direction.

column1: The blockchain adoption strategies of online retailer in a dual-channel supply chain
column2: Blockchain technology has emerged as a promising solution to address consumer distrust caused by the lack of transparency in online channels, thereby promoting the further growth of these channels. In this study, we focus on a dual-channel supply chain comprising a supplier, an online retailer, and an offline retailer, and offering two categories of products, convenience preference product (CPP) and trust preference product (TPP), based on consumers’ purchasing preference. Specifically, we consider three different blockchain adoption models: the online-retailer-based model (Model EB), the supplier-based model offering to solely the online retailer (Model SB), and the supplier-based model offering to both online and offline retailers (Model SA). We show that the online retailer always benefits from adopting blockchain for the CPP. However, for the TPP, only the cost coefficient of traceability by blockchain is low, and a Pareto improvement of blockchain adoption for all the players can be found under certain conditions. We also show that the online retailer benefits from Model SB when the cost coefficient is high, and from Model SA when the competition intensity is low (or high) and the cost coefficient is high (or small-medium). Furthermore, we compare the different blockchain adoption models’ impact on the players’ performance in pairs and inspect the online retailer's optimal blockchain adoption strategy. Through extended study, we find that blockchain adoption for the TPP consistently leads to an increase in social welfare. However, for the CPP, social welfare only improves when both the competition intensity and the cost coefficient are low.
column3: 7 Conclusion 7.1 Concluding remarks Taking into consideration factors such as the lack of transparency in online product information and the inconvenience of offline shopping, this study developed a three-party game model within a dual-channel supply chain. By comparing the model without blockchain with three distinct blockchain adoption models, we identified the necessary conditions for and impacts of blockchain adoption on the performance of the individual and the entire supply chain. We also inspected the online retailer’s optimal blockchain adoption strategy. The key findings are summarized as follows. First, for the CPP, the online retailer should consistently endorse blockchain traceability, whereas the supplier can benefit from blockchain adoption only when shopping convenience in the offline channel and the traceability cost coefficient are low. Conversely, for the TPP, the supplier consistently benefits from blockchain adoption, whereas the online retailer can benefit only when shopping convenience and blockchain cost coefficient are low. These results further emphasize the significance of comprehending the relative magnitudes of shopping convenience and cost coefficient prior to adopting blockchain. Second, for the CPP, if blockchain is only adopted in the online channel, there is the potential to achieve a triple-win situation when the shopping convenience and the traceability cost coefficient are moderate. Moreover, the lower the consumers’ trust in online products, the higher the likelihood of achieving a win-win-win with blockchain adoption. However, for the TPP, the key condition for achieving a win-win-win with blockchain adoption is the profitability of the offline retailer. The higher the consumers’ trust in the online channel, the greater the possibility of achieving a win-win-win situation. For CPP, if both online and offline channels adopt blockchain, the offline retailer can consistently benefit from blockchain adoption. However, for TPP, the offline retailer can only profit from blockchain adoption when the shopping convenience of the offline channel and the cost coefficient are low. Therefore, the potential for achieving a triple-win situation exists in both types of blockchain adoption models. Third, if the supplier exclusively offers blockchain solutions for the online channel and if the traceability cost coefficient is high, the online retailer will opt for a supplier-based blockchain model; otherwise, he will take the initiative to lead the blockchain implementation himself. Moreover, it is only when the online retailer leads the blockchain that both the supplier and the online retailer can benefit. However, if the supplier provides blockchain for both online and offline channels, the online retailer will choose a supplier-based blockchain model when competition intensity is low (or high) and the traceability cost coefficient is high (or low). Conversely, he will choose to lead the blockchain himself. The supplier-based blockchain model consistently favors both the supplier and the offline retailer. Moreover, when the online retailers consider themselves incapable of bearing the costs associated with blockchain traceability and opt for a supplier-based blockchain approach, they should choose suppliers that offer blockchain for both online and offline channels when the traceability cost coefficient is low. Conversely, when the traceability cost coefficient is high, the online retailer should select the supplier who exclusively provides blockchain for online channels. Fourth, our first extension suggests that blockchain adoption can enhance social welfare when consumers prefer convenience in purchasing products, provided that the convenience of the offline channel and the cost coefficient are low. However, if consumers prefer trust, blockchain adoption consistently contributes to social welfare. Moreover, our second extension confirms the stability of our findings by revealing similar conditions for blockchain adoption when invested by retailers. Additionally, in cases where both channels adopt blockchain, the choice of the investment party is influenced by the effectiveness of the blockchain and the intensity of channel competition.

column1: Price signal or blockchain technology? Quality information disclosure in dual-channel supply chains
column2: Quality information asymmetry regardless of online or offline channels have damaged the profits of high-quality manufacturers. Price signal and blockchain technology (BCT) are two strategies to eliminate this asymmetry, with BCT potentially incurring higher costs but also boosting demand potential. Therefore, in a dual-channel supply chain consisting of a manufacturer with private quality information and a retailer, we use a game-theoretic model to investigate which information strategy should be adopted by the high-quality manufacturer. Main results unveil a counterintuitive finding: the high-quality manufacturer may not reap greater benefits from BCT despite its ability to simultaneously boost prices and demands in both channels; conversely, the retailer can still derive benefits from BCT even if it fails to augment the expected demand in the retail channel. We attribute this phenomenon to two key effects of BCT: the information effect and the basic demand expansion effect. Additionally, we highlight the pivotal impact of channel market share on the value of these two strategies, as it not only affects the efficiency of information transmission through the price signal strategy but also the distinct demand enhancement that BCT offers to both channels. Specifically, for the products with a lower production cost difference and a higher market share in the retail channel, our research demonstrates that BCT has the potential to benefit the entire supply chain. This paper provides practical guidance for the strategic implementation of BCT in dual channels.
column3: 7 Conclusion The booming Internet and e-commerce have made online channels a popular distribution strategy for manufacturers. However, quality information asymmetry is prevalent in both online direct channel and offline indirect channel, undermining the profits of high-quality manufacturers. Therefore, they have an incentive to prevent imitation by low-quality manufacturers. In practice, two strategies (i.e., price signal and BCT) have been widely adopted. However, both strategies may involve costs, and the price signal cannot always achieve separation. Particularly, when prices in the two channels are used to signal quality, both vertical cooperation and horizontal competition makes the efficiency of price signals different from that in a single channel. Thus, this study provides valuable insights into supply chain managers to evaluate different information strategies. Our research underscores the significance of comprehending the dual effects of BCT, namely the information effect and basic demand expansion effect. Thus, for high-quality manufacturers, adopting BCT is not a one-size-fits-all solution but necessitates comprehensive evaluation. Particularly, for products with high production-cost differences, such as automobiles, the price signal strategy proves more efficient as it achieves separation without incurring information costs. Nevertheless, manufacturers should still opt for BCT when the basic demand expansion effect is substantial. As reflected in practice, BMW has established the PartChain organization to enhance transparency in raw materials and components within the global supply chain, which aims to build consumer trust and boost demand. Conversely, for luxury goods with moderate or low cost differences but high brand value (i.e., a high market share in manufacturers’ direct channels), BCT can convey quality information more effectively. Therefore, embracing BCT at a reasonable cost can be a profitable strategy for manufacturers to leverage the information effect. Retailers are advised to broaden their assessment of BCT beyond mere price and demand metrics. This is crucial because our findings indicate that even if BCT fails to augment expected demand in the retail channel, retailers can still benefit from the information effect. Moreover, our study uncovers a noteworthy revelation: retailers occasionally benefit more from information asymmetry than from the BCT strategy, which incurs an information cost and reduces retailers’ profitability of selling low-quality products. Consequently, retailers must judiciously assess the current market dynamics and the expenses related to achieving information symmetry when appraising the value of BCT. We also strongly recommend that when adopting BCT in a dual-channel supply chain, firms should keep an eye on the disparities in market shares between two channels. These disparities not only influence the information transmission efficiency of the price signal strategy but also yield varied demand expansion effects across the two channels under the BCT strategy. Specifically, if the unit-use cost of BCT remains reasonably low, high-quality manufacturers ought to embrace BCT when they hold a lower market share in their direct channel. Such a strategic choice further enhances the overall supply chain performance, as a higher market share in the retail channel concurrently amplifies the information effect and basic demand expansion effect of BCT for retailers. This paper can be further extended. We consider the case where manufacturers engage in dual channels. In practice, manufacturers have the flexibility to choose and adjust their sales channels in different scenarios. Thus, considering both channel market share and channel distribution strategies may lead to different BCT adoption strategies. In addition, because the deployment of BCT requires the consent of all supply chain enterprises, how to realize supply chain coordination under the BCT strategy is an interesting and meaningful research issue.

column1: The Genesis Effect: Digital Goods in the Metaverse
column2: This research shows that although the used and unused versions of a digital good (e.g., virtual apparel) are identical in every pixel and functionality, consumers tend to prefer the unused version. This “genesis effect” occurs because consumers tend to perceive used (vs. unused) digital goods as virtually contaminated and because being permanently listed as the first (vs. subsequent) owner in the ownership record can confer a greater sense of status. Specifically, in study 1, analyses of large-scale field data on purchases of digital goods in the metaverse showed that consumers paid substantially more to acquire the unused (vs. used) version of the same good. Studies 2–4 causally demonstrated the genesis effect and its underlying mechanism across metaverse product categories—participants were less likely to purchase digital goods described as used (vs. unused). Virtual contamination and virtual status jointly mediated the effect. Furthermore, being the first—at the genesis of a digital product’s usage history—was particularly special, such that participants were less sensitive to increases in the number of prior owners after the first one. Finally, showing participants that a used good had been digitally reconstituted attenuated the genesis effect. These findings add to the literature on consumer behavior in the metaverse and offer managerial insights on digital goods marketing.
column3:
GENERAL DISCUSSION
This research seeks to shed light on consumer behavior in the metaverse. I propose that although the used and unused versions of a digital good are identical in every pixel and functionality, consumers tend to prefer the unused version. This genesis effect occurs because consumers tend to perceive used (vs. unused) digital goods as virtually contaminated and because being permanently listed as the first (vs. subsequent) owner in the ownership record can confer a greater sense of status. Through empirical analyses of large-scale field data on transactions of digital goods in the metaverse and a series of controlled experiments, this research demonstrates the genesis effect and its underlying mechanism, investigates potential alternative accounts, and examines moderating factors.

This research makes several contributions. Complementing the literature on psychological processes of the mind as long-term evolutionary outcomes (e.g., Dennett 2017; Pinker 1997), the current work illustrates that the mind may not sufficiently adjust to consumption contexts involving radically new technologies. Specifically, this research shows that psychological processes associated with physical contamination (e.g., Argo et al. 2006) can be activated in virtual consumption contexts, even though those processes should not apply. At the same time, virtual contamination has unique characteristics—perceived contamination level of a digital good does not necessarily increase with the number of prior owners; digitally reconstituting a used good can attenuate perceived contamination. Furthermore, this research adds to the understanding of consumer behavior in the context of ownership history transparency. Complementing the research streams on consumers’ extended self (e.g., Belk 2013, 2016) and digital consumption (e.g., Atasoy and Morewedge 2018; Hofstetter et al. 2022; Schmitt 2019), this research shows that being permanently listed as the first (vs. subsequent) owner in ownership records can confer a greater sense of status for the metaverse self and hence shape consumer preference.

The findings of this research have important managerial implications. Given that virtual contamination degrades consumer preference, sellers of used digital goods should consider designing their metaverse stores to project cleanliness and avoid activating contamination-related cognitions. The current research shows that the virtual status derived from the ownership history of a digital good can influence consumer decision-making. This suggests that by highlighting certain virtual status (e.g., permanently ranked first), firms can bolster the effectiveness of their promotion endeavors in the metaverse. Further, study 1 findings indicate that the genesis effect can vary across product categories with different characteristics (e.g., virtual contact level, inherent status). These results inform how firms can better customize prices for used versus unused digital goods. Moreover, study 4 findings suggest that digitally reconstituting a used good can help reduce virtual contamination. Because of the digital nature of this type of approach (e.g., displaying the regeneration of each pixel of a virtual product), the marginal cost of the intervention is practically zero. But the increase in purchase likelihood can be substantial.

The findings of this research suggest several directions for future research. First, in study 1, analyses of large-scale field data on purchases of digital goods found that consumers were willing to pay a substantially higher price for the unused (vs. used) version of the same good across a wide spectrum of product categories. The subsequent experiments, which utilized controlled setups and large sample sizes, focused on investigating the underlying mechanism. While the genesis effect was consistently demonstrated across product categories, the size of the effect in the experiments was relatively moderate. Future research can leverage other approaches to further examine the phenomenon and, more importantly, uncover additional factors that accentuate or attenuate the effect. Second, the findings of this research suggest that the extent to which each of the two underlying factors drives the genesis effect depends on the consumption context. Like physical goods consumption in the offline world, digital goods consumption in the metaverse most often involves being virtually in contact with the goods. However, for goods that do not involve any virtual contact, the underlying role of virtual contamination may be attenuated. Further, the findings of this research suggest that digital goods can vary in their inherent status. Consumers may experience a substantial sense of status for acquiring, for instance, an exclusive product by an elite designer, even if the item has been previously owned. For such type of goods, being listed as a subsequent owner in the ownership history might not significantly reduce the sense of status. Relatedly, whether the first owner is the creator of the good (vs. a regular consumer) may also lead to different reactions. Future research can explore these possibilities and further delineate the conditions under which the two mediating factors may be more or less potent. Third, this research demonstrates a negative effect of prior usage on consumer preference for digital goods. Future research can explore situations in which the opposite pattern may occur. For example, extant research on offline entities suggests that when the previous owner is perceived to be highly positive (e.g., a beloved celebrity), consumers may perceive positive contamination and value the used items more (Newman, Diesendruck, and Bloom 2011; see Huang, Ackerman, and Newman 2017 for discussions). Future research can examine the extent to which such positive contamination occurs with used digital goods. Fourth, consumers’ chronic dispositions may influence their reactions to used (vs. unused) digital goods. For example, chronic sensitivity to physical contagion and/or spiritual contagion (Kim et al. 2023) may interact with different digital product categories to shape consumer preference. Future research can explore this direction and offer more insights on the psychology of virtual contagion.

More broadly, this research highlights the need to better understand consumer behavior in the metaverse. Digital goods have unique characteristics (see web appendix B) that remain unexplored. For example, unlike in the physical world, a diamond necklace/gold ring in the metaverse can cost the same to produce as a glass necklace/copper ring. Given the lack of differences in the preciousness of “raw materials” in the metaverse, research is needed to understand the implications for perceptions of value, rarity, and luxury. Moreover, it is important to examine how the metaverse may alter the psychology of ownership. For instance, prior research shows that the lack of physical interactions with digital goods makes it less likely for consumers to develop a sense of psychological ownership, causing them to value digital goods less than similar physical goods (Atasoy and Morewedge 2018; see Morewedge et al. 2021 for discussions). With the metaverse, consumers, in their avatars, are able to intimately interact with the digital goods they own. Future research can explore whether consumers develop a stronger level of psychological ownership toward certain digital possessions in the metaverse and whether the differences in valuations of digital versus physical goods may be attenuated or even reversed. It is also important to understand how the consumption of digital goods may impact that of physical goods and vice versa. Such insights can inform, for instance, when and how firms should offer a digital version of a physical product. Furthermore, this research examined non-fungible digital goods (e.g., a virtual lamp that has a unique ID and an associated ownership record in the blockchain is not perfectly interchangeable with another virtual lamp with a different ID and a different ownership record). Future research can explore how consumers react to digital items that are fungible (i.e., perfectly interchangeable). Finally, this research focused on common metaverse goods (e.g., virtual furniture, apparel). Future research can explore other classes of digital assets (e.g., virtual lands, houses, estates) and shed light on consumer decision-making involving those assets. Investigating potential research directions such as the above can help advance the theoretical understanding of consumer behavior in the metaverse and offer important managerial insights.

column1: International multimodal transport connectivity assessment of multimodal transport from mainland China to Europe
column2: In this study, we propose a novel International Multimodal Transport Connectivity (IMTC) index and assess the IMTC of multimodal transport from mainland China to Europe. We first present the definition of IMTC, which represents the ease of transporting export cargoes from a domestic origin to an overseas destination by an international multimodal transport network. Second, we propose two kinds of IMTC indexes and then give detailed measurement methods by considering the main modes (i.e., railway express and maritime shipping) in the international multimodal transport process. One is the monetary-based IMTC measured by the monetary cost shippers must pay for transporting export cargo to an overseas region. The other is the time-based IMTC, which is measured by the time cost of the international multimodal transport process and incorporates the time value of different export cargo categories and transport time uncertainty. Third, we assess the IMTC of the international multimodal transport from mainland China to Europe and we mainly compare the monetary-based and the time-based IMTCs via the CR Express or maritime shipping in the pre- and post-COVID years. The results indicate that monetary-based IMTCs from China to Europe via CR Express are significantly lower than those via maritime shipping in the pre-COVID year, while the trend reverses in the post-COVID year, and the monetary-based IMTCs via CR Express are much higher than those via maritime shipping. Moreover, in both the pre-and post-COVID years, the time-based IMTCs from China to Europe via CR Express were significantly higher than those via maritime shipping for all nine cargo categories. Our study offers a new perspective for assessing the convenience of international multimodal transport with the novel IMTC index and provides policy and managerial implications (e.g., real-time cargo tracking technology with blockchain, unified price control mechanism and subsidy strategy, and expansion of the CR Express capacity) to guide policymakers in improving the resilience of international multimodal transport.
column3: 5 Conclusions and policy implications This study proposed an IMTC index and assessed the IMTCs from mainland China to Europe in pre- and post-COVID years. Based on the main transport processes from domestic origins to overseas regions and shippers’ path choice behavior, we propose detailed measurement methods of IMTC by considering the monetary and time costs in the whole transport process via the main transport mode of railway express and shipping. The monetary-based IMTC is measured by the monetary cost the shippers must pay for transporting export cargo to an overseas region. The time-based IMTC is measured by the time cost of the whole international multimodal transport process and incorporates the time value of different export cargo categories and transport time uncertainty. In this case, we have chosen international multimodal transport from mainland China to Europe to conduct an empirical analysis. The results indicate significant differences in the monetary-based IMTCs from mainland China to Europe. In particular, the monetary-based IMTCs via the CR Express are significantly lower than those via maritime shipping in the pre-COVID year, while the trend reverses in the post-COVID years, and the monetary-based IMTCs via CR Express are much higher than those via maritime shipping. Concerning the time-based IMTCs from mainland China to Europe for different cargo categories, in both the pre-and post-COVID years, the time-based IMTCs via CR Express are significantly higher than those via maritime shipping for all nine cargo categories. We also analyze the spatial patterns of the IMTCs from domestic origins in mainland China to Europe in the pre- and post-COVID years, and the results show that the domestic origins with higher IMTCs via CR Express are mainly located in the central and western regions, while the domestic origins with higher IMTCs via shipping are mainly located in the southeast coastal regions. In addition, by combining the monetary cost and time cost to form a generalized transport cost, we further analyze the shipper’s main mode choice preference for maritime shipping and CR Express in international multimodal transport from mainland China to Europe. Overall, in the pre-COVID year, the shippers in mainland China do not have a strong preference for either CR Express or shipping. In the post-COVID years, CR Express gained a cost advantage, and shippers had a stronger preference for CR Express when transporting export cargoes to Europe. Possible implications for policymakers and industry are proposed to improve the resilience of international multimodal transport in the post-COVID era. First, as presented in the empirical study concerning the time-based IMTCs from mainland China to Europe in the pre-COVID and post-COVID years, higher transport time uncertainty in international shipping and the heavy port congestion in the post-COVID era has dramatically decreased the transport convenience from mainland China to Europe. Thus, an improvement in the port’s operational efficiency with limited resources and the usage of real-time cargo tracking technology (e.g., blockchain technology) would be helpful to improve the time-based IMTC from domestic origins to overseas regions. Second, high shipping prices of international shipping in the post-COVID era, especially in 2020 and 2021, have greatly impacted monetary-based IMTC via shipping from mainland China to Europe. A unified price control mechanism and subsidy strategy for different shipping companies from the regulatory authority are of great importance to speed up the recovery of the port and maritime shipping industries and further improve the resilience of international multimodal transport, as shipping is still the most environmentally friendly transport mode in international freight transport. Finally, CR Express has not been greatly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and thus, the IMTC via CR Express from mainland China to Europe also increased in the post-COVID years, while the shortage of CR Express lines and limited capacity have restricted the rapid development of CR Express in the post-COVID era. Therefore, we argue that an expansion of the CR Express capacity and frequency would be pivotal to support the rapidly growing bilateral trade demands between mainland China and Europe in the post-COVID era. Along with offering conclusions and implications, this paper leaves research directions for future study. First, in this study, we measure the IMTC using only the monetary cost or time cost of the whole transport process from domestic origins to overseas destinations. Since the decarbonization development of different transport modes has become increasingly vital in international cargo freight transport, the carbon emission cost could be included in the IMTC index to compare the emission cost advantages of different transport modes in the future. Second, this study assesses the international multimodal transport connectivity for export cargoes, but we believe that our proposed methodology for measuring the multimodal transport connectivity could also be applied to study the convenience of transporting import cargoes from overseas regions to domestic cities or regions. By comparing the multimodal transport connectivity of transporting export cargoes and import cargoes, the effects of IMTC on trade imbalance could be further analyzed in the future. Third, the parameters in the MNL model and the parameter θ used to capture the ‘tapering effect’ of domestic inland transport are set based on the literature, and we recommend calibrating these parameters based on data sourced from the Chinese inland transport market in future research. Finally, Europe is aggregated as one sole overseas destination in this study, and in future research, we can consider different cities or countries as destinations and evaluate the corresponding IMTCs from domestic origins in mainland China to these destinations. We believe that this study has set an ideal platform for researchers to address the important issue of transport connectivity in the post-COVID era.

column1: Integrating smart Green Product Platforming for carbon footprint reduction: The role of blockchain technology and stakeholders influence within the agri-food supply chain
column2: This study explores the integration of Blockchain Technology (BCT) with Green Product Platforming (GPP) in the agri-food industry, addressing the gap in empirical evidence about BCT's effective contribution to enhancing carbon and the economic performance of supply chains. It aims to analyze the impact of BCT-enabled GPP on reducing the carbon footprint and enhancing economic performance in the agri-food sector. In the agri-food sector, BCT-enabled platforms are emerging as critical methods. These platforms are characterized by their assortment of consistent modules and interfaces, adept at efficiently producing and digitally delivering diverse green products. The research combines quantitative surveys and qualitative interviews to examine the interplay of BCT as a digital technology and GPP and the significant role of stakeholders' stress in driving the effectiveness of BCT-enabled GPP, exploring the conditions of its positive impact on carbon and economic performance. The findings indicate the importance of aligning GPP initiatives with stakeholder expectations and leveraging BCT to navigate and capitalize on stakeholder pressures for improved carbon and economic performance. Highlighting actionable insights, this research offers a roadmap for agri-food managers to harness technological advancements to meet the dual objectives of sustainability and competitive advantage. Therefore, the paper presents a nuanced analysis of how BCT-enabled GPP can revolutionize the agri-food industry toward a more sustainable and efficient future. The study acknowledges limitations, notably, the variability in BCT implementation across the agri-food sector and the need for ongoing evaluation due to blockchain's evolving nature. Future research should explore BCT's diverse applications in agri-food contexts and its scalability within complex supply chains.
column3: 7 Conclusion, limitations, and future research BCT-enabled GPP serves as a fundamental framework for integrating sustainable practices. It provides a structured yet adaptable approach for developing and delivering green products, aligning with both environmental goals and economic performance. The platform-based model facilitates a more efficient and scalable means of innovation, effectively managing resources and reducing environmental impacts. This approach, therefore, stands as a cornerstone in the transition towards more sustainable agri-food supply chains. The study's findings suggest that such platforms' success relies on stakeholder stress. Our study significantly contributes to understanding the role of BCT in promoting GPP within the agrifood supply chain. It highlights the importance of stakeholder pressures in the adoption and effectiveness of BCT in GPP, offering novel insights into managing environmental and economic challenges in the sector. The findings emphasize the need for ongoing adaptation and alignment with evolving stakeholder expectations and technological advancements. This research paves the way for future studies to explore broader applications and long-term impacts of BCT in sustainable supply chain management. Acknowledging the study's limitations, a key aspect to consider is the potential variability in BCT implementation across different contexts within the agri-food sector. While the study integrates qualitative and quantitative methods, further research could delve into diverse agrifood supply chain models to ascertain the broader applicability of the findings. Additionally, the dynamic nature of blockchain technology calls for ongoing evaluation to keep pace with its evolving applications and implications in GPP. Therefore, future research should focus on exploring the variability of BCT applications in different agrifood contexts, continuously updating the understanding of BCT in GPP as technology evolves, and investigating the scalability of these applications in more extensive and complex supply chain structures.

column1: Technology-driven logistics and supply chain management for societal impacts
column2: In recent years, there has been substantial growth in the utilization of technologies within the logistics and transportation industries. This growth has resulted in the emergence of numerous novel and exciting applications, offering researchers valuable opportunities to develop innovative solutions. The field of operations management is well-positioned to contribute significantly to this development and promote socially responsible values. This paper investigates the impact of technology-driven logistics and supply chain management on various aspects of social values, categorized as technologies, platforms, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations. Additionally, it provides an introduction to the papers featured in this special issue. Lastly, the paper proposes future research directions to further advance the societal impacts of technologies in logistics and transportation applications.
column3:
5. Future research
We conclude this discussion paper by proposing future research directions based on the findings of the research studies featured in this special issue.
5.1. Prescriptive analytics for logistics and supply chains
With the increasing maturity of disruptive technologies such as blockchain, big data, AI, and robots, researchers have conducted extensive research on the impact and application scenarios of technology in logistics and supply chain management (Choi et al., 2018, Choi and Luo, 2019, Choi et al., 2019, Dutta et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2023, Klöckner et al., 2023, Xu et al., 2023, Yan et al., 2022, Wong et al., 2024). Existing research in this field mainly focuses on theoretical analysis or empirical estimation. However, as the complexity, uncertainty, multi-stage nature, and interactivity of supply chain systems become more significant, integrating empirical estimation with theoretical analysis. Prescriptive analytics has become a research trend in the field of logistics and supply chain operations (Qi et al., 2018, Guo and Choi, 2023).
It is worth noting that existing studies mainly discuss the economic and environmental sustainability of the supply chain (Zhou et al., 2023). However, when it comes to societal impacts, social sustainability may require more efforts (Meng et al., 2023). For example, in-depth analysis of people’s behavioral data will help recognize and predict consumer behavior and demand, further improving the accuracy of demand forecasting for products and raw materials, thereby enhancing decision-making efficiency at every link in the supply chain. Additionally, characterizing social welfare is of great significance as it helps policymakers develop relevant standards and incentive mechanisms to promote sustainable development of the supply chain and improve social well-being (Dou and Choi, 2023).
Furthermore, as the supply chain network continues to expand and involve more stakeholders, there is a need for further exploration of the coupling relationship between decision-making and resource consumption among multiple stakeholders hidden behind big data through machine learning and AI techniques. Quantitative scientific methods can be further applied to develop sustainable implementation plans. For example, the application of blockchain technology in networks consisting of multiple suppliers and multiple retailers is based on the fair mechanism for reasonable benefit division (Choi et al., 2021). By analyzing the data of production, logistics, and consumption at the front, middle, and end stages, and studying the patterns of business activities and resource consumption to predict future trends, it is expected that the results will contribute to the establishment and implementation of fair mechanisms in such a complex supply chain network.
Therefore, more research on prescriptive analytics is expected to be conducted, especially in sustainable supply chain operations (Chan et al., 2023), from economic, environmental, and social perspectives.
5.2. Policies and mechanisms for ESG enhancement driven by technologies
While technologies such as blockchain, IoT, and data analytics can play a significant role in collecting and analyzing information to strengthen ESG initiatives, it is important to recognize that these tools are only enablers. Another crucial aspect is the mechanisms for how policies can be derived by using the data collected and the information captured. In this line of research, the focus should not only be on the collection of data but on how that data is processed and used to derive effective policies and strategies. This requires a holistic approach that considers not just the technological aspects but also the social and economic factors that impact ESG. For example, in this special issue, Guo et al. (2021) demonstrate the positive societal impacts of a collaborative routing mechanism that utilizes an auction-based mechanism. Yuan et al. (2021) propose an AI-based automatic emissions permit trading system and develop a dynamic programming approach to coordinate transportation firms’ decisions. These studies also highlight the importance of considering financial aspects, such as the economics of adoption (Iyengar et al., 2023, Mohri et al., 2023), technology investment (Ma et al., 2021), and ESG investing (Halbritter and Dorfleitner, 2015, De Spiegeleer et al., 2023), for ESG enhancement.
Ultimately, the goal in this line of research should be to use technology as a tool to promote sustainability and responsible business practices, rather than as an end in itself. By integrating technological advancements with comprehensive policies and strategies, companies and organizations can effectively address ESG challenges and contribute to a more sustainable and socially beneficial future.
5.3. Data accessibility, authenticity, and security in supply chains
Data accessibility refers to the availability and ease of accessing relevant information throughout the supply chain network. This can be achieved through the adoption of technologies such as IoT, RFID, and real-time data sharing platforms. In this special issue, a few studies have presented the use of blockchain for data sharing (Dutta et al., 2020, Mangla et al., 2021, Niu et al., 2021). The research on data accessibility is highly relevant to studies in the context of supply chain visibility (Lee, 2002, Lee and Özer, 2007, Williams et al., 2013). It is essential for all stakeholders to have timely access to accurate data to make informed decisions and ensure smooth operations. In recent years, consumers are more concerned about companies’ and organizations’ ESG practices and have started to develop trust in ESG practices through improved supply chain visibility (Kraft et al., 2022).
Data authenticity refers to the trustworthiness and reliability of data. In supply chains, it is vital to ensure that the data collected and shared is accurate and has not been tampered with or manipulated. As discussed in Section 2.2, blockchain technology offers a promising solution by providing a decentralized and immutable ledger that can verify and authenticate data transactions. By leveraging blockchain, supply chain stakeholders can have confidence in the integrity and origin of the data, enhancing transparency and trust across the network. However, whether the adoption of blockchain is financially viable is still a key topic in the recent literature (Chod et al., 2020, Pun et al., 2021, Zhang et al., 2023, Tiwari et al., 2023).
Data security is another crucial aspect to safeguard sensitive information from unauthorized access, manipulation, or theft. As discussed in this special issue, Cheung et al. (2021) highlight the increasing risk of cyber threats and data breaches with the digitization of supply chains. Robust cybersecurity measures, such as encryption, firewalls, and access controls, must be implemented to protect data. Regular security audits and employee training on best practices can help mitigate risks and ensure data security. In particular, as the economy has accelerated from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0, the challenges related to cybersecurity in operations and supply chain management must be addressed (Kumar and Mallipeddi, 2022). Additionally, the role of governments in ensuring data security is an interesting research direction to study (Luo and Choi, 2022).
5.4. Platforms as an enabler for technology deployment for social impacts
Several studies in this special issue explore the utilization of platforms to deploy technologies with the ultimate aim of generating positive social impacts. For instance, Yuan et al. (2021) investigate the application of AI in transportation emissions trading platforms, while Guo et al. (2021) focus on enhancing social welfare through omnichannel on-demand logistics. By leveraging platforms, companies and organizations can gather valuable information, including user behavior, real-time system status, information sharing and reporting, and analysis (He et al., 2022, Mak and Max Shen, 2021). Furthermore, platforms facilitate collaboration among different supply chain participants, enabling them to optimize overall benefits while adhering to environmental regulations and social constraints set forth by the public and government entities (e.g., Guo et al., 2021, Yuan et al., 2021, Lai et al., 2023, Zheng et al., 2023). However, the effective utilization of platforms necessitates incentivizing companies to actively participate, provide accurate and valuable data, and make decisions that benefit the overall system and society as a whole. Thus, further research not is required focusing not only on the technical aspects of platform development, such as platform infrastructure and data collection and processing techniques, but also on effective incentive design and collaborative mechanisms that align the decisions and benefits of all stakeholders with the interests of society as a whole.
5.5. Human aspects of logistics and supply chain operations
Traditional research studies in logistics and supply chain management primarily focus on aspects such as production, movement, and sales of products, often neglecting the human element or considering human aspects only in aggregated demand modeling. However, there has been a recent shift towards incorporating human aspects into research in this field. As discussed in Section 5.4, the utilization of platforms offers significant benefits for organizations, companies, and customers by facilitating information sharing, collaboration, and individual and collective gains. The data collected from users through these platforms can provide valuable insights into their behaviors, enabling better decision-making in logistics and supply chain operations. For instance, Lin et al. (2021) present a research study that explores different matching strategies, such as “self-interested” and “hard-work-happy-life,” which incorporate user preferences in a matching process for a shared healthcare service delivery platform. In addition to platforms, sensing technologies have also played a role in capturing user behaviors at a more detailed level. For example, Ding et al. (2021) utilize video surveillance data to collect information on lost sales and understand user behavior regarding product substitution, with the aim of improving customer welfare through the application of such technology.
Furthermore, it is crucial to consider human worker behaviors in logistics operations. One emerging area in this regard is human–machine collaboration, which has gained popularity in warehouse operations (Lorson et al., 2023). In these warehouses, human pickers and robot transporters interact and collaborate, leveraging the flexibility of human workers in performing a wide range of picking operations, while robots offer efficiency and speed in product transportation without fatigue. The challenge lies in designing and coordinating the roles of human pickers and robots (Wang et al., 2022, Löffler et al., 2023). Additionally, ensuring a safe and healthy work environment for human workers is another critical issue that needs to be addressed, prioritizing their safety and mental well-being (Sheu and Choi, 2023).

column1: Manufacturer blockchain technology adoption strategies for different sales channels in an e-commerce platform supply chain
column2: Blockchain technology (BT) adoption in a platform supply chain can provide consumers with reliable product information traceability, thus meeting consumer needs and improving product image, but bringing high BT adoption costs to the supply chain members. This work focuses on a dual-channel e-commerce platform supply chain consisting of a manufacturer and two platforms, i.e., a reselling platform and an agent platform, both with established blockchain systems. All four strategies for the manufacturer to adopt and not to adopt BT on the two platforms are examined. The results show that intuitively the manufacturer should (not) adopt BT in the two platforms when its BT adoption cost is low (high). Interestingly, the commission rate charged by the agent platform affects the manufacturer BT adoption decision when the BT adoption cost is moderate, and the manufacturer should adopt BT only in the channel with the agent (reselling) platform if the commission rate is low (high). Counterintuitively, adopting BT in the e-commerce platform supply chain does not necessarily increase product demand. Four extensions are examined to broaden the applicability of the basic models, and some interesting findings are obtained.
column3: 7 Conclusions This study examines an e-commerce platform supply chain consisting of a manufacturer, a reselling platform and an agent platform, both with established blockchain systems. The manufacturer wholesales the products to the reselling platform in channel R, and sells the products directly to consumers by using and paying a commission to the agent platform in channel A. In this supply chain, the manufacturer has four BT adoption strategies, i.e., adopting BT in neither channel, in either channel R or channel A, and in both channels. The profit maximization models, as Stackelberg game models, are constructed and the equilibrium solutions are obtained through backward induction, for the four strategies. The manufacturer optimal BT adoption strategies are obtained for different sales channels under different conditions by comparing the manufacturer profits among the four strategies. The following are the principal findings obtained in this study. 1) Counterintuitively, adopting BT in the e-commerce platform supply chain does not necessarily increase product demand, although it helps meet consumer needs for product information traceability. 2) Intuitively, when there is no or a small difference between the product qualities provided by the manufacturer in the two channels, a low unit BT adoption cost motivates, and a sufficiently high unit BT adoption cost dampens, the manufacturer motivation to adopt BT in both channels. Interestingly, the manufacturer will adopt BT in only one of the two channels when the unit BT adoption cost is moderate. Consequently, the manufacturer adopts BT in channel A if the commission rate charged by the agent platform is low, and in channel R otherwise. When the difference between the product qualities provided by the manufacturer to the two channels is significant, the unit BT adoption cost, the commission rate charged by the agent platform, and the product quality heterogeneity will all affect the manufacturer optimal BT adoption strategy. In addition, if the platform makes the BT adoption decision, as the unit BT adoption cost increases, the platform equilibrium BT adoption strategy evolves from adopting BT in both platforms to adopting BT in only the agent platform, and finally to adopting BT in neither platform. 3) The reselling platform with strong power has the ability to change the manufacturer BT adoption decisions in channel A under certain conditions by threatening not to share the blockchain system with the manufacturer. However, this “threat” does not work if the BT adoption cost of the reselling platform is higher than that of the manufacturer. 4) Adopting BT is more likely to improve the manufacturer profits when the proportion of product information traceability sensitivity consumers is large in the market. Future research can be conducted in two directions. First, examining the manufacturer BT adoption strategies in a hybrid e-commerce platform where the manufacturer opens different sales channels may yield some interesting results, as such a setting is also common in reality. Second, future research can explore the manufacturer optimal BT adoption strategies in differentiated distribution channels composed of a large retailer like Walmart and some small retailers like local supermarkets.

column1: Antecedents of blockchain adoption in the poultry supply chain: An extended UTAUT model
column2: Currently, blockchain adoption as an emerging technology is in its infancy in most developing countries such as Iran. However, there is a current paucity of empirical research focusing specifically on the antecedents of blockchain adoption in the context of these countries. This study aims to investigate the behavioral intention (BI) to use blockchain by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model, incorporating subjective and objective knowledge, trust in technology, and information literacy. The proposed structural model was assessed by partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using the data from 275 senior managers of Iranian poultry supply chains. The results showed that effort expectancy and performance expectancy were the most influential variables in predicting the BI to use blockchain technology, respectively. Furthermore, objective knowledge had an impact on the intention to use blockchain. However, subjective knowledge was not found to have any effect. The proposed model including the moderating effects of trust in technology and information literacy showed a higher predictive power. Trust in technology moderated the relationship between performance expectancy and behavioral intention, and information literacy moderated the relationship between technical infrastructure, as one of the facilitating conditions, and behavioral intention. The theoretical and practical implications are discussed in the paper.
column3: 6 Conclusion and limitations This study set out to identify the predictors of the intention to adopt blockchain in the food supply chain of a developing country, Iran. To accomplish this purpose, we extended the original UTAUT model by adding the constructs of knowledge, TT, and IL. The main constructs of the UTAUT model, except for FCs, had a significant effect on BI in the context of this study. Unlike SK, OBK was found to be a strong predictor of BI to use BT. Furthermore, TT and IL were considered moderators in the research model. This study contributes theoretically and practically to the relevant literature. This study suffers from two limitations that should be addressed. First, the current study clarified the relationship between TT and BI. However, future research may provide further support for this relationship by adding perceived risk to the UTAUT model. This study was conducted in the context of a developing country where blockchain is treated as a fully emerging technology. Therefore, testing the model developed by this study in the context of developed countries that have successfully implemented blockchain may provide additional implications for theory and practice.

column1: Using blockchain or not? A focal firm's blockchain strategy in the context of carbon emission reduction technology innovation
column2: Recently, blockchain has been increasingly applied to low‐carbon supply chains, enabling consumers to track production process of low‐carbon products, thereby improving brand awareness and expanding the market. However, do the operation and construction costs of blockchain come at the expense of squeezing resources originally allocated for research and development (R&D) of carbon emission reduction (CER) or reducing firms profits? Given the varying capacities of different types of firms to bear the costs of blockchain in the process of R&D of CER, this paper considers two categories of firms, superior brand firms and inferior brand firms, and studies the impact of blockchain usage on CER and profits. Research shows that the usage of blockchain is not necessarily beneficial to CER and profits enhancement. Consumers' trust and low‐carbon preference, brand awareness, blockchain operation and construction costs, and R&D difficulty of CER are key factors. Superior brand firms can improve CER level and profits through blockchain when R&D difficulty is low and consumers' trust is high or when R&D difficulty is high but consumers' low‐carbon preferences and brand awareness are high. Inferior brand firms can improve CER level and profits through blockchain when R&D difficulty is low and consumers' trust is high or when R&D difficulty is high but brand awareness is low. This study provides strategic insights for brand firms considering the usage of blockchain in their CER initiatives, highlighting the importance of aligning blockchain integration with firm‐specific characteristics and market conditions to achieve both environmental and profit objectives.
column3: The usage of blockchain for low-carbon innovation poses a dilemma for focal firms. In this paper, we explore whether a firm with a superior or inferior brand should use blockchain. We investigate the relationship between the R&D difficulty of CER, brand awareness, consumers' low-carbon preference, consumers' trust, and the construction and operation costs of blockchain. Using Stackelberg models, we analyzed the impact of superior and inferior blockchain-based brands on CER and profits of focal firms. We provide the blockchain strategy by analyzing the profits and CER in the two scenarios of superior and inferior brand firms using and not using blockchain.There are some limitations to our work. The study presents a simplified view of the complexities in the real world by focusing on the impact of blockchain on CER and profits in a market where branded low-carbon products compete with non-low-carbon alternatives, not accounting for real-world nuances of cooperation and competition in CER technology development between firms. The model's reliance on specific assumptions and parameters may not fully capture the spectrum of real-world scenarios, thus limiting the generalizability of its predictions. A significant limitation is the lack of empirical validation, which is critical for confirming the theoretical model's relevance and accuracy in practical applications. Additionally, the model may not adequately reflect the dynamic and rapidly evolving nature of blockchain technology and environmental policies, which could diminish its predictive validity over time. To expand upon the current study's findings and address its limitations, future research could explore a multi-faceted approach that includes modeling complex real-world scenarios of both competition and cooperation among firms in CER technology development. By revisiting and testing the robustness of the underlying assumptions and parameters through sensitivity analysis and simulation models, researchers could better capture the dynamic market conditions. Empirical validation is essential; hence, incorporating real-world data to calibrate the theoretical model would enhance its practical applicability and accuracy. Moreover, considering the rapid evolution of blockchain technology and environmental policies, integrating dynamic components into the model would be crucial. This would allow for the examination of adaptive firm strategies in response to technological and policy changes, thereby offering a richer, more comprehensive understanding of blockchain's impact on low-carbon innovation.

column1: You jump, I jump? Herding behavior in blockchain application platforms
column2: Blockchain technology has brought opportunities and challenges to many fields, including operations and supply chain management. Due to the innovative characteristics of decentralization, transparency, immutability, and anonymity, blockchain applications break new ground for users' decision-making in an operations environment. There is a lack of evidence regarding herding in blockchain technology in general and its potential effect on blockchain application platforms in particular. In response to this new technological phenomenon, we studied whether and how herding behaviors take place in the context of blockchain applications for operations in this research. We propose two new variables related to the operation of the blockchain application (i.e., technical assurance and decentralized management efforts) and a new variable related to user identity (i.e., identifiability). We found evidence of the existence of herding by utilizing the objective data of approximately 0.1 million transactions on a leading blockchain application platform providing self-service and collateral-based lending services. Our empirical findings also reveal that technical assurance and decentralized management efforts reduce users' herding tendencies. Moreover, we found that the higher the identifiability, the lower the users' herding tendency, and the less they are affected by technical assurance and decentralized management efforts.
column3:
5. Discussion
5.1. Key findings
By analyzing data from a collateral-based lending application on the Ethereum platform, this study investigates how herding effects occur on blockchain applications and provides several findings.
Firstly, there is indeed a herding effect in blockchain applications. Specifically, blockchain users rely on the amount of loans their peers generate to adjust borrowing decisions. When users observe that a higher amount of Sai has been generated from CDPs, they tend to set a larger debt-to-collateral ratio for their CDP, even though such imitating behavior may put their CDPs at a higher risk.
In addition, two blockchain factors that can effectively reduce users' dependence on peer behaviors are identified. One is technical assurance, which is related to the operation of a blockchain application. Another is the decentralized management efforts relating to the management of blockchain applications. These two factors can effectively reduce the perceived uncertainty of blockchain applications and thereby reduce the herding tendency. This is consistent with the findings in the operation management study that operational transparency helps foster perceptions of efforts and trust [24].
Moreover, the user's identifiability may serve as another key factor in understanding the herding behaviors in the blockchain. Rich transaction-related information in blockchain enables users to build their identities. Despite being anonymized, users with high identifiability show different decision behaviors from others and are less likely to herd. The influences of technical assurance and decentralized management efforts on herding are reduced.
5.2. Theoretical contributions
The empirical evidence supports our operationalization and contextualization of the characteristics of blockchain platforms for business operations, emphasizing the need for theoretical modeling to address herding behaviors in blockchain platforms. To date, the extant research focuses primarily on the technical aspects in lieu of the managerial and operational impacts of blockchain [37]. A scarcity of research has attempted to discover and investigate herding effects in the blockchain context. Specifically, we innovatively explored users' herding behaviors in the blockchain environment. Using objective data from Ethereum, this study expands our understanding of how people navigate uncertainty in an innovative context. Our study discovers that technical assurance and decentralized management efforts, which are two factors related to the operation and management of the blockchain application, play a key role in regulating the tendency to herd. As with any emerging technology, the innovative artifacts of blockchain technology will take time to be accepted by the crowd.
Second, we are the first to explore how the unique characteristics of blockchain technology influence users' herding behaviors. Our findings show that decentralization, transparency, immutability, and anonymity in blockchain significantly impact users' decision-making behaviors. In particular, decentralization establishes distinct data storage, function development, and operational management in blockchain applications. Additionally, transparency and immutability can guarantee the quality of information visible on blockchain applications, including the behavioral records of the predecessors and details of the platform operations. Anonymity, while concealing users' real-world identities, still powerfully impacts their decision-making in this anonymized environment due to the abundant transaction record data and the universal address used in blockchain applications.
Third, we have substantially expanded the research paradigm of herding in the context of online lending by investigating users' decisions on a collateral-based lending application. Whereas the extant research on herding in online lending has focused mainly on P2P lending [21,38], less work has shed light on collateral-based lending, which is a traditional way of lending when credit rating information is insufficient. This study is an early attempt to depart from the lender-driven P2P environment and focus on understudied borrowers. Through this new perspective, we can exploit blockchain applications to unveil and study borrowers' herding behavior in generating collateral-based loans.
5.3. Managerial implications
Our theory-driven empirical study also has several implications for practitioners. First, using transaction data from a leading blockchain application platform providing self-service and collateral-based lending services, our results provide feasible solutions to regulating the herding tendency of users and helping blockchain application practitioners establish better user relationships. Previous studies have shown that when herding dominates, people tend to discount their private information and choose to follow the behavior of others [17]. Therefore, as people gradually obtain more information through subsequent uses, they may realize they have made choices that go against their preferences [39]. Such inconsistency may lead to dissatisfaction with the platform. The empirical results show that users, influenced by the high Sai supply, tend to set higher debt-to-collateral ratios, increasing the risk of system liquidation and user dissatisfaction. Thus, the Maker Protocol must encourage users to generate their collateral-based loans carefully. The current study's findings imply that showing users more about the efforts invested in the operation and management of the application is a feasible method.
Meanwhile, MakerDAO expands acceptive collateral to include both cryptocurrency and real-world assets. This indicates that in the future, the Maker Protocol may accept supply chain invoices as collateral and provide liquidity for small and medium-sized enterprises. Although how exactly this kind of business will be carried out is still unknown, the business will inevitably impact bank-centric supply chain finance due to the benefits brought by blockchain, such as visibility and automation [3].
5.4. Limitations and further research
As an early exploration of user behaviors in the blockchain environment from an operations perspective, our research aligns with the calls for technology-disrupting operations but suffers certain inevitable limitations.
