column1: Blockchain technology and vaccine supply chain: Exploration and analysis of the adoption barriers in the Indian context
column2: The vaccine distribution system, being a bio-pharmaceutical cold chain, is a complicated and sensitive system that must be effectively managed and maintained due to its direct impact on public health. However, vaccine supply chains continue to be affected by concerns, including vaccine expiry, inclusion of counterfeit vaccines, and vaccine record fraud. The blockchain technology integrated with the Internet of Things (IoT) can create a solution for global vaccine distributions with improved trust, transparency, traceability, and data management, which will help monitor the cold chain, tackle counterfeit drugs, surveillance, and waste management. Several theoretical models for vaccine management with blockchain have recently been published, and a few pilot studies for COVID-19 vaccine management using blockchain have been started in India. Still, full-scale adoption of blockchain technology in vaccine distribution and management has yet to be achieved due to underlying barriers. This study explores the adoption barriers utilizing Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework with the help of extant literature and inputs from administrators, academics, immunization, and blockchain experts and then analyzed using the Delphi and fuzzy Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) techniques. The finding shows that the requirement of change in organizational structure and policies is the most prominent barrier, and the barrier related to requirement of large-scale IoT infrastructure and lack of technical expertise are the most impactful barriers. The theoretical contribution of this study lies in the identification and analysis of barriers that should be addressed to achieve blockchain technology adoption in the vaccine supply chain.
column3: 7 Conclusion LMICs like India have several issues with their regular immunization programs, i.e., frequent stock-outs, vaccine spoilage due to temperature variation and mishandling, huge workforce for continuous surveillance, etc.; it becomes worse when mass vaccination for pandemics as well as regular immunization programs run simultaneously. This research explores IoT and blockchain's advancement to make VSC more transparent and efficient by addressing the challenges of VSC in the Indian context. Our initial goal was to explore the BT capabilities and VSC challenges to investigate how the new technology can transform vaccine distribution. With the help of the literature and several pilot projects, it is evident that BT is an innovative solution to counter VSC problems like temperature monitoring, tracking expired products, tracing counterfeit, securing IoT devices, and surveillance and feedback systems. BT will also play a crucial role in integrating immunization-related data into Electronic Health Record (EHR) to assess the efficacy of vaccination in the long term. The full-scale implementation of BT, despite its numerous ground-breaking capabilities and theoretical underpinnings, remains a distant dream due to underlying barriers. The next objective of this study is to identify the critical barriers that are limiting full-scale BT adoption in VSC. We used the TOE framework to identify the BT adoption barriers from public healthcare, humanitarian and cold chain pharmaceutical SC, screened the most relevant barriers using the Delphi technique, and finalized the barriers using a questionnaire survey. A total of 15 barriers are selected for final analysis. The fuzzy DEMATEL technique is used to prioritize the barriers based on their prominence and impact and segregate them into cause-and-effect groups. Finally, the results are discussed with the experts. The findings show that the barriers related to organizational context are the most prominent barriers, followed by the technological and environmental barriers, which are closely related to the organization and its stakeholders. This shows the VSC in its current configuration is not equipped to harness the potential of BT fully, and it may even render the system inefficient. The policymakers and stakeholders involved in immunization programs should make a road map for making necessary changes in organizational structure and policies, strategic investment in digital infrastructure and technically skilled personnel, and a global framework for regulation, conflict management, and data security. The unique contribution of this study is twofold. Firstly, barriers have been identified and finalized by taking into account VSC features related to the public health sector, humanitarian, and cold chain pharmaceutical SC. This gave a broader perspective to the study as well as identified some of the barriers specific to vaccine distribution that were not mentioned earlier in any study. The second aspect is the analysis of the findings with the help of experts. The in-depth discussion of findings with experts extends beyond the causal relationship established by the DEMATEL technique and will help policymakers systematically address the barriers to BT adoption in VSC. 7.1 Limitations and future scope This study has a few limitations. The findings are mostly based on the VSC stakeholder's opinion on the BT and blockchain experts involved in pilot projects related to immunization programs in India. For most of the data collected during the COVID-19 pandemic, the excessive load on VSC resulted in limited expert interactions. The inclusion of more experts from different countries will give a wider perspective to this study. This study is based on India's VSC, which is well established in comparison to low-income countries' VSC. Thus, to expand this result in other countries, the inclusion of local experts is necessary. The findings of this study are based on the pairwise comparison from the experts of different fields with equal weightage; hence the result may be biased. Also, as more organizations will start adopting the BT in VSC, their opinion on the barrier will provide the opportunity for future research. The result of this study can be empirically validated using the structural equation modeling (SEM) approach as a further extension of this study.

column1: Need for speed, but how much does it cost? Unpacking the fee-speed relationship in Bitcoin transactions
column2: Abstract The growing popularity of blockchain‐based cryptocurrencies is driven by the flexibility in transaction fee offerings, among other factors. To achieve service‐level differentiation among their users, many cryptocurrencies allow users to “name your own price,” giving rise to a large variation in fee offerings and hence, variation in confirmation times. Yet, the time it takes a cryptocurrency transaction to be confirmed in the blockchain is not only affected by the fee offered, but also by the contemporaneous congestion level and the inherent randomness in the verification process. Although it is generally expected that higher fees lead to quicker confirmation, the uniqueness of the cryptocurrency setting adds important nuances to the fee‐speed relationship. Using Bitcoin—the original and most heavily used cryptocurrency by far—as our empirical context, we stylize the transaction confirmation processes, propose a theoretical framework that maps the causal path from fee to speed, and estimate this framework using Bitcoin transaction data under periods of high volatility. Our results show strong evidence for two characteristics of fee's impact: congestion dependence and tail shrinkage. Our finding that the speed acceleration effect of fee is particularly strong on the tail of the confirmation time distribution motivates a target service level approach to fee recommendation. To put this finding into practice, we develop an efficient computational procedure that helps Bitcoin users accurately estimate fees based on their confirmation delay preferences. We discuss the implications of our analyses on future cryptocurrency development and the long‐term adoption of this revolutionary technology.
column3: Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin are revolutionary technologies that offer a decentralized and anonymous way to transfer payments. Compared with traditional money transfer services, Bitcoin transactions, on average, have considerably lower fees than wire transfers and much faster speeds than ACH transfers. Furthermore, unlike wire and ACH where a fee-speed schedule is predetermined by the financial institution, Bitcoin users can name their own prices or even choose to not pay any fee at all. Such benefits, however, come with certain trade-offs such as high volatility of transaction speed and the lack of transparency in the fee-speed relationship, which are consequences of the inherent Bitcoin protocol design. In this study, we adopt a process analysis perspective to unpack this nuanced fee-speed relationship among Bitcoin transactions.8.1 Theoretical contributionsIn his editorial piece on the scope of OM discipline, Browning (2020, p. 496) argues that “Working processes need to be discovered, described, and understood before they can be improved, controlled, and prescribed. Quite a bit of work is needed merely to describe some of the important activities, practices, processes, and operating systems utilized in diverse organizations. Only then can we begin to sink our teeth into developing better theories about how best to manage them.”The blockchain technology—in particular its cryptocurrency application—is widely regarded as an Industry 4.0 era disruptive technology that will have tremendous implications on productions and operations management (Choi et al., 2022). Yet, despite its first introduction by Nakamoto (2008) over a decade ago and its growing popularity since then, questions such as how blockchain transaction confirmation process works have been scantly investigated. Our paper aims to fill this gap by providing concise descriptions on various aspects of the Bitcoin system (the cryptocurrency of interest in this paper), such as the block size limit and miner's incentive structure. We further develop a framework that maps the causal path of transaction fee's impact on transaction confirmation times. The proposed framework depicts Bitcoin as a priority queueing system with flexible fees. Accordingly, it both draws on and contributes to two longstanding OM literature streams: NYOP and congested service pricing. While prior literature suggests that the magnitude of the fee-speed relationship likely depends on the system congestion level, the exact form of and the mechanisms behind this dependence would only come to light through our framework. We compare two preliminary analyses, which demonstrate what one would do without the proposed framework, with a set of framework-based analyses. The latter produces much richer results, especially regarding how congestion dependence is captured. The simplicity and clarity of our framework should facilitate future operational analyses of cryptocurrency systems.Babich and Hilary (2020) argue that classic service OM concepts can be instrumental in analyzing Bitcoin confirmation times. Our second theoretical contribution comes from the application of one of these concepts—that is, delay announcements. As demonstrated in congested service settings such as healthcare (Dong et al., 2019) and call centers (Akşin et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2016), announcement of waiting delays has positive effects on service quality outcomes. Akin to the mechanisms that forecast delays in those settings, the computational procedure proposed in this paper allows for an estimation of the waiting (i.e., confirmation) time distribution for a given range of fees. Accordingly, it expands the prior literature on delay announcement mechanisms to a new context—that is, the Bitcoin network.8.2 Practical implicationsFrom a practical standpoint, our study should be of great interest to various Bitcoin stakeholders. The first beneficiary is regular users—that is, transaction senders. It is evident that the lack of transparency in the fee-speed relationship can lead to overpayments in transaction fees (Easley et al., 2019). The scale of these overpayments is not trivial; we estimate that a Bitcoin user, on average, pays 48% more than the minimum fee needed to receive the same service (i.e., enter the same block).22 While it is impossible to perfectly predict the future state of the network, hence the exact confirmation block, the three-step procedure proposed in this study is a stepping-stone for improving the match between senders' speed preference and the potential fees needed for confirmation. Specifically, it takes a range of transaction fees as input and computes the resulting set of confirmation time distributions. This approach has obvious advantages over the existing average-time-based fee setting alternatives (e.g., Bitcoin Core Wallet) as users can name a target service level and be recommended a fee. Considering the large and rapidly growing total amount of fees paid (over $326 million in 2020), we believe improvements in fee recommendation have substantial customer welfare ramifications.Next, enhancing transparency into the fee-speed relationship also has long-run implications for the sustainability of the Bitcoin transaction system. Recall from Section 2.3 that the Bitcoin protocol dictates minting rewards to be halved roughly every 4 years, which gradually shifts the reliance of miner incentive scheme to the transaction fee revenue. Thus, it is to miners' benefit to gain more insights into how much extra speed an increase in fee is able to produce.Last, a longstanding discussion in the Bitcoin developer community is whether the block size limit should be relaxed to improve system processing capacity. Despite its evident capacity and hence consumer welfare benefits, a larger block size also fundamentally changes the current system congestion dynamics as it disincentivizes users to pay transaction fees. This concern has been grave enough to have instigated heated debates between influential software developers in the cryptocurrency ecosystem and eventually led to the creation of new currency systems such as Bitcoin Cash (Bogart, 2017). Our fee-speed findings are important inputs for the scalability debate (Price & Williams-Grut, 2017) and should be useful for the future development of cryptocurrency functionality. Overall, we believe more operational transparency on the fee-speed relationship creates a win-win-win situation for Bitcoin users, miners, and developers—a goal that many blockchain applications strive to achieve (Choi & Luo, 2019).8.3 Limitations and future workWe caution that our results must be interpreted within the boundaries of this research. One limitation is the use of data from a single cryptocurrency system—that is, Bitcoin. While it is plausible for our findings to be applicable to other cryptocurrencies that follow the same transaction fee mechanism as the Bitcoin system (e.g., Bitcoin Cash), future research can consider the heterogeneity across systems and investigate if there exist any unique features that can alter the fee-speed relationship in different settings. A second limitation is that per protocol, the Bitcoin transaction data do not include an authentic timestamp that identifies the precise transmission time of the transaction. However, this time can be proxied using the timestamp when the transaction has been received by a major mining node in the Bitcoin network. Calculating the difference between this timestamp and the blockchain publication timestamp of the block that the transaction was included in is a common approach to estimate the confirmation time of a transaction (Easley et al., 2019; Möser & Böhme, 2015), which we also follow. Future research can consider exploring different approaches to pinpoint transmission timestamps.

column1: Blockchain-enabled traceability and producerâ€™s incentive to outsource delivery
column2: ABSTRACT Applications of the blockchain technology in supply chains have attracted extensive attention in both academia and industries. However, little research has investigated the effects of the blockchain technology on firms’ operational strategies. In this paper, we investigate the impacts of the traceability enabled by the blockchain technology on a producer’s decision whether to outsource delivery to a third-party logistics firm. We find that without the blockchain technology, the logistics firm has a moral hazard—an incentive to set the delivery quality at the lowest level even though improving the delivery quality is for free. The traceability enabled by the blockchain technology can resolve the logistics firm’s moral hazard and encourage the producer to improve the production quality. Furthermore, when the delivery is cost-efficient for the producer, the traceability enabled by the blockchain technology motivates the producer to outsource the delivery to the logistics firm; otherwise, the producer’s outsourcing decision is not affected. When quality cost is low, the blockchain technology makes the logistics firm improve its delivery quality significantly and encourages the producer to improve the production quality. When the quality cost is moderate, only under certain conditions, the blockchain technology has effects on both parties’ decisions.
column3: This paper studies the impact of the traceability enabled by the blockchain technology on a producer’s decision in outsourcing delivery to a third-party logistics firm. In a supply chain without the blockchain technology, the producer cannot identify the defectiveness occurred during the delivering process. In a supply chain with the blockchain technology, the producer is able to identify and penalise the logistic firm’s delivery failure. The producer first determines its production quality and the wholesale price contract, with anticipation of the logistics firm’s response. Then the logistics firm decides whether to accept the contract. If the logistics firm accepts the contract, it determines the delivery quality. Then the demands are met. We first investigate the situations when outsourcing decision is exogenously given. We find that in a supply chain without the blockchain technology, the logistics firm will have a moral hazard—an incentive to lower the delivery quality, even if improving the quality is for free. The producer’s optimal production quality is either at the highest level, or at a relatively low level, depending on the cost efficiency of improving the production quality. In a supply chain with the blockchain technology, the logistics firm’s moral hazard can be resolved by designing a proper contract. This is because the logistics firm is impelled to improve the delivery quality to avoid the penalisation. Meanwhile, the producer also has an incentive to improve the production quality. We further explore the endogenous outsourcing decision. We find that when delivering is cost-efficient, the traceability enabled by the blockchain technology motivates the producer to outsource the delivery to the logistics firm; when delivery is cost-inefficient, the blockchain technology cannot affect the producer’s outsourcing decision. Moreover, in most cases, the blockchain technology makes the logistics firm improve its delivery quality significantly and encourages the producer to improve the production quality. Our research enriches the analytical research about the impacts of the blockchain technology on supply chains. Our results provide one possible explanation on how the blockchain technology can benefit the product quality in supply chains. This paper has two limitations. In this paper, we assume the wholesale price is determined by the producer. In practice, a contract is often negotiated between the two parties. How to design the contract between the producer and the logistics firm with different mechanisms will be worthy of research. Another limitation is that we do not consider the impacts of the blockchain adoption on consumers’ purchasing behaviours. In this paper, we focus on the impacts of traceability on the producer’s incentive in outsourcing delivery. From the consumers’ perspective, their purchasing behaviours will not change in the short term, but will change in the long term. This is because the adoption of the blockchain technology will affect the product quality and delivery quality, as derived in this paper. When the quality of the entire supply chain changes, the customers’ willingness to purchase will change in the long term. This is a very interesting direction of future research.

column1: Applying blockchain technology to ensure compliance with sustainability standards in the PPE multi-tier supply chain
column2: Because of the Covid-19 pandemic, urgent surging demand for healthcare products such as personal protective equipment (PPE) has caused significant challenges for multi-tier supply chain management. Although a given firm may predominantly focus on an arms-length solution by targeting the first-tier supplier, the firm can still struggle with extended multi-tier suppliers it cannot choose which use unsustainable practices. One key goal is compliance across various dimensions with production, environmental and labour standards across the multi-tier supply chain, a goal that blockchain technology can be applied to manage. Based on a comprehensive literature review, this research develops a system architecture of blockchain-based multi-tier sustainable supply chain management in the PPE industry designed to identify and coordinate standards in production and social and environmental sustainability in multi-tier PPE supply chains. The architecture was validated by theoretical basis, expert opinions and technical solutions. We conclude with managerial implications for implementing blockchain technology to advance sustainable multi-tier supply chain practices.
column3: Differing standards in production, environmental and social sustainability have created tremendous challenges for PPE multi-tier supply chains and caused huge amounts of loss and waste. Blockchain technology has the potential to enable the identification, coordination, and compliance of sustainability standards in multi-tier PPE supply chains, solving this issue. Our research offers several contributions. Firstly, it develops the literature on the integration of blockchain technology and sustainable supply chain management. This is one of the first studies to apply blockchain technology to sustainable multi-tier supply chain management in the PPE industry. It explores the identification and coordination of sustainability standards compliance, thus extending the depth of research on sustainability standards. There is a need to save costs and minimise losses through specific technical solutions in a sustainable PPE industry, so this topic is significant for further research. Secondly, this is a valuable pioneer endeavour in identifying and coordinating sustainability standards in multi-tier supply chains using a blockchain-based systematic architecture. Because some PPE multi-tier supply chains involve extended-tier suppliers following different levels of sustainability standards, there are highly complicated challenges such as standards identification and coordination. The proposed blockchain-based architecture constructs a comprehensive system from which practical solutions can be developed to solve the complex multi-tier supply chain structure problems. Its powerful operability can be achieved with detailed design and implementation process for the identification and coordination of sustainability standards. Lastly, considering the long-lasting and enormous demand for PPE products in pandemics now and in the future, this research has promising, practical implications for reducing waste and loss and on achieving social and environmental sustainability by protecting human rights and the living environment. This study has its limitations. Firstly, this research merely proposes a conceptual architecture even though the blockchain system is well designed with details in the five layers. Although the validity of the system has been validated by theoretical basis, expert opinions and technical solutions, the architecture needs to be taken into practical usage to test its functions. Secondly, this research focuses on new PPE products to reduce waste and loss in healthcare, but sustainable practice should also include used healthcare products. Lastly, this research focuses mostly on PPE, and future research needs to expand to other healthcare products and sectors. Qualitative case studies can be taken to explore the designed architecture in the real practice, followed by quantitative research to test the models.

column1: Innovative platform operations with the use of technologies in the blockchain era
column2: ABSTRACT With the development of ecommerce and digital technologies, we have witnessed a boom of platform operations. Amid their strong growth prospects, it is observed that platforms have created controversial issues and challenges, which could be potentially solved by the combination of blockchain features. More and more studies exploring the implementation of blockchain in platform operations have appeared in recent years. In this paper, motivated by the industrial practices of different types of product selling and service platforms, we first conduct a holistic literature review of the most representative papers relevant to platform operations. Examining the value of different blockchain features in operations management field, we further review the related works on platform operations with blockchain technologies. Afterwards, we analyse the innovative applications and challenges in platforms such as physical and virtual product selling platforms, rental/sharing and on-demand service platforms. A future research agenda is established which lays the solid foundation for further studies on platform operations in the blockchain era.
column3: 6.1 Future research agenda After our holistic review of literature of related papers and the introduction of blockchain implementation in innovative platforms, various promising and precious topics are found to be under-explored. We propose four future research directions in the field of platform operations with technologies build upon our findings in the review. Innovative features, functions and new challenges related with blockchain implementation in platform operations: The environment of different types of platform operations is rapidly developing due to technologies in the blockchain era. Based on the literature review, we observe that applications of many new configurations and innovative platform operations have not yet been examined. For instance, as shown in Section 5 that different blockchain frameworks and features are adopted by product selling platforms, which strategy is preferred by various platforms? Since transparency improves efficiency of customs clearance and traceability helps combat with counterfeits, it would be interesting to investigate the related impacts on cross-border/e-commerce platform operations in future studies. As some platforms provide resale service, it will also be interesting to investigate how blockchain technology helps in supporting security and transparency on such platforms. Literature like Niu et al. ( Citation 2021) and Pun, Swaminathan, and Hou ( Citation 2021) can be good references. In addition, the application of smart contracts in on-demand service platforms reconfigures the centralised platform into a decentralised system and accordingly deserves deep studies. More future analysis can be conducted on controversial issues, such as privacy, copyright and high costs for adoption and error correction (Lopez and Farooq Citation 2020; Babich and Hilary Citation 2020; Choi, Feng, and Li Citation 2020a). This is especially important for the virtual product selling platforms (e.g. Apple and Microsoft). Research opportunities under the coronavirus pandemic: COVID-19 outbreak prospers e-commerce platforms to a certain extent while has mixed effects on service platforms. Contactless delivery and logistics, traceability and reliable data about product and service agents supported by blockchain implementation blunts consumers’ health-safety concerns significantly. However, as we have reviewed in Sections 3 and 4, very few articles have explored related topics. This surprising finding should drive us to explore further on the analytical analysis about innovative platform operations with blockchain under pandemic. For example, some food platforms and their suppliers have adopted blockchain technologies to foster consumers’ trust during COVID-19. It would be interesting to investigate the firms’ incentives of blockchain adoption and related influences. For the service platforms, it is also a promising research direction which explores the impacts of traceability and reliable data on the on-demand hailing/food delivery platforms. Sustainability issues: Sustainability is critically important in operations management, especially for platforms that origin from sharing economy. In the blockchain era, platforms are able to utilise the accountable information of sustainable participation to attract eco-friendly consumers. However, sustainable practices are also traced by third-parties, such as Retraced, a German blockchain traceability platform, the fashion platforms may suffer from the joint responsibility of their unreliable suppliers. The existing works that focus on sustainable operations of platform with blockchain are rare, except Choi and Luo ( Citation 2019), Bai and Sarkis ( Citation 2020), Tozanlı, Kongar, and Gupta ( Citation 2020). Incorporating sustainability concerns into platform operations with blockchain technology is an important, meaningful and interesting future research direction. Security and cryptocurrency: Though cryptocurrency is originally related with the emergence of blockchain, some governments have not been favourable to crypto-economic system. However, it is worthy to note that as the development of technologies gradually releases the security issue, more and more governments are promoting permissioned blockchains with cryptocurrency. Then, what the role of government regulation in platform operations and blockchain implementation should be, has become an interesting research question. As the application of cryptocurrency are observed in platforms that provide crowdfunding, financial and on-demand service, future studies can be conducted to deeply examine the innovative business models. In addition, promising research opportunities can be found in cross-broad e-commerce platform operations, where cryptocurrency would play a crucial role in the future. 6.2 Conclusion There is no doubt that platform operations and related technology support are crucial topics in both the OM research field and business practices. As blockchain technology has emerged as disruptive technology, it is commonly believed that blockchain implementation has a huge potential to solve the challenges and difficulties emerging amid the burgeoning of platform operations. In this paper, we review the literature on platform operations in the blockchain era. By categorising the literature into operations management in product selling platforms and service platforms, we summarise the latest research progress on platform operations, as well as some important works on blockchain in operations management. As mentioned earlier, the key benefits of different blockchain features in innovative platform operations are the major aspects being unveiled in this review article, which are under-examined in the prior review papers. This work also summarises various innovative applications of blockchain in different categories of platforms with case studies in various sectors, such as physical and virtual product selling platforms, rental/sharing service platforms, on-demand service platforms and financing platforms. An extensive future research agenda in various blockchain functions in innovative platform operations within the current context has been proposed. Overall, this paper aims at establishing useful guidance that could inspire both scholars and practitioners to better understand and identify platform operations areas in which blockchain technology could be used, and proposing current trends, challenges, and potential scope for future research opportunities around the use of blockchain for platform operations.

column1: Blockchain adoption in food supply chains: a review and implementation framework
column2: Abstract Blockchain technology has received significant attention from the food industry; however, due to the scarcity of successful Blockchain projects and sector-specific studies, a step-by-step approach for implementing Blockchain in food supply chains (FSCs) is still missing. A systematic literature review of 69 high-quality, peer-reviewed articles is utilized to capture Blockchain adoption drivers and barriers, applications, and implementation stages within FSCs. Current Blockchain issues such as scalability, regulations, privacy, and incentivization are identified as future research opportunities. Following innovation adoption theory, a three-stage conceptual framework for Blockchain implementation in FSCs is developed. The proposed framework is novel and is expected to benefit food chain managers in establishing the suitability of Blockchain for their organization and/or wider supply network. Identified influential factors, case examples, and implementation stages are expected to guide practitioners in developing a roadmap for adopting Blockchain in the food industry.
column3: While attempting to address the defined research question What is the process for implementing Blockchain in FSCs? The study synthesized four major themes: implementation pro- cess, drivers and barriers to adopting Blockchain, and current uses of Blockchain within the FSC context. It was found that organizations typically go through the process of initiation adoption implementation to assimilate the technology. Further, increasing transparency and efficiency were identi- fied as two key internal drivers for Blockchain, whereas Figure 6. Conceptual stage model for Blockchain implementation in FSC. 14 N. VU ET AL. pressure from consumers, competitors and regulatory bodies were critical external drivers. The main barriers to adoption included the privacy versus transparency dilemma, high implementation cost, the supply chain s readiness for Blockchain, and the scalability of Blockchain technology. Facilitating end-to-end traceability and strengthening food safety and quality were found as the most prominent use of Blockchain. The study makes a novel contribution to the field of supply chains in general and FSCs in particular. The study provides academically strong findings regarding the overall state of Blockchain implementation for the food supply chain and a conceptual model for implementation. Descriptive ana- lysis of selected papers shows that this research stream is still in its infancy; nonetheless, the growth has been impres- sive and is expected to advance faster in the near future. The study suggests IA theories as a legitimate approach to understanding and guiding the implementation of Blockchain. A novel, conceptual framework for implementing Blockchain in FSCs was developed using the lenses of IA the- ories. Therefore, this framework can be used as a reference by academics and practitioners in examining Blockchain use in the food industry. Some implications for companies and regulatory bodies can be drawn from this study. First, managers gain an over- view of the Blockchain development in the FSC and funda- mental understandings about the implementation activities, potential, and challenges of a Blockchain application. Moreover, although conceptual, the framework can help managers plan their implementation process, utilizing the insights provided. For policymakers, it is possible to help leverage the use of Blockchain in the FSC by eliminating regulatory inhibitors, such as the lack of legal frameworks in recognizing smart contracts and, consequently, companies can adhere better to other regulations such as food trace- ability and food safety. column1: An analysis of strategies for adopting blockchain technology in the fresh product supply chain
column2: ABSTRACT This paper investigates the strategies for adopting blockchain technology in the fresh product supply chain (FPSC) consisting of a supplier, a third-party logistics service provider (3PL) and an e-tailer. We analyse the optimal strategies of FPSC members under the benchmark scenario where the FPSC does not adopt blockchain technology and those under the three scenarios where the supplier, 3PL and e-tailer lead the construction of the blockchain-based traceability system (BTS), respectively. We find that adopting blockchain technology is not always the optimal decision for the FPSC, which is related to the consumers’ acceptance degree for the product without blockchain technology, the deterioration rate of the fresh product and the allocation proportion of traceability cost of FPSC members when adopting blockchain technology. Regardless of the power and status of each member in the FPSC, it can lead the construction of the BTS. From the perspective of whole FPSC’s profit maximisation, the leader of the FPSC should lead the construction of the BTS under the coordination of a two-part tariff contract. This study provides valuable insights for FPSCs to adopt blockchain technology.
column3: Although cold chain logistics can greatly reduce the deterioration rate of fresh products, the quality of fresh products still cannot be effectively guaranteed. Blockchain technology is an emerging traceability technology. The use of this technology cannot only provide verifiable traceability information for consumers, but also help firms monitor product quality. Thus, blockchain technology has been concerned and applied by some firms, including production firms, logistics firms and e-commerce firms. To investigate the strategies for adopting blockchain technology in the FPSC, this paper considers an FPSC consisting of a supplier, a 3PL and an e-tailer. First, we analyse the optimal strategies for FPSC members under the benchmark scenario where the FPSC does not adopt blockchain technology. Then, under the scenario where the FPSC adopts blockchain technology, we analyse the optimal strategies of FPSC members when the supplier, 3PL and e-tailer, respectively, lead the construction of the BTS. By comparing the optimal results under the two scenarios, we identify the specific conditions that the FPSC adopts blockchain technology. Furthermore, by comparing the profits of whole FPSC under Cases CB-S, CB-L and CB-R, we obtain the specific conditions that the supplier, 3PL and e-tailer, respectively, lead the construction of the BTS. Finally, we design a coordination contract for the FPSC when adopting blockchain technology. Through this study, we can summarise the key findings as follows. First, under certain conditions, adopting blockchain technology can increase the overall profit of the FPSC. The conditions are related to the consumers’ preference for traceability information, fresh product deterioration, unit production costs of the supplier and 3PL, as well as the shares of FPSC members. Second, when the share of an FPSC member (either the supplier, the 3PL or the e-tailer) meets certain conditions, the profit of whole FPSC under the case where the member leads the construction of the BTS is greater than that under the case where other two members lead the construction of the BTS. In addition, the share of construction leader is the largest under Case CB-S and is the smallest under Case CB-R. Third, no matter which FPSC member leads the construction of the BTS, the FPSC cannot achieve profit maximisation, but adopting the two-part tariff contract can improve the profits of the FPSC members under Cases CB-L and CB-R and can coordinate the FPSC under Case CB-S. From our findings, we provide several useful managerial implications. When considering whether to adopt blockchain technology or deciding the traceability level, the firms should consider consumers’ preference for the traceability information and the traceability cost borne by the leader of the BTS construction. When the firm initiating the BTS construction bears less traceability cost and consumers’ preference for traceability information is higher, the FPSC should adopt blockchain technology to obtain as much traceability information as possible. Furthermore, any firm in the FPSC can be the leader of the BTS construction, the premise is that the leader should reasonably bear a certain proportion of traceability cost, and the proportion should decrease with the decrease of his/her power position in the FPSC. Moreover, to maximise the profit of the FPSC, the two-part tariff contract can be implemented. Finally, we note some potential directions for future research. First, this study is to consider the case of linear deterministic demand. The strategic analysis of adopting blockchain technology in the FPSC under stochastic demand also needs to be concerned. Second, in the case of adopting blockchain technology, FPSC members may use the crypto-currency for transaction and settlement. Thus, it would be interesting to examine the impact of digital currency or crypto-currency on the cash flow and FPSC structure.

column1: Psychological and System-Related Barriers to Adopting Blockchain for Operations Management: An Artificial Neural Network Approach
column2: This article aims to identify the barriers to adopting blockchain for operations management (BCOM). The barriers discussed include psychological barriers [information barrier (IB), usage barrier (UB), and functional risk barrier (FRB)] and system-related barriers [security and privacy barrier (SPB), compatibility and interoperability barrier (CIB), and system quality barrier (SQB)]. Data collected from 178 responses from manufacturing firms were analyzed using artificial neural network (ANN) to capture both linear and nonlinear relationships in the proposed model that comprises of psychological and systems-related barriers and resistance to BCOM. Nonlinear relationships of the barriers toward BCOM resistance were found. This is a significant contribution as previous studies only found linear relationships. Results also revealed that FRB has the highest level of importance toward blockchain resistance, followed by UB, SPB, and IB. CIB and SQB were found to have the least importance to BCOM. In addition, the negligible values of root-mean square of error concluded that the ANN model exhibits a good model fit. This article contributes to the understanding of BCOM by integrating psychological barriers and systems-related barriers to the current conceptual model. The study also offers practical guidelines and suggestions for future research.
column3: In conclusion, this article discussed obstacles that may be present for firms intending to explore BCOM. The barriers expounded in this article included both psychological and systems-related that have been considered in different innovation resistance studies. Psychology-related issues may limit a person's perceived value from innovation, resulting in the innovation not being able to address or fulfill the needs. Blockchain is still considered an immature technology, hence there are still concerns relating to security and privacy and users may still be sceptical about the technology. Other systems-related issues include challenges of interoperability and compatibility of integration because OM involves multiple stakeholders and blockchain should not be considered as a stand-alone system. System quality is also another factor of resistance—depending on the direction of these factors, they may limit adoption and increase resistance or vice versa. This article served as fundamental to the need for managing blockchain implementation for OM. Future research may incorporate the role of digital currency and the use of cryptocurrencies in supply chain structures. In addition, the impact of blockchain on supply chain trust and governance issues such as legal and security needs to be explored [118].

column1: Sustainability standards and blockchain in agro-food supply chains: Synergies and conflicts
column2: Blockchain-based technologies have emerged as a mechanism for governing sustainability in agro-food supply chain, where voluntary sustainability standards have been the main governance mechanisms over the past decades. Despite a growing body of research on blockchain-based technologies, the relationship between these two mechanisms for supply chains remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study aims at addressing this research gap and explaining their interaction. We described and assessed 16 cases of blockchain-based technologies and voluntary sustainability standards against twelve sustainability-related assessment criteria. The results show that the relationship between blockchain-based technologies and voluntary sustainability standards can be co-existing, synergistic, and antagonistic. While most cases fall under the co-existing relationship, we identified a few cases with synergistic relationships, and one case with an antagonistic relationship. We explain each type of relation and show how the system architecture and goal of a blockchain-based technology implementation are key determinants of this relationship. This study can support stakeholders in agro-food supply chain in better understanding the application of blockchain-based technologies for sustainability governance in relation to existing voluntary sustainability standards. It can further inform those stakeholders of possibilities to constructively collaborate and focus on positive social and environmental impacts within agro-food supply chains.
column3: 5 Conclusions We described in detail 16 VSS and BBT according to twelve sustainability-related assessment criteria and analyzed how the relationship between BBT and VSS can be synergistic, co-existing, and antagonistic. While most of the cases under analysis showed a co-existing relationship between BBT and VSS, we identified a few cases of synergy when BBT cases integrate VSS, and one case of antagonism occurring when a BBT becomes an alternative to existing VSS. We further identified specific characteristics of each relationship type. BBT cases that co-exist with VSS typically focus on making supply chain data available. Some also provide access to financial services to upstream actors in the supply chain. In cases where BBT and VSS have a synergistic relationship, VSS provide measures for positive impact, established structures, and a trusted label, while BBT increase transparency and make the existing label interactive providing access to additional product information. BBT cases that are antagonistic to existing VSS set up their own sustainability measures, make the outcome data transparent, and ultimately build an alternative to VSS. While VSS have shown mixed results in terms of effectiveness of their sustainability governance, BBT have been suggested as a solution to those shortcomings. However, it is doubtful if BBT can adequately fill all these gaps as the technology brings its own challenges and does copy some existing structural issues of VSS. Our findings provide a better understanding on how BBT and VSS interact. We show what advantages and drawbacks to sustainability governance in agro-food supply chains BBT can bring compared to VSS. This can inform stakeholders of the possibilities to cooperate constructively and ultimately bring positive social and environmental impacts to agro-food supply chains. With this study, we also intend to initiate a discussion on the relationship between BBT and VSS and its effects on governance of supply chain sustainability. To verify that BBT and VSS can have synergistic, co-existing, and antagonist relationships requires additional long-term research with larger sample sizes and additional empirical data. Research should also confirm that the additional and more transparent data that BBT provide to actors within the supply chain, such as brands and consumers, will in fact lead to positive impacts. Furthermore, research should investigate if consumers having access to more product-specific data foster more informed decisions leading to more sustainable consumption. Finally, research should analyze if private companies are better at innovating than more bureaucratic organizations such as VSS.

column1: The mediating role of supply chain quality management for traceability and performance improvement: Evidence among Chinese food firms
column2: With the frequent outbreak of food safety issues, supply chain traceability (SCT), using industry 4.0 technologies such as blockchain, Internet of Things, and cloud computing for end-to-end quality monitoring, has attracted increasing attention from academia and practitioners. However, whether and how supply chain focal firms can improve both quality and economic performance through SCT practices is still unclear and lacks studies. Built on the value of SCT and from the resource dependence theory (RDT) perspective, this study hypothesizes that supply chain quality management (SCQM) practices, including supply chain-based quality strategy and leadership (SCQSL), supply chain-based process integration and management (SCPIM), and quality-oriented supply chain relationship management (QSCRM), are necessary for focal firms to improve quality and gain economic benefit through SCT. Using survey data collected from 337 food firms in China, our structural equation modeling results reveal that SCT can bring quality performance while SCQSL and SCPIM are necessarily required. SCT can improve economic performance while SCPIM is essential and SCQSL is partially necessary. Moreover, SCRM is partially needed for firms to gain both types of performances. This study contributes new theoretical insights for food firms to highlight SCQM practices in support of their traceback investigation for associated performance gains.
column3: 6 Conclusions Based on the RDT, this paper develops a conceptual model to examine whether and how food firms can improve quality and economic performance through SCT practices. Statistical results reveal that SCT practices have significantly positive effects on both quality and economic performance. Traceability alone, however, cannot accomplish these goals. This study further confirms that the effects of SCT on both types of performances are fully mediated by SCQM practices, which distinguishes our contribution from past work. More specifically, SCPIM shows full mediation effects on both performances. SCQSL has a full mediation effect on the SCT-quality performance link, whereas partial mediation effect on the SCT-economic performance link. QSCRM plays the partial mediation roles in the linkage between SCT and two types of performances. Our empirical results provide food firms with decision support on how their SCT practices can drive the improvement of quality and economic performance through the better implementation of SCQM practices. Extant literature has not explicitly shed light on how SCT is linked to food quality and economic performance. This paper contributes as one of the first studies to develop SCT practices and their consequences for Chinese food firms, which also extends studies on SCT to a typical emerging market, China. This paper draws upon the RDT to propose a comprehensive definition for SCQM considering three kinds of practices, and test the mediation roles of SCQM and its three dimensions on the relationship between SCT and both types of performance, which contributes to the literature on SCT. This study extends the broader application of RDT by substantiating the theoretical claim that SCT practices cannot improve quality and economic performance directly but rather via SCQM resulting from traceability. Since increasing food firms lack confidence in traceability adoption, our findings provide them with useful insights into how SCQM practices can support their SCT to facilitate firm performance, especially in emerging markets where traceability has still been in the initial stage. Several limitations of our study are necessary to be addressed in future research. Firstly, we identified the content of the SCT construct from seven specific measurement items, which may be subdivided into more dimensions in future work, such as input traceability and output traceability, to examine how different types of traceability practices affect firm performance. Secondly, the purpose and findings of this study are oriented to food supply chains, and it is needed to test whether our conclusions are also applicable to other industry contexts. Since product traceability can affect many sectors, especially farming, future work may extend from a food supply chain to or including agricultural supply chains. Thirdly, this study only considers the potential quality and economic performance of SCT practices in the Chinese context. The prevalent discussion on the link between traceability and performance could be further considered by researchers beyond the Chinese context. For example, future studies can be extended to more performance types to examine the value output of SCT practices, such as operational performance and technical innovation performance. Moreover, researchers could explore the mediating factors other than SCQM practices or contingency factors (moderators) affecting the relationship between SCT and firm performance.

column1: Improving sustainability in the tourism industry through blockchain technology: Challenges and opportunities
column2: The tourism industry is extremely important to the world economy; yet, the industry falls short when it comes to economic, social, and environmental issues. Blockchain as an information technology can be utilized to help solve these issues and establish sustainable tourism globally. However, the challenges to blockchain adoption in the tourism industry have not yet been examined systematically. The goal of this study, therefore, is three-fold: we first identify the challenges to blockchain using literature review and expert opinions. Then, we examine them using the proposed rough Interpretive Structural Modeling - Cross-Impact Matrix Multiplication based on expert judgments. Finally, we link these challenges to diffusion of innovation theory. The results suggest that “lack of technical maturity” and “lack of interoperability” are the most important challenges of blockchain in the tourism industry. The findings of the study support macro- and micro-level decision-making in tourism industry's prospective applications of blockchain.
column3: 6 Conclusions Tourism has numerous benefits for both visitors and residents of host communities. Yet, these positive outcomes are often accompanied by adverse social and environmental impacts. Sustainable tourism enables more ecologic viability, economic feasibility, and societal desirability and helps maximize the potential benefits of tourism, while reducing or eliminating the drawbacks. Existing research suggests that blockchain, as s disruptive technology, may have a positive impact on sustainability of various industries. However, they also suggest that despite its advantages, blockchain has certain shortcomings and challenges with respect to scalability, data security, speed, regulations, interoperability, technological immaturity and so on. To date, several studies have been conducted on the challenges of adopting blockchain in various industries. Nonetheless, no prior analysis has been performed on the challenges to blockchain adoption in order to help improve sustainable tourism performance. Consequently, in this study, the first step was to identify the challenges to blockchain adoption using both a thorough literature review and consultation with an expert group. Then, a rough ISM and MICMAC based decision framework was proposed to discover the driving and dependence powers of the challenges based on the expert data. Finally, our findings indicated that lack of technical maturity and lack of interoperability are highly significant for the success of blockchain implementation in the industry. They also indicated that blockchain implementations in the tourism industry is still at the knowledge and persuasion stages through the theory of DOI. The results will contribute to better macro- and micro-level policymaking in the tourism industry. Our findings can also be used as a benchmark - as long as country-specific peculiarities are considered. The contributions of this study are as follows: (1) To date, there have been several industries and (or) country specific studies regarding the challenges to blockchain implementation. However, no prior research has scrutinized the challenges to blockchain adoption in order to improve the sustainability performance of the tourism industry. In this study, the list of challenges to blockchain adoption was determined via both a literature analysis and expert viewpoints. (2) To date, some research has been performed to reveal associations between the challenges to blockchain adoption. However, no study has analyzed the driving and dependency powers of the challenges towards the sustainability of the tourism industry based on expert data. In this study, rough ISM-MICMAC was proposed to demonstrate the associations among blockchain adoption challenges in order to improve the sustainability of the tourism industry. (3) Blockchain adoption challenges are linked to the innovation-decision process of DOI to identify the relevant stages of blockchain adoption. (4) Managerial and policy implications of our findings were also discussed. There are certain limitations of this study, which opens up a number of research opportunities. First, this study is based on data gathered from a small number of experts. Though the number of experts included in this study is adequate to support the study's primary conclusions, we believe that expanding the number of experts would be advantageous. Thus, further research might be undertaken with a larger expert group, as well as experts from other countries. In other words, country-specific studies should be conducted through considering several peculiarities for those countries. Moreover, a similar study in a different sector that has already adopted blockchain such as finance could be conducted to see the adoption stages of blockchain according to the theory of DOI and combine it with recommendations of how the industry has overcome the challenges of blockchain adoption. This practice may provide substantial benefits of facilitating the adoption of blockchain technology in the tourism industry. In a similar vein, future research can be conducted to evaluate blockchain diffusion using methods including Technology Acceptance Model and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology. Finally, to better manage the subjectivity of expert opinions, more robust methods based on new fuzzy and rough set extensions could be applied.

column1: Tunneling the barriers of blockchain technology in remanufacturing for achieving sustainable development goals: A circular manufacturing perspective
column2: As a concern with manufacturing industries, circular economy (CE) practices — often labeled “ circular manufacturing (CM) ” — are industrial tasks through which several circular economy principles have been integrated. Among these circular manufacturing strategies, “ 3R ” (recycle, refurbish/remanufacture, and reuse/redistribute) is the key strategy that assists the manufacturing industry with closing the loop for sustainability. An effective inclusion and management of 3R lead a firm to a greater likelihood of successfully integrating CE and CM. In recent years, remanufacturing has gained greater prominence, especially with the emergence of technology, including cyber-physical systems. These technologies assist the remanufacturing firm with efficient take-back systems through tracking. However, data transferred through these technologies among value chain partners in remanufacturing are not reliable. Due to the lack of trust and transparency, value chain partners are hesitant to participate in remanufacturing supply chains. To address the limitation of technologies in remanufacturing, blockchain has been introduced to secure the data. Despite the advantages of blockchain technology, practitioners face difficulties in integrating these blockchain technologies into the remanufacturing context. Several earlier studies addressed the challenges of implementing blockchain, but no earlier studies have specifically examined remanufacturing industries, which are entirely different from forward supply chain industries. Concerning the fact, this study identifies the barriers that exist with the implementation of blockchain technology in the application of the remanufacturing sector. A framework has been proposed and validated in a Danish automotive parts remanufacturing company. Multi-criteria decision-making method has been used to identify the effective and most influential barriers among common barriers. Results reveal that “ scaling of technology ” ( B6 ) is the key barrier of BCT implementation in remanufacturing context. This study concludes with useful discussions based on the results along with the recommendations to eradicate those influential barriers and their respective impacts on SDGs (SDG4, SDG8, SDG9
column3: This study examines the application of blockchain technology in remanufacturing context for achieving circular manufacturing. Due to the existing gap on the research for blockchain implementation in remanufacturing processes under the context of CM, this study attempts to explore the barriers of BCT implementation. A model framework has been proposed and validated with the Danish context. Initially, 20 common barriers of blockchain technology implementation in remanufacturing were identified with the assistance of literature review and experts' opinions. Further, the same was used to identify the essential barriers through ranking from the replies of case decision makers. Among the initial 20, 10 barriers are finalized for analyzing the interrelationship among the identified essential barriers. Further, the influential barriers have been identified through the application of DEMATEL. The results showed that “scaling of technology” (B6), “operational challenges” (B8), and “lack of awareness on blockchain risk” (B12) are the three key barriers that demonstrate high influence among other essential barriers of BCT implementation in remanufacturing. The results were explored with both acknowledgements of scientific literature and feedback from field experts and case managers. Based on exploitation of results, useful recommendations to eradicate the influential barriers have been shared with case industry managers. With these recommendations, the industrial managers can easily identify the influential barriers and prepare strategies to address those barriers for effective BCT implementation in remanufacturing. This study serves a serious contribution at practitioner's level by bridging the theoretical knowledge with real case scenario. Despite its contributions, this study includes some limitations. The major limitation is that this study considers case study methodology; i.e., the data obtained for this study is from a single source of application which might not be perfectly applicable to other remanufacturing applications. In addition, the results might also have an impact with the basic DNA of the case company. Hence, in future research, this study can be adapted with the proposed research framework with different fields of remanufacturing applications. This study only focuses on the application of BCT in remanufacturing under the circular manufacturing. It would be fruitful to extend this study with the comparison of BCT applications in both traditional manufacturing and remanufacturing. This kind of analysis could improve the understanding of practitioners towards the importance and uniqueness of remanufacturing under CM over traditional manufacturing processes.

column1: A conceptual framework for blockchain-based sustainable supply chain and evaluating implementation barriers: A case of the tea supply chain
column2: Abstract The increasing population and income inequality in the last decades have made it necessary to focus on the concept of sustainability. In the changing world order, with economic crises, instabilities, pandemics, and social media, sustainability awareness differs significantly from past years. In addition, developing new technologies and concepts (big data, blockchain, IoT, robotic, etc.) plays a crucial role in meeting social awareness in terms of sustainability. Food sustainability is also one of the most important pillars in this concept. The integration of new technologies in agriculture and food chains will enable the current world population to use resources more efficiently and sustainably. Blockchain, one of the technologies that emerged with the arrival of Industry 4.0, is a technology that can be used effectively in many sectors. Particularly in supply chain networks, it is seen as a technology that supports the sustainability concept due to its features such as decentralization, reliability, transparency, consensus standards, and traceability. However, since blockchain is an immature and new technology, there are some challenges with integrating it into existing conventional systems. This study aims to present a conceptual framework for the integration of blockchain technology to establish a sustainable tea supply chain, define possible actions, and prioritize the possible risks that may arise in this integration process; this will be done through the Spherical Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (SF‐AHP) approach. In this context, initially, the current tea supply chain will be considered and the activities carried out will be defined in terms of technological, environmental, and strategic sustainability. Then, the design that includes the integration of all activities with blockchain technology is presented. The proposed design covers the entire tea supply chain from end to end and is considered with regard to all sustainability dimensions. In the proposed framework, barriers that may be encountered and risks that may arise at each stage of the tea supply chain process are identified; managerial implications are then presented to eliminate these risks. To enhance the use of the recommendations made, risks and barriers are prioritized with SF‐AHP management. Thus, the problems that need to be solved primarily in the technological transformation process can be evaluated more clearly. The proposed theoretical framework is expected to extend to all agricultural practices and support technological advances throughout the agricultural sector.
column3: In today's world, the tea industry has still not solved the problems related to sustainability. One of the fundamental reasons for this is the lack of technology adaptation in the tea industry. To facilitate the supply chain process, this study proposes blockchain implementation in tea supply chain processes This will result in increased productivity, better control of payment arrangements, inventory regulation and enhancing current systems. It will ensure fair trade and pricing for all stakeholders in the tea industry. By presenting a framework in this context, it has been shown that blockchain provides transparency in all tea supply chain processes and that all transactions are documented at each stage. In addition, blockchain provides data security with its unchangeable feature and offers the tea industry opportunities that are free from manipulation. In this respect, blockchain technology's implementation provides the tea industry with increased transparency, greater sustainability and scalability, improved safety and security, fair trade and price equality. Through smart contracts, blockchain technology can eliminate intermediary institutions and bureaucratic barriers. Consequently, costs related to time and paper waste are eliminated.There are some challenges to implementing blockchain technology in the traditional tea industry. These difficulties need to be eliminated to allow technological transformation to take place. Also, we see that the challenges of digitalization come in a certain hierarchy. In this study, difficulties encountered in blockchain adaptation have been prioritized using the spherical fuzzy AHP method. When the results are examined, the biggest obstacle to technology transformation with blockchain is with organizational problems. Government support and establishing tea supply chain policies have an important place in technology transformation. Also, digitalization efforts should be supported financially. Managerial implications were made based on the results obtained; various suggestions have been proposed for those top managers who direct the tea industry and the decision-makers of the main tea producing countries.In this study, the spherical fuzzy AHP method was used for weighting the criteria. In addition, methods such as VIKOR, TOPSIS, ANP, ELECTRE, which are widely used in literature, and different versions of these methods (fuzzy, probabilistic) can be applied to existing criteria. Also, existing criteria can be expanded, or new criteria can be added for different supply chain models. Integrating new technologies such as IoT, big data, and machine learning can be introduced to the blockchain-based framework we present in this study. Unlike traditional supply chain models, new mathematical models of the proposed framework (with blockchain) can be developed.

column1: FUSION - Fog Computing and Blockchain for Trusted Industrial Internet of Things
column2: The industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is currently foreseen as a foundation to implement the Industry 4.0 vision. However, device heterogeneity and the need of integration and configuration exposes the industrial infrastructure to potential threats, such as black-hole, man-in-the-middle, and malicious configuration attacks. In this article, we investigate how to manage distributed trust information and to enable trusted configuration actions in the IIoT, by opportunistically intermingling blockchain with the software defined networking and container orchestration technologies. In particular, we focus on how the joint and coordinated adoption of such technologies can make technicians’ interventions on industrial equipment both easier and more trusted. To this purpose, we present the design of a software architecture to simplify the management, configuration, and assessment of IIoT systems, and we discuss our experiences with the application of the proposed architecture in a railways use case.
column3: In this article, we presented FUSION, a software platform born with the aim to show the advantages to combine the blockchain with SDN and container-based orchestration for the trusted management of devices in the IIoT. The platform was centered around the notion of FESNs as computing nodes for trusted IIoTs that can be flexibly reconfigured to act as end devices (L0FESN) or fog/edge nodes (L1FESN). We envisioned the use of the blockchain to both manage the trust information, in a federated way, and to securely manage FESN management in terms of reconfiguration. The presented railways business case has shown how the platform can simplify and make more trusted the intervention of technicians on equipment connected to edge devices, even when those technicians do not trust one another. This is also coupled with continuous assessment, which can be used to plan preventive maintenance, on the basis of tradeoffs between costs (e.g., how often to repair) and reliability, also taking into account possible changes that can happen during the life of the system. Again, monitoring information, collected by the trusted nodes of the system, is securely stored by FESNs using the blockchain.

column1: Green investment in a sustainable supply chain: The role of blockchain and fairness
column2: We study a green investment problem of a sustainable supply chain with one manufacturer who decides whether to implement blockchain and one retailer who has emotional fairness concerns. Although blockchain adoption is costly, it can raise customers’ green sensitivity level and exempt a firm from environmental taxes. A fair-minded retailer cares about disadvantageous inequity in addition to monetary payoffs. We compare the supply chain performance with and without blockchain, each in combination with and without emotional fairness concerns. We show that the manufacturer has the incentive to adopt blockchain if the operational cost is below a certain threshold, and this threshold increases in both tax rate and the blockchain-driven increment in customers’ green sensitivity. We find that fairness can encourage blockchain implementation if and only if the blockchain-driven increment in customers’ green sensitivity level is nominal. Moreover, blockchain adoption may weaken the positive impact of fairness on the supply chain performance such as the mitigation of double marginalization and consumer welfare improvement. We also find that blockchain can encourage green investment and benefit the retailer only if the blockchain-driven increment in customers’ green sensitivity level is relatively high; that is, an “all-win” situation for the supply chain can be achieved by blockchain adoption. Extended studies on consumption-based emission taxes and blockchain setup cost are also provided.
column3: 7 Conclusion 7.1 Major findings In this study, we investigate the green product design in a sustainable supply chain in which the manufacturer decides whether to implement blockchain and the retailer can be either fair minded or not. Blockchain adoption can exempt the manufacturer from environmental taxes and encourage consumers to be more eco-conscious. The fair-minded retailer has negative utility associated with disadvantageous inequity. By investigating the two cases without and with blockchain, each in combination with and without the retailer’s fairness concerns, we obtain the manufacturer’s incentive to adopt blockchain, the impact of blockchain implementation, and the interaction between blockchain and fairness. We find that the tax rate and the blockchain-driven increment in customers’ green sensitivity level are key factors to categorize supply chain decisions. Specifically, without the adoption of blockchain, fairness can increase both the wholesale price and the selling price if the tax rate is high; however, the retailer may obtain a higher profit if the green investment is considerably costly and the tax rate is sufficiently low. Furthermore, the manufacturer will adopt blockchain if the operational cost is below a certain threshold, and this threshold increases in both tax rate and the blockchain-driven increment in customers’ green sensitivity. The retailer’s emotional fairness concern can either encourage or discourage blockchain implementation, depending on whether the blockchain-driven increment in customers’ green sensitivity level is nominal or significant. Blockchain adoption, however, may cancel out the positive impact of fairness such as the increased consumer welfare and the mitigation of double marginalization. Blockchain implementation enhances the green investment level and increases the retailer’s profit only if the blockchain-driven green sensitivity level increment is significant, in which case the supply chain achieves “all-win” by blockchain adoption. The two extension studies on consumption-based taxes and a fixed set-up cost show the robustness of this work.

column1: Critical success factors for implementing blockchain-based circular supply chain
column2: Abstract The growing importance of the circular economy has emphasised optimal utilisation of resources within the constraints of economic development and protection of the environment. Digital technologies associated with Industry 4.0, such as blockchain, facilitate the implementation of circular economy principles throughout the supply chain. However, because blockchain implementation in the supply chain is still in the early stages, real‐world examples of the blockchain‐based circular supply chains (CSCs) are limited. The principal purpose of the paper is to examine the critical success factors (CSFs) for implementing blockchain‐based CSCs. Following that, 10 CSFs are identified through a short systematic literature review, and then, the integrated fuzzy cognitive mapping and fuzzy best‐worst method (FCM‐FBWM) is implemented to examine CSFs for the blockchain‐based CSC. The study's main findings demonstrate that network collaboration is the best CSF, while the shared circular economy toolbox is counted worst of all. This research enriches the literature by identifying the CSFs for implementing blockchain‐enabled CSCs to address the lack of a suitable decision‐making framework that assists managers in comprehending how blockchain technology can be adopted in the circular economy context. Implications for theory and practice are also discussed, offering new insights into the measures necessary to ensure successful blockchain implementations in CSCs.
column3: The main objective of this research study is to investigate the CSFs for blockchain-based CSC. Even though previous research gives a full overview of blockchain-related potential and challenges in the CE, few studies concentrate on adopting the technology in CSCs, and no study has yet examined the CSF and their relative importance for blockchain-enabled CSCs. First of all, a literature study was con- ducted, and the 10 most emphasised CSFs were determined. Then, a survey was prepared to examine these found CSFs following the FCM method, and a second survey was prepared following the FBWM method following the result of the FCM method. The novelty of this study can be specified as the integrated FCM-FBWM approach. Five companies actively implementing blockchain were included in this survey assessment. Afterward, an integrated FCM- FBWM study was carried out and the best-worst criteria necessary to start FBWM study were determined with FCM, then FBWM method was applied using IBM ILOG CPLEX Optimisation Studio 12 Software by using FCM results. Unlike other pair-wise comparison methods, this approach allows fewer comparisons and more reliable and consistent findings. Moreover, FBWM can manage the ambiguity and imprecision in judgments of experts. Through FCM, we were able to include feed- back loops among the tasks. In line with the results, CSF1, that is, net- work collaboration was the best criterion, while the Shared CE Toolbox, which was CSF7, was the worst criterion. Thus, considering them one by one is vital to successfully implementing blockchain tech- nology into the CSC. The evaluation of this CSF for blockchain- enabled CSC represents a decision-making procedure.
