which impact ﬁnance and revenue. Finally, the amount
of revenue that ﬁrms receive and capital they have
access to will affect a litany of other decisions the ﬁrm
makes, including marketing and technology adoption.

column1: Financing Product Development Projects in the Blockchain Era: Initial Coin Offerings Versus Traditional Bank Loans
column2: Nowadays, supported by the blockchain technology, initial coin offering (ICO) has emerged as a way to finance projects via crowdfunding. In this article, by building stylized theoretical models, we examine the product development project financing problem under the traditional bank case (Model TBK) and ICO case (Model ICO). Under a commonly used demand function in which product quality scales the price-dependent market demand, we theoretically derive and compare the optimal pricing and quality decisions for the project under both models. We identify the feasible conditions, which govern the feasibility of each financing model. We then develop the optimal rule, in the form of an algorithm, to determine the optimal financing choice. To show the robustness of the results and test the impacts of having a different form of demand function, we examine in the extended models the case when demand function is linear-additive to both price and quality. We find that the major results derived from the main models scenario remain valid in the extended models scenario. Some interesting subtle differences between the two models are also revealed. We conclude by highlighting that the two financing modes (TBK and ICO) are very different and have a substantial impact on the optimal pricing and quality decisions as well as the start-up company's profitability.
column3: A. Concluding Remarks With the development of blockchain technology, new opportunities have opened up for financing business operations such as start-up projects with innovative products such as “high-tech services.” In this article, motivated by the importance of acquiring funding for start-up company's PDP as well as the popularity of financing via ICO and TBK loan, we built stylized theoretical models to study the optimal choice between the two financing schemes. First, in the main models scenario, under a commonly used demand function in which product quality scales the price-dependent market demand, we theoretically derived and compared the optimal pricing and quality decisions for the new product proposed by the project under both models. We analytically derived the feasibility conditions, which are critical to govern whether a financing model can be used or not. We then developed the optimal rule (i.e., Algorithm 4.1) to determine the optimal financing choice. To develop more insights and show the robustness of the result, we examined in the extended models scenario the case when the demand function is linear-additive to both selling price and product quality. Similar to the main models scenario, we well-explored the problem under the extended models scenario. We analytically showed that the major results derived from the main models scenario all remain valid in the extended models scenario. We also highlighted the situations when differences between the two modeling scenarios would arise. B. Managerial Insights From the theoretically derived results, we obtained a few major insights. Implications of these findings can also be found. We discuss them one by one in the following. Under Model TBK, it is interesting to observe that the critical factors that determine the amount of loan as well as the expected profit after launching the project basically exhibit a simple pattern as the optimal pricing and quality decisions; to be specific, they are both increasing in the expected market potential and decreasing in the market volatility as well as the traditional bank's degree of risk aversion. Moreover, when the quality investment is more expensive, the loan and the expected profit will both be lower. Moreover, a key finding is that, owing to the risk averse attitude of the bank, the start-up company in general only obtains a limited amount of financing to support its PDP. As a result, the project's profitability is not maximized. This is a major drawback behind the traditional bank financing scheme. For feasibility of using Model TBK to acquire funding, the critical factor is the market interest rate i, which must satisfy both the participation constraints of the traditional bank and the start-up company. Of course, the traditional bank's degree of risk aversion as well as the market volatility also matter a lot. This finding explains why it is commonly argued that it is very difficult for start-up companies proposing innovative products to secure funding from traditional banks. ICO hence “comes to rescue.” Under Model ICO, the analytical expressions for the optimal pricing and quality decisions, the funding that is needed to successfully launch the project, as well as the expected profit are all very similar to the ones under Model TBK. The only difference is that, under Model ICO, if the campaign is successful, the start-up company can obtain funding to optimize its profitability derived from the project via launching the ICO campaign. A critical point to note is, for the optimal setting of initial token value under the ICO, it should not be “too small.” Of course, it also depends on the “investment capacity” of the investors and hence, cannot be ridiculously huge. Thus, the value of token governs whether or not the investors are willing to invest. For the start-up company, the blockchain's related costs are critical. If it is too expensive to operate, then ICO becomes infeasible to the start-up company as it will fail to achieve its minimum expected profit requirement. In the main models scenario, comparing between Model TBK and Model ICO, we can see some major differences in terms of optimal decisions. For example, the optimal pricing decision under Model ICO is always higher than the one under Model TBK. For the optimal quality decision, it depends on the degree of risk aversion of the traditional bank. If the bank is weakly risk averse, the optimal product quality level under Model ICO is higher than the optimal quality level under Model TBK. However, if the bank is sufficiently risk averse, the optimal product quality level under Model ICO is lower than the optimal quality level under Model TBK. For the amount of funding that can be acquired, it depends on the fixed cost required to have blockchain technology to support cryptocurrency and the start-up business operations. If it is sufficiently low, the funding secured from Model ICO is lower than that from Model TBK. This is intuitive, as issuing tokens helps to collect funding to support the PDP, which actually also includes the blockchain's fixed cost. Finally, comparing between the start-up company's optimal expected profits under Model ICO and Model TBK, we can see that the interest rate plays a crucial part. If it is sufficiently high, Model TBK outperforms Model ICO; otherwise, Model ICO is the more preferred financing option if both financing options are feasible. For the detailed steps to choose the optimal financing option, Algorithm 4.1 is developed. In the extended models scenario, Model TBK-X and Model ICO-X actually have very similar results as their respective counterparts in the main models (i.e., Model TBK and Model ICO, respectively). Overall speaking, the core insights developed under the main models and extended models are highly consistent. The only exception goes to some subtle cases which exist in terms of the sizes of the optimal pricing and quality decisions between TBK and ICO under the main models scenario and the extended models scenario (see Section V-D for the details). We hence conclude that the qualitative findings of the main models, including the algorithm to determine the optimal financing decision, remain robust with respect to the demand function. C. Further Extensions and Future Research8 In our current model, the estimation for initial token value and the feasibility check of ICO have not considered the uncertainty associated with the funding requirement. If a buffer is needed, we can scale the needed amount of funding by a factor (e.g., 25% up) and this extra amount of requested funding is termed as the “investment buffer.” As the mathematics is straightforward with the addition of such a factor, we do not repeat the mathematics here. Of course, adding such an investment buffer would increase the amount of funding to be collected via ICO, which also means that the feasibility of getting the needed funding via ICO will be lower. Even though ICO is an interesting financing scheme, it is far from perfect. In the industry, people are calling for regulations of ICO to avoid cases of cheating from happening. In fact, different countries and markets have different plans. It will be interesting to examine further how different rules may affect the effectiveness and performance of ICO for financing projects in the future. Moreover, some services of ICOs can be connected to the traditional supply chains, e.g., on product design [27]. Thus, future research can be conducted to investigate this type of ICO's impacts on supply chains. Last but not least, in future studies, one may more specifically explore the ICO funding scheme with the considerations of investor behaviors in a two-stage framework. Different types of investor behaviors, such as loss aversion or risk aversion, can be considered.

column1: A renewable energy microgrids trading management platform based on permissioned blockchain
column2: This paper presents an energy trading platform based on the permissioned blockchain for managing renewable energy microgrids. To accomplish low-cost and efficient renewable energy trading, a series of automated trading processes is designed for the trading platform, including the token trading mechanism and account management mechanism. Meanwhile, we actualise set of trading processes in the trading platform using smart contract and use the Internet of Things technology to facilitate the automatic execution of trading. Besides, we devised a homomorphic encryption scheme that provides an exceptional level of privacy protection without compromising trading efficiency to better safeguard users' privacy in the trading platform. Therefore, utilising the trading management platform for renewable energy we developed can increase user participation in trading. Finally, the proposed trading management platform has been constructed and deployed utilising the permissioned blockchain Hyperledger Fabric, and the effect of the homomorphic encryption scheme and the trading process has been tested. The simulation results demonstrate the practicability of the designed renewable energy trading management platform.
column3: 6 Conclusion The development and use of renewable energy is a contemporary topic of the utmost importance for managers, given the current dire scenario of energy deficit and worsening environmental degradation. Developing and utilising renewable energy rely on building and managing a trading market for renewable energy. To construct diverse, automated, and intelligent renewable energy trading platforms, it is essential to actively adopt and integrate cutting-edge technology into energy trading platforms through the continuous development and promotion of information technology. This study aims to address energy trading's efficiency and privacy challenges under the prosumer paradigm and propose a more efficient and safe solution for creating renewable energy markets. By integrating the most recent information technology, such as blockchain and IoT, we design a trading platform for renewable energy microgrids based on permissioned blockchain. This platform builds a synergy of multiple technologies and algorithms, including the physical, communication, and blockchain layers, to achieve business logic computing and privacy security protection. In contrast to other renewable energy trading platforms, our trading platform can automate collecting data from microgrids via IoT devices and record it on the blockchain through the security encryption method of smart contracts. Simultaneously, the smart contract can also complete the fine control of microgrid equipment through IoT according to the feedback data. Consequently, compared to the existing P2P energy trading platform, the architecture of the trading platform we built improves overall automation level of the platform, thereby improving the efficiency of transactions. By combining blockchain and IoT technologies, we can overcome the limitation of using only P2P communication in existing energy trading studies, drastically reduce labour costs, and provide an intelligent renewable energy trading platform for consumers and grid managers. To improve the efficiency of renewable energy trading, we design a trading platform with an automated trading process, including a token trading mechanism and an account management mechanism. The token trading mechanism focuses on the P2P trading of renewable energy, while the account management mechanism is primarily responsible for account management. By combining these two mechanisms, our trading platform can automate renewable energy trading’ payment and settlement activities, reducing trading clearing time and delivery loss. In contrast to other trading systems, ours includes a banking institution authorised by a government agency to monitor the trading activity of the entire platform. Although banks do not participate in or interfere with users' P2P trading, each transaction in the trading platform is logged and examined by banks, providing regulators with audibility and traceability. Moreover, we use smart contracts to automate the entire trading procedure. Using Hyperledger Fabric, we construct the energy blockchain for the trading management platform and implemented the smart contracts on the peer nodes of each business. Compared to other permissionless blockchain-based trading platforms, Fabric has superior trading performance. In addition, we apply the channel isolation mechanism in deploying the blockchain network, which effectively protects the security of user data. To validate the proposed renewable energy trading platform, this study simulates the trading processing flow for renewable energy trading in the trading platform. The results of these simulations indicate that our proposed trading management platform has some viability. In addition, taking into account the limits of permissioned blockchain in securing personal privacy data, we implement a homomorphic encryption method in the trading platform to further increase the protection capability of users' private data. Using the enhanced Paillier algorithm, certain personal data of platform users are encrypted while assuring that the encrypted data can participate in a certain degree of safe computing, allowing for the addition of later-added features like third-party data services and federal learning. To validate the enhanced Paillier algorithm, the Paillier algorithm was implemented in the trading platform, and its performance was subjected to the appropriate testing. Experimentally gathered data indicates that computer hardware in practice can execute the Paillier algorithm computation process well and can achieve parallel, expedited computation of the algorithm using multicore CPUs. This enables the trading platform to acquire a very high personal private data security at a very low computing cost. Thus, our trading platform not only improves the efficiency of renewable energy trading relative to existing energy trading platforms but also effectively protects users' privacy, providing governments and communities with an energy trading solution that combines efficiency and privacy protection. Overall, the adoption of blockchain technology has reshaped the trading process and trust relationship from the underlying technology level, enhancing the transaction efficiency while altering the transaction mode. Incorporating IoT technologies enhances the intelligent automation capabilities of the trading platform. Combined with homomorphic encryption technology, it significantly enhances the trading platform's capacity to safeguard the privacy and security of user information. Through the in-depth integration of these cutting-edge technologies, an intelligent trading platform that is both efficient and secure has been built, which is essential for the further promotion of renewable energy and sustainable development. To properly maintain the standardisation and stability of the renewable energy trading market, to prudently monitor and audit the various commercial activities within the trading platform, and to enhance the fairness and legality of the platform's trading, the government must be intimately involved in the construction and development of the renewable energy trading platform. In addition, the trading platform infrastructure must be integrated with the real economy, the P2P form of the energy-sharing economy must be vigorously developed, related enterprises must be stimulated to generate more green technology innovation, the renewable energy industry chain must be expanded, and the country's global competitiveness must be enhanced. Therefore, our study appeals to more governance efforts from stakeholders and higher legal protection and platform construction from policymakers to accelerate energy transition and carbon emission reduction. This study has a number of limitations. P2P energy trading is susceptible to external factors such as environment, technology and user density, thus the problem of technology adoption will be more complicated. On the one hand, the actual power equipment will affect energy, and the transaction cannot be completed unless the equipment is linked. Energy output conditions restrict the transaction management platform's network coverage. On the other side, municipal policies also influence energy trading. The absence of government regulatory norms and the insufficient collaboration of banking institutions will diminish the credibility and effectiveness of the transaction management platform, which will have an effect on the automated transaction process. Future research will therefore focus on developing easy and nuanced trade indicators for energy trading platforms that encompass comprehensive characteristics. In addition, another potential extension for this research would be to test the proposed energy trading platform with real-world trading data, which would be more beneficial to the platform's viability and the promotion, optimization, and enhancement of technology.

column1: Client use of blockchain technology: exploring its (potential) impact on financial statement audits of Australian accounting firms
column2: PurposeThe paper reports on a study that investigated the (potential) impact of client use of blockchain technology on financial statement audits of Australian accounting firms.Design/methodology/approachData were primarily collected from semi-structured interviews with a range of stakeholders including audit partners from first- and second-tier accounting firms in Australia. The interviews focused on the perceived (potential) impact of blockchain on the stages of obtain (retain) engagement, engagement planning, risk assessment, audit evidence and reporting of financial statement audits of clients that use blockchain technology. Perceptions of changes to financial statement audits were interpreted using the logics of professionalism and commercialism.FindingsAustralian accounting firms have either obtained or considered engagements with clients with a cryptocurrency business or that use a blockchain platform although they are a small group. There is a view that blockchain technology is distinctive and therefore poses risks not encountered before in audit engagements. These risks would most likely shift how firms plan, design audit methodologies and execute financial statement audits. The study showed that the logics of professionalism and commercialism are not conflicting but instead complementary. They present both opportunities and challenges for firms to apply and develop audit expertise in an emerging area in audit.Research limitations/implicationsBeing an exploratory study, the findings are tentative. A case study of an audit engagement with a cryptocurrency business will add to a nuanced understanding of the challenges posed to financial statement audits by blockchain technology.Originality/valueThis study is novel because of its focus on the impact of an evolving technology on the stages of financial statement audits.
column3: This study's purpose was to investigate the perceived (potential) impact of client use of blockchain technology on financial statement audits of accounting firms in Australia. As such, it addressed a need for research that identifies the perceived effects of blockchain on audit practice (Schmitz and Leoni, 2019). The impact of client use of blockchain technology was identified in decisions made at the stages of an audit: obtain (or retain) engagement, engagement planning, risk assessment, audit evidence and reporting (Louwers et al., 2015). Decisions made on each stage of the audit, including expertise and the need for specialists, were analysed as to whether they reflected a professional or commercial logic. This study found that the Big 4 and non-Big 4 accounting firms in Australia have either obtained or considered engagements with clients with a cryptocurrency business. Compared to their clients in other industries, audit clients that use a blockchain platform are a minority, which reflects the experimental stage of adoption of blockchain technology in Australia (cf. DISER, 2020). Like other clients, blockchain clients are (will be) subjected to protocols applied to other potential clients in accordance with relevant auditing standards on engagement. Deciding whether to accept or retain clients involves assessing client business models, going concern issues, internal control systems, risk management protocols, quality of personnel and management capability, which are in keeping with applicable auditing standards. Accounting firms also consider whether they have the requisite expertise and the effect of accepting clients on their reputation. Firms recognize that there is a potential for clients in the blockchain technology space to grow, hence, they are acquiring and developing expertise and designing appropriate methodology. Interestingly, there is a position that auditors should develop technology skills so that they are able to wholly provide audit services and be less reliant on specialists. It was revealed that there are no accounting standards on how to account and report cryptocurrency in the financial statements. Indeed, definitive guidelines from regulatory agencies and technology standards are currently being developed. Regarding engagement planning, there are two views on how client use of blockchain technology would impact on audit methodologies. The first view is that audit methodologies will not significantly change. This is confirmed by prior research that indicates that current audit methodologies already recognize the increasingly sophisticated use of IS and technology by clients (Bedard et al., 2005). Moreover, accounting firms have a well-entrenched practice of recruiting staff with expertise in IS (Janvrin et al., 2009) and accounting staff with industry specialization (Low, 2004) to enable them to effectively audit these clients. The second view is that the use of public blockchain platforms will pose a high level of risk to audit engagements that accounting firms have not encountered before. Consequently, there are firms that are already designing custom methodology for these clients. Here, it is anticipated that there will be a shift in how accounting firms plan, design audit methodologies and execute their financial statement audits. There is a perceived specific risk relating to permissionless blockchain platforms in that there are security vulnerabilities arising from a public ecosystem with many external parties. This risk arises from current challenges in the governance of blockchain applications and the democratization of a public blockchain network. There is also a risk with classification of blockchain transactions, which have two elements. The first element is unique for clients that deal with cryptocurrency. As indicated earlier there are no accounting standards on the classification of cryptocurrency. The second element is when and how to account for the costs of developing blockchain applications as assets or expenses. Despite claims that blockchain applications relating to financial statement reporting will greatly reduce audit costs of reconciling client ledgers and verifying client accounts (ICAEW, 2018), this study found that there is a view that reliance on controls on these applications will not eliminate substantive tests. It was also perceived that substantive testing will be different with IS on blockchain platforms. This stage of the audit proved very resource-intensive for one Australian accounting firm such that a further engagement was not entered into. However, the methodology adopted meant that there was sufficient, relevant and reliable audit evidence to issue an audit report. Pointedly, the absence of a relevant accounting financial framework for cryptocurrency transactions did not deter firms to accept audit engagements with blockchain clients. It was revealed that the Big 4 firms draw on the network of knowledge and experience across the global accounting firm to carry out this sort of engagements. The analysis of audit decisions made at each stage of the audit for (potential) clients that use blockchain technology reveals that both professional and commercial logics are at play when obtaining these clients. There appears to be a commercial incentive to prepare for the growth of this type of clients by building expertise and hiring of specialists, but also professional concerns relating to auditor expertise, relevant accounting standards and firm reputation. Similarly, with audit planning and risk assessment, there are both logics at play in the decisions by some firms to design bespoke risk matrices and audit methodologies to both uphold audit standards (professional logic) and be prepared for when clientele grows (commercial logic). The stages of audit evidence and reporting reflected both professional and commercial logics with the key consideration being the application of the firm's audit expertise. This reliance on firm-generated expertise is two-faceted. The adherence to an audit methodology that tests controls and generates audit evidence to verify transactions and account balances is mainly informed by audit standards, which reflect a professional logic. However, the use of a global network of knowledge and experience on cryptocurrency transactions seems to reflect a commercial logic given the lack of an applicable financial accounting framework. Further the decision by one accounting firm not to retain a blockchain client due to prohibitive cost of the initial engagement cements a commercial logic at play. This study demonstrated that the logics of professionalism and commercialism are not necessarily in conflict in audit decisions relating to blockchain clients. They appear not to have resulted in ambiguities in decisions relating to the audit of financial statements of clients using blockchain technology. Instead, they presented as complementary opportunities for accounting firms to apply, extend and create audit expertise to a new and forthcoming type of engagement. Importantly, this study's findings are aligned with Dermarkar and Hazgui's (2020) where commercial and professional logics were observed to be closely intertwined in a symbiotic relationship. We found that they functioned in support of developing bespoke audit expertise. Accounting firms are analysing the blockchain technology and its potential and preparing themselves. This study contributes to the accounting research and professional literature in four ways. Firstly, it addressed a research need to empirically identify the perceived (potential) impact of client use of blockchain on auditing practice, particularly of auditors. These effects include changes to audit methodology, which recognizes different approaches to risk assessment for public and private blockchain applications, and the development of requisite knowledge and expertise of auditors in Australia. Secondly, our study revealed a view that will reduce auditors' reliance on specialists by developing “hybrid auditors” with technology skills. This is an intriguing view in light of studies on professional identity and work jurisdiction that showed professional insecurity and discomfort among auditors with having specialists in audit engagements. Accounting firms could explore this view further to ascertain the appetite for developing technology skills amongst their auditors and respond accordingly. Thirdly, it highlighted the continued importance of multidisciplinary practice of accounting firms that enabled the accounting firms to respond to likely disruptions to financial statement audits arising from emerging and complex technologies like blockchain. The approach to tap into the global network of knowledge and expertise by the Big 4 firms put them at an advantage of being responsive to client needs in Australia. Non-Big 4 firms which may lack support due to a less developed or non-existent global network may look to partner with technology firms to enable a proactive response to client use of emerging technologies. Finally, the study supports a thesis by Malsch and Gendron (2013) that accounting firms continually test and push the boundaries of their work jurisdiction (commercial logic) while seeking to reaffirm their traditional claims to professional legitimacy (professional logic). It echoes Dermarkar and Hazgui (2020) that nowadays commercial and professional logics are closely intertwined in a symbiotic relationship. The advent of blockchain technology presented opportunities and challenges for accounting firms to apply, develop and extend audit expertise to an emerging type of audit engagement. The study's findings are subject to limitations. The first limitation is that the audit partners who participated in the study have either limited or no experience in auditing clients that use blockchain technology, which is understandable given the experimental stage of use of blockchain in Australia. Nonetheless, they are credible informants because of their lengthy experience in auditing clients which include those heavily invest in technology for their financial accounting systems. They can provide useful insights on how financial statement audits could be impacted by blockchain. Further, as audit partners, they can influence how accounting firms respond to blockchain including how to develop expertise. A second limitation is the exploratory nature of the study. While the use of semi-structured interviews allowed identification of a range of issues in client use of blockchain technology, further research of an audit engagement with a cryptocurrency business and/or an audit client operating as a member of a blockchain will add to a nuanced understanding of blockchain's unique opportunities for and challenges to financial statement audits. Another area for further research is an examination of the views of standard-setters and regulatory agencies that issue accounting standards on cryptocurrency and governance principles applicable to blockchain's ecosystem. Overall, the impact of blockchain technology on financial statement audits has been recognized by accounting firms in Australia. Blockchain technology and its unique features are expected to impact on the conduct of financial statement audits. This project was funded by The University of Sydney Accounting Foundation through its 2018 Engaged Research Scheme. The authors thank the interviewees for this study.

column1: The disruption of blockchain in auditing â€“ a systematic literature review and an agenda for future research
column2:
Purpose - This paper presents a systematic literature review, including content and bibliometric analyses, of the impact of blockchain technology (BT) in auditing, to identify trends, research areas, and construct an agenda for future research. 
Design/methodology/approach – We include studies from 2010 to 2020 in our Structured Literature Review (SLR), using accounting journals on the Scopus database, which yielded 40 articles with blockchain and auditing at its core. 
Findings – One of the contributions of our analyses is to group the prior research, and therefore also the agenda for future research, into three main research areas: 1) Blockchain as a tool for auditing professionals to improve business information systems to save time and prevent fraud; 2) Smart contracts enabling Audit 4.0 efficiency, reporting, disclosure and transparency; 3) Cryptocurrency and Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs) as a springboard for corporate governance and new venture financing. Our findings have several important implications for practice and theory. 
Implications for research and practice – The results of our study emphasize that 1) the disruption of blockchain in auditing is in a nascent phase and there is a need for compelling empirical studies and potential for the involvement of practitioners; 2) there may be a need to reconsider audit procedures especially suited for digitalisation and BT adoption; 3) standards, guidelines, and training are required to pivot towards and confront the challenge BT will represent for auditing; and 4) there are two sides to the BT coin for auditing, enthusiasm about the potential and risk upon implementation. These practical implications can also be seen as a template for future research in a quest to align theory and practice. 
Originality/value – Our SLR facilitates the identification of research areas and implications, forming a useful baseline for practitioners, professionals and academics, as we draft the state of the art on the disruption of blockchain in auditing, highlighting how BT is changing auditing activities and traditions.

column1: Can Bitcoin be Trusted? Quantifying the economic value of blockchain transactions
column2: Bitcoin is the largest blockchain, and provides the underlying UTXO architecture used by many other cryptocurrencies. We identify an inherent bias embedded in this architecture (the Notebreaker mechanism) which forces users to ‘spend’ the entire content of a wallet address in order to make a payment, receiving ‘change’ into a unique new address. This inflates both the apparent volume transacted and network users, as well as minimizing the apparent fees of transacting. We develop an innovative Transaction Identification Methodology (TIM) to quantify the economic value of transactions from raw blockchain data. Using four different algorithms across three stages, we achieve 95% accuracy in quantifying the degree of bias in these measures. Validated across more than 430 million Bitcoin transactions involving 600 million wallet addresses, our methodology reveals that the Notebreaker mechanism inflates transaction volumes 8 times, makes the actual costs of blockchain transactions appear 3–7 times more expensive than what is commonly reported, and inflates wallet counts – a common heuristic of unique adopter counts. We provide a remediation strategy to make Bitcoin blockchain data a more accurate representation of reality, and provide a daily data set of these remediated volumes and transaction fees.
column3: 5 Conclusion We examine 600 million Bitcoin wallet addresses involving 430 million Bitcoin transactions to assess the degree to which transaction volumes, user costs and wallet addresses on the Bitcoin protocol are biased and may obscure our understanding of adoption of that particular blockchain as well as obfuscate the true costs of transacting. Our novel Transaction Identification Methodology (TIM) algorithm achieves 95% accuracy at separating ‘economic value’ from ‘security value’ to provide a more accurate representation of reality, improving decision-making and reducing material distortion of adoption measures. Our results show that the unique mechanism present in Unspent Transaction Output (UXTO) blockchains that requires users to ‘spend’ the entire contents of a wallet address in order to make a payment, and then receive ‘change’ into a unique new address significantly inflates transaction volumes, obfuscates transaction costs and overstates unique user counts. We provide these daily adjusted metrics for use by future academics in the internet appendix. Our findings highlight the danger of extrapolating adoption levels of UXTO blockchains as the inflation of transaction numbers from auto-generated wallet accounts will only increase with rising fiat value of a token (such as bitcoin), creating the appearance of user growth even if no new users exist.

column1: Permissionless and Permissioned, Technology-Focused and Business Needs-Driven: Understanding the Hybrid Opportunity in Blockchain Through a Case Study of Insolar
column2: Blockchains can be public, permissionless networks implementing novel cryptocurrency-based technology features or permissioned, interorganizational networks championed by industry consortia. Some ventures operationalize a hybrid of these two network types to enhance adoption of their blockchain platforms by broadening their base of stakeholders or facilitating interoperability between heterogeneous blockchains. In this article, we synthesize literature and industry writings to identify four hybrid blockchain architectures: hybrid blockchain approach, connected hybrid blockchain, interoperable blockchain architecture, and hard-forked blockchain for enterprise use. We then analyze these architectures along dimensions of semantic modeling support between private and public networks, data connectivity between networks, syntactic interoperability support between networks with heterogeneous codebases, governance model, and technical features. We find that hybrid blockchain ventures make trade-offs: support API's, tools, and customized development so that a codebase is useful for private and public networks or provide such support for interoperation between heterogeneous codebases. We then conduct a case study of an exemplar for a hybrid blockchain approach, the startup Insolar. We identify characteristics that have led Insolar to be idiosyncratically agile and effective in its blockchain development, which together with our architecture analysis may be timely and prescriptive as enterprises grow interested in addressing blockchain hybridity and interoperability.
column3: In this article, we conducted a multimethod qualitative study entailing document analysis and analysis of interviews with Insolar—an exemplar venture developing a hybrid blockchain approach. We developed a framework that classifies four types that fall within the notion of hybrid blockchain as 1) hybrid blockchain approach, 2) connected hybrid blockchain, 3) interoperable blockchain architecture, and 4) hard-forked blockchain for enterprise use. We then identified key exemplar ventures from each type and benchmark them along dimensions of 1) support semantic modeling between private and public networks; 2) data connectivity between networks; 3) support for syntactic interoperability between networks with heterogeneous codebases; 4) governance model; and 5) technical features. We found that there are no truly complete hybrid blockchain ventures—i.e., those that fully support private and public networks, data interoperability, and heterogeneous networks as per our criteria. Our article indicates that developing a comprehensive hybrid blockchain architecture is difficult. Technical sophistication to capably integrate two modes of consensus for use in public and private networks is required. It also means expending resources and bearing responsibility to maintain connectivity between a venture's public network and various private networks, effectively requiring managing a platform that must somehow properly incentivize a wide base of stakeholders from online service providers, enterprise customers, to cryptocurrency holders. We then examined Insolar's blockchain development process more in-depth via analysis of interviews with its managers. We found that maintaining development foci—one, a technology-focus on its public MainNet, and the other, a use case/business needs-based focus on private networks—and having a disciplined software engineering approach were key for Insolar. Moreover, we found immaturity of blockchain technology as an impediment to the business needs-base focus, and software transparency and open source software as helpful for the technology focus. We noted Insolar's willingness to pivot from developing a platform for groceries to a general platform and servicing enterprise customers, and the blockchain development background in corporate setting that its technical leads brought to a startup when that was rare to find in other such ventures. Though the path that Insolar took has been extemporaneous, we posit that its arguably idiosyncratic commitment to organizational agility has been key to arriving where it has. Recall that the challenge in interoperability initiatives has been reconciling the disconnect between technology-focused and business needs-focused approaches [25]. Insolar's experiences from taking both approaches may be useful for blockchain interoperability providers: Commit to agility as an organization, whether that is being open to thinking even more in terms of enterprise use cases and business needs or hiring more people with corporate software/blockchain development experience. Facebook explicitly took this approach in its Libra initiative [88]. Though we addressed technology maturity as a factor that provides a challenge for Insolar taking a business needs focus, we did not address other aspects such as maturity of the IT organization and its business practices as well as IT strategy. Now that we have characterized a phenomenon regarding blockchain development, researchers may draw from research models from Capability Maturity Model [8] as well as Stages Theory [89], [90] to more rigorously pose research questions. In addition, we offer an avenue for scholars to extend our findings about the positive effect of software transparency on blockchain development. Prior studies [91], [92] highlight usability, informativeness, auditability, and accessibility of development process information as several factors that can improve software transparency. Most of these factors have been developed and tested before the boom of blockchain technology. Future studies can assess the precise influence of each factor on the perceived software transparency by users in the context of hybrid blockchain initiatives and its ultimate impact on performance benchmarks. Finally, future work could further delve into the reasons for the hybrid blockchain trade-off. Inasmuch as we observed and speculated upon this phenomenon, a rationale informed from further theory development was beyond the scope of this article and constitutes an opportunity for future contribution.

column1: Overcoming the Coordination Problem in New Marketplaces via Cryptographic Tokens
column2: New platforms such as peer-to-peer marketplaces frequently face a “coordination problem” in attracting users, as potential users may be reluctant to join given the uncertainty of other users joining, and this could cause the new platform to fail. There are several mechanisms in the literature to help address this coordination problem, such as subsidies for early users and promises of refunds or buybacks if the platform fails; these mechanisms, however, are likely to favor incumbent and larger firms with established reputation and financial resources. Platform-specific tradable cryptographic tokens allow a platform such as a marketplace to trade future revenue for present revenue, which then can be used to address the coordination problem. If the new platform is capital-constrained, as is often the case for new entrants and unproven technology applications, then tokens can offer an attractive alternative. As this benefit results from the tradability of the tokens, regulators and policy makers should facilitate or at least not unduly constrain the issuance of tradable utility tokens by new platforms. There is no corresponding benefit from user anonymity, and thus no corresponding drawback from identity regulations to establish accountability.
column3:
Much of the focus on ICOs has been in the context of using their proceeds as a primary or
secondary source of funds for the development of digital platforms such as new electronic
marketplaces. Several potential sources of value can be identified in this context, including
allowing entrepreneurs to tap a source of financing outside the traditional equity or debt
channels, and the potential of a prospective platform to gauge demand for its services based
on the demand for the digital tokens it issues.
 Our paper contributes to this discussion by addressing an aspect frequently overlooked:
the ability to issue tradable digital tokens required to access platform services can be used to
help address the coordination problem in fostering adoption by potential users. It is certainly

 34

true that transferable participation rights could be issued and traded without blockchain
and cryptographic token technology; however the extraordinary reduction in the associated
frictions, as well as the increase in functionality, awareness, popularity and acceptance of
these mechanisms, has resulted in a qualitative change that makes such mechanisms practical,
and, in fact, enjoying rapid growth.
 We employ a model that focuses on the coordination aspect of digital utility tokens issued
by a new marketplace. To simplify the model we assume:

 (1) The new marketplace is already developed and thus there is no uncertainty about its
 technological risk; this is consistent with the increase in the fraction of platforms that
 have achieved “minimum viable product” (MVP) before having an ICO.

 (2) There are two periods with arrival of early and late potential users, which captures
 the dynamic nature of new marketplace adoption, and the fact that the marketplaces
 may need to subsidize early users, but, if successful, are able to enjoy economic value
 in later periods.

 (3) The potential users expected to arrive in each of the two periods, their utility from
 joining the new marketplace, and the favorability of the market towards the platform
 (captured by the focality α of adopting the platform) are common knowledge.

 (4) Potential users that acquire a token in the first period also join the marketplace; these
 users can stay for the second period as long as they keep their token or they may exit
 in the second period and trade their token.

 (5) Tokens can be efficiently traded when issued and at resale, matching demand and
 supply and thus clearing the market, which reflects the extensive infrastructure that
 supports the issuance, distribution and trading of cryptographic tokens.

 35

 We find that cryptographic utility tokens can provide a novel mechanism to help solve
the coordination problem faced by a new platform such as a new digital marketplace. This
mechanism relies on the efficient tradability and credible commitments made possible by the
underlying blockchain and/or smart contracts technologies. It works by allowing early users
to share the benefit of platform success, as they can sell their tokens at a higher price when
the platform is successful. Early users essentially acquire an equity interest in the platform
and thus become vested in its success. As a result lower incentives are needed to get early
users to adopt, reducing the cost of addressing the coordination problem.
 Our main result is that tokens allow the platform to increase its revenue in period 1 at
the cost of lower revenue in period 2 and lower total revenue. While token sales to early
adopters result in higher revenue in period 1, they are offset by loss of revenue in period 2 as
these early adopters sell their tokens to future potential users. As more early users exit when
they can sell their token, the period 2 network is smaller, and the reduced network effect is
reflected in lower total revenue for the platform. If the platform faces no financial constraints,
then traditional strategies to address the coordination problem (such as a subsidy for early
users) will lead to higher total profits.
 If, however, the platform is capital constrained, tokens provide a mechanism to avoid the
cost of subsidizing period 1 users, and thus finance the solution of the coordination problem
faced by the platform. The benefit of issuing tokens increases when the platform is viewed
by the market as more risky, or when its cost of capital is higher.
 An important aspect of tokens is the ability to make token purchases (which in the case
of platform-specific tokens correspond to adoption decisions) observable by market partic-
ipants. This transparency on the platform’s progress in recruiting participants can affect
the resulting equilibria by changing the information structure and/or the sequence of moves
in the adoption game, which in some settings can resolve the coordination problem. This
mechanism, which has been studied in the literature, is distinct from the way tokens can

 36

help overcome the coordination problem in our setting, which follows from their tradability.
 In our analysis we assumed that the platform’s decision to issue tokens did not change
the market’s perception of the platform, and thus did not affect the focality of adopting the
platform in either period. If the mere fact of issuing tokens biases the market in favor of
adopting the platform (e.g., because offering tokens in an ICO creates a favorable impression
of the platform’s likely success or is otherwise desirable), then this will provide still another
reason why tokens can facilitate platform adoption.
 Our setting was intended to simplify the analysis and emphasize the central focus of our
model, which is using tokens to address the coordination problem of potential adopters. We
explored the robustness or our results by relaxing several of our assumptions in the Appen-
dices. In Appendix C we allow for early potential adopters to have different distribution of
types than later adopters, e.g., because early adopters could be more likely to have higher
value for the services of the platform. In Appendix D we allow for the platform and the
potential users arriving in period 1 to discount the future in period 2. In Appendix E we
allow the platform to commit upfront to supply a certain quantity of tokens in the second
period, as this is possible with cryptographic tokens and might lead to different token prices
when the market clears. In Appendix F we allow for investors that may acquire tokens
with the intent to trade their tokens in the second period, rather than use them to join the
platform as such investors are common in some real-world ICOs. In Appendices G.1 and
G.2 we allow uncertainty about the size of the market in the second period, for the cases
without and with investors respectively. In Appendix H we allow the platform to restrict the
number of tokens it makes available in the first period, as that could lead to more demand
in the second period. We find that consistent with our main results, when a resale market
for tokens can be sustained, employing tokens allows the platform to increase its first period
revenue at the cost of a lower second period as well as total revenue.43
 43
 Gan, Tsoukalas and Netessine (2021) study the impact of restricting the number of tokens made available

 37

 Relaxing other aspects in our setting can lead to several extensions and variations to our
work. For example, our setting can be extended to more than two periods. Another extension
would be to allow for heterogeneity of the potential users in their focality parameter with
respect to the platform, and in their willingness to pay as a function of network size. It
would also be interesting to combine the coordination features of our model with related
work that considers the use of tokens as a means for financing the development of a platform
or to gauge the demand for its services, which would allow us to explore potential strategic
interactions. Finally, while we analyzed a model one-sided platforms, our approach can
be used to study the use of tokens in resolving the coordination problem in two-sided or
multi-sided platforms.
 Another area for future research would be to consider competing platforms. If one of the
platforms is an incumbent with an existing user base, coordination is required for existing
and new users to move to the new platform; the new platform may be able to use tokens
to facilitate its entry. In the case of competing new platforms with similar functionality,
potential users face a layered coordination problem: first, they will only want to adopt if
other users adopt, but also, due to the network effects, if they do adopt, they want to adopt
the same platform as the other users. The platforms may compete by selling their respective
tokens in the first period below the price indicated in our analysis of the monopolistic case.44
While that would seem to make tokens less profitable, with competing platforms the required
subsidies would also need to be significantly larger, so issuing tokens may still be the preferred
strategy for a platform facing a high cost of capital.

column1: On the Profitability of Selfish Blockchain Mining Under Consideration of Ruin
column2: Mining blocks on a blockchain equipped with a proof of work consensus protocol is well known to be resource consuming. A miner bears the operational cost, mainly electricity consumption and IT gear, of mining and is compensated by a capital gain when a block is discovered. This paper aims at quantifying the profitability of mining when the possible event of ruin is also considered. This is done by formulating a tractable stochastic model and using tools from applied probability and analysis, including the explicit solution of a certain type of advanced functional differential equation. The expected profit at a future time point is determined for the situation when the miner follows the protocol as well as when the miner withholds blocks. The obtained explicit expressions allow us to analyze the sensitivity with respect to the different model components and to identify conditions under which selfish mining is a strategic advantage.
column3: In this paper we proposed a risk and profitability analysis framework adapted to the profit and loss profile of blockchain miners. The surplus of the miners is modelled as a stochas- tic process akin to the risk process in insurance risk theory. In addition to studying the standard ruin probability, we have defined a value function as the expected surplus over an exponentially distributed time horizon. This assumption allowed to work out closed form expressions for the expected profit of a miner that follows the prescribed protocol, and of a miner who seeks to optimize his expected profit by withholding blocks. The explicit solutions enabled a sensitivity analysis with respect to the model parameters and ingredients, and a profitability comparison between the two types of miners. We find that mining is a business for risk lovers as large expected profits are compensated by great odds of running out of financial resources. column1: The token economy as a key driver for tourism: Entering the next phase of blockchain research
column2: Abstract This is a research note in which I briefly outline the advantages of discussing tokens in tourism research rather than referring to the rather unspecific terms “cryptocurrencies” or “blockchain”.
column3: Reporting token applications in tourism research A clear description of a token application in a tourism or hospitality application helps to sharpen the focus and to understand its main characteristics and application scenarios. For example, in a comparison study of different decentralized applications (DApps), Ozdemir et al. (2020) included brief descriptions of the tokens that were used. We suggest taking this approach one step further by explicitly addressing three questions in every token study. Table 1 provides a general framework as a starting point: a) Question 1: What is the token used for? In a first step, researchers need to clarify the functionality, role, and purpose of a particular token. In the tourism industry, tokens can be used to pay for goods and services, present access rights to hotel rooms, facilitate bookings, help to create loyalty networks among consumers, or even represent a stake in a service provider, to name just a few. b) Question 2: How does the token work? To account for the numerous differences and intricacies of blockchain implementations from an end user perspective, researchers need to specify what the token represents, how the supply is managed, and the underlying incentive system and infrastructure, which also includes the governance model. Tokens that function as money to reward travelers and build customer relationships need to be designed very differently from tokens that guarantee bookings or solutions that accelerate data flows between travelers and custom agents. c) Question 3: Why is the token applied? Finally, the hypothesized impact of the token deployment needs to be described. This includes performance gains for tourism companies, changes in consumers' behaviors and attitudes, as well as the generation of positive and negative externalities, some of which might not have even been expected. Better service levels for travelers, for example, might go hand in hand with increased privacy concerns and legal complications. Taken together, these three questions provide a solid foundation for any blockchain study in tourism and hospitality research that goes beyond treating the technology as a uniform technology having a set of presumed characteristics. This is especially true for research that has an end user perspective. From an academic perspective, tokens can rather easily be integrated in rigorous theory-based research. For example, in Transaction Cost Analysis (TCA) digital assets can represent transaction costs and in principal agency theory (PAT) tokens can take over the roles of intermediaries. The Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework provides a model for analyzing the disruptive change of tokens at different levels, while the widely popular group of theories pertaining to technology adoption and acceptance helps to better understand the underlying motives for using a particular technology, or not. In a similar manner, tokens can easily be integrated in other models, frameworks, and theories as clearly specified antecedents or consequences of technological change. Again, it is crucial that specific applications are investigated instead of asking organizations and consumers simply about blockchain or cryptocurrencies in general. Summarizing, the analysis of blockchain-based applications in tourism and hospitality on the basis of the specific token applied gives a better understanding of the underlying rationale, technology, and functionality of an application than mere reference to a “blockchain solution”. Discussing a particular token and its respective use case therefore enables a clearer comparison of blockchain solutions to facilitate an incremental tourism research agenda as well as opening up a plethora of well-defined yet novel research opportunities.

column1: Fintech as a game changer: Overview of research frontiers
column2: Technologies have spawned finance innovations since the early days of computer applications in businesses, most recently reaching the stage of disruptive innovations, such as mobile payments, cryptocurrencies, and digitization of business assets. This has led to the emerging field called financial technology or simply FinTech. In this editorial review, we first provide an overview on relevant technological, pedagogical, and managerial issues pertaining to FinTech teaching and research, with a focus on market trading, artificial intelligence, and blockchain in finance. And then we introduce the articles appearing in this special section. We hope that our discussions of potential research directions and topics in FinTech will stimulate future research in the fields of information systems and finance toward making their unique marks in the FinTech evolution and the associated business and societal innovations.
column3: Every new advancement in technology inevitablypushes forward the progress of individuals, organi-zations, economies, and societies. FinTech has dem-onstrated tremendous power in fundamentally changinghow the ?nancial market is run.With the fast development of FinTech in businessapplications, exciting research opportunities arise. Inthis editorial review, we provide an overview ofrelevant technological, pedagogical, and managerialissues concerning FinTech research and teaching. We?rst give one speci?c example of how high-frequencytrading as an application of FinTech is transformingtrading itself and discuss the recent academic worksthat deepen our understanding of this technology.Then we focus on two most important technologiesthat supercharge the FinTech revolution: blockchainand arti?cial intelligence. We review pioneering worksin these two ?elds and conclude that they are both intheir infancy. Given the immediate importance of suchtechnologies in practice, academic work in this di-rection can lead to both theoretical breakthroughs andpractical relevance. We also review top FinTech edu-cation programs and call for further collaborationbetween IS and ?nance.

column1: Evolution of shares in a proof-of-stake cryptocurrency
column2: Do the rich always get richer by investing in a cryptocurrency for which new coins are issued according to a proof-of-stake (PoS) protocol? We answer this question in the negative: Without trading, the investor shares in the cryptocurrency are martingales that converge to a well-defined limiting distribution and, hence, are stable in the long run. This result is robust to allowing trading when investors are risk neutral. Then, investors have no incentive to accumulate coins and gamble on the PoS protocol but weakly prefer not to trade. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance.
column3:
We have analyzed the evolution of investor shares in a model of a cryptocurrency for
which new coin issuance follows a PoS protocol. This problem closely parallels the
evolution of color shares in a Polya’s urn. As in that literature, the shares of coins
owned by buy-and-hold investors are bounded martingales, and therefore have a limiting
distribution. Thus, investor shares are stable in the long run. With a constant reward
normalized to one coin, the limiting share distribution for buy-and-hold investors can be
computed in closed-form: it is a Dirichlet distribution, and in the case of two investors,
a beta distribution. Further, we show that when coin rewards are not increasing too
fast, the investor shares are stable in a stricter sense: they remain fairly close to the
