column1: Integrating the REA model and multisig architecture for blockchain-based supply chain traceability: An organisational-technical approach
column2: Blockchain-enabled supply chain traceability has transitioned from a new concept into a business practice and a customer expectation across industries. This paper explores an organisational-technical approach that integrates the structured business logic of the Resource-Event-Agent (REA) model with the security and accountability of multisig blockchain architecture to enhance blockchain-enabled supply chain traceability. This approach combines (i) an identity-based multisig mechanism, and (ii) unique REA-based traceable units to coordinate supply chain actors to propose, verify and register accountable data onto blockchain networks, while adhering to structured business practices for harmonised data traceability. The novelty of this approach lies in bridging blockchain's technical capabilities with business logic to mitigate garbage in and garbage out problems in achieving reliable and structured traceability in blockchain-enabled supply chains. The organisational-technical approach was developed and implemented to demonstrate its viability through an empirical pilot study in a food supply chain scenario. This paper offers theoretical advancements by integrating the REA ontological model with a multisig architecture to establish a robust framework for structured, secure, and accountable supply chain traceability, while providing practical insights through a scalable solution for industry adoption. By aligning technical innovations with organisational practices, this work makes a significant contribution to the digital transformation of supply chain ecosystems, fostering greater transparency, security, and trust to maximise social and economic impacts. • Builds on food traceability and information processing theory to advance blockchain-based supply chain traceability. • Proposes an organisational-technical framework to implement blockchain for enhanced supply chain transparency. • Integrates the REA model with multisig blockchain architecture for robust supply chain data governance. • Improves accountability and data harmonisation by aligning multisig mechanisms with REA business logic. • Develops and validates the approach through an empirical pilot in a real-world food supply chain scenario.
column3: 7 Conclusions This study presents an innovative organisational-technical approach that integrates the Resource-Event-Agent (REA) model with multisig blockchain architecture to enhance supply chain traceability, with a specific focus on the food industry. The REA-based multisig architectural framework offers a robust solution to align organisational processes with enhanced transparency and accountability in collecting, storing, and sharing data across the supply chain through unique traceable units linked to resources, events, and agents. The empirical pilot study, conducted within a beef supply chain scenario, successfully validated the technological feasibility, operational efficiency, and organisational-technical alignment of the REA-based multisig architecture. The integration of the REA model with identity-based multisig mechanisms ensures secure, accountable, and transparent traceability data collection and processing across the supply chain, while aligning with existing organisational processes to minimise operational disruptions. Through the demonstrable effectiveness, this study lays a foundation for ongoing efforts to develop a scalable and harmonised blockchain-based supply chain solution. Despite these achievements, it is important to acknowledge the limitations of this study, which signifies the directions for future research. The implementation was limited to a small-scale beef supply chain without fully exploring the scalability and complex technological integration issues. While this pilot offers significant insights, expanding to a larger sample size and diverse supply chain contexts could provide stronger empirical support. Future research could focus on: (i) scaling and testing in more complex, multi-tier supply chains; (ii) conducting benchmark analysis against industry standards; and (iii) exploring potential incentives mechanisms, such as token rewards and reputation scores, to encourage stakeholder participation and sustained engagement ( Jeanneret Medina et al., 2024 ). Technical complexities and feasibility in integrating with existing systems and processes were not fully investigated. Future work should not overlook the challenges faced in integrating blockchain with existing systems (e.g., IoT/RFID), including data synchronization issues and sensor reliability, which hinders practical applications. Great efforts are also highly needed to integrate data ownership and valorisation into the solution to enhance its economic and social value ( Bonvino and Giorgino, 2024 ). In addition, the status of product records is labelled as multi-verified, but without elaborating who are involved in the verification process. Future work will enable consumers to verify which stakeholders (e.g., producers, transporters) participated in the multi-signature validation process so as to strengthen accountability claims. Finally, this study focused on business-oriented architecture and user interfaces without exploring the consumer interface and traceability information access by consumers. Future research priority areas could include (i) designing and implementing consumer-faced user interfaces that accommodate NFC or QR codes, and (iii) evaluating the perceived value and accessibility of food traceability data by consumers. The development of consumer interfaces – particularly those leveraging QR codes – can significantly enhance access to verified provenance information and validation events, thereby empowering consumers to make more informed purchasing decisions.

column1: Does what happens on-chain stays on-chain? The dynamics of blockchain token transactions and prices
column2: Cryptoassets, particularly tokens, have garnered investor interest due to high returns, yet comprehensive studies examining on-chain transaction data to assess their intrinsic value remain limited. This study addresses this gap by introducing new on-chain transaction-based measures of token usage, crypto-exchange supply pressures, and aggregate transaction intention (trading versus usage/holding). Using over 180 million records of Ethereum-based-tokens’ transaction data, we categorize on-chain transactions as peer-to-peer usage or crypto-exchange-related. Our findings show that while increased token usage intensity, whether through peer-to-peer or exchange transactions, positively correlates with higher token returns, imbalances in exchange flows have the opposite effect. Specifically, increased token inflows to exchanges signal potential supply pressure and increased token deposits signal aggregate intention to trade, both contributing to price declines. This research underscores on-chain data as a reliable economic signal and its impact on token valuations.
column3: 5 Conclusion This study contributes to the growing body of literature on crypto-asset markets by introducing novel proxies for measuring real token usage intensity, CeDex token flow imbalance and aggregate intentions, and analysing their impact on token returns. By distinguishing between token use transactions and trading −related transactions, our approach offers fresh insights into how user behaviour influences token valuations. This separation allows us to empirically examine token usage within its ecosystem, shifting the focus from token adoption as a network effect to the actual functional use of tokens—a perspective previously unexplored in crypto-asset research. Our findings indicate that both token usage intensity and exchange-related transactions are correlated with token returns. This suggests that investors are concerned with the adoption, usage and network dynamics of tokens, as well as supply imbalances and aggregate transaction intention measures inferred from transaction activities involving CeDexs. These results offer important implications for investors and market participants. For investors, the findings underscore the relevance of monitoring exchange activity, as it appears to capture supply–demand imbalances and shift in aggregate intentions, which affect token pricing. Additionally, our analysis suggests that on-chain transaction data can serve as a reliable economic signal in assessing market conditions, providing a more direct indicator of users’ intentions than traditional measures related to market sentiment such search engine queries or social media activity. For market regulators, the results emphasize the need to understand how on-chain data reflects underlying market dynamics, offering potential tools for monitoring liquidity and aggregate intentions in token markets. A key limitation of our study is that our dataset ends in 2021. While this period already encompasses more than 180 million Ethereum-based token transactions, it does not capture the most recent structural developments in the digital token ecosystem, such as the increased participation of institutional investors. However, we do not expect these shifts to fundamentally alter the core behavioral patterns we document; if anything, they may reinforce the tendency of investors to observe and follow the actions of others. Future research could build on our findings by incorporating more recent data and explicitly examining how different types of market participants—retail versus institutional—contribute to these dynamics. Expanding the analysis to other blockchain ecosystems and cryptoasset types could further illuminate the unique drivers of value in different segments of the crypto market. Additionally, future studies could explore the relationship between other forms of on-chain activity, such as staking and governance participation, potentially offering a more comprehensive perspective on the diverse functions of blockchain assets. Finally, our methodology of using on-chain transactional data as a market liquidity and aggregate intention measure could serve as a foundation for the development of new tools and metrics that enhance market transparency and investor decision-making in the rapidly evolving field of token markets. *For their helpful comments, we are grateful to participants at the 5th Cryptocurrency Research Conference 2022,XXX and the 7th Cryptocurrency Research Conference 2024. column1: Decentralization, Blockchain, Artificial Intelligence (AI): Challenges and Opportunities
column2: New technologies like blockchain allow firms to decentralize core functions, forcing managers to reconsider the trade‐off between closed, proprietary control and open strategies that involve external contributors. While proponents often advocate for full decentralization, we argue this view overlooks important economic trade‐offs. We propose that the better strategy is selective decentralization: a disciplined approach to choosing where to centralize for efficiency and where to decentralize for innovation. We propose a three‐level framework—Infrastructure, Decision‐Making, and Operational Control—to guide this choice, helping managers analyze the specific costs and benefits at each layer. We apply this framework to the strategic adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), where the technology's powerful pull toward centralization provides a stark test case. Our analysis shows that an “open source AI” strategy—decentralizing operations to foster innovation while keeping infrastructure centralized for efficiency—is more pragmatic than full decentralization. Selective decentralization therefore emerges as a key managerial capability for capturing blockchain's benefits without sacrificing scale efficiencies.
column3: In an era of rapid technological change, managers must move beyond a simple binary choice between centralization and decentralization. We argue that the critical capability is selective decentralization, and we introduce a three-level framework—Infrastructure, Decision-Making, and Operational Control—to provide a structured approach for making this strategic choice.We illustrated the power of this framework through the conceptual application of AI adoption. This central case shows that a “one-size-fits-all” approach is flawed. Our analysis suggests that while full decentralization at the Infrastructure level is often impractical, the most powerful strategy is to decentralize at the Operational level. This “open source AI” strategy allows a firm to transform its tools into an ecosystem for innovation, driving long-term competitive advantage.Our analysis yields several critical lessons for managers. The first is to reframe technologies like blockchain not as products, but as tools for implementing selective decentralization, using our framework to diagnose where centralization is most costly. The second, drawn from our AI analysis, is to align the decentralization strategy with specific goals: using it to build trust at the Decision-Making level or, most powerfully, to catalyze an entire innovation ecosystem at the Operational level. Finally, managers must recognize that these are context-dependent choices, not universal mandates; the framework is a guide for structured thinking, not a single answer.The ultimate lesson is to view decentralization not as a technological mandate, but as a core strategic capability. The ability to diagnose where centralization creates risk or stifles innovation, and to then apply decentralizing tools in a targeted manner, is essential for navigating the modern technological landscape. This mindset allows a firm to move beyond being a mere user of technology and to become a leader of an innovation ecosystem.For future research, it will be fruitful to empirically investigate how firms are making these choices in practice and the resulting performance implications. Additionally, further conceptual work is needed to refine the hybrid governance models required for systems that blend centralized and decentralized control.

column1: A primer on oracle economics
column2: Oracle nodes enable smart contracts to access off-chain and cross-chain data, thus bridging information among digital networks and with the real economy. However, reliance on external input creates security and reliability risks in information aggregation and transfer. We describe the general oracle problem, introduce the Oracle Trilemma – highlighting the trade-offs between scalability, decentralization, and truthfulness – and discuss relevant economic issues concerning the role of oracles in applications such as DeFi, supply chain management, gaming, and prediction markets. In particular, we survey off-chain reporting, off-equilibrium alerting, and dynamic incentive design as promising approaches to resolving the trilemma. We further list oracle vulnerabilities and evaluate oracle sustainability through staking and tokenomics programs. Finally, we highlight empirical studies on how oracle integration affects DeFi adoption, token valuation, liquidity, and system risks. We conclude by presenting emerging trends and suggesting open research questions.
column3: 6 Conclusion This article systematically overviews the institutional foundations, economic mechanisms, and technical challenges underlying blockchain oracles. We introduce the Oracle Trilemma , highlighting the inherent tension among decentralization, truthfulness, and scalability, and show how partial solutions – such as off-chain reporting, off-equilibrium incentives, and dynamic reputation systems – mitigate but do not fully resolve this challenge. A comprehensive review of oracle vulnerabilities and empirical evidence demonstrates their critical role in blockchain interoperability, DeFi growth, real-world asset tokenization, etc. Our analysis shows that proper tokenomics and incentive design (e.g., staking protocols) can help sustain oracle networks by aligning participant incentives while balancing security trade-offs. Looking ahead, we outline promising directions for both scholarly research and industrial development, alongside expanding applications in DeFi, prediction markets, and beyond. Resolving the Oracle Trilemma. The Oracle Trilemma remains the primary challenge. Although current approaches achieve partial decentralization through committee-based validation or hybrid models, these solutions often sacrifice scalability or rely on centralized verification. Future research should prioritize developing recursive incentive mechanisms that preserve truthfulness in scalable systems, such as stake-weighted aggregation paired with sliding reputation windows. Cross-chain coordination protocols could standardize oracle consensus across heterogeneous ledgers, while formal verification frameworks should establish provable bounds for the accuracy of aggregation under adversarial conditions. Full decentralization may not be the ultimate objective; hybrid architectures that combine centralized and decentralized elements could better balance speed, cost, and security. In addition, exploring effective and robust governance models is essential to resolving the Oracle Trilemma and shaping a long-term sustainable governance structure.

column1: Bayesian Mechanism Design for Blockchain Transaction Fee Allocation
column2: Reliable Blockchain Transaction Fee Mechanisms with Revenue Guarantees In the paper “Bayesian Mechanism Design for Blockchain Transaction Fee Allocation” by Xi Chen, David Simchi-Levi, Zishuo Zhao, and Yuan Zhou, the authors address the critical challenge of designing reliable blockchain transaction fee mechanisms (TFMs) that ensure truthfulness, collusion-proofness, and desirable miner revenues. By proposing an innovative “auxiliary mechanism method,” the authors establish connections between Bayesian Nash Incentive Compatible (BNIC) and Dominant Strategy Incentive Compatible (DSIC) mechanisms through an “auxiliary-variation decomposition.” This breakthrough allows the proposed mechanism to bypass previous limitations in TFM design via the Bayesian game setting, achieving constant-ratio approximations of optimal miner revenues while providing strong incentive guarantees. The research not only advances the theoretical understanding of blockchain fee mechanisms but also demonstrates the potential versatility of the auxiliary mechanism method for designing and optimizing BNIC mechanisms across broader applications. This work represents a significant contribution to both blockchain economics and mechanism design, offering a pathway toward more reliable and efficient blockchain ecosystems.

column1: Proof-of-Work versus Proof-of-Stake: A Comparative Economic Analysis
column2: We develop an economic model to compare equilibrium security of Proof-of-Work (PoW) versus Proof-of-Stake (PoS) blockchains. We derive general conditions to determine when PoW blockchains are more secure than otherwise equivalent PoS blockchains and vice versa. Applying real-world parameter values to these conditions, we demonstrate that PoS blockchains are more secure than otherwise equivalent PoW blockchains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that PoS’s security advantage over PoW is particularly salient for high-scale blockchains. (JEL G0, O3)
column3:
In this paper we study the equilibrium relationship among blockchain scale, security, and adoption. Of particular note, we derive a condition to demonstrate the trade-off between PoW and PoS blockchain security. Notably, we clarify that, under current real-world conditions, PoS blockchains are likely to be more secure than PoW blockchains.

It is important to understand that our work is fundamental to the modern blockchain literature that focuses on tokenomics (see, e.g., Cong, Li, and Wang 2021; Gan, Tsoukalas, and Netessine 2021a; Gan, Tsoukalas, and Netessine 2021b; Goldstein, Gupta, and Sverchkov 2023; Mayer 2022) and Decentralized Finance (see, e.g., Lehar and Parlour 2025; Capponi and Jia 2022; Hasbrouck, Rivera, and Saleh 2022; John, Kogan, and Saleh 2023). In more detail, the ability for smart contracts and decentralized applications to operate as specified presumes that the blockchain is not disrupted. In turn, our paper provides a foundational economic framework to understand whether the welfare effects studied by the tokenomics and decentralized finance literature can actually be realized.

column1: How do circular economy and blockchain technology adoption relate to firm financial performance?
column2: Environmental challenges and increasing resource consumption may be mitigated through organizational circular economy (CE) practices. Implementing CE practices requires organizations to rethink, develop, and implement new initiatives and processes. It has been argued that blockchain technology (BCT) can support corporate and supply chain CE practices. However, empirical evidence on whether BCT adoption can complement corporate CE practices when considering firm financial performance is virtually non-existent. Using the resource-based view and a dataset of 1766 firm-year observations of Chinese listed companies, we investigate the relationship between corporate CE practices and financial performance, as well as the moderating effect of BCT adoption. Initial findings reveal a significantly positive relationship between corporate CE practices and financial performance. However, counterintuitively, BCT adoption not only directly negatively relates to firm financial performance but also weakens the positive relationship between CE practices and financial performance. Further analysis found that these direct and indirect negative effects of BCT adoption are only observed in resource-constrained firms, supporting our argument from a resource scarcity perspective. This study provides new insights into the nuanced relationship among CE practices, BCT adoption, and financial performance from the resource-based view. These insights provide new and valuable guidance for researchers and practitioners.
column3: 6 Conclusion This study investigated the relationship between corporate CE practices and firm financial performance, as well as the moderating role of BCT adoption by using a dataset of 1766 firm-year observations of Chinese listed companies. The key findings of this study include: (1) Corporate CE practices are positively associated with firm financial performance (measured by firm ROA and Tobin's Q), however, (2) BCT adoption not only has a negative relationship to firm financial performance but also significantly weakens the positive relationship between CE practices and financial performance; (3) the negative effects of BCT adoption, both direct and indirect, are only observed in resource-constrained firms (smaller firms). The findings of this study offer valuable implications for informing future research and practical applications in this field. This study also has some limitations that need further exploration. First, the sample is limited to Chinese listed companies, thus lacking empirical evidence on the relationship between CE practices, BCT adoption, and financial performance in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Given the potential significance of this relationship for resource-constrained firms, future research should aim to broaden the scope to include a wider range of firm sizes. Second, the generalizability of our findings to other countries and regions may be limited. Future research should seek to validate these results across diverse geographical and institutional settings to assess their broader applicability. There are also significant nuances and differences in CE and BCT definitions and adoption levels. A careful examination of various CE practices and BCT capabilities and their relationship with corporate financial performance is necessary. These multiple levels of resources and capabilities can provide much needed further insights as CE practices and BCT capabilities evolve and mature.

column1: What determines Bitcoin's price over the past decade?
column2: We employ a novel three-stage analysis method of ICEEMDAN-Van der Waerden Test-Elastic Net to analyze Bitcoin's price. Our research aims to explain how Bitcoin's price has been formed at different phases of development over the past decade. We have segmented the daily closing price of Bitcoin from November 1, 2013, to December 31, 2023, into five phases, utilizing the ICEEMDAN method to decompose them into intrinsic mode functions, followed by the reconstruction of high-frequency, low-frequency, and trend curves using the Van der Waerden Test. With Elastic Net, we identify the top ten factors impacting the high-frequency, low-frequency, and trend curves during each phase. Our findings reveal a strong correlation between the high-frequency curve, investor sentiment, and daily transaction frequency in the Bitcoin market. The significant rises and falls in the low-frequency curve correspond to important events in the Bitcoin market or global political and economic occurrences. The trend curve is decisive in determining the long-term trajectory of Bitcoin's price. Over the long term, our analysis indicates that Bitcoin's price is influenced predominantly by macroeconomic fundamentals and market vitality. Bitcoin's price is evolving, shifting from focusing on its internal production factors to relying more on external macroeconomic factors. Of the major asset classes, Bitcoin's correlation with stocks has grown the most significantly. Due to Bitcoin's increasing market vitality and the decrease in Bitcoin's issuance speed changing the supply-demand dynamics, Bitcoin's price is on an upward trajectory in the long term. Furthermore, our findings provide insights into Bitcoin's speculative and safe-haven properties. Our work also facilitates more accurate predictions of Bitcoin's future prices.
column3: 5.6 A summary of the five phases Overall weights offer a more direct approach to analyzing the changing influence of various factors on Bitcoin's price. Employing Elastic Net regression coefficients, we calculated overall weights of the five categories across the five phases: Factors of Macroeconomic Environment, Factors of Bitcoin Market Conditions, Factors of Bitcoin's Production and Transaction, Factors of Bitcoin's Supply-demand Dynamics, and Factors of Global Geopolitical Risks. Fig. 8 depicts the evolution of these overall weights across different phases. We observe an upward trend in the overall weights of Factors of Macroeconomic Environment, suggesting a strengthening link between Bitcoin and other financial assets such as stocks, currencies, and commodities. This indicates that macroeconomic environment is exerting a growing influence on Bitcoin's price, making it increasingly susceptible to economic fundamentals. While the overall weights of Factors of Bitcoin Market Conditions initially declined, they subsequently stabilized around a consistent value, signifying their enduring impact on Bitcoin's price. Conversely, the overall weights of Factors of Bitcoin's production and Transaction have steadily decreased, indicating that while these factors were initially critical to Bitcoin's pricing, their influence is diminishing. Factors of Bitcoin's Supply-demand Dynamics exerted a significant impact on Bitcoin's pricing during the COVID-19 Period. The influence of Factors of Global Geopolitical Risks on Bitcoin's price remains generally low. Fig. 9 delves into the overall weight changes within Factors of Macroeconomic Environment, focusing on its three subcategories: Factors of Stock Markets, Factors of Exchange Rates, and Factors of Commodity Markets. Notably, the sustained growth in the overall weights of this category is primarily driven by the increasing overall weights of Factors of Stock Markets. This signifies that the interconnectedness of Bitcoin market to stock markets is strengthening faster than its interconnectedness to other financial markets. The speculative or safe-haven nature of Bitcoin has changed as the market has evolved through different phases. In the Early Stage, despite some people considering Bitcoin a safe-haven asset following the Cyprus financial crisis, Bitcoin did not exhibit clear characteristics of a safe-haven asset. After its price exceeded $1000, it quickly fell. At this phase, Bitcoin's price was largely influenced by factors such as Bitcoin production and trading dynamics, as well as market conditions (such as market sentiment), and had low correlation with other financial assets. Therefore, Bitcoin in this phase displayed traits of a speculative asset. During the Burst and Developing phases, investor sentiment fluctuated significantly—initially rising sharply, catalyzed by the launch of Bitcoin futures by CBOE and CME in December 2017, and later dipping, influenced by the November 2018 Bitcoin Cash split into Bitcoin Cash ABC and Bitcoin Cash SV. After peaking at the end of 2017, Bitcoin's price rapidly dropped into a prolonged bear market that lasted over a year. Although Bitcoin's connection with the broader macro-financial environment strengthened during this period, it did not exhibit clear safe-haven characteristics and remained a speculative asset driven by short-term investor sentiment. In the COVID-19 Period, despite the rapid surge in Bitcoin's price in the first half of 2021, catalyzed by Elon Musk's strong interest in Bitcoin (which sparked similar strong interest from other investors), Bitcoin maintained a bull market throughout the pandemic. In this phase, Bitcoin could be viewed as a new emerging asset with both speculative and safe-haven properties. In the Post-COVID-19 Period, Bitcoin's correlation with the broader macro-financial environment continued to strengthen. During this phase, Bitcoin is often viewed as a tool for diversifying financial investment risks.

column1: Cross-channel influence of blockchain technology on green supply chains under asymmetric retail platform competition
column2: As consumer demand for eco-friendly products continues to grow, manufacturers are increasingly driven to enhance product greenness and disclose this information. Blockchain technology emerges as a pivotal enabler, facilitating credible communication of manufacturers’ sustainability efforts to consumers through retail platforms and influencing supply chain decisions concerning sustainability, pricing, and blockchain adoption. While existing research has extensively examined the positive moderating effect of blockchain technology on consumers’ perceived value of product greenness in retail competition or green supply chain contexts, there remains a significant gap regarding its cross-channel influence in situations of information disclosure asymmetry across retail platforms. To address this gap, we investigate the interactive dynamics of a green supply chain under asymmetric platform competition, where the incumbent platform offers blockchain services while the new platform does not. Our findings indicate that the manufacturer’s decision to adopt blockchain depends significantly on market conditions. Notably, the manufacturer’s inclination towards blockchain adoption widens for a broader range of blockchain costs when the cross-channel influence is pronounced. Moreover, the alignment of the manufacturer’s blockchain adoption strategy with the incumbent platform’s preference is not guaranteed. In scenarios where their interests diverge, joint efforts to reduce blockchain costs can be a viable strategy. Our parametric analysis further reveals that while the cross-channel influence contributes positively to enhancing product greenness and the manufacturer’s profit, it could diminish the profits of both platforms under certain conditions.
column3: 5 Conclusion 5.1 Concluding remarks and managerial implications In this paper, we explored a manufacturer’s blockchain adoption strategy under asymmetric platform competition, where the incumbent platform possesses an established market presence and provides blockchain services, while the new platform operates with a limited market presence and lacks blockchain capabilities. A key theoretical contribution of our study is the exploration of the cross-channel influence of blockchain technology, known as the spillover effect, which influences consumer valuation when purchasing from the new platform. While blockchain adoption in green supply chains has been studied, the spillover effect under asymmetric retail competition remains underexplored. Our findings yield several key insights that contribute to both the literature and managerial practice. Firstly, our analysis reveals that blockchain adoption becomes favorable when blockchain costs are low or when high costs are counterbalanced by a strong spillover effect. This implies that manufacturers should evaluate not only direct costs but also the broader impact of blockchain in increasing consumer trust and demand across channels. A real-world case is Walmart China’s pork industry blockchain initiative, where blockchain enhances transparency, increasing consumer trust in food safety. Manufacturers selling through Walmart’s blockchain-enabled platform benefit from heightened demand, even on non-blockchain platforms. 9 9 https://www.hyperledger.org/case-studies/walmart-case-study . These findings suggest that manufacturers should evaluate blockchain adoption not just as a cost but as a strategic tool for expanding market reach, particularly when targeting environmentally conscious consumers. This is particularly relevant in the food and beverage industry, where blockchain adoption remains in its early stages. Despite its potential benefits, adoption has been slow due to perceived complexity, financial constraints, and industry inertia. 10 10 https://www.foodengineeringmag.com/articles/101600-blockchain-technology-slow-on-the-uptake? . Addressing these barriers through cost-effective and scalable blockchain solutions can significantly enhance transparency, traceability, and consumer confidence in the industry. Secondly, we identified two equilibrium outcomes: (i) a win-win scenario, where the manufacturer and the incumbent platform both benefit from blockchain adoption, and (ii) a win-lose scenario, where only the manufacturer benefits while the incumbent platform incurs losses. The latter occurs when both blockchain costs and the spillover effect are high, counterintuitively harming the incumbent platform despite its own blockchain offering. To resolve misalignment, collaborative efforts to lower blockchain costs are essential. Blockchain platforms should explore cost-sharing models and customized blockchain solutions to ensure that blockchain services remain attractive to manufacturers. Amazon, for instance, collaborates with companies like Nestlé, Jinju Beer, and TrackX to tailor blockchain solutions to their operational needs, ensuring mutual benefits. 11 11 https://aws.amazon.com/managed-blockchain/customers/ . Moreover, blockchain platforms should adopt flexible pricing and modular blockchain solutions to lower the barriers to adoption in the food industry, making it easier for manufacturers to integrate blockchain into their operations. By offering scalable and cost-effective solutions, blockchain platforms can address concerns related to implementation complexity and financial constraints, thereby fostering widespread manufacturer adoption and ensuring long-term profitability. Thirdly, our parametric analysis highlights the complex interplay between the spillover effect, costs, and competition under the manufacturer’s blockchain adoption. While the spillover effect enhances product greenness and wholesale prices, yielding positive economic benefits for the manufacturer, it exerts a negative impact on the incumbent platform. Interestingly, the spillover effect demonstrates a double-edged sword effect on the new platform’s profit under lower blockchain costs, challenging the conventional belief that free-riding on the incumbent platform’s blockchain services always benefits the new platform. Furthermore, both blockchain costs and greenness improvement costs negatively impact product greenness and the manufacturer’s demand. However, their effects on wholesale prices and product selling prices differ, highlighting their distinct roles in shaping competitive dynamics. Lastly, greater consumer preference for the new platform enhances its profit when blockchain is adopted but reduces it in the absence of blockchain. This underscores the strategic advantage of blockchain adoption for the new platform, as it helps counterbalance the incumbent platform’s market dominance. Finally, our analysis highlights that reducing greenness improvement costs makes blockchain adoption more appealing to manufacturers. In green supply chain management, platforms play a crucial role in helping firms lower costs through collaborative sustainability initiatives and carbon footprint reduction strategies. Amazon Web Services (AWS) helps reduce customers’ carbon footprint by up to 80% compared to traditional on-premises computing, demonstrating how digital transformation supports both sustainability and cost efficiency. 12 12 https://www.forbes.com/sites/carolinamilanesi/2023/07/26/amazons-next-big-sustainability-push-to-focus-on-supply-chain/ . Similarly, Alibaba’s Energy Expert platform assists firms in tracking and minimizing carbon emissions, reducing long-term costs. 13 13 https://finance.yahoo.com/news/alibaba-blends-retail-technology-build-133500512.html . These examples illustrate how platforms can proactively assist manufacturers in adopting cost-effective, sustainable blockchain solutions. This can be achieved through resource-sharing initiatives and industry partnerships that streamline green supply chain management.

column1: Unlocking sustainable performance with blockchain technology: Insights from organizational learning theory
column2: Although blockchain technology (BT) has shown great potential, there remains a limited understanding of how to integrate it into business processes effectively. Drawing on organizational learning theory, we explore the drivers and outcomes of effective BT usage. Using survey data from 257 Chinese firms, we reveal that effective BT usage, whether for exploitation or exploration, hinges on both external knowledge acquisition and internal knowledge integration. Additionally, although both exploitation and exploration of BT can enhance economic and environmental performance, BT exploitation generally has a more substantial impact. This disparity arises because BT exploitation often involves optimizing existing processes (e.g., improving supply chain transparency), leading to more immediate performance improvements. In contrast, BT exploration involves experimental and innovative applications (e.g., developing new BT-based business models) that require a longer time frame to realize benefits. Finally, we discuss the heterogeneity between manufacturing and information technology firms. Our study contributes to the existing literature by elucidating how firms can achieve sustainable outcomes through BT usage. Our findings also assist managers in adapting their BT strategies to an increasingly competitive environment.
column3: 7 Conclusions Drawing from organizational learning theory, we reveal the differences in how manufacturing and IT firms use BT and how these patterns relate to sustainable performance. For manufacturing firms, the relationship between external knowledge acquisition and BT exploitation is not significant, suggesting a reliance on internal processes. In contrast, IT firms exhibit a strong link between external knowledge acquisition and BT exploitation, highlighting their need for external insights in a fast-paced digital environment. Further, both sectors recognize the importance of external knowledge acquisition in BT exploration, indicating a shared understanding of the value of innovation. Internal knowledge integration positively influences BT exploitation in both sectors; however, it only significantly affects BT exploration in IT firms, suggesting that IT firms leverage internal knowledge for innovative exploration more so than manufacturing firms. Finally, BT exploitation emerges as a strong predictor of economic and environmental performance in both types of firms. However, BT exploration shows a significant impact on economic and environmental performance exclusively in IT firms, indicating that the benefits of exploration may take longer to materialize in manufacturing contexts. According to these findings, our study contributes to the existing literature by providing guidance on how firms can unlock the potential of BT to achieve sustainable outcomes. We also offer actionable insights for managers seeking to adapt their BT strategies to thrive in a competitive landscape.

column1: Distributed ledgers and the governance of money
column2: Distributed ledgers promise to enable the classical vision of money as a universal transaction record. But is it ever optimal to update a ledger through decentralized consensus? Analyzing an exchange economy with credit, we show that centralized updating is optimal when long-term rewards are more valued, minimizing redundant validation costs and maximizing economic surplus. Decentralization becomes preferable under weaker intertemporal incentives and when validators are drawn from market participants. We show how competing ledgers – anonymous or identified, permissioned or permissionless – can achieve socially optimal outcomes even in low-trust environments. Our framework provides a foundation for designing robust and efficient ledger systems.
column3: 5 Conclusion In this paper, we have presented an economic analysis of decentralized ledger technology in an economy where money is essential. To our knowledge, our analysis is the first economic analysis of DLT in such a context. It links a ledger validation game to monetary exchange, establishes the uniqueness of the equilibrium via a global game approach, and characterizes the optimal supermajority voting rule, number of validators, and size of transactions. We believe our analysis is timely, as DLT is rapidly becoming an industry standard for digital currencies and in other applications. In particular, our results can shed light on the burgeoning literature on central bank digital currency (CBDC) and stablecoins insofar as it gives conditions under which a central authority should manage the ledger of transactions. 55 55 See the stock-taking exercise of pursued technological designs in Auer et al. (2020) . The discussion of technology and the economics of central bank digital money has thus far centered on the balance sheet effects and related systemic implications. 56 56 See, among others, Andolfatto (2020) , Brunnermeier and Niepelt (2019) , Fernandez-Villaverde et al. (2020) , Keister and Monnet (2020) . Here, we focus not on balance sheets and the issue of how the value of a currency can be guaranteed (central backing is of the essence for a CBDC irrespective of our analysis), but on the governance of a societal record-keeping device used as a substitute for money. Of course, we have made simplifying assumptions in order to better grasp the basic economics of money as memory. Future work should relax some of these. For instance – to simplify the analysis – we have assumed that validators all agree to accept bribes in unison. It would be interesting to also study the cooperative games between validators in more detail. We have also taken as given that agents use a private ledger, as they want to preserve their anonymity in trades. Tirole (2020) and Chiu and Koeppl (2020) make progress on this front. In order to better compare the different types of ledger, future work should also include the benefit from preserving anonymity. Also our mechanism design approach implies that we have ignored every industrial organization aspect of DLT, which might be significant if this technology were to be widely adopted in the future.

column1: The Impact of Blockchain Technology on Firms' Environmental Innovation: A Technological Push Perspective
column2: Environmental innovation helps to achieve sustainable utilization of resources and represents an important measure for promoting the coordinated development of human and environment. Adopting the perspective of technological push—based on information asymmetry theory, cognitive orientation theory, and the resource‐based view—this study constructs a research model capturing the impact of blockchain technology on firms' environmental innovation. This study uses multiple regression analysis to examine the impact of blockchain technology on firms' environmental innovation. It also observes the mediating effect of proactive orientation and the moderating effect of venture capital. The results show that blockchain technology positively impacts firms' environmental innovation, with proactive orientation playing a mediating role between blockchain technology and environmental innovation and venture capital enhancing the positive effect. By analyzing the mechanism between blockchain technology and environmental innovation, this study provides a new theoretical basis for better applying blockchain technology to environmental innovation at the firm level.
column3: 5.1 ConclusionThis study utilizes A-share listed companies from the period 2012 to 2022 as the research sample to investigate the impact of blockchain technology on environmental innovation, and obtains several main conclusions.First, blockchain technology exhibits a positive effect on firms' environmental innovation. This study confirms that adopting blockchain technology can positively promote environmental innovation in firms. Blockchain technology can help firms solve not only certain management problems (Saberi et al. 2019) but also problems such as information asymmetry (Li et al. 2024) by providing technical support for the innovation and development of firms' ecological activities (Chin et al. 2021). Furthermore, blockchain technology positively promotes collaboration and information exchange among participants in firms' environmental innovation (Benzidia, Makaoui, and Subramanian 2021), encouraging greater enthusiasm from stakeholders and enhancing the performance of firms in environmental innovation.Second, proactive orientation serves as a mediator in the relationship between blockchain technology and firms' environmental innovation. The rapid development of blockchain technology provides technical support for firms to enhance operational capabilities and improve management models (Pan et al. 2020), which has a positive promoting effect on improving the proactive orientation level. Proactive orientation can give firms a clear advantage in terms of creating new technologies and discovering new markets (He et al. 2023), which is conducive to promoting environmental innovation. In addition, proactive orientation can reduce production and operating costs for firms (Morris, Kuratko, and Covin 2011; Yang, Jiang, and Zhao 2019) and stimulate enthusiasm for firms' environmental innovation.Third, venture capital moderates the influence of blockchain technology on firms' environmental innovation, amplifying its positive effect on promoting firms' environmental innovation. The participation of venture capital helps firms not only obtain more financial support—enabling them to optimize blockchain technology (Yi et al. 2023)—but also solve the problem of long-term and sufficient financial support for environmental innovation (Owen, Brennan, and Lyon 2018). Meanwhile, the knowledge acquisition and integration capacities provided by venture capital institutions can further leverage blockchain technology to eliminate information asymmetry (De Clercq and Dimov 2008; Yi et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024). To some extent, this can further leverage the positive effect of blockchain technology on firms' environmental innovation.5.2 Theoretical ImplicationsFirst, this study explores the impact of blockchain technology on environmental innovation from a technology push perspective, thereby enriching and broadening the existing research on the antecedents of environmental innovation. Currently, there is ongoing debate in the literature regarding the impact of blockchain technology on firms' environmental innovation (Mubarak et al. 2021; Chin et al. 2022; Schinckus 2020). By confirming the influence of blockchain technology on firms' environmental innovation, this study contributes to the understanding of the driving factors behind such innovation, thereby advancing the field of research. Second, based on cognitive orientation theory, this study confirms proactive orientation which plays a mediating role in the relationship between blockchain technology and firms' environmental innovation, deepening understanding of the mechanics of blockchain technology's impact on environmental innovation. Finally, this study validates that venture capital acts as a moderating factor in the link between blockchain technology and firms' environmental innovation. This finding further elucidates the boundary conditions under which blockchain technology influences firms' environmental innovation.5.3 Managerial ImplicationsFirst, firms need to enhance investment in blockchain technology and improve the level of environmental innovation. Blockchain technology can provide support for the virtual currency in the virtual world and has become a key technology for enhancing firm value, as well as a practical and feasible means of optimizing operation models (Saberi et al. 2019; Chang et al. 2020; Sternberg, Hofmann, and Roeck 2021; Zhou et al. 2023). However, the number of firms using blockchain technology is insufficient. Firms can apply blockchain technology, establish and improve blockchain platforms, integrate blockchain technology with firm management, utilize the advantages of blockchain technology to improve and optimize management models, and strive to enhance the environmental innovation ability of firms and improve environmental innovation efficiency. Second, firms should choose a proactive development strategy. Proactivity represents the core of firms' innovation behavior, reflecting the degree to which firms take advantage of new opportunities, attempt change, and mobilize forward-thinking agents (Morgan and Strong 2003). Firms should actively improve their proactive orientation level, promote the effective integration of internal and external information resources, and optimize business management to meet the internal and external conditions required for environmental innovation. In this way, they can foster the development of environmental innovation. Third, venture capital institutions should support the green development of firms. In addition to providing financial support for firms, venture capital can also provide abundant nonfinancial resources and diversified resources for firms (Yi et al. 2023). Venture capital institutions, especially state-owned venture capital institutions, should focus on not only profit but also their social responsibility, which means using their resources to empower firms, and attending to the sustainable green development of firms. Meanwhile, venture capital institutions should closely follow policy trends, implement the concept of green development, fully utilize the cooperation relationship with invested firms to play supervisory and managerial roles, help firms coordinate economic development and environmental protection, and encourage and supervise firms to actively perform environmental innovation activities.5.4 Limitations and Suggestions for Future ResearchDespite yielding certain results through the empirical analysis of the relationship between blockchain technology, proactive orientation, venture capital, and firms' environmental innovation, this study is not devoid of limitations. First, this study only explores the impact of blockchain technology on firms' environmental innovation from a technology push perspective. In addition to blockchain technology, other information technologies may also impact environmental innovation. However, limitations related to data and other factors prevented this study from comprehensively examining the impact of other information technologies. Second, the assessment of proactive orientation was based on the overall occurrence of pertinent keywords in the annual reports, rather than utilizing publicly available authoritative data. Therefore, future research needs to adopt more scientific measurement methods to measure proactive orientation. Third, the sample selected for this study is listed companies. Due to differences in the development stages and external environment of firms, this research's results lack generalizability. Therefore, future research can expand the sample size to further test this study's conclusions.

column1: What drives female travelers to use blockchain-enabled booking applications?
column2:
Purpose
Adopting appropriate technology, such as blockchain-enabled hotel booking applications (BHB apps), empowers female travelers to control their lives and gain flexibility, safety and economic benefits while traveling. This study aims to examine elements shaping their expectations when using hotel booking applications.

Design/methodology/approach
This study used partial least squares structural equation modeling, multigroup analysis and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis to offer comprehensive reviews of how independent factors (e.g. openness to change, social influence, hedonic motivation, perceived benefits, perceived risks) influence travelers’ intentions toward decentralized booking solutions in international contexts.

Findings
Two studies were conducted in the Asian region where there is a shortage of studies on female tourists, specifically in Vietnam (n = 241) and South Korea (n = 323). The findings indicate that social influence and perceived benefits most affect Vietnamese travelers’ intentions, whereas Korean travelers are primarily influenced by hedonic motivation and perceived benefits.

Research limitations/implications
This study delves into female travelers’ behaviors toward BHB apps, focusing on the often-overlooked Asian markets. Cultural influences shape differences in travel choices across countries and future studies should examine the impact of cultural dimensions and socioeconomic factors in more detail.

Originality/value
This study uses the extended valence framework to provide new insights into the advantages of blockchain-based products that help travelers control their trips.
column3: The results showed that openness to change, social influence, hedonic motivations, perceived benefits and perceived risks are key determinants shaping the behavior of using BHB apps for travel-related purposes. The extent to which these factors influence traveler behaviors differs across countries. In Vietnam, openness to change, social influence and hedonic motivation significantly influence the perceived benefits and risks of BHB apps. These findings align with the research of Albayati et al. (2020), Hien et al. (2024) and Park et al. (2019). Among the three antecedents, social influence exerts the strongest positive impact on perceived benefits, whereas hedonic motivation has the largest negative effect on perceived risks. This indicates that recommendations from social circles help to boost the perceived benefits of apps, making them appear more appealing. Moreover, when Vietnamese tourists are driven by entertainment value, it tends to reduce their risk perception regarding using the apps. Both perceived benefits and risks significantly affect attitudes, supporting the results of Al-Debei et al. (2015) and Chen (2013). The influence of perceived benefits on attitude is stronger than that of perceived risks. Moreover, only perceived benefits and attitudes significantly influence behavioral intention toward BHB apps, whereas the impact of perceived risks does not. This highlights the fact that the benefits of apps (e.g. features, convenience, effectiveness, financial value) are crucial in motivating travelers to use them. In Korea, hedonic motivation is the only factor significantly influencing perceived benefits and risks, and it has the strongest impact. This reveals that BHB apps align with tourists’ demand for entertainment values, and it will enhance their perception of their benefits. However, if the apps do not meet their expectations, tourists may focus on the drawbacks of apps. Surprisingly, openness to change does not influence these two factors. This implies that regardless of how open individuals are to novel technology, their perception of the apps’ benefits and risks may remain unaffected by personal traits. Similar to Vietnam’s results, perceived benefits and risks have opposing effects on attitude, with perceived benefits having greater impacts on attitude than perceived risks. Specifically, perceived risks still do not impact the intention to use BHB apps. This highlights the importance of emphasizing the benefits of the BHB app in business strategies to drive adoption. The multigroup analysis reveals more about the differences in behavior across the two countries. The extent to which openness to change and social influence impact perceived benefits and risks is higher in Vietnam than in Korea. Such disparities in new technology adoption probably originate from the culture of each nation. Due to the highly collectivist culture and uncertainty avoidance, Korean people’s approach to novel technologies is more conservative than that of the Vietnamese (Hong-Xoan and Earl, 2020; Yoo et al., 2014). Although 91.1% of Vietnamese women use mobile phones to access information and government services, they remain responsible for family care, a barrier to their participation in technological activities (United Nations Vietnam, 2023). Meanwhile, Korean women play crucial roles in shaping the technology industry, accounting for 25% of the tech workforce (Baldacchino, 2023). Hence, Vietnamese travelers are less familiar with technology than Korean travelers and they rely more on references from close individuals to evaluate the pros and cons of new technology. Hedonic motivation has a stronger positive influence on perceived benefits in Korea, whereas its negative impact on perceived risks is stronger in Vietnam. This means that Korean travelers primarily perceive BHB apps as tools for entertainment and enjoyment, making people perceive the apps as offering valuable benefits. Conversely, Vietnamese travelers often overlook the risks of BHB apps (e.g. security risks, adaptation issues) as they are motivated by the pleasure of using the technology. In addition, Vietnamese travelers are less influenced by perceived benefits in shaping their attitudes and intentions than Korean travelers. This may be because the level of familiarity with digital tools varies between countries. Vietnamese travelers are less accustomed to using travel apps compared to Koreans. Hence, they might not fully appreciate the benefits of apps, resulting in a weaker impact on their behaviors. The fsQCA results reveal additional insights into the data, showing that openness to change and social influence not only directly impact Vietnamese travelers’ behavior, but also combine with hedonic motivation and perceived risks to lead to high intention toward BHB apps. This strongly confirms the notion that openness in Vietnamese culture and the opinions of others (such as family, peers or societal norms) are crucial in shaping Vietnamese travelers’ decisions regarding blockchain. Surprisingly, openness to change coordinates with perceived benefits and perceived risks to lead to Korean travelers’ high intentions. This indicates that Korean travelers are open to BHB apps when they have comprehensive views of the benefits and risks of this technology. Theoretical implications This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of the antecedents underpinning female travelers’ intentions toward blockchain. This study enriches knowledge about female tourist behavior in Asia, where blockchain technology is more advanced than in Europe and other regions, rather than solely adopting Western-centric perspectives that are dominant in previous studies. Personal traits and social norms significantly influence female consumption behavior, particularly in the context of Confucian cultures and collectivist societies (Kapser et al., 2021; Kulik, 2016; Phuong-Mai et al., 2005; Sung et al., 2023). To better align with gender and cultural perspectives, we incorporated personal traits and intrinsic rewards like openness to change, social influence and hedonic motivation into EVF to shape the perceptions of the benefits and risks of using blockchain applications, thereby enhancing its predictive ability regarding travelers in Asian countries where collectivism has strong impacts. Instead of using traditional technology models (e.g. TAM, UTAUT) that only focus on functional benefits or technological aspects, this study uses EVF to offer a clearer perspective on how positive and negative perceptions shape user behavior. This is a crucial contribution since motivation and resistance are the two essential aspects of consumers’ behaviors and might considerably affect consumers’ acceptance of novel technologies. Effort expectancy, performance expectancy, price value, risk barriers and tradition barriers are integrated into the benefits and risks of EVF to provide a deeper insight into the diverse advantages and threats that female travelers encounter when using BHB apps. Hence, this study has played a part in developing second-order measurement in the future. The study contributes to the growing body of research by conducting a comparative analysis across Asian countries, each with its distinct cultural and economic landscapes. A mixed-method design combining qualitative (fsQCA) and quantitative (PLS-SEM) methods were used to compare travelers’ behavior in Vietnam and Korea. This approach highlights the differences in travelers’ behavior toward blockchain adoption, driven by cultural, economic and technological development disparities. The findings confirmed that openness to change and social influence significantly impact developing countries with cultures that blend individualism and collectivism, such as Vietnam. Meanwhile, developed countries such as Korea prioritize hedonic motivation. Both countries value the benefits of BHB apps over concerns about drawbacks. Practical implications Social norms strongly influence collectivistic societies such as Vietnam and Korea (Phuong-Mai et al., 2005). It is essential to leverage the effect of influential figures (e.g. women’s organizations, female celebrities) to introduce BHB apps to potential customers. Enhancing customers’ acknowledgment of blockchain-powered hotel apps to attract them is a difficult mission for individual companies (Strebinger and Treiblmaier, 2022). Hence, tech companies should partner with leading tourism and marketing firms to develop effective marketing strategies. Specifically, Vietnamese companies should target young and educated travelers – who are open to change and quick to adopt BHB apps – by offering special promotions or rewards for first-time customers. Meanwhile, Korean travelers value the exciting experiences of new products. Hence, Korean companies can incorporate entertainment features (e.g. experience sharing, gamified elements) into BHB apps. As travelers from both countries pay attention to the benefits of BHB apps rather than the risks, advertising campaigns should emphasize their advantages for travelers, including ensuring safety, cost savings and flexible reservations. Furthermore, making booking convenient for customers is essential to improve their experiences (Hien et al., 2024). Hence, tech companies should organize product testing campaigns to gather feedback for enhancing the user-friendly interfaces and intuitive features of BHB apps. The apps should generate a customized travel plan including recommendations for destinations, activities and accommodation that aligns with a user’s desires, while being safe for women. Tech companies can reduce customers’ perceived risks toward BHB apps by providing transparent information about the apps. Importantly, policymakers should ensure that the apps’ transactions comply with relevant laws and regulations. This can strengthen public trust and minimize the risk of legal issues. Moreover, social media, blogs and press releases are good channels to share positive information about BHB apps. User reviews also help build trust with potential customers and encourage widespread adoption. Limitations and future research directions This study mentioned cultural aspects influencing female traveler behavior but has not yet evaluated them. In addition, most participants were young and educated, potentially having different attitudes toward BHB apps than older people. Hence, further research can add sociodemographic variables to improve this current model. Moreover, scholars can examine the influence of Hofstede’s cultural dimensions on women’s intentions toward this technology and the moderating effects of factors such as age, education level and socioeconomic status. The study focused solely on female travelers and did not consider male travelers, which may limit the contributions of blockchain to promoting gender equality. Therefore, future studies should compare the behavior of female and male travelers regarding BHB apps.
