column1: Tokenized assets in a decentralized economy: Balancing efficiency, value, and risks
column2: The emergence of blockchain technology is compelling firms to rethink traditional operations and management strategies, with asset tokenization presenting a transformative potential to optimize transaction processes and redefine value chains. This study explores how blockchain-enabled asset tokenization influences transaction efficiency, value creation, and risk distribution across different market contexts. Utilizing a multiple-case study design, this research analyzes four asset tokenization business cases in multiple sectors —real estate, gold, gaming assets, and carbon credits—through 30 semi-structured interviews with participants from each case. Our research findings indicate that while tokenization significantly enhances transaction efficiency and creates new value propositions, it also introduces complexities in governance and risk distribution, which may challenge market stability. This study contributes to the contemporary blockchain literature by empirically illustrating how asset tokenization alters traditional asset management and investment models, highlighting the importance of tailored regulatory frameworks to address this emerging blockchain-enabled business models. Additionally, the research offers practical insights for business practitioners, suggesting that a balanced approach is necessary to leverage the benefits of asset tokenization while safeguarding market trust and sustainability.
column3: 6 Conclusion 6.1 Theoretical contributions This study makes several significant theoretical contributions to the literature on blockchain-enabled asset tokenization ( Gan et al., 2021 ; Wankmüller et al., 2023 ; Guggenberger et al., 2024 ), particularly in understanding its impact on transaction efficiency, value creation, and the unintended consequences on risk distribution and market trust. First, by employing TCT as a framework ( Williamson, 1985 ; Coase, 1993 ), this research extends its application to emerging decentralized systems, illustrating how asset tokenization alters traditional cost structures. The findings emphasize that while decentralization reduces transaction costs and improves access to fractional ownership, it introduces new forms of risks, such as heightened security vulnerabilities and regulatory uncertainty. This nuanced understanding contributes to the literature ( Schmidt and Wagner, 2019 ) by offering a balanced view of both the benefits and risks associated with decentralization, enriching the ongoing debate surrounding asset tokenization and blockchain applications' potential for disintermediation and its broader market implications. Second, this research addresses a gap in the literature concerning the unintended consequences of decentralization in tokenized asset markets. Existing literature primarily focuses on the efficiency gains brought by blockchain and smart contracts ( Gan et al., 2021 ; De Giovanni, 2020 ); this study brings forward critical insights into how the lack of centralized oversight and governance structures can create new risks. By offering propositions grounded in empirical findings from cases across multiple industries (e.g., real estate, gold, carbon credits, and bonds), this research critically examines the balance between decentralization and market stability. The study contributes to a deeper theoretical understanding of how decentralized systems impact not only market trust but also the capacity for self-regulation, raising important questions about how decentralized governance and regulatory mechanisms should evolve. Finally, this research adds to the broader discourse on the future of tokenized assets by challenging the overly optimistic narrative of blockchain as inherently trust-enhancing ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Bhatia et al., 2024 ). The insights presented here illustrate that while blockchain's transparency and immutability offer significant advantages for regulatory compliance and fraud prevention ( Lu and Wu, 2024 ), these characteristics also introduce rigidities that may hinder adaptive responses to market manipulation and errors. This dual perspective enriches theoretical debates on the long-term viability of blockchain-enabled markets ( De Giovanni, 2020 ; Wankmüller et al., 2023 ), positioning this study as a critical voice in discussions surrounding the evolving role of blockchain technology in global asset markets.

column1: The economics of Constant Function Market Makers
column2: We use microeconomic theory to describe the inner workings of Constant Function Market Makers (CFMMs). We show that standard results from consumer theory apply in this new context, endowing us with powerful tools to characterize the optimal design of CFMMs. We employ them to analyze the externalities that traders and liquidity providers exert on each other when interacting through a CFMM. Liquidity providers reduce the execution costs by flattening the bonding curve on which trades are executed. Arbitrageurs impose an adverse selection cost on liquidity providers by unfavorably rebalancing their portfolio. We show that the strengths of these two externalities are pinned down by the curvature of the bonding curve and are inversely related to each other, thereby identifying the fundamental economic tradeoff that market designers have to address.
column3: 9 Conclusion We have shown in this paper that standard microeconomic theory sheds a powerful light on the inner workings and optimal design of CFMMs. First, we explained how the main properties of CFMMs, such as their ability to provide reliable oracles for off-chain prices, naturally follow from established results in consumer theory. Transposing the insights of consumer theory enabled us to narrow the design space, for instance by showing that only homothetic trading functions can prevent liquidity providers from scrambling the price signal. After having established these fundamental results, we used our new tools to gather deeper insights into the economic externalities connecting traders and liquidity providers. Focusing first on traders, we provided explicit conditions under which their costs of using a CFMM are decreasing in the liquidity of the pool. Then, we turned our attention to liquidity providers, explaining why their impermanent losses are decreasing in the curvature of the bonding curve. Finally, we connected both sides, establishing that the externalities exerted by liquidity providers and by traders are inversely proportional. This finding has important implications for the design of CFMMs since it shows that the preferences of traders are fundamentally divergent from that of liquidity providers: Traders favor CFMMs with low curvature whereas liquidity providers favor CFMMs with high curvature. The challenge for the designer therefore consists in identifying the curvature that strikes an optimal balance between liquidity attraction and fees collection. Solving this mechanism design problem is beyond the scope of the models considered in this paper since it requires specifying the law of motion of prices. We intend to follow this roadmap in future research by leveraging the apparatus laid-out in our paper and extending it to a dynamic setting.

column1: Quality improvement and evaluation for profile responses in cloud-based additive manufacturing processes
column2: The 3D printing cloud service platform integrates 3D printing with cloud manufacturing to enable resource sharing and transition manufacturing from mass production to personalised customisation. However, the unstable process of 3D printing, which results in high variability and low repeatability, impedes the application of cloud 3D printing platforms. How to economically and effectively monitor and control the process stability of 3D printers, especially in blockchain-based cloud 3D printing networks, has become a critical technical bottleneck. The authors propose a novel method to monitor and stabilise the fused deposition modelling (FDM) 3D printing process. This method uses profile responses to obtain sufficient quality data and reliable optimisation results from just a few specimens. First, the spatio-temporal Gaussian process model is combined with the Latin hypercube design to investigate the relationship between profile responses and process parameters. Second, under the Bayesian optimisation framework, find the optimal parameter settings that make the predicted profiles maximally conform to the specification region. Finally, evaluate the printing process under the optimal parameter settings by multivariate process capability indices. Verification tests show that the proposed method is feasible and cost-effective, promoting the application of a cloud 3D printing platform.
column3: With the integration and application of advanced information technology and manufacturing technology, intelligence, collaboration, customisation, service, and platform have become essential development trends in 3D printing. In this ‘small sample, poor information’ and ‘high variation’ manufacturing environment, this paper combines the STGP model, Bayesian optimisation, and process capability index to create a method for continuously improving and evaluating the stability of the 3D printing process. The specific contributions are summarised as follows: Experimental results show that a stabler printing process can be achieved under the optimal parameter settings obtained by the proposed STGP model compared to the BHME model. This reduces the defect rate of the 3D printing process, lowering production costs and improving productivity. Validation tests show that the process stability monitoring and optimisation of the FDM 3D printer based on profile response is reliable using a small number of specimens. This indicates that the proposed novel method in this paper is more cost-effective than traditional methods, which require large amounts of specimens. Since the 3D printing process is unstable, this paper uses multivariate control charts and process capability indices to monitor and control the 3D printing process regularly under the optimal parameter settings. This helps stabilise the FDM 3D printing process in a blockchain-based cloud 3D printing network. To our knowledge, no paper has been found to meaningfully address quality monitoring and improvement of FDM 3D printing equipment in blockchain-based cloud additive manufacturing processes. This paper develops an effective quality improvement and evaluation strategy to stabilise the FDM 3D printing process based on profile response. This novel technology supports the practical application and development of 3D printing cloud service platforms. It also offers a promising approach for improving other costly, uncertain manufacturing processes, such as micro/nano-machining. It should be noted that when using the STGP model, choosing separable covariances may result in information loss, while non-separable covariances are computationally more complex. Therefore, employing more general stationary and non-stationary STGP models or tensor regression models to address the modelling problem of profile responses is a worthwhile topic for future research. In addition, different methods can be evaluated and compared from multiple dimensions, such as printing accuracy, surface quality, material usage efficiency, and computational cost, to provide more comprehensive experimental data support.

column1: Combating the Global Food Crisis with Agricultural Technologies: Potential Research Opportunities
column2: The ongoing global food crisis is exacerbated by rising food demand and dwindling natural resources. Combating this crisis requires interventions beyond government subsidies to sustain the agricultural sector. In this article, we discuss various agricultural technologies leveraging AI, drones, blockchain, mobile apps, and solar technology that can help smallholder farmers in developing countries gain access to financial resources, information, and knowledge about crop management, market selection, and fair selling processes. Although these technologies hold great promise, encouraging farmers to invest in and adopt them remains to be a major challenge. This challenge, in turn, creates future research opportunities for operations management researchers to explore.
column3: The global food crisis is a complex and multifaceted issue that requires innovative solutions to ensure food security and alleviate farmer poverty. This article explores various agricultural technologies, including AI, drones, mobile apps, blockchain, and solar energy, which hold promise in addressing these challenges. These technologies can empower smallholder farmers in developing countries by providing them with access to financial resources, knowledge about crop management, market information, and fair-trading processes. However, the realized benefits are not fully understood, and the adoption of these technologies by farmers remains a significant challenge. Future research opportunities for OM researchers include evaluating the economic value of these technologies, developing mechanisms to encourage their adoption, and understanding the factors that influence farmers' willingness to invest in and use these technologies. By addressing these research questions, OM researchers can contribute to the development of more effective and sustainable interventions that improve the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and enhance global food security. In addition to analytical and empirical studies, OM researchers can play a crucial role in designing and conducting field experiments to assess the real-world benefits of agricultural technologies. By doing so, OM researchers can help create societal value by addressing the unique challenges faced by smallholder farmers and promoting the widespread adoption of innovative agricultural technologies.

column1: Advancing corporate sustainability via big data analytics, blockchain innovation, and organizational dynamicsâ€”A cross-validated predictive approach
column2: In today's business landscape, the paramount focus of firms is to achieve advanced corporate sustainability. This objective has led to the development of big data analytics, reliable big and cloud data analytics capabilities, and blockchain technology as powerful tools worldwide that have helped firms increase sustainable performance. Capitalizing on these technologies, this study provides new insight into the role data‐driven competitive sustainability, data‐driven culture, and organizational management information in steering firms' performance. Using a quantitative research approach, data was collected through a structured survey administered to managers and IT professionals across various industries. The relationships between the variables were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM), confirming that all proposed hypotheses were supported. The results demonstrate the significant positive impact of big data analytics capabilities, reliable big and cloud data analytics capabilities, and blockchain technology on corporate sustainable performance and data‐driven competitive sustainability. Furthermore, data‐driven competitive sustainability was found to mediate the relationships between BDA, RBCDA, blockchain technology, and corporate sustainable performance. Additionally, OMIS‐fit and data‐driven culture were identified as critical moderators that enhance the effects of these technological capabilities on competitive sustainability and corporate performance. These findings provide valuable insights for organizations seeking to leverage advanced technological capabilities to achieve a sustainable competitive advantage in emerging economies.
column3: In the current business scenario, customer demand is rapidly evolving, with the new tools keeping pace. In recent years, advanced technological developments have inspired global institutions to embrace new digital tools. Technological development is the engine that drives an organization's interest in technical capabilities, thus creating a data-driven organizational culture of competitive sustainability. However, despite the increasing role of digital inventions, it is still difficult to determine the impact of these innovations on firms' sustainable performance. Leveraging digital technologies has been a challenge previously, yet today, it has become a prominent tool for analyzing historical and real-time data. The study findings showed positive results, revealing a significant relationship between BDA, RBCDA, and BCT, and sustainable performance and DDCS. The study confirmed the positive mediating role of DDCS and moderation of DDC and OMIS-F. Indeed, this is a significant study that holds implications for global organizations concerning technology implementation in the world's major sectors. The study findings advise organizations' management to invest in new developments for establishing a data-driven environment of competitive sustainability, leading to sustainable performance.

column1: The influence of blockchain technology on circular economy implementation in the automotive sector: From a GMM model to a new machine learning algorithm
column2: This investigation explores the integration of blockchain technology (BCT) with circular economy (CE) principles within the automotive sector, leveraging a dataset from the years 2011 to 2019. Employing advanced analytical techniques, including machine learning models and the system generalized method of moments (GMM), the study meticulously assesses BCT's impact on CE practices over the specified period. The dataset, curated from esteemed sources such as CSRHub, Thomson Reuters, and Bloomberg, enhances the reliability and validity of our analysis. Results indicate a positive influence of BCT on the adoption and effectiveness of CE practices in the automotive industry, suggesting that CE practices can bolster firm performance. Notably, the analysis reveals that support vector machines (SVM) and neural networks (NNs) exhibit superior efficacy over the random forest (RF) model in capturing the nuances of the BCT‐CE interplay. This is evidenced by their lower root‐mean‐square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE), signifying greater predictive accuracy. The findings illuminate BCT's potential to revolutionize CE practices, optimize resource use, and foster sustainability in the automotive field.
column3: While this study delineates the positive correlation between CE practices and firm performance, enhanced by BCT adoption, it acknowledges several limitations. The specific sample period and industry focus on the automotive sector limit the generalizability of the findings. Future research should extend beyond these confines to examine the enduring impact of CE and BCT in different sectors and over longer periods. Additionally, exploring additional moderating factors, such as regulatory environments and market conditions, could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics at play. Incorporating complementary technologies, such as Internet of Things (IoT) and artificial intelligence (AI), could also shed light on how these technologies interact with BCT to foster circular practices. Despite these limitations, the study's implications for managers and policymakers are profound, advocating for a strategic embrace of CE principles and BCT to cultivate sustainability and enhance corporate performance. Future inquiries across various industries and employing qualitative methodologies will enrich our understanding of CE and BCT's multifaceted impact on firm performance, guiding more effective sustainable practice strategies.In conclusion, this study provides a robust and comprehensive analysis of the relationship between CE, BCT, and firm performance. The findings underscore the significant positive correlation between CE practices and FP metrics, including ROA, ROE, ROIC, and Tobin's Q, supporting the notion that companies embracing CE principles tend to achieve higher returns and market valuations (Doe et al., 2021; Smith & Johnson, 2020). Moreover, the study offers compelling evidence to support Hypothesis 2, indicating that the adoption of BCT can indeed enhance a firm's CE performance (Brown et al., 2019; Green & White, 2022). The statistically significant positive relationship between BCT and CE further emphasizes the role of BCT as a catalyst for promoting sustainability and resource efficiency within firms (Clark et al., 2020).The K-means clustering scatter plot analysis of automotive firms reveals four distinct groups based on their BCT investments and CE practices. The clusters show varying levels of BCT adoption and integration with CE practices. One cluster indicates firms successfully leveraging BCT to enhance CE, while other clusters suggest either a nascent stage of BCT adoption or a misalignment between BCT investments and CE practices. The conclusion drawn from the analysis is that while some firms are capitalizing on the synergy between BCT and CE for sustainability, there remains significant untapped potential within the industry. The insights from the clustering encourage firms to refine their strategies for BCT implementation to advance CE practices. Policymakers are also advised to facilitate environments that promote such technological adoption, contributing to the sector's overall sustainability.The automotive sector emerges as a prime beneficiary of integrating BCT. Leveraging BCT's capabilities in secure and transparent SCM empowers automakers to trace materials and components' origins, ensuring compliance with sustainability standards and identifying opportunities for recycling and reuse (Miller & Davis, 2019; Taylor et al., 2021). BCT's facilitation of peer-to-peer transactions and smart contracts streamlines remanufacturing and refurbishment processes, fostering circular business models, and sharing economies (Adams et al., 2020). The data-sharing capabilities of BCT also enable collaborative efforts among stakeholders, optimizing resource utilization and implementing product-as-a-service models, thereby extending vehicle lifespans and minimizing waste (Robinson & Lee, 2019).In summary, this study reinforces the significance of CE practices and BCT adoption in driving firm performance and supporting sustainable business practices. By embracing CE and leveraging BCT's transformative capabilities, industries can pave the way for a more resilient and environmentally responsible global economy (Khan & Singh, 2021; Patel & Gomez, 2022).

column1: Platform pricing and blockchain adoption for capacity sharing with cross-network externality and supply risk
column2: Platform-based capacity sharing is a new business format of sharing economy to reallocate spare production resources via industrial internet, generating collaborative manufacturing related platform operations issues. This paper examines the impact of cross-network externality and supply risk of the two-sided market on the pricing and blockchain adopting decisions of capacity sharing platforms. The mean–variance model is employed to depict the impact of purchasers’ or suppliers’ risk-sensitive types on platform pricing, where purchasers’ or suppliers’ risk-sensitive types can be identified by blockchain technology and be intertwined by the cross-network externality. The obtained platform’s optimal pricing under two scenarios with risk-sensitive capacity purchasers (D) and risk-sensitive suppliers (S) shows that the platform charges risk-seeking, risk-neutral and risk-averse users in descending order for the platform side containing risk-sensitive users, regardless of the comparison of bilateral cross-network externalities. However, for risk-neutral side users, the price ranking under three risk-sensitive types depends on the relative size of bilateral cross-network externalities. In addition, blockchain technology always decreases the surplus of risk-sensitive side users, whereas it increases the surplus of risk-insensitive side users. Further, we find that platform prefers to introduce blockchain technology when the fixed cost of introducing it is less than the profit increment it brings. In addition, by comparing platform profits and blockchain value in the two scenarios, we argue that platforms need to comprehensively balance the comparison of fixed costs of introducing blockchain on both sides and the importance of risk-preferring and risk-averse users to improve their profitability. Introducing blockchain technology to the side where the cost of blockchain technology is higher may result in higher blockchain value for the platform. Finally, we examine the platform with two-sided risk-sensitive users and the results are robust. This study proposes theoretical explanation for platform pricing considering the cross-network externality and risk-sensitive users, as well as some management insights for the application of blockchain technology in platform operations.
column3: Inspired by the reality fact that platform users risk tendency to capacity supply variation affects the efficiency of platform-based capacity sharing economy, this paper investigates how risk attitudes and cross-network externality impact capacity-sharing platform pricing, platform profit and surplus of two sides. Specifically, this paper discusses three scenarios: hybrid risk- sensitive purchasers (scenario D), hybrid risk-sensitive suppliers (scenario S), and hybrid risk- sensitive purchasers and suppliers (scenario B). The analysis of above three situations yields some managerial insights. In scenario D, we first discuss the platform pricing when the purchasers show the same risk- sensitive types. The result shows that the price on the demand side, the platform profit, and the surplus of bilateral users are higher with risk-seeking purchasers. However, the impact of risk- sensitive types on supply-side pricing depends on the relative size of the bilateral cross-network externalities. The supply-side pricing is higher with risk-seeking purchasers when the cross- network externality of the supply side is greater than that of the demand side; otherwise, the supply-side pricing is higher with risk-averse purchasers. The result is different from Choi et al. (2020b), which only focuses on demand-side pricing. Secondly, we discuss two pricing mechanisms of the platform when purchasers show different risk attitudes: common pricing (without considering the risk-sensitive types of purchasers) and customized pricing (charging different usage fees in terms of purchasers risk-sensitive types based on blockchain technology). We find the blockchain improves the surplus of suppliers but it hurts purchasers surplus by comparing the above pricing schemes. The result is the opposite in scenario S. However, Choi et al. (2020b) show that whether blockchain technology is beneficial to consumers depends on the significance of risk-averse and risk-seeking consumers in the market. Song et al. (2022) conclude that blockchain technology always hurts consumer surplus with the high application cost of blockchain. Furthermore, we find that it is wise for the platform to introduce blockchain technology when the fixed cost of introducing blockchain technology is less than the profit added for the platform. While Wu and Wang (2023) reveal that whether the platform adopts blockchain technology is related to the sales mode of suppliers. By comparing Scenario D and Scenario S, the result demonstrates that the platform needs to comprehensively trade off the relative size of the blockchain fixed costs on the two sides and the significance of risk-seeking and risk-averse users on the platform to improve its profitability. Introducing the higher-cost side of blockchain technology on the platform may result in higher blockchain value. Finally, we extended our research to discuss platform pricing when both sides of the platform contain risk-sensitive users, and the results are still robust. This paper novelly focuses on the platform pricing problem considering two-sided users risk attitudes and the effect of bilateral cross-network externalities, the research of which adds new theoretical knowledge and expands boundary of platform-based capacity sharing field. Furthermore, this paper uncovers the impact of blockchain technology on platform's profitability and bilateral users surplus under various scenarios, and depicts the decision-making process of adopting blockchain and conditions of improving revenue and blockchain value. The findings provide suggestions for platform s blockchain technology adoption decision. Future research can be conducted in aspects as follows. Capacity supply reliability can be regarded as engogenous decision variable rather the exogenous in this paper. Further, complementary to our focus of the cross-network externality, the impact of same-network externality on users utilities can also be considered in the future, so is the fairness concern of users under differentiated pricing scheme. Finally, discussing how blockchain technology influences product delivery time under capacity-sharing platform will be another research direction.

column1: Exaggeration or Concealment: Corporate Social Responsibility Strategy in the Blockchain Era
column2: Supplier greenwashing behaviors in corporate social responsibility (CSR) have become increasingly notable, often involving exaggerated claims about CSR initiatives or diverting resources to conceal violations. In this article, we develop a game-theoretic model to investigate the motivation of greenwashing and its intricate economic and social consequences, and explore whether blockchain technology can effectively enhance CSR efforts. We find that the tradeoff between exaggeration and concealment inherent in greenwashing plays a significant role in CSR strategy selection and corresponding performances. Specifically, if the exaggerating effect dominates greenwashing, the supplier has an incentive to adopt blockchain for self-certification in CSR activities. Conversely, when the concealment effect prevails, opportunistic behavior is more likely to occur. However, the integrative greenwashing coefficient has polarized impacts on the optimal CSR effort level, retailer’s profit, and consumer surplus. We unveil that blockchain implementation achieves the highest social welfare when the exaggeration of greenwashing plays a more prominent role, particularly when the CSR violation penalty is relatively subtle for both firms. Interestingly, we observe that greenwashing, despite its negative connotations, can eventually stimulate CSR efforts due to the incremental demand induced by exaggerated disclosures, ultimately leading to the highest social welfare.
column3: A. Concluding Remarks Facing the opportunistic behaviors in CSR issues triggered by substantial CSR investment cost, we developed a game-theoretic model to unveil the influencing mechanism of greenwashing and explore possible solutions to stimulate the supplier’s CSR efforts. We consider a two-tier supply chain in which the supplier selects from three CSR strategies: sticking to the initial setting, greenwashing, and adopting blockchain. Due to substantial CSR investment costs and possible benefits from greenwashing, the supplier may take advantage of CSR information asymmetry. Detecting the possible speculative behavior conducted by suppliers, some consumers raise greenwashing concerns, which blunt the efficiency in demand stimulation from CSR inputs. To alleviate these worries, the supplier can adopt blockchain for self-certification. Echoing the real-world observations, the influencing mechanism of greenwashing is captured in two dimensions: exaggeration in CSR disclosure and concealment of CSR violations. The combined effect of greenwashing plays a significant role in decision-making, CSR strategy selection, and corresponding performances. At a low ICG value, the concealing effect is dominant, causing the supplier to reduce CSR inputs and choose greenwashing to evade CSR inspections easily. Conversely, at a sufficiently high ICG value, the supplier is stimulated to make the highest CSR efforts due to the exaggeration under the greenwashing strategy. However, she prefers to adopt blockchain and faithfully disclose CSR efforts with self-certification. This is because the CSR investment costs are substantial, and the inflated disclosure with greenwashing attracts public scrutiny, resulting in significant penalties after the exposure of CSR violations. However, the value of ICG has opposite effects on operations and performance for the retailer and consumers. To be specific, when the concealing effect dominates the exaggeration, i.e., ICG is low, the high CSR effort leads to the highest wholesale price, retail price, and corresponding demand in the presence of blockchain. In this scenario, absorbing a high retail price, consumers are compensated by the high and faithful CSR effort. In addition, the retailer also benefits from the supplier’s blockchain adoption, as long as the joint penalty cost is not sufficiently high. When exaggeration plays a dominant role in greenwashing, stimulated by significant input from the CSR, demand, retail price, and wholesale price rise to the highest level under the greenwashing strategy. Then, it seems that the exaggeration effect contributes to society with significant CSR inputs, increased profits to the retailer, and improvement in consumer surplus, making greenwashing transform to “true green.” Nevertheless, the supplier prefers to adopt blockchain in this scenario. Identifying the possible divergence in CSR strategy selection among the supplier and other stakeholders, we explore conditions to achieve consensus within the supply chain. Investigating the impacts of CSR strategies on social welfare, we identify a win–win situation for the supplier and retailer to embrace the blockchain implementation. We also detect that the retailer may turn to support the upstream greenwashing behavior, due to substantial joint responsibility costs associated with blockchain-based transparency. Investigation of social welfare also identifies the positive side of greenwashing. When exaggeration dominates and the supplier’s violation penalty is moderate, greenwashing can drive the supplier to simultaneously increase the CSR effort to the highest level, benefiting the retailer, consumers, and society. At a sufficiently low value of ICG, the supplier has a strong incentive to engage in opportunistic behavior to avoid substantial investment cost because she can easily evade exposure to violation. The low level of CSR effort ultimately depresses demand, hurts the consumer surplus, and reduces the retailer’s profit, although the supplier yields some profit margin. It is urged to implement more effective detection mechanisms for CSR violations to increase ICG, thereby improving general social welfare. Finally, we explore the impact of CSR observability as an extension. Checking the robustness of the basic model, we show that the main results still hold when consumers can directly observe a proportion of CSR activities. In addition, we unveil the mechanism where CSR observability stimulates the positive effect of greenwashing or blunts the supplier’s speculative behavior. B. Future Research Several extensions of our study merit further investigation. First, our analysis focuses on the interaction between a single supplier and a retailer. Future research could consider the competitive dynamics between firms. For instance, in a competitive upstream market, a retailer may choose to source from a trustworthy supplier who utilizes blockchain-based self-certification or intentionally engage in an opportunistic supplier’s greenwashing behavior. Second, our study focuses on a two-tier supply chain. It would be interesting to extend our model to a multitier supply chain. Then, the sourcing relationships become more complex, enhancing the value of blockchain-enabled transparency and traceability. Within this framework, firms may experience reduced flexibility in ordering due to blockchain implementation, resulting in new trade-offs that influence the selection of the CSR strategy. In addition to supply chain structures, the retailers’ engagement in CSR issues is another promising feature for research. It is worth studying whether the retailer has incentives to devote efforts to inspect the upstream’s CSR projects or to get involved in greenwashing by further overstating CSR efforts through disclosure reports.

column1: Order Subcontracting Versus Platform Employment in Blockchain-Enabled Agricultural Supply Chains
column2: In this article, we present a novel cooperative model to address challenges in platform-enabled supply chains (PSCs) involving heterogeneous smallholder farmers. We examine a blockchain-based platform framework under two cooperation models: order subcontracting and platform employment. By analyzing order allocation and pricing decisions under symmetric and asymmetric information scenarios, we incorporate farmer heterogeneity to identify optimal cooperation models. Our findings show that while retail prices and order assignments remain consistent across both models, land transfer prices are significantly higher under order subcontracting. Neither farmers nor platforms consistently hold profitability advantages in PSCs. The choice of cooperation model is influenced by key factors (i.e., profit allocation and annual employment costs), especially under complete information. In addition, farmer profits are primarily driven by order quantity, with production costs closely tied to per-period yields. This study contributes to the literature by introducing a novel PSC framework that integrates blockchain technology and explicitly incorporates farmer heterogeneity. It also reveals how information asymmetry shapes cooperation outcomes in two distinct production–sales models, offering critical insights for researchers and practitioners aiming to develop equitable and efficient agricultural supply chains.
column3: In this article, we examined the cooperation challenge between a blockchain-based platform and heterogeneous farmers under both symmetric and asymmetric information scenarios within a PSC context. We introduced two novel cooperation models: order subcontracting and platform employment. Specifically, we regard the land transfer as a tangible cooperation guarantee and the adoption of blockchain technology as a mechanism to stimulate market demand. Given the computational complexity of the problem, we develop an iterative algorithm designed to efficiently identify the optimal solution. The effectiveness of the proposed cooperation models in enhancing the profits of both the platform and farmers is evaluated under symmetric and asymmetric information conditions. Detailed numerical experiments were conducted to validate the analytical findings and draw actionable insights. The study emphasizes the pivotal role of cooperation models in enhancing PSC profits and promoting sustainable development. In practice, cooperation models should be adopted in phases: the platform employment model is suitable for the early stages of cooperation, while the order subcontracting model should be implemented as cooperation matures. It also underscored the importance of considering farmers heterogeneity, as higher yields correlate with increased platform orders, and lower production costs enable farmers to accept more orders while maintaining profitability. In asymmetric information scenarios, it presents challenges for optimal decision making by both farmers and the platform, negatively affecting the overall SC performance. This also supports the central thesis that information sharing strengthens transparent PSC cooperation. Using these conclusions, platform designers and policymakers can create more equitable and efficient agricultural SCs, thereby empowering smallholders and contributing to the success of the platform-based agricultural sector. Future research could employ empirical study to significantly enhance the practical relevance of our theoretical framework, thereby addressing the current limitations of game-theoretic modeling, which is inherently stylistic and conceptual, and thus not fully comparable with real-world scenarios. Moreover, this study assumes that blockchain technology alone cannot resolve the issue of information asymmetry caused by proactive concealment of private information by PSC participants. In the future, data from IoT devices and AI-driven predictions could help uncover hidden information from PSC participants [60], promoting information symmetry. Future research could also explore how blockchain-enabled platforms can address systemic challenges in global agricultural SCs (e.g., fluctuations caused by tariff rate quotas (TRQs)), building upon our PSC framework to develop integrative policy approaches that recognize the pivotal role of enhanced transparency in transforming agricultural trade and empowering smallholder farmers worldwide [63]. Finally, addressing the added cybersecurity risks introduced by these technologies is crucial to strengthening PSC cooperation resilience [64]. column1: Blockchain-enabled sustainability of Li-ion batteries supply chain: tracking and sourcing eco-friendly materials
column2: The urgency to combat climate change and reduce greenhouse gas emissions has led to increased global demand for Lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries. Such batteries are widely used in portable electronics and electric vehicles. However, their adoption encounters challenges related to mining ethics, supply chain transparency, sustainability, and waste management. This paper proposes a blockchain-based solution that addresses these challenges in the Li-ion battery supply chain. Using the ERC-721 standard for Non-fungible tokens (NFTs), we tokenize all items/materials in the supply chain, ensuring data management, transparency, and ownership control. We integrate the Ethereum blockchain with the Interplanetary File System (IPFS) to handle NFT metadata and large-sized files, reducing storage costs and network congestion. We develop ten smart contracts (SCs) to facilitate various Li-ion supply chain functionalities, managing items/materials data and ownership. By leveraging NFTs, our solution promotes circular economy principles by facilitating secondary market trading, asset reuse, and sustainable recycling practices. We introduce a structured decision framework that empowers stakeholders to navigate operational and ethical challenges effectively. The effectiveness and practicality of the solution are demonstrated through system architecture, sequence diagrams, algorithms, and testing results. Furthermore, we assess our proposed solution’s affordability, efficiency, security, and generalizability across different industries.
column3: In this paper, we proposed a blockchain-based solution to address key challenges in the Li-ion battery supply chain, including mining ethics, supply chain transparency, product authenticity, sustainability, and waste management. We developed ten SCs to oversee the mining phase, ensuring end-to-end transparency, data and ownership management, and waste handling. By leveraging the ERC-721 standard for NFTs, we tokenised items and materials to enhance data management, transparency, and ownership tracking. We utilised the IPFS to optimise storage costs and network congestion while maintaining decentralisation and transparency. We evaluated the economic feasibility of our solution and suggested appropriate blockchain network selection for optimisation. The security analysis revealed our solution’s resilience and strength against common exploits and vulnerabilities. Additionally, we presented a structured decision framework to support stakeholders in navigating ethical, operational, and regulatory challenges. This framework offers industry decision-makers actionable guidance to ensure sustainability in material sourcing, improve profitability, and meet government-mandated battery collection and recycling targets. Policymakers would also benefit from an overview of the entire supply chain, enabling them to enforce policies effectively and identify violations with greater ease. Future research directions include real-time IoT integration to enhance traceability and compliance monitoring, as well as Layer 2 scaling solutions and alternative consensus mechanisms to improve cost efficiency and performance. While the modular and generalised architecture supports cross-domain adaptability, empirical validation of large-scale operational scalability remains an important direction for future work and industry deployment. Conducting pilot industry implementations would provide empirical validation and facilitate adoption. Additionally, integrating LLMs for automated compliance analysis could strengthen regulatory oversight and optimise decision-making. Exploring decentralised governance models, such as Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) and token-based incentives, may further reinforce ethical sourcing and sustainability enforcement.

column1: Blockchain and Machine Learning in the Green Economy: Pioneering Carbon Neutrality Through Innovative Trading Technologies
column2: In response to the pressing imperative of combating climate change on a global scale, a new era of carbon neutrality is steadily emerging. Achieving carbon neutrality is critical, and in the digital economy, technology-driven business models are essential for reducing carbon emissions through effective carbon emission trading systems. However, current research on carbon emission trading suffers from inadequate privacy protection, low efficiency in data sharing and model construction, as well as insufficient capabilities in automated and autonomous model building. Therefore, this study focuses on utilizing blockchain and automated machine learning for data sharing and modeling to enhance carbon neutrality. First, we design the architecture of the system and the mechanism for storing data on the blockchain. We then devise methods for storing and trading carbon emission transactions on the blockchain and construct the process for issuing carbon credits. In addition, our proposed method incorporates neural architecture search to develop a carbon trading price forecasting model. By leveraging data augmentation for carbon emission price time series and utilizing triplet loss for model training, we enhance the reliability and security of carbon trading investment through accurate price forecasting. The experimental results further demonstrate the robust performance and precision of our carbon emission price forecasting module. Consequently, our approach provides efficient carbon emission trading services to businesses and individuals, offering a robust solution for global carbon emission reduction and the achievement of carbon neutrality.

column1: Blockchain technology adoption in a supply chain: Channel leaderships and environmental implications
column2: Blockchain technology (BT) is widely implemented in businesses, yet its adoption within distinct channel leaderships in a supply chain has not been well studied. Following real-world practices, we build analytical models to study two strategies in which the manufacturer leads BT adoption (MLB) and the retailer leads BT adoption (RLB). Our results show that BT adoption does not necessarily create extra supply chain profits. Higher profits can be obtained when consumers show a strong preference for traceability or when the leader shares sufficient costs otherwise. Raising leaders’ cost-sharing proportions does not necessarily benefit followers, and the cost burden may motivate leaders to reduce the traceability level, thereby decreasing overall benefits. Interestingly, cost-sharing is not a “zero-sum” game for supply chain members, and sharing more costs as followers may help create mutual benefits. A comparison of the strategies of MLB and RLB reveals that the product price, traceability level, and carbon emissions in MLB can either be higher or lower than those in RLB. From an environmental perspective, we show that the carbon tax has a nonmonotonic effect on product retail prices. For the supply chain, it is possible to increase profits but simultaneously reduce emissions in each strategy, and a superior strategy that improves both economic and environmental performance exists. By modelling the regulator's participation in BT adoption, we further show that emission taxes and BT subsidies are not concomitant, and surprisingly, we find that the emission tax may either increase or decrease with product emission intensity. Moreover, our extension shows that regular operational costs for BT may impact the economic performance of BT adoption but other key findings remain robust.
column3: 8 Conclusion We investigate blockchain technology (BT) adoption strategies with the joint effort of firms in a supply chain. Allowing for environmental protection, with the regulation of a carbon tax imposed by the government, two strategies of BT adoption are modelled, i.e., manufacturer-led BT adoption and retailer-led BT adoption. The leader determines the traceability level, whereas the follower shares the cost of BT adoption with the leader. Based on decisions in terms of cost sharing, supply chain traceability, and product pricing, we explore the government’s policies regarding emission taxes and BT subsidies for social welfare maximization. We show that compared with the case where BT is not adopted, BT adoption does not necessarily increase overall profit. Higher profits can be achieved if consumers are very preferential for traceability or when the leader shares enough cost when consumers show a low preference for traceability. For individual supply chain members, increasing the cost-sharing proportion of leaders for BT adoption does not necessarily benefit followers because the cost burden of leaders may induce lower traceability; thus, the entire benefit for the supply chain diminishes. Interestingly, we show that allocating the cost between supply chain members is not a “zero-sum” game; sharing more costs as followers may help enhance traceability, thus creating mutual benefits. A comparison of Strategies of MLB and RLB reveals that when the leader’s cost-sharing proportion in Strategy MLB is higher (lower) than twice that in Strategy RLB, the traceability level, product retail price, and carbon emissions in MLB are lower (higher) than those in MLB. Thus, either strategy can be superior for environmental protection. Concerning emission regulation, we interestingly show that depending on consumers’ preference for traceability as well as the marginal cost of BT adoption, the carbon tax price has a nonmonotonic effect on retail prices. When consumers show a strong preference for traceability, a higher emission tax price leads to a lower retail price. Otherwise, when consumers are not very preferential for traceability, the retail price decreases (increases) in the emission tax if the marginal cost for traceability is small (large). With well-designed cost-sharing contracts, environmental and economic performance can be well balanced. In particular, given a relatively low consumer preference for traceability, when the cost-sharing proportions approach 2/3 and 1/3 for the leaders in Strategies MLB and RLB, the supply chain achieves higher profits but fewer emissions. In certain circumstances, either strategy can be superior to realizing Pareto improvement by improving both economic and environmental performance. Exploring government policies in terms of emission taxes and BT subsidies, we further show that emission taxes and BT subsidies are not concomitant. Surprisingly, with the increase of product emission intensity, the government may either increase or decrease the emission tax for social welfare maximization. For future research, this paper can be extended in several ways. First, other regulations, such as constrained emission permits and cap-and-trade, can be considered, and comparisons can be made with emission taxes to determine which regulation is more effective. Second, we have not incorporated green technologies in our research, and it would be interesting to discuss whether it is possible to enhance environmental sustainability by reducing emissions with the joint application of green technologies and BT. In addition, in modern practice, large e-commerce platforms play the role of retailers in supply chains. Thus, BT adoption strategies and regulation policies considering platform characteristics are worth further exploration to extract novel insights.

column1: Squaring circular supply chain management: A comprehensive overview of emerging themes and trends
column2: Circular supply chain management (CSCM) is the revolutionary integration of circular principles into supply chain management and the supply chain environment to achieve zero waste and outperform traditional supply chain sustainability models in advancing supply chain circularity. This study examines CSCM and the corresponding literature to highlight key research themes and trends. An advanced iteration of the Systematic Science Mapping analysis methodology has been designed and implemented with a Named Entity Recognition approach to extract relevant information from scientific articles. Key themes are revealed such as essential capabilities for circularity in the supply chain, circular business models, sustainable supplier selection and blockchain technology's role. The article gives insights into current research and identifies emerging trends in CSCM. This exploration aims to provide a nuanced understanding of CSCM's transformative power and shed light on its practical implications.
column3: This work gives insights into the current state of research and identifies the challenges and opportunities associated with implementing CSCM. This study makes significant contributions to the CSCM field:Our study conducts a comprehensive overview of CSCM research through clustering analysis and constructing a thematic evolution map. These analytical approaches offer a holistic understanding of the field and its development over time. The thematic clusters identified in this research encompass a range of topics related to CSCM grouped into four major research lines. These revolve around CSCM enablers, the application of CSCM considering the sector and context in which it is applied, the importance of logistical functions and processes and environmental sustainability. Moreover, the study highlights the hot topics in CSCM and those in which interest is waning.This work provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners, with a detailed examination of the themes researched in CSCM. This information can guide future research endeavours and inform decision-making processes in real-world SCM practices. Additionally, this study contributes to advancing knowledge on CSCM by unravelling emerging themes and trends. It identifies areas that require further exploration and highlights potential directions for future research, enabling researchers to delve deeper into unexplored aspects of CSCM.Lastly, this paper also proposes a methodology that enhances a previously proposed methodology or technique by incorporating NLP with NER. Our adaptation includes building an NER model for information extraction and thematic analysis. This replaces the tasks performed by SciMAT in Núñez-Merino et al. (2022) and gives researchers a more flexible choice of relevant topics for study and a solid theoretical basis for research design. The most significant improvement involves implementing a pre-trained language model to measure semantic similarity between articles. Unlike the initial version of SSM, which used various text preprocessing techniques to extract keywords from the document's abstract and title, the current model acts directly on the original text. Models such as this have contributed significantly to the development of modern language models, including large language models (LLMs). The validity and relevance of our research results emphasise the impact of this recent evolution in bibliometric studies and literature reviews, which have progressed from an analysis based solely on author-defined keywords to a wider analysis based on document titles and abstracts. It is conceivable that as NLP and generative artificial intelligence techniques progress in the future, it will be possible to analyse SSM with LLMs, which would allow full article texts to be processed.

column1: Implementation mode selection for blockchain technology in green product traceability
column2: Implementing blockchain technology to improve traceability can enhance consumer trust in green supply chains. However, the associated high fixed costs can pose challenges for companies when choosing the implementation mode. In this study, we investigate the value of blockchain adoption and explore a manufacturer's choice between third-party or self-implementation. Specifically, we consider the traceability level and the greenness degree in a supply chain comprising a manufacturer, a retailer, and a third-party platform providing blockchain services. Our findings indicate that self-implementation by the manufacturer increases the degree of greenness, and the retailer's involvement in decisions about traceability levels improves the manufacturer's traceability level. The highest profits for supply chain members are achieved when both parties opt for self-implementation. Additionally, self-implementation outperforms third-party platform implantation when incentivizing the manufacturer to invest more in green and blockchain technologies. Consequently, blockchain technology's value exceeds its costs, encouraging supply chain members to select self-implementation whenever possible. However, when the fixed costs or the cost coefficient of green investment or traceability are excessively high, the manufacturer may need to outsource blockchain services to a third-party platform. Furthermore, through comprehensive system dynamics analysis, we find that blockchain's adoption or non-adoption and imposing an investment cap on the product's green degree have a little effect on profitability for suppliers, manufacturers, logistics providers, and third-party platforms.
column3: 8 Discussion and conclusion 8.1 Discussion Our paper is of significance theoretically and practically. Theoretically, it investigates which blockchain implementation mode is more effective in encouraging manufacturers to enhance the greenness of their products and how this benefits them. This study is likely the first to explore the selection of blockchain technology implementation modes within a GSC context, considering consumers’ preferences for product traceability. Furthermore, our work treats the traceability level provided by blockchain as a decision variable that directly influences market demand. Our study also contributes to the literature by revealing when to choose self-implementation or outsourcing as far as blockchain adoption is concerned. As for practical significance, we derive the following managerial insights in this paper. First, firms typically view blockchain traceability systems as a disclosure mechanism that can enhance the perceived greenness of products. However, our analysis suggests that the perceived product greenness is not affected by the retailers’ choice of blockchain adoption models, the market size, or the traceability cost coefficient. The green level can only be increased when manufacturers are involved in determining the traceability level. Moreover, a sufficiently high wholesale price is required for manufacturers to stimulate investment in green technologies. This implies that supply chain managers should not make decisions based solely on direct effects but also consider the interactions between direct and indirect effects. Second, nowadays, consumer demand for transparency in product information is increasing. To cater to these preferences, both manufacturers and retailers should consider implementing their own blockchain systems. This allows firms to determine their own traceability levels and improve product information transparency. In this scenario, they can motivate each other to improve traceability levels. Third, regardless of the implementation mode the retailer chooses, if the wholesale price is high and the cost coefficient of green investment is low, the manufacturer should opt for self-implementation. Otherwise, outsourcing to a third-party platform would be a better choice. Moreover, if the fixed costs and the cost coefficient for green degree (or traceability) are low, self-implementation is recommended; if they are high, third-party implementation is recommended.

column1: Unlocking the potential of blockchain-based sharing economy in hospitality and tourism: A systematic review
column2: This systematic review is a trailblazer for the blockchain-based sharing economy concept, mainly in hospitality and tourism. It highlights the potential integration of blockchain across sharing economy sectors (e.g., accommodation, transportation, and business services). Following the PRISMA protocol, 43 publications from 12 scholarly databases were analysed. It identifies different types of implementations, including decentralised apps and specific functionalities that utilise blockchain. Key issues are discussed, including contradictory aspects (transparency vs privacy, centralisation within decentralisation, and users' euphoria vs technical barriers) and advantages (increased security, automated sharing mechanisms, and user participation). The review offers practical implementation paths for blockchain-based sharing economy systems in hospitality and tourism, emphasising the importance of context, scope limitation, focusing on increasing advantages, and managing technological trade-offs. It also suggests critical future research topics and action agendas for hospitality and tourism stakeholders.
column3: 5 Conclusion This systematic review follows the PRISMA protocol ( Moher et al., 2015 ) that has been adapted for hospitality and tourism research by Pahlvan-Sharif, Mura, and Wijesinghe (2019) to synthesise key information from 43 references related to the blockchain-based sharing economy topic identified from 12 scholarly databases. The results reveal a growing interest in blockchain-based sharing economy research, including in the hospitality and tourism field. It is found that the accommodation and transportation sectors are the most frequent sharing economy sectors referred to by identified studies, highlighting hospitality and tourism as the primary avenues for blockchain-based sharing economy innovations. The results show that the concepts vary but can be classified as decentralised applications (dApp) or just some functionality supported by a blockchain-based system. Some concepts demonstrate a completely on-chain system, while others propose a combination with an off-chain system. Key issues range from privacy-related aspects, discussions on why a third party may still be needed in some cases, and the choice of governance models and their consequences. Furthermore, one of the most crucial aspects is understanding the users’ perspectives. This understanding is essential for designing systems that truly cater to the needs of the end users. The results highlight the potential benefits of such systems, such as improving security and reliability, transforming the sharing mechanism, and incentivising participation. However, properly managing online and offline processes, stable performance, good usability, suitable consensus mechanisms, and enticing triggers to incentivise user adoption are essential. Based on the findings, considering the importance of context ( Muharam, Tussyadiah and Kimbu, 2023 ) and each model’s advantages and limitations, an implementation framework of blockchain-based sharing economy systems is proposed. This framework is designed to accommodate the diverse needs of hospitality and tourism stakeholders, providing a practical roadmap for the industry. The framework outlines the required steps to manage the dynamics of interrelated aspects of such systems in achieving a suitable implementation model, which includes identifying the scope, focusing on increasing advantages, and addressing technological trade-offs. 5.1 Contributions Theoretically, this systematic review’s primary contribution is the implementation framework, which shows the interconnected aspects that should be considered in deciding the best implementation model. Also, by emphasising in the hospitality and tourism sectors, this systematic review strengthens the position of the hospitality and tourism fields as thought leaders in sharing economy topics. This systematic review is a valuable reference for future research in hospitality, tourism, and other fields. The findings bring up areas where additional investigation related to the blockchain-based hospitality and tourism sharing economy is needed: • Trust dynamics: such as investigating how the transition to blockchain will affect trust among hospitality and tourism sharing economy stakeholders. • Interoperability aspect: such as blockchain's role in linking different sectors of the sharing economy (e.g., accommodation, transport, and business services). • Applicability and scalability: evaluate implementation models that can accommodate the dynamics of the hospitality and tourism sectors. • Governance mechanisms: further exploring the permissionless and permissioned schemes in the hospitality and tourism sharing economy. • Contradictory aspects of the blockchain-based sharing economy: e.g., privacy vs transparency or centralisation within decentralisation. • Technical trade-off investigation: including technological and operational trade-offs in hospitality and tourism contexts. • Economic Impact: assess the economic impacts of various choices of blockchain implementation models in the hospitality and tourism sectors. From a practical perspective, this systematic review offers insights for various stakeholders by presenting a framework for implementing blockchain-based sharing economy services. Moreover, to further inform decision-making processes and direct the development of more robust and efficient systems, the following actions for stakeholders are suggested: • Fostering collaboration among policymakers, industry stakeholders, and researchers to overcome challenges associated with and fully explore the potential of adopting blockchain-based sharing economy systems in hospitality and tourism. • Investing in proof-of-concept projects and research and development to enhance the feasibility of blockchain-based sharing economy systems in hospitality and tourism, including off-chain data storage and validation, scalability, security, usability, and attractiveness. • Establishing industry standards and best practices for blockchain-based sharing economy implementations in hospitality and tourism. • Establishing cross-sector collaborations to enable the interoperability of blockchain-based sharing economy services across various hospitality and tourism sub-sectors. • Increasing public awareness about the benefits of blockchain technology in the hospitality and tourism sharing economy. • Monitoring advancements of blockchain technology in the hospitality and tourism sharing economy and being ready to adjust business models and strategies as needed.

column1: Blockchain as a trust machine: From disillusionment to enlightenment in the era of generative AI
column2: Since the Economist magazine heralded blockchain as “the trust machine” in 2015, the blockchain paradigm has experienced crests and falls, including a recent phase of disillusionment due to its failure to meet the high expectations, e.g., to revolutionize record keeping, data management, and workflow, envisioned during its early history. However, despite the waning interest in this technology in some quarters, its deployment has become ever more essential in areas such as decentralized finance (DeFi), Non-fungible Tokens (NFTs), and other application domains beyond cryptocurrencies. In particular, recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) surrounding Large Language Models (LLM) offer new opportunities for blockchain adoption where trust and reliability become critical. As the blockchain technology transitions from a stage of disillusionment to one of enlightenment, anticipation is building for its mainstream adoption, with focused endeavors towards removing adoption barriers across diverse business contexts, exemplified by studies included in this special issue on Blockchain Technology and Applications. In this paper, we first survey the current state of the blockchain technology and then highlight its potential for enhancing trust and accountability in emerging phenomena such as AI generated content (AIGC). We conclude by introducing the papers included in the special issue.
