column1: Blockchain and value systems in the sharing economy: The illustrative case of Backfeed
column2: This article explores the potential of blockchain technology in enabling a new system of value that will better support the dynamics of social sharing. Our study begins with a discussion of the evolution of value perceptions in the history of economic thought. Starting with a view on value as a coordination mechanism that defines meaningful action within a certain context, we associate the price system with the establishment of capitalism and the industrial economy. We then discuss its relevance to the information economy, exhibited as the techno-economic context of the sharing economy, and identify new modalities of value creation that better reflect the social relations of sharing. Through the illustrative case of Backfeed, a new system of value is envisioned, comprising three layers: (a) production of value; (b) record of value; and (c) actualisation of value. In this framework, we discuss the solutions featured by Backfeed and describe a conceptual economic model of blockchain-based decentralised cooperation. We conclude with a tentative scenario for blockchain technology that can enable the creation of commons-oriented ecosystems in a sharing economy.
column3: 5 Conclusions The main motivation of this article was to explore an ongoing transformation in the economy, in response to technological changes. We focused on the role of value systems in relation to the wider logic that determines actions as meaningful within a certain context. The object of study was the sharing economy, and the main research question concerned how value could be assessed and distributed, based on the dynamics of social sharing. We began our theoretical inquiry with a historical account of value in the economic thought. A set of arrangements were identified that established capitalism as a dominant mode of production and determined exchange power as the main expression of value. Afterwards, we examined the context of the information economy, insofar it improves our understanding of the factors that have spawned the sharing economy as a new modality of resource allocation and exchange in societies. The transformation of productive relations was examined focusing on the changing conditions of labour and the nature of information. In response, a new modality of production, namely commons-based peer production (CBPP), was identified as the sphere within which a genuine sharing economy could function. Finally, the potential of blockchain technology was discussed as a medium of value that could crystallise the dynamics of CBPP, as the dominant rationality of a new economic system. Three interrelated layers associated with value were elaborated to decipher the components that would integrate a new system of value. The first layer, production of value, is related to the dynamics of CBPP and the sharing of use values, with the communities of contributors at the core. For the second layer, we examined blockchain technology as a medium for value record that could effectively determine the value of contributions to CBPP. We introduced a mechanism for decentralised consensus through the case of Backfeed, which relies on participatory evaluations and reputation-based influence. Finally, a token-based economic model was presented, which tentatively integrates this new system of value, providing the final layer of value actualisation. The tokens issued through collaborative processes represent a fair share of the created value and a reward for the contributors, and simultaneously they reflect the perceived value of the products and services they produce. Certain opportunities and limitations have been identified in relation to Backfeed and blockchain technology. On one hand, the Backfeed protocol can help productive communities, which engage in social sharing to create commons, to enact their own systems of value, through an inclusive, consensus-based approach. Simultaneously, it allows them to interface with one another and the market, and eventually scale and become sustainable. It thus can help us envision an ecosystem composed by a variety of value systems that fuel the circulation of commons in a sharing economy. In such an ecosystem value would become perceptible in a way that it shifts away from the logic of utility maximisation, towards the general benefit for the society. On the other hand, the application of Backfeed, and in fact any similar system of evaluation, poses certain challenges to the internal relations in productive communities, related to trust, reciprocity and intrinsic motives. Moreover, the technology is still at a very early stage and more empirical data are necessary to support its real life application. More generally, there are well-justified doubts on the extent that the blockchain alone can help communities solve issues concerning power and influence. At the same time, with the technology yet to reach a dominant design, it is too early to predict how it would operate on large scale. In any case, regardless of the development of blockchain technology or the eventual success of Backfeed as a project, its conceptual model allegedly presents an interesting scenario for the sharing economy and the role the latter can play in societies.

column1: Designing a fair and inclusive digital asset-based name-image-likeness marketplace
column2: Regulatory changes have enabled American student-athletes to profit from their name, image, and likeness (NIL). However, only a fraction of the student-athlete population is actually profiting from their NIL, which raises questions concerning fairness and inclusiveness. Motivated by that scenario, we look at technological solutions capable of sharing a limited amount of financial resources fairly and inclusively. Following a design science methodology, we define design requirements for such technological solutions after interviewing student-athletes, which leads us to establish the inclusive-meritocratic fairness criterion. Subsequently, we determine design principles that artifacts aiming at helping student-athletes should satisfy. We find that a solution that satisfies the proposed design principles is to associate student-athletes with digital collectibles represented as non-fungible tokens (NFTs). The core idea behind our artifact is that student-athletes receive royalties in primary markets after NFTs are randomly minted, plus deterministic royalties in secondary markets whenever a transaction involving their collectibles happens. Interviews with student-athletes validate our design. We conclude the paper by discussing how our ideas give rise to a new NIL design theory. • A framework for fair and inclusive name-image-likeness compensation is proposed. • Relevant design requirements, principles, and features are defined. • An NFT-based solution satisfies all design requirements and principles. • The NFT-based solution is validated with US athletes. • A new design theory for fair NIL systems in creator economies is proposed.
column3: 8 Conclusion We note that our design theory is highly prescriptive in nature; it can guide researchers and practitioners when designing fair and inclusive NIL projects while being abstract and flexible enough to capture different application needs. Moreover, our work touches on all the phenomena of interest for design research, as determined by Gregor and Jones [ 28 ]: 1) we instantiate a concrete artifact; 2) we create a theoretical and, thus, abstract description of the artifact; and 3) the previous points are guided by human understanding of the artifact, done by means of evaluations and requirement elicitation. In terms of future work, it is worthwhile to contemplate potential applications of our design beyond traditional sports. The fundamental principles of inclusive-meritocratic fairness that we propose are highly generalizable, as the challenge of equitably distributing revenue and recognition is not unique to NIL. Exploring other domains would allow us to refine our solution and make further contextual knowledge claims [ 31 ], as we believe our model offers a robust blueprint for other creator-centric economies where individual rights and royalties are critical, such as music, art, and digital content. For example, in the music industry, our solution could be adapted to support a collective of emerging, independent artists. Instead of athlete collectibles, a platform could issue NFTs representing a micro-share of streaming royalties, exclusive B-side tracks, or digital liner notes. The primary market would function as a discovery engine, where fans could purchase randomized packs of these assets. This mechanism would provide all participating artists with crucial initial funding and exposure, fulfilling the inclusiveness requirement. Subsequently, the secondary market would allow fans to trade these assets, with the value of an artist's tokens naturally increasing as their popularity grows. Similarly, in the art world, our design could empower a collective of digital artists, e.g., a gallery or platform could launch a curated collection where each NFT is initially sold in a randomized loot box format [ 32 ] at a uniform price. This approach would guarantee every artist in the collective a sale and an entry point into the market. As collectors begin to trade the individual pieces in the secondary market, the artists who garner the most acclaim would see the value of their work and their subsequent royalties increase. Whereas our qualitative evaluation through stakeholder interviews provided valuable insights into the fairness and inclusiveness of our proposed solution, we acknowledge that future work could benefit from complementary quantitative validation approaches. For example, controlled experimental simulations could be designed to measure behavioral responses to different fairness criteria and randomization mechanisms, thus enabling a more rigorous assessment of user engagement as well as deriving causal knowledge claims [ 31 ]. Additionally, willingness-to-pay studies could offer a quantifiable perspective on how fans value different NFTs, thereby enriching our understanding of demand-side incentives. These methods would serve to triangulate findings from our qualitative evaluation and support the refinement and validation of our artifact. While our proposed artifact promotes fairness and inclusiveness in NIL monetization via NFTs, it is essential to recognize associated ethical and regulatory challenges. Privacy concerns may arise from the storage and sharing of athlete data on public blockchains, which are inherently transparent and immutable. To mitigate such risks, our design avoids recording sensitive personal or biometric data on-chain and instead uses minimal identifiers linked to verified athlete identities. Additionally, speculative risks tied to the NFT market, such as price volatility or artificial scarcity, can expose student-athletes to reputational or financial harm. To minimize these risks, the proposed system focuses on royalty-based compensation, rather than asset speculation, and incorporates mechanisms (e.g., randomized minting) that discourage manipulative trading behavior. Lastly, concerns about exploitation are addressed through automated, transparent royalty distribution, ensuring athletes receive fair and traceable compensation. Future work could explore formal mechanisms for athlete consent and data governance on blockchain platforms, as well as longitudinal studies on the financial and reputational impacts of NFT participation. In addition, developing design adaptations that account for emerging NIL regulations across jurisdictions is critical to ensure compliance and scalability. Given the exciting future research directions above, we believe our work marks a meaningful step toward more just and participatory NIL platforms.

column1: Online quality endorsement to improve consumer trust: Blockchain or self-hosted livestream?
column2: Online products have long suffered from consumer distrust, putting them at a disadvantage when online brands compete with offline brands. To address this issue, many online brands have adopted blockchain as a means of quality endorsement to improve consumer trust. Alternatively, livestream e-commerce has shown the capability of both quality endorsement and demand creation by real-time interactions with consumers because the application of AR/VR technology and the use of online sales force can effectively induce the herding mentality. For many small and medium-sized online brands, it remains unclear which approach is better, so we formulate the key tradeoffs in the online brand's choice to improve consumer trust in the presence of offline brand's competition. Our research delves into the influence of three key factors on livestream e-commerce: the cost associated with adopting blockchain technology, the strength of positive network externality, and the potential downside of consumer returns. Contrary to conventional wisdom, we find that when the return cost is high and the network externality in livestream is weak, opting for livestream as a quality endorsement can actually benefit the online brand. We also find that the online brand is capable of mitigating the return cost by transferring it to consumers through charging a high retail price, which increases the likelihood of favoring livestream. Our findings shed light on the building and improvement of online consumer trust, contributing to the high-quality development of online-offline business in the new era of consumption.
column3: 6 Conclusion 6.1 Theoretical contributions In the e-commerce era, consumers often have limited trust in online products, making them reluctant to purchase. To address this distrust, the online brand has adopted two strategies for product quality endorsement. One involves adopting blockchain technology, which is effective due to its immutability, ensuring the life cycle traceability of authentic products. The other is to apply AR/VR technology to proceed with the self-hosted livestream. While this strategy removes the consumers’ ex-ante distrust, there still exist ex-post returns. Therefore, we are interested in which strategy is more effective for the online brand to ensure quality endorsement and improve consumer trust. We formulate the key properties of these two strategies and identify two important effects that shape the online brand's preferences: the “ loss aversion effect ” and the “ return cost transfer effect ”. These two effects underscores the importance of minimizing return risk and transferring the return cost to consumers. We further identify a “quantity coordination zone” that softens the competition between online and offline brands and mitigates the channel system efficiency loss. Our analysis reveals that when the livestream return cost is high and the network externality has a weak impact, the online brand may benefit more by choosing livestream for product quality endorsement, where the “ loss aversion effect ” and the “ return cost transfer effect ” are the key driving forces. In this situation, the competitive offline brand's profit also improves due to the quantity coordination effect, which allows the two brands to soften competition and achieve mutually beneficial outcomes.

column1: Artificial intelligence, cloud computing, blockchain, and the energy market in the era of energy transition
column2: This study explores the spillover effects between artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing (CC), blockchain (BC), and eight traditional and renewable energies using cross-quantilogram and quantile time–frequency connectedness approaches. The findings reveal a distinct inverse relationship between the lowest energy return quantile and the highest digital technology quantile. We also find that spillovers change over time, frequency, and quantile levels with hydrogen energy remaining a primary risk transmitter and crude oil as a receiver. Additionally, while digital technologies may impose short-term negative shocks on the energy market, their influence on hedging risks and stabilization is more prominent in comparison. Furthermore, the dependence between AI, CC, BC, and energy indices was insignificant before the COVID-19 pandemic but increased significantly afterward. This analysis is based on high-frequency data from Wind. This study extends the literature by constructing a comprehensive spillover network integrating digital technologies and energy markets. In addition, we conduct a dynamic analysis of asymmetric spillovers across short- and long-term time horizons, while also emphasizing the hedging and stabilizing functions of digital technology within energy markets. Our findings provide actionable insights for promoting digital transformation and strengthening international cooperation.
column3: 7 Conclusion This study fouces on the performance of digital technologies and energy markets under extreme conditions. The following three aspects summarize the main points of the empirical analysis. First, according to the analysis of the cross-quantilogram analysis, the energy indices are significantly negatively correlated with AI at the upper quantile level - indicating that AI can still play a crucial role in stabilizing the energy market even in the face of shocks such as the COVID-19 crisis. Second, we analyze the spillovers between digital technologies and the energy indices across different time, frequency, and quantile levels. The results show that HE and CO are the main risk transmitters and receivers, respectively. Third, the long-term spillover effects show asymmetry, with higher spillovers under extreme negative conditions compared to extreme positive conditions. This paper incorporates digital technologies with different types of energy indices into a unified framework and dynamically analyzes long-term and short-term asymmetries. It also identifies the main risk transmitters and receivers, highlights the importance of digital technologies in energy markets under extreme conditions and designs rational investment strategies. This paper provides some useful implications. First, investors should build diversified portfolios. According to the results of time-domain spillover, HE has the highest positive spillover effects which is the main transmitter of the eight energy indices. In addition to traditional fossil energy, investors are advised to diversify market risks by increasing investments in clean energy (CE) sources. This can be achieved through exchange – traded funds (ETFs) focused on renewable energy or direct investment in HE - related projects. By diversifying funds across asset classes, industries, geographic regions and investment styles, investors can reduce the impact of volatility in a single asset or market on their overall portfolios. Second, enterprises need to proactively promote the process of digital transformation. According to the results of cross-quantilogram, energy investment returns have not been fully eroded, and digital technology remains pivotal. In response to the increased spillover effects after the epidemic, enterprises should leverage AI algorithms to construct energy price prediction models. These models can analyze historical price data and geopolitical factors to forecast price movements. Enterprises should also establish specialized departments to enhance employees' skills in digital technologies (e.g., CC for data storage and analysis) and ensure a unified understanding of the value of digital transformation. Third, governments should play a policy - led role. Although the correlation between digital technology and the energy indices at different quantile levels shows that digital technology can have a negative influence on energy market, its positive effect far outweighs the negative one of the shocks. Governments should encourage the adoption of digital technologies in energy management through policy guidance - for example, promoting the development of smart grids that use AI for real-time monitoring and optimization of energy distribution. Furthermore, governments can allocate special funds for direct investment in or subsidy of HE technology research and development, as well as infrastructure construction. This can stimulate innovation in the clean energy sector, contributing to a more sustainable and efficient energy market. This study also has some limitations. First, due to the data availability constraints, we were unable to use panel data to analyze different countries globally. In the future, when each countries' data are more complete, we will conduct heterogeneity analysis across developed and developing countries, OECD and non-OECD countries, and G20 and non-G20 countries. Second, a wider range of technologies is now being used worldwide beyond AI, CC, and BC. When new technologies emerge, we will incorporate them into our research and conduct specific analysis.

column1: A process model of governance adaptation and performance outcomes in e-commerce permissioned blockchain networks
column2: E-commerce-permissioned Blockchain networks are enablers of new governance mechanisms, leveraging Blockchain technology to enable parties in e-commerce supply chains to collaborate on and coordinate transactions. Despite the widespread interest in forming these business networks, there is little understanding of how joining these networks affects the established contractual and relational governance mechanisms among supply chain partners. Consequently, this study adopts an input-process-outcome (IPO) process model to examine the effects of Blockchain-enabled governance mechanisms on traditional governance (contractual and relational) in e-commerce permissioned Blockchain networks and performance outcomes. We employ a quantitative research design and collect data from e-commerce permissioned Blockchain consortium members worldwide, analysing data from 361 individual respondents using CFA and SEM. The findings show that as the Blockchain platform's transaction-level and administrative-level capabilities increase, so do the changes in contractual and relational governance mechanisms employed by supply chain actors. Furthermore, changes in relational governance have a significant positive correlation with performance outcomes. However, changes in contractual governance negatively impact performance outcomes. Managers in e-commerce permissioned Blockchain networks can enhance performance by prioritising relational governance, adopting flexible contracts, streamlining administrative processes, and proactively managing risks, thus maximising the potential benefits of Blockchain technology.
column3: 4.4 Summary of findings Adopting an IPO model, the study examined the effects of Blockchain-enabled governance mechanisms on traditional governance (contractual and relational) in e-commerce permissioned Blockchain networks and performance outcomes. The proposed research model ( Figs. 1 and 2 ) exhibited strong explanatory power in predicting changes in contractual governance mechanisms (CCG), changes in relational governance mechanisms (CRG) and performance outcomes (PER). The findings could be summarised as follows: 1) the greater the perceived capability of the permissioned Blockchain structure (at both transaction and administrative levels), the greater the changes are in contractual governance utilised by supply chain actors; 2) the greater the perceived capability of the permissioned Blockchain structure (at both transaction and administrative levels), the greater the changes are in relational governance utilised by supply chain actors; and 3) changes in both contractual and relational governance utilised by Blockchain participants are correlated with performance outcomes. First, the two predictor variables examined in the study (TLM and ALM) demonstrated significant predictive power for changes in contractual governance mechanisms (CCG), explaining approximately 90.6 % of the variance in CCG. Additionally, TLM was found to be the most influential predictor (β = 0.780), followed by ALM (β = 0.205). This finding suggests that as transactional and administrative-level mechanisms become more effective, there is a corresponding increase in changes within the contractual governance mechanisms. That is, when permissioned Blockchain networks improve the effectiveness of their transactional and administrative processes, procedures and practices, this process triggers adjustments or modifications in the contractual governance practices of their members. The study identified five changes in traditional contractual governance mechanisms: fewer written contracts, less complex contracts, fewer formal written rules, fewer third-party intermediaries and less interpretation required of contractual terms due to the automated nature of contracts. Second, the two predictor variables examined in the study (TLM and ALM) demonstrated significant predictive power for changes in relational governance mechanisms (CRG), explaining approximately 56.7 % of the variance in CRG. Beyond this, ALM was found to be the most influential predictor (β = 0.567), followed by ALM (β = 0.484). The positive path coefficient suggests that as transactional and administrative-level mechanisms become more effective, a corresponding adaptation develops in relational governance mechanisms. Thus, private Blockchain networks with robust and efficient transactional and administrative-level mechanisms are more likely to experience positive changes in relational governance practices among participants. The study identified four changes in relational governance mechanisms that can be anticipated, including a lower level of trust, less risky trading partners, fewer informal rules and procedures and less reliance on the promises of vendors. Third, CCG and CRG demonstrated significant predictive power for performance outcomes, explaining approximately 98.3 % of the variance in PER. Although CRG was found to be the most influential positive predictor (β = 1.610), CCG was found to be a significant negative predictor (β = −0.709). Most importantly, the findings suggest that modifications to relational governance mechanisms improve performance outcomes. This finding implies that organisations that focus on modifying their relational governance mechanisms, such as a lower level of trust, less risky trading partners, fewer informal rules and procedures and less reliance on the promises of vendors, are more likely to achieve better performance outcomes. On the other hand, the negative path coefficient between CCG and PER suggests that as changes in contractual governance mechanisms increase, performance outcomes tend to decrease. This finding implies that when organisations implement or undergo changes in their contractual governance mechanisms, such as modifying contractual terms, their performance outcomes suffer. In the next section, we will reflect on these findings in light of governance theory and the existing literature to deepen our understanding of the implications for Blockchain-enabled governance in e-commerce networks.

column1: Online operations in a multichannel supply chain under service cost difference: The adoption of blockchain technology
column2: E-commerce has been growing at an unprecedented rate over the last decade. Nowadays, products are sold either on online e-platforms or at traditional offline stores. Two online operation modes between suppliers and e-platforms are dominant: reselling and agency. We examine the supplier's trade-offs for blockchain technology adoption in both online operation modes. There are two potential win–win scenarios in which the supplier and e-platform could mutually benefit. The advent of blockchain technology has not impacted the competition between online and offline channels or the selection of online operation modes. The decision of the supplier to adopt blockchain technology is also not contingent on the online operation mode. Blockchain adoption may lead to an increase in the wholesale price of products, but will not necessarily promote an increase in product demand. However, the supplier adopting blockchain technology produces an all-win effect, When the blockchain operational cost is low, all supply chain members’ attitudes toward blockchain adoption are aligned. When consumers’ trust in product information is lower, the relative effectiveness of adopting blockchain technology increases. Finally, we find that the government subsidy enables all supply chain members to achieve Pareto improvement, and supply chain coordination can be achieved through the provision of government subsidies.
column3: 8 Conclusions In this study, we consider a multichannel comprising a supplier, an e-platform, and a physical store. The supplier is suggested to carefully consider whether to implement blockchain technology, as well as the selection of operation cooperation modes between it and the e-platform. With and without blockchain technology, we compare the profits of supply chain members and the consumer surplus in the reselling mode/agency mode. We analyze the range of parameter thresholds that affect the choice of online operation modes and the incentive conditions for the supplier to implement blockchain technology. We also discuss the supply chain coordination with government quantity subsidy. The following paragraphs present a summary of the main findings and insights that emerged from this study. Without blockchain technology, an increase in consumer trust in product information has the potential to encourage the supplier to provide more precise product information. The online-offline channel competition remains unaffected by blockchain technology. In the reselling mode, the greater the bargaining power of the platform, the more favorable the wholesale price, and the more profits can be obtained. In the agency mode, a higher commission rate for the e-platform would increase its profit. The supplier’s choice of online operation mode also remains unaffected by blockchain technology. There exist two win–win situations wherein the supplier and e-platform could mutually benefit from an operation cooperation mode. With the improvement of the e-platform’s bargaining power, it tends to prefer a reselling mode, while the supplier tends to prefer an agency mode. The threshold limitations on commission rate and service cost differences that affect the supplier (or e-platform) to choose the reselling mode become tighter (or relaxed). In practice, Tmall.com typically charges a commission rate of 2 %-5% for most products, JD.com generally takes a commission rate of 5 %-12 %, while Amzon.com charges a commission rate of 6 %-25 %. It is more favorable for suppliers with smaller production scales to join Tmall.com . Large home appliance suppliers such as Gree, Midea, and Haier may choose to adopt a reselling mode with JD.com . Suppliers can refer to product service costs, industry characteristics, and commission rates to choose a profitable cooperation mode suitable for their development. Blockchain technology adoption may lead to an augmented wholesale price of products, and the other members of the supply chain can take a ride as well. However, this does not guarantee an increase in demand for the product. The lower the consumer’s trust in the product, the higher the relative effectiveness of the supplier in adopting blockchain technology. The decision of suppliers to adopt blockchain technology is not contingent on the online operation mode. The unit operational cost of blockchain is a crucial factor in evaluating the influence of blockchain technology on consumer surplus and social welfare. The lower the unit operational cost of blockchain technology, the more pronounced the relative effectiveness of the supplier adopting this technology. When the unit operational cost of blockchain technology is low, the adoption of blockchain by the supplier has a win–win–win effect: not only the supplier but also other members and consumers can benefit from blockchain technology. The high operational cost associated with blockchain technology may prove an insufficient incentive for suppliers to invest. Therefore, collaboration between supply chain members and the government is necessary to encourage the promotion and application of blockchain technology in supply chain management. This will benefit all parties involved, creating a mutually beneficial outcome. We also find that a Pareto improvement in profits can be achieved for both supply chain members when the government subsidizes the supplier. The supply chain coordination under government subsidy can be achieved when the operational cost and per-unit subsidy meet threshold conditions. For instance, this was seen in the cases of the Zhejiang Food Chain and the Shandong Pingyin Rose Industry. 19 19 https://sdxw.iqilu.com/w/article/YS0yMS0xMzY3MTAzOQ.html . The government could incentivize suppliers to adopt blockchain technology by offering subsidies and promoting supply chain coordination. Government-led construction of product traceability platforms and bearing the set-up cost can reduce the cost burden of suppliers. This would be beneficial for improving overall social and economic benefits and promoting harmonious development. In addition, we extend our model to verify the robustness of our main conclusions. We further consider another aspect of consumer heterogeneity, that is, consumer heterogeneity regarding the authenticity of products sold on the e-platform. Then we examine consumers’ privacy concerns regarding blockchain technology. Finally, we consider that the government subsidy has a maximum budget. When we do so, the results do not lead to any changes in our key insights. Our work may be expanded in various directions. First, the present study only addresses the optimal choice between reselling and agency modes. Future research may explore the possibility that the upstream supplier may sell its product in both the agency and reselling modes, that is, a hybrid operation mode ( Zhang et al., 2022 ). Secondly, we consider the impact of the consumer channel preference and service cost differences between supply chain members on the online-offline channel competition. In real-world practices, the sales of one channel may have an impact on another channel ( Yan et al., 2018 ; Shen et al., 2021). Such cross-channel effects should be explored for the online-offline channel competition, as well as the optimal choice of operation modes. Thirdly, it would be interesting to investigate the endogenous choices of commission fees ( Zennyo, 2020; Tsunoda and Zennyo, 2021; Kittaka et al., 2022 ).

column1: Dynamic optimization of e-commerce supply chains for fresh products with blockchain and reference effect
column2: Due to information asymmetry, consumers often rely on reference freshness when purchasing fresh products online. We employ blockchain technology to address this issue and enhance transparency in the fresh product supply chain. Specifically, using product freshness and goodwill as state variables, we develop a fresh product supply chain model involving a supplier and an e-commerce platform, based on differential game theory. By comparing traditional supply chain models with those utilizing blockchain technology, this study reveals that blockchain implementation encourages suppliers to increase their freshness-keeping efforts during distribution. Meanwhile, the e-commerce platform may reduce its advertising efforts. This strategic shift can result in a higher long-term equilibrium freshness compared to scenarios without blockchain implementation. Additionally, the research demonstrates that goodwill significantly improves when blockchain investment efficiency reaches a sufficient threshold. However, the study also highlights how reference freshness can lower the level of blockchain traceability. These findings provide valuable insights into the application of blockchain in managing fresh products on e-commerce platforms.
column3: 7 Conclusion Inspired by emerging practices in the fresh e-commerce industry, this paper proposes a dynamic decision management model for a fresh product supplier and an e-commerce platform in the presence of freshness reference effects among consumers. In model N, the fresh product supplier and the e-commerce platform decide on freshness and advertising efforts, while consumers make purchase decisions based on uncertain freshness information. Businesses can adjust their information traceability levels and decisions using BT in model B. Subsequently, consumers make purchase decisions based on updated freshness information. Our findings reveal that when customers heavily rely on the platform’s goodwill to shape their expectations, optimal freshness-keeping and advertising levels decrease. As RFE increases, the optimal freshness-keeping effort level increases, while advertising effort decreases, and the platform may be less inclined to adopt a higher level of BT traceability. Furthermore, optimal freshness-keeping efforts are elevated with BT, demonstrating its significant impact on the supplier’s freshness-keeping investment decisions. Simultaneously, advertising efforts tend to decline with BT implementation, reducing advertising costs significantly. Under steady-state conditions, the freshness achieved surpasses the traditional case when BT is implemented. When the BT implementation efficiency is sufficiently high, it results in greater goodwill. When considering the numerical example, we additionally observe that BT enables the supply chain to adjust and adapt to market changes more quickly. The following are critical managerial insights. First, when the supplier joins a system that adopts BT, they should also allocate additional resources to maintain freshness. For instance, MOA Planet, a South Korean O2O blockchain-based e-commerce platform, enables its suppliers with higher product freshness to disclose their freshness levels, distinguishing them from regular suppliers. Additionally, platforms can utilize BT to provide verifiable information, thereby reducing advertising activities. Meanwhile, managers are required to evaluate the balance between goodwill, freshness expectations, and BT’s investment efficiency to inform business decisions. For example, during a leafy green safety crisis, Walmart deployed BT to reduce the traceability time for contaminated products from days to seconds. This rapid response alleviated consumer concerns and reinforced Walmart’s goodwill as a reliable platform. Moreover, collaboration between suppliers and platforms is essential to optimizing strategies, ensuring product quality, and meeting customer needs. The impact of RFE depends on joint decisions made by suppliers and platforms, such as optimizing freshness-keeping measures, advertising strategies, and BT implementation. Management can be improved by promoting collaboration, transparency, and freshness. Additionally, FPSC operational investment efficiency can be optimized, ensuring continued success in the ever-changing market landscape. Combining the freshness reference effects with blockchain will produce meaningful and exciting outcomes. Future research can focus on the following directions. First, a model can be established from the perspective of BT to evaluate additional quality attributes of fresh food, such as sweetness and taste, and assess blockchain’s effectiveness in improving consumer satisfaction. Second, the coordination contract between supply chain members should be explored. This includes focusing on effectively combining the freshness reference effect with BT through coordination and cooperation, further optimizing supply chain management and product quality control.

column1: Shaping the future through developing and managing breakthrough innovations: A new conceptual framework
column2: Breakthrough innovations and technologies have gained increasing attention and have the potential to contribute to the development of a better society. Important breakthrough innovations and emerging technologies include fifth generation (5G) telecommunications technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), internet of things, digital platforms and businesses, autonomous vehicles, blockchain, e-payment/e-commerce technologies, and renewable energies. By reviewing recent papers published in Technological Forecasting and Social Change, this study proposes a novel conceptual framework for the development and design of such breakthrough technologies. There are three levels in this pyramidal framework: (i) exploring and identifying breakthrough innovations and emerging technologies; (ii) analyzing and managing breakthrough technological innovations and their innovation ecosystems; (iii) synthesizing and strategizing breakthrough innovations such as through digital platforms and businesses. This study makes two important contributions. First, by reviewing a set of coherent studies that shed light on the theoretical and empirical boundaries of research and knowledge in this area, this study pushes these boundaries with the goal of advancing the development and management of breakthrough innovations. Second, this study proposes a novel, integrative conceptual framework which encompasses different levels of activities associated with breakthrough innovations which could help develop and manage breakthrough innovations for the society of tomorrow.

and relationships between firms and their key stakeholders in fostering
the development of breakthrough innovations in the era of AI and digital
transformation.

column1: Blockchain adoption for product freshness traceability under platform competition
column2: ABSTRACT With the rapid development of e-commerce, a large number of online platforms specialising in fresh product have entered the market. Previous studies have rarely considered how to efficiently deliver the product’s freshness status to customers. In this paper, we establish a game model that consists of two competitive online platforms, which operate vertically differentiated fresh product on the same market. The product freshness is uncertain due to the opaque delivery process and consumers may have the risk-averse attitude, while platforms could opt to deploy blockchain to trace the product’s logistic information in real time and eliminate the consumer’s risk-averse attitude. Our finding shows that when the platform competition and the consumer’s risk-averse attitude are high, both platforms would like to adopt blockchain technology; With the moderate platform competition and the consumer’s risk-averse attitude, neither platform wants to adopt blockchain technology. Otherwise, only one platform would like to adopt blockchain technology. Moreover, when one platform deploys blockchain, the other one can free ride and become better off. Finally, we analyse consumer surplus and social welfare under different scenarios. A win-win-win situation can be achieved among platforms, consumer surplus, and social welfare when both platforms deploy blockchain technology.
column3: The fresh product industry is highly competitive with multiple platforms vying for market share. Consumers pay more attention to safe, healthy, high-quality fresh product when purchasing online. In the presence of the uncertain product freshness status, consumers may have risk-averse behaviour. To eliminate the freshness status uncertainty, blockchain technology can be utilised to trace the logistic information of the fresh product’s delivering process. However, the implementation of blockchain technology would heighten the competition among platforms and there is a cost to deploying blockchain. The platforms have to weigh the benefits and drawbacks to make a decision on whether to adopt blockchain. Therefore, we consider a game model that involves two platforms competing with the other while offering different product, and consumers are risk-averse. The platforms have the option to incorporate blockchain technology, which would help eliminate uncertainty that consumers may have regarding the freshness of the product. This, in turn, would increase consumer trust in the platforms. Some important results are summarised as follows. First, in highly competitive platform environments with the high consumer’s risk-averse attitude, both platforms would adopt blockchain. When the consumers’ risk-averse attitude and platform competition are moderate, neither of the platforms tends to adopt blockchain technology. Otherwise, only one platform adopts blockchain technology. Second, compared to neither of platforms using blockchain technology, only one platform using blockchain technology can also have a positive impact on the rival platform due to the free rider tendency. Third, we find when the consumer’s risk-averse attitude among consumers and the intensity of competition between the two platforms are high, a win-win-win situation for platforms, consumer surplus, and social welfare can be achieved. We also identify the conditions for maximising social welfare under different scenarios, showing that social welfare can be maximised in all four scenarios. This paper can provide management suggestions for all parties in the supply chain. First, the superior platform should adopt blockchain technology when the consumer’s risk-averse attitude is high; While for the inferior platform, it should adopt blockchain technology when either the consumer’s risk-averse attitude or the intensity of competition between the two platforms is high. Second, for consumers, they should pay regular attention to the quality of product and services provided by fresh food platforms, and fully understand the source of product, transportation routes and other information to help platforms improve and enhance product quality and service levels. Finally, for the entire society, the relevant departments should promote the application and development of blockchain technology in the field of fresh food e-commerce through policy support and financial investment. They should encourage the technological innovation of the entire industry, and prompt the platform to continuously improve product quality and service level, so as to realise a multi-win situation. There are several potential directions for future research. First, this paper only analyses the competition between the two platforms. In practice, considering the competition between two supply chains may get some new implications and deserve to be discussed in the future. Second, future study can consider either the platform or the third-party logistic could exert effort to increase the freshness of the product. column1: Fight Against Counterfeits: Traditional Anticounterfeiting Versus Blockchain Adoption
column2: Counterfeits have spread across nearly every product category, posing significant financial and reputational threats to brand companies. In response, companies are adopting various strategies to address this issue, including blockchain adoption and traditional anticounterfeiting. Specifically, anticounterfeiting aims to reduce or eliminate counterfeits from the market, increasing the likelihood that consumers will purchase the authentic product. In contrast, blockchain adoption allows consumers who engage with it to fully recognize the authentic product. In this article, we build analytical models to explore a brand company’s optimal strategies by considering a market where consumers are categorized into two groups based on their awareness of counterfeits: informed consumers and uninformed consumers. Our findings suggest that the brand company should implement anticounterfeiting when there are more uninformed consumers and the initial proportion of the authentic product is high. Otherwise, blockchain adoption is the better strategy. Furthermore, while both strategies effectively combat counterfeits, they should not be viewed solely as substitutes. When the initial proportion of the authentic product is low and the reputation loss is not significant, the company tends to earn more from anticounterfeiting when adopting blockchain compared to when blockchain is not used. In other words, the two strategies are complementary.
column3: Due to the prevalence of counterfeits in nearly every industry, consumers inevitably make mistaken purchases of counterfeit products, posing significant challenges for brand companies that produce the authentic product. On one hand, this trend erodes the market share of brand companies, leading to decreased sales. On the other hand, when consumers unknowingly buy counterfeits, they may develop negative attitudes toward the brand, resulting in substantial reputation loss. Given these challenges, it is crucial for brand companies to implement effective strategies to combat counterfeiting. Two particularly important and commonly used strategies are blockchain technology and traditional anticounterfeiting. Blockchain offers a revolutionary approach by providing consumers with the ability to verify the authenticity of products through secure and transparent digital records. In contrast, traditional anticounterfeiting encompasses a range of tactics, such as enhancing barriers to imitation and implementing legal enforcement strategies. These efforts aim to eliminate counterfeits and increase the likelihood that consumers will successfully acquire the authentic product. In this article, we build analytical models to capture consumer purchase behavior and firms’ payoffs, and quantitatively compare two strategies: blockchain adoption and traditional anticounterfeiting. In particular, we distinguish between informed and uninformed consumers based on their counterfeit awareness, and explore the interaction between the two combating strategies through mathematical analysis. Furthermore, our results are validated through extensive robustness checks, ensuring the reliability of our findings. Our main findings are summarized as follows. We show that the brand company has a stronger incentive to adopt blockchain technology when the potential reputation loss from uninformed consumers purchasing counterfeits is significant. In addition, the effects of the initial proportion of the authentic product and the proportion of informed consumers on the brand company’s incentives are nonmonotonic. Furthermore, when the brand company implements anticounterfeiting, it will completely eliminate counterfeits if the initial proportion of the authentic product is relatively high. However, if this proportion is lower, the company may tolerate some counterfeits. Interestingly, as the initial proportion of the authentic product increases, the brand company is likely to invest more efforts into anticounterfeiting, even if it cannot completely remove all counterfeits. By comparing the two strategies, our results indicate that the brand company should implement anticounterfeiting when there are more uninformed consumers and when the initial proportion of the authentic product is high. Conversely, in other situations, the company is better off adopting blockchain technology. It is important to note that while both strategies can effectively combat counterfeits, our findings surprisingly suggest that the brand company should not view them solely as substitute methods. Specifically, when the initial proportion of the authentic product is low and the potential reputation loss is not significant, the company exerts more anticounterfeiting efforts when adopting blockchain compared to when blockchain is not utilized. Besides, with one strategy in place, the other has a more significant impact on improving the payoff. In other words, the two strategies are complementary. Our study is among the first to compare blockchain technology with traditional anticounterfeiting in combating counterfeits. There are several potential future research directions. First, this article focuses on deceptive counterfeits and only considers the decisions made by the brand company. However, when considering nondeceptive counterfeits, it is important to note that the pricing strategies and production levels of counterfeit producers may influence consumer purchasing behavior. Future research could extend to examine these decisions and explore how brand companies strategically respond to the actions of counterfeit producers. Second, this article focuses on consumers intending to purchase the authentic product. However, in reality, there may be consumers who intentionally buy counterfeits, especially in the luxury industry. It would be insightful to explore the brand company’s anticounterfeiting strategies when there are different types of consumers. Third, our model can be extended to a supply chain setting that includes both producers and sellers. It would be insightful to investigate which firm should take responsibility for combating counterfeits.

column1: Can Blockchain-Based Authenticity Disclosures Increase Consumer Trust in Online Advertising?
column2: Fake advertising is a type of commercial disinformation that has profound negative implications for the online advertising ecosystem. However, it is often ignored in societal discourse and scientific research. Whereas disinformation labeling literature suggests fact-checking labels to be an effective solution to minimize the effects of disinformation, these labels are not always trusted by users and may decrease belief in accurate information. In two studies conducted in different contexts (Instagram and Google search ads), this paper investigates whether using blockchain-based disclosures of advertising authenticity could help increase consumer perceptions of ad and brand credibility. It also examines whether such authenticity disclosures lead to more favorable attitudes. The results of both studies show that this is not the case: blockchain-based authenticity disclosures do not positively affect credibility or attitudes. However, further analyses of different disclosure communication strategies show that disclosures communicating the ad source without mentioning the use of blockchain are perceived as more understandable, translating to positive ad- and brand-related effects. These findings have significant implications for existing blockchain-based solutions that guarantee online information integrity and product authenticity, and for future implementation of the European Union’s Digital Product Passports.
column3: 2011). Second, this study applies and empirically tests the framework of communication strategies for labeling online information described by Spradling, Straub, and Strong ( 2021). Our findings reveal that an evaluative communication strategy, or a strategy that combines both informative and evaluative elements, is most effective at enhancing perceptions of information credibility via increasing the understandability of the label. Therefore, our study contributes to research on advertising disclosures by demonstrating this framework’s applicability for developing disclosures of advertising authenticity—and information labeling more broadly—showcasing its relevance beyond its original setting. Furthermore, the study broadens the framework’s scope to developing strategies for communicating the use of a complex and poorly understood technology. Finally, our findings on participants’ previous experience with fake advertising demonstrate that it is prevalent in the current digital landscape and beyond, thereby highlighting the importance of dedicating research to investigating how the harmful effects of this issue can be minimized. These findings also demonstrate the variety of fake advertising types to which consumers are exposed and exemplify their varied experiences with this form of deception. Unfortunately, existing disinformation taxonomies fall short in fully capturing the complexity of deceptive advertising as a type of commercial disinformation by failing to account adequately for the variety of forms that it can take (e.g., Bakir and McStay 2018; Ferreira, Robertson, and Kirsten 2019; Kapantai et al. 2021; Tandoc, Lim, and Ling 2018). At best, these taxonomies categorize some deceptive advertising types as varieties of disinformation (e.g., native advertising, Tandoc, Lim, and Ling ( 2018); clickbait and fake reviews, Kapantai et al. 2021). This calls for the development of taxonomies dedicated to differentiating between various forms of deceptive advertising. Doing so is essential because there is not a “one-size-fits-all” solution to addressing deceptive advertising. For instance, the purpose of this study was to test the efficacy of blockchain-based disclosures of advertising authenticity to communicate that advertising is authentic because it came from a legitimate source. While this type of solution has the potential to address fake advertising (defined earlier as advertising that involves deception from a source external to the brand featured in the ad), it cannot necessarily help to address false advertising (in which the brand itself is involved in disseminating deception) because blockchain does not have the ability to verify claims. Therefore, distinguishing between different types of advertising deception opens new avenues for research. This study takes the first step in this direction, drawing on theoretical and legal definitions of similar constructs to introduce and define the concept of fake advertising. In this way, the study helps to differentiate fake advertising from other forms of advertising deception and thus helps to increase the conceptual clarity of this construct. In turn, future research can draw on this definition as a starting point for differentiating between other forms of advertising deception and developing a dedicated, comprehensive taxonomy of deceptive advertising types. By distinguishing fake from false advertising, this study also clarifies the direction that future research can take in order to develop targeted interventions that more effectively address these deceptive advertising types. For instance, the distinction between fake and false advertising clearly demarcates the source of deception. In the case of false advertising, the source of deception is apparent (i.e., the brand itself). Therefore, future research on false advertising may continue to focus on the ad content itself—specifically: (a) what characteristics distinguish false advertising claims, and (b) how advertising literacy interventions can be improved to help consumers identify and refute misleading information in practice. Alternatively, the source of fake advertising is often unclear. Therefore, future research on fake advertising may focus on identifying its source, analyzing diffusion patterns (e.g., via bots, fake social media accounts) to improve algorithmic detection. In turn, this could enable digital media platforms to more effectively detect and label (or remove) fake advertisements. The study findings also provide valuable insights for shaping policies on advertising malpractice. By identifying fake advertising to be just one form of deceptive advertising and demonstrating the different types of fake advertising that consumers encounter, this study advocates for a more nuanced approach to regulating deception in advertising. To this end, policies regulating deceptive advertising should make more granular distinctions between its various forms in order to address them more effectively. Doing so will also help to identify which types of advertising deception are in urgent need of addressing, and which may be tolerated as a “necessary evil.” Practical Implications Although this study focused on using blockchain-based disclosures to communicate ad-related information to consumers, the findings may also have implications for firms already utilizing blockchain-based labels for communicating other types of commercial (e.g., product- or brand-related) information, and for regulators in relation to the recent implementation of the EU’s Digital Product Passports. It seems that, from a consumer perspective, blockchain-based disclosures may not be the most effective way of communicating this information. Therefore, firms and regulators must carefully evaluate the efficacy of such solutions to bring added value to consumers. Currently, Instagram and Google have already implemented disclosures that communicate basic ad source metadata to their consumers. Our results support the efficacy of this practice, demonstrating that simple disclosures providing a contextual explanation of how the information should be interpreted seem to be the best way to communicate ad provenance information to consumers. Future research could investigate whether this approach also applies to communicating other types of commercial information, such as product-related information, as required by the EU’s Digital Product Passports. Furthermore, the high incidence of previous experience with deceptive advertising and high perceptions of the seriousness of this issue in our samples suggest that deceptive advertising is a societal problem requiring urgent attention alongside other forms of disinformation. However, our results also suggest that consumers do not see blockchain as a viable solution to this problem. As mentioned earlier, this view could be attributed to a need for more trust in blockchain technology. Practitioners should be cautious about disposing with blockchain for information integrity altogether: indeed, simply stating the source origin of an advertisement or other piece of content without verification may encourage fraudsters to do the same. Therefore, we recommend that practitioners continue to implement blockchain-based solutions for information integrity, albeit on the back end at present. Such an approach is successfully adopted by various blockchain-based information integrity solutions (e.g., Provenance). In the meantime, we encourage regulators to develop educational campaigns about blockchain’s true characteristics and possibilities. These actions will increase consumer understanding, trust and adoption of blockchain (Antsipava et al. 2024b), allowing this technology’s full potential for information integrity to be realized. Limitations and Suggestions for Future Research From a signaling theory perspective, this study did not measure consumer perceptions of information asymmetry or blockchain trust. It may be that for blockchain-based authenticity disclosures to signal ad credibility effectively, consumers must first: a) perceive an information asymmetry between themselves and the brand, b) believe that blockchain-based authenticity disclosures help to reduce this asymmetry, and c) develop trust towards blockchain technology in this context. Therefore, future research could examine whether blockchain-based authenticity disclosures help reduce information asymmetry and which types of information help to facilitate this. Furthermore, future research could investigate whether technological trust is a necessary pre-condition for reducing information asymmetry, in order to extend the application of signaling theory to technological contexts. From a methodological perspective, disclosure understandability and trust were measured prior to ad and brand credibility and attitude variables, which may have primed participants to question their perceptions of understandability and trust toward the disclosure. This approach may have led to a suppression effect, resulting in less favorable perceptions of ad and brand credibility and trust than they had initially, and it could explain the lack of significant positive effects of blockchain-based disclosures on these variables. Therefore, future studies should avoid the potential effects of priming by carefully considering question-order effects. Furthermore, this study tested the efficacy of blockchain-based disclosures in the context of ads for one product category. It may be that the risks of fake advertising are higher in other product categories, such as health or luxury goods, which could influence the effectiveness of blockchain-based disclosures in such contexts. Therefore, replication studies are needed to generalize the results to other product categories. Ultimately, this study tested just one solution to address fake advertising, and future research must continue investigating alternative solutions to reduce its impact. column1: Team Experience and ICO Success: An Empirical Study of Entrepreneurs in Blockchain Projects
column2: Initial coin offering (ICO), based on the blockchain technology, has emerged as a new fundraising mechanism in entrepreneurial finance for ventures to raise capital via crowdfunding. Building upon the limited yet growing body of literature on the interaction of entrepreneurship, crowdfunding, and organizational learning, this article aims to investigate the relationship between entrepreneur teams’ functional-based experience and crowdfunding success with a focus on the ICOs of blockchain projects. We also examine the moderating roles of the characteristics of blockchain projects on the relationship. The study collects empirical data on 428 blockchain projects which had completed their ICOs. Logistic regression models are developed to test hypotheses. The results show that entrepreneurial teams’ technically related ICO experience has a positive impact on their ICO success while commercially related ICO experience has a negative impact. Further examination shows that the sector factor significantly moderates both impacts. The moderating effect of soft caps is found insignificant. These findings add to the existing literature by highlighting the impact of entrepreneurs’ experience on the success of their ICO projects and have implications for practice on managing entrepreneurial team to improve crowdfunding performance
