column1: Introducing blockchain into low-carbon e-commerce supply chains: a differential game analysis in monopoly and oligopoly markets
column2: This paper proposes a dynamic game theory model based on the brand goodwill to examine how Blockchain Technology (BT) improves the performance of Low-carbon e-commerce supply chain (LC-ECSC) and what factors facilitate the introduction of BT in both monopoly and oligopoly competition market. Through analytical models, this paper finds that BT can improve LC-ECSCs performance through the brand premium effect and brand attraction effect in monopoly markets. However, in oligopoly competition markets, these effects of BT diminish as competition intensifies. In terms of introduction, in monopoly markets, the introduction of BT has consistently proven to be the optimal strategy for LC-ECSCs. In oligopoly competition markets, the optimal strategy of introducing BT will be affected by the degree of competition and the degree of BT to enhance brand loyalty. Specifically, both manufacturers could introduce BT when BT’s enhancement degree is significant and competition is low; otherwise, individual introduction strategies are preferable. Furthermore, for the stability of the LC-ECSC, only under an extremely low degree of competition can all members reach a stable strategy. This paper serves as a roadmap for enterprises to introduce cooperation in BT and provide valuable evidence for the government to promote the introduction of BT.
column3: 7.1. Conclusions It has been demonstrated by earlier research and business practices that BT is crucial to traceability and transparency. Based on this, this paper focuses on introducing BT to address the issues of decreasing consumer trust and damaged brand goodwill in LC-ECSC. It also explores the impact of BT on the operational decisions of different stakeholders in LC-ECSC, as well as the conditions for introducing BT, in the monopoly and oligopoly competition markets. In terms of specific research, this paper solves the optimal decisions of manufacturers, e-commerce platforms, and BT companies in different market structures by using differential game theory. It then blends theoretical formulation with empirical investigation to analyse how BT affects the equilibrium strategies of distinct LC-ECSC members under varied market arrangements. Finally, by comparing the profits of the LC-ECSC, the optimal decisions for introducing BT are determined. Therefore, this paper has tackled the three research questions that were previously posed, providing the following answers. First, whether in a monopolistic market or in an oligopolistic competitive market, introducing BT impacts the emission reduction efforts and retail prices of manufacturers, the big data marketing efforts of e-commerce platforms, and the BT traceability efforts of BT companies through the brand premium effect and brand attraction effect. For manufacturers, introducing BT not only enhances emission reduction efforts but also indirectly raises the retail prices of their products by increasing goodwill and potential demand. The conclusion is consistent with that of Ma and Hu ( Citation 2022) and Huang ( Citation 2023). However, it is worth noting that in the oligopoly competition market, the competition between emission reduction technology and BT affects the two effects of BT. When only one manufacturer introduces BT, the manufacturer has a major competitive advantage in both emission reduction technology and BT competition. In this case, the two effects of BT are significant, and the manufacturer could set higher retail prices. Furthermore, different from Ma and Hu ( Citation 2022) and Huang ( Citation 2023), it is also found that introducing BT does not necessarily lead to an increase in product prices. When all manufacturers in the market introduce BT and face competition from rivals, the two effects of BT are limited, and the manufacturer gradually lowers the price. For the e-commerce platforms, the two effects of BT would not only encourage them to increase their efforts in promoting manufacturers’ responsibility but also increase their commission income. However, in the oligopoly competition market, the profit of platforms is positively connected with the positive impact of competition on brand goodwill. And, the profit of BT companies is only positively connected with the number of manufacturers introducing BT and the degree of competition in BT. Second, the main factors affecting the introduction of BT are the cost of introducing BT, the competition between emission reduction technology and BT, and the degree of BT to enhance the brand loyalty. In the monopoly market, introducing BT is always the optimal decision for each member of the LC-ECSC. However, in the oligopoly competition market, when the coefficient of operating costs is high, the decision of not introducing BT is the ultimate choice for both manufacturers. Different from Li, Fan, and Wu ( Citation 2023) and Ghosh, Seikh, and Chakrabortty ( Citation 2020), it is found that only when the degree of improvement in consumer loyalty by BT is equal for both competing manufacturers and under appropriate levels of competition, dose the decision of both manufacturers introducing BT become the final choice. With the increase in competition in BT, the decision of one manufacturer introducing BT becomes the optimal strategy. However, if there is a significant difference in the improvement, the decision of both manufacturers introducing BT is the optimal choice under limited competition in BT. In intense competition in BT and for those manufacturers that introduce BT earlier or have a significant improvement, the decision of a single manufacturer introducing BT is the best choice. For those manufacturers that introduce BT later or have a less significant improvement, the decision for both manufacturers introducing BT is the optimal decision. It should be noted that as the increasing difference in the degree of improvement in consumer loyalty by BT and the intensification of competition in BT, the latter decision of not introducing BT becomes the best decision. Finally, in monopoly markets, manufacturers and e-commerce platforms could always achieve stable strategies on introducing BT. However, in oligopoly competition markets, manufacturers and e-commerce platforms could achieve stable strategies on introducing BT only when the competition between BT and emission reduction technology is extremely low, which is different from Wang et al. ( Citation 2021) and Saberi et al. ( Citation 2019), This is because platforms are more sensitive to the competition between BT and emission reduction technology compared to manufacturers. Moreover, as the competition intensifies between BT and emission reduction production technology, the revenue from distribution for the platforms may not be able to cover the cost of big-data marketing. Therefore, introducing BT is the optimal decision for platforms, but the region of this optimal decision is smaller than the choice range for manufacturers. This paper found that the decision of introducing BT is the optimal decision for both manufacturers and platforms only when the competition between BT and emission reduction technology is extremely low. Therefore, manufacturers and platforms can only achieve coordination under conditions of extremely low competition. 7.2. Management recommendations The LC-ECSC has faced hurdles like low consumer trust and inaccurate information. BT is key to overcoming these obstacles and ensuring the LC-ECSC’s ongoing development. The study proposes strategic advice for introducing BT across enterprises and regulatory suggestions for market competition by the government. For enterprises operating in the monopoly and oligopoly competition markets, the timely introducing BT is imperative for all low-carbon enterprises. However, not all companies should introduce BT sooner rather than later. The developed brands are advised to introduce BT early and offset any associated costs by setting higher retail prices during the initial product phase. Conversely, the developing brands could introduce BT before the product cycle to maintain stable retail prices. Start-ups are encouraged to first establish a pricing advantage and then introduce BT to gain a competitive edge. Nevertheless, the increased demand for targeted promotion of products following BT introduction may elevate big data marketing costs for platforms, thereby impacting profits and hindering BT acceptance. In light of this, e-commerce platforms should focus on two main areas for improvement: cost reduction and efficiency enhancement. On the cost reduction front, it is suggested that platforms establish designated low-carbon shopping sections or organise shopping events to consolidate resources. This approach can reduce the promotion and identification costs of products while verifying and ensuring their low-carbon credentials, thereby jointly enhancing the green image of both the platform and the manufacturers. In terms of efficiency enhancement, it is recommended that platforms accurately pinpoint the low-carbon competitive advantages of products. By improving the targeting and precision of promotional efforts, the effectiveness of marketing campaigns can be significantly boosted, leading to a substantial increase in revenue. Moreover, the revenue of BT companies is directly related to the demands of manufacturers and their willingness to pay. Therefore, BT enterprises should accelerate the pace of technological innovation, provide customised services, expand their business scope, and establish an open-source community through collaboration to share the fruits of innovation. For the government, it is evident that not all low-carbon enterprises will proactively introduce BT in a competitive market. To drive the sustainable advancement of LC-ECSC, government intervention is required to incentivise leading enterprises to utilise BT for recording their ‘carbon footprints’ and leveraging its ripple effect to enhance the profitability of the entire low-carbon sector. Furthermore, moderate market competition is instrumental in encouraging the introduction of BT, thereby invigorating the sustainability of the industry. Accordingly, the government can regulate market competition through tax policies, such as providing tax incentives to companies meeting specific emission reduction criteria. Simultaneously, it is recommended that deter ‘greenwashing’ and excessive emissions by imposing penalties and tax regulations. Excessive competition may impede the stable progress of LC-ECSC, necessitating the government to regulate the blockchain industry's access licensing system to modulate competitive intensity and ensure the healthy evolution of LC-ECSC. 7.3. Future work Future research can consider the autonomous development of BT, exploring market conditions where manufacturers choose to develop independently or collaborate with BT companies under government subsidy policies. Furthermore, although brand goodwill is one of the significant factors influencing consumers’ purchase of low-carbon products, price also plays a crucial role in consumer purchasing decisions. Consequently, future research could incorporate dynamic pricing mechanisms into market competition models. Finally, real-world market competition is not confined to duopolistic markets but encompasses fully competitive markets with multiple participants. Therefore, a key focus for future research should be on addressing the decision-making issues surrounding the introduction of BT among multiple competing entities.

column1: Exploring determinants of non-fungible token creatorsâ€™ engagement behaviors on metaverse-based NFT platforms: A multi-analytical SEM-IPMA method
column2: The advancing technologies of blockchain and Web 3.0 are transforming the decentralized nature of the Internet. Token-based services, particularly nonfungible tokens (NFTs), are innovative methods of performing financial transactions that have contributed to the growth of crypto commerce. Previous studies on NFT have focused on the role of investors, with a limited understanding of NFT creators. This study aims to provide a comprehensive examination of how NFT technology is utilized in cryptographic art by NFT creators. Based on the uses and gratifications (U&G) theory, the research utilizes a mixed-method approach combining in-depth interviews and online surveys of 1331 NFT creators from eight prominent NFT platforms. The results demonstrated that content and reward gratification were associated with NFT creation identification, whereas social gratification facilitated community identification. Both NFT and community identification facilitate consumption and creation behaviors. We also discussed theoretical and practical implications for stakeholders.
column3: 7 Conclusion This study provided valuable insights into the motivations and behaviors of NFT creators, extending the application of U&G theory to the emerging Web 3.0 context. Employing a two-stage approach combining qualitative interviews and quantitative surveys, the findings of the study highlight the importance of artistic value, content richness, extrinsic rewards, intrinsic rewards, self-image expression, and recognition in shaping NFT creation and community identifications and how these identifications influence creation and consumption behavior. Our study contributes to the growing body of knowledge of NFTs and offers practical implications for NFT platform providers, marketers, and policymakers. As the NFT landscape continues to evolve rapidly, it is crucial for researchers and practitioners to deepen their understanding of its complex dynamics and unlock the full potential of this transformative technology.

column1: Blockchain Adoption in a Supply Chain with Manufacturer Market Power
column2: We examine a supply chain with a single risk-averse manufacturer who purchases from suppliers and sells to consumers. Within this context, we focus on two channels that drive blockchain adoption by the manufacturer: manufacturer risk aversion and consumer information asymmetry. Regarding the first channel, blockchain enables efficient tracing of defective products so that the manufacturer can selectively recall defective products rather than conducting a full recall. This tracing ability reduces the risk involved in the manufacturer purchasing from multiple suppliers and thereby leads the manufacturer to endogenously diversify across suppliers when blockchain is adopted. The diversification enhances the manufacturer’s welfare due to the manufacturer’s risk aversion and thus drives the manufacturer to adopt blockchain. With regard to the second channel, blockchain stores details from the manufacturing process and reveals them to consumers, thereby ameliorating consumer information asymmetry. This reduction in information asymmetry improves consumer decision making that, in isolation, would enhance consumer welfare. However, the manufacturer responds by increasing the consumer price, thereby transferring potential consumer welfare gains to the manufacturer, and consequently serving as a second channel to drive blockchain adoption by the manufacturer. This paper was accepted by Lin William Cong, finance.
column3:
Our analysis establishes that blockchain adoption generically arises in equilibrium when the man-

ufacturer has market power. In particular, when the manufacturer has the power to adjust prices

and thereby extract gains accrued to other supply chain participants, then blockchain adoption is

incentive-compatible for sufficiently small adoption costs. Our main result contrasts with that of

Iyengar et al. (2023), which establishes that blockchain adoption does not arise in equilibrium when

the manufacturing sector is competitive. Thus, our work highlights market structure as a crucial

determinant of whether blockchain adoption arises.

 Our results also clarify the role of two different economic channels in blockchain adoption. We

find that both manufacturer risk aversion and consumer information asymmetry drive blockchain

adoption. The blockchain enables the manufacturer to diversify across suppliers, and thereby reduce

risk. However, this risk reduction increases the manufacturer’s welfare only if she is risk-averse.

The blockchain reduces consumer information asymmetry and thereby increases consumer welfare.

The manufacturer responds optimally to the increased consumer welfare by increasing the consumer

price, and extracting all the welfare gains. Thus, the reduction in consumer information asymmetry

serves as a second incentive for the manufacturer to adopt blockchain and compel such adoption

for her suppliers as well.

column1: In blockchain we trust? Demystifying the â€œtrustâ€ mechanism in blockchain ecosystems
column2: The purpose of the paper is to conceptualize and redefine trust within the blockchain ecosystem by exploring the trust construct across academic disciplines and its applicability in the blockchain context. We develop a conceptual model and testable propositions that extend the work of McKnight et al. (2001, 2002, 2011) to the blockchain ecosystem based on an integrative literature review. We conceptualize trust as a multidimensional, multi-object construct combining three major objects of trust: algorithmic trust in the blockchain protocol (platform), trust towards peers and services providers, and trust in decentralized applications (product). The model reflects the process of building a trust layer for users and institutions on top of the trustless technology. The paper demystifies the trust building process, from initial trust to knowledge-based trust, and its dimensions within the blockchain ecosystem, and, consequently, helps practitioners to build strategies that increase users' trust. The contribution to the academic literature resides in the unification of multiple perspectives on trust within an integrative conceptual framework to point out the mechanisms of trust building process, as well as to identify future research directions.
column3: 8 Conclusion The purpose of this paper is to conceptualize trust within the blockchain ecosystem by exploring the trust construct across academic disciplines and its applicability in the blockchain context. We propose an integrative conceptual model that extends the work of Mcknight and Chervany (2001, 2002) to the blockchain ecosystem. The model delineates the perceived risks and challenges of three objects of trust – the platform, peers and service providers, and the dApp. It also incorporates the process of building trust from initial to knowledge-based trust. Our model and propositions help researchers to examine trust towards blockchain technology in a novel way that includes trusting beliefs towards different objects in the blockchain ecosystem. The model is theoretical and invites an empirical investigation into its predictive validity. For example, it could be useful for both practitioners and academics to explore how well the model holds for the DeFi ecosystem. Specifically, the composability feature of DeFi - a function of high interdependence of the DeFi stack layers and ecosystem actors – is a major systemic risk for the ecosystem at large; and if one of the layers collapses, trust may be permanently breached. Future research could also test the model to identify the constructs that have an impact on trust towards each object within the blockchain ecosystem, as well as the relative importance of each construct in the model in explaining trust. As the model is holistic and combines constructs grounded in different disciplines, it risks losing some of the meanings related to trust in each field. In addition, some constructs (e.g., trusting beliefs in the dApp vs in the blockchain platform) may not be discriminant in empirical studies and might tend to factor together. Thus, testing the model and building measurement scales in relation to trusting beliefs for each object could also be a research priority. The literature has already operationalized most concepts in the model – e.g., disposition to trust measured by the subconstructs “faith in humanity” and “trusting stance” ( McKnight et al., 2002 ). The new organizational form, DAO (a decentralized autonomous organization), represents an opportunity for researchers to explore trust in uncertain and algorithmically driven autonomous organizations with no formal hierarchy. Testing the impact of challenges associated with the dApp (e.g., UX, network effect), peers and service providers (e.g., reputation, law compliance) and technology-specific challenges (e.g., scalability, Sybil attacks) on trust would add value to the blockchain literature. Individual differences regarding trust and contextual factors could have important implications for the study of users' trust towards blockchain. Researchers can also consider the list of questions we propose in Table 4 . Given that trust-building is a dynamic process, an investigation of the issue of trust repair once trust in the blockchain ecosystem is broken, as we have recently seen with the FTX collapse, may be particularly topical, both from theoretical and practical perspectives. Such research could investigate the process, mechanisms, principles, best practices, and costs and benefits of trust repair after a large-scale ecosystem failure (see, e.g., Gillespie and Dietz, 2009 ; Kähkönen et al., 2021 ). From a practical perspective, to build trust towards blockchain and its applications, the entire ecosystem should be trustworthy. The regulatory framework must be well defined for consumer and investor protection and compliance; the technical difficulties and vulnerabilities should be resolved, and transparent standards and protocols for protecting privacy and security should be developed, with the goal to increase institutional-based trust. This paper has produced insights into trust building towards blockchain ecosystems, which would be of interest to academics, practitioners, and policy makers. We hope that other researchers will extend our work.

column1: Optimal pricing and financing decision of dual-channel green supply chain considering product differentiation and blockchain
column2: This paper constructs a dual-channel green supply chain model that includes a well-capitalized retailer and e-commerce platform, as well as a capital-constrained manufacturer. The manufacturer sells two different green quality products through the e-commerce platform and the retailer. There are two portfolio financing strategies for the manufacturer to choose and decide whether to use blockchain. We establish four models of whether to use blockchain under the EP financing strategy (e-commerce platform financing and prepayment financing) and the EB financing strategy (e-commerce platform financing and bank financing). By comparing the optimal solutions under four models, we discover some results. Firstly, we discover that the wholesale price will be higher than the selling price of the online channel when the product greenness difference between the two channels is large, and the optimal expected profit of the retailer is not related to product green differences. Secondly, the EP financing strategy is the optimal financing strategy choice for the manufacturer regardless of whether blockchain is used or not. Thirdly, when the cost per unit of using blockchain is greater than a certain threshold, the manufacturer should choose not to use blockchain. Finally, the manufacturer's acceptable blockchain usage threshold under the EP financing strategy is higher than under the EB financing strategy, and it decreases with the smaller product greenness difference between the two channels under the EP financing strategy. In addition, we also make an extension that verifies our model and findings are robust.
column3: With the growth of e-commerce in recent years, academics and enterprises have been concentrating more on dual-channel selling. Research on green supply chains has also gained popularity as a means of addressing the world's serious environmental problems. However, using two channels to sell the same product can result in channel disputes and conflicts of interest, and in practice, manufacturers frequently have limited funding. Therefore, this study adds product heterogeneity and supply chain financing into dual-channel green supply chain management and considers the effects of blockchain usage. According to the different financing strategies of the manufacturer under the use of blockchain or not, we construct four models. In addition, we also make an extension in accordance with the different selling strategy choices of the manufacturer, and the conclusions drawn from the extension are consistent with the previous section, which also verifies that our model and findings are robust. By solving and analyzing the four models and numerical simulation, our findings are shown as follows. Firstly, the optimal expected profit of the retailer is not related to , and the wholesale price will be higher than the selling price of the online channel when the product greenness difference between the two channels is large. Secondly, by comparing the optimal solutions under the four models, we find that the optimal pricing when using blockchain is always greater than not using it. The optimal pricing of retailer under the EP financing strategy is always lower than it is under the EB financing strategy, no matter whether the blockchain is used; and the advance financing rate and the bank loan interest rate have an impact on the relationship between the size of the optimal wholesale price under different models, but have no influence on that of the optimal pricing of the online and the retail channel. Thirdly, through numerical simulation, we observe that the optimal expected profits of retailer and manufacturer are greater under the EP strategy than under the EB strategy no matter whether the blockchain is used, so the EP financing strategy is optimal for the manufacturer. Finally, when the cost per unit of using blockchain is greater than a certain threshold, the manufacturer will choose not to use blockchain, and we also discover that the blockchain usage cost threshold is always higher under the EP strategy than under the EB strategy for the manufacturer's and retailer's optimal expected profits, and for the manufacturer's optimal expected profit, the blockchain usage cost thresholds for the EP strategy are decreasing as increases. The research findings above allow us to derive the following management insights. Firstly, when using dual-channel for selling, providing differentiated products is beneficial for retailers, and the greater the product difference between the two channels, the more advantageous for retailers. Secondly, when manufacturers in the supply chain face capital constraints, actively providing financial support for retailers is a win–win choice. Finally, when using blockchain in supply chain management, supply chain members should consider their acceptable usage costs rather than blindly adopting. Although we explore the impact of blockchain use and product heterogeneity on dual-channel supply chain members' pricing, profitability, and financing strategy choices in this paper, there are some limitations. First, supply chain members often include more than one manufacturer and retailer, and future research could further consider more complex dual-channel supply chain structures. Second, we only explore the impact of blockchain use and the size of product heterogeneity on the pricing and profitability of supply chain members and do not consider whether there is an impact on the overall supply chain utility improvement. Finally, in this paper we only consider the ameliorating effect of blockchain use on market demand instability, and other effects of blockchain technology use on supply chain such as reducing transaction cost and improving the market potential deserve further exploration.

column1: Sales mode selection and blockchain technology adoption decisions in a platform supply chain
column2: In recent years, some large-scale e-commerce platforms have established blockchain systems (BSs) to improve consumer product quality trust degrees (QTDs). However, whether the BSs work eventually depends on the upstream manufacturer strategic decision on whether to join the BSs to provide product quality information authentication. The impacts of the platform sales mode selection between the agency and the reselling modes on the manufacturer blockchain technology (BT) adoption decision are examined, and the equilibrium strategy combinations between the platform sales mode selection and the manufacturer BT adoption decisions are obtained. Furthermore, the impacts of the platform and the manufacturer strategic decisions on the product quality decision are analyzed. The results show that the manufacturer may have more incentive to join the BS under the agency mode than under the reselling mode. In addition, the manufacturer should set a higher product quality level under the agency mode than under the reselling mode, after joining the BS only if the unit BT adoption cost is low. Finally, the QTD, the quality improvement cost and the unit BT adoption cost determine the equilibrium strategy combinations. The double marginalization effect in the channel and the platform channel power advantage are used to explain the above findings. Several extensions are provided to verify the robustness of the results and to broaden the applicability of the model and method.
column3: 8 Conclusions This work investigates a platform supply chain consisting of a platform with an established BS and a manufacturer, where the platform makes the sales mode selection between the reselling and the agency modes and the manufacturer decides whether to join the BS. All four strategy combinations, represented by RN, RB, AN and AB, are examined. The platform and the manufacturer profit functions are constructed and the equilibrium solutions are derived by backward induction for each strategy combination. The impacts of the sales mode selection and the BT adoption decisions on the product quality decision are then analyzed. Furthermore, by investigating the interaction between the two supply chain members, the impacts of the platform sales mode on the manufacturer BT adoption decisions are discussed, and the platform and manufacturer equilibrium strategy combinations are determined for different unit BT adoption cost, quality cost coefficient and consumer QTD. The major findings are summarized as follows. First, the product quality level may be lower under the agency mode than under the reselling mode in the platform supply chain if BT is adopted with a low unit cost. This result is controversial to the earlier results in the literature ( Xu, 2009 ; Ha et al., 2016 ). In addition, the manufacturer improves the product quality after joining the BS if the unit BT adoption cost is low. Second, the manufacturer BT adoption decision is dependent on the quality cost coefficient and the unit BT adoption cost. On the one hand, the BT adoption improves the consumer QTD and stimulates consumer purchase. If the BT adoption cost is not too high, the income from market expansion will outweigh the adoption cost so that the manufacturer will benefit from the BT adoption. On the other hand, the improvement of the consumer QTD will affect the manufacturer product quality decision and a lower quality improvement cost lowers the barrier for the manufacturer to adopt BT. In addition, the platform may encourage the manufacturer to join the BS by selecting the agency mode. Third, the platform and the manufacturer equilibrium strategy combinations are determined by the unit BT adoption cost, the quality cost coefficient and the consumer QTD. When the platform is the first mover, the equilibrium strategy combination is RN if both the quality cost coefficient and the unit BT adoption cost are relatively high, RB if the quality cost coefficient is high and the unit BT adoption cost is low, AB if the quality cost coefficient is low or if the quality cost coefficient is relatively moderate and the unit BT adoption cost is relatively low, or AN only if the quality cost coefficient is relatively moderate, the unit BT adoption cost is high and the consumer QTD is sufficiently high. When the manufacturer is the first mover, the equilibrium strategy combination changes from RN to AB in part of the area determined by the quality cost coefficient and the unit BT adoption cost. Fourth, a higher platform unit BT adoption cost raises the barrier for the manufacturer to adopt BT. In addition, the platform may not incentivize the manufacturer to join the BS by sharing the manufacturer BT adoption cost. This incentive works only when the quality cost coefficient or the consumer QTD is low. The manufacturer publicizing false product quality information will not be interested in adopting BT, but will choose to publicize false product quality information, under the reselling mode. When the market size is relatively large and the manufacturer unit BT adoption cost is relatively low, the platform can choose the agency mode to attract the manufacturer to adopt BT to eliminate product quality deception. Intuitively, the barrier for the manufacturer to adopt BT will increase when BT adoption cannot completely eliminate consumer distrust. A high commission rate or an endogenous commission rate will attract the platform to choose the agency mode. The above findings are insightful for any e-commerce platform with an established BS making sales mode selection decisions and any manufacturer making BT adoption and quality decisions in cooperation with the platform. The following suggestions are helpful to the platforms and manufacturers. BT can ensure the authenticity of product quality information and can increase product demand. However, the change in the consumer QTD will affect the product quality decision. Therefore, the manufacturer should comprehensively consider the quality cost coefficient and the BT adoption cost while making the BT adoption decision. The higher the quality cost coefficient is, the higher the cost is for the manufacturer to improve product quality, including R&D spending, equipment upgrades, etc. The profits brought by quality improvement may be squeezed by the high quality improvement cost, and the increase in revenue may hardly cover the BT adoption cost. Therefore, the manufacturer should join the BS only when either the quality cost coefficient or the BT adoption cost is relatively low. The consumer QTD, reflecting the degree of consumer trust in the product quality advertised by e-commerce firms, is also an important factor affecting the BT adoption decision. A high QTD indicates that consumers highly trust the advertised product quality. The QTDs of imported products and some consumer products, such as foods, drugs, cosmetics, etc., are often low since consumers usually have concerns over the quality information of these products. Manufacturers producing products with low QTD should join the BS to provide product quality authentication. Platforms with established BSs, such as JD.com , Amazon and Taobao.com , can encourage, although cannot force, manufacturers to join the BS by choosing the agency mode. Specifically, the platform should sign an agency contract with the manufacturer to induce the manufacturer to join the BS if the quality cost coefficient is low and the unit BT adoption cost is moderate. Future research can be conducted in several directions. First, incorporating platform competition into the research framework of this work may engender some interesting results since competition between platforms is very common. Second, future works can explore the impacts of the BT application in addressing information asymmetry on the manufacturer and the platform decisions since information asymmetry is a common issue in supply chains and the use of BT provides a feasible solution to resolve this issue. Third, counterfeiting in the platform supply chain is an interesting topic ( Zhao et al., 2021a ), but beyond the scope of this study. Therefore, future work can explore the BT value in addressing the counterfeiting issues. Fourth, it is worthwhile exploring the possibility for the platform to provide an additional contract to the manufacturer with a single contract already to form a hybrid sales mode. The impacts of the hybrid sales mode on the manufacturer BT adoption decisions can be examined. Fifth, important factors like traffic and clicks usually affect the actual contract and transactions in a platform supply chain, and future works may explore the impacts of such factors on the platform sales mode selection and the manufacturer BT adoption decisions.

column1: The role of fintech startups and big banks in shaping trust expectations from blockchain use in mainstream financial markets
column2: Through two qualitative case studies we explore the role of a fintech and a big bank in shaping trust expectations of blockchain use in mainstream financial markets. Drawing on Zucker's theory of trust we explore adaptations to the original blockchain made by these actors, and show how such changes may impact trust expectations from blockchain use. Our analysis identifies a blockchain innovation trajectory involving the co-evolution between technological changes and trust expectations as it moves from supporting cryptocurrency exchanges to mainstream business settings. Furthermore, we show that fintech startups and established big banks align their strategies with the widespread generalization and acceptance of blockchain as a sector-wide information infrastructure and position themselves in co-dependent relationships within the emerging blockchain marketplace. Industry practitioners may gain insights on how to best navigate this innovation space.
column3: 6 Conclusions In this paper we explore the role of a fintech and a big bank in shaping trust expectations from blockchain use as the technology is adapted for use in mainstream corporate settings in the financial services sector. Our analysis reveals a notable shift in trust expectations – transitioning from full visibility of transaction information to embracing a range of visibilities. This shift is a response to the adaptation of the blockchain protocol, introducing layered transparency to address the privacy and security concerns of mainstream users. The study highlights that fintech firms and big banks wield considerable influence in re-writing constitutive expectations of trust. At the same time, these key actors, strategically position themselves – fintechs as suppliers of innovative ideas and expertise and big banks as adopters and resourceful champions in the burgeoning blockchain marketplace. In addition to re-shaping trust dynamics these key players contribute to the broader generalization of trust expectations from blockchain use. This extends beyond isolated transaction events to foster a perception of blockchain as a taken-for-granted infrastructure. For example, they introduce, select and pursue promises and organizing visions related to blockchain, exemplified through relevant use cases. Subsequently, by interpreting these ideas and mobilizing financial resources, market forces and industry influence, they seek to propel them on a mass scale. 6.1 Contributions In this study we have identified a research gap in relation to the ways in which trust expectations from blockchain use may change when it is adapted for use in mainstream business settings, and the role of two key actors (banks and fintechs) in this process. We devised two research questions to specifically address this research gap. Below we present our analysis' contributions to theory and industrial practice. 6.1.1 Theoretical contribution: blockchain innovation trajectory Our analysis leverages Zucker's theory of trust as constitutive and background expectations of participants in a market exchange. By examining how these expectations change alongside adaptations of a technology in a new business context, we contribute to the theoretical understanding of the coevolution between technological change and trust expectations. Specifically, we identify an innovation trajectory between changes in blockchain technology (i.e. from full to layered transparency in the blockchain protocol) and trust expectations from its use (i.e. from full visibility to a range of visibilities), as blockchain is disentangled from associations with cryptocurrencies and reinvented as a mainstream technology for financial services. We suggest that looking forward, and if blockchain achieves infrastructure status, generalized background trust expectations will become more prevalent, while the meaning of transparency will shift from “visible” to “opaque” during transactions as constitutive expectations become less needed.

column1: Minimizing block incentive volatility through Verkle tree-based dynamic transaction storage
column2: Transaction fees are a crucial revenue source for miners in public and consortium blockchains. However, while public blockchains have additional revenue streams, transaction fees serve as the primary income for miners in consortium blockchains formed by various financial institutions. These miners allocate different levels of computing resources to process transactions and earn corresponding fees. Nonetheless, relying solely on transaction fees can lead to significant volatility and encourage non-standard mining behaviors, thereby posing threats to the blockchain's security and integrity. Despite previous attempts to mitigate the impact of transaction fees on illicit mining behaviors, a comprehensive solution to this vulnerability is yet to be established. To address this gap, we introduce a novel approach that leverages Dynamic Transaction Storage (DTS) strategies to effectively minimize block incentive volatility. Our solution implements a Verkle tree-based storage mechanism to reduce bandwidth consumption. Moreover, to configure the DTS strategies, we evaluate several optimization algorithms and formulate the challenge as a Vehicle Routing Problem. Our experiments conducted using historical transactions from Bitcoin and remittance data from the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China reveal that the strategy focusing on time-based transaction incorporation priority, while excluding a designated space for small-fee transactions, as discovered by the gradient-based optimizer algorithm, proves most effective in reducing volatility. Hence, the DTS strategy can sustain stable block incentives irrespective of transaction types or user bidding behavior. Furthermore, the inclusion of higher-fee transactions, often smaller in size, can alleviate propagation delays and the occurrence of forks.
column3: 5 Conclusion Our research begins by examining the role of blockchain in the financial sector, emphasizing the importance of a Consortium Blockchain for streamlining transactions among institutions. Institutions encounter a significant challenge related to transaction fees impacting block incentives, leading to potential deviant mining behaviors like Selfish Mining , Undercutting , Mining Gap , and Pool Hopping . These behaviors are largely influenced by the volatility of block incentives To tackle these challenges, our study builds upon the DTS strategies proposed by Zhao et al. [15] , focusing on reducing block-incentive volatility. We enhance these strategies by integrating the Verkle Tree mechanism, organizing transactions while integrating DTS with current and prospective scalability solutions. This integrated approach alleviates network bandwidth congestion. Additionally, we abstract the optimization of DTS strategies using the framework of the VRP. By treating DTS as a VRP, we leverage established VRP solution techniques, ranging from heuristic to machine learning algorithms. This application of VRP techniques to the DTS problem allows us to effectively determine near-optimal solutions. We utilized five optimization algorithms—PSO, DE, GA, CMA-ES, and GBO—to identify the most effective DTS strategy. Extensive experimentation with a historical dataset of 400,000 bitcoin transactions reveals that Verkle-Tree-based DTS strategies can significantly mitigate block-incentive volatility. The most effective strategy identified is the “Time-based transaction incorporation priority without designated space for small-fee transactions” (refer to Table 6 ). Expanding our methodology and dataset, we assess the DTS strategy’s effectiveness using historical market data from Bitcoin and remittance data from the ICBC Macau. These experiments demonstrate the robustness of the proposed DTS strategy, ensuring block incentive stability even amidst irrational user bidding behavior. Consequently, transaction fees can transition from merely incentivizing miners to include transactions in their blocks, to becoming a primary source of block incentives. 5.1 Future work As discussed in Section 5 , the expedited consensus speed of the Fee-based DTS strategy reduces the risk of forking attacks on blocks involving high-fee transactions. This approach can be expanded in the future by integrating additional transaction characteristics like business type, priority, and execution order into the factors affecting block size. This incentivizes miners to prioritize transactions based on specific attributes, thereby reducing the likelihood of block forking. The fee-based DTS strategy could also address Miner Extractable Value (MEV) [24] issue which stems from miners’ inability to precisely control the order of transactions when included in a block through distributed means.

column1: Introduction to the Special Section: Blockchain and Nonfungible Tokens in Electronic Commerce
column2:
We are pleased to present two articles that will help build an understanding of blockchain and nonfungible tokens (NFTs) and offer guidance on how the special nature of these technologies can help organizations and customers realize new forms of value. These articles describe a range of ways in which blockchain and NFTs can add value to an organization�s products and services, improve privacy, and partially address concerns about online content created by the latest generation of artificial intelligence. Taken together, these articles will help information systems (IS) researchers examine blockchain and NFTs within their own domains of study.

In the eye of the public, NFTs have risen and fallen in both prominence and esteem. Initially, they were obscure, unknown to all but those few with a technical background and an interest in the shadowy benefits of anonymous financial transactions. Then, as the prices of the NFTs associated with artwork rose stratospherically, the popular press showered them with attention, and this technology became the basis of a craze. Like most crazes, the NFT craze developed into a bubble, and like most bubbles, that bubble burst. As much as the popular press broadcasted the rise of NFTs, it covered the spectacular financial losses realized by NFT owners with even more enthusiasm. As a result, most people only associate NFTs with financial gains and losses.

However, research can uncover ways that NFTs offer more to society than their ability to make some people rich and to bankrupt others. This special section considers how industry can use NFTs to create value for their customers in ways other than buying and selling tokens associated with art. This new technology is fundamentally different from previous technologies, creating novel opportunities for organizations willing to look beyond NFTs mere monetary value as investments. This special section features two articles that may serve as the basis for exciting new research in information systems on a topic that, while currently rarely understood (and disgraced by a very public price crash), will likely become well known for value well beyond financial gain and loss.

The first article in this section is �NFTByBrands: A Proposed Value Framework for Analysis and Design of NFT Initiatives.� This work extends a well-known framework by explaining how its value typology can be adapted to embrace the special nature of NFTs. In addition to being valuable for its own contributions, this work can serve as an example of how to blend the normally technical NFT literature with the societally oriented literature of IS research. In doing so, it will help IS researchers integrate the dramatically novel and often misunderstood technology of smart contracts into their research agendas.

Our second article, �Redefining the Customer Service Relationship Through Blockchain,� is broader in scope in that its focus is on how blockchain technology, not only NFTs, can be applied to a prominent topic in management and IS. This work casts light on how NFTs create new opportunities for more secure, private, and sophisticated transactions for patients in the medical field, as well as a means for better privacy for Web users. It also explains how the special nature of smart contracts can address validity concerns about online content in the age of �deep fake� videos.

This special section was the product of feedback from the Societal and Economic Dynamics of the Metaverse, Smart Contracts, and Non-Fungible Tokens Minitrack of the Internet, within the Digital Economy track at the 56th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences. We thank track chairs Alan Dennis and Joe Valacich, as well as the anonymous reviewers of these works for IJEC publication. Without reviewers, who are rarely rewarded for their work, our field cannot make progress. We give special thanks to Vladimir Zwass, Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal of Electronic Commerce, for allowing us to serve as guest editors.

This work casts light on how NFTs create new opportunities for more secure, private, and sophisticated transactions for patients in the medical field, as well as a means for better privacy for Web users. It also explains how the special nature of smart contracts can address validity concerns about online content in the age of “deep fake” videos.

column1: Blockchain-Empowered Market Entry Strategy for a Green Product
column2: It is often difficult for consumers to predict the greenness of a new green product, reducing their willingness to purchase the product. Numerous companies have recently started adopting blockchain to demonstrate their products' quality. In this study, a market is considered where consumers decide what to buy when they know the greenness of existing products but are unsure about the greenness of new green products. This research presents a game theory model to examine the incumbent's entry-deterrence strategy and the entrant's blockchain adoption strategy. We examine the conditions under which blockchain can help an entrant's market entry, and the impact of blockchain adoption on firms' pricing strategies and profits, consumer surplus, and social welfare. The findings denote that blockchain adoption makes the incumbent more inclined to tolerate the entrant when the blockchain adoption cost is negligible. In addition, blockchain adoption can result in a “win-win” outcome for the two firms when the cost of the green products is low and the proportion of high-type consumers is high. However, blockchain adoption may not always benefit the entrant even if the blockchain adoption cost is negligible, particularly when consumers' perceived greenness of green products is significant enough. Furthermore, blockchain adoption may not be beneficial for consumer surplus and social welfare when green products' cost is moderate. Finally, blockchain adoption may drive the entrant to improve or reduce product greenness, depending on the proportion of high-type consumers and their uncertainty about the greenness.
column3: In this article, we analyze the two-stage Stackelberg competition between an incumbent and an entrant in a market composed of heterogeneous consumers with different valuations of product greenness. The incumbent sells ordinary products with low greenness, and the entrant sells green products with high greenness. Low-type consumers will only consider buying ordinary products, while high-type consumers will consider buying two products. Without blockchain, consumers do not know the real greenness of green products. However, all consumers in the market know the real greenness of products after blockchain adoption. This difference highlights that blockchain adoption has the function of quality (greenness) disclosure. We study the entry conditions of the entrant before and after blockchain adoption, the circumstances under which the entrant adopts blockchain, and the impact of blockchain adoption on firms' pricing strategy, social welfare, and consumer surplus. Our analysis leads to the following conclusions. First, regardless of whether the entrant adopts blockchain technology or not, the incumbent will accommodate the entrant's entry when the product cost of green goods is below a certain threshold and will deter the entrant when the product cost of green goods is high. However, blockchain adoption makes it easier for the entrant to enter the market when the blockchain adoption cost is negligible. Second, blockchain adoption is not always beneficial for the entrant even if the blockchain adoption cost is negligible. When green products' cost is low and the proportion of high-type consumers is high, both the entrant and the incumbent can benefit from blockchain adoption. Furthermore, whether blockchain adoption is beneficial to consumer surplus and social welfare is related to market conditions and consumer characteristics. In some cases, blockchain adoption is beneficial for firms but not social welfare; thus, it may not encourage blockchain adoption from the government's perspective. Finally, when the greenness of ordinary products remains unchanged, blockchain adoption ensures that consumers understand the real greenness of green products, encouraging the entrant to improve product greenness only when consumer uncertainty about green product's greenness is high, or uncertainty about green product's greenness is moderate and the proportion of high-type consumers is small. Our model can be extended in the following aspects. First, we only consider the competition of firms selling different greenness products but do not consider the entire supply chain. Hence, integrating a manufacturer's role may enrich the results [9], [27]. Second, this study assumes that consumers are uncertain about the product greenness of the entrant, and we could further consider the greenness uncertainty of the incumbent. It would be interesting to examine the case in which both the incumbent and the entrant need to determine whether to adopt blockchain [50] and product greenness. Third, this study does not consider the impact of legal maturity and culture on blockchain adoption. For example, some consumers will support the use of blockchain because of their aversion to risk, while others will oppose it for fear of privacy disclosure, due to cultural influences. Therefore, the impact of different consumer attitudes on blockchain adoption can be considered [24].

column1: Risk-Averse Ride-Hailing Platform Operations With Safety Risk-Averse Consumers Under Pandemics: Roles of Blockchain Technology and Government Sponsors
column2: Today, ride-hailing platform operations are popular. Facing pandemics (e.g., COVID-19) some customers feel unsafe for the ride-hailing service and possess a “safety risk-averse” (SRA) attitude. The proportion of this type of SRA customers is unfortunately unknown, which makes it difficult for the ride-hailing platform to decide its optimal service price. In this article, understanding that blockchain technology (BT) based systems can help improve market estimation for the proportion of SRA customers, we conduct a theoretical study to explore the impacts that the BT-based system can bring to the platform, customers, and drivers. We consider the case in which the platform is risk-averse (in profit) and serves a market with both SRA and non-SRA customers. We analytically prove that using BT, the optimal service price will be increased and BT is especially helpful for the case with a more risk-averse ride-hailing platform. However, whether it is more or less significant for the more risk-averse SRA customers depends on their degree of risk aversion. We uncover that when the use of BT is beneficial to the customers, it will also be beneficial to the drivers, and vice versa. We derive in closed-form the analytical conditions under which the use of BT can be beneficial to the ride-hailing platform, customers, and drivers (i.e., achieving “all-win”). When all-win cannot be achieved automatically, we explore how governments can provide sponsors to help. We further extend the analysis to consider the general case in which BT incurs both a fixed cost as well as a cost increasing in demand. We prove that the main conclusion remains robust. In addition, we reveal that the required amount of government sponsor to achieve all-win is the same between the two different costing models explored in this article.

Based on the theoretically derived findings, we have the following managerial insights and practical implications. Optimal service price: For the platform managers, using BT will mean an increased optimal service price. The interesting thing is that even under the use of BT with a fixed cost, the optimal service price is increased. Another finding is that when the cost of BT is larger (i.e., under the case with both the fixed cost and demand-increasing variable cost), the optimal service price is even higher. This fits our intuition. However, a higher service price does not necessarily mean that customers suffer as consumer surplus can be higher or lower depending on other parameters (such as the unit benefit (enhanced trust utility) brought by using BT). Achieving all-win with BT deployment: Whether using BT is good or not to customers, ride- hailing platform and drivers depends on many factors such as the unit benefit brought by using BT (b). Achieving an all-win situation may not be automatic though. In other words, in general, when using BT is beneficial to the ride-hailing platform, it need not benefit the drivers and customers. It is interesting to note that the drivers and customers will both be benefited by the use of BT under the same condition. In other words, when using BT is good for the drivers, it will also be good for the customers (and vice versa). As such, for policy makers, the way to achieve all win only requires to provide the right incentive (i.e., sponsor) to make sure the ride-hailing platform will vote for using BT if it is beneficial to customers (and hence also the drivers). This makes the policy easier to implement. Degrees of risk-aversion: We reveal an insight that using BT is especially beneficial to the more risk-averse ride-hailing platform. In other words, if the ride-hailing platform s manager is more risk averse, using BT is especially significant. However, for the SRA customers, whether it is especially significant for the case with the more risk-averse SRA customers depends on their specific degree of 22 risk aversion. In particular, if the existing SRA customers are already substantially risk-averse (i.e., their fear to safety is sufficiently high), then the benefit of using BT is especially prominent to them. Comparisons of two different costing models: When we compare the two costing models, under the case when government sponsor S is needed to achieve the all-win situation, it is most interesting to find that the required sponsor amount is the same under the two examined costing models. This implies that for the implementation of government sponsorship scheme, it is in fact easy to do so and policy makers of governments do not need to worry too much about the costing structure. Similar to other analytical studies, we admit a few non-trivial limitations which call for further research. To be specific, in this paper, we focus on the analytical models with which we do not consider the specific arrival patterns of customers. Future research can consider this factor by making it a queueing model based study. In this study, we focus our analysis on safety risk while not putting emphasis on environmental sustainability related issues [51, 52, 53, 54]. column1: The interplay of manufacturer encroachment and blockchain adoption to combat counterfeits in a platform supply chain
column2: Consumers’ perception of product value when purchasing is a critical issue relative to online platform commerce. This is especially true when the brand manufacturer authorises only a third-party reseller to sell through the platform, a practice that may provide opportunities to counterfeiters. To address this issue, we establish a theoretical model in which one brand manufacturer wholesales its products to a third-party reseller who then sells through an online platform. The platform acts as a marketplace, while multiple counterfeiters also exist on the platform, which may deceive consumers. In particular, we consider that the manufacturer can encroach with a direct channel and that the platform can adopt blockchain technology to help consumers identify authenticity. The results show that the platform could induce the brand manufacturer to encroach by deploying blockchain technology. Furthermore, an interesting result indicates that although either manufacturer encroachment or blockchain technology used alone can effectively boycott counterfeits, the coexistence of two strategies can raise the demand for counterfeit products. Finally, we find that when the brand manufacturer encroaches on the platform and the platform adopts blockchain technology, the brand manufacturer, platform, reseller and social welfare can achieve Pareto improvement, while the consumer surplus may be worse off.
column3: With the rapid growth of e-commerce, brand manufacturers are moving into online platforms to occupy a larger market. However, the proliferation of counterfeit goods on online platforms has led to a lack of trust in both brand manufacturers and consumers. Therefore, the online platform has an incentive to combat counterfeit goods to keep the growth of transaction volumes on the platform market and to achieve higher profits. Blockchain is a new anti-counterfeiting technology due to its highly transparent and tamper-evident nature. However, the deployment of blockchain costs a lot, and whether it deserves to be adopted is a controversial and unresolved issue. In this context, this paper studies the anti-counterfeiting strategy of online platforms and the encroachment strategy of brand manufacturers. We also analyse the anti-counterfeiting value of these strategies and their impacts on consumer surplus and social welfare. Through the analysis, we can conclude an optimal strategy solution. If both the blockchain setup cost and the encroachment cost are both high (low), ‘no encroachment, no blockchain’ (‘encroachment, blockchain’) would be the best strategy combination for the brand manufacturer and the online platform. If the blockchain setup costs much (little) but the encroachment costs little (much), ‘encroachment, no blockchain’ (‘no encroachment, blockchain’) would be the best strategy combination. Additionally, without blockchain technology, if the cost of encroachment is too high, brand manufacturers are reluctant to open direct sales channels in vain. Otherwise, when the platform adopts blockchain technology, no matter how large the encroachment cost is, the brand manufacturer always encroaches on the platform. Our results have several management implications. First, for the brand manufacturer, this paper provides an encroachment strategy on how to weigh the potential market demand against the negative impact of counterfeits and encroachment costs in an online platform market. Facing an online platform without blockchain, the manufacturer should do encroachment when it costs low to combat counterfeits. The more counterfeits there are in the online platform, the more effective encroachment works. After encroaching, the brand manufacturer should mitigate competition between the dual-channel through pricing strategy, such as lowering the wholesale price, which is shown in the Pareto area. Therefore, brand manufacturers should consider all aspects and then decide whether to adopt an encroachment strategy to combat counterfeits. Especially with the development of information technology, many new anti-counterfeit strategies, such as blockchain, will interfere with the encroachment of brand manufacturers. As this paper shows, the blockchain technology adopted by the platform can induce manufacturer encroachment. However, manufacturers should be careful at this time because the effect of encroachment on boycotting counterfeits decreases with the existence of blockchain. Second, for an online platform, the paper first proposes a way to combat counterfeiting: blockchain technology, which can completely disclose products’ quality. However, the platform needs to weigh the anti-counterfeiting value and construction cost of blockchain. Interestingly, as mentioned above, the platform can motivate the brand manufacturer to encroach by adopting blockchain, and the result of interplay increases the demand for counterfeits, whose crackdown on counterfeits is even lower than the solo strategy. That is connected to the fierce competition among genius markets, which leaves spares for counterfeiters. Therefore, the platform can not only use blockchain technology to resist counterfeits but also use the adoption strategy of blockchain to adjust the strategies of other supply chain members to benefit itself more. Finally, if the brand manufacturer or the platform cares about enterprise social responsibility, the paper finds that blockchain adoption and brand manufacturer encroachment can improve the profitability of the overall supply chain and the overall social welfare at the same time under certain conditions. Therefore, considering social welfare, the two members can make some contributions without hurting their own benefits. Table 3 summarises the specific action guidance for operations managers.
