First, we have not taken into account the phenomenon that the brand manufacturer has an offline sales channel simultaneously. Therefore, future research can consider a platform supply chain with online and offline channels at the same time to further verify our results. Second, consumers’ attitudes toward blockchain (e.g. their recognition of anti-counterfeiting value, their trust in transparency, and privacy issues) are also crucial to affect the adoption of blockchain and are worth studying in the future. Finally, whether other supply chain members, such as the brand manufacturer and the authorised reseller, should share the construction cost of the blockchain (e.g. whether authorised resellers need to bear the cost of tie-in use) and how much they should undertake need to be paid close attention. Additionally, how blockchain can be rolled out to small-sized brand companies and the role of government and leading enterprises are worth examining.

column1: Improving operational efficiency through blockchain: evidence from a field experiment in cross-border trade
column2: Abstract Based on the practical needs of cross-border trade between Yunnan Province, China, and Southeast Asian countries, this paper studies the impact of blockchain technology usage on operational performance. Owing to immutability and traceability, the implementation of a blockchain-based platform solves several existing problems of cross-border trade. We conducted a field experiment to verify the effect of blockchain technology on the operational efficiency of cross-border trade companies. The results show that operational, agency, and time costs significantly decrease. Blockchain usage reduces the intermediary agencies of cross-border trade and settlement payment for traders, also improves the timeliness of business processing and the efficiency of cross-departmental business collaboration. This study provides new insights on the interface of blockchain technology and supply-chain operation management.
column3: Based on the actual needs of cross-border trade between Yunnan Province of China and Southeast Asian countries, we developed a cross-border trade and payment settlement platform based on blockchain technology. The unique features of immutability and traceability of blockchain enable us to address the pain points existing in the traditional cross-border trade business process. Taking advantage of the closed beta testing period, we compared the cross-border transaction data with and without the platform. This allowed us to conduct a field experiment to explore the effect of blockchain technology on the operational efficiency of cross-border trade enterprises. Our field-based study responds to the current need for research on the application of blockchain technology and the call for empirical evidence regarding its operational effectiveness and efficiency. We constructed an innovative business framework for blockchain technology in cross-border trade applications, providing new insights for the application of blockchain technology in supply-chain operations management. There has been very little empirical research on the implication of blockchain technology on operational efficiency (Pan et al. Citation 2020). This study attempts to fill this void in the literature by conducting a field experiment with real import and export transaction data. With these data provided by the industry collaborators, our findings provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of blockchain implementation in the cross-border trade business. Our blockchain-based platform connects the information channels of overseas companies, logistics agencies, payment agencies, service agencies, and regulatory agencies, and solves the long-standing problems of information exchange in the cross-border trade business between Yunnan Province and Southeast Asian countries. The theoretical contribution of this study mainly includes the following three aspects. First, we constructed an innovative business framework for the application of blockchain technology in cross-border trade, providing insights for the development of blockchain technology and its integration with supply-chain operational management. Although many people are aware of the potential of blockchain now, there are few concrete plans for implementation (Ying, Jia, and Du Citation 2018). We applied a blockchain-based platform for cross-border trade business, inspiring academia and enterprises to explore the practical application of blockchain technology. Second, we conducted a field experiment with real import and export orders, which empirically indicates that blockchain technology improves the efficiency of business operations. Since blockchain is still an emerging technology, academic research on it is in a fledgling period. Scant empirical studies use the transaction data of enterprises, let alone research the impact of blockchain implementation on the operational capabilities of enterprises (Ying, Jia, and Du Citation 2018). Our results lay a foundation for research on the effects of blockchain implementation in real-life business by examining cross-border trading data with and without platform usage. Third, our research background is in the actual needs of Yunnan Province of China to conduct cross-border trade with Southeast Asian countries, which proves the feasibility of adopting blockchain in industry. The blockchain-based platform provides solutions to the long-term pain points and difficulties existing in traditional cross-border trade business processes and provides a decision-making reference for enterprises to improve operational efficiency and reduce operating costs. This study contributes to innovative business practices in three aspects, which, we hope, will be helpful for the management of cross-border trade operations for enterprises. First, the new blockchain-based platform revolutionizes the cross-border trade service model. In contrast to the existing cross-border trade business service model, this study proposes a new cross-border trade business collaboration model based on blockchain technology, which heavily integrates the scattered resources of foreign trade enterprises, logistics institutions, payment institutions, service institutions and regulatory authorities. We hope to inspire practitioners to open their information-sharing channels across business departments and enable an open and trustworthy data collaboration platform to connect all partners in the trade chain for multi-win and value-sharing. Second, the empirical findings of our field experiment inform innovation on integrated application of blockchain technology. We offer empirical evidence that applying blockchain in industry improves operational efficiency and reduce operating costs, which serves as an incentive for supply-chain managers to rely on new industry 4.0 technologies such as blockchain to improve operations. Third, our research has implications for other trade-related third-party regulators, such as governments and customs, not just buyers and sellers. Adopting blockchain has more significance than the exchange of goods; we establish a set of computerized systems with data exchange, sharing, and business collaboration models, seamlessly connecting to the management systems of core enterprises and regulators in the cross-border trade chain. The management system guarantees the authenticity of the data by uploading the source data to the chain and ensures data traceability and security with the inherent technical attributes of blockchain. It provides corresponding information for the government monitoring processes and product quality tracing. Our study has some limitations that serve as avenues for future research opportunities. We focus on the benefits of blockchain but without considering the cost of implementation. On the one hand, the costs are difficult to measure. The cost of adopting blockchain technology are related to the technology. For example, developing a blockchain-based platform requires professional architects to plan how to integrate blockchain technology into business scenarios and improve business efficiency, cryptography experts to carry out reasonable encryption design to ensure the immutability of blockchain, and professional programmers coding to develop and launch the platform. On the other hand, once the technology innovation is adopted by business, it can continuously save costs and improve efficiency for business operations. One-time costs and continuous benefits should be considered when comparing gains and losses. The longer the platform is in use, the less its marginal cost. We carried out a field experiment in the closed beta test period before the platform was officially launched. The platform was not used over a long period of time, and the cost of technical expenses was not effectively shared. In addition, the cost of some of the hardware facilities required for blockchain adoption, such as hard discs, computers and more, cannot be accurately measured since the platform was not officially launched during the field experiment period in this study. Alternatively, a future study could examine the effect of adopting blockchain from the perspective of both cost and benefits, which may make our findings more convincing. Along with the benefits, the other aspects of the application should also be fairly addressed. In the context of our study, Shanghai WinJoin Information Technology Co., Ltd. was commissioned by Yunnan traders to develop the blockchain-based platform and is mainly responsible for running and maintaining the platform. Future research should determine who controls, operates, and maintains innovative technologies based on actual business needs and context. In addition, we expect to explore the application of blockchain technology in strengthening the complete traceability of logistics flow in the future. By recording the full-track dynamic information of logistics on the blockchain, we enable the retrieval and traceability of cargo movement, and enhance the transparency and authenticity of information in the logistics supply chain. Based on ample real transaction data in the platform, a risk control and credit model should be established to integrate with the resources of commercial banks, insurance, trust, and other financial institutions. Future research can thus provide online supply-chain finance solutions for small- and medium-sized trade enterprises and logistics enterprises and improve the capital turnover rate and reducing capital costs.

column1: The impacts of blockchain adoption on pricing and efforts decisions in online game supply chains with information asymmetry
column2: This study investigates the impact of blockchain adoption on online game supply chain pricing and enterprises' investment decisions in situations of information asymmetry. Our analyses reveal that, first, with high market demand, enterprises will consistently adopt blockchain only when the combined effect of input-output on quality is significant and when players' price tolerance after blockchain adoption is moderate. Additionally, when the combined input-output effect on quality is minimal, and players’ price tolerance after blockchain adoption is more significant, enterprises will consistently adopt blockchain with low market demand. Second, when players have a higher price tolerance after blockchain adoption, product pricing and platform efforts can be enhanced regardless of market demand state. However, market demand state and price elasticity will significantly impact product pricing and platform effort decisions when players have less price tolerance after blockchain adoption. Third, developers tend to improve the quality of the game product in blockchain adoption when market demand is high. In contrast, when market demand is low, developers may prefer to increase the quality effort using blockchain if and only if players have higher price tolerance after adopting it.
column3: 6 Conclusion This paper has presented the impact of blockchain adoption on product pricing and investment in the online game supply chain based on the property of traceability. First, we have established two scenarios of online game supply chain decisions for blockchain usage: no blockchain adoption and blockchain adoption. In the situation of no blockchain adoption, there is no information-sharing about market demand across the supply chain, lowering player perceptions of the product's value. Meanwhile, in blockchain adoption, demand information is shared across the supply chain, increasing player perceptions of the product's value. Second, we have obtained optimal pricing and efforts strategies of enterprises in the supply chain via Nash game equilibrium analysis, which enables insights into the mechanism responsible for the impact of blockchain adoption on these. Our analysis highlights several main findings. First, if market demand and the product's quality input-output combined effect are large, enterprises prefer to adopt blockchain consistently when the players' price tolerance following blockchain adoption is moderate. Thus, increasing price elasticity requires higher player price tolerance to mitigate this adverse effect. In contrast, if the demand and the product's quality input-output combined effect are low, enterprises tend to adopt blockchain consistently when player price tolerance following blockchain adoption is significantly higher. Therefore, the consistent selection in blockchain adoption in a depressed market environment is more limited by the developer, who requires the players' higher acceptance of blockchain products to meet its increased effort in products, more than its higher market forecasts. Second, player price tolerance directly impacts product pricing and platform effort. Whether market demand is low or high, adopting blockchain can improve product pricing and platform investment when the player's price tolerance is high after blockchain adoption. However, when the player's price tolerance is low after blockchain adoption, the operator's platform effort and pricing decisions will be comprehensively affected by the market demand situation and price elasticity. Third, the actual market demand situation will considerably impact quality decisions concerning online game products. Adopting blockchain makes developers increase their quality efforts under conditions of high market demand. Meanwhile, under conditions of low market demand, the developer's quality efforts will also be influenced by the price tolerance of players. Thus, market demand and player price tolerance determine the change in quality effort. This paper's conclusions provide a theoretical reference point for decisions to adopt blockchain in the operational practices of online game supply chains and provide a basis for supply chain enterprises' product pricing and effort decisions of following blockchain application. Future research can expand on two main aspects of this paper's inquiries. On the one hand, it can focus on the risk-averse characteristics of enterprises in the online game supply chain ( Hu et al., 2020 ) and examine the impact of those characteristics on blockchain adoption. On the other hand, it can attend to the competition between multiple game developers producing largely homogeneous products. For example, if a product adopting blockchain and a product not adopting blockchain are launched simultaneously on an operating platform, it is worth exploring the impact on pricing, operator investment, and player response to the two products.

column1: The Value of Smart Contract in Trade Finance
column2: Problem definition: Smart contract improves the supply chain efficiency by enabling the supplier’s commitment to postshipment financing decisions, which mitigates the bank’s lending risk exposure and thereby reduces the financing cost. This paper investigates how smart contract adoption could facilitate trade finance activities and create value for supply chain firms. Academic/practical relevance: As the emerging blockchain technology could potentially reshape the trade financing landscape, understanding the impact of smart contract adoption and its interaction with trade finance activities is practically relevant and of great importance. Methodology: We develop a two-stage game-theoretic model and adopt supply chain finance theory to characterize the strategic interactions between supply chain firms in the presence of both operational risk (demand uncertainty) and financial risks (credit and liquidity risks). Results: We find that the value of smart contract depends critically on the trade finance structures, including both preshipment and postshipment financing schemes. Under the baseline trade finance model (with purchase order financing as preshipment financing and factoring as postshipment financing), smart contract alleviates the supplier’s overpricing behavior caused by commitment frictions and helps restore the supply chain efficiency. When buyer direct financing serves as an alternative preshipment financing, smart contract might discourage the retailer from offering buyer direct financing, which significantly hurts the supplier and thus reduces the supply chain profit. When invoice trading serves as the alternative postshipment financing, the supplier always chooses invoice trading over factoring because of its trading flexibility, which in turn, makes the commitment frictions ubiquitous and unresolvable (namely, commitment trap). As a result, invoice trading could unexpectedly lead to a lower supplier’s profit. Luckily, such an adoption dilemma can be resolved by smart contract adoption in conjunction with factoring. Managerial implications: Our findings provide guidelines for and insights into when smart contract should be adopted and its interactions with different trade finance schemes. In particular, smart contract adoption does not always benefit the supply chain.
column3:
The increased attention to blockchain-related technologies and emerging application scenarios (e.g.,
DeFi: decentralized finance, NFT: non-fungible token, Web 3.0, etc.) has brought smart contract
into sharper focus. A central premise of smart contracts (and more broadly blockchain technology)
has been that the automated algorithmic execution based on mapping states of the world to
corresponding contractual actions, which can create creditable commitments that previously would
be expensive or impossible to enforce. In our analysis, we investigate to what extend smart contract
indeed allows for this premise to be realized in the trade finance domain; we find that while smart
contracts can indeed mitigate the commitment frictions, in many cases the ability to add value to
the supply chain critically depends on the underlining trade finance structures.
We have several main findings. First, under the baseline trade finance model, the commitment
frictions between the bank and the supplier could lead to either the supplier’s opt-out of factoring
or adoption with overpricing. Smart contract resolves such issues, reduces the supplier’s financing
cost, and thus benefits both supply chain members. Second, when BDF is available as an alternative
pre-shipment financing scheme, we find that smart contract might hurt the supplier and even the
supply chain system. This is because smart contract discourages the self-interest retailer from
offering BDF, which transfers the financing burden to the more cost-sensitive supplier’s shoulder.
As a result, the supplier can only charge a rather high wholesale price, leading to a fairly low order
quantity and thus a sharp decline in overall supply chain profit. Third, when invoice trading is
available to the supplier as an additional post-shipment financing choice, we find, unexpectedly,
that such financing option could make the supplier worse-off due to the adoption dilemma. That is,
the supplier always prefers invoice trading over factoring due to its trading flexibility which, in turn,
leads to a commitment trap (i.e., ubiquitous and unresolvable commitment frictions). Luckily, such
an adoption dilemma can be resolved by adopting smart contract in conjunction with factoring.
Our main contribution is to propose a general supply chain finance model framework that enables
us to quantify the value of smart contract when different types of trade finance instruments are in
place. Our theory can help “debias” the value of smart contract (as might be incorrectly promoted
by many FinTech firms) and promote more legitimate implementations of this technology in the
trade finance domain (or more broadly, the supply chain area). Caution is warranted if one merely
considers the direct positive impact of smart contract (e.g., allow creditable commitments that
previously would be expensive to enforce), but largely overlooks its indirect effect on supply chain
firms’ incentives as well as their strategic choice of different trade financing schemes.
We conclude by pointing out some model limitations and proposing several potential future
directions. First, we have only studied the supply chain structure with one supplier and one
retailer. In many business environments, however, large retailers such as Walmart have multiple
suppliers and large suppliers such as Intel have multiple downstream buyers. We expect studying
such supply chains with retailer or supplier competition might bring in new findings and insights.
Second, we only consider a simplified version of FinTech-driven digitalization. In practice, the
benefit of digitalization can go beyond lowering the bank premium and may provide other benefits
such as improving data-driven decision making and better information sharing among different
supply chain members. These could be interesting directions to further explore the value of
FinTech-driven digitalization.

column1: The Conceptual Flaws of Decentralized Automated Market Making
column2: Decentralized exchanges (DEXs) are an essential component of the nascent decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystem. The most common DEXs are so-called automated market makers (AMMs): smart contracts that pool liquidity and process trades as atomic swaps of tokens. AMMs price transactions with a deterministic liquidity invariance rule that only uses the AMM’s token deposits as inputs and that has no precedent in traditional finance. Yet, in the context of transparent and open blockchain operations, any liquidity invariance pricing function allows so-called sandwich attacks (akin to front running) that increase the cost of trading and threaten the long-term viability of the DeFi ecosystem. Invariance pricing is also not regret free. Linear pricing rules have similar problems except for uniform pricing, which has regret-free prices and limits sandwich attack profits but which invites excessive order splitting. Comparing trading costs using a model of liquidity provision, constant product pricing is often cheaper except when the variance of the underlying asset is small or when the order is large. column3:
In practice, only a small minority of the thousands of stocks listed on traditional
stock exchanges have a liquid market. Liquidity is a chicken-and-egg problem: pro-
fessional liquidity providers have no interest in assets with low turnover, but without
liquidity, there is no trading. Lack of liquidity makes trading more expensive, it makes

assets unattractive for many investment strategies, it raises the funding costs for is-
suers, and it limits the attractiveness of stock options in compensation packages. Might
an automated market maker-type arrangement be a solution to the illiquidity of many
traditional markets? A key innovation of automated market makers is that risk and

 41

fees are pro-rated, so that liquidity providers don’t compete. This feature allows un-
sophisticated traders to supply their token holdings as liquidity and earn fee income,
possibly eliminating the need for intermediaries to supply liquidity.
 The existing AMM systems have several nice features. For instance, many have very

intuitive user interfaces and are easy to use. Conceptually, most have a “self-contained”
pricing function: the only necessary data are the deposits in the liquidity pool. These
pricing functions also discourage order splitting, which reduces network traffic. How-
ever, there are challenges. The lack of time priority and the default transparency
of unsettled orders in a blockchain’s mem-pools allow for front-running “sandwich”

trades: an attacker would submit a round trip transaction so that one gets processed
before the original one and the return trip right after. The problem is that these at-
tacks are unboundedly profitable for any pricing function that is based on a (convex)
liquidity invariance rule. The invariance rule is not the issue. A linear pricing rule that

resembles limit order book pricing has the same problem.
 Invariance and limit order book-type pricing are not regret free, nor do they allow
liquidity providers to break even in expectation. Therefore, AMM need a reward
separate mechanism to compensate liquidity providers. In the current iterations, the fee

is exogenous and there are, at best, broad groups (e.g., 1, 5, and 30 bps for UniSwap).
As Hasbrouck, Rivera, and Saleh (2022) show, setting the right level of fees is a separate
problem and the one-size-fits-all approach is unlikely to work. An optimal AMM
design is therefore much more complicated than the simple implementations that we
are currently seeing.

 Uniform pricing, which often emerges in economic models, fares better in that

 42

sandwich attack profits are bounded and a separate fee is not necessary. However,
under this rule order splitting is beneficial and allows users to achieve the same price as
under limit order book-type pricing. Therefore, an implementation of uniform pricing
would merely resemble discriminatory pricing, with all its downsides.

 Thinking beyond the decentralized finance world, arguably, sandwich attacks would
not be a problem in traditional markets because these rely on centralized systems
that can enforce time priority. Which pricing rule then would markets prefer? To
address this question, I develop a liquidity provision model in which liquidity demanders
account for the so-called “impermanent/divergence loss” caused by changes in the

underlying fundamental value. In numerical computations, constant product pricing is
often cheaper for liquidity demadners, except for large order sizes or very low levels of
variance of the fundamental.

A Appendix: Background on Crypto-Asset Trading

 Blockchain tokens and coins can be traded on centralized platforms and with de-
centralized protocols. A platform is centralized if trades are arranged and processed
in a firm’s proprietary system, and if the user surrenders custody to the venue. De-
centralized trading utilizes a blockchain’s decentralized processing capacity to arrange
and process transactions, and the user retains control over their assets. This appendix

reviews the institutional features of crypto-asset trading with the caveat that the world
of crypto-asset trading is fast-moving and this overview is therefore merely a snapshot.

 43

Centralized Trading. There are two main types of centralized exchanges: fiat con-
nected and crypto-only ones. The former are connected to the payments’ rails of
traditional finance; examples are Coinbase, Upbit, Kraken, and Bitbuy. The latter
are not directly connected to the world’s traditional payments networks, and they are,

therefore, not directly connected to the traditional world of finance. Examples for these
markets are Poloniex, Binance, OKEx, Huobi, or Kucoin. According to the website
CryptoCompare, non-fiat venues have processed about twice the volume of the fiat-
connected venues from 2020-22. Although there are some 500 different crypto asset
trading platforms worldwide, most volume is concentrated on a handful of platforms.

For fiat-connected venues, users can fund their account by wire transfer, similar to
an account with a traditional investment brokerage. Crypto-only venues do not ac-
cept wire transfers, but some allow users to fund their accounts using the expensive
work-around of a credit card transaction. On fiat-linked venues users can trade crypto

assets directly against fiat currencies. On crypto-only platforms, all trades are between
crypto assets, where one is most commonly a stablecoin (e.g., USDT or USDC).
 There are two ways for users to buy crypto assets. First, many venues allow users
to buy crypto assets directly from the platform operator. This service is a money

exchange. Second, crypto exchanges have trading platforms that are usually organized
as a public limit order book where users can submit market, limit, and specialized
orders and thus trade with one another rather than with the exchange. Some token
issuers or exchanges additionally enlist the services of specialized market making firms
to ensure a liquid market.

 Custody. By now most crypto asset trading platforms are categorized as money

 44

services businesses and must therefore abide by international anti money-laundering
rules. Therefore, users must first register with the platform and usually complete a
KYC process before they can use the venue. To trade a crypto asset at a centralized
exchange, users need to either buy the asset on the exchange as described above or

transfer a crypto-asset that they own to the exchange. Deposits and withdrawals from
centralized exchanges involve fees, and these can be substantial; 50-150 basis points
of the transaction value is not uncommon at the time of writing. Notably, standard
blockchain wallets such as MetaMask hold users’ private keys and therefore users have
full control over their assets. In contrast, when depositing crypto-assets at an exchange,

users transfer control over their assets to the platform. These public addresses are also
referred to as custodial wallets because the exchange has custody of the private keys.
After a user transfers crypto assets to their exchange/custodial wallet, there is usually
a second step whereby the assets are transferred from the custodial wallet to one of the

exchange’s omnibus wallets. After that, all transactions and transfers are recorded only
in the exchange’s own siloed system and not on the blockchain. For this reason, assets
in omnibus wallets are often referred to as “off chain.”9 Since trades are arranged and
recorded on the exchange’s proprietary infrastructure, these venues are referred to as
 9
 The concept of an off-chain asset may be confused with the concept of a so-called “cold storage
wallet.” Most commonly, a cold storage wallet is a device that stores private keys and that is not
connected to any network, in particular not the internet; wallets that are connected to the internet
are sometimes referred to as “hot wallets.” Using the private keys from a cold storage wallet to sign a
transaction requires a multi-step process. First, users create a QR code for the transaction information
with an internet-connected app. Second, the user scans this QR code with the cold storage device.
Third, the user creates the signature on the cold storage device (usually by entering a pass-phrase)
and the device then creates another QR code. Fourth, the user goes back to the online device and
scans scans the signature QR code from the offline device. The online device can then transfer the
signature together with the transaction information to the blockchain network. This process ensures
that the private keys cannot be remotely hacked. However, even cold storage wallets have a private
key that has been generated from a seed phrase. Therefore, if someone has the seed phrase, they can
re-create and use the private keys.

 45

centralized.
 Almost all centralized crypto-exchanges are startups that operate on shoe-string
budgets, grow fast, and often have a messy internal structure. At the same time, cen-
tralized exchanges have control of millions and sometimes billions worth of customer

assets, often without any oversight. For instance, it is often unclear how crypto ex-
changes handle assets in their omnibus wallets, if users have real-time 365-24-7-access,
if exchanges separate their own assets neatly from their customers’, and if exchanges
actually have the assets that they owe their customers.
 By now there is a body of evidence showing that it is risky to keep tokens at a

centralized exchange. For instance, QuadrigaCX sold customers crypto-assets that the
platform did not own. FTX used Alameda Research (both owned by the CEO and
founder of FTX) as a market maker, and then allegedly used their customers’ assets to
cover losses of their market maker. Very few jurisdictions have established frameworks

that regulate how these platforms ought to operate, and often the development of
frameworks is further complicated by the uncertain legal status of the traded crypto-
assets. In contrast, regulated financial institutions usually either have complex, stress-
tested compliance systems that ensure that their assets always match their liabilities

or they use a tightly supervised third-party custodian for their assets. At the time of
writing the hope in the industry is that the 2022 collapse of the platform FTX will at
the very least prompt platforms to use the inherent transparency of the blockchain to
prove control over their crypto-related assets and liabilities.
 Finally, crypto exchanges have also been linked to a number shady practices, such

as wash trading (see Cong, Li, Tang, and Yang (2021)), pump-and-dump schemes (see

 46

Li, Shin, and Wang (2022)) and tax-loss harvesting (see Cong, Landsman, Maydew,
and Rabetti (2022)).

Decentralized Trading. As I outline in the introduction of this paper, AMMs are

one example of a genuine innovation and new market structure that blockchain technol-
ogy enables. As a “smart contract,” an AMM is but a piece of code that is registered on
a public blockchain. Once deployed, this code can be used by anyone who has access to
the blockchain. Regulators and law enforcement bodies may be able to block websites

that provide access services, but it is much more difficult to prevent the blockchain
network from processing smart contracts. Changes to the code are usually governed by
a so-called Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO), and governance is DAO-
token based.

 As discussed in the main body of the paper, the AMM trading process has several
novel trading-related features. AMMs pool liquidity, so that retail investors need no
specialized skills or expensive equipment to become a liquidity provider. Beyond trad-
ing, AMMs play an important role in the DeFi eco-system. As Lehar and Parlour (2022)

show, AMMs are, for instance, often used in DeFi loan liquidations. Well-functioning
AMMs are, therefore, crucial for the long-term viability of the DeFi ecosystem.
 In addition to AMMs, there are also “rollup” based decentralized trading systems.
An example is dYdX with runs on Validium, a zero-knowledge based roll-up technology.
A rollup is a process that efficiently bundles or “rolls up” many transactions into

one, which resembles end-of-day netting in CCPs or CSDs. The basic principle of a
roll-up based exchange is not too dissimilar from a centralized exchanges: users first
deposit funds into a rollup-contract. Traders then submit cryptographically signed

 47

transactions, processed by the roll-up operator, and if there are matching buyers and
sellers, either the actual trade or a change in balances (often bundled for many together)
is sent to the blockchain for processing. The advantage of using a roll-up over the
blockchain mainnet is that only the roll-up validator handles the signed orders, not

all network nodes. The advantage over a centralized exchange is that no single third
party has control over the assets in the rollup. Although the rollup validator processes
the transactions, users can either challenge and revert demonstrably wrong/fraudulent
transactions, using the blockchain mainnet (for the case of optimistic roll-ups) or the
rollup organizer has to provide an unforgeable cryptographic proof of the validity of

the processed transactions. Therefore, the kind of embezzlement of customer funds
that happened prior to the FTX collapse are in principle not possible in roll-ups. In
addition to saving on fees for orders, a roll-up is very efficient when posting (bundling)
transactions. Theoretically, according to Buterin (2021), a rolled-up transaction should

use less than 1% of the gas (the measure for computational cycles on blockchains) of a
normal transaction.

Differences between Crypto-Asset and Equity Trading. Traditional equity
markets require several different data infrastructures to work in unison, and customer-
firm relationships are fundamentally different. Namely, for an equity trade to occur,
numerous infrastructures must be linked: the investor, their broker, the exchanges or
trading systems, the broker’s custodian, the clearinghouse, the securities depository,

the beneficiary ownership recordkeeper, and the payments network (which too is a
collection of various infrastructures). Notably, in equity trading, a key relationship is
between the broker and the trading venue because usually the brokers make the decision

 48

of where to send their customer’s order. Since the traditional system has numerous
intermediaries that touch an investor’s asset and that ought to act in the investor’s
best interest, there is a complex regulatory regime to oversee this world. Despite the
complexity, the system is “convenient” for regulators: since brokers handle trades and

accounts, regulators can delegate the enforcement of a variety of rules such as trading
conduct.
 A blockchain subsumes many functions of the traditional infrastructures. Investors
can choose self custody and thus deploy their assets as liquidity providers in an AMM
or DeFi lending protocol or use crypto-assets such as utility or DAO tokens for their

intended use cases without going through an intermediary. The lack of go-to entities
and gatekeepers in DeFi, however, makes regulatory enforcement and oversight sig-
nificantly more difficult. For instance, regulators can delegate trading conduct rules
in traditional finance to oversee a handful of brokers and their trading desks because

users have no choice but to go through intermediaries. In the extreme case where all
crypto-asset trading occurs in DeFi applications, trading conduct rules would need to
be enforced directly on the general population of investors, and that would require a
fundamental shift in the operation and reach of today’s regulators. Crypto-exchanges,

on the other hand, are not only go-to entities with a business address, they also operate
like broker-dealers and have custody of customer funds, which is why they are facing
increased regulatory scrutiny — although, as the world learned in the case of FTX,
oversight is still lacking.

column1: Channel selection and pricing strategy with supply chain finance and blockchain
column2: Some emerge technologies (e.g., blockchain) and new business models (e.g., e-commerce platform) are utilized to promote the digitalization of supply chains. In this paper, we study the channel selection (direct channel/e-commerce platform) and pricing (wholesale pricing/agency pricing) strategies for a capital constrained supplier in the digital supply chain with the consideration of supply chain finance and blockchain. The supplier can sell through the direct channel or the e-commerce platform. When selling through the e-commerce platform, it can choose agency pricing or wholesale pricing mode, as well as whether to obtain financial supports through supply chain finance with blockchain technology. We show that the application of supply chain finance is not always beneficial for the supplier. The initial capital of the supplier plays an important role in channel selection. Besides, the adoption of blockchain technology can promote the development of supply chain finance. Regardless of wholesale pricing or agency pricing, the adoption of blockchain technology is always beneficial to suppliers. However, for the e-commerce platform, the adoption of blockchain technology can bring an increase in the interest and increase the profits of the e-commerce platform, only when the initial capital of the supplier is relatively low.
column3: 8 Conclusions In this paper, we study the channel selection and pricing strategies with consideration of supply chain finance and blockchain. The supplier can choose to sell in direct channel or e-commerce platform with wholesale and agency pricing. The supplier has a limited capital for the production, and capital constraint can be alleviated when selling on the e-commerce platform. Adopting blockchain technology can also enhance the transparency between supply chain members. Our study initially shows that selling in the direct channel is always beneficial to the supplier in the absence of supply chain finance. However, in the presence of supply chain finance, the supplier obtains loans from e-commerce platforms, and she prefers selling on such platforms when the initial capital is low and the loan rate is high. Second, adopting blockchain technology promotes the development of supply chain finance. It can increase the profit of the supplier regardless of wholesale or agency pricing strategies. For the e-commerce platform, when the supplier has less initial capital and can acquire more loans through blockchain, the increased interest and demand can raise the profit of the e-commerce platform. Moreover, in cases of without capital constraint and adopting blockchain technology, the supplier and the e-commerce platform will choose the same pricing strategy when the supplier can obtain sufficient capital to support production. Specifically, we show that the supplier and the e-commerce platform prefer agency pricing when the revenue sharing rate is moderate, whereas both of them prefer wholesale pricing when the revenue sharing rate is high. Our results provide some practical implications as follows. First, for large e-commerce enterprises, such as JD.com and Alibaba, providing supply chain financial services can effectively relieve the financial pressure of suppliers and attract SMEs to sell on e-commerce platforms while appropriately increasing the loan ratio, thereby improving the production capacity of suppliers and benefitting all supply chain members. Second, our results provide a theoretical explanation for the phenomenon of many companies developing blockchain technology in supply chains. For example, some companies, such as Ant Financial and Suning Financial, take advantage of large e-commerce platforms to create the mode of “blockchain + supply chain finance,” realize the visualization of supply chain finance, and reduce the financing costs of SMEs based on securely sharing information in the whole chain. Moreover, some companies implement agency and wholesale pricing strategies. For example, Alibaba uses wholesale pricing in Tmall and agency pricing in Taobao. Then, e-commerce platforms decide the revenue sharing rate and lead the suppliers to sell by wholesale or agency pricing to achieve a win–win situation. Nevertheless, our model still has some limitations, which also provide future research directions. First, in this paper, we consider that the supplier chooses to either sell in the direct channel or sell on the e-commerce platform. In future research, we can extend our model to consider a dual channel, in which the supplier sells in the direct channel and on the e-commerce platform at the same time. Second, in our paper, adopting blockchain technology is considered to solve the credit problems between the supply chain members. However, in reality, adopting blockchain technology also has some other values, such as smart contract and increasing the credibility of products, which may affect consumers’ behaviors. The influences of these characteristics on channel selection and pricing strategies should be studied in future research. Finally, we do not consider uncertainties for suppliers and e-commerce platforms. In future research, we can extend to consider demand and supply uncertainties in the supply chain.

column1: Competition between green and non-green products in the blockchain era
column2: Blockchain technology has been used to certify the green level of green products, which changes the competition landscape between green and non-green products. We explore the important issue concerning how blockchain adoption affects the duopoly game between green and non-green products. We first examine a benchmark case where blockchain is not used. Then we develop two pricing models to analyze the value of blockchain adoption and the competition landscape between green and non-green products, where one concerns a green product manufacturer that applies blockchain to certify the green level of its product, and the other concerns a non-green product manufacturer. To assess the robustness of the results, we extend the models to consider two important cases, namely (i) substitutability between green and non-green products, and (ii) mixed competition including the simultaneous presence of conventional, blockchain-enabled, and non-green products in the marketplace. We show that the green product manufacturer does not necessarily increase its price when adopting blockchain, whereas the non-green product manufacturer does. Specifically, when the green level is high, the GPM's blockchain adoption decreases price competition between green and non-green products, causing both the green and non-green product manufacturers to raise prices. In addition, it is intriguing to find that the presence of more sustainable consumers in the market does not cause the green product manufacturer to charge a higher price than the non-green product manufacturer. Under the mixed competition scenario, as a result of blockchain adoption, the blockchain-enabled green product manufacturer charges a higher price than the green and non-green product manufacturer. However, this does not inherently result in a higher profit margin for the blockchain-enabled green product manufacturer.
column3: 6 Conclusions 6.1 Conclusion discussion and managerial insights Having seen blockchain being used in the real world to verify the greenness of green products, we are driven to investigate the competition landscape for manufacturers of both green and non-green products in the age of blockchain. To address the issue, we consider two types of consumers in the market according to their preferences for the green attribute of products. We develop two pricing models of a blockchain-enabled green product manufacturer and a non-green product manufacturer to perform the analysis. We derive the optimal pricing decisions and profits of the two firms. We then analyze how the GPM can win the competition with the NGPM by comparing the optimal solutions of the two models. To assess the robustness of our results, we extend the models to consider two important factors, namely (i) substitutability between the green and non-green products, and (ii) the mixed competition case. We obtain the following major findings: (i) In a highly competitive market, an intriguing result is that blockchain is not necessarily helpful and valuable. Under the condition that the proportion of sustainable consumers in the market is moderate, the GPM outperforms the NGPM, although the increasing proportion of sustainable consumers can potentially reduce the GPM's price and profit. This result holds when the green level of the GP is sufficiently high. This is because the low green level scarcely satisfies green consumers' requirements regarding environmental friendliness. Even if blockchain is adopted, consumers are unlikely to pick the green product. (ii) It is possible that blockchain adoption mitigates the price competition between the GPM and NGPM. This result means that blockchain adoption boosts the prices of the NGPM and GPM, leading them to gain more profits. We demonstrate, however, that such anti-competitive effects only occur when both the green level and the proportion of SCs in the market are sufficiently high. This result is rationalized by the fact that SCs are more concerned with the green level than the price. When there are a sufficient number of SCs in the market, and the green level of the GP is high, it is acceptable for the GPM to charge a greater price, not to mention that blockchain increases SCs' confidence in the green level. As blockchain adoption reduces market competition, the NGPM can also increase the price proportionally. (iii) When the green level is insufficient, it will not be prudent for the GPM to use blockchain because doing so will raise the NGPM's profit but not its own. We derive this result from comparing the optimal results in the cases with and without blockchain. We indicate further that blockchain is not inherently advantageous to the GPM. In addition to the low quality that prevents the BGPM from benefiting from blockchain adoption, we claim that if the green level of the BGP is high, the BGPM's blockchain adoption promotes the NGPM to enhance product quality to regain market share. Consequently, the NGPM embraces blockchain as well. (iv) Substitutability between the green and non-green products leads to a narrowed range within which the optimal solutions exist, but does not qualitatively alter the variation trends of most of the optimal solutions with the model parameters. Consumer privacy concerns dominate this result. Thus, the BGPM should be cautious about blockchain adoption when consumers are sensitive to privacy. (v) The BGPM has the potential to win the competition if the market contains conventional green products, non-green products, and green products enabled by blockchain. In particular, the BGPM is more likely to win the competition with the NGPM rather than the GPM. This is because the green level requirement for the BGPM is lower than that for the GPM due to blockchain adoption. Importantly, we also show that using blockchain is not necessarily wise. This result shows the robustness of the results we derive from the main models.

column1: Blockchainâ€™s role in e-commerce sellersâ€™ decision-making on information disclosure under competition
column2: In e-commerce, sellers can disclose product information (such as quality, size information, function, and so on) to make consumers understand the products. However, in the process of information disclosure, consumers often fall into information distortion or information loss. Because of its immutability and traceability, blockchain can help e-commerce sellers improve information disclosure and ensure the efficiency of information transmission. We study a duopoly competitive e-commerce market in which two e-commerce sellers compete in information disclosure. According to whether to apply blockchain, we divide the sellers’ decision-making into four research scenarios (NN, BN, NB, BB). Based on the above four scenarios, we get the market demand of different products depending on the consumer utility, and further establish the game model in the competitive environment. This paper explores the impact of blockchain on information disclosure and consumer surplus, and achieves the Nash equilibrium of blockchain application for both sides. In the expansion model, we study e-commerce sellers’ risk aversion and capital constraints, and further explore their impact on blockchain in practice. Finally, combining with blockchain’s characteristics, we also analyze the impact of the application of blockchain at other aspects on the supply chain. We find that when consumers' trust in information is low or the cost of blockchain applications is low, all e-commerce sellers in competition will adopt blockchain. In addition, when consumers have low trust in information, it will be difficult to achieve complete equilibrium in the application of blockchain as their risk aversion increases. For capital constrained sellers, when the cost of blockchain application is low, it will be difficult to achieve full equilibrium for blockchain applicants as the bank financing rate increases.
column3:
Blockchain can ensure the validity and authenticity of information transmission in e-commerce supply chain. On the basis of fully considering the competitive relationship in e-commerce market (such as the competition between JD and Taobao), we regard the information disclosure as the competitive decision of two e-commerce sellers, and divide e-commerce sellers’ decision-making into four research scenarios (neither of the two e-commerce sellers should use the blockchain, and the e-commerce seller applies the blockchain, e-commerce seller 2 applies blockchain, and both e-commerce sellers use blockchain). After solving the equilibrium results, the influence of blockchain is analyzed from the e-commerce sellers’ and consumers’ viewpoint. After that, we analyze the Nash equilibrium region of the blockchain applied by the e-commerce sellers. Considering the uncertainty of the utility of consumers buying products and the inadequate funds of e-commerce sellers, we expand these two cases in the expansion model. Our research is only carried out on the basis of ensuring the authenticity of information in the blockchain, but the role of the blockchain is much more than that. We make a further analysis in Sect. 5 in view of the many functions of the blockchain in the information disclosure supply chain, and some conclusions are drawn.

To sum up, the main conclusions of this paper are as follows:

(1)

If only one seller uses blockchain, when the cost of blockchain application is very small, the high trust of consumers will drive the seller's, information disclosure. For consumer surplus, if the cost of blockchain application is relatively high, the results show that the blockchain application will reduce consumer surplus, and more consumer surplus will be reduced by self-application than by competitors, and the more the application subjects, the more the consumer surplus will be reduced. For the applied blockchain equilibrium, we give the equilibrium region about the blockchain cost and consumer trust.

(2)

Risk aversion will make the two competitive platforms set a high level of product information disclosure and obtain high consumer surplus. However, after the blockchain application, the level of information disclosure will be lower, but it has no effect on the increase of consumer surplus. In addition, the high cost of using blockchain will increase sellers' sensitivity to demand fluctuations. Based on the analysis of the equilibrium results, it is found that if the information is not transmitted relatively effectively before the blockchain application (the degree of trust of consumers to the product), with the increase of risk aversion, it is more difficult to achieve the Nash equilibrium of the blockchain application.

(3)

Under financial constraints, increasing lending rates will reduce the information disclosure and consumer surplus. Interestingly, if the cost of applying blockchain is high, applying blockchain will reduce this impact. If the blockchain is applied, the high cost reduces the seller's sensitivity to the loan interest rate. Based on the analysis of the equilibrium results, it is found that if the information is transmitted relatively high effectively before the blockchain application (the degree of trust of consumers to the product) is relatively high, with the increase of the bank loan interest rate, it will be more difficult to achieve the Nash equilibrium of the blockchain application.

We further analyze the other functions of blockchain: blockchain can accurately predict the utility of consumers to buy products, blockchain reduces bank lending rates, and blockchain increases consumer preference. We find that what we have in common under these three effects is that e-commerce sellers will increase the information disclosure after applying blockchain. But for themselves, whether to increase the information disclosure depends on the cost of applying blockchain.

Our study assumes that the information disclosure ability for two sellers is homogeneous. In the future, we can extend the study to the fact that it (unit information disclosure cost) is heterogeneous. And we can also consider exploring the impact of the two e-commerce sellers' information transmission efficiency and blockchain costs on their optimal decision-making.

column1: Combating counterfeits with the Blockchain-technology-supported platform under government enforcement
column2: The intrinsic value of brand names has led to the widespread presence of counterfeits in multi-industries. Although government enforcement plays a role in combating counterfeits, it is difficult to fundamentally curb counterfeiting. This paper examines how the brand-name firm adopts the blockchain-technology-supported (BTS) platform in dealing with counterfeits under government enforcement. We consider a market with a manufacturer (i.e., a brand-name firm) and a counterfeiter. First, we develop a signaling game model to analyze the negative impact of deceptive sales. The results show that, under weak government enforcement and a high rampancy level of counterfeits, deceptive sales will decrease the expected demand for authentic products, the manufacturer's expected profit, the expected consumer surplus, and the expected social welfare. Although government enforcement forces the counterfeiter to implement non-deceptive sales, it will decrease the expected consumer surplus under symmetric quality information. Then, we develop a Stackelberg game model to analyze the manufacturer's adoption strategy for the BTS platform. We find that weaker government enforcement will incentivize the manufacturer to adopt the BTS platform. However, the manufacturer does not always adopt the BTS platform even if the counterfeiter implements deceptive sales. Finally, we analyze the effect of adopting the BTS platform under government enforcement. We reveal that the role of the BTS platform in improving consumer rights is stronger than that in combating counterfeits, and the effect of adopting the BTS platform will strengthen as government enforcement weakens.
column3: 7 Conclusions This paper examines how the brand-name firm adopts the BTS platform for dealing with counterfeits under government enforcement. We consider a market consisting of a manufacturer (i.e., a brand-name firm) and a counterfeiter. The counterfeiter sells counterfeits with low quality but a high physical resemblance to authentic products. The manufacturer can choose whether to adopt the BTS platform. If the BTS platform is not adopted, the counterfeiter may implement deceptive sales. We develop a Stackelberg game model and a signaling game model under the scenarios with and without the BTS platform, respectively. We present several major findings and managerial insights as follows. First, deceptive sales have a serious negative impact on the market. Under weak government enforcement and a high rampancy level of counterfeits, deceptive sales will decrease the expected demand for authentic products, the manufacturer’s expected profit, the expected consumer surplus, and the expected social welfare. Although government enforcement can eliminate asymmetric quality information, it is not beneficial for consumers. Therefore, in order to improve the interests of itself and consumers, the manufacturer should consider adopting the BTS platform to solve the problem of asymmetric quality information. Second, although adopting the BTS platform can eliminate asymmetric information, it is not always beneficial to the manufacturer. Whether the manufacturer should adopt the BTS platform depends on specific market conditions. However, weak government enforcement will incentivize the manufacturer to adopt the BTS platform. Third, adopting the BTS platform can increase the expected demand for authentic products, the expected consumer surplus, and the expected social welfare, while decreasing the counterfeiter’s expected profit. However, if the quality of the counterfeit is relatively low, adopting the BTS platform will also increase the expected demand for counterfeits. Therefore, the role of the BTS platform in improving consumer rights is stronger than that in combating counterfeits. In addition, both the improving effect and the combating effect of the BTS platform will strengthen as government enforcement weakens. We point out some potential directions for future research. First, as observed in practice, there may be different types of counterfeits in the market for a certain brand name product (e.g., low-quality type and high-quality type). Therefore, it would be interesting to analyze how brand-name firms adopt the BTS platform in the market where there are different types of counterfeits. Second, our paper assumes that the government combating level is exogenously given. Another possible extension of our research would be to consider that the government combating level is endogenously determined based on welfare.

column1: The Choice Strategy of Authentication Technology for Luxury E-Commerce Platforms in the Blockchain Era
column2: Blockchain technology, as an emerging information technology, has attracted much attention. Some luxury e-commerce platforms have focused on the adoption of blockchain technology to provide electronic certificates for consumers, which helps to increase consumers’ trust in luxury goods. However, due to the high authentication cost of blockchain technology, some platforms still adopt manual technology with lower authentication costs to provide paper certificates for consumers. So whether platforms choose to adopt manual technology or blockchain technology for authentication is a problem worthy of attention. In this article, we investigate the choice strategy of authentication technology for luxury e-commerce platform(s) in the monopoly and duopoly markets, respectively. The results show that the choice of authentication technology for platform(s) depends on the cost difference between manual technology authentication and blockchain technology authentication. When the cost difference is small (large), platform(s) should adopt blockchain (manual) technology. In particular, in the duopoly market, the competition between the two platforms will improve their motivation to adopt blockchain technology, but the two platforms may trap into a prisoner's dilemma when they both adopt blockchain technology. Moreover, in the monopoly and duopoly markets, adopting blockchain technology is likely to improve consumer surplus and social welfare at the same time.
column3: In this article, we investigated the choice strategy of authentication technology for luxury e-commerce platform(s) in the monopoly market and the duopoly market, respectively. In the monopoly market, we analyzed the optimal decision and profit of the platform that adopts different authentication technologies and identified the conditions for the platform to adopt manual technology or blockchain technology. In the duopoly market, we considered two platforms that engage in a Cournot competition. We analyzed the equilibrium results of the two platforms in different scenarios (i.e., scenarios BB, BN, and NN). Comparing the profit of each platform in different scenarios, we analyzed the equilibrium strategies of authentication technology choice for the two platforms. Some important findings are summarized as follows. First, in the monopoly market, the choice strategy of authentication technology for the platform is related to the cost difference between manual technology authentication and blockchain technology authentication. When the cost difference is small, the platform should adopt blockchain technology to acquire higher profit, and in this situation, consumer surplus and social welfare will also be improved. Otherwise, manual technology will become the first choice for the platform. Second, in the duopoly market, the two platforms will reach equilibrium when they adopt the same authentication technology. Specifically, when the cost difference is small, scenario BB (i.e., both platforms adopt blockchain technology) is the unique Nash equilibrium. Otherwise, scenario NN (i.e., both platforms adopt manual technology) is the unique Nash equilibrium. Further, when both platforms adopt blockchain technology, they may trap into a prisoner's dilemma. In this case, although the profit of each platform is higher in scenario NN, neither of them will unilaterally deviate from adopting blockchain technology. Moreover, the existence of the prisoner's dilemma will reduce social welfare. In addition, compared with the monopoly market, blockchain technology is more likely to be the best choice for the platforms in the duopoly market. Third, with the increase of the operation cost, the motivation of the platform adopting blockchain technology will be reduced, and the possibility of adopting blockchain technology to achieve a win-win situation between the platform and consumers will also be reduced. In addition, when the platform establishes its own blockchain-based system, the high blockchain technology investment cost attracts the platform to prefer manual technology. This article can provide several practical insights for luxury e-commerce platforms to choose authentication technology. First, when the platform is faced with the choice between manual technology and blockchain technology, it should fully evaluate the authentication cost difference between the two technologies. If the cost difference is small, the platform should adopt blockchain technology to provide electronic certificates for consumers. Otherwise, the platform should adopt manual technology to provide paper certificates for consumers. Second, for the use of different authentication technologies, the platform should make a reasonable ordering decision to achieve better performance. Third, if the platform wants to adopt blockchain technology, it is necessary to improve the operation efficiency and reduce the operation cost. This study can be extended in the following aspects. First, in a supply chain system with blockchain technology, it will be interesting to examine the impact of profits redistribution between the third-party blockchain institution and the platform on the choice strategy of authentication technology. Second, in the future, we can study the choice strategy of authentication technology for the platforms in the case of information asymmetry. For example, the quality information between platforms and consumers is asymmetric, and the quality or the demand information among platforms is asymmetric.

column1: Blockchain adoption and firm performance: The contingent roles of intangible capital and environmental dynamism
column2: Despite the purported benefits of blockchain technology for business applications, it is unclear how blockchain adoption affects firm performance, and large-scale empirical evidence on this relationship remains scarce. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities perspective, we examine the relationship between blockchain adoption and firm performance using a sample of 4994 firm-year observations from 2017 to 2021. Using a dynamic System GMM approach, we show that blockchain adoption significantly increases Tobin's Q (a market-based measure of expected future earnings); however, it has no relation with the current accounting performance measured using return on equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA). We find that a firm's intangible capital and environmental dynamism positively moderate the relationship between blockchain adoption and Tobin's Q. The former finding reflects market expectations that firms with high intangible capital are better equipped to benefit from blockchain adoption. The latter finding suggests that blockchain adoption strengthens firms' dynamic capabilities, and thus it enables firms to undertake proactive and innovative initiatives in response to an uncertain business environment.
column3: 7 Conclusion Despite growing interest in commercial applications of the BCT, large-scale evidence regarding the impact of BCT adoption on firm performance remains scant. This study uses the dynamic capabilities perspective to examine the effect of BCT adoption on firm performance. An empirical analysis using a sample of global listed firms with 4994 firm-year observations from 2017 to 2021 partially supports our hypothesis. We measure firm performance using a market-based measure (Tobin's Q) and two accounting measures: return on equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA). Our results suggest that blockchain adoption enhances firm performance, and firms with a higher level of intangible capital can create more value from blockchain adoption. Further, blockchain adoption is valued more in a dynamic business environment. Our findings are consistent with the core arguments of the dynamic capabilities perspective and advance the notion that BCT adoption enhances firms' capabilities to sense and seize opportunities in the dynamic and uncertain business environment.

column1: Financing and operating strategies for blockchain technology-driven accounts receivable chains
column2: We focus on blockchain technology (BCT) adoption in a three-echelon supply chain in which upstream sellers offer trade credits to capital-constrained downstream buyers, forming an accounts receivable chain. According to different supply chain partners adopting BCT, we analyze the game equilibrium of the no, upper-stream, lower-stream, and entire BCT-driven accounts receivable chains (NBC, UBC, LBC, and EBC) to understand participants’ motivation and condition to adopt BCT and the different roles of participants in blockchain introduction. We find that trade credit management cost-saving and repayment risk-sharing effects, as facilitated by BCT, help increase the equilibrium order quantity, thereby increasing supply chain efficiency and participants’ profits, although BCT cannot fully coordinate the supply chain. Regarding supply chain efficiency, EBC is superior to LBC, which is better than UBC or NBC. As a supply chain leader and creditor, the supplier plays a passive role in achieving the positive effect of BCT. Given that the retailer and manufacturer are supply chain followers and debtors, their adoption of BCT is the key to enhancing supply chain efficiency and profits. The BCT platform can set appropriate technology-usage fees to guide participants to form the EBC structure through different paths. Meanwhile, the retailer's initial working capital can evaluate the risk-sharing degree of the supply chain, and the stable EBC selection region defined by the risk-sharing degree can be ascertained. We further find that with the trade credit insurance premium increasing, supply chain participants have become more active in adopting BCT.
column3: 9 Concluding Remarks In this study, we analyze and compare supply chain participants’ actions and performance in various (no, upper-stream, lower-stream, and entire) BCT-driven accounts receivable chains. Regarding the motivations and conditions for adopting BCT, we find that BCT can facilitate trade credit management cost-saving and repayment risk-sharing effects. These two effects build the foundation for supply chain efficiency improvements and can also increase profits for all participants under certain conditions. Regarding the strength and limitation of BCT adoption, we find that EBC can obtain the largest equilibrium order quantity in all BCT-driven accounts receivable chain types. Meanwhile, EBC achieves a higher supply chain efficiency than that in LBC as well as a higher supply chain efficiency than that in UBC or NBC. However, we find that although EBC can enhance supply chain efficiency, it cannot fully coordinate participants’ actions as in the integrated supply chain. This reveals both the strength of BCT in supply chain efficiency improvement and its limitation in supply chain coordination. Regarding the choice among different BCT-driven accounts receivable chains, we find that the supplier, as the creditor and leader of the supply chain, has the most motivation to adopt BCT himself and hopes the downstream members of the supply chain adopt BCT as well because of the unconditional additional profits he can obtain through EBC or LBC. We find that only when the retailer can receive enough benefits from the repayment risk sharing facilitated by BCT—namely when the retailer’s initial working capital is high enough—does it choose to participate in blockchain through EBC or LBC. For the manufacturer, as the intermediary in the supply chain (being both the creditor and debtor), only when the risk-sharing degree is in the medium range—namely, when the retailer has a medium amount of initial working capital—does the manufacturer have incentive to adopt BCT through EBC or LBC. This reveals the conditions for participants to adopt BCT through EBC or LBC. These conditions for choosing EBC or LBC are still valid in the same repayment priority case. Supply chain participants’ choices for BCT schemes reveal their different roles in BCT introduction. We find that the supplier has unconditional reasons for choosing EBC and that he can get the highest profit in EBC. However, there needs to be certain conditions for the retailer and manufacturer in EBC to outperform in other accounts receivable chains. Therefore, encouraging followers of the supply chain—namely, the retailer and the manufacturer—to adopt BCT is key. This indicates that the leader of both the supply chain and the accounts receivable chain cannot necessarily play a dominant role in facilitating BCT’s effects; instead, followers’ participation determines BCT’s positive functions. Our analytical results also suggest that the BCT platform can play a crucial role in BCT implementation. Considering the mutual influence of partners in choosing BCT schemes, we ascertain the stable EBC selection region defined by the repayment risk-sharing degree, in which the BCT platform can charge appropriate technology-usage fees to guide participants to form the EBC structure through different paths. We also find that with the trade credit management cost (or the insurance premium) increasing, the participants become more active in adopting BCT. Participants in industries with different material production costs will choose different BCT-driven accounts receivable chains. In the industry with low material production cost, UBC is the final choice for all participants; In the industry with high material production cost, NBC is the final choice; In the industry with medium material production cost, all participants choose EBC. Our study opens some directions for future research. First, when multiple accounts receivables exist in the BCT-driven supply chain, information pertaining to these accounts receivables is symmetrical under BCT’s transparency feature, and creditors can then raise money by issuing asset-backed medium-term notes based on their accounts receivables. This new BCT-driven SCF mode requires further investigation. Second, our study examines the BCT-driven supply chain when buyers have capital constraints. Further studies can focus on the BCT-driven supply chain in which the supplier has funding constraints for production and explore the game equilibrium of participants in this case. Third, our study finds that BCT can increase supply chain efficiency but cannot achieve supply chain coordination. Future studies can focus on the BCT platform’s role in designing supply chain coordination contracts and allocating surplus profits among supply chain participants. Fourth, our research benchmark is the traditional supply chain without BCT in which debtors repay the loan in full under the trade credit insurance system. It is also an interesting benchmark that in the traditional supply chain, the creditor does not purchase trade credit insurance, and the debtor repays the loan with a probability. Fifth, further studies can use supply chain empirical data before and after BCT is adopted by different supply chain participants to validate our theoretical results and analyze more influential factors of BCT implementation. Overall, BCT research has much potential given its increasing adoption in the SCF field.

column1: Conflicted Analysts and Initial Coin Offerings
column2: This paper studies the contribution of analysts to the functioning and failure of the market for initial coin offerings (ICOs). The assessments of freelancing analysts exhibit biases because of reciprocal interactions of analysts with ICO team members. Even favorably rated ICOs tend to fail raising some capital when a greater portion of their ratings reciprocate prior ratings. Ninety days after listing on an exchange, the market capitalization relative to the initial funds raised is smaller for tokens with more reciprocal ratings. These findings suggest that conflicts of interest help explain the failure of ICOs. This paper was accepted by Bruno Biais, special issue of Management Science: blockchains and crypto economics.
